stem:
A 28-year-old man on methadone 100 mg daily for opioid use disorder is found unresponsive in a Newcastle community park after combining methadone with diazepam in an attempt to potentiate sedation. He is brought to the ED 30 minutes after the witnessed event with RR 6, GCS 8, SpO2 86 percent on room air, pinpoint pupils, no track marks suggesting concurrent injection.

He responds briefly to 400 microgram IV naloxone with respiratory rate rising to 12 and GCS improving to 12 over 90 seconds. He then deteriorates again over the next 30 minutes back to RR 8 and GCS 9. Bedside glucose 5.4 mmol/L, T 36.4, BP 102/68.

data_table.Vital signs: RR 6 (improved to 12 with naloxone bolus then back to 8), GCS 8 -> 12 -> 9, SpO2 86% RA -> 96% with BVM, BP 102/68.
data_table.Examination: Pinpoint pupils, no track marks, no aspiration evidence, no head injury signs.
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 5.4, paracetamol level pending, ECG sinus normal axis QRS 86 QTc 460.

lead_in: Why has he re-sedated after initial response, and what is the single most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Naloxone has worn off because its half-life (~60 min) is much shorter than methadone (~24 h); commence naloxone infusion at two-thirds the effective bolus dose per hour (0.4 mg/h)
options.rationale: MECHANISM: naloxone is a competitive mu-opioid receptor antagonist with a short half-life (~60 minutes). Methadone has a half-life of ~24 hours (8-59 hour range). The bolus reverses receptor occupancy briefly; as naloxone redistributes and is cleared, methadone re-binds receptors and re-sedation follows. AU practice (eTG Toxicology): commence naloxone infusion at two-thirds the cumulative effective bolus dose per hour. So if 400 microgram bolus produced response, infuse 0.4 mg/h (267 microgram/h rounded). Titrate to RR >=12 and adequate consciousness for airway. Source: eTG Toxicology; NSW Poisons Information Centre.

options.text: Methadone causes tolerance, so additional doses of methadone should be given to maintain consciousness
options.rationale: This is the opposite of correct - methadone is the toxin causing sedation. Giving more methadone deepens toxicity. Source: eTG.

options.text: Diazepam reversal with flumazenil 0.2 mg IV is the priority
options.rationale: Flumazenil reversal in patients with chronic benzodiazepine use risks seizures; it is rarely indicated in mixed-overdose patients especially with opioid co-ingestion. Source: NSW PIC.

options.text: Intubation under RSI rather than continued naloxone, since recurrent doses prolong ED length of stay
options.rationale: Intubation is appropriate in failure of medical reversal, but the standard pathway is naloxone infusion first - intubation is reserved for failure of infusion to maintain airway. Source: eTG.

options.text: Activated charcoal 50 g orally to reduce further methadone absorption
options.rationale: Methadone was taken hours earlier and the patient has reduced GCS - charcoal is contraindicated due to aspiration risk and is past its absorption window. Source: eTG.

explanation.summary: Pharmacokinetic mismatch is the central reasoning step: naloxone (half-life ~60 minutes) reverses opioid receptor occupancy briefly, while methadone (half-life ~24 hours, can extend to 59 hours due to autoinduction and tissue redistribution) continues to bind. After bolus, naloxone is cleared while methadone is still toxic. AU practice is naloxone INFUSION at two-thirds the cumulative effective bolus per hour, titrated to RR >=12 and adequate airway maintenance. Continuous monitoring for at least 24 hours given methadone's prolonged effect. Buprenorphine overdose may NOT respond to naloxone due to high receptor affinity. Always consider co-ingestion: benzodiazepine (synergistic respiratory depression but flumazenil rarely indicated) and paracetamol (delayed hepatotoxicity).
key_points: Naloxone t1/2 ~60 min; methadone t1/2 ~24 h (up to 59 h)
AU practice: naloxone infusion at 2/3 effective bolus dose per hour
Titrate to RR >=12 and airway maintenance, not full reversal
Buprenorphine overdose may not respond to naloxone (high affinity)
Observe at least 24 hours for methadone overdose
explanation.pearls: Avoid over-aggressive naloxone in chronic opioid-dependent patients - precipitated withdrawal is unpleasant, increases aspiration risk, and may not be needed. Aim for RR >=12 and airway maintenance, not awake-and-talking.

subtopic_detail: Naloxone infusion for methadone overdose - pharmacokinetic mismatch

stem: A 24-year-old previously well woman is admitted to a Gosford acute mental health unit with 3 weeks of progressive anxiety, paranoid delusions, and disorganised speech. Over the past 5 days she has developed orofacial dyskinesias (intermittent lip-smacking and chewing movements), choreoathetoid limb movements, low-grade fever (37.8), and one witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure. She had previously been started on risperidone 2 mg BD 8 days ago for presumed first-episode psychosis with no improvement. She has a history of menstrual irregularity. No personal or family history of psychiatric illness. No drug use confirmed on urine toxicology screen.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.8, HR 118 sinus, BP 142/88, RR 22, SpO2 98% RA.
data_table.Examination: Disorganised speech, orofacial dyskinesias, choreoathetoid limb movements, no focal weakness, no rash, mild abdominal mass on bimanual palpation.
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFT normal. TSH normal. Urine toxicology negative. CT brain normal. LP CSF: lymphocytosis 36 (mostly lymphocytes), protein 0.52 g/L, glucose normal, ANTI-NMDA-receptor antibodies STRONGLY POSITIVE in CSF; serum anti-NMDA also positive. EEG generalised slowing with delta brushes.

lead_in: Which is the unifying diagnosis, and what additional investigation must be requested urgently?

options.text: First-episode schizophrenia with neuroleptic malignant syndrome from risperidone; cease risperidone and supportive care
options.rationale: NMS presents with rigidity, hyperthermia, autonomic instability, raised CK - not orofacial dyskinesias, choreoathetoid movements, seizures, or anti-NMDA antibody positivity in CSF. The serology and EEG findings are diagnostic. Source: eTG Neurology.

options.text: Anti-NMDA-receptor encephalitis; urgent abdominal/pelvic imaging for ovarian teratoma
options.rationale: ANTIBODY PATTERN: CSF anti-NMDA-receptor antibodies are diagnostic of anti-NMDA-receptor encephalitis. Classic clinical phases: prodromal viral-like illness -> psychiatric symptoms (anxiety, psychosis, mood lability) -> seizures + orofacial dyskinesias + choreoathetoid movements -> autonomic instability + dyskinesias. EEG delta brushes are pathognomic. In young women, ~50 percent have an underlying ovarian teratoma producing the antigen - urgent abdominal/pelvic imaging (transabdominal/transvaginal USS + CT/MRI) and tumour removal is the curative step alongside immunotherapy (steroids + IVIG or plasmapheresis as first line; rituximab/cyclophosphamide as second line). Source: ANZAN; Australian Encephalitis Network; eTG Neurology.

options.text: Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM); high-dose methylprednisolone alone
options.rationale: ADEM is a post-infectious demyelinating disease with multifocal neurology and characteristic MRI white-matter lesions; the antibody and EEG findings here are diagnostic of NMDA-receptor encephalitis. Source: ANZAN.

options.text: Limbic encephalitis (anti-Hu); CT chest for small-cell lung cancer
options.rationale: Anti-Hu paraneoplastic encephalitis is associated with small-cell lung cancer in older smokers; demographics, antibody profile, and CT chest are not appropriate first investigation in a 24-year-old woman with NMDA-positive CSF. Source: ANZAN.

options.text: Substance-induced psychosis from undetected synthetic cannabinoid; urine ELISA for synthetic cannabinoids
options.rationale: Synthetic cannabinoid psychosis does not produce CSF antibody positivity, EEG delta brushes, or orofacial dyskinesias as a constellation. Source: NSW Health.

explanation.summary: Anti-NMDA-receptor encephalitis is one of the most important psychiatric mimics. It typically affects young women and presents in stereotyped phases: viral prodrome -> psychiatric symptoms (anxiety, psychosis, mood lability, behavioural change) -> seizures and movement disorders (orofacial dyskinesias, chorea) -> autonomic instability + reduced consciousness. CSF anti-NMDA antibodies are diagnostic. EEG delta brushes are pathognomic. In women aged 18-35, approximately half have an underlying ovarian teratoma producing the antigen - imaging and tumour removal is curative alongside immunotherapy (first-line steroids + IVIG or plasmapheresis; second-line rituximab + cyclophosphamide). Prognosis is good with early treatment. Cognitive recovery may take 12-24 months.
key_points: Classic phases: prodrome -> psych -> seizures + dyskinesia -> autonomic
CSF anti-NMDA antibody is diagnostic
EEG delta brushes are pathognomic
~50% of young women have ovarian teratoma - REMOVE the tumour
First-line immunotherapy: steroids + IVIG or plasmapheresis
explanation.pearls: Any first-episode psychosis in a young woman with new seizures, movement disorder, dysautonomia, or refractory presentation should trigger urgent LP for NMDA antibodies. Antipsychotics worsen the movement disorder and may precipitate NMS-like reactions.

subtopic_detail: Anti-NMDA-receptor encephalitis psychiatric mimic + teratoma search

stem:
A 22-year-old man is brought to ED at John Hunter Hospital after using crystal methamphetamine at a nightclub 90 minutes ago. He is agitated and combative. Initial parenteral midazolam 5 mg IV has reduced agitation partially. His BP remains markedly elevated and he is now developing chest pain radiating to the left arm with diaphoresis. ECG shows ST elevation in the inferolateral leads.

Bedside echo shows preserved LV function and no regional wall motion abnormality at rest. The cardiology registrar asks for pharmacological management of his hypertension prior to angiography, recognising the agent he has used is a presynaptic monoamine releaser causing massive endogenous noradrenaline release acting at both alpha-1 and beta-1 receptors.

data_table.Examination: Agitated but redirectable after midazolam, BP 198/118, HR 142 sinus, temperature 38.1, diaphoretic, mydriatic pupils 6 mm, chest pain 7/10 retrosternal.
data_table.Investigations: Troponin I 180 ng/L (rising), ECG ST elevation II, III, aVF and V5-V6 with reciprocal change, urine drug screen positive amphetamines, ABG pH 7.32 lactate 4.1 mmol/L.

lead_in: Which agent is the single most appropriate first-line for blood pressure control in this setting?

options.text: Glyceryl trinitrate infusion titrated to BP and chest pain
options.rationale: In sympathomimetic-induced coronary vasospasm, nitrates relieve epicardial spasm directly and lower BP via venodilation without unopposed alpha effects. Australian toxicology guidance (NSW PIC, eTG) endorses benzodiazepines first, then GTN and phentolamine for ongoing hypertension or chest pain in cocaine/amphetamine ACS. Beta-blockers are avoided because of the theoretical risk of unopposed alpha-mediated coronary vasoconstriction.

options.text: Metoprolol 5 mg IV
options.rationale: Non-selective and selective beta-blockade is relatively contraindicated in sympathomimetic ACS because of the unopposed-alpha hypothesis; in Australian practice labetalol (mixed alpha-beta) is preferred over pure beta-blockade if a beta-blocker is essential. Would be wrong (Source: eTG).

options.text: Atenolol 25 mg orally
options.rationale: Same concern as metoprolol; oral route also inappropriate in acute coronary syndrome with active hypertension. Would be wrong (Source: AMH).

options.text: Adrenaline 1 mg IV
options.rationale: Adrenaline would worsen the sympathomimetic state catastrophically; not indicated. Would be wrong (Source: ARC Guidelines).

options.text: Verapamil 5 mg IV
options.rationale: Non-dihydropyridine CCB has negative inotropic effect risky in ACS with possible LV strain; not first-line. Would be wrong (Source: eTG).

explanation.summary: The mechanism-counter-mechanism logic: methamphetamine causes massive monoamine release with both alpha-1 (vasoconstriction, coronary spasm) and beta-1 (chronotropy, contractility) stimulation. The dangerous component in ACS is alpha-1 coronary vasoconstriction. Pure beta-blockade leaves alpha-1 unopposed which can worsen spasm; benzodiazepines lower central sympathetic outflow indirectly, GTN relieves spasm directly, and phentolamine provides pure alpha-1 blockade if needed. The discriminator is recognising why beta-blockade alone is contraindicated.
key_points: Sympathomimetic ACS first-line: benzodiazepines + GTN
Avoid pure beta-blockade; labetalol acceptable if beta-blocker essential
Phentolamine for refractory alpha-mediated HTN
Cooling for hyperthermia >39 degrees Celsius
Consult NSW PIC 13 11 26 early
explanation.pearls: The unopposed-alpha concern is best supported in cocaine ACS but extended to amphetamine by Australian guidelines. If the patient needs a beta-blocker for tachyarrhythmia, labetalol is the agent of choice because it has alpha-1 blockade built in.

subtopic_detail: Pharmacological reversal logic in sympathomimetic ACS

stem:
A 34-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has been stable on clozapine 450 mg nocte for 11 months, attending a Newcastle community mental health clinic. He smokes 20 cigarettes daily and has been advised against changing his smoking behaviour without consultation. He presents today with 4 days of intermittent sharp left-sided chest pain, mild dyspnoea on exertion (climbing one flight of stairs), and a single self-recorded resting heart rate of 122.

He denies fever, cough, sputum, syncope, or recent travel. His most recent FBC, UEC, LFT, and CK are within 7 days and normal except WCC 7.2 (with neutrophils 4.8) and CK 142 U/L. He has gained 8 kg over 11 months.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9, HR 118 sinus, BP 124/82, RR 22, SpO2 97% room air.
data_table.Examination: Heart sounds normal, no rub, mild bibasal fine crackles, no peripheral oedema, no calf tenderness, no rash.
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus tachycardia 118, no ST changes. Troponin I 142 ng/L (ULN 14). NT-proBNP 380 pg/mL. CXR mild cardiomegaly. FBC: WCC 7.2 N 4.8; UEC normal; CK 142; LFT normal.

lead_in: Which clozapine-associated adverse effect is the single most likely explanation for this presentation, and what is the immediate monitoring response?

options.text: Clozapine-induced agranulocytosis; cease clozapine and admit for haematology review
options.rationale: Neutrophil count is 4.8 (well above the 1.5 mandatory cessation threshold); agranulocytosis is not occurring. The presentation does not fit; agranulocytosis typically presents with sepsis from infection, not chest pain and troponin rise. Source: Australian Clozapine Monitoring Protocol.

options.text: Clozapine-induced myocarditis; cease clozapine, admit, urgent echocardiogram and cardiology consult
options.rationale: Clozapine-induced myocarditis occurs in 0.7-3 percent of patients, peaks 14-21 days after initiation but can occur later (especially with smoking-related metabolism changes). Presentation: tachycardia + chest pain + dyspnoea + raised troponin + raised CRP/NT-proBNP in a clozapine patient is myocarditis until proven otherwise. Mandatory cessation; cardiology review; echocardiogram for LVEF assessment; cardiac MRI for confirmation. Re-challenge generally not recommended. Source: RANZCP Clozapine Position Statement; Australian Clozapine Monitoring Protocol.

options.text: Clozapine-induced metabolic syndrome and weight gain; commence atorvastatin 40 mg daily and dietitian referral
options.rationale: Metabolic syndrome is a recognised clozapine effect but does not present acutely with chest pain and raised troponin in a young patient. The acute presentation demands cardiac evaluation. Source: RANZCP.

options.text: Clozapine-induced sialorrhoea; commence hyoscine hydrobromide 0.4 mg sublingually nocte
options.rationale: Sialorrhoea is a common clozapine side effect but is unrelated to acute cardiac presentation. Source: AMH.

options.text: Clozapine-induced ileus; nil orally, IV fluids, urgent abdominal X-ray
options.rationale: Gastrointestinal hypomotility is a serious clozapine effect but does not explain tachycardia + troponin + dyspnoea; the presentation is cardiac. Source: RANZCP.

explanation.summary: Clozapine's adverse-effect profile is broad and side-effect-specific monitoring schedules are mandatory in Australian practice. Mapping the presentation back to the side effect determines whether the drug must be stopped or continued. Acute chest pain + tachycardia + troponin elevation + dyspnoea in a clozapine patient is myocarditis until proven otherwise; mandatory cessation, cardiology consult, echocardiogram + cardiac MRI confirm. Other key clozapine adverse effects with their monitoring: agranulocytosis (FBC weekly 18 weeks then monthly), seizure (EEG/dose review at high doses), GI hypomotility (constipation history at each visit), metabolic syndrome (HbA1c + lipids 3-monthly first year), pulmonary embolism (high index of suspicion), sialorrhoea (clinical), hypotension (BP at each visit).
key_points: Clozapine myocarditis: peaks 14-21 days but possible later; mandatory cessation
Workup: ECG + troponin + CRP + NT-proBNP + echocardiogram + cardiac MRI
Smoking induces CYP1A2 - smoking cessation can double clozapine plasma level
Mandatory FBC monitoring: weekly x18 weeks, fortnightly x18 weeks, then monthly indefinitely
Re-challenge after myocarditis is not generally recommended in Australia
explanation.pearls: Smoking cessation in a clozapine patient is a pharmacokinetic event - plasma level can double within 1-2 weeks. Always consult before any smoking change, including admission to a non-smoking ward.

stem:
A 31-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder presents to a Gosford perinatal mental health clinic at 7 weeks gestation. Her bipolar history includes two manic episodes requiring hospitalisation 5 and 8 years ago, three depressive episodes between, and one suicide attempt by overdose 3 years ago. She has been euthymic for 18 months on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily as monotherapy.

She has now stopped valproate on her own initiative 2 weeks ago after discovering the pregnancy. She has a personal history of acne treated with isotretinoin 8 years ago (now resolved), no thyroid disease, normal renal function (Cr 65), and a strong family history of bipolar disorder in her mother. She is keen to continue the pregnancy and plans to breastfeed. She has a supportive partner.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no psychotic symptoms, MSE unremarkable, judgment intact.
data_table.Investigations: TSH 1.8 mIU/L, free T4 normal. Cr 65 micromol/L. LFT normal. Beta-hCG confirms 7-week pregnancy.

lead_in: Which mood stabiliser strategy best satisfies ALL the following constraints: minimal teratogenic risk, established efficacy in bipolar maintenance, compatibility with breastfeeding, and minimum complexity of monitoring?

options.text: Restart sodium valproate at half-dose with 5 mg folate; the second trimester is past the highest teratogenicity window
options.rationale: Valproate is contraindicated in pregnancy at any gestation (neural-tube defects, autism, lower IQ) and is single-strongest absolute contraindication in the Australian Pregnancy Category D listings for bipolar. Restarting is wrong. Source: RANZCP Perinatal Position Statement; AMH.

options.text: Quetiapine 300-600 mg daily as monotherapy; trimester-specific dose reviews; compatible with breastfeeding
options.rationale: Quetiapine satisfies all four constraints: teratogenic risk is among the lowest of mood stabilisers/atypical antipsychotics in pregnancy (Pregnancy Category B3), has good evidence for bipolar maintenance, is breastfeeding-compatible (low RID typically <1 percent), and requires minimal additional monitoring beyond standard antenatal. Lithium is more efficacious but requires intensive monitoring (TFT, renal, lithium level), 12-week fetal echo for Ebstein anomaly, and is excreted in breast milk at significant levels. Source: RANZCP Perinatal Position Statement; Bipolar Disorder Australian Treatment Guide; LactMed.

options.text: Lithium 750 mg daily; weekly levels first trimester; 12-week and 20-week fetal echo for Ebstein anomaly; cease at 6 weeks postpartum to enable breastfeeding
options.rationale: Lithium is highly effective and reasonable in pregnancy if antenatal monitoring is feasible, but the question asks for the strategy that minimises monitoring complexity AND maintains breastfeeding compatibility - lithium requires intensive monitoring and is not first-line for breastfeeding women (high RID, neonatal toxicity risk). Source: RANZCP.

options.text: Carbamazepine 600 mg daily; 5 mg folate daily; vitamin K 20 mg from 36 weeks to prevent neonatal haemorrhage
options.rationale: Carbamazepine is teratogenic (NTD, craniofacial defects) and is no longer recommended for bipolar in women of reproductive age in Australian guidance. Source: RANZCP; AMH.

options.text: Cease all mood stabilisers; weekly psychiatry review; restart only if relapse occurs
options.rationale: Wait-and-see strategy in a patient with two prior manic admissions and one suicide attempt is unsafe - relapse risk during pregnancy off all maintenance approaches 80 percent in 6 months. Source: RANZCP.

explanation.summary: Constraint stacking forces the candidate to weigh teratogenicity (favours lamotrigine, quetiapine over valproate, carbamazepine, lithium), efficacy in bipolar maintenance (favours lithium, valproate, quetiapine, lamotrigine, olanzapine), breastfeeding compatibility (favours lamotrigine, quetiapine, sertraline, olanzapine; avoid lithium, valproate, carbamazepine), and monitoring complexity (favours quetiapine, lamotrigine over lithium). Quetiapine satisfies all four; lamotrigine is reasonable for bipolar depression maintenance but less effective for mania prevention. Patient autonomy and shared decision-making frame the discussion: each option's evidence and trade-off should be discussed explicitly.
key_points: Valproate: absolutely avoid in women of reproductive age unless no alternative
Lithium: most efficacious but intensive monitoring; not first-line in BF
Quetiapine: best balance of efficacy, safety, BF compatibility, simplicity
Lamotrigine: best for bipolar depression maintenance; titration risk of SJS/TEN
Sudden discontinuation of mood stabiliser in pregnancy: relapse risk approaches 80% in 6 months
explanation.pearls: When discussing pregnancy planning in any woman of reproductive age on valproate, document the discussion explicitly - PBS access in Australia now requires a pregnancy-prevention attestation.

subtopic_detail: Mood stabiliser selection under multiple pregnancy/BF constraints

stem:
A 22-year-old woman with severe restricting-type anorexia nervosa over 5 years is brought to John Hunter Hospital ED by her mother. The patient is refusing admission. She weighs 38 kg (height 168 cm, BMI 13.5), heart rate 38 bpm sinus, BP 78/48 supine and 65/40 standing, T 35.2 degrees Celsius, glucose 2.8 mmol/L, K 2.6 mmol/L, P 0.42 mmol/L, Mg 0.62 mmol/L.

ECG shows sinus bradycardia with QTc 510 ms. She is alert, coherent, and capable of stating she understands she could die but does not want medical treatment because she fears weight restoration. She has no other psychiatric comorbidity and no acute psychosis. Her mother has lasting power of attorney for property only.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 38 sinus, BP 78/48 supine to 65/40 standing, T 35.2 deg C, weight 38 kg (BMI 13.5), SpO2 95%.
data_table.Examination: Cachexia, lanugo hair, dry mucous membranes, peripheral cyanosis, alert and oriented, MSE no thought disorder, insight present for medical consequences but absent for need for treatment.
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 2.8 mmol/L, K 2.6 mmol/L, P 0.42 mmol/L (low), Mg 0.62 mmol/L (low), ECG sinus brady 38 with QTc 510 ms. Cr 75, urea 4.

lead_in: Which combination of MARSIPAN-AU admission criteria and NSW Mental Health Act 2007 framework most appropriately governs her treatment, given that she is refusing care?

options.text: Discharge against advice with daily outpatient follow-up; her capacity is intact so no involuntary admission is possible
options.rationale: MARSIPAN-AU criteria for mandatory medical admission are met (BMI <14, HR <40, postural BP drop >20 mmHg systolic, T <35.5, glucose <3, K <2.5 [borderline], QTc >500 ms). Discharge would be negligent regardless of stated capacity, because severe AN classically presents with intact superficial reasoning but a circumscribed inability to weight-restore. NSW MHA Section 14 mental illness criteria can be met for severe AN where the eating disorder substantially impairs judgment. Source: MARSIPAN-AU; NSW MHA 2007.

options.text: Admit to a medical ward under NSW MHA 2007 Schedule 1 (involuntary mental health assessment) with refeeding under specialist eating-disorder protocol; commence oral phosphate, low-dose IV thiamine 300 mg BD, refeed at 5-10 kcal/kg/day initial rate; daily P/Mg/K; cardiac monitoring for QTc and bradycardia
options.rationale: Combined trigger: ALL MARSIPAN-AU admission criteria are met (BMI 13.5, HR 38, postural BP drop, T 35.2, glucose 2.8, QTc 510). Under NSW MHA 2007, severe AN with refusal of care meets Schedule 1 criteria when the eating disorder is judged to substantially impair the patient's ability to make safe treatment decisions about feeding/weight restoration. Refeeding starts low (5-10 kcal/kg/day; progress per protocol over 5-7 days) to prevent refeeding syndrome; phosphate and thiamine pre-treatment are mandatory; cardiac monitoring for QTc and arrhythmia. Family is consulted; the eating-disorder service is involved early. Source: MARSIPAN-AU; NSW MHA 2007; RANZCP Eating Disorders Position.

options.text: Admit voluntarily and commence standard adult enteral nutrition at 30 kcal/kg/day via nasogastric tube to rapidly restore weight
options.rationale: Starting at 30 kcal/kg/day in severe AN triggers refeeding syndrome (intracellular phosphate/magnesium/potassium shift causing arrhythmia, cardiomyopathy, encephalopathy). MARSIPAN-AU protocol starts at 5-10 kcal/kg/day and titrates. The patient is also refusing care - voluntary admission cannot be assumed. Source: MARSIPAN-AU.

options.text: Apply for guardianship through the NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal (NCAT) for medical treatment authority; defer treatment until order is granted
options.rationale: Guardianship orders take days to weeks; her condition is acutely life-threatening. NSW MHA 2007 provides immediate involuntary admission authority for psychiatric emergencies. Guardianship may be a longer-term consideration. Source: NSW MHA 2007.

options.text: Sedate with IM midazolam 5 mg, intubate for airway protection, commence IV TPN 25 kcal/kg/day with continuous insulin infusion to manage hyperglycaemia
options.rationale: Sedation and intubation are inappropriate in an alert cooperative-to-discussion patient. TPN is reserved for failed enteral nutrition; oral or NG is preferred. Rate of 25 kcal/kg/day day 1 risks refeeding syndrome. Source: MARSIPAN-AU.

explanation.summary: Severe AN with medical instability + treatment refusal is one of the few situations where the medical and mental health systems intersect operationally. MARSIPAN-AU (Management of Really Sick Patients with Anorexia Nervosa - Australia/New Zealand) gives objective criteria for medical admission: BMI <14, HR <40, postural BP drop >20 mmHg, T <35.5, glucose <3, K <2.5, P <0.4, ECG QTc >500 or rhythm abnormality. When the patient refuses, NSW MHA 2007 Section 14 mental illness criteria (with eating disorder substantially impairing decision-making capacity around feeding) provides involuntary admission authority - even where surface capacity appears intact. Refeeding starts at 5-10 kcal/kg/day with pre-treatment phosphate + thiamine and progresses over 5-7 days under daily electrolyte monitoring. The principle: capacity to refuse weight restoration is not equivalent to capacity to refuse life-saving treatment for the underlying disorder.
key_points: MARSIPAN-AU admission triggers: BMI<14, HR<40, postural drop>20, T<35.5, gluc<3, K<2.5, QTc>500
NSW MHA 2007 Section 14 covers severe AN with treatment refusal
Refeed start: 5-10 kcal/kg/day, titrate over 5-7 days
Pre-treatment: phosphate + thiamine before any kcal
Cardiac monitoring mandatory: QTc, bradycardia, arrhythmia
explanation.pearls: Aboriginal Mental Health Worker referral is essential when the patient identifies as Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander; cultural-safety governance under NSW MHA 2007 includes consultation with the patient's preferred community supports.

subtopic_detail: MARSIPAN-AU admission threshold + NSW MHA 2007 framework

stem:
A 58-year-old man with bipolar I disorder on lithium carbonate 750 mg nocte for 12 years presents to Gosford ED with 5 days of nausea, coarse tremor, ataxia, slurred speech and increasing confusion. He started ramipril 5 mg 3 weeks ago for new hypertension. Three weeks ago he also started ibuprofen 400 mg TDS for chronic shoulder pain. He has had no fluid losses, no fever, no diuretics.

His last documented serum lithium 6 months ago was 0.7 mmol/L. Today: lithium 2.4 mmol/L, creatinine 138 micromol/L (baseline 84), Na 142, K 4.2, TSH normal, glucose 5.8. ECG sinus rhythm with U waves and prolonged QT.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8, HR 102 sinus, BP 142/88, RR 16, SpO2 98% RA, GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6).
data_table.Examination: Coarse upper-limb tremor at rest, hyperreflexia 3+, ataxic gait, dysarthria, dysmetria, no focal weakness, confusion to recent events.
data_table.Investigations: Lithium 2.4 mmol/L (therapeutic 0.6-1.0), Cr 138 (baseline 84), Na 142, K 4.2, glucose 5.8. ECG sinus 102 with prolonged QT, U waves. TSH normal.

lead_in: Which is the single best explanation for the cerebellar and basal ganglia signs described, and which clinical scenario most predictably reproduces this mechanism?

options.text: Lithium interferes with neuronal sodium-potassium ATPase and Purkinje-cell function in cerebellum; recurs predictably when CYP450 inhibitors are added to the regimen
options.rationale: Lithium is not metabolised by CYP450 (it is purely renally excreted). CYP enzyme interactions are not the mechanism. The other half of the option (Na-K ATPase + Purkinje cell effect) is partially correct as a mechanism, but the predictability claim is wrong. Source: AMH; eTG Toxicology.

options.text: Lithium accumulates in neurons via secondary active transport substituting for sodium; clearance falls when GFR drops or proximal tubule sodium reabsorption increases (NSAID, ACEI, dehydration, low salt intake)
options.rationale: MECHANISM: lithium is freely filtered at the glomerulus and reabsorbed in the proximal tubule via sodium-coupled transporters. Anything that reduces GFR (NSAIDs via prostaglandin-mediated afferent arteriolar constriction, ACEIs via efferent arteriolar dilation) OR increases proximal sodium reabsorption (dehydration, low-salt diet, thiazides) causes lithium reabsorption to rise and serum level to climb. Cerebellar and basal ganglia neurons accumulate lithium because it substitutes for sodium in active transport. The triple combination of lithium + ACEI + NSAID is the classic Australian general-practice prescribing trap. Source: AMH; eTG Toxicology; Murray's Toxicology Handbook.

options.text: Lithium is hepatically metabolised by CYP3A4 and accumulates when CYP3A4 inhibitors are added; clarithromycin and grapefruit juice are the classic triggers
options.rationale: Lithium is NOT hepatically metabolised - it is purely renally excreted unchanged. CYP3A4 is irrelevant. Source: AMH.

options.text: Lithium chelates calcium and reduces parathyroid hormone production; chronic toxicity produces hypocalcaemic tetany and Trousseau sign
options.rationale: Lithium actually INCREASES PTH (causes hyperparathyroidism over years), producing hypercalcaemia not hypocalcaemia. Tetany is not the clinical picture described. Source: AMH.

options.text: Lithium directly inhibits muscarinic receptors causing central anticholinergic toxicity; trigger is co-administration with other antimuscarinic agents
options.rationale: Lithium is not an antimuscarinic. Anticholinergic toxidrome is different (hot, dry, flushed, mydriasis, ileus) and not the cerebellar-extrapyramidal picture described. Source: eTG Toxicology.

explanation.summary: Lithium is purely renally cleared. Its handling follows sodium: it is freely filtered and ~80 percent is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule by sodium-coupled mechanisms. Anything that reduces GFR (NSAID afferent constriction, ACEI efferent dilation in low-perfusion states) or upregulates proximal sodium reabsorption (volume depletion, low-salt diet, thiazide) causes lithium reabsorption to climb and serum levels to rise. The narrow therapeutic index (0.6-1.0 mmol/L; toxicity 1.5+; severe 2.5+) and the neurotoxic accumulation (substitutes for sodium in CNS Na-coupled transport, accumulates in Purkinje cells and basal ganglia) produce the classic cerebellar + extrapyramidal syndrome. Management: stop lithium, stop the precipitant (NSAID, ACEI), aggressive IV crystalloid to restore renal lithium clearance, haemodialysis when level >4.0 mmol/L acute or >2.5 with neurological signs (lithium has small Vd, dialyses readily).
key_points: Lithium = 100% renal clearance; never hepatic
Triple-trap interaction: lithium + NSAID + ACEI (or diuretic)
Therapeutic 0.6-1.0; toxicity >1.5; severe >2.5
Dialysis indications: level >4 acute, or >2.5 with neuro signs, or AKI
Long-term lithium adverse: nephrogenic DI, hypothyroidism, hyperparathyroidism, renal interstitial fibrosis
explanation.pearls: When commencing any new medication for a patient on lithium, ask: does this drug change renal sodium handling? If yes, monitor lithium level within 1-2 weeks. The classic exam vignette is the patient with new-onset hypertension started on an ACEI without lithium re-monitoring.

subtopic_detail: Lithium toxicity mechanism + drug interaction predictability

stem: You are the consultation-liaison psychiatry registrar reviewing a 62-year-old woman in clinic. She has been on lithium 750 mg nocte for bipolar I disorder for 14 years and remains euthymic. Her last lithium level 4 months ago was 0.7 mmol/L. Her eGFR has declined gradually from 78 to 62 mL/min/1.73m^2 over 2 years. She is asymptomatic and her urine albumin to creatinine ratio is 2.1 mg/mmol. There is no NSAID use and her blood pressure is well controlled on perindopril 5 mg daily.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic affect; no tremor; no oedema; no goitre; abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Na 139, K 4.3, Cr 92, eGFR 62, TSH 3.8, fT4 14, corrected calcium 2.36, lithium 0.7 (target 0.6 to 0.8), HbA1c 5.4%
data_table.Medications: Lithium carbonate 750 mg nocte, perindopril 5 mg mane

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue lithium; recheck lithium level, U&E, TSH and calcium every 3 to 6 months with nephrology referral
options.rationale: Long-term lithium requires lithium level, U&E, TSH and calcium every 3 to 6 months once stable; eGFR below 60 warrants nephrology input for shared decision-making about continuation. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Mood Disorders)

options.text: Cease lithium and switch to sodium valproate; arrange psychiatry review within 2 weeks for cross-titration
options.rationale: Stable bipolar I on therapeutic lithium with stage 2 CKD does not mandate cessation; abrupt switch risks relapse and valproate carries its own monitoring burden. Continue with closer surveillance unless eGFR falls below 45 or declines by more than 4 mL/min/year. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Mood Disorders)

options.text: Reduce lithium to 375 mg nocte; recheck lithium level, U&E and TSH at 7 days then again at 4 weeks
options.rationale: Halving a therapeutic dose risks subtherapeutic levels and mood relapse without clear renal benefit; dose reduction is reserved for levels above the target range or symptomatic toxicity. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Lithium)

options.text: Add candesartan 8 mg daily for renoprotection; recheck eGFR, electrolytes and lithium level in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Adding a second renin-angiotensin blocker is not indicated and ARB plus ACE inhibitor combination increases acute kidney injury and hyperkalaemia risk. (Source: KHA-CARI: CKD management)

options.text: Arrange an urgent renal tract ultrasound and refer to nephrology for renal biopsy within the next 14 days
options.rationale: Slow eGFR decline with minimal albuminuria does not meet criteria for urgent imaging or biopsy; lithium nephropathy is a clinical diagnosis with stable trajectory in most patients. (Source: KHA-CARI: CKD management)

explanation.summary: Long-term lithium therapy requires structured surveillance for renal, thyroid and parathyroid effects. Once a patient is stable, lithium level, U&E, TSH and corrected calcium are checked every 3 to 6 months. An eGFR below 60 mL/min/1.73m^2 warrants nephrology input to weigh ongoing lithium against relapse risk. Abrupt cessation or aggressive dose reduction is reserved for clear toxicity or rapid renal decline.
key_points: Routine lithium monitoring is lithium level, U&E, TSH and calcium every 3 to 6 months when stable
Refer to nephrology when eGFR is below 60 or declines rapidly
Avoid combined ACE inhibitor plus ARB therapy
Lithium nephropathy is usually a clinical diagnosis without biopsy
explanation.pearls: Nephrology referral threshold: eGFR below 60 mL/min/1.73m^2 OR decline greater than 4 mL/min per year.

subtopic_detail: Lithium-induced hypothyroidism in early pregnancy planning
stem: You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 31-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder, stable on lithium 900 mg nocte for 5 years. She and her partner are planning pregnancy in 6 months. She has gained 3 kg, feels cold, and reports new constipation over 8 weeks. Her last manic episode required ICU admission and her psychiatrist regards her as high relapse risk. She is using condoms reliably. The pre-pregnancy bloods are back.

data_table.Examination: Mildly dry skin; slow ankle reflex relaxation; no goitre; affect euthymic; no tremor
data_table.Investigations: TSH 8.4, fT4 11 (low-normal), TPO antibody positive, lithium 0.8, Cr 76, eGFR 92, beta-hCG negative
data_table.Medications: Lithium carbonate 900 mg nocte; folic acid 500 micrograms daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Cease lithium immediately and substitute quetiapine 300 mg nocte; refer to obstetric psychiatry for monitoring
options.rationale: Sudden lithium cessation in a high relapse risk patient is associated with manic recurrence; lithium nephrotoxicity is not the issue here and hypothyroidism is correctable. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Mood Disorders)

options.text: Continue lithium at current dose and commence levothyroxine 50 micrograms daily; recheck TSH and fT4 in 6 weeks
options.rationale: Lithium-induced hypothyroidism is managed with thyroxine replacement rather than lithium withdrawal in a stable bipolar patient at high relapse risk; pregnancy planning increases the imperative for euthyroid status before conception. (Source: AMH: Levothyroxine)

options.text: Continue lithium and start carbimazole 5 mg daily; recheck thyroid function and lithium level in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Carbimazole is used for hyperthyroidism; the patient has biochemical hypothyroidism and thyroxine is required. (Source: AMH: Thyroid disorders)

options.text: Reduce lithium to 600 mg nocte and start levothyroxine 25 micrograms daily; recheck TSH and lithium in 2 weeks
options.rationale: Reducing lithium in a high relapse risk patient risks decompensation; subtherapeutic dosing is not justified by hypothyroidism which is independently treated. (Source: AMH: Lithium)

options.text: Continue lithium, withhold levothyroxine and recheck TSH in 12 weeks before any decision on thyroid replacement
options.rationale: Delay risks worsening hypothyroidism through pregnancy planning and conception; TSH above 4 in a woman planning pregnancy with positive TPO antibody warrants treatment now. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Lithium-induced hypothyroidism affects up to 1 in 5 patients on long-term therapy and is more common in women, especially with positive TPO antibodies. The standard approach is to treat with levothyroxine rather than to discontinue lithium, particularly in patients at high relapse risk. In a woman planning pregnancy, achieving euthyroid status before conception reduces fetal neurodevelopmental risk. Lithium itself is teratogenic but the absolute Ebstein anomaly risk is lower than historically taught and continuation may be appropriate with shared decision-making.
key_points: Lithium hypothyroidism is treated with levothyroxine, not by stopping lithium
Target TSH below 2.5 mIU/L preconception and in first trimester
TPO antibody positivity predicts lithium hypothyroidism
High relapse risk bipolar warrants continuation through pregnancy planning
explanation.pearls: Levothyroxine 50 micrograms daily is a reasonable starting dose in non-pregnant adults; titrate by TSH at 6 weeks.

stem: You are the early psychosis registrar reviewing a 24-year-old man who started olanzapine 10 mg nocte 3 months ago after a first episode of schizophrenia. He reports a 4 kg weight gain and increased appetite. He smokes 10 cigarettes daily, drinks no alcohol, and has a strong family history of type 2 diabetes. He is otherwise asymptomatic, attending TAFE, and adherent to treatment.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/78, HR 78, RR 14, SpO2 99% RA, T 36.7; waist 96 cm, BMI 27
data_table.Examination: Settled affect; no EPS; no tremor; no acanthosis nigricans
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 5.5, HbA1c 5.8%, total cholesterol 5.2, LDL 3.4, HDL 1.0, triglycerides 2.0, ALT 32, prolactin 280 (normal)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management strategy?

options.text: Continue olanzapine; arrange lifestyle counselling and recheck weight, fasting glucose and lipids at 6 months
options.rationale: While lifestyle counselling is correct, a single recheck at 6 months delays detection of rapid metabolic decline during the first year on a high-risk antipsychotic. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia)

options.text: Switch to aripiprazole 10 mg daily over 4 weeks; recheck weight, fasting glucose and lipids in 3 months
options.rationale: Premature switching after only 3 months of effective treatment risks relapse; metabolic side effects should first be addressed with lifestyle and surveillance, with switch reserved for established intolerance or inefficacy. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia)

options.text: Continue olanzapine with lifestyle intervention; arrange 3-monthly weight, BP, fasting glucose and lipids in year 1
options.rationale: First year on a metabolically active antipsychotic requires 3-monthly metabolic monitoring including weight, waist circumference, BP, fasting glucose and lipids; lifestyle intervention is first line for weight gain at this stage. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia)

options.text: Continue olanzapine; add metformin 500 mg twice daily and recheck weight, HbA1c and fasting lipids in 3 months
options.rationale: Metformin for antipsychotic weight gain is considered when lifestyle measures fail and after at least 3 to 6 months; HbA1c 5.8% does not meet diabetes criteria and lifestyle is the first step. (Source: AMH: Metformin)

options.text: Stop olanzapine; switch to risperidone 2 mg twice daily and commence atorvastatin 20 mg nocte for CV risk
options.rationale: Risperidone is also metabolically active and may worsen prolactin; statin therapy is not indicated by current lipid profile or absolute cardiovascular risk in a 24 year old. (Source: AMH: Antipsychotics)

explanation.summary: Second-generation antipsychotic metabolic monitoring follows a structured schedule, especially in the first year. Weight, waist, blood pressure, fasting glucose and lipids are checked at baseline, 3 months, then 3 to 6 monthly. Olanzapine carries the highest metabolic burden alongside clozapine. Lifestyle intervention is first line for weight gain before adjunct metformin or antipsychotic switch.
key_points: Baseline, 3 month then 3 to 6 monthly metabolic monitoring during the first year
Olanzapine and clozapine carry the highest metabolic risk
Metformin is second line for antipsychotic weight gain after lifestyle fails
Switch to a lower metabolic burden agent is reserved for established harm
explanation.pearls: Metformin can be added if weight gain exceeds 5% over 3 months despite lifestyle and the patient is otherwise well controlled on antipsychotic.

stem: You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 28-year-old woman with schizophrenia, stable on risperidone 4 mg daily for 18 months. She reports 4 months of amenorrhoea, breast tenderness and recent galactorrhoea. She is not pregnant. She is otherwise mentally well and has previously failed olanzapine due to weight gain. Her prolactin is 1850 mIU/L (normal less than 500 in non-pregnant adult).

data_table.Examination: Galactorrhoea bilateral on expression; no visual field defect; no acromegalic features
data_table.Investigations: Prolactin 1850, beta-hCG negative, TSH 1.8, fT4 14, oestradiol low, LH and FSH low-normal; MRI pituitary normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue risperidone and commence cabergoline 0.25 mg twice weekly; recheck prolactin in 6 weeks
options.rationale: Dopamine agonists antagonise antipsychotic action and risk psychotic relapse; they are not first line for antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinaemia. (Source: AMH: Cabergoline)

options.text: Reduce risperidone to 2 mg daily; arrange endocrinology review and recheck prolactin within 4 weeks
options.rationale: Dose reduction in a stable patient risks relapse and rarely normalises prolactin from this range; switch to a prolactin-sparing agent is preferred. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia)

options.text: Continue risperidone at current dose; reassure that mild prolactin rise is expected and recheck symptoms in 6 months
options.rationale: Symptomatic hyperprolactinaemia with amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea is not acceptable to leave untreated due to bone density loss and quality of life impact. (Source: eTG: Endocrinology)

options.text: Switch risperidone to aripiprazole 10 mg daily over 4 weeks; recheck prolactin and review symptoms at 6 weeks
options.rationale: Aripiprazole is prolactin-sparing and often partially reverses antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinaemia; switch is preferred over add-on cabergoline. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia)

options.text: Cease risperidone abruptly; commence quetiapine 100 mg twice daily and refer to gynaecology for amenorrhoea workup
options.rationale: Abrupt antipsychotic cessation risks rebound and psychotic relapse; quetiapine is reasonable but cross-titration is needed, and gynaecology referral is unnecessary if antipsychotic switch resolves the prolactin. (Source: AMH: Antipsychotics)

explanation.summary: Symptomatic hyperprolactinaemia from risperidone, paliperidone and amisulpride is managed by switching to a prolactin-sparing agent such as aripiprazole, quetiapine or olanzapine. Aripiprazole has the most evidence for prolactin reduction without antipsychotic withdrawal. Dopamine agonists are avoided where possible because they may precipitate psychotic relapse. Persistent symptomatic hyperprolactinaemia causes bone density loss in both sexes.
key_points: Risperidone, paliperidone and amisulpride are high-prolactin agents
Aripiprazole is the prolactin-sparing switch of choice
Dopamine agonists risk psychotic relapse
Long-term hyperprolactinaemia causes osteoporosis
explanation.pearls: Adjunctive aripiprazole 5 to 10 mg added to risperidone is an alternative when switching is not possible; partial dopamine agonism normalises prolactin in many patients.

stem: You are the adult psychiatry registrar reviewing a 26-year-old man with newly diagnosed ADHD-combined type confirmed on DIVA-5 interview and corroborated by partner and parents. Childhood symptoms documented in school reports. He has no current substance use disorder, no cardiac history, no family history of sudden cardiac death and is otherwise well. He drives a car as part of his work delivering parcels. His ECG and BP are normal.

data_table.Examination: Distractible during interview; otherwise normal; ECG sinus rhythm QTc 410 ms
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative; TSH normal; FBC, U&E and LFTs normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacological choice and the most important counselling point about driving?

options.text: Commence atomoxetine 40 mg daily; advise that he must surrender his licence to Vicroads while on stimulant medication
options.rationale: Atomoxetine is second line for adults and licence surrender is not required for legally prescribed stimulants. (Source: Austroads: Assessing Fitness to Drive)

options.text: Commence guanfacine extended release 1 mg daily; advise that driving is contraindicated for the first 6 weeks of treatment
options.rationale: Guanfacine is third line for adult ADHD and there is no 6-week driving ban; only sedation while titrating should be considered. (Source: AMH: Guanfacine)

options.text: Commence bupropion 150 mg daily; advise that ADHD without comorbid depression rarely requires pharmacotherapy
options.rationale: Bupropion is not approved for adult ADHD in Australia and the premise that ADHD rarely requires medication is incorrect. (Source: AMH: Bupropion)

options.text: Commence dexamfetamine 5 mg twice daily; counsel that he must inform police about stimulant use at every interaction
options.rationale: Dexamfetamine is a reasonable agent but the advice on police disclosure is incorrect; patients only need to comply with general driving licence and medical reporting rules. (Source: Austroads: Assessing Fitness to Drive)

options.text: Commence lisdexamfetamine 30 mg morning; counsel that untreated ADHD increases crash risk and treated driving is generally safe
options.rationale: Lisdexamfetamine is first line for adult ADHD per RANZCP guidance and Austroads recognises that treated ADHD is associated with lower crash risk than untreated ADHD. (Source: RANZCP CPG: ADHD)

explanation.summary: First-line pharmacotherapy for adult ADHD in Australia is a long-acting stimulant, with lisdexamfetamine or methylphenidate as preferred options. ECG and cardiovascular history are checked before initiation but routine cardiac imaging is not required without risk factors. Austroads guidance supports driving on stimulants when symptoms are controlled and there is no impairment, because treated ADHD has lower crash rates than untreated. Atomoxetine, guanfacine and bupropion are non-stimulant options reserved for stimulant failure, substance misuse risk or contraindications.
key_points: Lisdexamfetamine and methylphenidate are first-line for adult ADHD
ECG and BP at baseline; no routine cardiac imaging without risk factors
Treated ADHD has lower crash risk than untreated
Atomoxetine is second line
explanation.pearls: Lisdexamfetamine starting dose 30 mg morning; titrate weekly to 50 to 70 mg based on response and tolerability.

stem: You are the GP registrar reviewing a 48-year-old man with COPD who smokes 30 cigarettes per day. He has tried nicotine patches alone twice unsuccessfully and wants to quit before a planned hip replacement in 12 weeks. He has stable schizophrenia on aripiprazole, no recent self-harm, no current depressive symptoms and no recent suicidal ideation. He is keen to try something more effective.

data_table.Examination: Mood euthymic; affect reactive; no thought disorder; no suicidal ideation
data_table.Investigations: FBC, U&E, LFTs normal; PHQ-9 score 4 (minimal); spirometry FEV1 62% predicted
data_table.Medications: Aripiprazole 10 mg daily; tiotropium inhaler; salbutamol PRN

lead_in: Which pharmacotherapy is most appropriate for this patient?

options.text: Varenicline 0.5 mg daily for 3 days, then 0.5 mg twice daily for 4 days, then 1 mg twice daily; quit day at 8 to 14 days
options.rationale: Varenicline is the most effective single agent for smoking cessation and is appropriate in stable schizophrenia without active suicidality; modern guidance supports use with monitoring rather than avoidance. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines)

options.text: Bupropion 150 mg daily for 6 days then 150 mg twice daily for 12 weeks; quit day at 7 to 14 days from start
options.rationale: Bupropion is reasonable but less effective than varenicline and lowers seizure threshold; in schizophrenia varenicline now has the best evidence base. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines)

options.text: Nicotine replacement patch 21 mg daily with 4 mg gum PRN for breakthrough cravings for 12 weeks total
options.rationale: Combination NRT is reasonable but the patient has already failed two NRT-based attempts; escalation to varenicline is appropriate. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines)

options.text: Nortriptyline 25 mg nocte titrated to 75 mg nocte over 4 weeks; quit day at 14 to 21 days from start
options.rationale: Nortriptyline is fourth line and not appropriate when varenicline is available and tolerated; antidepressant effect is unwanted here. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines)

options.text: Clonidine 50 micrograms twice daily titrated to 150 micrograms twice daily; quit day at 7 to 10 days from start
options.rationale: Clonidine is rarely used due to side effects and is reserved for failure of first and second line agents; it offers no advantage over varenicline. (Source: AMH: Clonidine)

explanation.summary: Varenicline is the most effective single agent for smoking cessation with approximately a doubling of long-term quit rates compared with placebo. Previous neuropsychiatric safety concerns have been substantially refuted by the EAGLES trial, and varenicline can be used in stable schizophrenia and depression with appropriate monitoring. Combination NRT or escalation to varenicline is recommended after monotherapy NRT failure. Quit day is typically set 8 to 14 days after starting varenicline to allow steady state.
key_points: Varenicline is first line for high-dependence smokers and after NRT failure
EAGLES trial supports use in stable mental illness with monitoring
Quit day 8 to 14 days after varenicline initiation
Bupropion is second line and lowers seizure threshold
explanation.pearls: Smoking is a CYP1A2 inducer; cessation can raise clozapine and olanzapine levels by 30 to 50 percent, requiring dose adjustment.

stem: You are the emergency medicine registrar called to a 32-year-old man in the resus bay who arrived via police. He is shouting, swinging at staff and security, and refusing oral medication. There is no obtainable history beyond that he was found wandering on a freeway. Five staff and two security officers have established physical containment in lateral recumbent position. There is no IV access. His airway is patent.

data_table.Vital signs: BP estimated 150/90 by manual, HR 132, RR 28, SpO2 unmeasured, T not yet measured; finger-prick glucose 6.8
data_table.Examination: Sweating, dilated pupils, dry mucosa, no obvious trauma, no track marks visible
data_table.Investigations: ECG not yet feasible; capillary glucose 6.8; venous gas pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first parenteral medication?

options.text: Midazolam 10 mg intramuscular into deltoid; reassess at 15 minutes and repeat 5 mg if not adequately settled
options.rationale: Midazolam alone is associated with greater respiratory depression than droperidol in this setting and is second line in current Australian ED practice. (Source: ACEM/ACEP Guideline: Acute Behavioural Disturbance)

options.text: Droperidol 10 mg intramuscular into deltoid; reassess at 15 minutes and repeat once if not adequately settled
options.rationale: Droperidol 10 mg IM is first-line for severe acute behavioural disturbance in Australian emergency practice; onset 10 to 20 minutes and good safety profile in agitated patients without known long QT. (Source: ACEM/ACEP Guideline: Acute Behavioural Disturbance)

options.text: Haloperidol 5 mg with lorazepam 2 mg intramuscular into deltoid; reassess at 30 minutes for response
options.rationale: The haloperidol plus lorazepam combination is widely used internationally but has slower onset than droperidol monotherapy; current Australian guidance preferences droperidol. (Source: ACEM/ACEP Guideline: Acute Behavioural Disturbance)

options.text: Olanzapine 10 mg intramuscular into deltoid; await onset over 20 minutes before considering further sedation
options.rationale: Olanzapine IM is an option but reserved when droperidol is contraindicated; combined olanzapine plus benzodiazepine within 1 hour increases hypotension and oversedation risk. (Source: AMH: Olanzapine IM)

options.text: Ketamine 4 mg/kg intramuscular into deltoid as immediate dissociative sedation pending ICU transfer for intubation
options.rationale: Ketamine is reserved for failure of first and second line sedation; routine first-use ketamine in an undifferentiated patient is not standard and risks laryngospasm without airway preparation. (Source: ACEM/ACEP Guideline: Acute Behavioural Disturbance)

explanation.summary: Droperidol 10 mg IM is the first-line parenteral sedative for severe acute behavioural disturbance in Australian emergency departments based on the DORM and DORM II studies. It offers fast onset, predictable duration and a favourable safety profile when QT prolongation risk factors are absent. Second-line options include olanzapine IM or midazolam IM, and ketamine is reserved for refractory cases. Continuous monitoring of airway, oxygenation and circulation begins as soon as feasible after sedation.
key_points: Droperidol 10 mg IM is first line for severe ABD in Australian EDs
Onset 10 to 20 minutes, repeat in 15 minutes if needed
Olanzapine IM avoided within 1 hour of benzodiazepines
Ketamine reserved for failure of standard sedation
explanation.pearls: Monitor for respiratory depression and check ECG once safe; QTc above 500 ms or known long QT favours olanzapine over droperidol.

stem: You are the emergency medicine consultant overseeing the resuscitation of a 26-year-old man with suspected methamphetamine intoxication. He has received droperidol 10 mg IM 25 minutes ago and a repeat droperidol 10 mg IM 10 minutes ago. He continues to thrash against restraints despite a brief period of partial settling. His core temperature is now 39.1, HR 168 sinus on monitor, BP 168/104, and he has bitten his lip with blood in airway. There is one functional IV line. The team is preparing to intubate.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.1, HR 168 sinus, BP 168/104, RR 36, SpO2 92% on 15 L NRB; capillary glucose 8.2
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, rigid, clenched jaw, lip laceration with airway blood; pupils 6 mm reactive
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.18, lactate 8.2, K 5.8, Na 142; CK 4200; troponin pending; ECG sinus tachycardia, QTc 480
data_table.Medications: Droperidol 10 mg IM x2 in last 25 minutes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Ketamine 4 mg/kg intramuscular as immediate sedation; defer intubation until obtainable cooperation for nasal airway placement
options.rationale: IM ketamine in this patient is acceptable as a rescue strategy but defers definitive airway control in a patient with active aspiration and severe acidaemia; the team is already preparing intubation, and IV access exists. (Source: ACEM/ACEP Guideline: Acute Behavioural Disturbance)

options.text: Repeat droperidol 10 mg IM and add midazolam 5 mg IV; reassess in 10 minutes before considering airway intervention
options.rationale: Third dose of droperidol with benzodiazepine in an unstable patient with airway compromise wastes time and risks dropping BP without addressing temperature; intubation is required. (Source: ACEM/ACEP Guideline: Acute Behavioural Disturbance)

options.text: Rapid sequence intubation with ketamine 1.5 mg/kg IV and rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg IV; commence active cooling with cold IV fluids
options.rationale: Sympathomimetic toxidrome with hyperthermia above 39, rhabdomyolysis, acidaemia and airway compromise meets criteria for definitive airway control; ketamine RSI avoids sympathetic surge from suxamethonium and active cooling addresses the principal driver of mortality. (Source: ACEM/ACEP Guideline: Acute Behavioural Disturbance)

options.text: Dantrolene 1 mg/kg IV with active surface cooling; transfer to ICU and defer airway intervention
options.rationale: Dantrolene is for malignant hyperthermia and NMS, not sympathomimetic hyperthermia which responds to sedation, paralysis and external cooling; airway must be secured first. (Source: AMH: Dantrolene)

options.text: Suxamethonium 1.5 mg/kg IV alone with bag mask ventilation; insert nasogastric tube for activated charcoal administration
options.rationale: Suxamethonium without sedation is inhumane; further hyperkalaemia in rhabdomyolysis is dangerous; charcoal is not indicated for sympathomimetic intoxication. (Source: AMH: Suxamethonium)

explanation.summary: Severe sympathomimetic toxidrome with hyperthermia above 39, severe lactic acidaemia, rhabdomyolysis and airway compromise mandates definitive airway control rather than further procedural sedation. Ketamine RSI is preferred over suxamethonium because suxamethonium can exacerbate hyperkalaemia in rhabdomyolysis and induces sympathetic surge. Active cooling with cold IV fluids and exposure is the principal disease-modifying intervention; hyperthermia drives multi-organ failure. Dantrolene is for malignant hyperthermia and NMS, not psychostimulant toxicity.
key_points: Hyperthermia above 39 in sympathomimetic toxidrome warrants immediate cooling and airway control
Ketamine RSI preferred over suxamethonium with rhabdomyolysis and hyperkalaemia
Dantrolene has no role in psychostimulant hyperthermia
Repeated sedation without airway control wastes resuscitation time
explanation.pearls: Cold IV crystalloid at 30 mL/kg over 30 minutes plus surface cooling can drop temperature by 1 degree per 30 minutes; target below 38.5 within 1 hour.

stem: You are the consultation-liaison psychiatry registrar reviewing a 28-year-old woman admitted under medicine for dehydration and reduced oral intake over 5 days. She has known schizophrenia previously stable on aripiprazole. She is mute, holds bizarre postures for minutes at a time, and appears to be staring at the wall. Bush-Francis catatonia rating scale is 14. CT brain unremarkable. EEG, infection screen and lithium not contributory. Her aripiprazole was stopped on admission by the medical team.

data_table.Examination: Mute, waxy flexibility, posturing arms above head 60 seconds, no tremor, no rigidity, no fever
data_table.Investigations: CK 320 (mildly elevated), Na 142, K 4.0, WCC 8.4, CRP 6, TSH normal, CT brain normal, lumbar puncture deferred
data_table.Medications: Aripiprazole ceased on admission; IV maintenance fluids

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Restart aripiprazole 10 mg orally daily; continue intravenous maintenance fluids and reassess catatonia at 48 hours
options.rationale: Restarting an antipsychotic without first addressing catatonia risks precipitating neuroleptic malignant syndrome; lorazepam is required first. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Catatonia)

options.text: Administer haloperidol 5 mg intramuscularly with promethazine 25 mg intramuscularly and reassess in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Antipsychotics can worsen catatonia and precipitate NMS, especially in malignant catatonia; first-generation high-potency agents are particularly avoided. (Source: AMH: Haloperidol)

options.text: Refer urgently for electroconvulsive therapy without prior pharmacological challenge; consent through guardianship board
options.rationale: ECT is second line after lorazepam fails, although highly effective in malignant catatonia; a trial of lorazepam should normally precede ECT. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Catatonia)

options.text: Administer lorazepam 2 mg intravenously and reassess Bush-Francis score within 10 to 15 minutes for response
options.rationale: Lorazepam challenge with 1 to 2 mg IV is the diagnostic and initial therapeutic step for catatonia; a 50 percent reduction in Bush-Francis score within 10 to 15 minutes is supportive and guides ongoing scheduled lorazepam. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Catatonia)

options.text: Administer amantadine 100 mg orally twice daily; arrange MRI brain with contrast over the next 48 hours
options.rationale: Amantadine is third line after lorazepam and ECT; structural imaging has already been done and contrast is not indicated for catatonia workup at this stage. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Catatonia)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is diagnosed clinically using Bush-Francis criteria and confirmed by a lorazepam challenge. Lorazepam 1 to 2 mg IV given over a few minutes with reassessment at 10 to 15 minutes is both diagnostic and the first treatment step. A clear response supports scheduled lorazepam 6 to 24 mg daily titrated to effect. Antipsychotics, especially high-potency first generation agents, can worsen catatonia and precipitate malignant catatonia or NMS and should be withheld until catatonia resolves. ECT is highly effective second-line treatment.
key_points: Bush-Francis is the standard catatonia rating tool
Lorazepam 1 to 2 mg IV is both diagnostic and therapeutic
Avoid antipsychotics during active catatonia
ECT is second line and definitive treatment for refractory cases
explanation.pearls: Scheduled lorazepam doses of 6 to 24 mg per day are often tolerated without sedation when catatonia is active because of altered GABA tone.

stem: You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 22-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder. She has been stable on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily for 3 years. She has a new male partner and reports inconsistent condom use. She does not currently want to become pregnant but is open to pregnancy in 2 to 3 years. She has not been counselled about valproate and pregnancy. Her TGA-listed indication and the AU pregnancy prevention requirements apply.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no tremor, no peripheral oedema, normal gait
data_table.Investigations: FBC normal, LFTs normal, valproate 480 micromol/L (target 350 to 700), beta-hCG negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue valproate; arrange annual ultrasound screening for ovarian morphology and reassess teratogenic counselling in 12 months
options.rationale: Polycystic ovary morphology is a recognised valproate effect but routine annual ultrasound surveillance is not standard; teratogenic counselling cannot wait. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Mood Disorders)

options.text: Switch valproate to lamotrigine 200 mg daily; commence folic acid 5 mg daily and continue current condom-only contraception
options.rationale: Premature switch may destabilise bipolar; condom-only contraception is not reliable enough for a teratogenic medication; counselling and effective contraception should come first. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Mood Disorders)

options.text: Continue valproate; commence high-dose folic acid 5 mg daily and reassure that contraception is not yet necessary
options.rationale: Folic acid does not mitigate valproate teratogenicity meaningfully and effective contraception is required during valproate exposure regardless of pregnancy plans. (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention)

options.text: Cease valproate abruptly; bridge with quetiapine 300 mg nocte and arrange psychiatry review within 2 weeks for stability
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation risks relapse and quetiapine is not equivalent to valproate for bipolar maintenance; managed switch is appropriate but only after counselling. (Source: AMH: Sodium valproate)

options.text: Continue valproate; arrange counselling on teratogenic risk and ensure highly effective contraception is in place
options.rationale: Valproate carries up to 10 percent major congenital malformation risk and 30 to 40 percent neurodevelopmental risk; Australian guidance mandates documented teratogenic counselling and reliable contraception for women of reproductive potential, with consideration of switch when planning pregnancy. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Mood Disorders)

explanation.summary: Valproate is the most teratogenic anticonvulsant and is associated with major malformations in about 10 percent of exposed pregnancies and neurodevelopmental impairment in up to 40 percent. The TGA in 2023 introduced Pregnancy Prevention Program requirements for valproate, including documented annual counselling, effective contraception and acknowledgement forms for women of reproductive potential. Switching is considered when pregnancy is planned but must be done in a stable patient with bridging therapy. Lamotrigine and lithium are commonly used alternatives.
key_points: Valproate has 10 percent malformation risk and 30 to 40 percent neurodevelopmental risk
TGA Pregnancy Prevention Program mandates annual documented counselling and contraception
Folic acid does not negate valproate teratogenicity
Switch to lamotrigine or lithium when planning pregnancy in stable bipolar
explanation.pearls: Long-acting reversible contraception (LARC) such as etonogestrel implant or copper IUD is preferred for women on valproate due to user-independent reliability.

stem: You are the community mental health team registrar reviewing a 26-year-old woman with borderline personality disorder. She has had 4 self-harm episodes by superficial cutting in the last 6 weeks and 1 emergency presentation with paracetamol ingestion of 8 g 3 weeks ago, managed conservatively. She is currently on no psychotropic medication and is willing to engage in psychological therapy. She has chronic feelings of emptiness, fear of abandonment and intense unstable relationships. There are no psychotic features.

data_table.Examination: Multiple superficial healing forearm lacerations; mood reactive; no psychosis; no acute suicidality at interview
data_table.Investigations: FBC, U&E, LFTs (post-paracetamol) normal; urine drug screen negative

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first-line management strategy?

options.text: Refer for dialectical behaviour therapy with weekly individual and weekly skills group for at least 12 months
options.rationale: DBT is the most evidence-based first-line treatment for BPD with recurrent self-harm, with reductions in self-harm, suicide attempts and hospitalisation in randomised trials. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD

options.text: Commence quetiapine 100 mg nocte; arrange GP review in 4 weeks; defer psychological therapy until mood is more stable
options.rationale: Medication is not first-line for BPD and quetiapine is not indicated for emotion dysregulation alone; psychological therapy is the primary treatment. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy of 12 sessions focused on cognitive restructuring for self-harm thoughts
options.rationale: Standard CBT is less effective for BPD than structured therapies (DBT, MBT, schema-focused therapy); 12 sessions is also too short. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD

options.text: Admit for inpatient stabilisation under the Mental Health Act; arrange psychiatric review for medication initiation
options.rationale: Inpatient admission is generally avoided in BPD outside of brief crisis admission; involuntary admission and routine pharmacotherapy worsen long-term outcomes. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg daily; refer to GP-led mental health treatment plan for 10 sessions of supportive counselling
options.rationale: SSRI is not first-line for BPD without comorbid major depression; supportive counselling is less effective than structured BPD-specific therapy. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD

explanation.summary: The NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD recommends structured psychological therapy such as DBT, MBT or schema-focused therapy as first-line treatment, particularly with recurrent self-harm. DBT has the strongest evidence and reduces self-harm, suicide attempts and inpatient days. Medication is reserved for clearly identified comorbid disorders and is not the primary treatment for BPD itself. Prolonged inpatient admission is generally avoided due to risk of regression and dependency.
key_points: DBT, MBT and schema-focused therapy are first-line for BPD
Pharmacotherapy is for comorbid conditions, not BPD per se
Avoid prolonged inpatient admission
Standard CBT and supportive counselling are less effective
explanation.pearls: Standard DBT comprises weekly individual therapy, weekly skills group, phone coaching and therapist consultation team for at least 12 months.

sources.label: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD

stem: You are the emergency registrar reviewing a 34-year-old woman who took her dosette tray of amitriptyline 50 mg tablets approximately 90 minutes ago after a relationship breakup. She estimates 28 tablets ingested. On arrival she is drowsy but rousable, with dry mucous membranes and an ECG showing sinus tachycardia. She has just had one self-terminating generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting 45 seconds. The ECG is in front of you.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 92/58, HR 132, RR 18, SpO2 96% on 6 L Hudson mask, T 37.2, GCS 12 (E3 V4 M5)
data_table.Examination: Dry mucosa, dilated pupils, hyperreflexia, no focal deficit, no airway compromise after seizure
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus tachycardia HR 132, QRS 140 ms, terminal R wave aVR 5 mm; pH 7.28, lactate 3.4, K 3.6, paracetamol negative
data_table.Medications: Amitriptyline 50 mg nocte usually; no other regular medications

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer flumazenil 200 micrograms IV; commence intravenous normal saline 1 L over 30 minutes and recheck ECG
options.rationale: Flumazenil is contraindicated in mixed overdose or TCA toxicity due to seizure precipitation; the drowsiness here is anticholinergic plus TCA, not benzodiazepine. (Source: AMH: Flumazenil)

options.text: Administer sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol IV bolus and prepare an infusion; intubate if GCS drops or seizures recur
options.rationale: QRS above 100 ms in TCA toxicity is an indication for sodium bicarbonate; bolus 1 to 2 mmol/kg with reassessment is the standard antidote and reduces cardiotoxicity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Administer activated charcoal 50 g orally; commence intravenous diazepam 5 mg for sedation and seizure prophylaxis
options.rationale: Activated charcoal in a drowsy patient without secured airway risks aspiration; benzodiazepines treat established seizures but bicarbonate is the priority for cardiotoxicity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Administer magnesium sulfate 2 g IV over 10 minutes; commence amiodarone 300 mg infusion for arrhythmia prophylaxis
options.rationale: Magnesium has no evidence in TCA toxicity and amiodarone can worsen sodium channel blockade; class IA, IC and III antiarrhythmics are contraindicated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Administer intravenous lipid emulsion 1.5 mL/kg over 1 minute; commence noradrenaline infusion for hypotension control
options.rationale: Intralipid is rescue therapy in refractory TCA cardiac arrest; not first line; sodium bicarbonate precedes it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

explanation.summary: TCA toxicity causes sodium and potassium channel blockade leading to QRS widening, prolonged QT and ventricular arrhythmia, plus anticholinergic features and seizures. Indications for sodium bicarbonate include QRS above 100 ms, terminal R in aVR greater than 3 mm, ventricular dysrhythmia or hypotension. Standard regimen is 1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus followed by infusion to target pH 7.5. Avoid class IA, IC and III antiarrhythmics; treat seizures with benzodiazepines; intralipid is reserved for refractory arrest.
key_points: QRS above 100 ms is the trigger for sodium bicarbonate in TCA toxicity
Target arterial pH 7.5 with bicarbonate infusion
Avoid amiodarone, lidocaine and procainamide
Intralipid is rescue therapy in refractory arrest
explanation.pearls: Bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg IV bolus, repeat every 5 minutes if QRS remains widened, then infusion at 100 to 150 mmol in 1 L D5W at 250 mL/h.

stem: You are the neurology registrar reviewing a 28-year-old teacher with 4 weeks of right leg weakness preventing her from walking unassisted. There is no antecedent trauma. She is currently on workers' compensation for unrelated stress leave. Examination shows Hoover sign positive on the right leg, give-way weakness throughout the right leg with normal tone and reflexes, and a non-anatomical sensory loss. MRI brain and spine are normal. Nerve conduction studies are normal.

data_table.Examination: Right leg 2/5 power on direct testing with give-way pattern; Hoover sign positive; sensory loss to fingertip threshold non-anatomical; reflexes 2+; toes downgoing
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain and spine normal; NCS and EMG normal; B12, TSH, glucose normal

lead_in: Which statement most accurately describes the diagnostic framework?

options.text: Defer diagnosis; arrange repeat MRI with contrast and lumbar puncture in 4 weeks to exclude inflammatory disease conclusively
options.rationale: Repeated negative investigations reinforce the sick role and delay treatment; FND is a positive diagnosis not requiring exclusion of all alternatives. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Somatic Symptom Disorders)

options.text: Diagnose malingering based on the workers' compensation context and refer to occupational physician for capacity assessment
options.rationale: Malingering requires intentional production of symptoms for external gain; the patient cannot consciously generate a positive Hoover sign and presence of secondary gain does not establish intentionality. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Diagnose factitious disorder imposed on self based on absence of physical findings and presence of psychosocial stressor
options.rationale: Factitious disorder requires conscious deception without external gain; positive clinical signs and absence of evidence of deception point to FND. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Diagnose functional neurological disorder based on positive Hoover sign and rule-in clinical features; explain the diagnosis collaboratively
options.rationale: FND in DSM-5-TR is a rule-in diagnosis based on positive clinical signs such as Hoover sign and tremor entrainment; it does not require exclusion of all organic disease nor evidence of psychological stressor. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Somatic Symptom Disorders)
