options.text: Diagnose generalised anxiety disorder based on the work-related stress; commence sertraline 50 mg daily and refer for CBT
options.rationale: GAD does not cause focal weakness with positive Hoover sign; SSRI is not first-line treatment for FND without comorbid anxiety. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Somatic Symptom Disorders)

explanation.summary: Functional neurological disorder is a positive diagnosis in DSM-5-TR based on clinical signs such as Hoover sign, hip abductor sign, tremor entrainment and dissociative seizure features. Psychological stressor is no longer required for diagnosis. Communication of the diagnosis using clear language and pathophysiological explanation improves outcomes. First-line treatment involves physiotherapy for motor FND and CBT for cognitive aspects; antidepressants are reserved for comorbid mood or anxiety disorders.
key_points: FND is a rule-in diagnosis based on positive clinical signs
Psychological stressor is no longer a DSM-5-TR diagnostic requirement
Repeated investigations reinforce illness; collaborative explanation is first step
Physiotherapy and CBT are mainstay treatments
explanation.pearls: Hoover sign: passive hip extension power on the weak side is restored when the patient is asked to flex the contralateral hip against resistance, indicating selective central engagement.

subtopic_detail: Refeeding syndrome prevention in severe anorexia
stem: You are the medical registrar admitting a 19-year-old woman with anorexia nervosa restricting subtype. BMI is 13.4, she has been eating less than 500 kcal per day for 8 weeks and her phosphate on admission is 0.65 mmol/L. She has no oedema. Her ECG shows sinus bradycardia at 38 with QTc 470 ms. She is awake and oriented. The eating disorder service has requested admission for refeeding under their protocol.

data_table.Examination: Cachectic, lanugo, cool peripheries, no peripheral oedema, mild orthostatic drop
data_table.Investigations: Na 140, K 3.1, phosphate 0.65 (low), Mg 0.62 (low), Cr 64, glucose 3.4, Hb 102, WCC 3.2, LFTs ALT 78, ALP 92, INR 1.1, ECG QTc 470, HR 38

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial refeeding strategy?

options.text: Commence enteral feed at 30 kcal/kg per day with daily electrolyte monitoring; replace phosphate and magnesium intravenously
options.rationale: 30 kcal/kg/day at this BMI exceeds safe starting rate per ANZAED guidance and risks severe refeeding hypophosphataemia; starting rate should be 5 to 10 kcal/kg/day in highest-risk patients. (Source: ANZAED Refeeding Guidelines)

options.text: Defer feeding for 24 hours; correct electrolytes first then start enteral feed at 20 kcal/kg per day with weekly electrolytes
options.rationale: Delaying nutrition does not prevent refeeding syndrome; structured low-rate feeding with concurrent electrolyte replacement is the standard approach with daily electrolyte monitoring. (Source: ANZAED Refeeding Guidelines)

options.text: Commence parenteral nutrition at 25 kcal/kg per day; replace electrolytes intravenously and start propranolol for bradycardia
options.rationale: Enteral is preferred over parenteral when the gut works; beta blockade in extreme bradycardia of anorexia is dangerous and contraindicated. (Source: ANZAED Refeeding Guidelines)

options.text: Commence oral diet ad libitum with appetite-led portions; check phosphate and magnesium twice weekly during refeeding admission
options.rationale: Ad libitum feeding in severe anorexia risks rapid refeeding syndrome and is not standard; structured low-rate refeeding with daily electrolytes is required. (Source: ANZAED Refeeding Guidelines)

options.text: Commence oral feed at 5 to 10 kcal/kg per day with cardiac monitoring; replace phosphate, magnesium and potassium and give thiamine 200 mg IV daily for 3 days
options.rationale: BMI under 14 with hypophosphataemia and bradycardia is highest refeeding risk; start at 5 to 10 kcal/kg/day, replace electrolytes pre-emptively and give thiamine 100 to 300 mg IV daily for the first 3 to 5 days. (Source: ANZAED Refeeding Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Refeeding syndrome risk is highest in BMI under 14, weight loss greater than 15 percent in 3 months, minimal intake for more than 10 days and pre-existing electrolyte derangement. ANZAED guidance recommends starting at 5 to 10 kcal/kg/day in highest-risk patients with daily electrolyte monitoring and pre-emptive replacement of phosphate, magnesium and potassium. Thiamine 100 to 300 mg IV daily for 3 to 5 days precedes carbohydrate to prevent Wernicke's encephalopathy. Calorie titration upwards is guided by electrolyte stability and clinical tolerance.
key_points: BMI under 14 is highest refeeding risk - start 5 to 10 kcal/kg/day
Pre-emptive phosphate, magnesium and potassium replacement
Thiamine before glucose load
Daily electrolyte monitoring in first week of refeeding
explanation.pearls: Phosphate falls 1 to 3 days into refeeding; check daily and replace IV if below 0.6 mmol/L or symptomatic at any level.

stem: You are the community mental health registrar reviewing a 24-year-old woman with a 4-year history of intense unstable relationships, recurrent self-harm by superficial cutting, chronic feelings of emptiness, and impulsive spending. She has had 3 brief inpatient admissions for safety after threats of self-harm. She is not currently suicidal. There is no active substance use disorder, no eating disorder, and her PHQ-9 today is 7 (mild). She wants to feel more stable in herself.

data_table.Examination: Healed superficial linear scars on forearms; reactive affect; no current SI; no thought disorder; no psychotic features
data_table.Investigations: PHQ-9 7, GAD-7 9, ASRS negative, AUDIT 3; FBC, U&E, TSH normal

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate evidence-based first-line intervention?

options.text: Refer for dialectical behaviour therapy; arrange care coordination with crisis plan and skills coaching access
options.rationale: Structured psychological therapy is first-line in BPD; DBT has the strongest evidence base, with mentalisation-based therapy and schema-focused therapy as alternatives. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Personality Disorders)

options.text: Commence olanzapine 5 mg nocte and arrange psychiatry review in 4 weeks for response and side effects
options.rationale: Antipsychotics are not first-line and are reserved for short-term symptom-targeted use (transient psychotic phenomena, severe anger); psychotherapy comes first. (Source: NICE BPD Guideline)

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg daily; review at 4 weeks for response and adverse effects with structured measurement
options.rationale: Antidepressants are not first-line for BPD without comorbid major depression; symptom-targeted prescribing in BPD has limited evidence and may delay psychotherapy access. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Personality Disorders)

options.text: Arrange weekly individual supportive psychotherapy alone; review every 12 weeks with non-structured care coordination
options.rationale: Supportive therapy alone is inferior to structured therapies designed for BPD such as DBT, MBT or schema-focused therapy. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Personality Disorders)

options.text: Admit for short-term inpatient psychiatric care; commence quetiapine 50 mg nocte during stabilisation phase
options.rationale: Prolonged inpatient care is not recommended in BPD and can worsen outcomes; community-based structured therapy is the standard. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Personality Disorders)

explanation.summary: Borderline personality disorder is treated primarily with structured evidence-based psychological therapies. Dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT) has the strongest evidence base, with mentalisation-based therapy and schema-focused therapy as effective alternatives. Pharmacotherapy is symptom-targeted, short-term, and reserved for crisis or comorbidity; no medication is licensed for BPD itself. Prolonged inpatient care is avoided. Crisis plans, care coordination and skills coaching access are key adjuncts.
key_points: DBT is the most evidence-based first-line therapy
MBT and schema-focused therapy are effective alternatives
No medication is first-line for BPD itself
Avoid prolonged inpatient care
explanation.pearls: DBT consists of weekly individual therapy plus group skills training across mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation and interpersonal effectiveness, typically over 12 months.

stem: You are the GP registrar reviewing a 32-year-old man who was a passenger in a fatal car accident 6 months ago. He has flashbacks 3 times daily, sleep disturbance with nightmares 4 nights per week, avoids driving on motorways, and is hypervigilant. He drinks 2 standard drinks per week, no other substance use. He has no past psychiatric history. He is keen to engage in treatment and prefers psychological therapy over medication. PHQ-9 today is 14 (moderate).

data_table.Examination: Anxious but cooperative; intrusive thoughts of the accident on direct questioning; intact thought form; no psychosis; no SI
data_table.Investigations: PCL-5 score 52; PHQ-9 14; AUDIT 3; thyroid and CMP normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg daily titrated to 100 mg at 4 weeks; review response at 6 weeks
options.rationale: SSRIs are effective but psychological therapy is preferred first-line where available and acceptable; this patient prefers therapy and meets criteria for it. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Refer for trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy; review response after 8 to 12 sessions
options.rationale: Trauma-focused CBT (including prolonged exposure and cognitive processing therapy) and EMDR are first-line treatments for PTSD with the strongest evidence; psychological therapy is preferred over pharmacotherapy where accessible. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Commence prazosin 1 mg nocte titrated for nightmares; review and add sertraline at 4 weeks if no response
options.rationale: Prazosin can target nightmares but is adjunctive, not first-line for PTSD as a whole; trauma-focused therapy addresses the broader syndrome. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Recommend supportive counselling and watchful waiting for 3 months before commencing any active intervention
options.rationale: Active PTSD at 6 months post-trauma warrants treatment now; watchful waiting is appropriate only in the first 4 weeks post-trauma. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Commence quetiapine 50 mg nocte for sleep and anxiety; review response at 4 weeks for symptom control
options.rationale: Quetiapine is not first-line for PTSD and exposes the patient to metabolic and movement side effects without addressing trauma memory processing. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)

explanation.summary: First-line treatment for adult PTSD is trauma-focused psychological therapy, with prolonged exposure, cognitive processing therapy or EMDR carrying the strongest evidence. Where therapy is unavailable, unacceptable to the patient, or insufficient, SSRIs (sertraline, paroxetine) or venlafaxine are first-line pharmacotherapies. Watchful waiting is for the first 4 weeks post-trauma only. Prazosin and atypical antipsychotics are adjunctive options for specific symptoms.
key_points: Trauma-focused CBT and EMDR are first line
SSRIs (sertraline, paroxetine) or venlafaxine when psychotherapy unavailable
Watchful waiting only in the first 4 weeks post-trauma
Avoid benzodiazepines for PTSD
explanation.pearls: Prolonged exposure and cognitive processing therapy show effect sizes around 1.0; benefit usually emerges within 8 to 12 weekly sessions.

subtopic_detail: Adult ASD recognition in women with masking
stem: You are the GP registrar reviewing a 28-year-old woman with a 12-year history of recurrent burnout from work and social demands. She describes feeling like she is acting in social situations and reports intense sensory sensitivity to fluorescent lights and clothing tags. She has narrow restricted interests in 19th century botany. She has a history of anorexia nervosa and a previous diagnosis of social anxiety. Her cousin has autism. She has come because she suspects she might be autistic.

data_table.Examination: Eye contact intermittent; affect appropriate; no thought disorder; no psychotic features; settled mood
data_table.Investigations: AQ-50 score 38, RAADS-R score 168, no hearing or vision deficit; previous PHQ-9 8

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure that adult diagnosis of autism is uncommon in women; address presenting anxiety with CBT and lifestyle measures
options.rationale: Adult diagnosis of autism in women is increasingly recognised due to masking and previous misdiagnosis; this presentation warrants formal assessment. (Source: RANZCP: Autism Spectrum Disorder in Adults)
source_refs: RANZCP: Autism Spectrum Disorder in Adults

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg daily for social anxiety; review in 4 weeks for response and tolerability
options.rationale: Antidepressants address comorbid anxiety but do not constitute assessment for autism, which would change formulation and support needs. (Source: RANZCP: ASD in Adults)
source_refs: RANZCP: Autism Spectrum Disorder in Adults

options.text: Refer for formal multidisciplinary autism assessment using ADOS-2 and developmental history with collateral
options.rationale: Suggestive screening scores plus presenting features warrant formal multidisciplinary assessment using gold-standard tools (ADOS-2, ADI-R or developmental history with collateral); adult women often receive late diagnoses due to masking. (Source: National Guideline for ASD Assessment Australia)
source_refs: National Guideline for ASD Assessment Australia

options.text: Refer for borderline personality disorder assessment with DBT consideration; defer autism workup pending personality diagnosis
options.rationale: Sensory sensitivity, masking and restricted interests are not core BPD features; misattribution to BPD is a common pitfall in autistic women. (Source: RANZCP: ASD in Adults)
source_refs: RANZCP: Autism Spectrum Disorder in Adults

options.text: Recommend reading on social skills training and self-directed online ASD modules; review at 6 months
options.rationale: Self-directed reading does not substitute for assessment; missing the diagnosis prolongs distress and burnout and delays NDIS access. (Source: RANZCP: ASD in Adults)
source_refs: RANZCP: Autism Spectrum Disorder in Adults

explanation.summary: Autism in adult women is frequently missed because of camouflaging or masking behaviour, internalising symptoms, restricted interests in socially typical topics, and overlapping diagnoses such as anxiety, eating disorders and BPD. Formal assessment uses the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS-2), Autism Diagnostic Interview-Revised (ADI-R) and developmental history with collateral informants. Diagnosis enables NDIS access, autism-specific supports and reframing of previous diagnoses.
key_points: Adult women with ASD often masked or misdiagnosed
Sensory sensitivity, narrow interests, and burnout cues to assessment
Gold-standard assessment uses ADOS-2 plus developmental history
Diagnosis enables NDIS support and reframing
explanation.pearls: RAADS-R cutoff above 65 and AQ-50 above 32 in adults are suggestive but not diagnostic; formal multidisciplinary assessment is needed.

sources.label: RANZCP: Autism Spectrum Disorder in Adults
National Guideline for ASD Assessment Australia

stem: You are the inpatient psychiatry registrar reviewing a 27-year-old man on admission. Over the past 8 weeks he has been hearing third-person voices commenting on his actions and believing the government is monitoring him through his phone. For the last 3 weeks of that period he has been elated, sleeping 2 hours per night, hyperactive and grandiose, spending $20,000 on cryptocurrency. He has a prior depressive episode 18 months ago. He denies substance use, urine drug screen negative.

data_table.Examination: Pressured speech, flight of ideas, grandiose delusions, third-person auditory hallucinations; thought broadcasting; no insight
data_table.Investigations: FBC, U&E, LFTs, TSH normal; urine drug screen negative; CT head normal

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis and the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.text: Bipolar I disorder with mood-congruent psychosis; start olanzapine 10 mg nocte and lithium 750 mg nocte with monitoring
options.rationale: Psychosis predates the mood episode by 5 weeks, which does not fit mood-congruent psychotic bipolar; schizoaffective should be considered. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia)

options.text: Schizophreniform disorder; commence risperidone 2 mg twice daily and refer to early psychosis intervention service
options.rationale: Schizophreniform does not account for clearly demarcated mood episode; the presence of a 3-week manic episode within the psychotic illness shifts the formulation. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia)

options.text: Substance-induced psychosis; observe over 7 days off all substances and reassess for diagnostic clarification
options.rationale: Urine drug screen is negative and the presentation extends over 8 weeks beyond plausible intoxication or withdrawal; substance-induced disorder is unlikely. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia)

options.text: Schizoaffective disorder bipolar type; commence olanzapine 10 mg nocte plus mood stabiliser (lithium) with ongoing monitoring
options.rationale: Psychotic symptoms persisting at least 2 weeks without mood symptoms within an illness that includes a 3-week manic episode meets schizoaffective bipolar criteria; antipsychotic plus mood stabiliser is first line. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia)

options.text: Brief psychotic disorder; commence aripiprazole 10 mg daily; review for resolution over 1 month before further treatment
options.rationale: Brief psychotic disorder is limited to less than 1 month; 8 weeks of symptoms and a co-occurring mood episode rule it out. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia)

explanation.summary: Schizoaffective disorder is diagnosed when psychotic symptoms persist for at least 2 weeks in the absence of prominent mood symptoms, within an illness that also includes a major mood episode (manic for bipolar type, depressive for depressive type) over a substantial portion of the total illness duration. Bipolar I with psychotic features requires psychotic symptoms occurring only during mood episodes. Differentiating the two has prognostic and treatment implications: schizoaffective typically requires both antipsychotic and mood stabiliser long term.
key_points: Schizoaffective: psychosis 2+ weeks without mood symptoms in same illness
Bipolar with psychosis: psychosis only during mood episode
Schizoaffective treatment: antipsychotic plus mood stabiliser
Long-term prognosis intermediate between schizophrenia and bipolar
explanation.pearls: Olanzapine plus lithium is a common Australian first-line combination for schizoaffective bipolar type; clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistance.

stem: You are the consultation-liaison psychiatry registrar reviewing a 34-year-old woman admitted with left-sided weakness for 3 days. The neurologist has ruled out stroke (MRI, CTA and CSF normal) and a video EEG of an episode shows preserved consciousness with normal background. She demonstrates Hoover sign with weakness ablating on contralateral hip extension. She works as a teacher and is not facing legal proceedings or insurance claims. She is distressed by her symptoms and wants to return to work.

data_table.Examination: Left hemiparesis 3/5 globally; positive Hoover sign; normal reflexes and tone; intact sensation to pinprick; tremor entrainment positive
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain and CTA normal; CSF normal; video EEG normal background during episode; FBC, U&E, TFT normal

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis and the most appropriate management?

options.text: Malingering; document discrepancy, withdraw analgesia and refer to occupational health for fitness for duty
options.rationale: Malingering requires external incentive (e.g. compensation, legal advantage); none is identified, and the patient is distressed and wishes to return to work, against malingering. (Source: DSM-5-TR; AAN FND Guidance)

options.text: Factitious disorder; transfer to psychiatry under involuntary section for ongoing observation and confrontation with team
options.rationale: Factitious disorder involves intentional symptom production for the sick role; positive rule-in signs of FND such as Hoover sign suggest a positive diagnosis of FND, not factitious. (Source: AAN FND Guidance)

options.text: Somatic symptom disorder; commence sertraline 50 mg daily and refer for CBT for somatic symptoms over 12 weeks
options.rationale: SSD requires excessive thoughts, feelings or behaviours related to somatic symptoms; the central feature here is positive rule-in motor signs, consistent with FND rather than SSD. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Stroke mimic with conversion overlay; arrange thrombectomy review and add aspirin 100 mg daily for secondary prevention
options.rationale: Stroke has been excluded by MRI and CTA; secondary prevention is not warranted and labelling stroke risks unnecessary medication. (Source: NHMRC Stroke Guidelines)

options.text: Functional neurological disorder; explain diagnosis using positive signs and refer to physiotherapy with FND-specific approach
options.rationale: FND is diagnosed positively from rule-in signs such as Hoover sign and tremor entrainment, not by exclusion; explaining the diagnosis using the positive signs plus referral to FND-experienced physiotherapy is first-line. (Source: AAN FND Guidance)

explanation.summary: Functional neurological disorder is diagnosed positively using rule-in neurological signs (Hoover sign for limb weakness, tremor entrainment, dissociative seizure features on video EEG with preserved consciousness) rather than by exclusion. Patient explanation using the positive signs themselves and referral to FND-experienced physiotherapy and psychological therapy form the core management. Malingering and factitious disorder require evidence of intentional symptom production with or without external incentives, which is uncommon and not implied by clinical examination findings.
key_points: FND is a positive rule-in diagnosis using neurological signs
Patient explanation grounded in the positive signs is key to engagement
FND-specific physiotherapy and psychological therapy are first line
Malingering needs evidence of external incentive
explanation.pearls: FND has a similar prevalence to multiple sclerosis in neurology clinics; early diagnosis and FND-specific physio improve recovery, especially within the first 6 months.

stem: You are the medical registrar admitting a 19-year-old woman with severe anorexia nervosa (BMI 13.4, weight 36 kg, recent 5 kg loss over 4 weeks) to a general medical ward. She has been eating less than 500 kcal per day for 2 months and reports occasional dizzy spells. She is alert, hydrated and apyrexial. Bloods on arrival show low normal electrolytes and the dietitian has commenced a structured refeeding plan starting at 20 kcal/kg/day.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.2, HR 48 sinus, BP 88/52, RR 14, SpO2 99% RA
data_table.Examination: Cachectic; lanugo hair; dry skin; reduced subcutaneous fat; alert, no focal deficits
data_table.Investigations: Na 137, K 3.4, urea 4.2, Cr 76, phosphate 0.74, magnesium 0.68, glucose 4.0, ALT 22, ECG QTc 470 ms

lead_in: Which prophylactic regimen is most appropriate before commencing the refeeding plan?

options.text: Oral thiamine 300 mg daily, oral phosphate 500 mg three times daily, and daily phosphate, magnesium and potassium monitoring for 7 days
options.rationale: Severe malnutrition with BMI under 14 and 2 months of low intake meets very high refeeding-risk criteria; prophylactic thiamine, phosphate replacement and daily electrolyte monitoring for 7 to 10 days are standard. (Source: ANZAED/RANZCP Eating Disorders Guidelines)

options.text: Intravenous insulin 0.05 unit/kg/hour to maintain glucose between 4 and 6 mmol/L during refeeding; routine vitamin replacement
options.rationale: Insulin is not used in refeeding; insulin surge from carbohydrate reintroduction is the underlying mechanism of refeeding syndrome and pharmacological insulin worsens this. (Source: ANZAED/RANZCP Eating Disorders Guidelines)

options.text: Rapid escalation to 40 kcal/kg/day from day 2 with weekly biochemistry monitoring; restrict thiamine to symptomatic patients
options.rationale: Rapid escalation in severe malnutrition causes refeeding syndrome (severe hypophosphataemia, cardiac arrhythmia, Wernicke); slow escalation with daily monitoring is standard. (Source: ANZAED/RANZCP Eating Disorders Guidelines)

options.text: Withhold nutrition for 48 hours; correct electrolytes intravenously first before any oral intake; defer thiamine
options.rationale: Withholding nutrition prolongs starvation; refeeding is started cautiously with electrolyte replacement and thiamine before the first calories. (Source: ANZAED/RANZCP Eating Disorders Guidelines)

options.text: Parenteral nutrition only for 5 days; resume enteral feeding at 30 kcal/kg/day once electrolytes have normalised
options.rationale: Parenteral nutrition increases line infection and metabolic complication risk; enteral feeding is preferred when the gut is functional, even in severe malnutrition. (Source: ANZAED/RANZCP Eating Disorders Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Refeeding syndrome is precipitated by carbohydrate reintroduction in severe malnutrition; insulin surge drives intracellular shift of phosphate, potassium and magnesium causing severe hypophosphataemia, cardiac arrhythmia, cardiac failure and Wernicke encephalopathy. Australian guidance for high-risk eating disorder admissions starts at 20 kcal/kg/day, escalates over 7 to 10 days, prescribes prophylactic thiamine 300 mg daily, phosphate replacement, and daily monitoring of phosphate, magnesium, potassium and ECG. ECG monitoring is essential as QTc prolongation and arrhythmia are leading causes of death.
key_points: Start refeeding at 20 kcal/kg/day in high-risk patients
Prophylactic thiamine 300 mg daily and phosphate replacement
Daily electrolytes and ECG for 7 to 10 days
Avoid parenteral nutrition when gut functional
explanation.pearls: Phosphate below 0.6 mmol/L during refeeding warrants IV phosphate replacement (e.g. 30 mmol over 12 hours) and slowing calorie escalation.

stem: You are the emergency medicine registrar managing a 26-year-old woman 90 minutes after deliberate ingestion of 60 amitriptyline 50 mg tablets (3 g total). She is drowsy with GCS 9 (E2V3M4). The team has secured the airway with a nasopharyngeal adjunct and applied oxygen. Vitals and bloods are back. A first 12-lead ECG shows broad complexes with QRS 140 ms and a tall terminal R wave in aVR.

data_table.Vital signs: GCS 9, BP 88/52, HR 128 sinus, RR 22, SpO2 96% on 6 L mask, T 36.4
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, mydriasis 6 mm reactive, dry skin, urinary retention; absent bowel sounds; lateral chest clear
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.30, lactate 3.0, K 3.6; ECG QRS 140 ms, terminal R in aVR 4 mm, QTc 510 ms; paracetamol negative

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Intravenous lipid emulsion 20 percent 1.5 mL/kg bolus over 1 minute; defer sodium bicarbonate until ECG worsens
options.rationale: Lipid emulsion is reserved for cardiovascular collapse refractory to standard measures including sodium bicarbonate; first-line for TCA-induced QRS widening is bicarbonate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus and prepare for intubation; recheck ECG and pH 5 minutes after bolus
options.rationale: QRS above 100 ms or terminal R in aVR above 3 mm in TCA overdose indicates sodium-channel blockade with high risk of seizures and arrhythmia; IV sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg with airway protection is first line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg every minute to a maximum of 1 mg; arrange psychiatric review for risk assessment
options.rationale: Flumazenil is contraindicated in TCA overdose because it can precipitate seizures; benzodiazepines are not the toxin here. (Source: AMH: Flumazenil)

options.text: Synchronised DC cardioversion at 100 J for the broad-complex tachycardia; followed by lidocaine infusion 1 mg/kg loading
options.rationale: Sinus tachycardia with QRS widening from sodium channel blockade does not require cardioversion; class Ic and Ia antiarrhythmics worsen sodium channel blockade. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Activated charcoal 50 g via nasogastric tube; defer airway intervention and observe for 4 hours before further escalation
options.rationale: Charcoal in a patient with GCS 9 without secured airway risks aspiration; airway protection precedes decontamination, and bicarbonate is the priority. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

explanation.summary: TCA overdose causes sodium-channel blockade with QRS widening, terminal R wave in aVR, hypotension and seizure risk. QRS above 100 ms or terminal R in aVR above 3 mm predicts arrhythmia and seizures. First-line treatment is IV sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg, repeated to maintain QRS below 100 ms and arterial pH 7.45 to 7.55, alongside airway protection and benzodiazepines for seizures. Lipid emulsion is reserved for refractory cardiovascular collapse. Hypertonic saline is an alternative source of sodium load when bicarbonate excess limits use.
key_points: Terminal R in aVR above 3 mm or QRS above 100 ms = sodium channel toxicity
Bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg IV first line
Avoid class Ia and Ic antiarrhythmics and flumazenil
Lipid emulsion for refractory collapse
explanation.pearls: Aim arterial pH between 7.45 and 7.55 with serial bicarbonate boluses; sodium load and alkalinisation both reduce sodium channel blockade.

stem: You are the psychiatry registrar admitting a 28-year-old man with schizophrenia who has failed adequate trials of risperidone and olanzapine at therapeutic doses over the last 18 months. He has ongoing positive symptoms and severe functional impairment. He has been counselled regarding clozapine therapy and has consented. He has no cardiac history, no fever, no neutropenia, and pre-clozapine baseline bloods including FBC, ECG, lipids and HbA1c are normal. He is registered on the clozapine patient monitoring system.

data_table.Examination: Settled, no extrapyramidal features; no abnormal cardiac findings
data_table.Investigations: FBC: WCC 6.8, neutrophils 4.2; ECG: normal sinus, QTc 410 ms; troponin pending baseline; HbA1c 5.2; lipids normal
data_table.Medications: Olanzapine 20 mg daily (to taper); lorazepam 1 mg PRN

lead_in: What is the most appropriate clozapine initiation regimen?

options.text: Start at 200 mg twice daily and continue full dose without titration; monitor only WCC and neutrophils for safety
options.rationale: Starting at therapeutic dose causes severe orthostasis, sedation, seizures and arrhythmia; gradual titration is mandatory. (Source: AMH: Clozapine)

options.text: Defer clozapine and switch to aripiprazole 30 mg as a fourth antipsychotic trial; reserve clozapine for failure of aripiprazole
options.rationale: Treatment-resistant schizophrenia is defined as failure of 2 adequate antipsychotic trials; further antipsychotic delay clozapine, which is the only agent with proven superior efficacy in this group. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia Guidelines)

options.text: Start at 100 mg twice daily and continue without dose titration unless side effects occur; monthly FBC monitoring is sufficient
options.rationale: Starting at 100 mg twice daily exceeds safe initiation rates and risks orthostasis, sedation and seizure; monthly FBC misses the high-risk neutropenia window in weeks 6 to 18. (Source: AMH: Clozapine)

options.text: Start at 25 mg twice daily with monthly FBC monitoring throughout the first 18 weeks regardless of dose changes
options.rationale: Starting dose is too rapid and monthly FBC misses the high-risk neutropenia period; weekly FBC for 18 weeks is the Australian standard. (Source: AMH: Clozapine)

options.text: Start at 12.5 mg in the evening on day 1; titrate by 25 to 50 mg per day to a target of 300 to 450 mg by 3 to 4 weeks with weekly FBC
options.rationale: Australian clozapine titration begins at 12.5 mg with gradual upward titration to therapeutic dose over 2 to 4 weeks; weekly FBC monitoring is mandatory for 18 weeks then monthly, with troponin and CRP weekly for first 4 weeks for myocarditis surveillance. (Source: AMH: Clozapine)

explanation.summary: Clozapine is the only antipsychotic with proven superiority in treatment-resistant schizophrenia. Initiation requires gradual titration starting at 12.5 mg evening day 1, then 25 mg day 2, increasing by 25 to 50 mg per day to a target of 300 to 450 mg by 3 to 4 weeks. Weekly FBC monitoring for the first 18 weeks then monthly captures clozapine-induced neutropenia (peak risk weeks 6 to 18). Weekly troponin and CRP for the first 4 weeks screens for myocarditis. Patients must be on a clozapine patient monitoring system. Seizure threshold lowered: avoid drugs and triggers.
key_points: Initiation: 12.5 mg day 1, titrate by 25 to 50 mg per day
Weekly FBC for 18 weeks, monthly thereafter
Weekly troponin and CRP first 4 weeks for myocarditis
Target 300 to 450 mg per day by 3 to 4 weeks
explanation.pearls: Smoking cessation can double clozapine plasma levels via CYP1A2 induction loss; warn patients and adjust dose monitoring if smoking status changes.

stem: You are the GP reviewing a 42-year-old man with schizophrenia who has been stable on olanzapine 15 mg nocte for 18 months. His last metabolic review was 9 months ago. He has gained 8 kg over the past year and reports increased thirst and polyuria. His mother has type 2 diabetes. He smokes 10 cigarettes daily and walks for 20 minutes most days. He drinks 2 standard drinks twice weekly. His latest set of bloods is back.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 142/88, HR 84, RR 16, SpO2 99% RA, T 36.6; BMI 33 (up from 29)
data_table.Examination: Central adiposity; no acanthosis nigricans; no thyroid mass
data_table.Investigations: HbA1c 7.4 percent, fasting glucose 8.6 mmol/L; total cholesterol 5.8, LDL 3.6, HDL 0.9, triglycerides 3.2; ALT 48; eGFR 92; TSH 1.8

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Continue current antipsychotic and lifestyle changes alone; defer diabetes pharmacotherapy until HbA1c above 8 percent at next review
options.rationale: HbA1c 7.4 with symptomatic hyperglycaemia warrants pharmacotherapy initiation per Australian diabetes guidance; deferral risks complications. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Stop olanzapine abruptly and substitute haloperidol 5 mg daily as a lower-metabolic-risk first-generation antipsychotic option
options.rationale: Abrupt switch risks relapse and discontinuation syndrome; first-generation antipsychotics carry higher extrapyramidal burden and are not the standard substitute. (Source: RANZCP Metabolic Monitoring)

options.text: Continue olanzapine unchanged and add metformin 500 mg twice daily for newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes; lifestyle measures and statin discussion
options.rationale: Olanzapine has the highest metabolic risk among antipsychotics; switching is one option but in a patient stable for 18 months on a single agent, initiating metformin while continuing the antipsychotic is reasonable per Australian psychiatric metabolic guidance, with antipsychotic switch as a parallel consideration. (Source: RANZCP Metabolic Monitoring)

options.text: Switch olanzapine to clozapine to address treatment resistance and metabolic syndrome together as a single intervention
options.rationale: Clozapine has higher metabolic risk than olanzapine and is reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia; switching solely for metabolic reasons worsens not improves the metabolic phenotype. (Source: AMH: Clozapine)

options.text: Cease olanzapine and offer cognitive behavioural therapy for schizophrenia as monotherapy until metabolic parameters normalise
options.rationale: Stopping antipsychotic in stable schizophrenia carries a 70 percent 1-year relapse rate; CBT is adjunctive not substitutive. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Antipsychotic-induced metabolic syndrome is most pronounced with olanzapine and clozapine. RANZCP monitoring schedule: weight, waist, BP, fasting lipids and glucose, HbA1c at baseline, 3 months, 6 months and annually. New onset metabolic disease (type 2 diabetes, dyslipidaemia, hypertension) is managed in parallel with antipsychotic optimisation: lifestyle (diet, exercise, smoking cessation), metformin first-line for diabetes (also has modest antipsychotic-associated weight benefit), statin per absolute CV risk, antihypertensive per BP. Switch to a lower-risk antipsychotic (aripiprazole, lurasidone) is considered if disease is severe and switch is acceptable to the patient.
key_points: Olanzapine and clozapine highest metabolic risk
RANZCP monitoring: baseline, 3 months, 6 months, annual
Metformin first-line for new T2DM; statin per CV risk
Switch to aripiprazole or lurasidone if severe and acceptable
explanation.pearls: Metformin 500 to 2000 mg daily reduces antipsychotic-induced weight gain by 3 to 5 kg over 12 weeks even without diabetes; consider in patients with greater than 7 percent weight gain on antipsychotic.

stem: You are the consult psychiatry registrar called to ED for a 64-year-old woman brought in by her family because of 5 days of progressive immobility, mutism and refusal of food and fluid. She has a history of bipolar I disorder controlled on lithium and valproate. She was discharged 2 weeks ago after a depressive episode. On examination she stares fixedly, holds postures imposed by the examiner, and does not respond verbally. There is no fever, no rigidity, no rash and no recent medication change. Her observations are otherwise normal.

data_table.Examination: Mutism; immobility; posturing (maintains examiner-placed arm position 90 seconds); waxy flexibility; staring; no rigidity, no clonus
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 280, FBC normal, electrolytes normal, lithium 0.7, valproate 480, BSL 5.8, urine bHCG negative; ECG normal sinus
data_table.Medications: Lithium 750 mg nocte; sodium valproate 1000 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence intramuscular haloperidol 5 mg as a first-line antipsychotic to treat presumed psychotic stupor and observe for response
options.rationale: Antipsychotics may worsen catatonia and increase risk of neuroleptic malignant syndrome; lorazepam is the established first-line challenge. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Administer IV lorazepam 2 mg as a diagnostic and therapeutic challenge; observe response over 30 to 60 minutes for partial reversal
options.rationale: Lorazepam 1 to 2 mg IV is the standard catatonia challenge: 70 to 80 percent of catatonia responds at least partially within 10 to 60 minutes, supporting both diagnosis and treatment plan. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Discontinue lithium and valproate and observe over 48 hours for clinical improvement before any further pharmacological intervention
options.rationale: Untreated catatonia carries risk of dehydration, venous thromboembolism, pressure injury and aspiration pneumonia; immediate intervention rather than withdrawal observation is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Arrange urgent electroconvulsive therapy as first-line therapy without a prior lorazepam trial or other diagnostic intervention attempt
options.rationale: ECT is highly effective in catatonia but is generally reserved for lorazepam-refractory or life-threatening cases (malignant catatonia, NMS-like presentation); lorazepam trial is first. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence subcutaneous heparin and intravenous fluids only; defer catatonia-specific intervention until psychiatric consultant review tomorrow
options.rationale: Supportive measures (DVT prophylaxis, hydration) are important adjuncts but are not the primary intervention; lorazepam challenge should not be deferred. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a syndrome of psychomotor disturbance with mutism, immobility, posturing, waxy flexibility, negativism, echolalia and stupor. DSM-5 requires 3 or more of 12 features. Causes include mood disorders (most common in Australia), psychosis, autoimmune encephalitis, metabolic and toxic. Lorazepam 1 to 2 mg IV is both diagnostic challenge (response in 70 to 80 percent within 30 to 60 minutes) and therapeutic; titrate to effect, often 8 to 24 mg daily. ECT is highly effective and indicated for lorazepam non-response or malignant catatonia (autonomic instability, rigidity, hyperthermia).
key_points: Lorazepam 1 to 2 mg IV is diagnostic and therapeutic
70 to 80 percent partial response within 60 minutes
Avoid antipsychotics (worsen or precipitate NMS)
ECT for refractory or malignant catatonia
explanation.pearls: Malignant catatonia includes fever, autonomic instability and rigidity overlapping clinically with NMS; both are treated with urgent ECT plus benzodiazepines and stopping the offending drug.

subtopic_detail: Smoking cessation pharmacotherapy in psychiatric patient
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 38-year-old man with paranoid schizophrenia stable on aripiprazole 15 mg daily for 3 years. He smokes 25 cigarettes daily, smokes within 15 minutes of waking, and has tried cold turkey 4 times unsuccessfully. He is motivated to quit and asks for the best option. He has no history of depression, no recent suicidality, no cardiovascular disease, no seizure history. His current mental state is stable. He has tried 8 weeks of nicotine patches alone last year with relapse at week 4.

data_table.Examination: Stable mental state, no thought disorder; nicotine staining on fingers
data_table.Investigations: FBC, LFT, UEC normal; ECG normal sinus rhythm; PHQ-9 score 4

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Repeat nicotine patch monotherapy at higher dose (21 mg per 24 hours) for 12 weeks without combination or alternative therapy
options.rationale: Patch monotherapy was tried last year and failed at week 4; escalation to varenicline or combination NRT is more effective. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines)

options.text: Avoid varenicline due to historical black box warnings and use bupropion 150 mg twice daily as the safer first-line agent in schizophrenia
options.rationale: The black box warning was removed in 2016 after the EAGLES trial showed no excess neuropsychiatric harm; bupropion lowers seizure threshold and is less effective than varenicline. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines)

options.text: Commence varenicline 0.5 mg daily titrated up to 1 mg twice daily over 7 days; set quit date for 8 days; review at 4 weeks for mood and tolerance
options.rationale: Varenicline is the most effective single-agent smoking cessation pharmacotherapy and is safe in stable psychiatric disease per the EAGLES trial; standard titration over 7 days reaches 1 mg twice daily. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines)

options.text: Refer to behavioural counselling only without pharmacotherapy given his stable psychiatric illness and previous medication trials
options.rationale: Behavioural support alone has lower quit rates than combined behavioural plus pharmacotherapy; both are recommended together. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines)

options.text: Prescribe nortriptyline 75 mg nocte for cessation as a tricyclic with proven cessation efficacy and antidepressant effect
options.rationale: Nortriptyline is second-line for smoking cessation with cardiac and anticholinergic risks; varenicline is first-line in motivated patients without contraindication. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Smoking cessation in psychiatric patients is safe and improves both physical and mental health. First-line pharmacotherapies are varenicline, combination NRT (patch plus short-acting), or bupropion. Varenicline is the single most effective agent. The EAGLES trial established safety in stable schizophrenia, depression and other psychiatric conditions, leading to removal of the FDA black box warning in 2016. Standard varenicline titration: 0.5 mg daily for 3 days, 0.5 mg twice daily for 4 days, then 1 mg twice daily, set quit date at day 8, continue for 12 weeks. Bupropion is avoided in seizure disorder, eating disorders and abrupt alcohol or sedative withdrawal.
key_points: Varenicline most effective single agent for cessation
EAGLES trial: safe in stable psychiatric disease
Bupropion lowers seizure threshold
Combine pharmacotherapy with behavioural support
explanation.pearls: Smoking induces CYP1A2 metabolism; quit reduces clozapine and olanzapine clearance and may require 30 to 50 percent dose reduction over 1 to 4 weeks.

stem: You are the GP reviewing a 34-year-old former paramedic with 8 months of intrusive memories of a multi-fatality road traffic crash, nightmares 3 to 4 nights per week, avoidance of driving on highways, hyperarousal, sleep onset insomnia and irritability. He drinks 6 standard drinks 3 nights per week to sleep. He scores 56 on the PCL-5. He has no current suicidal ideation and has not commenced any treatment. There is no active psychosis. He is willing to engage in therapy or medication.

data_table.Examination: Hypervigilant; mildly tremulous; PHQ-9 score 14
data_table.Investigations: PCL-5 score 56; LFTs mildly raised (GGT 92); FBC and UEC normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line management?

options.text: Recommend cannabidiol oil under specialist prescribing for sleep and intrusive symptoms; defer formal trauma-focused therapy referral
options.rationale: Cannabidiol is not established first-line for PTSD; trauma-focused CBT or EMDR with concurrent alcohol use management is first-line. (Source: Phoenix Australian Guidelines for PTSD)

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg daily titrated to 200 mg over 8 weeks as first-line monotherapy; defer psychological therapy until response
options.rationale: SSRIs are recommended but psychological therapy is the preferred first-line; pharmacotherapy is offered when therapy is unavailable or insufficient, not as a substitute. (Source: Phoenix Australian Guidelines for PTSD)

options.text: Prescribe oral benzodiazepine (diazepam 5 mg three times daily) for hyperarousal and insomnia; consider therapy at 3-month review
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are not recommended for PTSD; they impair fear extinction learning, are addictive and risk worsening avoidance. (Source: Phoenix Australian Guidelines for PTSD)

options.text: Commence quetiapine 25 mg nocte for sleep and arousal; review at 4 weeks to consider trauma-focused therapy referral and engagement
options.rationale: Atypical antipsychotics are not first-line and risk metabolic harm; trauma-focused psychological therapy is the cornerstone of PTSD treatment. (Source: Phoenix Australian Guidelines for PTSD)

options.text: Refer for trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy or EMDR; address harmful alcohol use in parallel with support
options.rationale: Australian PTSD guidance places trauma-focused CBT (or EMDR) as first-line, with concurrent management of comorbid alcohol use as adjunct; SSRI is added if therapy alone is insufficient or unavailable. (Source: Phoenix Australian Guidelines for PTSD)

explanation.summary: Australian PTSD guidance recommends trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy or eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing as first-line treatment, with 8 to 12 sessions. Pharmacotherapy (SSRI: sertraline, paroxetine or venlafaxine) is reserved for patients declining or unable to access therapy, or as adjunct when therapy is insufficient. Benzodiazepines are contraindicated. Antipsychotics are not first-line. Comorbid substance use (especially alcohol) requires concurrent management; complete sobriety is not required to commence therapy. Co-occurring depression, dissociation and chronic pain are common and addressed simultaneously.
key_points: Trauma-focused CBT or EMDR is first-line
SSRI as adjunct or when therapy unavailable
Benzodiazepines contraindicated (impair extinction)
Concurrent management of comorbid alcohol use
explanation.pearls: Prazosin 1 to 10 mg nocte has evidence for reducing trauma nightmares and is included as second-line adjunct in Australian guidance for nightmare-predominant PTSD.

stem: You are the medical registrar admitting a 19-year-old woman with severe anorexia nervosa for medical stabilisation. She has lost 18 kg over 8 months. BMI is 13.4. She has minimal oral intake for 3 weeks. The eating disorders team plans to commence nutritional rehabilitation. Her admission bloods are back. Her ECG shows sinus bradycardia with QTc 478 ms. She has no purging behaviour. She is on no medications. She accepts admission and refeeding under supervision.

data_table.Examination: Cachectic; lanugo; cold peripheries; capillary refill 3 s; muscle wasting; alert oriented; no proximal myopathy yet
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 3.0, phosphate 0.62, magnesium 0.65, sodium 134, glucose 3.6, albumin 32, LFT mildly raised, FBC: Hb 102 microcytic; ECG sinus bradycardia, QTc 478, no U waves

lead_in: What is the most appropriate refeeding plan?

options.text: Commence enteral feeds at 1500 to 2000 kcal/day from day 1 to rapidly correct undernutrition; defer electrolyte correction until refeeding established
options.rationale: High-calorie initiation in severely underweight patients precipitates refeeding syndrome; start at 5 to 10 kcal/kg/day and correct electrolytes first. (Source: ANZAED/RANZCP Eating Disorders Guidelines)

options.text: Refuse admission for refeeding because BMI 13 is unsafe outside intensive care; arrange community day-program review next week
options.rationale: BMI under 14 with bradycardia and hypotension requires inpatient medical stabilisation; community care is unsafe at this severity. (Source: ANZAED/RANZCP Eating Disorders Guidelines)

options.text: Withhold feeds entirely for the first 48 hours and rehydrate with 4 L per day of dextrose 5 percent in saline to correct dehydration first
options.rationale: Carbohydrate-rich rehydration without thiamine and electrolyte correction precipitates Wernicke encephalopathy and severe refeeding syndrome; controlled feeding with thiamine is preferred. (Source: ANZAED/RANZCP Eating Disorders Guidelines)

options.text: Replace phosphate, potassium, magnesium and start thiamine; commence feeds at 10 kcal/kg/day on day 1 with daily electrolyte monitoring and slow titration
options.rationale: Severe anorexia with electrolyte derangement and bradycardia mandates pre-emptive electrolyte correction, thiamine before any carbohydrate, and cautious caloric ramp from 5 to 10 kcal/kg/day with daily electrolyte monitoring. (Source: ANZAED/RANZCP Eating Disorders Guidelines)

options.text: Commence total parenteral nutrition at full caloric requirement immediately and defer oral or enteral nutrition for 7 days
options.rationale: Parenteral nutrition is reserved for failure of enteral access and carries higher refeeding risk if initiated at full caloric load; enteral or oral feeding with cautious ramp is preferred. (Source: ANZAED/RANZCP Eating Disorders Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Refeeding syndrome arises when carbohydrate-rich nutrition triggers intracellular shift of phosphate, potassium and magnesium in a chronically starved patient, causing arrhythmia, heart failure, seizure, rhabdomyolysis and death. High-risk features include BMI under 16, weight loss over 15 percent, minimal intake for 10 days, or pre-existing electrolyte abnormality. Management: thiamine 100 to 300 mg daily IV or oral starting before any feeds; correct hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypophosphataemia and hypocalcaemia before and during refeeding; commence feeds at 5 to 10 kcal/kg/day with daily electrolyte monitoring; ramp up over 7 to 10 days. Inpatient medical admission for BMI under 14, bradycardia under 40, hypotension, hypothermia, hypoglycaemia or syncope.
key_points: Thiamine 100 to 300 mg before any feed
Correct phosphate, potassium, magnesium pre-emptively
Start feeds 5 to 10 kcal/kg/day, ramp over 7 to 10 days
BMI under 14 + bradycardia requires inpatient admission
explanation.pearls: Hypophosphataemia below 0.5 mmol/L during refeeding triples mortality risk; replace IV phosphate (e.g. potassium phosphate 20 mmol over 6 hours) before increasing calories further.

stem: You are the GP shared-care registrar reviewing a 26-year-old man with first-episode schizophrenia who started olanzapine 10 mg nocte at discharge from inpatient care 12 weeks ago. His mental state has stabilised and he attends the appointment with his community mental health nurse. He reports increased appetite, has gained 5 kg since discharge and notices a thicker waist. He has no chest pain, no family history of premature cardiovascular disease and is a never smoker. He drinks two standard drinks per week.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/78, HR 78, weight 84 kg (was 79 at discharge), waist 102 cm, BMI 27
data_table.Examination: Mental state stable; no extrapyramidal signs; no acanthosis nigricans; cardiovascular examination unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: No bloods since discharge; ECG at discharge QTc 412 ms; HbA1c at discharge 5.4 percent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate investigation panel today?

options.text: Fasting glucose only with deferral of lipid profile until the 12-month annual review according to the standard antipsychotic monitoring schedule recommended for ongoing therapy
options.rationale: Fasting lipids are part of the 12-week panel not deferred to annual review; metabolic effects emerge within weeks and require early detection for intervention. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Antipsychotic monitoring)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Antipsychotic monitoring

options.text: Serum olanzapine concentration as the priority biochemistry test today to assess therapeutic blood drug level guidance for any further olanzapine dose adjustment
options.rationale: Olanzapine therapeutic drug monitoring is reserved for non-response, toxicity or adherence concerns; routine monitoring is metabolic biochemistry rather than serum drug levels. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Antipsychotic monitoring)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Antipsychotic monitoring

options.text: Echocardiogram and 24-hour ambulatory ECG monitoring as the first-line cardiac screening for any patient stable on antipsychotic therapy at the 12-week review milestone
options.rationale: Routine ambulatory cardiac monitoring is not indicated; baseline and 12-week ECG are sufficient unless QTc prolongation, syncope or family sudden death history exists. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Antipsychotic monitoring)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Antipsychotic monitoring

options.text: Fasting lipid profile, fasting glucose or HbA1c, urea and electrolytes, liver function tests and prolactin to complete the 12-week metabolic monitoring panel today
options.rationale: Antipsychotic 12-week metabolic monitoring includes fasting lipids, glucose, weight, blood pressure, waist, prolactin and ECG QTc; this is the time point for the first post-initiation set of bloods. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Antipsychotic monitoring)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Antipsychotic monitoring

options.text: Sleep-deprived electroencephalogram and brain magnetic resonance imaging as the standard structural and electrophysiological review at three months of antipsychotic therapy
options.rationale: Routine EEG and MRI are not part of antipsychotic monitoring; they are reserved for atypical presentations, new neurological signs or specific clinical suspicion. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Antipsychotic monitoring)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Antipsychotic monitoring

explanation.summary: Antipsychotic metabolic monitoring follows a structured schedule: baseline (weight, waist, BP, FBC, UEC, LFTs, fasting lipids, fasting glucose or HbA1c, prolactin, ECG), then weight and BP weekly for the first 4 weeks, weight and BP at 12 weeks, then fasting biochemistry at 12 weeks, 6 months and annually. Olanzapine and clozapine have the highest metabolic risk; aripiprazole and lurasidone the lowest. Intervention triggers include weight gain over 5 percent, waist increase over 5 cm, new dyslipidaemia, prediabetes (HbA1c 5.7 to 6.4 percent) or diabetes (HbA1c above 6.5 percent), and warrant lifestyle counselling and consideration of switching to a lower-risk agent.
key_points: Baseline plus 12 weeks plus 6 months plus annual biochemistry
Olanzapine and clozapine highest metabolic risk
Switch trigger: weight above 5 percent gain or new dyslipidaemia or dysglycaemia
Prolactin only if clinical symptoms of hyperprolactinaemia
explanation.pearls: Adding metformin 500 mg twice daily reduces antipsychotic-induced weight gain and improves insulin sensitivity in patients with significant weight gain who must remain on the offending agent.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Antipsychotic monitoring

stem: You are the GP reviewing a 42-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder who has been stable on lithium carbonate 1000 mg nocte for the past five years with euthymia and full functional recovery. She attends every six months for routine review. She has no symptoms of lithium toxicity, no tremor and no polyuria. She uses ibuprofen occasionally for menstrual pain but has not taken any over the past two weeks. She has no acute illness or change in fluid status today and is keen to complete her routine 12-monthly biochemistry panel.

data_table.Examination: No fine tremor; no goitre; cognition intact; cardiovascular and neurological examination unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Last six months: lithium 0.78 mmol/L, creatinine 75, TSH 2.1, calcium 2.42; today's bloods not yet drawn
data_table.Medications: Lithium carbonate 1000 mg nocte; quetiapine 50 mg nocte for sleep; combined contraceptive pill

lead_in: What is the most appropriate investigation panel today?

options.text: Lithium concentration, urea, electrolytes and creatinine, estimated glomerular filtration rate, thyroid function, calcium and weight as the comprehensive annual monitoring
options.rationale: Lithium 12-month review covers lithium concentration plus renal function, thyroid function and calcium to detect nephropathy, hypothyroidism and hyperparathyroidism as long-term adverse effects. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Lithium concentration alone given that recent thyroid and renal function were normal at six months and she remains clinically euthymic without tremor or polyuria
options.rationale: Annual review includes lithium, U and E, eGFR, TSH and calcium together; lithium concentration alone misses the cumulative organ-specific toxicities that emerge over time. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Lithium concentration plus full blood count and liver function tests as the annual review panel reflecting standard antipsychotic monitoring transposed onto her current bipolar therapy
options.rationale: FBC and LFTs are not specifically affected by lithium; renal function, thyroid function and calcium are the lithium-specific surveillance tests required annually. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Echocardiogram and 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure as a cardiovascular screen reflecting concern about long-term lithium-related cardiovascular toxicity in stable euthymic patients
options.rationale: Routine echocardiogram is not part of lithium monitoring; ECG at baseline is recommended but ongoing cardiac imaging is reserved for symptoms or specific risk factors. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Defer all blood tests until next clinically indicated review or annual review the following year because she has been entirely stable on her current dose for the past five years
options.rationale: Annual review is mandatory regardless of clinical stability because lithium nephropathy and hypothyroidism develop insidiously over years; deferring misses early intervention. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Lithium long-term monitoring includes lithium concentration (target 0.4 to 0.8 mmol/L for maintenance, 0.6 to 1.0 mmol/L for acute mania, taken 12 hours post-dose), renal function (U, E, creatinine, eGFR), thyroid function (TSH, free T4 if abnormal) and calcium (lithium causes hyperparathyroidism in around 5 to 10 percent of long-term users). Frequency is 3-monthly for the first 6 months then 6-monthly to 12-monthly for stable patients. ECG at baseline. Toxicity risk increases with NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, thiazides, dehydration and reduced renal function; review medications and fluid status at every visit.
key_points: Annual lithium, UEC, eGFR, TSH, calcium for stable patients
Maintenance target 0.4 to 0.8 mmol/L 12 hours post-dose
NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, thiazides raise lithium concentration
Hyperparathyroidism prevalence 5 to 10 percent in long-term lithium
explanation.pearls: An eGFR fall over 25 percent within a year on lithium warrants nephrology review and consideration of switching to valproate or lamotrigine; nephropathy may progress despite lithium cessation.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Bipolar guidelines

stem:
You are the GP reviewing a 48-year-old man who wants to stop smoking. He has smoked 20 cigarettes per day for 30 years and his Heaviness of Smoking Index is high (first cigarette within 5 minutes of waking). He has never tried pharmacotherapy. He has well-controlled depression on sertraline 100 mg daily for the past three years with no recent suicidal ideation.

He has no cardiovascular disease and no current alcohol use. He is keen to quit before his daughter's wedding in six months and wants the most effective pharmacotherapy.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 130/82, HR 76, BMI 26, expired carbon monoxide 18 ppm
data_table.Examination: No respiratory distress; chest clear; mental state euthymic with no suicidality elicited on screen
data_table.Investigations: Lipid profile shows mildly elevated LDL; baseline ECG sinus rhythm, QTc 410 ms

lead_in: What is the most effective first-line pharmacotherapy option?

options.text: Nicotine replacement therapy patch 21 mg over 24 hours combined with as-needed nicotine lozenge 4 mg for breakthrough craving across the standard quit period
options.rationale: Combination NRT is effective first-line but varenicline has higher quit rates at 12 weeks in heavy smokers; both are valid choices, varenicline preferred where suitable. (Source: RACGP: Supporting smoking cessation)

options.text: Bupropion sustained release 150 mg daily for three days then 150 mg twice daily for 12 weeks, started two weeks before set quit date with seizure precautions discussed
options.rationale: Bupropion is effective but has lower quit rates than varenicline and a seizure risk; it is reserved when varenicline and NRT are contraindicated or have failed. (Source: RACGP: Supporting smoking cessation)

options.text: Varenicline 0.5 mg daily for three days, then 0.5 mg twice daily for four days, then 1 mg twice daily for 12 weeks with set quit date one week into therapy
options.rationale: Varenicline has the highest quit rates at 12 weeks for heavy smokers and is first-line where not contraindicated; titration over week 1 reduces nausea before reaching maintenance dose. (Source: RACGP: Supporting smoking cessation)

options.text: Behavioural counselling alone via the Quitline telephone service with no pharmacotherapy because his depression contraindicates all pharmacological options for cessation today
options.rationale: Stable depression on SSRI is not a contraindication to varenicline; combining behavioural support with pharmacotherapy is more effective than counselling alone. (Source: RACGP: Supporting smoking cessation)

options.text: Electronic nicotine delivery system (vape) prescription as the first-line cessation therapy with the goal of complete vape cessation by three months after quit date achieved
options.rationale: Nicotine vaping is reserved for patients who have failed first-line pharmacotherapy combined with behavioural support; it is not first-line under TGA prescription pathway. (Source: RACGP: Supporting smoking cessation)

explanation.summary: Smoking cessation pharmacotherapy options ranked by quit rate are varenicline (most effective), combination nicotine replacement therapy (patch plus oral form for breakthrough cravings), single-form NRT, bupropion sustained release and nortriptyline. Varenicline is started one week before quit date, titrated over the first week and continued for 12 weeks; an additional 12 weeks reduces relapse. Stable depression is not a contraindication to varenicline but patients should be monitored for neuropsychiatric changes. Cardiovascular events are uncommon but warrant caution in recent acute coronary syndrome. Behavioural support (Quitline, brief intervention) doubles quit rates whatever pharmacotherapy is chosen.
key_points: Varenicline first-line for heavy smokers without contraindication
Combination NRT (patch plus oral) is second-line
Start one week before set quit date; titrate to reduce nausea
Behavioural support doubles quit rates when added to pharmacotherapy
explanation.pearls: Varenicline can be safely continued in cardiovascular disease except recent acute coronary syndrome (within 2 weeks) where waiting for stabilisation is reasonable; benefits of quitting outweigh risks.

stem:
You are the GP reviewing a 28-year-old woman who self-refers requesting assessment for adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. She describes lifelong difficulty sustaining attention, procrastinating on tasks, losing her keys regularly and missing deadlines at her marketing job. She recalls being told she daydreamed in primary school but never received formal assessment. She is otherwise well, with no past psychiatric history.

She does not use illicit substances. She has read about adult ADHD online and asks what the next step in formal diagnosis would be from primary care today.

data_table.Examination: Mental state: euthymic; thought form linear; no psychotic features; cognition grossly intact
data_table.Investigations: Recent FBC, UEC, TFT, B12 normal; ECG sinus rhythm with QTc 405 ms; not pregnant

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe a trial of methylphenidate immediate release 10 mg twice daily for two weeks as a diagnostic trial to confirm adult ADHD by symptomatic response
options.rationale: Stimulant prescription is restricted to authorised paediatric, psychiatric or other authorised prescribers in Australia and cannot be initiated empirically without specialist diagnosis. (Source: RANZCP: Australian evidence-based clinical practice guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: RANZCP: Australian evidence-based clinical practice guideline for ADHD

options.text: Order overnight polysomnography and brain magnetic resonance imaging as the standard initial workup investigations for any presentation of adult attentional concerns
options.rationale: Routine imaging and polysomnography are not required for adult ADHD diagnosis; they are reserved for atypical presentations such as new-onset symptoms or focal neurology. (Source: RANZCP: Australian evidence-based clinical practice guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: RANZCP: Australian evidence-based clinical practice guideline for ADHD

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg daily empirically as initial pharmacotherapy because anxiety is more likely than ADHD in adult women presenting with attentional symptoms
options.rationale: Empirical antidepressant treatment without diagnosis risks missing primary ADHD and delays correct treatment; specialist diagnostic assessment should occur first. (Source: RANZCP: Australian evidence-based clinical practice guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: RANZCP: Australian evidence-based clinical practice guideline for ADHD

options.text: Reassure her that adult-onset ADHD is not a recognised diagnostic entity and recommend cognitive behavioural therapy for non-specific attention concerns from primary care
options.rationale: Adult ADHD is a recognised diagnosis when childhood symptoms can be demonstrated to predate age 12; dismissing the presentation denies access to evidence-based treatment. (Source: RANZCP: Australian evidence-based clinical practice guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: RANZCP: Australian evidence-based clinical practice guideline for ADHD

options.text: Refer to a psychiatrist or paediatrician authorised to assess and prescribe for adult ADHD with collateral history from childhood and adult symptom rating scales
options.rationale: Adult ADHD diagnosis requires specialist assessment including DSM-5 criteria, childhood symptom evidence (school reports, parental collateral), adult symptom scales and exclusion of differentials. (Source: RANZCP: Australian evidence-based clinical practice guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: RANZCP: Australian evidence-based clinical practice guideline for ADHD

explanation.summary: Adult ADHD diagnosis requires DSM-5 criteria: five or more inattention or hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms (over six for under 17), symptoms present in two or more settings, evidence symptoms began before age 12, and significant functional impairment with other causes excluded. Workup includes childhood collateral (school reports, parents), adult self-report scales (Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale, Connors), psychiatric history, substance use review and basic biochemistry to exclude differentials. Stimulant prescription in Australia is restricted to authorised psychiatrists, paediatricians and selected other specialists under state-based authority schedules. GP shared-care arrangements are common after stabilisation.
key_points: DSM-5 requires childhood onset before age 12
Specialist diagnostic assessment in Australia before stimulant prescription
Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale is a validated screening tool
Comorbidity with anxiety, depression and substance use is common
explanation.pearls: Stimulant prescribing in Australia requires individual state-based authority approval which is renewed annually; GPs may continue prescribing under shared care after specialist initiation in most jurisdictions.

sources.label: RANZCP: Australian evidence-based clinical practice guideline for ADHD

stem: You are the GP reviewing a 35-year-old woman who was the driver in a serious motor vehicle accident eight months ago. She describes intrusive flashbacks, hypervigilance, avoiding driving, nightmares disrupting sleep four nights a week, and irritability with her partner. Symptoms have not improved spontaneously and now meet DSM-5 criteria for post-traumatic stress disorder. She has no history of depression, no current suicidal ideation, no substance misuse and is keen to engage in evidence-based therapy. She is wary of medication and asks what will help her most.

data_table.Examination: Mental state: anxious affect, no psychotic features; cognition intact; insight retained
data_table.Investigations: Recent FBC, UEC, TFT all normal; PTSD Checklist score 56 of 80

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line management?

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg daily titrated to 200 mg as the first-line pharmacological treatment in preference to trauma-focused psychological therapies for this presentation
options.rationale: SSRIs are effective but trauma-focused psychological therapies have superior evidence as first-line; pharmacotherapy is reserved for inadequate response or patient preference. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for the prevention and treatment of PTSD)
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for the prevention and treatment of PTSD

options.text: Refer for trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy or eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing therapy as the evidence-based first-line treatment in PTSD
options.rationale: Trauma-focused CBT and EMDR are the first-line psychological treatments for PTSD with the strongest evidence base for symptom reduction and sustained remission. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for the prevention and treatment of PTSD)
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for the prevention and treatment of PTSD

options.text: Prescribe prazosin 1 mg nocte and a long-acting benzodiazepine for sleep restoration and to suppress traumatic re-experiencing symptoms before any psychological therapy starts
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are not recommended in PTSD as they impair extinction learning and worsen long-term outcomes; prazosin alone is reserved for nightmare reduction adjunctively. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for the prevention and treatment of PTSD)
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for the prevention and treatment of PTSD

options.text: Provide supportive counselling alone through generalist primary care without referral to specific evidence-based trauma-focused psychological therapy in the first six months
options.rationale: Generic supportive counselling is less effective than trauma-focused therapy and does not address core PTSD symptoms; first-line trauma-focused therapy should be offered. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for the prevention and treatment of PTSD)
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for the prevention and treatment of PTSD

options.text: Refer for inpatient psychiatric admission to a tertiary trauma service for intensive group-based therapy because symptoms have persisted for eight months without intervention
options.rationale: Inpatient admission is reserved for risk to self or others, severe functional decompensation or treatment failure; outpatient trauma-focused therapy is first-line. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for the prevention and treatment of PTSD)
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for the prevention and treatment of PTSD

explanation.summary: PTSD first-line treatment is trauma-focused psychological therapy: trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy (including prolonged exposure and cognitive processing therapy) or eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing. Both have strong evidence for symptom reduction over 8 to 12 weekly sessions. Pharmacotherapy (SSRI sertraline, paroxetine or fluoxetine) is reserved for patients who decline or cannot access psychological therapy, who have inadequate response, or who have comorbid depression. Benzodiazepines are contraindicated as they impair extinction learning and worsen long-term outcomes. Prazosin is an evidence-based adjunctive treatment for distressing nightmares.
key_points: First-line: TF-CBT or EMDR for 8 to 12 sessions
Sertraline, paroxetine, fluoxetine: SSRIs as second-line
Benzodiazepines contraindicated in PTSD
Prazosin adjunctive for distressing nightmares
explanation.pearls: Prazosin 1 mg nocte titrated weekly to 5 to 10 mg specifically reduces PTSD trauma nightmares; first-dose hypotension warrants supine titration and warning patients about postural symptoms.

sources.label: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for the prevention and treatment of PTSD

stem: You are the GP reviewing a 26-year-old woman with established borderline personality disorder confirmed by community mental health team assessment two years ago. She has a five-year history of recurrent superficial wrist cutting in response to perceived rejection, two prior low-lethality paracetamol overdoses in the past three years, and unstable interpersonal relationships. She has previously had supportive counselling without sustained benefit. She is not currently suicidal and is engaged in care. She asks what intervention would most reduce her self-harm and admissions over time.

data_table.Examination: Old linear scars on bilateral forearms; mental state: euthymic, no acute risk; cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Recent FBC, UEC, LFTs, urine drug screen all normal; no current pregnancy
data_table.Medications: Quetiapine 50 mg nocte for sleep; nil other

lead_in: What is the most appropriate evidence-based recommendation?

options.text: Commence high-dose fluoxetine 60 mg daily as first-line pharmacotherapy for the core features of borderline personality disorder with quarterly review and dose titration
options.rationale: No medication has approval or strong evidence as first-line treatment for borderline personality disorder; structured psychological therapy is the cornerstone of management. (Source: NHMRC: Clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder)
source_refs: NHMRC: Clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder

options.text: Refer for inpatient psychiatric admission whenever she presents with self-harm to interrupt the behaviour and provide containment until stable for outpatient discharge
options.rationale: Routine admission for self-harm in borderline personality disorder reinforces the behaviour and worsens long-term outcomes; brief crisis admissions are used only when imminent risk warrants. (Source: NHMRC: Clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder)
source_refs: NHMRC: Clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder

options.text: Recommend electroconvulsive therapy as the next escalation in management given previous failure of supportive counselling and ongoing high-risk behaviours over years
options.rationale: ECT is reserved for severe treatment-resistant depression or catatonia; it has no role in core borderline personality disorder treatment without comorbid mood diagnosis. (Source: NHMRC: Clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder)
source_refs: NHMRC: Clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder

options.text: Refer for a structured dialectical behaviour therapy program combining weekly individual therapy with group skills training over 12 months as the recommended intervention
options.rationale: Dialectical behaviour therapy has the strongest evidence base for reducing self-harm, hospital admissions and treatment dropout in borderline personality disorder over a 12-month program. (Source: NHMRC: Clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder)
