explanation.pearls: Brief admissions for BPD have been associated with reduced self-efficacy and increased re-presentation in AU cohorts; aim for community resilience-building rather than inpatient sanctuary unless safety cannot be maintained.

subtopic_detail: Smoking cessation pharmacotherapy in stable schizophrenia
stem: You are the GP registrar reviewing a 42-year-old man with stable schizophrenia on aripiprazole 15 mg daily for 4 years. He smokes 25 cigarettes daily and wants to quit. He has tried nicotine replacement patches without success twice. He has no depression, anxiety, or active substance use. He has a normal ECG, BP, lipids, and HbA1c. He is keen to discuss varenicline after seeing television advertising.

data_table.Examination: Mental state stable; no thought disorder; no suicidal ideation
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, HbA1c, lipids, TSH normal
data_table.Medications: Aripiprazole 15 mg daily; no other regular

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase aripiprazole to 20 mg daily to reduce reward salience associated with nicotine craving
options.rationale: Dose escalation of aripiprazole is not an evidence-based smoking cessation strategy and risks increased side effects. (Source: RANZCP)

options.text: Avoid varenicline because of an absolute contraindication to its use in any patient with a primary psychotic illness
options.rationale: Varenicline is no longer contraindicated in psychotic disorders; the previous black box warning was removed after the EAGLES trial. (Source: AMH)

options.text: Start varenicline 0.5 mg daily titrated over the standard 12 week course with mood monitoring at each review
options.rationale: Varenicline is safe and effective in stable schizophrenia and is supported by AU smoking cessation guidance with routine monitoring for neuropsychiatric symptoms. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation; AMH)

options.text: Start bupropion sustained release 150 mg daily titrated to 300 mg over the first week of treatment
options.rationale: Bupropion lowers seizure threshold and may interact with antipsychotic metabolism; varenicline is preferred when not contraindicated. (Source: AMH)

options.text: Refer for an inpatient detoxification program as the only safe approach in patients with schizophrenia
options.rationale: Inpatient nicotine detoxification is not standard in AU; outpatient pharmacotherapy with monitoring is the recommended approach. (Source: RACGP)

explanation.summary: Smoking prevalence in schizophrenia is over 50 percent and is the leading driver of cardiovascular mortality in this population. Varenicline and combination nicotine replacement are first-line pharmacotherapy with similar safety in stable mental illness as in the general population since the EAGLES trial. Behavioural support combined with pharmacotherapy doubles quit rates compared with either alone. Cytochrome P450 1A2 metabolism slows when smoking stops, which can increase clozapine and olanzapine plasma levels by up to 50 percent.
key_points: Varenicline safe in stable psychotic illness post-EAGLES
Combination NRT effective alternative
Behavioural support doubles quit rates
Clozapine and olanzapine levels rise on smoking cessation
explanation.pearls: When smokers on clozapine quit, reduce dose by 20 to 30 percent over the first 2 weeks and monitor levels and side effects; failure to do so risks sedation, seizure, and toxicity.

subtopic_detail: Lorazepam challenge dose and route in suspected catatonia after recent antipsychotic exposure
stem: You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar reviewing a 38-year-old woman on the medical ward who has become mute, immobile, and waxy on examination over the last 36 hours. She was admitted 5 days ago with sepsis from cellulitis and received haloperidol 5 mg twice daily for delirium for 3 days, ceased 24 hours ago. She has a long history of bipolar disorder. Her sepsis is resolving. She is afebrile, normotensive, and her CK is mildly elevated at 380.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8, HR 86, BP 116/72, RR 18, SpO2 98 percent
data_table.Examination: Mute, immobile, posturing left arm, waxy flexibility, no rigidity, no tremor, eyes open
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, calcium, magnesium normal; CK 380; CRP 22 falling; urine drug screen negative; MRI brain unremarkable; EEG no electrographic seizure
data_table.Medications: Ceftriaxone day 5 of 7; lithium 800 mg nocte; haloperidol ceased 24 hours ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate diagnostic and therapeutic next step?

options.text: Commence bromocriptine 2.5 mg orally three times daily as first-line dopaminergic treatment for catatonia
options.rationale: Bromocriptine is not first-line for catatonia; lorazepam and ECT are the evidence-based treatments. (Source: RANZCP)

options.text: Arrange urgent electroconvulsive therapy tomorrow as first-line treatment before any pharmacological trial
options.rationale: ECT is first-line for malignant or refractory catatonia and benzodiazepine non-responders; a lorazepam trial first is standard. (Source: RANZCP)

options.text: Start dantrolene infusion at 2.5 mg/kg over 30 minutes to address suspected neuroleptic malignant syndrome
options.rationale: Dantrolene is reserved for NMS where temperature rises and rigidity dominate; the picture here lacks hyperthermia and severe rigidity. (Source: RANZCP)

options.text: Administer lorazepam 1 mg IV as a single challenge dose and reassess catatonic features within 10 minutes
options.rationale: A lorazepam challenge of 1 to 2 mg IV is both diagnostic and therapeutic in catatonia; a robust response within 10 minutes supports the diagnosis and guides ongoing therapy. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia)

options.text: Re-initiate haloperidol 2.5 mg twice daily as low dose maintenance to treat suspected residual delirium tonight
options.rationale: Antipsychotics can worsen catatonia and precipitate NMS; they should be ceased or avoided when catatonia is suspected. (Source: RANZCP)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is recognised by mutism, posturing, waxy flexibility, negativism, echo phenomena, and immobility. The lorazepam challenge of 1 to 2 mg IV is the diagnostic and therapeutic first step; response within 10 minutes supports diagnosis and ongoing oral or IV lorazepam typically 6 to 16 mg daily. Antipsychotics should be ceased as they may precipitate or worsen catatonia and increase NMS risk. Refractory or malignant catatonia warrants urgent ECT.
key_points: Lorazepam challenge 1 to 2 mg IV diagnostic and therapeutic
Ongoing lorazepam 6 to 16 mg daily commonly required
Cease antipsychotics in suspected catatonia
ECT for refractory or malignant catatonia
explanation.pearls: Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale of 2 or more items present for over 24 hours satisfies DSM-5 criteria for catatonia and supports proceeding to lorazepam trial.

subtopic_detail: Discrimination of cannabis-induced psychosis from first episode schizophrenia
stem: You are the early psychosis service registrar assessing a 21-year-old man brought in by his family with 3 weeks of persecutory delusions, auditory hallucinations, and disorganised speech. He has been using high-potency cannabis daily for the past 6 months, increasing in the month before symptom onset. He has no prior psychiatric history but maternal half-brother has schizophrenia. He last used cannabis 9 days ago and remains symptomatic with positive symptoms unchanged after 1 week of olanzapine 10 mg nocte.

data_table.Examination: Disorganised speech, persecutory delusions, second-person auditory hallucinations, blunted affect
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain unremarkable; FBC, UEC, LFTs, TFTs, syphilis serology, HIV negative; urine drug screen positive for THC on admission, negative on day 9

lead_in: Which clinical feature most strongly supports an evolving primary psychotic disorder rather than substance-induced psychosis at this point?

options.text: Persistence of positive symptoms beyond a month after cessation of cannabis use most strongly favours a primary psychotic disorder
options.rationale: DSM-5 distinguishes substance-induced psychosis from primary psychotic disorder by symptom resolution within about a month of substance cessation; persistence supports primary diagnosis. (Source: RANZCP First Episode Psychosis; DSM-5)

options.text: Presence of negative symptoms during the first month of illness rules out substance-induced psychosis entirely
options.rationale: Negative symptoms can occur in both substance-induced and primary psychotic disorders during the acute phase. (Source: RANZCP)

options.text: Negative urine drug screen at presentation is required before a primary psychotic disorder can be diagnosed
options.rationale: Urine drug screen reflects recent use, not aetiology of psychotic symptoms, and is not a diagnostic gateway. (Source: RANZCP)

options.text: Onset of positive symptoms during heavy cannabis use is itself sufficient to diagnose substance-induced psychosis
options.rationale: Temporal association alone does not exclude primary psychotic disorder; cannabis is both a trigger and risk factor for primary psychosis. (Source: RANZCP)

options.text: Positive family history of psychotic illness in a maternal half-brother is sufficient to confirm a primary psychotic disorder
options.rationale: Family history raises risk but alone does not distinguish between substance-induced and primary psychosis. (Source: RANZCP)

explanation.summary: Cannabis-induced psychosis typically resolves within days to weeks of cessation; persistence beyond a month supports an evolving primary psychotic disorder under DSM-5. Heavy use of high-potency cannabis approximately doubles lifetime risk of schizophrenia. Treatment with a second-generation antipsychotic, cannabis cessation support, and engagement with early psychosis services are central. Family history, premorbid functioning, and negative symptoms can all inform prognosis but none alone is diagnostic.
key_points: Substance-induced psychosis typically resolves within a month of cessation
Persistence beyond a month suggests primary psychotic disorder
High-potency cannabis doubles schizophrenia risk
Family history raises risk but does not confirm diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Up to 50 percent of patients with cannabis-induced psychosis transition to a primary psychotic disorder within 3 years; early intervention services should follow these patients for at least 2 years.

subtopic_detail: Choice of first-line trauma focused therapy in adult PTSD with single index event
stem: You are the community psychiatry registrar reviewing a 34-year-old woman with 4 months of intrusive memories, avoidance, hyperarousal, and nightmares after a single motor vehicle crash. She is mid-grade depressed but not suicidal. She is reluctant to take medication and is asking about psychological treatment options. She has access to both a clinical psychologist with EMDR training and a clinical psychologist with TF-CBT training within the same service.

data_table.Examination: Mental state alert, mood low-mid, no psychosis, no suicidal ideation
data_table.Investigations: Nil indicated; PCL-5 score 52, PHQ-9 score 13

lead_in: Which statement is the most accurate first-line recommendation under AU guidance?

options.text: Eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing has clearly superior outcomes to trauma focused CBT in adult PTSD
options.rationale: Head-to-head trials show comparable outcomes between TF-CBT and EMDR; neither is clearly superior. (Source: Phoenix Australia)

options.text: Generic supportive counselling has equivalent efficacy to trauma focused therapy and is preferred in mild PTSD
options.rationale: Supportive counselling is less effective than trauma focused therapy for PTSD across severity levels. (Source: Phoenix Australia)

options.text: Trauma focused CBT and EMDR have comparable first-line evidence in adult PTSD and choice is guided by patient preference and clinician training
options.rationale: Both TF-CBT and EMDR are first-line for adult PTSD in AU; choice is guided by availability, clinician expertise, and patient preference. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD)

options.text: Sertraline is the recommended first-line treatment for adult PTSD before any trauma focused psychological therapy is offered
options.rationale: Trauma focused psychological therapies are first-line; SSRIs are an alternative or adjunct, not the recommended first step. (Source: Phoenix Australia)

options.text: Critical incident debriefing within a single session is the recommended first step in management of all adult PTSD
options.rationale: Single-session debriefing is not effective and may be harmful; structured trauma focused therapy is recommended instead. (Source: Phoenix Australia)

explanation.summary: Adult PTSD is treated first-line with a trauma focused psychological therapy. The Phoenix Australia guidelines recommend TF-CBT and EMDR as comparable first-line options. SSRIs (sertraline, paroxetine, fluoxetine, venlafaxine) are an alternative or adjunct, particularly for patients who decline psychotherapy or have prominent comorbid depression. Single-session debriefing is not recommended. Co-occurring substance use, depression, or chronic pain are addressed concurrently with PTSD treatment rather than sequentially.
key_points: TF-CBT and EMDR equally first-line for adult PTSD
SSRIs are alternative or adjunct treatment
Single-session debriefing not recommended
Treat comorbid depression or substance use concurrently
explanation.pearls: Prazosin 1 to 4 mg nocte can reduce trauma related nightmares in PTSD where sleep disturbance dominates; consider adding when nightmares persist despite psychotherapy.

subtopic_detail: Choosing between varenicline and combination NRT for adult smoker seeking quit attempt
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 52-year-old man who smokes 25 cigarettes daily and wants to quit before an elective knee replacement in eight weeks. He has had three prior failed quit attempts using nicotine patches alone. He has stable mood with no history of suicidal ideation, no seizures, no untreated cardiovascular disease, and no contraindication to varenicline. He prefers oral medication and is willing to set a quit date in two weeks.

data_table.Mental state: Euthymic, no suicidal ideation, no recent depressive episode
data_table.Past history: Hypertension on amlodipine; no seizure disorder; no liver disease; eGFR over 60 mL/min/1.73m2
data_table.Smoking: 25 per day for 30 years; Fagerstrom score 7

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Varenicline 0.5 mg daily titrated up to 1 mg twice daily starting one week before quit date
options.rationale: Varenicline has the highest single-agent cessation efficacy and suits a planned quit attempt with no contraindications. (Source: RACGP: Smoking cessation; Therapeutic Guidelines)

options.text: Repeat nicotine patch monotherapy for another six week course as the proven single agent strategy
options.rationale: Repeat patch monotherapy after prior failure has low success; escalation to varenicline or combination NRT is recommended. (Source: RACGP: Smoking cessation)

options.text: Bupropion 150 mg daily for three days then 150 mg twice daily for nine weeks from the quit date
options.rationale: Bupropion is third-line behind varenicline and combination NRT and is contraindicated in seizure disorder, but here varenicline is preferred. (Source: RACGP: Smoking cessation)

options.text: E-cigarette as the primary cessation strategy given preference for oral nicotine substitution device
options.rationale: E-cigarettes are not a first-line cessation strategy in Australia and are recommended only after registered therapies fail. (Source: RACGP: Smoking cessation)

options.text: Brief advice and motivational counselling only without any pharmacotherapy this consultation
options.rationale: Behavioural advice alone is insufficient in a heavy smoker with prior failed attempts; pharmacotherapy adds substantial benefit. (Source: RACGP: Smoking cessation)

explanation.summary: Varenicline and combination NRT (patch plus short acting form) are the most effective pharmacotherapies for smoking cessation in adults. Varenicline is started one week before the quit date and continued for 12 weeks, with consideration of a 12-week maintenance course in high relapse risk. Combination NRT is a reasonable alternative for those who cannot take varenicline. Bupropion is third-line and contraindicated in seizure disorder. Behavioural support roughly doubles success rates of pharmacotherapy.
key_points: Varenicline and combination NRT are first-line
Start varenicline one week before the quit date
Treat for at least 12 weeks; consider maintenance
Add behavioural support to pharmacotherapy
explanation.pearls: Varenicline achieves 6-month cessation around 25 percent versus 18 percent for single patch alone in heavy smokers; the FDA boxed warning for psychiatric effects was removed in 2016 after the EAGLES trial showed no excess risk.

subtopic_detail: Choice of SSRI when starting antidepressant treatment in a breastfeeding mother
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 32-year-old woman at 10 weeks postpartum with moderate depressive symptoms confirmed by EPDS of 18 and clinical interview. She is exclusively breastfeeding her well 10-week-old son. She has not had antidepressant treatment previously. There is no suicidal ideation, no psychotic features, and no manic history. She wishes to start an antidepressant and continue breastfeeding.

data_table.Mental state: Tearful, low mood for six weeks, sleep disturbance beyond infant feeds, anhedonia, no suicidal ideation, no psychotic features
data_table.Past history: Nil regular medication; no thyroid disease; TSH 1.8 mIU/L
data_table.Infant: Term, well, gaining weight on the 25th centile

lead_in: Which antidepressant has the most supportive safety data in this setting?

options.text: Fluoxetine 20 mg daily orally with infant monitoring during initiation and dose titration
options.rationale: Fluoxetine has the longest half-life of the SSRIs and accumulates in breastfed infants more than alternatives. (Source: COPE; LactMed)

options.text: Citalopram 20 mg daily orally with weekly infant clinical review during the first two weeks
options.rationale: Citalopram is acceptable but has slightly higher infant exposure than sertraline and is not preferred first-line in lactation. (Source: COPE; LactMed)

options.text: Mirtazapine 15 mg nightly orally with infant weight and sedation review during the first two weeks
options.rationale: Mirtazapine has less safety data in lactation and is not the preferred first-line agent for postnatal depression. (Source: COPE)

options.text: Sertraline 50 mg daily orally with infant clinical review for sedation and feeding during initiation
options.rationale: Sertraline has the lowest measured infant serum concentrations among SSRIs and is the preferred first-line agent in breastfeeding women. (Source: COPE; LactMed)

options.text: Venlafaxine 75 mg daily orally with blood pressure and infant review during the first two weeks
options.rationale: Venlafaxine has higher discontinuation symptoms and is not first-line in postnatal lactation. (Source: COPE)

explanation.summary: Sertraline is the preferred first-line antidepressant in breastfeeding women because of the lowest measured infant serum concentrations among SSRIs. Paroxetine is an alternative. Fluoxetine has the longest half-life and active metabolite, leading to greater infant accumulation. Citalopram and escitalopram are acceptable alternatives if previously effective. Treatment should be combined with structured psychological therapy and a planned review at one and four weeks. Mothers should be reassured that breastfeeding does not need to be stopped.
key_points: Sertraline is the first-line SSRI in lactation
Fluoxetine accumulates more in breastfed infants
Add psychological therapy
Review at one and four weeks for response and tolerability
explanation.pearls: Infant serum sertraline levels are typically less than 2 percent of weight-adjusted maternal dose, which is the lowest of the SSRIs and underpins the COPE recommendation as first-line in lactation.

subtopic_detail: Initial inpatient feeding plan for severe anorexia nervosa with refeeding risk markers
stem: You are the medical registrar admitting a 19-year-old woman with anorexia nervosa to an adolescent ward. She has BMI 13.6, has eaten less than 500 kcal daily for four weeks, and has lost 12 kg in three months. Bloods show phosphate 0.65 mmol/L, magnesium 0.7 mmol/L, and potassium 3.2 mmol/L. She is normotensive supine but with HR 38 supine. She has no severe organ failure and is consenting to treatment.

data_table.Vital signs: T 35.8, HR 38 supine, RR 14, BP 92/56 supine, BMI 13.6
data_table.Examination: Cachectic, peripheral oedema +, lanugo, no organomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Na 138, K 3.2, Mg 0.7, PO4 0.65, glucose 3.6 mmol/L; LFTs ALT 84; ECG QTc 470 ms
data_table.Mental state: Engaged, cognitively intact, no suicidal ideation, agrees to treatment

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial feeding plan?

options.text: Commence oral feeds at 5 kcal/kg/day with thiamine and replace electrolytes before any oral intake
options.rationale: Starting feeds at 5 kcal/kg/day is too restrictive and delays nutritional recovery; current ANZAED guidance starts higher with vigilance. (Source: ANZAED: Refeeding)

options.text: Commence oral feeds at 20 kcal/kg/day with thiamine 300 mg IV and daily phosphate magnesium potassium
options.rationale: Starting feeds at 20 kcal/kg/day with thiamine and daily electrolyte monitoring is current ANZAED guidance for high-risk refeeding. (Source: ANZAED: Refeeding)

options.text: Commence oral feeds at 40 kcal/kg/day with weekly bloods and no parenteral thiamine prescribed
options.rationale: 40 kcal/kg/day at BMI 13.6 with electrolyte derangement carries high refeeding risk; weekly bloods is insufficient. (Source: ANZAED: Refeeding)

options.text: Commence total parenteral nutrition through central venous access with daily electrolyte review
options.rationale: TPN is reserved for failed enteral feeding or contraindications; oral or NG feeding is preferred. (Source: ANZAED: Refeeding)

options.text: Commence nasogastric continuous feeds at 60 mL/hour without electrolyte preloading or thiamine
options.rationale: High continuous feed without electrolyte and thiamine preloading risks refeeding syndrome and cardiac complications. (Source: ANZAED: Refeeding)

explanation.summary: Severe anorexia with electrolyte derangement, bradycardia, and prolonged starvation is high risk for refeeding syndrome. ANZAED guidance starts feeds at 20 kcal/kg/day with thiamine supplementation and daily monitoring of phosphate, magnesium, potassium, and glucose for the first week, with electrolyte replacement as needed. Bradycardia and orthostasis are markers of medical instability requiring inpatient monitoring. Psychological therapy and family work continue alongside medical stabilisation.
key_points: Start 20 kcal/kg/day, increase as electrolytes allow
Thiamine 300 mg IV before feeds in high-risk patients
Daily phosphate, magnesium, potassium, and glucose
Bradycardia and orthostasis are medical instability markers
explanation.pearls: Refeeding hypophosphataemia typically develops 24 to 72 hours after starting feeds; the threshold for replacement is phosphate under 0.6 mmol/L with IV potassium phosphate at about 0.3 mmol/kg over 6 hours.

subtopic_detail: Initial mental health assessment of an Aboriginal man presenting with low mood in regional GP
stem: You are the rural GP reviewing a 45-year-old Aboriginal man presenting with three months of low mood, broken sleep, and reduced engagement with family. He attends with his sister who provides collateral. He recently lost his mother and has begun attending Sorry Business in his community. He has no suicidal ideation, no psychotic features, and no alcohol or drug use. He is reluctant to see a mainstream mental health service.

data_table.Mental state: Withdrawn, congruent affect, no suicidal ideation, no perceptual abnormality
data_table.Past history: Nil regular medication; chronic lower back pain; no prior mental health treatment
data_table.Social: Lives with extended family; cultural and community connections important

lead_in: What is the most culturally appropriate first step?

options.text: Refer urgently to a mainstream community psychiatric team for inpatient assessment as a priority
options.rationale: Mainstream urgent referral is disproportionate without risk features and may worsen engagement with care. (Source: RACGP: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health)
source_refs: RACGP: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health

options.text: Start oral sertraline 50 mg daily as monotherapy without further mental health team involvement now
options.rationale: Pharmacotherapy alone does not address social and emotional wellbeing or cultural context; partnership care is preferred. (Source: RACGP: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health)
source_refs: RACGP: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health

options.text: Document the consultation and review in six weeks without offering any therapeutic plan today
options.rationale: Six-week passive review without active engagement risks deterioration; supportive care should commence now. (Source: RACGP: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health)
source_refs: RACGP: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health

options.text: Discharge with online self-help resources and a fact sheet about depression in adult patients now
options.rationale: Self-help leaflets alone do not address SEWB context or family-centred preferences and underuse local services. (Source: RACGP: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health)
source_refs: RACGP: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health

options.text: Offer co-ordinated care with the local Aboriginal community-controlled health service and SEWB worker
options.rationale: Engagement with the Aboriginal community-controlled health service and SEWB worker centres cultural context, family, and continuity of care. (Source: RACGP: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health)
source_refs: RACGP: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health

explanation.summary: Social and emotional wellbeing is the holistic framework for mental health in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities, recognising connection to country, family, culture, spirituality, and community as integral. The first step in an engaged primary care assessment is partnership with an Aboriginal community-controlled health service and SEWB worker where available. Pharmacotherapy and psychological therapy can be added once a therapeutic relationship and cultural support are in place. Grief and loss responses, including Sorry Business, are part of cultural context and shape presentation.
key_points: SEWB framework rather than medical-model only
Partner with ACCHS and SEWB worker
Add pharmacotherapy and therapy once engaged
Recognise grief and loss in cultural context
explanation.pearls: The Kessler-5 is the validated screening tool for psychological distress in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander populations and replaces the K10 in this context; scores 12 or above warrant further SEWB assessment.

sources.label: RACGP: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health

subtopic_detail: Pre-treatment cardiovascular screening before adult stimulant initiation in newly diagnosed ADHD
stem: You are the psychiatrist starting methylphenidate for a 34-year-old man with newly diagnosed adult ADHD after a comprehensive assessment. He has no syncope, no chest pain, and no exertional symptoms. His father had a sudden cardiac death at 42 years from a documented arrhythmia. The patient has not had cardiology assessment previously. He is otherwise well, not on any other medication, and has no substance use.

data_table.Examination: Cardiovascular examination unremarkable, no murmurs, no displaced apex
data_table.Investigations: ECG not yet performed; baseline bloods unremarkable
data_table.Family history: Father sudden cardiac death at 42 from documented arrhythmia

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step before initiating stimulant?

options.text: Refer to cardiology for ECG and echocardiogram review before commencing any stimulant medication
options.rationale: First-degree family history of sudden cardiac death warrants cardiology workup before stimulant initiation. (Source: RANZCP: Adult ADHD)

options.text: Commence methylphenidate 10 mg twice daily and review symptoms at four weeks with a BP recheck
options.rationale: Stimulants can unmask arrhythmia or structural disease; family history of SCD requires workup first. (Source: RANZCP: Adult ADHD)

options.text: Commence atomoxetine 40 mg daily as non-stimulant alternative without cardiology referral now
options.rationale: Atomoxetine also affects blood pressure and pulse and is not exempt from cardiac workup with this family history. (Source: RANZCP: Adult ADHD)

options.text: Order outpatient 24-hour Holter monitor alone without further cardiology input before treatment now
options.rationale: Holter alone does not screen for structural disease; cardiology assessment with ECG and echocardiogram is preferred. (Source: RANZCP: Adult ADHD)

options.text: Defer all pharmacotherapy indefinitely and refer for ongoing CBT alone without further investigation
options.rationale: CBT alone is insufficient for most adult ADHD; pharmacotherapy is the first-line intervention after cardiac workup. (Source: RANZCP: Adult ADHD)

explanation.summary: Stimulants raise heart rate and blood pressure modestly and can unmask underlying structural cardiac disease or arrhythmia. Pre-treatment screening involves cardiovascular history, family history of sudden cardiac death under 40 years, examination, blood pressure and pulse, and ECG if any red flags. Cardiology referral with echocardiogram is indicated for first-degree family history of sudden cardiac death, syncope, or examination abnormality. Atomoxetine and guanfacine also affect cardiovascular parameters and are not exempt.
key_points: Family history SCD under 40 in first-degree relative: cardiology review
Syncope and structural exam findings need workup
Both stimulants and non-stimulants affect cardiovascular parameters
Continue BP and pulse monitoring throughout treatment
explanation.pearls: Methylphenidate typically raises resting heart rate by 5 to 10 bpm and systolic blood pressure by 2 to 5 mmHg; absolute cardiovascular event rates are low in healthy adults but family history of SCD under 40 mandates pre-treatment workup.

sources.label: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

subtopic_detail: Recommended initial screening tool for refugee mental health in primary care first visit
stem: You are the refugee health GP reviewing a 28-year-old man from Syria three weeks after arrival on a humanitarian visa. He reports broken sleep, nightmares, irritability, and avoidance of crowds. He spent three years in transit including time in detention. He speaks limited English and an Arabic interpreter is present. He has no acute suicidal ideation and is engaged in the consultation but cautious.

data_table.Examination: Wary, intermittent eye contact, no current acute distress
data_table.Past history: Reported torture survivor; no diagnosed mental illness; nil regular medication
data_table.Social: Recent arrival; living with extended family; engaged with settlement service

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial mental health screening approach?

options.text: Use a translated PHQ-9 self-report tool today and book a six-week follow-up for routine review
options.rationale: Generic PHQ-9 has limited validity in refugee populations and a six-week passive review delays specialist input. (Source: FASSTT; RACGP)

options.text: Refer for inpatient psychiatric admission for diagnostic clarification and trauma therapy initiation
options.rationale: Inpatient admission is disproportionate in a man without acute risk and may retraumatise a detention survivor. (Source: FASSTT)

options.text: Start oral sertraline 50 mg daily empirically for presumed PTSD before any formal mental health assessment
options.rationale: Empiric pharmacotherapy without trauma-informed assessment misses culture and engagement priorities. (Source: FASSTT)

options.text: Decline to discuss trauma and provide general lifestyle advice with social settlement support only today
options.rationale: Avoiding mental health topics misses an opportunity to engage and signpost specialist trauma services. (Source: FASSTT)

options.text: Use a culturally validated screening tool such as the RHS-15 with an accredited interpreter and onward referral
options.rationale: The Refugee Health Screener RHS-15 with an accredited interpreter is the recommended initial screening and gates onward STARTTS referral. (Source: FASSTT; RACGP)

explanation.summary: Refugee health assessment requires trauma-informed care, accredited interpreters, and validated screening tools. The Refugee Health Screener RHS-15 is the recommended initial screening tool for distress, anxiety, depression, and PTSD symptoms in primary care. Onward referral to specialist services such as the state Survivors of Torture and Trauma services (STARTTS, FASST, ASeTTS) is indicated for positive screens or complex presentations. Pharmacotherapy is added after engagement with specialist trauma services where possible.
key_points: Use RHS-15 with accredited interpreter as initial screen
Refer positive screens to specialist torture and trauma services
Engage trauma-informed care principles
Pharmacotherapy follows specialist input where possible
explanation.pearls: The RHS-15 takes about 10 to 15 minutes, is available in over 15 languages, and uses a positive screen cut-off of 12 or above which flags about 80 percent of refugees with significant mental health needs.

subtopic_detail: Bicarbonate threshold and indication in tricyclic antidepressant overdose with widened QRS
stem: You are the ED registrar reviewing a 22-year-old woman two hours after ingestion of an unknown quantity of amitriptyline tablets in a suicide attempt. She had a witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure on arrival lasting one minute. ECG shows sinus tachycardia at 130 bpm with QRS 140 ms and right axis deviation in lead aVR with terminal R wave 4 mm. She is now drowsy with shallow breathing.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8, HR 130, RR 10, BP 86/54, SpO2 92 percent, GCS 9
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, dry mucosa, mydriasis, hyperreflexia, no focal weakness
data_table.Investigations: ECG QRS 140 ms with terminal R wave in aVR 4 mm; VBG pH 7.30 lactate 3.8 mmol/L; bedside glucose 5.2
data_table.Medications: No regular medications; ingestion 2 hours ago

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Administer intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg bolus and titrate against conscious level for reversal
options.rationale: Flumazenil is contraindicated in TCA overdose as it lowers seizure threshold further. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre; Therapeutic Guidelines)

options.text: Administer intravenous adenosine 6 mg rapid push to terminate the wide complex tachycardia rhythm
options.rationale: This rhythm is sinus with sodium channel blockade, not a re-entrant SVT; adenosine has no role here. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre)

options.text: Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg as a bolus to narrow the QRS interval
options.rationale: QRS over 100 ms with R wave in aVR over 3 mm indicates sodium channel blockade and is the threshold for IV sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre)

options.text: Administer intravenous glucagon 5 mg slow push for refractory hypotension and bradycardia presumed
options.rationale: Glucagon is for beta-blocker overdose; she is tachycardic with sodium channel blockade requiring bicarbonate. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre)

options.text: Administer activated charcoal 50 g via nasogastric tube for late presentation decontamination first
options.rationale: Charcoal is contraindicated with reduced GCS and unprotected airway; secure airway and correct sodium channel blockade first. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre)

explanation.summary: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose causes sodium channel blockade with QRS widening, terminal R wave in aVR, hypotension, and seizures. Treatment of QRS over 100 ms or R wave in aVR over 3 mm is intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus repeated until QRS narrows. Hypertonic saline is an alternative. Lidocaine is reserved for refractory ventricular arrhythmia. Activated charcoal is contraindicated with unprotected airway. Intralipid is a salvage option in cardiac arrest.
key_points: QRS over 100 ms or R in aVR over 3 mm = sodium channel blockade
Sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg IV bolus
Flumazenil contraindicated due to seizure risk
Secure airway before any oral charcoal
explanation.pearls: A terminal R wave in aVR greater than 3 mm predicts arrhythmia in TCA overdose with sensitivity around 80 percent; QRS over 160 ms predicts ventricular arrhythmia and indicates aggressive sodium bicarbonate dosing.

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing very late onset schizophrenia from delusional disorder in 72-year-old woman
stem: You are the consultation-liaison psychiatrist asked to review a 72-year-old woman with a six-month history of fixed persecutory belief that her neighbour is poisoning her water supply. She has installed cameras and tested her water. She has no hallucinations, no thought disorder, no negative symptoms, and remains otherwise able to manage her household and pay bills. There is no family history of schizophrenia, no recent drug use, normal MMSE, and unremarkable MRI brain.

data_table.Mental state: Calm, fixed non-bizarre delusion, no hallucinations, no thought disorder, mood euthymic, insight nil
data_table.Investigations: MMSE 28/30; MRI brain unremarkable; bloods normal; urine drug screen negative; TSH 2.4
data_table.Functional: Independent in activities of daily living, paying bills, shopping, driving

lead_in: What is the single most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Very late onset schizophrenia-like psychosis with intact higher cognition and preserved function
options.rationale: Very late onset schizophrenia-like psychosis typically includes hallucinations or thought disorder; this is absent here. (Source: RANZCP; ICD-11)

options.text: Alzheimer disease with associated paranoid behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia first
options.rationale: Alzheimer disease usually shows cognitive impairment on MMSE and imaging changes; her cognition is preserved. (Source: RANZCP)

options.text: Substance-induced psychotic disorder from her recent over-the-counter and prescription medications
options.rationale: No substance use is identified and urine drug screen is negative; substance-induced disorder is not supported. (Source: RANZCP)

options.text: Delusional disorder persecutory type with circumscribed non-bizarre belief and preserved function
options.rationale: Circumscribed non-bizarre persecutory delusion with no hallucinations or thought disorder and preserved function defines delusional disorder. (Source: RANZCP; ICD-11)

options.text: Schizoaffective disorder with mood instability and persistent delusion across affective phases now
options.rationale: Schizoaffective requires both affective and psychotic features with characteristic phasic pattern, which is absent. (Source: RANZCP)

explanation.summary: Delusional disorder is characterised by one or more non-bizarre delusions for at least one month with otherwise preserved function, no prominent hallucinations or thought disorder, and no significant negative symptoms. Persecutory type is the most common subtype in late life. Very late onset schizophrenia-like psychosis usually includes hallucinations or thought disorder. Cognitive testing and imaging help exclude dementia. Treatment is challenging because insight is typically nil; second-generation antipsychotics at low dose are first-line with strong attention to therapeutic alliance.
key_points: Non-bizarre fixed delusion with preserved function
No prominent hallucinations or thought disorder
Persecutory subtype most common in late life
Second-generation antipsychotic at low dose first-line
explanation.pearls: Risperidone 0.5 to 2 mg daily is the most commonly used first-line agent in late-life delusional disorder, but adherence is the rate-limiting step because insight is typically absent and the therapeutic alliance is fragile.

subtopic_detail: Valproate pregnancy prevention program in a woman with bipolar I disorder of childbearing potential
stem: You are the consultant psychiatrist reviewing a 28-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder maintained on sodium valproate 1500 mg daily for 4 years following a manic episode. She has had no further admissions and is now in a stable relationship. She is using condoms only as contraception. She raises the possibility of starting a family within the next 2 years. Liver function and full blood count are normal.

data_table.Bloods: Valproate level 350 micromol/L (therapeutic), LFTs normal, FBC normal, beta hCG negative
data_table.Reproductive history: Nulliparous, regular cycles, no fertility concerns
data_table.Current medications: Sodium valproate 1500 mg daily, no other psychotropics

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue valproate at current dose and review again in 6 months when pregnancy planning becomes active
options.rationale: Valproate carries dose-dependent risk of major congenital malformation up to 11 percent and neurodevelopmental disability up to 30 to 40 percent; delaying change is unsafe in a woman of childbearing potential. (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program)

options.text: Counsel on teratogenicity, switch to lithium, and enrol in the valproate pregnancy prevention program
options.rationale: Australian guidance requires women on valproate to be counselled annually, use highly effective contraception until cessation, and be transitioned off where possible; lithium is the standard maintenance alternative in bipolar I. (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program)

options.text: Add high-dose folate 5 mg daily and continue valproate at the current dose throughout pregnancy
options.rationale: Folate does not negate the high baseline malformation and neurodevelopmental risks of valproate exposure; substitution is required. (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program)

options.text: Reduce valproate to 750 mg daily and continue indefinitely as a safer dose in pregnancy
options.rationale: There is no safe valproate dose in pregnancy; risk is dose-related but persists at any therapeutic dose. (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program)

options.text: Cease valproate today without alternative and arrange community mental health follow-up review weekly
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation without a replacement mood stabiliser substantially increases relapse risk in a woman with established bipolar I disorder. (Source: RANZCP: Bipolar disorder clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Bipolar disorder clinical practice guideline

explanation.summary: Sodium valproate carries the highest teratogenic burden of any common psychotropic, with major congenital malformation in 9 to 11 percent and dose-related neurodevelopmental disability in 30 to 40 percent of children exposed in utero. The TGA imposed a Pregnancy Prevention Program in 2023 requiring annual specialist review, signed acknowledgement of risk, and use of at least one highly effective contraceptive method (long-acting reversible contraception preferred) in any woman of childbearing potential. Switching to lithium, lamotrigine (better in bipolar II), or olanzapine for maintenance is preferred well before conception, with relapse risk weighed against teratogenicity.
key_points: Major malformation risk 9 to 11 percent on valproate in pregnancy
Neurodevelopmental disability risk approximately 30 to 40 percent
Annual specialist review and signed risk acknowledgement required
Highly effective contraception required while on valproate
Lithium is the standard alternative for bipolar I maintenance
explanation.pearls: If valproate cannot be substituted because of refractory illness, the woman must use a long-acting reversible contraceptive (intrauterine device or implant) and document the decision in the Pregnancy Prevention Program annual review.

sources.label: RANZCP: Bipolar disorder clinical practice guideline

subtopic_detail: Anticholinergic burden when escalating tricyclic antidepressant in an older adult with comorbidities
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 76-year-old man with chronic neuropathic pain and depression maintained on amitriptyline 25 mg nocte for 3 months. He has had a partial mood response and his pain remains poorly controlled. He also takes oxybutynin 5 mg twice daily for urge incontinence, donepezil 10 mg daily for mild Alzheimer dementia, and citalopram 20 mg daily was ceased 2 months ago when amitriptyline was started.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.6, HR 88, BP 132/80 mmHg supine, 110/72 mmHg standing
data_table.Cognitive status: MMSE 24 of 30, mild short-term recall impairment, attention intact
data_table.Bloods: Sodium 138 mmol/L, eGFR 62 mL/min/1.73m^2, ECG QTc 440 ms
data_table.Medications: Amitriptyline 25 mg nocte, oxybutynin 5 mg twice daily, donepezil 10 mg daily, ramipril 5 mg daily

lead_in: Which medication change is most appropriate?

options.text: Increase amitriptyline to 50 mg nocte for stronger antidepressant and neuropathic effect
options.rationale: Higher anticholinergic burden in dementia worsens cognition and falls and counteracts donepezil; nortriptyline at a low dose is preferred when a tricyclic is needed in older adults. (Source: AMH; eTG)

options.text: Switch amitriptyline to duloxetine 30 mg daily and titrate based on response and tolerability
options.rationale: Duloxetine is a reasonable option but does not address the immediate concurrent anticholinergic burden of oxybutynin and amitriptyline opposing donepezil. (Source: AMH; eTG)

options.text: Increase donepezil to 23 mg daily to overcome the anticholinergic burden affecting cognition
options.rationale: The 23 mg dose is not available in Australia and treating prescriber-introduced anticholinergic burden by escalating a cholinesterase inhibitor is not appropriate. (Source: AMH; eTG)

options.text: Cease oxybutynin and review bladder symptoms with non-anticholinergic alternatives in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Stopping oxybutynin alone is reasonable but does not address the amitriptyline contribution to anticholinergic burden, the dominant culprit. (Source: AMH; eTG)

options.text: Substitute amitriptyline with nortriptyline 10 to 25 mg nocte and cease oxybutynin with bladder retraining
options.rationale: Nortriptyline has substantially lower anticholinergic and orthostatic burden than amitriptyline in older adults and ceasing oxybutynin addresses the other major contributor while donepezil continues. (Source: AMH; eTG)

explanation.summary: Anticholinergic burden in older adults causes cognitive decline, falls, urinary retention, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, and orthostatic hypotension. Drugs with high burden include tricyclics, especially tertiary amines (amitriptyline, imipramine), oxybutynin, hyoscine, and first-generation antihistamines. Nortriptyline and desipramine are secondary amines with lower anticholinergic burden. In patients on cholinesterase inhibitors for dementia, anticholinergic drugs directly oppose treatment and worsen cognitive trajectory. Bladder retraining, mirabegron, or topical oestrogen are alternatives to oxybutynin for urge incontinence.
key_points: Anticholinergic burden causes falls, cognitive decline and retention
Amitriptyline carries higher burden than nortriptyline
Anticholinergics oppose donepezil effect in dementia
Mirabegron and topical oestrogen are non-anticholinergic incontinence alternatives
Postural hypotension is a marker of cumulative burden
explanation.pearls: The Anticholinergic Cognitive Burden scale gives oxybutynin and amitriptyline 3 points each; combined exposure above 3 points carries clinically significant cognitive risk in older adults.

subtopic_detail: Lorazepam challenge in suspected catatonia complicating major depressive episode
stem: You are the consultant liaison psychiatrist asked to review a 22-year-old man with a known history of severe major depression admitted under medicine for 4 days of not eating or drinking, mutism, posturing, and waxy flexibility. He is medically cleared, with a normal CT brain, lumbar puncture, and metabolic screen. He has had no fevers, autonomic instability, or rigidity. He is not on any antipsychotic.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8, HR 88, BP 116/72 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99 percent
data_table.Mental state: Mute, immobile, waxy flexibility on right upper limb, no rigidity, no autonomic instability
data_table.Investigations: CK 230 U/L (normal), TSH normal, urine drug screen negative, CT brain and CSF normal
data_table.Bush-Francis catatonia rating: Score 16 with 6 of 14 screening items positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence oral olanzapine 10 mg daily and review the response again in 48 hours
options.rationale: Antipsychotics may worsen catatonia and precipitate neuroleptic malignant syndrome; they are not first-line. (Source: RANZCP catatonia guidance)

options.text: Refer for urgent electroconvulsive therapy without a benzodiazepine trial in the next 24 hours
options.rationale: ECT is highly effective for refractory catatonia but is reserved for failure of the benzodiazepine challenge or malignant catatonia. (Source: RANZCP catatonia guidance)

options.text: Administer parenteral lorazepam 1 to 2 mg and observe over 5 to 10 minutes for clinical response
options.rationale: A parenteral lorazepam challenge produces a marked reduction in catatonic signs within minutes in over half of cases and confirms the diagnosis and pathway. (Source: RANZCP catatonia guidance)

options.text: Start scheduled diazepam 5 mg orally three times a day and review response again in 48 hours
options.rationale: Oral diazepam is too slow and pharmacokinetically poor in this context; parenteral lorazepam is the standard test dose and treatment. (Source: RANZCP catatonia guidance)

options.text: Reassure the medical team this is psychogenic and arrange psychotherapy review in the community
options.rationale: Catatonia is a neuropsychiatric syndrome with substantial mortality if untreated; dismissing it as psychogenic is unsafe and incorrect. (Source: RANZCP catatonia guidance)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is identified clinically using the Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale and confirmed pharmacologically by response to a parenteral lorazepam challenge. The standard dose is 1 to 2 mg IM or IV with marked reduction in catatonic signs within 5 to 10 minutes considered a positive response. Treatment continues with scheduled lorazepam, titrated as tolerated (often 6 to 24 mg daily total in divided doses). Refractory catatonia, malignant catatonia (with autonomic instability and hyperthermia), or NMS-like presentation responds best to ECT. Antipsychotics may exacerbate catatonia and risk NMS, so are avoided unless the catatonia is clearly settled.
key_points: Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale screens 14 items
Parenteral lorazepam 1 to 2 mg is diagnostic and therapeutic
Marked reduction in 5 to 10 minutes confirms catatonia
ECT is first-line for malignant or refractory catatonia
Avoid antipsychotics until catatonia clearly settled
explanation.pearls: Malignant catatonia (with hyperthermia, autonomic instability, raised CK) is clinically indistinguishable from neuroleptic malignant syndrome and is treated identically with cessation of dopamine antagonists, supportive care, lorazepam, and early ECT.

subtopic_detail: DSM-5 timing rule discriminating schizoaffective disorder from bipolar disorder with psychotic features
stem: You are the consultant psychiatrist reviewing a 27-year-old man on an extended inpatient admission. Over the past 12 months he has had two confirmed episodes of mania each lasting around 2 weeks accompanied by persistent grandiose delusions. Between these manic episodes, the family describe approximately 6 weeks of continued grandiose delusions and auditory hallucinations without mood disturbance. He has had ongoing psychotic symptoms for most of the last 12 months. He is currently euthymic but continues to describe special abilities.

data_table.Substance use: Nil illicit substances on urine drug screen, no alcohol misuse
data_table.Medical workup: CT brain, full medical workup, autoimmune encephalitis screen negative
data_table.Mental state: Euthymic mood, hyperreligious content, paranoid persecutory delusions, no formal thought disorder
data_table.Family history: Father with bipolar I disorder, paternal aunt with schizophrenia

lead_in: Which diagnosis best fits the DSM-5 timing rule?

options.text: Schizoaffective disorder bipolar type is the best fit given the longitudinal pattern of symptoms
options.rationale: DSM-5 requires delusions or hallucinations for 2 weeks or more in the absence of a major mood episode, with mood symptoms present for the majority of the total illness duration; both criteria are met here. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Bipolar I disorder with mood-congruent psychotic features is the most accurate single diagnosis
options.rationale: Bipolar I with psychotic features requires psychosis only during mood episodes; psychosis here persists outside manic episodes. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Schizophrenia with comorbid bipolar I disorder is the most accurate combined diagnosis
options.rationale: Comorbid diagnosis is not used when criteria for schizoaffective disorder are met; schizoaffective is the integrating diagnosis. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Brief psychotic disorder with marked stressor is the most accurate diagnosis presently
options.rationale: Brief psychotic disorder requires symptoms to last less than 1 month; 12 months of psychotic illness excludes this. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Delusional disorder grandiose type is the most accurate single diagnosis in this presentation
options.rationale: Delusional disorder requires absence of other psychotic features beyond delusion and minimal functional impairment; hallucinations and manic episodes exclude this. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

explanation.summary: Schizoaffective disorder is the integrating DSM-5 diagnosis when psychosis persists for at least 2 weeks in the absence of a major mood episode and mood episodes are present for the majority of the total illness. The bipolar subtype includes manic episodes; the depressive subtype includes depressive episodes only. Discrimination from bipolar I with psychotic features hinges on whether psychotic symptoms persist outside mood episodes. Treatment uses second-generation antipsychotics (paliperidone has the only FDA indication) and a mood stabiliser; the choice of lithium or anticonvulsant depends on episode polarity and individual factors.
key_points: Psychosis for 2 weeks or more without mood episode is required
Mood episodes must be present for majority of total illness
Bipolar subtype includes mania; depressive subtype does not
Comorbid schizophrenia plus bipolar is not assigned when criteria met
Antipsychotic plus mood stabiliser is the standard treatment
explanation.pearls: Family history of both schizophrenia and bipolar disorder is over-represented in schizoaffective disorder, supporting it as a distinct genetic entity rather than a coincidence of the two main psychoses.

subtopic_detail: Discriminating cannabis-induced psychotic disorder from first-episode primary psychosis
stem: You are the registrar in the early psychosis service reviewing a 19-year-old man who is 7 days post-discharge from an inpatient unit following a first presentation with persecutory delusions, auditory hallucinations and disorganised thinking. Symptoms began acutely 4 weeks ago after heavy daily cannabis use over 6 months. He has been abstinent from cannabis for 14 days under family supervision. Olanzapine 10 mg nightly was started during admission with marked improvement.

data_table.Mental state: Euthymic affect, persecutory ideas now overvalued not fixed, no hallucinations, fully oriented
data_table.Family history: Paternal cousin with schizophrenia, maternal grandmother with depression
data_table.Substance history: Daily high-potency cannabis 0.5 to 1 g for 6 months, no other substances, no withdrawal
data_table.Medical workup: Urine drug screen positive cannabis at admission, repeat now negative; CT brain normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan now?

options.text: Stop olanzapine immediately as it is no longer required following discharge from inpatient unit
options.rationale: Even substance-induced psychotic episodes typically need antipsychotic continuation for several months and abrupt cessation risks relapse. (Source: RANZCP psychosis guideline)

options.text: Refer for a Mental Health Act community treatment order to enforce ongoing antipsychotic medication
options.rationale: Voluntary engagement with family support is appropriate; a CTO is not justified in a cooperative young person with insight. (Source: RANZCP psychosis guideline)

options.text: Switch olanzapine to amisulpride to avoid future metabolic risk and review at 6 months only
options.rationale: Switching agents during a successful response is unnecessary; metabolic monitoring with continued olanzapine is the standard initial path. (Source: RANZCP psychosis guideline)

options.text: Continue olanzapine for at least 6 months with brief structured cannabis use intervention and headspace follow-up
options.rationale: Australian early psychosis guidance recommends maintaining antipsychotic for at least 6 to 12 months after first-episode psychosis with intensive cannabis cessation support; persistence of symptoms beyond 1 month off cannabis would reclassify the disorder. (Source: RANZCP psychosis guideline)

options.text: Provide reassurance and discharge to the GP for a single follow-up appointment in 3 months
options.rationale: Discharge without intensive early-psychosis follow-up loses the highest-impact window of intervention. (Source: RANZCP psychosis guideline)

explanation.summary: Cannabis-induced psychotic disorder shares features with first-episode primary psychosis, but discrimination requires longitudinal observation. DSM-5 substance-induced psychotic disorder requires psychotic symptoms during or within 1 month of intoxication or withdrawal AND attribution beyond mere co-occurrence. If psychotic symptoms persist for more than 1 month after substance cessation, a primary psychotic disorder diagnosis is favoured. Even in confirmed substance-induced episodes, approximately 30 to 50 percent transition to a primary psychotic disorder within 3 years, especially with heavy use of high-potency cannabis from a young age and a family history. Early psychosis services provide intensive support during this critical window.
key_points: Persistence of psychosis more than 1 month after cessation suggests primary disorder
Approximately 30 to 50 percent transition to primary psychosis within 3 years
High-potency cannabis and youth amplify transition risk
Continue antipsychotic at least 6 to 12 months after first episode
Intensive early psychosis service and substance support reduce relapse
explanation.pearls: Heavy cannabis use before age 15 confers roughly four-fold increased risk of adult schizophrenia in cohort studies, with the COMT Val/Val polymorphism implicated in mediating risk.

subtopic_detail: Recognition of GHB overdose presenting with rapid fluctuation in conscious state
stem: You are the emergency registrar reviewing a 23-year-old woman brought in by ambulance from a music festival. She was found unresponsive in a portable toilet and on arrival has fluctuating GCS rapidly between 4 and 12 over 20 minutes. She has no signs of trauma, miosis, or pupillary asymmetry. Her vital signs are stable. Bystanders saw no injectables and no prescription containers. She has woken briefly, become agitated, and then dropped GCS again twice.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.6, HR 64, BP 110/70 mmHg, RR 12, SpO2 99 percent on 4 L oxygen via Hudson
data_table.Examination: No trauma, pupils 4 mm reactive, no needle tracks, no neck rigidity
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.36, lactate 1.8, glucose 5.4 mmol/L, paracetamol and salicylate negative, ethanol 0.04
data_table.Urine toxicology: Pending; rapid amphetamine and opioid panel negative

lead_in: Which is the most likely cause of her presentation?

options.text: Acute opioid overdose despite negative urine drug screen and absence of typical examination signs
options.rationale: Opioid overdose produces persistent miosis and respiratory depression rather than rapid swings between alertness and unconsciousness. (Source: NSW Toxicology Service)

options.text: Gamma-hydroxybutyrate intoxication producing characteristic rapid fluctuation in conscious state
options.rationale: GHB intoxication classically produces rapid swings between deep coma and combative wakefulness over short periods, typically resolving within 4 to 6 hours, and is undetectable on standard urine panels. (Source: NSW Toxicology Service)

options.text: MDMA toxicity with serotonin syndrome accounting for the presentation and observed symptoms
options.rationale: MDMA toxicity produces hyperthermia, hypertension, hyponatraemia, and serotonin syndrome features rather than coma fluctuation. (Source: NSW Toxicology Service)

options.text: Acute methamphetamine intoxication producing rapid swings between agitation and unresponsiveness
options.rationale: Methamphetamine intoxication produces sustained sympathomimetic features (tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia) rather than reduced GCS. (Source: NSW Toxicology Service)

options.text: Cannabis intoxication producing acute psychosis with associated rapid fluctuation in conscious state
options.rationale: Cannabis intoxication rarely depresses GCS in healthy young adults and does not produce minute-to-minute fluctuation. (Source: NSW Toxicology Service)

explanation.summary: Gamma-hydroxybutyrate (GHB) and the pro-drugs GBL and 1,4-butanediol are colourless, odourless liquids commonly used at festivals. Intoxication is characterised by rapid fluctuation between deep coma and combative wakefulness over a 4 to 6 hour course. Bradycardia, mild respiratory depression, and vomiting are common. Standard urine drug screens do not detect GHB and the diagnosis is clinical. Management is supportive with airway protection, lateral positioning, oxygen and observation; intubation is reserved for sustained loss of airway reflexes or aspiration. Withdrawal in dependent users is dangerous and resembles severe alcohol withdrawal with delirium and seizures; treatment is with high-dose benzodiazepines.
key_points: Rapid fluctuation between coma and arousal is the hallmark of GHB
Effects resolve within 4 to 6 hours with supportive care
GHB is not detected on standard urine drug screens
Co-ingestion (alcohol, benzodiazepines) prolongs and deepens coma
GHB withdrawal needs benzodiazepines and may need ICU
explanation.pearls: Flumazenil and naloxone do not reverse GHB intoxication and giving them risks precipitating mixed benzodiazepine or opioid withdrawal when there has been co-ingestion.

subtopic_detail: Discriminating functional neurological disorder from malingering and factitious disorder
stem: You are the neurology registrar consulted on a 38-year-old woman with sudden right-sided weakness on awakening 5 days ago. There was no headache, dysphasia, or facial droop. MRI brain and MR angiography are normal. Examination shows positive Hoover sign on the right leg, sudden weakness that reverses with distraction, and intact reflexes. She is distressed by the symptoms, has missed work, and is requesting a second neurological opinion. There is no ongoing legal claim and no external secondary gain identified.

data_table.Examination: Hoover sign positive, give-way weakness in right upper and lower limb, deep tendon reflexes 2+ symmetric, no clonus
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain, MR angiography, glucose, electrolytes, CK all normal
data_table.Psychosocial: Distressed by symptoms, no compensation claim, no military or insurance context
data_table.Behaviour: Cooperative with examination, willing to engage with physiotherapy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate diagnosis and next step?

options.text: Malingering: discharge with safety-net advice and no further follow-up needed at present
options.rationale: Malingering requires an identifiable external incentive (avoiding work, compensation, criminal proceedings), which is absent here. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Factitious disorder imposed on self: refer for psychiatric management and avoid further investigation
options.rationale: Factitious disorder requires intentional deception to assume the sick role; willingness to engage with physiotherapy and distress about symptoms argues against this. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Conversion disorder: order CT angiogram of the carotids to rule out a missed structural cause
options.rationale: Further imaging is not indicated when MRI and MR angiography are already normal and positive functional signs are present; FND is a rule-in diagnosis. (Source: ANZAN FND consensus)

options.text: Stroke mimic: admit for observation on stroke unit with 24-hour neurological observations performed
options.rationale: FND with positive signs and normal imaging does not require stroke unit admission. (Source: ANZAN FND consensus)

options.text: Functional neurological disorder: explain diagnosis using positive signs and refer for specialist FND physiotherapy
options.rationale: FND is now a positive rule-in diagnosis based on internal inconsistency signs (Hoover, distractibility), with neurologist-led explanation and specialist FND physiotherapy as the evidence-based first step. (Source: ANZAN FND consensus)

explanation.summary: DSM-5 frames functional neurological symptom disorder (conversion disorder) as a positive rule-in diagnosis: incompatibility between symptoms and recognised neurological disease, plus internal inconsistency on examination such as Hoover sign, hip abductor sign, drift without pronation, or distractibility. Malingering and factitious disorder both require intentional symptom production; malingering for external incentive, factitious to assume the sick role. Most patients with FND have neither; they have genuine, distressing, involuntary symptoms. Management is led by neurology with positive explanation of the diagnosis using demonstration of the signs to the patient, structured physiotherapy with FND-trained therapists, and CBT or psychiatric input when comorbid depression or trauma is present.
key_points: FND is a positive rule-in diagnosis with internal inconsistency signs
Hoover sign and distractibility have high specificity for FND
Malingering requires identifiable external incentive
Factitious disorder requires intentional deception for sick role
Specialist FND physiotherapy is evidence-based first treatment
explanation.pearls: Demonstrating Hoover sign to the patient at the bedside as part of the diagnostic explanation produces a higher rate of acceptance and engagement with FND physiotherapy than the explanation alone.

stem: A 28-year-old software engineer presents to your general practice clinic asking about adult ADHD assessment after his partner suggested it. He describes lifelong difficulty completing projects at work, frequently losing his keys, interrupting in meetings, and being unable to sit through long presentations since primary school. School reports from age 9 documented inattention and disruptive behaviour. He has used cannabis socially on weekends for years and drinks four to six standard drinks two nights per week, which he describes as helping his racing thoughts settle. There is no personal history of mood disorder or psychosis. His mother had similar inattention as a child.

data_table.Examination: Mildly fidgety, well groomed, normal mental state examination
data_table.Investigations: Adult Self-Report Scale (ASRS-v1.1) part A: 6 of 6 positive screening items

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his ADHD assessment?

options.text: Refer to a psychiatrist after a four-week substance-free observation period from alcohol and cannabis
options.rationale: Adult ADHD diagnosis in Australia requires specialist (psychiatrist or paediatrician) confirmation under PBS authority, and DSM-5 requires symptoms are not better explained by substance effects, so a substance-free observation period improves diagnostic accuracy before specialist review. (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Practice Guideline 2022)

options.text: Commence methylphenidate immediate release as a four-week diagnostic and therapeutic primary-care trial
options.rationale: Initiating stimulants without specialist diagnosis breaches PBS authority requirements for adult ADHD and exposes a patient with active alcohol and cannabis use to diversion and cardiovascular risk without baseline ECG or substance stabilisation. (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Practice Guideline 2022)

options.text: Order brain MRI and quantitative EEG to confirm the diagnosis before any specialist referral
options.rationale: Neuroimaging and quantitative EEG have no validated role in routine adult ADHD diagnosis under the RANZCP guideline; diagnosis remains clinical using DSM-5 criteria with corroborative collateral history. (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Practice Guideline 2022)

options.text: Reassure that adult ADHD is unlikely given his tertiary attainment and review routinely in twelve months
options.rationale: Tertiary attainment does not exclude adult ADHD; many adults compensate at high cognitive cost and present in their twenties when role demands exceed compensatory capacity, so this represents a missed diagnosis pathway. (Source: NICE NG87 ADHD: diagnosis and management 2019)
source_refs: NICE NG87 ADHD: diagnosis and management 2019

options.text: Refer directly for cognitive behavioural therapy targeting inattention without prior diagnostic clarification
options.rationale: CBT for ADHD is an evidence-based adjunct but is delivered after diagnostic clarification because the formulation and skills target ADHD-specific deficits; bypassing diagnosis also forfeits stimulant access if criteria are met. (Source: NICE NG87 ADHD: diagnosis and management 2019)
source_refs: NICE NG87 ADHD: diagnosis and management 2019

explanation.summary: Adult ADHD assessment in Australia requires specialist confirmation under PBS authority before stimulant initiation, with DSM-5 explicitly requiring exclusion of substance-attributable symptoms. Concurrent alcohol and cannabis use materially impairs diagnostic accuracy because both can produce inattention and emotional dysregulation that mimic ADHD. Best practice is to refer to a psychiatrist while requesting the patient observe a defined substance-free period to optimise the assessment. Stimulant trials in primary care, neuroimaging, and reflexive reassurance based on educational attainment are all common pitfalls.
key_points: Adult ADHD diagnosis in AU requires psychiatrist or paediatrician confirmation for PBS-authority stimulants
DSM-5 requires symptoms are not better explained by substance use
Cannabis and alcohol both mimic inattention; a four-week substance-free window aids assessment
Neuroimaging and qEEG are not validated diagnostic tools for adult ADHD
explanation.pearls: When a patient drinks four or more standard drinks more than twice weekly or uses cannabis regularly, arrange specialist referral with a planned four-week minimum substance-free assessment window rather than initiating methylphenidate or lisdexamfetamine in primary care.

sources.label: NICE NG87 ADHD: diagnosis and management 2019

stem: A 54-year-old taxi driver presents to your general practice clinic motivated to quit smoking. He has smoked 25 cigarettes per day for 35 years and his last serious quit attempt with patches alone failed at four weeks. He has stable major depressive disorder on sertraline 100 mg daily with no recent suicidal ideation. He has well-controlled hypertension and a history of recurrent vivid dreams when he tried mirtazapine briefly two years ago. He drinks alcohol occasionally, has no renal impairment, and asks for the most effective pharmacotherapy to combine with brief counselling.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 76, BP 132/80, RR 14, SpO2 96% on room air
data_table.Examination: Mood euthymic, no current passive or active suicidal ideation; PHQ-9 score 5
data_table.Investigations: eGFR 88 mL/min/1.73m2; LFTs within reference range
data_table.Medications: Sertraline 100 mg daily; perindopril 5 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy to recommend?

options.text: Nicotine patch 21 mg daily as monotherapy starting on his planned quit day without short-acting NRT
options.rationale: Single-form NRT has lower quit rates than combination NRT or varenicline and has already failed in this patient; monotherapy patch is not the best next-line choice. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation 2021)

options.text: Varenicline with standard titration to 1 mg twice daily, commenced one to two weeks before a planned quit day
options.rationale: Varenicline produces the highest single-agent quit rates and is appropriate in stable depression on SSRI; the standard titration to 1 mg twice daily and start one to two weeks pre-quit date allows nicotinic receptor saturation by the quit day. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation 2021)

options.text: Bupropion titrating from 150 mg daily to 150 mg twice daily, commenced one week before a planned quit day
options.rationale: Bupropion is a reasonable option but its combination with sertraline raises serotonergic and seizure-threshold considerations, and head-to-head data favour varenicline for quit-rate efficacy. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation 2021)

options.text: Nortriptyline 75 mg nocte for cessation after cross-tapering sertraline off over the preceding fortnight
options.rationale: Nortriptyline is a second-line cessation option with worse tolerability and would require disrupting effective antidepressant therapy without sound clinical justification. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation 2021)

options.text: Defer pharmacotherapy and refer for hypnotherapy and acupuncture as first-line cessation interventions
options.rationale: Hypnotherapy and acupuncture lack robust evidence for sustained cessation and deferring proven pharmacotherapy in a motivated heavy smoker reduces the probability of quitting. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation 2021)

explanation.summary: Varenicline remains the most efficacious single-agent smoking cessation pharmacotherapy in Australian primary care and is appropriate in patients with stable, well-treated depression. Standard titration is 0.5 mg once daily for three days, then 0.5 mg twice daily for four days, then 1 mg twice daily, commenced one to two weeks before the planned quit day. Combination NRT (patch plus short-acting) is the alternative when varenicline is contraindicated or not tolerated. Bupropion and nortriptyline are second-line and complicated by interactions with SSRIs.
key_points: Varenicline > combination NRT > single NRT > bupropion > nortriptyline for quit-rate efficacy
Standard titration ends at 1 mg twice daily; start one to two weeks before quit day
Stable, well-managed depression is not a contraindication to varenicline under RACGP guidance
Patient has already failed monotherapy patch; do not repeat the same approach
explanation.pearls: For a motivated heavy smoker with previous patch-only failure, prescribe varenicline started one to two weeks before quit day rather than repeating single-form NRT - PBS subsidises 12 weeks of varenicline once per year with twice-yearly access criteria documented in the RACGP guideline.

stem: A 27-year-old man with a first episode of schizophrenia commenced olanzapine 10 mg nightly six weeks ago in your community mental health clinic. He attends for routine review feeling more settled with reduced auditory hallucinations, but reports increased appetite and a 4 kg weight gain. He has no personal or family history of diabetes. He has not had any pre-treatment baseline metabolic bloods taken because he was acutely unwell at initiation. He smokes ten cigarettes per day and drinks no alcohol. He asks how often you will be checking his physical health.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 84, BP 128/78, RR 14, SpO2 99%, weight 86 kg (baseline 82 kg), waist 96 cm
data_table.Examination: Morning sedation only, no abnormal movements, BMI 27.8
data_table.Investigations: Pending: fasting lipids, fasting glucose or HbA1c, prolactin

lead_in: Which metabolic monitoring schedule best matches Australian best-practice for olanzapine?

options.text: Fasting glucose or HbA1c, fasting lipids and waist at three months and then twelve-monthly while stable
options.rationale: Three-month intervals miss the peak window for olanzapine-induced metabolic change, which occurs in the first 12 weeks; the recommended early review is at 6 and 12 weeks. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia 2016)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia 2016

options.text: Fasting lipids only at six months with weight and waist circumference checked at twelve-monthly intervals
options.rationale: This schedule under-monitors glucose despite olanzapine being among the highest-risk antipsychotics for new-onset diabetes; weight at annual intervals also misses early intervention windows. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia 2016)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia 2016

options.text: Weight and waist at every visit; fasting glucose or HbA1c and fasting lipids at baseline, twelve weeks, then yearly
options.rationale: Baseline (because none was done), 12-week reassessment, and at least annual review thereafter is the RANZCP-endorsed minimum schedule for high metabolic-risk antipsychotics like olanzapine, with weight and waist at each contact. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia 2016)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia 2016

options.text: ECG and prolactin only at six and twelve months without routine glucose or lipid testing during the first year
options.rationale: Olanzapine has minimal QT impact and low prolactin elevation; the priority metabolic targets (glucose, lipids, weight) are not addressed by this schedule. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia 2016)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia 2016

options.text: Two-yearly OGTT only, with no routine fasting lipid, weight or waist monitoring required during the interval
