explanation.pearls: AMH guidance: valproate prescribing in women of childbearing potential requires pregnancy prevention plus active plan for switch to lithium or lamotrigine before conception.

stem: A 34-year-old man attends his general practice seeking assessment for adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. He reports lifelong difficulty completing tasks, frequent job changes due to disorganisation, and being told he was disruptive at primary school. School reports from year 4 confirm restlessness and inattention. He scored highly on a self-administered Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS-v1.1). He has a remote past of cannabis use (ceased 5 years ago), no current substance use, no current depressive episode, and is otherwise medically well. He has no history of cardiac disease and his resting ECG is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 70, BP 122/78, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Engaged, fidgety, no thought disorder; affect bright; school reports support childhood symptoms
data_table.Investigations: ASRS-v1.1 part A positive (6/6); ECG sinus rhythm; thyroid function normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his diagnostic pathway?

options.text: Commence a trial of methylphenidate immediate-release 10 mg three times daily for 4 weeks and reassess response
options.rationale: Adult ADHD prescribing of stimulants in Australia is restricted to specialist initiation under state-based authority arrangements; GP-initiated trial is not permitted. (Source: RANZCP CPG: ADHD; State Health Department Stimulant Approvals)

options.text: Refer to a psychiatrist or paediatrician with adult ADHD experience for diagnostic assessment and treatment authority
options.rationale: Adult ADHD in Australia is diagnosed and treated by a specialist (psychiatrist or paediatrician with adult experience) who can obtain the state-based stimulant approval; GPs may then continue prescribing under shared-care arrangements. (Source: RANZCP CPG: ADHD)

options.text: Refer for neuropsychological testing as a prerequisite to any specialist clinical assessment for adult ADHD
options.rationale: Neuropsychological testing supports complex cases but is not a prerequisite; AU guidance is clinical diagnosis based on history, collateral, and DSM-5 criteria. (Source: RANZCP CPG: ADHD)

options.text: Provide reassurance, cognitive behavioural therapy referral, and reassess in 12 months without diagnostic workup
options.rationale: Established functional impairment and a positive screen warrant specialist assessment; deferring CBT alone without diagnosis is inadequate. (Source: RANZCP CPG: ADHD)

options.text: Prescribe atomoxetine 40 mg daily as a non-stimulant alternative bypassing the need for specialist diagnostic assessment
options.rationale: Atomoxetine still requires the same specialist diagnostic assessment as stimulants; non-stimulant choice does not bypass diagnostic pathway. (Source: RANZCP CPG: ADHD)

explanation.summary: Adult ADHD diagnosis in Australia requires DSM-5-TR criteria fulfilment with childhood-onset features, collateral history, functional impairment in two or more domains, and exclusion of alternative explanations. Pharmacological treatment is specialist-initiated: psychostimulants (methylphenidate, dexamfetamine, lisdexamfetamine) require state-based authority approvals, while atomoxetine and guanfacine are non-stimulant alternatives. Once stable, GPs may continue prescribing under shared-care arrangements. Driving safety, cardiovascular history, and substance misuse are formal risk-assessment domains.
key_points: AU adult ADHD requires specialist (psychiatrist or paediatrician) diagnosis and treatment initiation
Stimulants require state-based authority
Childhood-onset features must be documented
Cardiovascular and driving risks must be assessed before stimulant initiation
explanation.pearls: AU adult ADHD: specialist (psychiatrist or paediatrician) initiates stimulants under state-based authority; GPs continue under shared care.

sources.label: AADPA Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

subtopic_detail: Bipolar I maintenance with depressive predominance
stem:
A 34-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder presents to your community psychiatry clinic 8 weeks after recovering from her most recent depressive episode. Her illness pattern over 6 years includes one hypomanic episode 5 years ago and four depressive episodes, the most recent requiring inpatient admission. She is currently euthymic and tolerated her acute treatment of quetiapine and sertraline well, but has gained 8 kg and complains of sedation.

Her renal function is normal. She is sexually active and uses a copper intrauterine device. She wants a single maintenance agent with the best evidence for preventing further depressive relapse.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 72, BP 124/78, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 36.5
data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no psychomotor change, no suicidal ideation; BMI 28.4 kg/m^2
data_table.Investigations: TSH 2.1; UEC normal; LFTs normal; eGFR > 90

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate maintenance pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Continue sertraline as the sole maintenance agent and review every 3 months in psychiatry clinic
options.rationale: Antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar I disorder raises the risk of mood switching and rapid cycling and is contraindicated as a maintenance strategy; an effective mood stabiliser is required. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

options.text: Switch to carbamazepine titrated to a target serum level for relapse prevention
options.rationale: Carbamazepine has efficacy in bipolar mania but is less effective than lamotrigine for preventing the depressive pole and carries significant CYP3A4 induction and rash burden. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Continue quetiapine 300 mg nocte indefinitely as the established maintenance choice in bipolar I disorder
options.rationale: Quetiapine has bipolar maintenance evidence but the patient has weight gain and sedation that are unlikely to remit; a switch to an agent with depressive-pole evidence and a better metabolic profile is appropriate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Initiate sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily and titrate to a maintenance serum trough level
options.rationale: Valproate is teratogenic and is not first-line for women of reproductive age; it also has weaker evidence than lamotrigine in preventing the depressive pole of bipolar I. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Initiate lamotrigine with slow titration to a target maintenance dose with monitoring for skin reaction
options.rationale: Lamotrigine has the strongest evidence for preventing the depressive pole of bipolar I disorder, is metabolically neutral, and is acceptable in women of reproductive age; slow titration over 6 weeks minimises the risk of serious cutaneous reaction. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

explanation.summary: Maintenance pharmacotherapy in bipolar I disorder is tailored to the predominant pole of relapse. Lithium remains gold standard for overall prevention but lamotrigine has the strongest evidence for preventing the depressive pole, with a clean metabolic and reproductive safety profile. Valproate is teratogenic and avoided in women of reproductive age. Antidepressant monotherapy is contraindicated due to manic switch risk. Quetiapine has maintenance evidence but its metabolic burden often drives a switch. Slow lamotrigine titration over 6 weeks reduces the risk of serious cutaneous adverse reactions.
key_points: Lamotrigine prevents depressive relapse in bipolar I with the strongest evidence base
Antidepressant monotherapy is unsafe in bipolar I disorder
Valproate is teratogenic and avoided in women of reproductive age
Lamotrigine titration is slow and the patient must report any new rash
explanation.pearls: Lamotrigine for the depressive pole, lithium for overall relapse prevention; combine when needed. Titrate lamotrigine over 6 weeks and stop on any rash.

stem:
A 38-year-old woman with treatment-resistant major depression is brought to the emergency department by family after 4 days of progressive withdrawal. Today she has been mute, has not eaten or drunk, and has remained in awkward postures for hours. On examination she stares ahead without blinking, will hold an arm raised when placed there for over a minute, and shows a positive grasp reflex.

Her father remembers her stopping olanzapine 3 weeks ago. Bloods show a creatine kinase of 1500, normal renal function, normal calcium, and a venous pH of 7.39. Temperature is normal and there is no rigidity.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, BP 124/76, Temp 36.6
data_table.Examination: Mute, immobile with waxy flexibility on positioning; staring without blinking; no tremor or rigidity
data_table.Investigations: CK 1500, UEC normal, calcium normal, glucose 4.8, urine drug screen negative; CT brain unremarkable

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Intravenous lorazepam 1 to 2 mg now and reassess catatonia signs within 10 minutes
options.rationale: The lorazepam challenge of 1 to 2 mg intravenously confirms the diagnosis and provides the first-line treatment in benzodiazepine-responsive catatonia; a clear response supports continued scheduled lorazepam with ECT planned for non-response. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Position Statement)

options.text: Intramuscular haloperidol 5 mg with promethazine 25 mg for behavioural containment of agitation
options.rationale: Antipsychotics worsen catatonia and risk precipitating neuroleptic malignant syndrome, particularly in a recently neuroleptic-exposed patient; behavioural agents are inappropriate when the picture is hypokinetic. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Position Statement)

options.text: Commence intravenous dantrolene as empirical treatment for suspected neuroleptic malignant syndrome
options.rationale: NMS is excluded by the absence of fever, rigidity, and autonomic instability; CK elevation alone in immobile catatonia does not justify dantrolene and delays specific therapy. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Position Statement)

options.text: Transfer to a medical ward for nutritional support and observation without psychiatric intervention
options.rationale: Catatonia carries significant mortality from dehydration, venous thromboembolism, and pneumonia if untreated; transfer without first-line lorazepam delays definitive care. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Position Statement)

options.text: Restart olanzapine at her previous maintenance dose with intravenous fluid support as needed
options.rationale: Resuming the antipsychotic she stopped 3 weeks ago risks NMS in this state and does not treat catatonia; lorazepam is the first-line agent regardless of underlying mood or psychotic disorder. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Position Statement)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a neuropsychiatric syndrome characterised by stupor, mutism, posturing, waxy flexibility, negativism, and stereotypies, occurring across mood, psychotic, neurological, and medical conditions. The Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale supports diagnosis. First-line treatment is intravenous lorazepam 1 to 2 mg as a challenge dose, with rapid response supporting continued scheduled benzodiazepine therapy. ECT is the definitive treatment for malignant or non-responsive catatonia. Antipsychotics worsen catatonia and risk neuroleptic malignant syndrome; they are avoided until catatonia resolves.
key_points: First-line treatment is intravenous lorazepam 1 to 2 mg as a challenge dose
Antipsychotics are avoided as they worsen catatonia and risk NMS
ECT is the definitive treatment when benzodiazepines fail
Catatonia is missed when CK elevation triggers a presumed NMS workup without checking catatonic signs
explanation.pearls: Bush-Francis score >=2 plus a positive lorazepam challenge defines treatable catatonia. Plan ECT early if no response within 24 to 48 hours.

stem:
A 24-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by ambulance 5 hours after taking approximately 50 of her mother's amitriptyline 25 mg tablets in a deliberate self-harm episode. She has had a brief seizure during transit. On arrival she is drowsy with a GCS of 11, dry mucous membranes, mydriasis, and a tachycardia of 130. Her blood pressure is 90/58.

An ECG shows sinus tachycardia with a QRS duration of 140 ms and a terminal R wave in aVR of 5 mm. Capillary glucose is 5.2 and pH from a venous gas is 7.30 with a lactate of 4.0.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 130, RR 22, SpO2 98% on 6 L mask, BP 90/58, Temp 36.8
data_table.Examination: GCS 11; dry mucous membranes; mydriasis; warm dry skin; bowel sounds absent
data_table.Investigations: ECG: sinus tachycardia QRS 140 ms, R wave in aVR 5 mm; venous pH 7.30, lactate 4.0; glucose 5.2

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Administer activated charcoal 50 g via nasogastric tube as the immediate priority for decontamination
options.rationale: Activated charcoal is reserved for presentations within 1 to 2 hours with a protected airway; at 5 hours and a depressed conscious level it adds aspiration risk without meaningful absorption benefit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Administer intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg to reverse the depressed conscious level
options.rationale: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, not TCAs, and in mixed overdose risks precipitating seizures; it is contraindicated in TCA toxicity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg as a bolus targeting a serum pH of 7.45 to 7.55
options.rationale: QRS prolongation above 100 ms in TCA overdose indicates cardiotoxicity and warrants sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg to a target pH of 7.45 to 7.55, which displaces TCA from sodium channels and narrows the QRS; bolus is repeated as needed and infusion may follow. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Administer intramuscular physostigmine as an anticholinergic reversal agent for the toxidrome
options.rationale: Physostigmine in TCA overdose precipitates asystole and seizures and is contraindicated; the cardiotoxicity is sodium channel blockade, not pure anticholinergic excess. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Administer intravenous calcium gluconate 10 percent 10 mL to stabilise the cardiac membrane
options.rationale: Calcium is used in hyperkalaemia and in calcium channel blocker overdose; it has no role in TCA cardiotoxicity, where sodium loading with bicarbonate is the specific intervention. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

explanation.summary: TCA overdose causes sodium channel blockade with QRS prolongation, anticholinergic toxidrome, seizures, hypotension, and refractory ventricular arrhythmias. ECG features predictive of toxicity include QRS above 100 ms and a terminal R wave in aVR above 3 mm. Sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg is the specific antidote, working through sodium loading and alkalinisation to narrow the QRS and stabilise the membrane; it is repeated until QRS narrows and pH reaches 7.45 to 7.55. Adjuncts include benzodiazepines for seizures, intubation, and noradrenaline for refractory hypotension. Lipid emulsion is considered for refractory cardiotoxicity. Flumazenil and physostigmine are contraindicated.
key_points: QRS above 100 ms or R wave in aVR above 3 mm predicts TCA cardiotoxicity
Sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus is the specific antidote
Target pH is 7.45 to 7.55 with QRS narrowing as the clinical endpoint
Flumazenil and physostigmine are contraindicated in TCA overdose
explanation.pearls: The R wave in aVR is the most sensitive ECG predictor of TCA toxicity; above 3 mm warrants pre-emptive bicarbonate even if QRS is still under 100 ms.

subtopic_detail: Schizoaffective disorder vs bipolar with psychosis
stem: A 28-year-old woman is admitted for the third time in two years with persecutory delusions, auditory hallucinations of two voices arguing, and disorganised thought. Records show two distinct presentations: an 8-week episode of severe depression with congruent psychotic features 18 months ago, and a 3-week manic presentation with grandiose delusions 10 months ago. Between episodes she has continued to report ongoing auditory hallucinations and persecutory beliefs persisting for at least 4 weeks at a stretch without prominent mood symptoms. Substance use and medical causes are excluded.

data_table.Examination: Disorganised speech; second-person auditory hallucinations; persecutory delusions; mood currently mildly elevated
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative; TSH normal; CT brain unremarkable; B12 normal

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type, given mood episodes alongside persistent psychotic symptoms without mood
options.rationale: DSM-5 schizoaffective disorder requires a major mood episode concurrent with criterion A schizophrenia symptoms plus at least 2 weeks of psychotic symptoms without prominent mood; presence of both manic and depressive episodes qualifies as the bipolar subtype. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Bipolar I disorder with psychotic features only present during episodes of mania or major depressive disturbance
options.rationale: Bipolar I with psychotic features confines psychosis to mood episodes; documented psychosis lasting at least 2 weeks without prominent mood symptoms rules this out. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Schizophrenia with secondary mood symptoms occurring as a brief minor reaction to ongoing psychotic experience
options.rationale: Schizophrenia requires that any mood episodes be brief relative to the total duration of psychosis; here two distinct full mood episodes meeting duration criteria exclude that pattern. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Major depressive disorder with mood-congruent psychotic features and incidental persistent perceptual phenomena later
options.rationale: MDD with psychotic features cannot account for a manic episode meeting full duration and symptom criteria; a manic episode mandates a bipolar spectrum diagnosis. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Brief psychotic disorder with mood instability emerging in the post-episode recovery and stabilisation phase
options.rationale: Brief psychotic disorder requires symptoms under one month with full return to premorbid function; recurrent presentations over two years with persistent psychosis exclude this. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

explanation.summary: Schizoaffective disorder bridges schizophrenia and mood disorder spectra. DSM-5-TR criteria require a major mood episode concurrent with criterion A schizophrenia symptoms, at least 2 weeks of delusions or hallucinations in the absence of prominent mood symptoms across the lifetime of the illness, and that mood symptoms are present for the majority of the total duration. Bipolar subtype is used when manic episodes have occurred; depressive subtype when only depressive episodes have.
key_points: Schizoaffective needs at least 2 weeks of psychosis without prominent mood
Bipolar subtype requires a manic episode
Bipolar I with psychotic features confines psychosis to mood episodes
Schizophrenia requires mood episodes to be brief relative to overall illness
explanation.pearls: Key DSM-5 differentiator: at least 2 weeks of psychosis WITHOUT prominent mood symptoms makes schizoaffective; psychosis only during mood episodes makes bipolar I with psychotic features.

sources.label: RANZCP Practice Guidelines: Schizophrenia and Related Disorders

stem: A 44-year-old man with bipolar I disorder has been stable on lithium 1000 mg nocte for 6 years with steady-state levels of 0.7 mmol/L. He attends for his routine review with you as his community psychiatry registrar. His baseline 6 years ago showed normal renal function with creatinine 78 micromol/L. He has no new symptoms, takes no nephrotoxic medications, drinks alcohol minimally, and adheres well to his lithium regimen. Today's bloods are reviewed alongside his historical trends.

data_table.Examination: No tremor; no oedema; mental state stable euthymic
data_table.Investigations: Lithium level 0.7 mmol/L; Cr 102 micromol/L (baseline 78); eGFR 68 mL/min/1.73m2 (baseline 92); TSH 3.2 mIU/L; calcium 2.42 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step regarding his renal monitoring?

options.text: Continue 6-monthly U+E and increase frequency only when the eGFR falls below the routine clinical action threshold
options.rationale: A persistent eGFR decline of around 25 percent from baseline over 6 years signals chronic lithium nephrotoxicity and warrants escalation rather than waiting for a worse eGFR. (Source: RANZCP Lithium Monitoring Guidance)

options.text: Repeat U+E and eGFR within 4 weeks, calculate the rate of decline, and arrange nephrology review for shared planning
options.rationale: A trajectory of progressive decline with eGFR drop of 25 percent over years signals lithium-induced chronic interstitial nephropathy; confirming the rate and involving nephrology for risk-benefit re-evaluation is the recommended pathway. (Source: RANZCP Lithium Monitoring Guidance)

options.text: Cease lithium today and start sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily as the immediate substitute mood stabiliser regimen
options.rationale: Abrupt lithium cessation increases relapse risk markedly; switching is a deliberate decision after nephrology input and consideration of alternatives and tapering. (Source: RANZCP Lithium Monitoring Guidance)

options.text: Add an angiotensin receptor blocker to reduce intraglomerular pressure and continue the existing lithium dose unchanged
options.rationale: Adding ARB risks lithium toxicity through reduced renal perfusion and sodium handling and does not arrest lithium nephropathy; nephrology assessment first guides safe management. (Source: RANZCP Lithium Monitoring Guidance)

options.text: Halve the lithium dose now to reduce nephrotoxic exposure and target a level of 0.4 mmol/L at the next steady state
options.rationale: Halving dose risks loss of mood control and subtherapeutic levels without nephrology input; arbitrary dose reduction is not the appropriate response to a declining eGFR trend. (Source: RANZCP Lithium Monitoring Guidance)

explanation.summary: Lithium chronic interstitial nephropathy presents as gradual eGFR decline over years. Routine monitoring is 3-monthly lithium and 6-monthly renal, thyroid, and calcium tests. Decline of around 25 percent from baseline or eGFR under 60 prompts confirmation of rate and nephrology referral to weigh continuation, dose reduction with closer level monitoring, or switching. Abrupt cessation risks relapse and is not done without a parallel plan.
key_points: Routine lithium monitoring: 3-monthly level, 6-monthly renal/thyroid/calcium
25 percent eGFR drop or eGFR under 60 triggers escalation
Confirm trajectory before changing therapy
Nephrology involvement guides continuation vs switch
explanation.pearls: Lithium nephropathy thresholds: confirm trajectory, refer nephrology when eGFR falls 25 percent from baseline or below 60 mL/min, do not stop lithium abruptly because relapse risk is high.

stem: A 52-year-old man with a 30 pack-year smoking history attends his general practice motivated to quit. He has previously attempted nicotine patches alone twice without success and finds withdrawal craving the major barrier. He has stable coronary artery disease, no history of seizures, and no current depression or psychiatric symptoms. He sleeps reasonably and has no nightmares. He is open to combination pharmacotherapy and is supported by his partner. He is keen to know the most effective evidence-based option.

data_table.Examination: No acute respiratory distress; clear chest; no neurological deficits
data_table.Investigations: Routine bloods unremarkable; spirometry FEV1/FVC 75 percent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy option?

options.text: Bupropion 150 mg daily monotherapy escalating to twice daily after 7 days of treatment for 12 weeks total
options.rationale: Bupropion is effective but its abstinence rates are lower than varenicline and its seizure risk excludes it in some patients; varenicline is preferred when not contraindicated. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines)

options.text: Varenicline 0.5 mg daily titrated to 1 mg twice daily over 1 week, started 1 week before nominated quit date
options.rationale: Varenicline is the most effective single agent for smoking cessation; the standard schedule is titrate from 0.5 mg daily up to 1 mg twice daily started 1 week before quit day, with treatment to 12 weeks (or 24 in some). (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines)

options.text: Nicotine replacement therapy patches alone at the same strength previously tried with planned 8-week reducing regimen
options.rationale: The patient has already failed patch monotherapy twice; repeating the same approach without escalation is unlikely to succeed and combination NRT or varenicline is more effective. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines)

options.text: Brief advice and follow-up review in 3 months because all pharmacotherapy options carry significant adverse event risks
options.rationale: Brief advice alone is less effective than combined behavioural and pharmacological support; pharmacotherapy in this motivated patient is appropriate and standard. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines)

options.text: Electronic cigarette substitution with nicotine vaporiser as a less harmful alternative under prescription
options.rationale: Nicotine vaporisers are available on prescription in Australia for cessation when first-line options fail or are unsuitable; they are not the first-line option for a motivated patient with no contraindication to varenicline. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Australian smoking cessation guidance places varenicline as the most effective single agent with continuous abstinence rates at 12 weeks roughly double that of placebo and superior to NRT or bupropion monotherapy. Combination NRT (patch plus oral) is an alternative when varenicline is contraindicated. Behavioural support such as Quitline counselling improves outcomes. Nicotine vaporisers are second line in Australia.
key_points: Varenicline is first-line single agent
Combination NRT (patch + oral) is alternative
Behavioural support always added
Vaporisers on prescription are second line in AU
explanation.pearls: Varenicline regimen: start 0.5 mg daily 1 week before quit day, titrate to 1 mg BD by day 8, continue 12 weeks; double abstinence rate over placebo; mental health symptoms now NOT a contraindication per updated PBS criteria.

stem: A 24-year-old woman is referred to community mental health by her general practitioner after her third presentation in 6 months with non-suicidal self-harm and emotional dysregulation. She meets DSM-5-TR criteria for borderline personality disorder, with affective instability, intense interpersonal relationships, identity disturbance, and recurrent suicidal gestures. She is not currently psychotic, not in a major depressive episode, and is not using substances problematically. She is motivated to engage with structured treatment and has stable housing. She works part-time.

data_table.Examination: Linear superficial cuts on forearm; reactive mood; intact insight; no acute psychotic features; no suicidal intent today
data_table.Investigations: Routine bloods and TSH normal; urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line intervention for the disorder itself?

options.text: Long-term hospitalisation in a specialist personality disorder inpatient unit for 6 to 12 months of intensive containment
options.rationale: Prolonged inpatient admission for BPD reinforces dependency and undermines self-regulation skills; community-based structured psychotherapy is the first-line. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD

options.text: Lifelong second-generation antipsychotic such as quetiapine 200 mg nightly as the primary therapeutic intervention
options.rationale: There is no medication approved as first-line monotherapy for BPD; medications are used adjunctively for specific co-morbidities. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD

options.text: Brief solution-focused cognitive behavioural therapy over 6 weeks targeted only at self-harm reduction at presentation
options.rationale: Brief CBT is insufficient for BPD; structured longer-term therapies such as DBT, mentalisation-based therapy, or schema therapy have evidence for sustained improvement. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD

options.text: Structured psychological therapy such as dialectical behaviour therapy for at least 12 months with case management support
options.rationale: The NHMRC BPD guideline recommends structured psychological therapy (DBT, MBT, schema therapy, or transference-focused psychotherapy) for at least 12 months as the first-line treatment, with crisis planning and case management. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD

options.text: Discharge to primary care with crisis line contact details and an SSRI prescription for emotional dysregulation
options.rationale: Discharge without structured therapy misses the evidence-based intervention; SSRIs are not specifically effective for BPD as monotherapy. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD

explanation.summary: Borderline personality disorder is best treated with structured psychological therapy delivered over at least 12 months: dialectical behaviour therapy, mentalisation-based therapy, schema therapy, or transference-focused psychotherapy. Medication is adjunctive for co-morbid depression, anxiety, or psychotic-like symptoms but not first-line monotherapy. Brief admissions for safety are acceptable; long admissions are counterproductive. Crisis planning, written safety plans, and consistent case management are foundational.
key_points: Structured psychotherapy at least 12 months is first-line
DBT, MBT, schema, or TFP are evidence-based
Medications adjunctive only
Avoid prolonged inpatient stays
explanation.pearls: NHMRC BPD guideline: structured psychotherapy (DBT/MBT/schema/TFP) for at least 12 months is the first-line; long admissions worsen outcomes through dependency.

sources.label: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD

subtopic_detail: Antipsychotic metabolic monitoring at baseline and 12 weeks
stem: A 27-year-old man with first-episode schizophrenia was commenced on olanzapine 10 mg nocte 12 weeks ago. He has had a good clinical response with reduction in positive symptoms and minimal extrapyramidal effects. He attends today for the 12-week metabolic review. His baseline measurements showed normal weight, fasting glucose 4.8, lipids unremarkable, and BP 118/72. He has gained 6 kg since commencing treatment. He has no family history of diabetes or premature cardiovascular disease and has otherwise stayed well.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78, BP 134/88, weight 86 kg (baseline 80), waist 102 cm
data_table.Examination: No EPS; mental state stable; no acute distress; no acanthosis nigricans
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 5.8 mmol/L (baseline 4.8), HbA1c 5.6 percent, total cholesterol 5.4 mmol/L, LDL 3.5, HDL 1.1, TG 2.4, ECG QTc 442 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue olanzapine unchanged and rely on routine 12 monthly reviews because no parameter exceeds a threshold for action
options.rationale: Multiple metabolic parameters have moved adversely (weight, waist circumference, fasting glucose, lipids, BP), reflecting evolving metabolic syndrome; intervention rather than annual review is needed. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Metabolic Monitoring)

options.text: Add metformin 500 mg twice daily empirically and continue olanzapine without further behavioural or dietary intervention
options.rationale: Metformin can mitigate antipsychotic weight gain but is added alongside diet, exercise, and consideration of antipsychotic switch where appropriate, not as the sole intervention. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Metabolic Monitoring)

options.text: Cease olanzapine abruptly and start ziprasidone 80 mg twice daily today as a metabolically neutral antipsychotic option
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation with cross-taper to ziprasidone, which has QTc concerns and is not currently PBS-listed in Australia, is not appropriate as the immediate response. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Metabolic Monitoring)

options.text: Stop all antipsychotic therapy because metabolic adverse effects outweigh symptomatic response in a first episode case
options.rationale: First-episode psychosis benefits from at least 12 to 24 months of maintenance treatment to reduce relapse; abandonment of antipsychotic therapy after metabolic concerns alone is inappropriate. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Metabolic Monitoring)

options.text: Implement lifestyle intervention, consider switch to aripiprazole given metabolic trajectory, and arrange repeat metabolic panel in 12 weeks
options.rationale: RANZCP recommends combining lifestyle intervention with consideration of switching to a less weight-and-glucose-adverse antipsychotic such as aripiprazole when metabolic deterioration develops; reassessment within 12 weeks confirms response. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Metabolic Monitoring)

explanation.summary: Antipsychotic metabolic monitoring requires baseline weight, waist circumference, fasting glucose, lipids, blood pressure, and ECG. Reassessment at 6 and 12 weeks then 3-monthly to 1 year is recommended for second-generation agents, with annual review thereafter if stable. Deterioration prompts lifestyle intervention, consideration of switching to less metabolically active agents (such as aripiprazole), and adjuncts such as metformin where appropriate. Continued treatment is essential in first-episode psychosis.
key_points: Baseline + 6, 12 week, 3-monthly to 1 year, then annual
Aripiprazole less weight/glucose adverse than olanzapine
Metformin adjunct can mitigate weight gain
Lifestyle intervention always added
explanation.pearls: Olanzapine carries highest metabolic burden of second-generation antipsychotics; switching to aripiprazole when deterioration occurs improves the metabolic trajectory while maintaining psychosis treatment.

stem: A 31-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has been stable on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily for 4 years. She presents to your community psychiatry clinic having recently entered a new relationship and wishes to consider pregnancy in the next 12 to 24 months. She has been counselled previously about valproate risks but asks for a detailed plan. Her mood has remained euthymic with no episodes for 3 years on valproate monotherapy. She is otherwise well, takes no other medications, and has no contraindications to alternative mood stabilisers. She has no children.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic mental state; no tremor; full insight; capacity preserved
data_table.Investigations: Valproate level 540 micromol/L; LFTs normal; FBC normal; pregnancy test negative; folate level adequate

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue valproate at the current dose with prescribed high-dose folate 5 mg daily for 3 months before conception
options.rationale: Valproate causes neural tube defects in around 10 percent and cognitive impairment in around 30 to 40 percent of exposed offspring; folate supplementation does not mitigate these risks. (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention)

options.text: Reduce valproate to 500 mg daily to lessen teratogenic exposure during planned conception while maintaining mood stability
options.rationale: Teratogenicity is dose-related but no dose is considered safe in early pregnancy; reducing dose risks relapse and does not eliminate teratogenicity. (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention)

options.text: Switch to carbamazepine 400 mg twice daily as an alternative mood stabiliser with comparable mood-stabilising properties
options.rationale: Carbamazepine is also teratogenic (around 3 percent neural tube defects, hand abnormalities, and cardiac defects) and is not the preferred substitute in women planning pregnancy. (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention)

options.text: Cross-taper to a safer mood stabiliser such as lamotrigine, document highly effective contraception throughout, and refer to perinatal psychiatry
options.rationale: Australian TGA pregnancy-prevention guidance for valproate requires highly effective contraception in women of childbearing potential, transition to a safer mood stabiliser such as lamotrigine before conception, and specialist perinatal psychiatric input. (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention)

options.text: Stop valproate today without substitution and rely on psychological therapy alone until pregnancy is confirmed
options.rationale: Untreated bipolar disorder during planned conception risks severe relapse with associated maternal and fetal harm; substitution rather than monotherapy cessation is required. (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention)

explanation.summary: Sodium valproate is associated with around 10 percent neural tube defects, cleft palate, hypospadias, and 30 to 40 percent neurodevelopmental impairment in exposed offspring. TGA guidance restricts valproate prescription in women of childbearing potential to those for whom no alternative is appropriate, mandates highly effective contraception (LARC or sterilisation), and requires annual review with risk acknowledgement. Cross-taper to lamotrigine or low-dose lithium are preferred when planning pregnancy, with perinatal psychiatry support.
key_points: Valproate teratogenicity: ~10 percent major malformation, 30 to 40 percent neurodevelopmental
TGA pregnancy prevention program mandatory in women of childbearing potential
Switch to lamotrigine or low-dose lithium before conception
Perinatal psychiatry referral for planning
explanation.pearls: Valproate in pregnancy: 10 percent major malformation and 30 to 40 percent neurodevelopmental harm; TGA mandates highly effective contraception and transition to lamotrigine before planned conception.

subtopic_detail: SSRI discontinuation syndrome recognition versus relapse
stem:
A 34-year-old woman returns to her GP 6 days after stopping paroxetine 20 mg daily, which she has taken for 14 months for a single episode of major depression now in stable remission. She stopped after running out of script while travelling and forgot to refill. She reports vivid 'electric shock' sensations in her head when she moves her eyes, dizziness when standing, nausea, vivid disturbing dreams, and feeling anxious and irritable.

Her mood is reactive, she is enjoying her usual activities, sleeps well after initial dreaming subsides, eats normally, and denies anhedonia, hopelessness, or suicidal thoughts.

data_table.Examination: Alert, oriented, full affect range, eye movements normal, no focal neurology, gait normal
data_table.Investigations: Nil performed today
data_table.Medications: Paroxetine 20 mg daily ceased 6 days ago; combined oral contraception

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Switch to fluoxetine 20 mg daily as a long half-life bridge then taper fluoxetine over 4 weeks instead of paroxetine
options.rationale: Fluoxetine bridging is reserved for severe persistent discontinuation symptoms despite reintroduction of the original SSRI; first step is to resume the original drug and taper. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Antidepressant Discontinuation)

options.text: Commence prochlorperazine 5 mg three times daily and ondansetron 8 mg three times daily for symptomatic relief of nausea and dizziness
options.rationale: Symptomatic treatment with antiemetics does not address the underlying serotonergic withdrawal and adds prochlorperazine-related extrapyramidal risk; addressing the cause is preferable. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Antidepressant Discontinuation)

options.text: Reassure that symptoms will resolve spontaneously within 7 days and recommend continued cessation without resuming any medication
options.rationale: Symptoms are functionally limiting and last 1 to 3 weeks if untreated with paroxetine (highest-risk SSRI for discontinuation due to short half-life); resumption and slow taper is recommended over watchful waiting. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Antidepressant Discontinuation)

options.text: Diagnose major depressive recurrence and restart paroxetine 20 mg with referral for outpatient psychiatry assessment within 4 weeks
options.rationale: Mood remains in remission with reactive affect, preserved enjoyment, sleep, appetite, and no suicidality; symptom timing and physical features (paraesthesia, electric shocks) point to discontinuation syndrome rather than depressive recurrence. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Antidepressant Discontinuation)

options.text: Restart paroxetine 20 mg daily and taper over 4 to 6 weeks once symptoms resolve, with close follow-up to monitor for recurrence
options.rationale: Onset within days of cessation with classic FINISH features (flu-like, insomnia, nausea, imbalance, sensory paraesthesia, hyperarousal) plus preserved mood and reactivity strongly favours discontinuation syndrome; resumption resolves symptoms within 24 to 48 hours then slow taper prevents recurrence. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Antidepressant Discontinuation)

explanation.summary: SSRI discontinuation syndrome appears within 1 to 7 days of stopping or markedly reducing an SSRI/SNRI and is most common with paroxetine and venlafaxine (short half-lives). Features (FINISH mnemonic) include flu-like symptoms, insomnia, nausea, imbalance, sensory disturbance (electric-shock paraesthesia), and hyperarousal. Distinguish from depressive recurrence by rapid onset, prominent physical/sensory features, preserved mood reactivity, and resolution within 24 to 48 hours of reinstating the SSRI. Management is restart and slow taper, with fluoxetine bridging reserved for resistant cases.
key_points: Onset 1-7 days post stop; resolves within 1-3 weeks if untreated.
Paroxetine and venlafaxine highest risk.
FINISH: flu, insomnia, nausea, imbalance, sensory, hyperarousal.
Restart + slow taper; fluoxetine bridge only if persistent.
explanation.pearls: Taper paroxetine by 5 mg every 1 to 2 weeks (or slower) and watch for re-emergence at each step; agomelatine and bupropion have low discontinuation rates and may be preferable in patients with poor taper tolerance.

subtopic_detail: Borderline personality disorder acute self-harm crisis management
stem:
A 24-year-old woman with established borderline personality disorder under a community mental health team (currently in week 14 of an 18-month dialectical behaviour therapy program) presents to the emergency department after taking 14 paracetamol tablets at 9 pm following an argument with her boyfriend. It is now 11 pm. She immediately told her mother who brought her in. She has had three similar low-lethality overdoses in the past 18 months.

She is calm now, regrets the act, and says she 'just wanted to feel something stop'. She denies current suicidal intent and has agreed verbally to use her crisis card and call her DBT therapist tomorrow morning. Her therapist is contactable now if needed.

data_table.Examination: Alert, full conversation, no signs of intoxication, no fresh self-harm wounds, mood reactive, no psychotic features
data_table.Investigations: Paracetamol level pending (4 h sample at 1 am); ALT 22, INR 1.0, creatinine 68
data_table.Medications: Currently nil regular; trialled three SSRIs previously with no benefit

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management approach after treating the paracetamol overdose?

options.text: Treat the overdose, liaise with her DBT and crisis teams, activate her agreed safety plan, and discharge home with mother and 24-hour follow-up
options.rationale: NHMRC guidelines recommend avoiding lengthy psychiatric admission for BPD self-harm and instead coordinating with the existing structured treatment (DBT) team, activating an agreed safety plan, ensuring rapid follow-up and engaging family/carer support; this preserves therapeutic momentum and avoids reinforcing maladaptive coping. (Source: NHMRC Borderline Personality Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: NHMRC Borderline Personality Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Commence quetiapine 100 mg nocte as ongoing mood stabilisation and discharge with a 7-day pharmacy supply for self-administration
options.rationale: There is no PBS-recognised medication that treats BPD itself; quetiapine has unproven benefit, sedates, contributes to metabolic side effects, and a 7-day supply hands a vulnerable patient potential overdose means. (Source: NHMRC Borderline Personality Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: NHMRC Borderline Personality Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Request an inpatient Mental Health Act assessment for involuntary admission to enforce safety despite her stated agreement to use the crisis plan
options.rationale: Involuntary admission for chronic recurrent low-lethality self-harm in BPD is not therapeutic, breaches least-restrictive principles, and may damage the established therapeutic relationship; criteria for compulsion are not met. (Source: NHMRC Borderline Personality Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: NHMRC Borderline Personality Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Admit to an acute mental health inpatient unit for at least 7 days for observation, behavioural stabilisation, and medication review
options.rationale: Brief admission for BPD self-harm is associated with worsening behaviour, regression, and dependency; Australian guidelines advise the shortest possible admission only when there is acute risk that cannot be managed in the community. (Source: NHMRC Borderline Personality Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: NHMRC Borderline Personality Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Discharge without communication to the community mental health team and advise her to call Lifeline if distress returns at any point
options.rationale: Discharge without contacting the existing care team fragments care and misses the opportunity to align with her individualised crisis and safety plan; this is the commonest preventable adverse outcome after ED presentation in BPD. (Source: NHMRC Borderline Personality Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: NHMRC Borderline Personality Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline

explanation.summary: For self-harm crises in BPD, Australian NHMRC guidelines emphasise active coordination with the existing structured psychotherapy team (DBT, MBT, schema), use of the patient's individualised safety plan, family/carer involvement when agreed, and avoiding both lengthy inpatient admission (which can reinforce maladaptive behaviour) and reflexive involuntary detention. Brief admission is reserved for risk that cannot be managed in community. No psychotropic medication has been shown to treat the core features of BPD; pharmacotherapy is reserved for clearly diagnosed comorbid disorders and reviewed regularly. Rapid follow-up within 24 to 72 hours is critical.
key_points: Avoid prolonged admission for BPD self-harm.
Coordinate with existing DBT/MBT/schema team.
Activate individualised safety plan + carer involvement.
No drug treats BPD; treat clear comorbidities only.
explanation.pearls: Means restriction (small quantities of analgesics, locked supply with carer) reduces lethality of impulsive overdoses; document the safety plan jointly and share it with the GP and DBT team before discharge.

sources.label: NHMRC Borderline Personality Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline
RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for BPD

subtopic_detail: Anorexia nervosa medical admission threshold criteria
stem: A 19-year-old woman is reviewed at her university health service after losing 14 kg over 6 months. She has restricted intake and exercises 2 hours daily. She denies binge or purge behaviour. Her menses ceased 3 months ago. Today she felt dizzy on standing and her family is alarmed. She is intelligent, insightful that her behaviour is harmful, but ambivalent about gaining weight. There is no suicidal ideation. She has no prior psychiatric history and is not on medication.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 38 supine and 62 standing, BP 86/52 supine and 76/40 standing, RR 16, T 35.4, weight 38 kg, height 1.66 m (BMI 13.8)
data_table.Examination: Cachectic, dry skin, lanugo, cold peripheries, no focal neurology, alert, oriented, no thought disorder, mood low-normal reactive
data_table.Investigations: Na 132, K 3.0, phosphate 0.62, magnesium 0.62, glucose 3.4, urea 8.2, creatinine 88, LFT mildly raised, FBC normal, ECG QTc 478 ms with U waves

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Arrange day-program treatment with structured meals and group therapy three times weekly with regular weight and electrolyte monitoring
options.rationale: Day programs suit medically stable patients with BMI typically above 14 to 15; current vital signs and biochemistry require inpatient cardiac monitoring and supervised refeeding. (Source: ANZAED Eating Disorder Treatment Guidelines)

options.text: Admit to a medical or eating disorders inpatient unit for cardiac monitoring, cautious nutritional rehabilitation and electrolyte correction
options.rationale: Multiple ANZAED medical admission criteria are met (BMI 13.8, HR 38, postural BP drop, hypoglycaemia, hypokalaemia, QTc 478, hypothermia 35.4); inpatient medical admission for cautious refeeding with cardiac monitoring is required to prevent arrhythmia and refeeding syndrome. (Source: ANZAED Eating Disorder Treatment Guidelines)

options.text: Initiate olanzapine 2.5 mg nocte to promote appetite and weight gain and review in 2 weeks to assess the effect on eating behaviour
options.rationale: Olanzapine has weak evidence in anorexia and does not address the acute medical instability; medical stabilisation is the priority and pharmacotherapy is adjunctive at best. (Source: ANZAED Eating Disorder Treatment Guidelines)

options.text: Refer to the community eating disorders team for weekly outpatient review with weight checks and food diary for the next 6 weeks
options.rationale: She meets multiple ANZAED medical admission criteria (BMI under 14, bradycardia under 40, postural drop over 20 mmHg, hypoglycaemia, hypokalaemia, hypothermia, QTc above 460); outpatient management is unsafe at this acuity. (Source: ANZAED Eating Disorder Treatment Guidelines)

options.text: Discuss using the Mental Health Act to detain her for treatment given the high risk of death without immediate involuntary intervention at this stage
options.rationale: She has capacity, insight and is engaged; voluntary admission should be attempted first. Mental Health Act use is reserved for refusal of life-saving treatment when capacity is lost. (Source: ANZAED Eating Disorder Treatment Guidelines)

explanation.summary: ANZAED and RANZCP criteria for medical inpatient admission in anorexia include BMI under 14 (or under 15 in some thresholds), HR under 40, postural drop above 20 mmHg or postural HR rise above 20, hypothermia under 35.5 C, hypoglycaemia under 3.0, hypokalaemia under 3.0, hypophosphataemia, QTc above 460 ms, syncope, severe dehydration, or organ failure. Admission allows cardiac monitoring, supervised refeeding (start at 20 to 30 kcal/kg/day with daily phosphate and electrolyte checks), and management of refeeding syndrome. Family-based or CBT-E therapy follows once medically stable.
key_points: Medical admit: BMI<14, HR<40, postural drop, QTc>460.
Hypophosphataemia and hypokalaemia are red flags.
Refeed at 20-30 kcal/kg/day, monitor phosphate daily.
Family-based or CBT-E once stable.
explanation.pearls: Phosphate falls within 24 to 72 hours of refeeding starting; supplement prophylactically with oral or IV phosphate when baseline is at or below 0.7 mmol/L, and consider thiamine 100 mg before any carbohydrate-containing fluids.

subtopic_detail: ECT indication in severe depression with food refusal and psychomotor retardation
stem: A 68-year-old man is admitted involuntarily under the Mental Health Act with severe psychotic depression. He has lost 8 kg in 6 weeks, refuses food and drink for the past 4 days, has stopped speaking, lies motionless in bed and is incontinent. He has had two adequate trials of antidepressants (sertraline 200 mg for 8 weeks, then venlafaxine 300 mg for 6 weeks) augmented with quetiapine and lithium in turn over the past 14 months with no improvement. He has no significant comorbidities other than hypertension. His son provides next-of-kin consent and the consultant psychiatrist is requesting urgent treatment.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 64, BP 138/82, T 36.2, weight 62 kg (was 70 kg)
data_table.Examination: Mute, immobile, reactive to noxious stimuli only, no rigidity or waxy flexibility, no focal neurology, dehydrated
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 138, urea 9.4, creatinine 102, glucose 4.2, LFT and TFT normal, ECG normal QTc 410, CT brain age-related atrophy only
data_table.Medications: Venlafaxine 300 mg, lithium 800 mg nocte (level 0.7), perindopril 4 mg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in this patient's treatment?

options.text: Refer for transcranial magnetic stimulation in a private centre as the next evidence-based step before considering electroconvulsive therapy
options.rationale: rTMS has good evidence for moderate treatment-resistant depression but slower onset and is not recommended for severe psychotic depression with imminent food refusal where ECT is first-line. (Source: RANZCP ECT Position Statement)

options.text: Continue venlafaxine, increase lithium target to 0.8 to 1.0 mmol/L, and review response in 4 weeks at outpatient follow-up appointment
options.rationale: Two adequate antidepressant trials with augmentation have failed and the man is at imminent risk from dehydration and starvation; further pharmacotherapy alone is not safe at this acuity. (Source: RANZCP ECT Position Statement)

options.text: Trial intranasal esketamine 84 mg twice weekly in a registered TGA Risk Management program centre while continuing current oral antidepressants
options.rationale: Esketamine has TGA approval for treatment-resistant depression but is not indicated in patients with imminent risk needing rapid stabilisation, and is contraindicated when patients cannot safely follow post-dose monitoring requirements. (Source: RANZCP ECT Position Statement)

options.text: Refer for an urgent course of electroconvulsive therapy with anaesthetic preassessment and bridging intravenous fluids while awaiting first session
options.rationale: Life-threatening severe depression with food refusal, psychomotor retardation, treatment resistance, and psychotic features has level-1 evidence for ECT in Australian guidelines with rapid onset of action (1 to 2 weeks); intravenous fluids bridge dehydration. (Source: RANZCP ECT Position Statement)

options.text: Switch venlafaxine to tranylcypromine 30 mg daily after washout and add olanzapine 10 mg as augmentation for treatment-resistant depression
options.rationale: MAOI switch requires a 1 to 2 week washout (longer for fluoxetine) and would not act in time to address food refusal and dehydration; ECT is the indicated rapid treatment in this acuity. (Source: RANZCP ECT Position Statement)

explanation.summary: ECT is first-line in severe depression with high suicide risk, food/fluid refusal, severe psychomotor retardation or stupor, psychotic features, catatonia, treatment-resistance, or in pregnancy when medication risk is unacceptable. It has 70 to 90 percent response rate with onset within 1 to 2 weeks (faster than pharmacotherapy). In Australia it is delivered under general anaesthesia and muscle relaxant, typically 2 to 3 times weekly for 6 to 12 sessions, with maintenance ECT as appropriate. Major risks are anaesthetic, transient anterograde and retrograde memory disturbance (which usually resolves), and headache.
key_points: Indications: severe depression, food refusal, catatonia, suicidality, resistance.
Onset 1-2 weeks; 70-90 percent response.
2-3 sessions/week, 6-12 acute, maintenance considered.
Memory loss usually transient anterograde.
explanation.pearls: Bilateral ECT is faster acting but with more cognitive side effects than right unilateral; in elderly patients with severe psychotic depression bilateral is often preferred for life-threatening illness.

sources.label: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for Mood Disorders

subtopic_detail: Antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinaemia with amenorrhoea switch strategy
stem: A 27-year-old woman with schizophrenia in clinical remission for 18 months on risperidone 4 mg daily presents to her community psychiatrist with secondary amenorrhoea of 7 months, galactorrhoea, loss of libido, and bone pain in the hips. She has had no positive or negative symptoms during this remission. She is not pregnant. She has been adherent to risperidone with good clinical response and is reluctant to change because of previous relapses on quetiapine. Her bone densitometry shows a Z-score of -1.8 at the lumbar spine.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral galactorrhoea, no thyroid mass, normal visual fields, normal neurological examination, intact secondary sexual characteristics
data_table.Investigations: Prolactin 2640 mU/L (upper normal 500); TSH normal, beta-hCG negative, FSH and LH suppressed, oestradiol low, MRI pituitary normal
data_table.Medications: Risperidone 4 mg daily, vitamin D 1000 IU

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Halve the risperidone dose to 2 mg daily to lower prolactin while accepting the increased risk of psychotic relapse for the next several months
options.rationale: Risperidone-related prolactin elevation is dose-related but reductions often do not normalise prolactin without losing efficacy; aripiprazole switch achieves both goals. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Antipsychotic Adverse Effects)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Antipsychotic Adverse Effects

options.text: Switch directly from risperidone to amisulpride 400 mg daily as the next antipsychotic and reassess prolactin and bone density in 6 months
options.rationale: Amisulpride raises prolactin more than risperidone and would worsen amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea and bone loss; it is the wrong switch in this scenario. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Antipsychotic Adverse Effects)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Antipsychotic Adverse Effects

options.text: Continue risperidone unchanged and add cabergoline 0.5 mg twice weekly to normalise prolactin while preserving the current antipsychotic response
options.rationale: Dopamine agonist add-on in patients with schizophrenia is generally avoided because it risks worsening psychotic symptoms by stimulating mesolimbic dopamine; switching to a prolactin-sparing antipsychotic is the recommended first step. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Antipsychotic Adverse Effects)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Antipsychotic Adverse Effects

options.text: Cross-titrate risperidone down while introducing aripiprazole 10 to 15 mg daily to lower prolactin while maintaining symptomatic control
options.rationale: Aripiprazole (partial D2 agonist) reliably lowers prolactin and is the standard switch in antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinaemia with adverse effects; cross-titration over 2 to 4 weeks minimises relapse risk. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Antipsychotic Adverse Effects)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Antipsychotic Adverse Effects

options.text: Refer to endocrinology for transsphenoidal pituitary biopsy to exclude prolactinoma despite the normal magnetic resonance imaging study
options.rationale: MRI pituitary is normal and prolactin elevation is consistent with risperidone effect; invasive biopsy is not indicated and the cause is iatrogenic. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Antipsychotic Adverse Effects)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Antipsychotic Adverse Effects

explanation.summary: Risperidone, amisulpride, and paliperidone reliably cause hyperprolactinaemia by D2 blockade in the tuberoinfundibular pathway. Symptomatic patients (amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea, sexual dysfunction, bone loss, gynaecomastia) should be switched to a prolactin-sparing agent: aripiprazole (best evidence), olanzapine, quetiapine, or clozapine. Aripiprazole is added or switched (cross-titration over 2 to 4 weeks) and effectively normalises prolactin within weeks. Cabergoline is generally avoided in schizophrenia because of relapse risk. Bone density assessment is indicated if amenorrhoea has lasted over 6 months.
key_points: Prolactin-raising: risperidone, paliperidone, amisulpride.
Prolactin-sparing: aripiprazole, olanzapine, quetiapine, clozapine.
Switch or add aripiprazole 10-15 mg as standard intervention.
Cabergoline avoided - psychosis relapse risk.
explanation.pearls: Document baseline prolactin before starting risperidone or paliperidone and at 3 months; ask routinely about menstrual cycle, sexual function and galactorrhoea, which patients often do not volunteer.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Antipsychotic Adverse Effects

stem:
A 32-year-old man with schizophrenia has had persistent auditory hallucinations and paranoid delusions causing significant functional impairment over the past 3 years despite treatment. He completed an adequate 8-week trial of risperidone 6 mg daily (with documented adherence on long-acting injectable for 6 months), then an adequate 10-week trial of olanzapine 20 mg daily, both with minimal response. He has gained 14 kg on olanzapine and has impaired fasting glucose.

He has no other major comorbidities and lives with his parents who support treatment. He has read about clozapine and is willing to engage with monitoring.

data_table.Examination: Mildly thought-disordered, third-person auditory hallucinations described, paranoid ideation, no acute risk
data_table.Investigations: FBC normal (neutrophils 4.2 x10^9/L), HbA1c 5.8 percent, lipids LDL 3.1, LFT normal, ECG QTc 410 ms
data_table.Medications: Olanzapine 20 mg nocte, metformin 1 g BD

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his pharmacological management?

options.text: Commence clozapine titration under monitoring with weekly FBC for 18 weeks then monthly, plus baseline ECG and lipid panel before titration begins
options.rationale: Treatment-resistant schizophrenia after two adequate antipsychotic trials is the standard indication for clozapine; mandatory monitoring includes weekly FBC for 18 weeks, then monthly, with cardiac and metabolic baselines because of agranulocytosis and myocarditis risk. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG)

options.text: Add lithium 500 mg nocte to the current olanzapine regimen as augmentation and review response over the next 8 weeks at outpatient clinic
options.rationale: Lithium augmentation of antipsychotics has limited efficacy in primary schizophrenia (better evidence in schizoaffective with mood features); clozapine remains the indicated treatment after two failed trials. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG)

options.text: Trial repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation targeted at the temporoparietal cortex for auditory hallucinations before any further drug change
options.rationale: rTMS for hallucinations has limited and inconsistent evidence; clozapine remains first-line for treatment-resistant schizophrenia after two adequate antipsychotic trials. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG)

options.text: Continue olanzapine at maximum 30 mg daily and add high-dose sertraline as augmentation for the residual positive symptoms over the next 12 weeks
options.rationale: He meets Australian criteria for treatment-resistant schizophrenia (two adequate trials of different antipsychotics) and clozapine is the recommended next step with strongest evidence; high-dose olanzapine augmentation has limited evidence. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG)

options.text: Switch directly to long-acting paliperidone palmitate monthly injections to ensure adherence before considering clozapine in 6 months
options.rationale: Adherence has been confirmed during the 6 months of risperidone LAI, so non-adherence is not the cause; he meets clozapine criteria now and further antipsychotic trials delay benefit. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG)

explanation.summary: Treatment-resistant schizophrenia is defined as failure to respond to two adequate trials (4 to 6 weeks at therapeutic dose with confirmed adherence) of different antipsychotics, at least one of which is not clozapine. Clozapine is the only antipsychotic with superior efficacy in this group and is recommended as the third antipsychotic. Monitoring is mandatory: weekly FBC for 18 weeks then monthly indefinitely for agranulocytosis; baseline and serial ECG plus troponin in the first 4 weeks for myocarditis; weight, glucose, and lipids for metabolic syndrome.
key_points: Definition: two adequate trials at therapeutic dose with adherence.
Clozapine third antipsychotic - unique efficacy.
Weekly FBC 18 weeks then monthly for agranulocytosis.
ECG + troponin first 4 weeks for myocarditis.
explanation.pearls: Stop clozapine for neutrophils below 1.5 x10^9/L (red zone); rechallenge requires haematology review and is generally only for life-threatening psychosis without alternative. Avoid co-prescribing other agents that lower neutrophils (e.g. carbamazepine).

stem: A 44-year-old man attends the practice asking for help to quit smoking. He has smoked 20-25 cigarettes daily for 25 years and is highly nicotine dependent (Fagerstrom score 7). He has tried short-acting nicotine replacement gum once before unsuccessfully. He has no significant mental health history and is not on any psychiatric medications. He has well-controlled type 2 diabetes and asthma. His renal function is normal and he is keen to set a quit date for 2 weeks from now.

data_table.Examination: Chest clear, no cyanosis, no oral changes
data_table.Investigations: HbA1c 6.8 percent, fasting glucose 6.4, eGFR 92, urinalysis unremarkable, PHQ-9 score 3 (none-minimal)

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first-line pharmacological smoking cessation therapy?

options.text: Combination of long-acting nicotine patch 21 mg per 24 hours together with short-acting nicotine inhaler used in response to cravings for the next 12 weeks as outpatient
options.rationale: Combination NRT is a valid choice but varenicline has higher quit rates and remains first-line in highly dependent smokers without contraindication. (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation)

options.text: Bupropion sustained release 150 mg daily for 3 days then 150 mg twice daily for 7 to 12 weeks starting today, with quit date set in the first 2 weeks of therapy as planned
options.rationale: Bupropion is effective but second-line; it lowers seizure threshold and varenicline has higher quit rates as first-line therapy. (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation)

options.text: Varenicline 0.5 mg daily for 3 days then 0.5 mg twice daily for 4 days then 1 mg twice daily for 12 weeks with a quit date set in week 2 of treatment
options.rationale: Varenicline titrated over week 1 with quit date in week 2 is first-line in nicotine-dependent smokers without contraindication and outperforms NRT and bupropion. (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation)

options.text: Brief intervention with motivational interviewing alone without pharmacotherapy and arranging a follow-up appointment in 4 weeks to discuss further options if no progress made
options.rationale: Brief intervention without pharmacotherapy in a highly nicotine-dependent smoker underuses effective treatment and lowers quit success rates. (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation)

options.text: Clonidine 0.1 mg twice daily as off-label smoking cessation pharmacotherapy with planned monitoring of blood pressure during the first 4 weeks of titration therapy
options.rationale: Clonidine is third-line because of sedation and rebound hypertension and is rarely used in Australia compared with first and second-line options. (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation)

explanation.summary: Combined behavioural and pharmacological therapy doubles quit rates. Pharmacological first-line options in Australia for nicotine-dependent smokers are varenicline, combination NRT (patch plus short-acting), or NRT alone. Varenicline (alpha-4 beta-2 nicotinic receptor partial agonist) has the highest quit rates; titrate from 0.5 mg daily over week 1 to 1 mg twice daily for 12 weeks, with quit date in week 2. Monitor for nausea (most common), sleep disturbance, vivid dreams; warnings on neuropsychiatric symptoms have been downgraded after EAGLES trial showed no significant increase. Bupropion is second-line; avoid in seizure or eating disorder history.
key_points: Combine behavioural and pharmacological for best quit rates.
Varenicline first-line in nicotine-dependent smokers.
Titrate varenicline over week 1 to 1 mg BD; quit date in week 2.
Combination NRT (patch plus short-acting) is equally effective alternative.
Bupropion second-line; avoid with seizure or eating disorder.
explanation.pearls: Varenicline can interact with insulin needs in diabetes - improved cessation often improves glycaemic control quickly so monitor home BSL closely in the first 4 weeks and titrate hypoglycaemic medications down as needed.

subtopic_detail: Smoking cessation in established mental illness
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 46-year-old man with chronic schizophrenia stable on clozapine for 8 years. He smokes 30 cigarettes daily, wants to quit, and is asking what works best. He has no past suicide attempts but had one major depressive episode in his 20s. He has no cardiovascular disease, no renal impairment, and no current substance use. His mental state is stable with no recent psychotic symptoms. His care coordinator and treating psychiatrist support the plan to quit. He has tried nicotine gum unsuccessfully twice in the past.

data_table.Examination: Settled mood, no thought disorder, no psychotic symptoms, no extrapyramidal signs, smoker's cough
data_table.Investigations: Clozapine trough level 480 ng/mL on 350 mg nightly, eGFR 85, ECG normal, fasting glucose 5.4, LDL 3.0

lead_in: Which pharmacotherapy is most appropriate?

options.text: Bupropion 150 mg daily titrated to 150 mg twice daily commenced 1 to 2 weeks before quit date, with reassurance that this antidepressant has no interactions with the antipsychotic regimen
options.rationale: Bupropion lowers seizure threshold and combined with clozapine substantially increases seizure risk; this combination is generally avoided. (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation)

options.text: Varenicline 0.5 mg daily titrated over 1 week to 1 mg twice daily commenced 1 week before quit date, with monitoring for mood change and proactive clozapine level review after he has quit
options.rationale: Varenicline is first-line, safe in stable schizophrenia, and clozapine levels rise on quitting (cytochrome P450 1A2 induction by cigarette smoke is lost) so monitoring is needed. (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation)

options.text: Combination nicotine replacement therapy with 21 mg patch plus rapid release lozenges on cravings, with reassurance that no monitoring of clozapine level is required after he successfully quits
options.rationale: Combination NRT is effective but he has previously failed monotherapy NRT; clozapine levels still rise on quitting and require monitoring. (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation)

options.text: Refer for hypnotherapy and acupuncture as primary therapy without pharmacological cover, given the lack of robust evidence for medication efficacy in patients with chronic psychotic illness
options.rationale: Hypnotherapy and acupuncture have weak evidence; smokers with serious mental illness benefit equally from first-line pharmacotherapy. (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation)

options.text: Switch clozapine to olanzapine to reduce the smoking-clozapine interaction, then prescribe varenicline 1 mg twice daily without further clozapine monitoring during the cessation attempt
options.rationale: Stable clozapine should not be switched; varenicline can be used with clozapine but levels must still be monitored. (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation)

explanation.summary: Smoking cessation halves cardiovascular mortality regardless of psychiatric comorbidity. First-line pharmacotherapy is varenicline; combination NRT (patch plus short-acting) is the alternative. Varenicline was previously flagged for neuropsychiatric adverse effects but the EAGLES trial showed safety in stable severe mental illness. Bupropion is third-line and avoided with clozapine because of compound seizure risk. Cigarette smoke induces CYP1A2, the enzyme that metabolises clozapine and olanzapine, so plasma levels rise on cessation; dose reduction is often needed and toxicity may occur. Behavioural support adds independent benefit and Quitline support should be offered routinely.
key_points: Varenicline or combination NRT is first-line.
EAGLES trial: varenicline safe in stable severe mental illness.
Avoid bupropion with clozapine due to seizure risk.
Monitor clozapine and olanzapine levels after quitting.
Add behavioural support and Quitline referral.
explanation.pearls: After quitting smoking, expect clozapine plasma concentration to rise by around 50% over 1 to 2 weeks; pre-empt with a 25% dose reduction in heavy smokers and recheck a trough level at 2 weeks.

subtopic_detail: Borderline personality disorder - acute distress in ED
stem: You are the ED registrar reviewing a 25-year-old woman with known borderline personality disorder brought in after superficial forearm cuts following an argument with her partner. She is engaged in a DBT program and has a safety plan. She is calm now and apologetic, says she does not want to die, can identify the trigger, and feels regretful. She is housed, has supportive friends, and the GP is contactable in the morning. The wounds do not need suturing. She has had multiple similar presentations over the past 12 months.

data_table.Examination: Superficial linear lacerations to left forearm, dressed, no neurovascular compromise; mental state: euthymic, congruent affect, no thought disorder, no current suicidal ideation or plan, oriented
data_table.Investigations: None required
data_table.Medications: Quetiapine 25 mg PRN nocte; sertraline 100 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate disposition?

options.text: Admit voluntarily for 72 hours to the acute psychiatric inpatient unit to provide safety and reset her crisis plan, with daily DBT individual sessions for the duration of admission
options.rationale: Brief admissions for self-harm in BPD without acute risk worsen outcomes by reinforcing crisis behaviour and disrupting community DBT; community management is preferred. (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guideline)

options.text: Commence regular oral diazepam 5 mg three times daily for 2 weeks to reduce emotional reactivity, then have the GP gradually wean it once her mood stabilises and crises become less frequent
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are not recommended in BPD; they cause disinhibition, dependence and worsen long-term outcomes. (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guideline)

options.text: Discharge home with wound care advice, review her DBT crisis plan together using a chain analysis approach, ensure outpatient DBT therapist follow-up, and arrange GP review the following day
options.rationale: Community-based management with structured follow-up and engagement of existing DBT supports is the evidence-based approach for BPD self-harm without acute suicidal intent. (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guideline)

options.text: Apply an inpatient treatment order under the Mental Health Act for involuntary admission given the repeated pattern of self-harm presentations, then transfer her to the acute unit overnight for safety
options.rationale: Mental Health Act admission requires acute mental illness with imminent risk; chronic self-harm in BPD without acute risk does not meet criteria. (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guideline)

options.text: Increase sertraline to 200 mg daily and add olanzapine 10 mg at night as augmentation given the recurrent self-harm pattern, with psychiatrist outpatient appointment within 2 weeks for review
options.rationale: Polypharmacy is not recommended in BPD; medications target specific comorbid symptoms only, and self-harm itself is treated with psychotherapy. (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guideline)

explanation.summary: Borderline personality disorder is treated primarily with structured psychotherapy (DBT, MBT, schema therapy, transference-focused therapy). Brief involuntary or voluntary admissions for chronic self-harm do not improve outcomes and may worsen them by reinforcing crisis behaviour and disrupting community treatment. Inpatient care is reserved for acute psychiatric emergencies, severe comorbid depression with imminent suicide risk, or where outpatient resources are not available. Pharmacotherapy is symptom-targeted (eg short courses of antipsychotic for psychotic-like symptoms) and not first-line; benzodiazepines are best avoided because of disinhibition and dependence. Engaging existing community supports and family is central.
key_points: Structured psychotherapy is the primary treatment.
Avoid brief inpatient admissions for chronic self-harm.
No first-line pharmacotherapy for BPD itself.
Avoid benzodiazepines.
Engage existing community supports and family.
explanation.pearls: Use chain analysis collaboratively at every contact - mapping prompting event, vulnerabilities, links and consequences - to convert each crisis into a DBT skill-building opportunity rather than an isolated incident.

stem: You are the GP reviewing a 28-year-old IT worker who requests assessment for ADHD after reading about it online. He describes lifelong difficulty completing tasks, frequent job changes, chronic disorganisation, losing items and being easily distracted. School reports from primary school describe him as bright but unable to focus and impulsive. He has no current substance use, no past psychosis, and his mood is stable. He sleeps adequately. He has not previously been on any psychiatric medication. He is now in a stable relationship.

data_table.Examination: Alert, restless, normal mental state otherwise, no thought disorder, no psychotic symptoms
data_table.Investigations: Not yet performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?
