options.text: Commence a trial of dexamfetamine 5 mg twice daily for 4 weeks and review symptom response, with referral to specialist ADHD service only if the medication trial does not show clear benefit
options.rationale: Stimulant prescription requires specialist diagnosis and an authority script; trial first is not appropriate in primary care. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Order brain MRI, sleep study, urine drug screen, and thyroid function to exclude organic mimics of inattention before any referral to mental health services is initiated by primary care
options.rationale: Routine neuroimaging and sleep study are not standard ADHD work-up; selected screening tests may be appropriate but not all of these. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Reassure the patient that adult-onset ADHD does not exist and arrange counselling for procrastination, with cognitive behavioural therapy as the primary intervention for organisational difficulty
options.rationale: ADHD persists into adulthood in 50 to 70% of childhood cases; refusing assessment is not appropriate when symptoms are present since childhood. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Refer to a psychiatrist or paediatrician credentialed in adult ADHD assessment to confirm diagnosis using DSM-5 criteria, collateral history, and validated rating scales before any pharmacotherapy
options.rationale: Formal diagnosis by an appropriately credentialed specialist using DSM-5 criteria and collateral history is required before stimulant prescription. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Prescribe atomoxetine 40 mg daily for 4 weeks as a non-stimulant trial, since it requires no authority script in adults and is safe to initiate in general practice without specialist input
options.rationale: Atomoxetine in adults still requires specialist diagnosis; first prescription is by a specialist with GP shared care thereafter. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

explanation.summary: Adult ADHD diagnosis requires DSM-5 criteria: five or more symptoms of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity, several present before age 12, present in 2 or more settings, causing functional impairment, and not better explained by another condition. Assessment uses clinical interview with validated tools (DIVA-5, ASRS) and collateral history. Comorbidities are common - anxiety, depression, substance use, sleep disorders, ASD - and require parallel management. Stimulants (methylphenidate, lisdexamfetamine, dexamfetamine) are first-line treatment; non-stimulant atomoxetine or guanfacine are alternatives. Specialist credentialling rules vary by state but all currently require psychiatrist or paediatrician initiation in Australia.
key_points: DSM-5 needs childhood onset and 2+ settings.
Use validated rating scales and collateral history.
Screen for common comorbidities.
Stimulants are first-line; non-stimulants second.
Specialist diagnosis required for first prescription.
explanation.pearls: Lisdexamfetamine has lower abuse potential than immediate-release dexamfetamine because it requires red cell hydrolysis to produce active drug, giving a smoother onset and longer duration.

sources.label: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

stem:
You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar called to a 67-year-old man on the medical ward 5 days after admission for community-acquired pneumonia, which has resolved. Nursing staff report he has stopped eating and drinking and has not spoken for 48 hours. He had a major depressive episode 2 years ago that responded to sertraline, which his wife stopped during this admission because of new medications.

On examination he is awake but mute, holds his left arm in an awkward raised posture for over a minute when placed, and resists passive movement with stiff opposition.

data_table.Examination: Mute, immobile, eye contact reduced, waxy flexibility, mitgehen, no rigidity outside posturing, no tremor, no fever, no autonomic instability
data_table.Investigations: FBE normal, UEC Na 138 K 4.2 creatinine 78, CK 220, TSH 1.8, CRP 12, CT brain unremarkable, urine MCS no growth
data_table.Medications: Withheld sertraline; received ceftriaxone, azithromycin during admission, now ceased

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer intravenous lorazepam 1 to 2 mg as a diagnostic and therapeutic challenge with reassessment for clinical response at 5 to 10 minutes after the dose has been given
options.rationale: Lorazepam challenge is both diagnostic and therapeutic for catatonia and is the standard first step before considering ECT. (Source: RANZCP CPG Mood Disorders, BMJ Best Practice Catatonia)

options.text: Commence intravenous haloperidol 5 mg with promethazine 50 mg now to address agitation and restore behavioural control quickly, with nasogastric feed if intake remains poor overnight
options.rationale: Antipsychotics, especially typicals, can precipitate or worsen catatonia and provoke neuroleptic malignant syndrome; they are contraindicated. (Source: BMJ Best Practice Catatonia)

options.text: Arrange urgent electroconvulsive therapy for first treatment within 24 hours without a lorazepam challenge given the severe presentation and the patient's prior depressive history
options.rationale: Lorazepam challenge is the standard initial test and treatment; ECT is reserved for lorazepam non-response or malignant catatonia. (Source: BMJ Best Practice Catatonia)

options.text: Restart sertraline 50 mg orally daily and observe for 1 week, supporting nutrition with nasogastric feeding, and review progress at the next ward round before considering escalation
options.rationale: SSRI alone takes too long and does not treat acute catatonia; lorazepam is the immediate intervention. (Source: BMJ Best Practice Catatonia)

options.text: Commence intravenous dantrolene and bromocriptine combination for presumed neuroleptic malignant syndrome based on rigidity, mutism and recent hospitalisation with antibiotic exposure
options.rationale: NMS requires fever, marked autonomic instability and very high CK; this patient lacks these features and there has been no antipsychotic exposure. (Source: BMJ Best Practice Catatonia)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a syndrome of psychomotor disturbance characterised by features such as mutism, immobility, posturing, waxy flexibility, mitgehen, negativism, echolalia and stereotypies. It complicates mood disorders, schizophrenia and general medical conditions. Diagnosis is supported by the Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale; 2 or more of 14 signs supports the diagnosis. The lorazepam challenge (1 to 2 mg IV) gives both diagnostic confirmation and therapeutic benefit in around 70 to 80% within hours. Maintenance is regular lorazepam 6 to 24 mg daily titrated to response. ECT is the most effective treatment and is preferred for malignant catatonia (fever, autonomic instability, rigidity) which approaches NMS in mortality. Avoid antipsychotics.
key_points: Diagnose using Bush-Francis criteria (2 of 14 signs).
Lorazepam challenge: diagnostic and therapeutic.
Avoid antipsychotics - may precipitate NMS.
ECT for lorazepam non-response or malignant catatonia.
Identify underlying cause: mood, psychotic, or medical.
explanation.pearls: Mitgehen is the anglepoise-lamp sign where the patient's arm moves with even the lightest touch despite instructions to resist - one of the most specific catatonic signs.

stem:
You are the GP reviewing a 34-year-old female paramedic 4 months after a fatal multi-casualty incident on a highway. She describes intrusive flashbacks several times daily, nightmares, avoidance of driving past the site, hypervigilance at work, irritability and low mood. She is no longer enjoying activities she once loved. There is no substance misuse. She had a brief depressive episode in her 20s.

She is functioning at work with difficulty and has supportive family. She is not suicidal and has no current self-harm. She has not previously had psychotherapy.

data_table.Examination: Mood low, affect reactive, hypervigilant during interview, no thought disorder, no psychotic symptoms, oriented
data_table.Investigations: Not required

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line therapy?

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg daily as first-line pharmacotherapy and provide psychoeducation, with referral for psychological therapy only if symptoms have not responded after 12 weeks of medication
options.rationale: Trauma-focused psychological therapy is first-line for PTSD; pharmacotherapy is second-line or used in parallel when psychotherapy is unavailable. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Refer for trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy or eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing, either delivered by a trained therapist over 8 to 12 sessions as first-line management
options.rationale: TF-CBT or EMDR are first-line for PTSD with strongest evidence; both are equally effective. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Prescribe benzodiazepine clonazepam 0.5 mg twice daily for anxiety and sleep disturbance, combined with stress management techniques and lifestyle advice in primary care without further referral
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines worsen PTSD outcomes by impairing fear extinction learning and risk dependence; they are contraindicated. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Provide single-session psychological debriefing focused on the index incident, with review at 4 weeks to determine whether additional structured therapy will be needed for any persisting symptoms
options.rationale: Single-session debriefing does not prevent PTSD and may worsen outcomes; structured trauma-focused therapy is required. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Refer for inpatient psychiatric admission for stabilisation and intensive group therapy given the severity of intrusive symptoms and the operational role she holds in emergency services
options.rationale: PTSD without psychosis, suicidality or inability to function is managed in the community; admission is not indicated. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)

explanation.summary: PTSD is diagnosed when characteristic symptoms (intrusion, avoidance, negative cognition/mood, arousal) follow exposure to a traumatic event and persist beyond 1 month with functional impairment. First-line treatment is trauma-focused psychological therapy delivered by a trained clinician: trauma-focused CBT and EMDR both have strong evidence. Pharmacotherapy with sertraline, paroxetine or venlafaxine is second-line or adjunct when therapy is unavailable, declined, or insufficient. Benzodiazepines are contraindicated because they impair fear extinction. Prazosin is added for trauma nightmares. Antipsychotic augmentation is for severe treatment-resistant cases. Single-session debriefing is no longer recommended.
key_points: Trauma-focused CBT or EMDR are first-line.
Sertraline, paroxetine or venlafaxine if pharmacotherapy needed.
Avoid benzodiazepines.
Add prazosin for trauma-related nightmares.
Single-session debriefing does not prevent PTSD.
explanation.pearls: Prazosin reduces noradrenergic activity through alpha-1 blockade and is started at 1 mg at night titrated to 5 to 15 mg; first-dose hypotension is the main precaution especially in older adults.

stem: You are the ED registrar on the late shift when security calls for help. A 30-year-old man with known schizophrenia is shouting, pacing, threatening staff and refusing to engage. He has been brought in by police under emergency apprehension for self-neglect. He has previously responded to oral olanzapine in similar presentations. Verbal de-escalation by senior nursing staff over 20 minutes has not reduced agitation, and the team is now concerned for the safety of other patients and staff in the department. He has no known allergies.

data_table.Vital signs: Not yet measurable, observed alert with regular respirations, no pallor, no diaphoresis
data_table.Examination: Pacing, shouting, raised arms, persecutory and grandiose content, refusing assessment
data_table.Investigations: Not yet performed
data_table.Medications: Documented past response to oral olanzapine; on community paliperidone depot, last dose 5 weeks ago (overdue)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Restrain physically and administer intramuscular zuclopenthixol acetate 100 mg for sustained tranquillisation, then re-dose after 24 hours if behavioural disturbance has not fully settled
options.rationale: Long-acting zuclopenthixol acetate is not appropriate for acute behavioural disturbance because its 48 to 72 hour effect cannot be titrated. (Source: SHPA Acute Behavioural Disturbance Statement)

options.text: Administer intramuscular droperidol 10 mg plus midazolam 5 mg without offering oral therapy, given the level of disturbance and the risk to other patients in the department
options.rationale: Oral medication should be offered first when feasible; combination IM droperidol plus midazolam carries respiratory depression risk and is reserved for failure of monotherapy. (Source: SHPA Acute Behavioural Disturbance Statement)

options.text: Administer intravenous ketamine 200 mg as procedural sedation by the consultant, with rapid sequence intubation prepared because of the level of agitation and refusal to engage with staff
options.rationale: Ketamine sedation is reserved for severe refractory cases requiring physical restraint with anaesthetic backup; not first-line. (Source: SHPA Acute Behavioural Disturbance Statement)

options.text: Administer intramuscular haloperidol 10 mg with promethazine 50 mg as a single combination injection, then commence regular oral antipsychotic once cooperative for the remainder of the admission
options.rationale: High-dose haloperidol with promethazine carries QT prolongation and over-sedation risk; modern Australian practice favours droperidol or olanzapine first. (Source: SHPA Acute Behavioural Disturbance Statement)

options.text: Offer oral olanzapine wafer 10 mg as the first pharmacological step alongside continued de-escalation, accepting that intramuscular medication is offered only if oral is refused
options.rationale: Oral medication is preferred over IM where the patient can accept it; olanzapine wafer is rapid-onset and matches his past response. (Source: SHPA Acute Behavioural Disturbance Statement)

explanation.summary: Acute behavioural disturbance management follows a stepped approach: verbal de-escalation first, then offered oral medication, then intramuscular monotherapy, then IM combination if needed. Olanzapine wafer 5 to 10 mg is a fast-acting oral option that matches the patient's previous response. IM options are droperidol 10 mg or olanzapine 10 mg; combination IM droperidol plus midazolam is reserved for severe disturbance with respiratory monitoring. Avoid IM olanzapine within 1 hour of IM benzodiazepine because of respiratory depression. Continuous monitoring of airway, breathing and circulation is mandatory after any IM sedation. Document Mental Health Act status and review medication regularly.
key_points: Verbal de-escalation always first.
Offer oral medication before IM where possible.
Droperidol or olanzapine IM are monotherapy options.
Avoid IM olanzapine with IM benzodiazepine within 1 hour.
Continuous airway, breathing and circulation monitoring after IM.
explanation.pearls: Droperidol carries a black box QT warning but at typical sedation doses (5 to 10 mg IM) the absolute torsades risk is very low and ECG screening is reserved for risk factors or repeated dosing.

stem: You are the GP reviewing a 38-year-old man with bipolar I disorder, well-controlled on lithium for the last six years at a stable level. He has had no manic or depressive episodes in three years. He attends today asking for a script for ibuprofen for two weeks for an acute mechanical back strain after lifting at work. He has no past history of renal disease, hypertension or peptic ulceration. He is on no other regular medications and is otherwise well.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/74 mmHg, HR 72 bpm, T 36.6°C, weight 84 kg
data_table.Examination: Lumbar paraspinal tenderness only, no neurology, no abdominal tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Last lithium level 4 weeks ago: 0.7 mmol/L, eGFR 92 mL/min/1.73 m^2, TSH 2.1 mIU/L, sodium 138 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe oral celecoxib 200 mg daily as a COX-2 selective alternative without lithium monitoring
options.rationale: COX-2 selective NSAIDs interact with lithium similarly to non-selective NSAIDs and offer no safe-co-prescription advantage in this context. (Source: AMH; eTG: Psychotropic)

options.text: Prescribe oral ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily and recheck lithium level after the two-week course
options.rationale: Co-prescribing an oral NSAID with lithium is generally avoided; checking the level afterwards manages the consequence rather than preventing it. (Source: AMH; eTG: Psychotropic)

options.text: Prescribe oral paracetamol 1 g four times daily and topical diclofenac gel rather than oral NSAID
options.rationale: Oral NSAIDs reduce renal lithium clearance and can raise lithium levels by 30 to 60%, precipitating toxicity; paracetamol and topical NSAIDs avoid this interaction. (Source: AMH; eTG: Psychotropic)

options.text: Prescribe oral oxycodone 5 mg as required and review back pain weekly for the next month
options.rationale: Opioids for mechanical low back pain risk dependence and falls and are not first-line; non-opioid options that do not interact with lithium are preferred. (Source: AMH; eTG: Pain)

options.text: Withhold lithium for two weeks while the patient uses oral ibuprofen and resume lithium afterwards
options.rationale: Stopping lithium risks relapse of bipolar disorder; abrupt withdrawal also increases the risk of rebound mania within weeks. (Source: AMH; eTG: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Lithium has a narrow therapeutic index. NSAIDs reduce prostaglandin-mediated renal afferent arteriolar dilation, lowering glomerular filtration and lithium clearance. Plasma lithium levels can rise 30 to 60% over 7 to 10 days of NSAID co-administration. Paracetamol with topical NSAIDs is a safer analgesic strategy. If an oral NSAID is unavoidable, the lithium dose is reduced empirically by 25 to 50% and a level checked within 5 to 7 days, alongside close monitoring of renal function and clinical signs of toxicity.
key_points: Oral NSAIDs raise lithium levels by 30 to 60% within 7 to 10 days.
Paracetamol with topical NSAIDs avoids the interaction.
If oral NSAIDs are unavoidable, reduce lithium dose and check level within a week.
explanation.pearls: Co-prescription of an oral NSAID with lithium raises lithium levels by up to 60% within 7 days; if unavoidable, drop the lithium dose by a quarter and check the level at day 5.

stem: You are the psychiatry registrar in an early intervention clinic seeing a 19-year-old man with a four-month history of social withdrawal, persecutory delusions and auditory hallucinations. He has not used illicit substances and screens negative for cannabis, methamphetamine and synthetic cannabinoids. He is medication-naive and has no relevant past medical history. He is engaged in shared decision-making and is willing to start an antipsychotic but is concerned about weight gain because his older brother gained 18 kg on olanzapine.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 122/72 mmHg, HR 78 bpm, T 36.7°C, BMI 22 kg/m^2
data_table.Examination: Calm, formal thought disorder, persecutory delusions, second-person auditory hallucinations, no insight
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 4.8 mmol/L, total cholesterol 4.2 mmol/L, ECG normal sinus rhythm with QTc 410 ms, prolactin within normal range

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial antipsychotic choice?

options.text: Oral clozapine 12.5 mg daily titrated according to protocol with weekly FBC monitoring
options.rationale: Clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia after two adequate trials of other antipsychotics; using it first-line is not supported. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders)

options.text: Oral aripiprazole 10 mg daily titrated weekly with monthly metabolic monitoring
options.rationale: Aripiprazole has a lower metabolic burden than olanzapine while maintaining efficacy in first-episode psychosis and aligns with the patient's stated concern. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders; eTG: Psychotropic)

options.text: Oral olanzapine 10 mg daily titrated weekly with monthly metabolic monitoring
options.rationale: Olanzapine is effective but carries the greatest weight-gain risk of the second-generation agents; given this patient's stated concerns it is not the best first choice. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders)

options.text: Oral haloperidol 5 mg daily titrated weekly with extrapyramidal symptom monitoring
options.rationale: First-generation antipsychotics have higher rates of EPS and tardive dyskinesia and are not preferred first-line for medication-naive young men with first-episode psychosis. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders)

options.text: Oral lorazepam 1 mg three times daily as monotherapy until clear diagnosis is established
options.rationale: Benzodiazepine monotherapy does not treat psychotic symptoms; antipsychotic therapy should not be delayed once first-episode psychosis is diagnosed. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders)

explanation.summary: RANZCP guidance for first-episode psychosis emphasises early treatment, lower starting doses, shared decision-making and avoidance of olanzapine where metabolic concerns are present. Aripiprazole and risperidone are reasonable first-line options. Baseline weight, waist circumference, fasting glucose, lipids, prolactin and ECG should be measured before starting and reviewed at 3 and 12 months. Long-acting injectables should be discussed early as an option after stabilisation to support adherence.
key_points: Aripiprazole and risperidone are first-line for first-episode psychosis.
Olanzapine has the highest metabolic burden; discuss this explicitly.
Baseline metabolic, cardiac and prolactin screening precedes antipsychotic start.
explanation.pearls: First-episode psychosis starts with low-dose aripiprazole or risperidone, baseline weight, fasting glucose, lipids and ECG, with metabolic review at 3 and 12 months.

stem: You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 26-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia who started clozapine 18 days ago and is on day 18 of titration at 200 mg daily. The community nurse phones because he reports increasing fatigue, mild central chest discomfort and a low-grade temperature. He has had no respiratory symptoms and his clozapine clinic baseline ECG was normal. He has no past cardiac history. Examination shows sinus tachycardia and mild bibasal crackles.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 122 bpm, BP 108/62 mmHg, T 37.6°C, RR 22, SpO2 96% on room air
data_table.Examination: Mild bibasal crackles, no murmurs, no peripheral oedema, JVP not raised
data_table.Investigations: Troponin I 380 ng/L (baseline less than 14), CRP 78 mg/L, ECG sinus tachycardia with non-specific T wave changes, FBC unchanged, ferritin within normal range

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Add oral prednisolone 50 mg daily and continue clozapine 200 mg daily with weekly troponin and CRP checks
options.rationale: Steroid therapy does not allow continued clozapine exposure in established myocarditis and there is no evidence base for routine corticosteroid use here. (Source: RANZCP: Clozapine)

options.text: Reduce clozapine to 100 mg daily and recheck troponin and CRP in 72 hours as outpatient at the clozapine clinic
options.rationale: Dose reduction does not protect against ongoing myocarditis; continued exposure risks fulminant cardiomyopathy. (Source: RANZCP: Clozapine)

options.text: Continue clozapine at 200 mg daily and review with the general practitioner at 7 days for symptom progression
options.rationale: Continuing the offending drug in suspected clozapine myocarditis is dangerous and contradicts the recommended cessation pathway. (Source: RANZCP: Clozapine)

options.text: Cease clozapine today, admit for cardiac monitoring and arrange urgent transthoracic echocardiogram and cardiology review
options.rationale: Within the first 4 weeks of clozapine titration any constitutional symptoms with troponin rise, CRP rise or tachycardia mandate immediate clozapine cessation; rechallenge requires specialist cardiology and psychiatry input. (Source: RANZCP: Clozapine; AMH)

options.text: Switch to oral olanzapine 20 mg daily and ignore the cardiac investigations pending outpatient psychiatry review
options.rationale: Cardiac workup must continue regardless of antipsychotic switch; ignoring the troponin and CRP rise misses cardiomyopathy. (Source: RANZCP: Clozapine)

explanation.summary: Clozapine-induced myocarditis is most common in the first 4 weeks of treatment. Surveillance includes baseline and weekly troponin, CRP and clinical review during titration. A troponin rise above twice the upper limit, a CRP above 100 mg/L, fever, tachycardia disproportionate to dose or any unexplained constitutional symptoms triggers immediate clozapine cessation, cardiology referral and echocardiography. Rechallenge has been described under highly specialised circumstances but is not routine.
key_points: Clozapine myocarditis peaks in the first 4 weeks of titration.
Cease clozapine immediately when troponin rises or constitutional symptoms appear.
Echocardiography and cardiology referral guide diagnosis and prognosis.
explanation.pearls: During clozapine titration any troponin above twice the upper limit, CRP above 100 mg/L or unexplained tachycardia in the first 4 weeks means stop the drug today and call cardiology.

stem: You are the perinatal psychiatry registrar urgently called to the postnatal ward to assess a 30-year-old woman on day 3 after an uncomplicated vaginal birth of her first baby. The midwives report 24 hours of insomnia, pressured speech, religious grandiosity and now disorganised thought. She is breastfeeding and is reluctant to be separated from the baby. She has a family history of bipolar disorder in her sister. She has been medication-naive throughout pregnancy and has had no obstetric complications.

data_table.Examination: Pressured speech, flight of ideas, grandiose religious delusions, partial insight, no acute medical findings, no fever, no neurology
data_table.Investigations: FBC, urea, electrolytes, calcium, magnesium, TSH all within normal limits, urinalysis clear, no infective focus

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management plan?

options.text: Admit to a general adult psychiatry ward, commence oral diazepam 5 mg three times daily and suspend breastfeeding
options.rationale: General adult wards separate mother and baby unnecessarily; benzodiazepine monotherapy does not treat psychosis or mania. (Source: COPE: Perinatal mental health)

options.text: Discharge home with the baby on oral lithium 600 mg daily with paediatric monitoring of the breastfed infant
options.rationale: Outpatient management of postpartum psychosis is unsafe; lithium also has lower breastfeeding compatibility than olanzapine and is rarely first acute choice. (Source: COPE: Perinatal mental health)

options.text: Admit to a mother-baby unit, commence oral olanzapine 5 mg at night and arrange consultant psychiatry review in 24 hours
options.rationale: Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency requiring inpatient care; olanzapine is compatible with breastfeeding, has rapid antimanic effect and is the preferred first-line acute treatment in this setting. (Source: COPE: Perinatal mental health; RANZCP: Perinatal)

options.text: Arrange community perinatal psychiatry follow-up in 48 hours with no medication changes made today
options.rationale: Deferring treatment for 48 hours in postpartum psychosis exposes both mother and baby to substantial harm including infanticide and maternal suicide risk. (Source: COPE: Perinatal mental health)

options.text: Admit for urgent unilateral electroconvulsive therapy today as the first-line treatment without an oral antipsychotic trial
options.rationale: ECT is highly effective in postpartum psychosis but is reserved for severe non-response, catatonia or refusal of oral therapy; oral antipsychotic is the standard first step. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal)

explanation.summary: Postpartum psychosis affects approximately 1 in 1000 births and clusters in women with bipolar disorder or a family history. Onset is typically within the first 2 weeks postpartum with rapid escalation of insomnia, mood lability, psychosis and risk to mother and baby. Management is psychiatric emergency: admission to a mother-baby unit, antipsychotic plus mood stabiliser where indicated, and ECT for severe or refractory presentations. Olanzapine is preferred for breastfeeding-compatible rapid antimanic effect.
key_points: Postpartum psychosis is an emergency with rapid escalation.
Admit to a mother-baby unit when available; start oral antipsychotic immediately.
Olanzapine is the preferred initial breastfeeding-compatible antipsychotic.
explanation.pearls: Day 3 to 14 postpartum onset of insomnia, mood elevation and delusions is postpartum psychosis until proven otherwise - admit today and start olanzapine 5 to 10 mg at night.

subtopic_detail: Depression with psychotic features in older adults
stem: You are the consultation-liaison psychiatry registrar reviewing a 76-year-old woman admitted under geriatrics with weight loss of 8 kg over 2 months, reduced oral intake and persistent low mood. She has nihilistic delusions that her bowels have rotted and refuses food because of this. She has tried sertraline at 100 mg daily for 8 weeks and mirtazapine at 30 mg daily for 6 weeks as outpatient with no response. She has no past history of psychosis. She has retained capacity and is willing to consider further treatment.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/68 mmHg, HR 76 bpm, T 36.5°C, weight 48 kg, BMI 18 kg/m^2
data_table.Examination: Psychomotor retardation, nihilistic delusions, MMSE 28 of 30, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, TSH, B12, folate, calcium all within normal limits, ECG normal sinus rhythm with QTc 440 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in treatment?

options.text: Switch mirtazapine to oral venlafaxine 75 mg daily titrating over 4 weeks and review at 8 weeks
options.rationale: A third sequential antidepressant trial delays definitive treatment in a malnourished psychotically depressed older patient; ECT has superior response rate and speed. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders)

options.text: Add oral aripiprazole 5 mg daily to existing mirtazapine and continue for 8 weeks before reassessment
options.rationale: Antipsychotic augmentation is reasonable for non-psychotic treatment-resistant depression, but slow onset and inadequate efficacy in nihilistic delusions with malnutrition make ECT preferable here. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders)

options.text: Refer for bilateral electroconvulsive therapy after written informed consent and anaesthetic assessment
options.rationale: Psychotic depression in older adults responds rapidly to ECT and is the preferred next step when two adequate antidepressant trials have failed and there is malnutrition or risk to life. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders; eTG: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence oral lithium 250 mg twice daily for augmentation aiming for level 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L
options.rationale: Lithium augmentation in an older adult with reduced GFR and dehydration risk is high-risk and slow-acting, not the optimal next step here. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders)

options.text: Refer for transcranial magnetic stimulation as outpatient over the next 6 weeks
options.rationale: TMS lacks adequate evidence in psychotic depression and is generally avoided in this subgroup; inpatient ECT is preferred. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders)

explanation.summary: Major depression with psychotic features in older adults carries a high mortality from suicide and physical decline. Adequate antidepressant trial is at least 6 to 8 weeks at therapeutic dose. After two such failures, particularly with malnutrition or active suicide risk, ECT is the preferred next step with response rates of 70 to 90% within 6 to 12 sessions. Capacity should be assessed and informed consent obtained; involuntary treatment under the relevant Mental Health Act may apply when capacity is lost.
key_points: Two adequate antidepressant trials precede ECT in non-emergent cases.
Psychotic depression with malnutrition or suicide risk justifies earlier ECT.
Capacity assessment and informed consent precede ECT where possible.
explanation.pearls: Older adult with psychotic depression refusing food after 2 antidepressant failures should be offered ECT within days; expected response rate is 70 to 90% in 6 to 12 sessions.

stem: You are the consultation-liaison psychiatry registrar reviewing a 22-year-old woman admitted with mutism, immobility and refusal to eat or drink for 4 days. She has a first presentation of a probable mood disorder. Medical workup including computed tomography of the brain, lumbar puncture, autoimmune encephalitis panel and toxicology has been unremarkable. An intramuscular lorazepam 2 mg trial 48 hours ago produced a brief partial improvement that lasted 2 hours. She has since had two further 2 mg doses without sustained benefit. She has developed pressure areas and has stopped passing urine.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/86 mmHg, HR 110 bpm, T 37.4°C, RR 18, SpO2 98% on room air
data_table.Examination: Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale 28 of 69, mutism, posturing, waxy flexibility, no rigidity, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 480 U/L, Na 134 mmol/L, K 4.2 mmol/L, creatinine 110 micromol/L, lactate 1.6 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence intravenous amantadine 200 mg twice daily as the next step in management while continuing lorazepam
options.rationale: NMDA antagonists are an unproven third-line option after benzodiazepines and ECT have failed; they should not displace ECT in this presentation. (Source: RANZCP: ECT)

options.text: Increase lorazepam to 8 mg orally over 24 hours and continue for a further 5 days before considering ECT referral
options.rationale: Lorazepam non-response within 48 to 72 hours alongside complications mandates escalation to ECT rather than further dose increases; prolonged immobility risks rhabdomyolysis and DVT. (Source: RANZCP: ECT)

options.text: Commence oral olanzapine 10 mg daily as the next step in management and re-evaluate at 7 days for response
options.rationale: Antipsychotics can worsen catatonia and may precipitate neuroleptic malignant syndrome; they are generally avoided until catatonia has resolved. (Source: RANZCP: ECT)

options.text: Refer for bilateral electroconvulsive therapy starting within 24 hours with daily anaesthetic and physical review
options.rationale: Catatonia not responding to a lorazepam challenge requires prompt ECT, particularly when there is dehydration, immobility complications and creatine kinase elevation suggesting evolving malignant catatonia. (Source: RANZCP: ECT; eTG: Psychotropic)

options.text: Stop all psychotropic medications and continue supportive care for 7 days before reassessment of catatonic features
options.rationale: Watchful waiting in a dehydrated immobile patient with rising CK risks progression to malignant catatonia with multi-organ failure. (Source: RANZCP: ECT)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a transdiagnostic syndrome of mutism, immobility, posturing, waxy flexibility, mutism and stupor. The Bush-Francis scale screens and grades severity. First-line treatment is a lorazepam challenge of 1 to 2 mg with response monitored; titration up to 8 to 24 mg daily may be needed. ECT is indicated when benzodiazepines fail, when malignant catatonia evolves with autonomic instability and elevated CK, or when life-threatening complications such as dehydration emerge. Antipsychotics may precipitate or worsen catatonia and are avoided until resolution.
key_points: Bush-Francis screening confirms catatonia; lorazepam challenge is first-line.
ECT is the next step when benzodiazepine fails or malignant catatonia evolves.
Avoid antipsychotics during active catatonia.
explanation.pearls: When a lorazepam challenge gives only transient benefit and CK rises with autonomic instability, malignant catatonia is evolving and ECT should start within 24 hours.

stem: You are the GP reviewing a 26-year-old man with first-episode schizophrenia commenced on risperidone 3 mg daily 12 weeks ago. Symptoms are improved and he tolerates the medication. He has gained 6 kg since starting treatment. He smokes 10 cigarettes per day, drinks no alcohol and has no family history of cardiovascular disease. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. Baseline metabolic parameters were normal. He is asymptomatic and lives independently.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 128/82, HR 78, RR 16, BMI 28, waist circumference 99 cm
data_table.Examination: Well-appearing, no extrapyramidal signs, no tardive dyskinesia, no orthostatic hypotension
data_table.Investigations: Baseline (12 weeks ago) fasting glucose 5.0 mmol/L, lipids normal, HbA1c 33 mmol/mol, ECG normal

lead_in: What metabolic monitoring is most appropriate at this visit?

options.text: Repeat fasting glucose and lipids at 12 months from baseline review and not before then
options.rationale: Australian guidance recommends fasting glucose and lipids at 12 weeks after starting an antipsychotic to detect early metabolic shift; 12 months is the next routine interval after that. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Monitoring)

options.text: Check serum prolactin and weight only because metabolic risk is minimal in young men
options.rationale: Young men are at meaningful metabolic risk on antipsychotics and a full panel is recommended at the 12-week review, not selective monitoring. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Monitoring)

options.text: Check fasting glucose, lipids, weight, waist and blood pressure and review the lifestyle plan
options.rationale: RANZCP and Australian guidelines recommend full metabolic monitoring at 12 weeks plus lifestyle counselling, given the early-onset weight gain seen in this patient. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Monitoring)

options.text: Switch to aripiprazole now to reduce future metabolic risk even though he is tolerating risperidone
options.rationale: Switching antipsychotics should be considered after weight gain is confirmed and lifestyle measures trialled; routine switch at 12 weeks is not recommended. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Monitoring)

options.text: Order oral glucose tolerance test plus 24-hour urinary cortisol to exclude secondary causes today
options.rationale: OGTT and cortisol are not part of routine antipsychotic monitoring; standard fasting glucose and lipid screening is the recommended baseline at 12 weeks. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Monitoring)

explanation.summary: Australian antipsychotic monitoring guidance recommends baseline assessment of weight, waist circumference, blood pressure, fasting glucose, lipids, ECG and prolactin and review at 6 weeks, 12 weeks, then yearly. Risperidone causes early weight gain and dyslipidaemia in younger patients. The 12-week review is the critical decision point: if metabolic shift is evident, intensify lifestyle measures, consider metformin, and discuss switching to a lower-risk antipsychotic such as aripiprazole if change persists. Smoking cessation should also be addressed because of independent cardiovascular and CYP1A2 effects.
key_points: Repeat metabolic panel at 6 and 12 weeks post-initiation.
Yearly metabolic review thereafter is the standard.
Intensify lifestyle measures and consider metformin early.
Switching to lower-risk agent is appropriate if changes persist.
explanation.pearls: Metformin 500 mg twice daily has good evidence for attenuating antipsychotic-induced weight gain in patients with at least 5 kg gain in 3 months; start it alongside structured lifestyle support rather than after a metabolic syndrome has developed.

subtopic_detail: Sertraline in third-trimester pregnancy and neonatal adaptation
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 31-year-old at 34 weeks pregnant with a history of moderate depression. She has been on sertraline 100 mg daily for 18 months and is well, with no current symptoms. She is anxious about effects on the baby and considering stopping the medication before delivery. She has no other medications, no risk of postpartum psychosis and has supportive family. She has booked at a tertiary centre.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/74, HR 78, T 36.6 °C, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Soft uterus, cephalic, fetal heart 138 reassuring, no oedema, EPDS score 7
data_table.Investigations: Not required

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice regarding sertraline continuation in late pregnancy?

options.text: Stop sertraline now to reduce neonatal adaptation syndrome risk and restart after delivery completed
options.rationale: Stopping antidepressants in late pregnancy carries a substantial relapse risk in postpartum depression and is not recommended in stable, well patients. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal)

options.text: Continue sertraline 100 mg daily and arrange neonatal adaptation review at 24 to 48 hours after birth
options.rationale: Australian practice is to continue effective antidepressants through pregnancy and breastfeeding, with paediatric review for neonatal adaptation syndrome in the first 24 to 48 hours after birth. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal)

options.text: Halve the sertraline dose now and stop it completely two weeks before the expected date of delivery
options.rationale: Tapering before delivery to reduce neonatal symptoms increases maternal relapse risk and is not recommended in well stable patients on a maintenance SSRI. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal)

options.text: Switch sertraline to fluoxetine to maintain a longer half-life and reduce neonatal withdrawal effects
options.rationale: Fluoxetine has a long half-life and may extend exposure rather than reduce neonatal symptoms; switching well-tolerated treatment in late pregnancy is not recommended. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal)

options.text: Substitute psychological therapy alone now and discontinue sertraline before the third trimester begins
options.rationale: Switching from effective pharmacotherapy to psychological therapy alone late in pregnancy risks relapse; both modalities can be combined when clinically indicated. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal)

explanation.summary: Australian perinatal psychiatry guidance favours continuing effective antidepressants in pregnancy because relapse risk often outweighs the small absolute risk of neonatal adaptation syndrome. Sertraline is one of the SSRIs with the most reassuring breastfeeding data. Neonates exposed in the third trimester should be observed for 24 to 48 hours for jitteriness, feeding difficulties and respiratory symptoms. Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn is a rare and largely transient association. A maternal mental health plan and EPDS monitoring postpartum are routine.
key_points: Continue effective antidepressants in stable pregnant women.
Watch for neonatal adaptation in the first 24 to 48 hours.
Sertraline and paroxetine have lower breast milk concentrations.
Add EPDS at 6 weeks and 3 months postpartum to detect relapse.
explanation.pearls: Neonatal adaptation syndrome occurs in around 30 percent of SSRI-exposed infants, peaks at 24 to 48 hours and resolves within a week without specific treatment; rooming-in plus paediatric observation is sufficient in most term babies.

subtopic_detail: Valproate pregnancy prevention in bipolar disorder
stem: You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 23-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder who has been stable for 18 months on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily. She has a long-term partner and uses condoms only. She is not currently planning pregnancy but is unsure about her contraception. She is aware valproate has risks in pregnancy. She has no other psychiatric or medical conditions and her last manic episode required hospital admission.

data_table.Examination: Stable mood, euthymic, no extrapyramidal signs, no tremor
data_table.Investigations: FBC, LFTs, valproate level within range; beta-hCG negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step regarding her treatment plan?

options.text: Reassure that condoms are adequate contraception and continue valproate at the current dose long-term
options.rationale: Valproate has a 10 percent major congenital malformation and 30 to 40 percent neurodevelopmental impairment risk; highly effective contraception is required throughout treatment. (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention)

options.text: Plan a slow valproate taper over four weeks and start lamotrigine 25 mg daily titrating up cautiously
options.rationale: Tapering a stabilising mood stabiliser without secured alternative cover risks severe relapse with prior psychiatric hospitalisation; secure contraception is the immediate priority. (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention)

options.text: Switch to lithium today and provide both verbal and written information about teratogenicity risks
options.rationale: Switching mood stabilisers in a stable patient introduces relapse risk; the immediate need is highly effective contraception while continuing the stabilising agent. (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention)

options.text: Continue valproate and add a combined oral contraceptive without other contraceptive review or plan
options.rationale: Combined oral contraception alone meets effectiveness criteria but the pregnancy prevention program requires annual review and documented risk acknowledgement, not contraception alone. (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention)

options.text: Insert an etonogestrel subdermal implant today and document the pregnancy prevention program plan
options.rationale: Australian and TGA-aligned pregnancy prevention program requires highly effective contraception such as a LARC plus documented annual risk acknowledgement when valproate is used in women of reproductive potential. (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention)

explanation.summary: Sodium valproate carries a 10 percent risk of major congenital malformation and 30 to 40 percent risk of neurodevelopmental impairment with fetal exposure. Australian pregnancy prevention program guidance requires highly effective contraception such as long-acting reversible contraception, annual reauthorisation, and documented patient acknowledgement of risks. In women planning pregnancy, switch to a safer mood stabiliser such as lithium or lamotrigine before conception. Folic acid 5 mg daily is added if conception is planned despite valproate.
key_points: Use LARC for highly effective contraception on valproate.
Document the pregnancy prevention plan and review annually.
Switch to safer agents before planned conception.
Prescribe 5 mg folic acid daily if conception is planned.
explanation.pearls: The risk of neural tube defects with valproate exposure is highest in the first 28 days; brief pre-conception switching may not eliminate risk if the embryo is already implanted, so LARC is preferable to depending on a planned switch alone.

stem: You are the consultation-liaison psychiatry registrar reviewing a 32-year-old woman on the medical ward. She has had no significant medical history but has become mute, immobile and resistant to passive limb movement over the last 24 hours. Her examination shows waxy flexibility, mutism and posturing without focal neurological signs. She has had two previous episodes of psychotic depression. CT head and basic metabolic screen are unremarkable. NMS, encephalitis and serotonin syndrome are not supported by current findings.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 °C, HR 88, RR 16, BP 124/74, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Mutism, immobility, waxy flexibility, posturing of left arm; no rigidity, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: CT head normal; FBC, U&E, LFT, glucose, calcium, magnesium normal; CK 220, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate diagnostic and therapeutic step?

options.text: Order a lumbar puncture and MRI brain before commencing any specific pharmacological therapy today
options.rationale: Imaging and CSF analysis are appropriate when organic causes are suspected, but a lorazepam challenge can proceed in parallel because basic screening is normal. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia)

options.text: Begin oral olanzapine 10 mg now to treat presumed underlying psychosis prior to other interventions
options.rationale: Antipsychotics in untreated catatonia can precipitate neuroleptic malignant syndrome; benzodiazepines or ECT are first-line until catatonia resolves. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia)

options.text: Refer for urgent electroconvulsive therapy without trial of any benzodiazepine challenge first
options.rationale: ECT is reserved for malignant or benzodiazepine-resistant catatonia; a lorazepam challenge should be tried first because most catatonia responds to benzodiazepines. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia)

options.text: Commence intramuscular haloperidol 5 mg as needed for behavioural control on the ward overnight
options.rationale: High-potency antipsychotics in catatonia significantly increase the risk of neuroleptic malignant syndrome and worsen the catatonia itself. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia)

options.text: Administer intravenous lorazepam 2 mg and reassess catatonia features after 10 minutes
options.rationale: An IV lorazepam challenge is both diagnostic and therapeutic; reduction in Bush Francis catatonia features within 10 minutes supports the diagnosis and guides ongoing benzodiazepine use. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a clinical syndrome of stupor, mutism, posturing, waxy flexibility and other motor features that can occur with mood, psychotic and organic disorders. Intravenous or intramuscular lorazepam at 1 to 2 mg gives a 60 to 80 percent response within 10 minutes and is both diagnostic and therapeutic. Antipsychotics should be withheld until catatonia resolves because they predispose to neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Failure to respond to benzodiazepine should prompt early ECT under the relevant mental health act framework.
key_points: Lorazepam 1 to 2 mg IV is the recommended challenge dose.
Antipsychotics worsen catatonia and increase NMS risk.
Reserve ECT for benzodiazepine-resistant or malignant catatonia.
Investigate for organic and mood disorder causes simultaneously.
explanation.pearls: Persistent autonomic instability, hyperthermia above 38 °C or rising CK in a catatonic patient signals malignant catatonia; transfer to ICU and arrange ECT urgently because untreated mortality exceeds 50 percent.

subtopic_detail: TCA overdose with QRS widening management
stem: You are the ED registrar at a metropolitan hospital seeing a 28-year-old man brought in 90 minutes after ingestion of about 40 amitriptyline 25 mg tablets in a suicide attempt. He is drowsy but responsive, with dry mouth and dilated pupils. His ECG shows sinus tachycardia with a QRS of 140 ms and right axis deviation of the terminal R wave in aVR. He has no seizures and a single dose of activated charcoal has been administered. Toxicology has been notified.

data_table.Vital signs: GCS 13, HR 124, BP 96/58, RR 18, SpO2 98% room air, T 36.7 °C, BSL 6.2
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, dry mucous membranes, mydriasis, no focal neurological deficit, no clonus
data_table.Investigations: ECG: sinus tachycardia, QRS 140 ms, terminal R in aVR >3 mm; venous blood gas pH 7.30, lactate 3.2 mmol/L, K 3.6 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus and reassess QRS width and pH
options.rationale: QRS above 100 ms with terminal R wave in aVR signifies sodium channel blockade in TCA toxicity; sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus reverses the conduction abnormality. (Source: NSW Poisons Information)

options.text: Commence intravenous lipid emulsion 1.5 mL/kg as a first-line antidote prior to alkalinisation therapy
options.rationale: Lipid emulsion is reserved for cardiovascular collapse refractory to bicarbonate in lipophilic drug toxicity; sodium bicarbonate is first-line for TCA QRS widening. (Source: NSW Poisons Information)

options.text: Give intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg titrated until alert as the immediate next reversal step today
options.rationale: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines and has no role in TCA overdose; it can precipitate seizures in mixed ingestions. (Source: NSW Poisons Information)

options.text: Begin intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g over 10 minutes as the recommended sodium channel antidote
options.rationale: Magnesium is an adjunct for torsades de pointes and refractory dysrhythmia, not the primary therapy for TCA-induced sodium channel blockade. (Source: NSW Poisons Information)

options.text: Commence intravenous procainamide 17 mg/kg to control sinus tachycardia and prevent further conduction loss
options.rationale: Class 1a antiarrhythmics are sodium channel blockers themselves and will worsen TCA cardiotoxicity; they are contraindicated. (Source: NSW Poisons Information)

explanation.summary: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose causes sodium channel blockade, anticholinergic toxicity, alpha-adrenergic blockade and seizures. A QRS above 100 ms predicts seizures and ventricular arrhythmia; a terminal R in aVR above 3 mm is a sensitive marker. Sodium bicarbonate boluses of 1 to 2 mmol/kg narrow the QRS and reverse hypotension. Aim for arterial pH 7.50 to 7.55 and sodium 145 to 155 mmol/L. Lipid emulsion is rescue therapy for collapse not responding to bicarbonate, with toxicology input.
key_points: QRS above 100 ms drives bicarbonate therapy decision.
Aim for pH 7.50 to 7.55 and sodium 145 to 155 mmol/L.
Avoid class Ia, Ic and III antiarrhythmics.
Lipid emulsion is reserved for refractory collapse.
explanation.pearls: Seizures cause profound metabolic acidosis that worsens TCA cardiotoxicity within minutes; treat with benzodiazepines first-line and avoid phenytoin which is also a sodium channel blocker and may precipitate ventricular tachycardia.

subtopic_detail: Discrimination of NMS from serotonin syndrome with hyperthermia
stem: You are the ED registrar reviewing a 24-year-old man with treatment-resistant depression on phenelzine. He took two doses of tramadol from his mother's medication this evening. Two hours later he is agitated, sweating, with hyperthermia, hypertension, ocular clonus, hyperreflexia and inducible lower limb clonus. His muscles are not lead-pipe rigid and his mental status fluctuates with marked agitation. No antipsychotic exposure. CK is 220 IU/L. Toxicology has been contacted and ICU is aware.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.6 °C, HR 132, BP 168/102, RR 24, SpO2 98% room air, BSL 6.4
data_table.Examination: Agitated, mydriasis, hyperreflexia greater in lower limbs, sustained clonus at ankles, ocular clonus, sweating
data_table.Investigations: CK 220 IU/L, lactate 3.6 mmol/L, creatinine 92, sodium 138, ECG sinus tachycardia

lead_in: What is the most appropriate specific therapy in addition to supportive care?

options.text: Give intramuscular adrenaline 10 micrograms/kg and intravenous methylprednisolone for autonomic crisis
options.rationale: Adrenaline and steroids have no role and may worsen hypertension and hyperthermia; benzodiazepines plus cyproheptadine are first line. (Source: NSW Poisons Information)

options.text: Start oral bromocriptine 2.5 mg three times daily and intravenous dantrolene for muscle rigidity now
options.rationale: Bromocriptine and dantrolene are reserved for neuroleptic malignant syndrome which features lead-pipe rigidity and bradyreflexia; this presentation is serotonin syndrome. (Source: NSW Poisons Information)

options.text: Administer intravenous haloperidol 5 mg for control of agitation and continue all current medications
options.rationale: Antipsychotics worsen autonomic instability and can precipitate NMS; agitation in serotonin syndrome is treated with benzodiazepines and removal of serotonergic agents. (Source: NSW Poisons Information)

options.text: Restart phenelzine immediately and add oral mirtazapine to block serotonin syndrome symptoms tomorrow
options.rationale: Mirtazapine has 5HT2A blocking properties but should never be restarted with phenelzine; both serotonergic drugs must be ceased. (Source: NSW Poisons Information)

options.text: Cease serotonergic drugs, give midazolam titrated and oral cyproheptadine 12 mg loading dose now
options.rationale: The Hunter criteria pattern of inducible clonus, ocular clonus and hyperreflexia fit serotonin syndrome; benzodiazepines and the 5HT2A antagonist cyproheptadine are the specific Australian-recommended therapy. (Source: NSW Poisons Information)

explanation.summary: Serotonin syndrome from MAOI plus tramadol is a clinical diagnosis using Hunter criteria: spontaneous or inducible clonus, ocular clonus, agitation, hyperreflexia, hypertension and hyperthermia. NMS instead features lead-pipe rigidity, bradyreflexia and slow onset after antipsychotic dose escalation. Treatment is removal of serotonergic agents, intravenous fluid, cooling, benzodiazepines for agitation and rigidity, and cyproheptadine if symptoms persist. Severe hyperthermia above 41 °C warrants intubation, paralysis and active cooling in ICU.
key_points: Clonus and hyperreflexia favour serotonin syndrome over NMS.
Benzodiazepines plus cyproheptadine are specific therapy.
Avoid antipsychotics in serotonin syndrome.
Intubate and paralyse if T above 41 °C with rigidity.
explanation.pearls: Cyproheptadine loading is 12 mg orally, then 2 mg every 2 hours up to 32 mg in 24 hours; if the patient cannot swallow, crush and give via nasogastric tube because there is no parenteral preparation in Australia.

stem: You are the GP seeing a 42-year-old man who smokes 25 cigarettes a day, has done so for 20 years, and is highly motivated to quit. He has a Fagerstrom score of 7 indicating high dependence. He had one mild depressive episode treated with sertraline 5 years ago, has been off SSRI for 4 years and reports no current depression, anxiety, suicidal ideation or cardiovascular disease. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Examination: Cardiovascular and respiratory examination unremarkable; no signs of liver disease; PHQ-9 score 3
data_table.Investigations: FBC, LFTs, eGFR all normal; ECG unremarkable; carbon monoxide breath test elevated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy plan?

options.text: Combination nicotine patch and bupropion together with weekly counselling
options.rationale: Combination NRT plus bupropion lacks superior outcomes over single agent and increases the chance of adverse effects without clear benefit. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guideline)

options.text: Nicotine 21 mg/24 hour patch alone with as needed lozenges for cravings
options.rationale: Combination NRT is acceptable but varenicline has higher quit rates and is preferred first-line in patients without contraindication. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guideline)

options.text: Bupropion 150 mg twice daily combined with nortriptyline 25 mg at night
options.rationale: Combining noradrenergic agents increases seizure and serotonergic risk and is not first-line; nortriptyline is rarely used now. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guideline)

options.text: Hypnotherapy alone without pharmacological support and a quit date in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Hypnotherapy has no robust evidence of benefit in tobacco dependence and delays the chance of a pharmacologically supported quit. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guideline)

options.text: Start varenicline 0.5 mg daily titrating to 1 mg twice daily with quit date in week 2
options.rationale: Varenicline is first-line pharmacotherapy in Australian guidance for highly dependent smokers without significant psychiatric instability; titration over the first week reduces nausea. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guideline)

explanation.summary: Varenicline produces higher continuous abstinence rates than bupropion or single-agent NRT in tobacco dependence. RACGP guidance recommends varenicline first-line for highly dependent smokers without recent suicidal ideation, severe mood disorder or pregnancy. Initiation is staged over the first week with a quit date in week 2 to maximise tolerability. Combination NRT is reserved as second-line and bupropion as third-line; behavioural support adds to all options.
key_points: Varenicline produces the highest continuous abstinence rates.
Start at 0.5 mg daily and titrate over a week.
Quit date is set in week 2 of treatment.
Combination NRT is second-line; bupropion is third-line.
explanation.pearls: Varenicline can intensify the effects of alcohol with reports of disinhibition and amnesia; counsel patients to avoid alcohol particularly during the first few weeks and re-question carefully at follow-up because behaviour change can be subtle.

subtopic_detail: Adult ADHD pathway with childhood symptom evidence
stem: You are the GP seeing a 30-year-old man with long-standing inattention, distractibility, poor organisation, frequent lateness, and recent loss of his job after repeated forgotten deadlines. His mother provides childhood school reports from age 8 documenting 'does not pay attention in class' and 'difficulty completing tasks'. PHQ-9 is 4 and GAD-7 is 3. He drinks 2 standard drinks a week and has no illicit drug use. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Examination: Cardiovascular examination unremarkable; no thyroid mass; cognitive screen unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: TFTs normal; B12 and ferritin normal; ECG unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to a psychiatrist for formal ADHD diagnostic assessment using DSM-5 criteria and collateral
options.rationale: Adult ADHD diagnosis and stimulant initiation in Australia requires a psychiatrist or paediatrician with collateral evidence of pre-12-year symptoms; this case has both childhood documentation and current functional impairment. (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guidelines)

options.text: Commence a trial of methylphenidate 10 mg twice daily from the GP and review in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Stimulant initiation in adult ADHD in Australia is restricted to authorised specialists (psychiatrist or paediatrician); GP initiation is not permitted without prior specialist diagnosis. (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guidelines)

options.text: Order thyroid function tests alone and review again with a working diagnosis at 2 weeks
options.rationale: TFTs are already normal in this case; thyroid disease is excluded as an organic mimic and further screening alone delays definitive diagnosis. (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guidelines)

options.text: Refer to occupational therapy for cognitive strategies and defer any psychiatric assessment
options.rationale: Occupational therapy alone cannot establish the diagnosis or initiate appropriate pharmacotherapy if indicated; psychiatric assessment is the formal pathway. (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guidelines)

options.text: Trial of methylphenidate sustained release as a diagnostic-therapeutic probe in clinic
options.rationale: Therapeutic trials are not the diagnostic pathway; stimulants must follow a formal specialist diagnosis under Australian regulation. (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Adult ADHD diagnosis in Australia requires DSM-5 criteria including pervasive symptoms in two or more settings, functional impairment and evidence of childhood symptoms before age 12. Diagnostic assessment must currently be made by a psychiatrist or paediatrician, who may also initiate stimulant therapy. Collateral information from family, employers or old school reports strengthens the diagnostic process. Comorbid mood, anxiety and substance disorders should be screened for and managed concurrently.
key_points: DSM-5 requires childhood symptoms before age 12.
Specialist diagnosis is mandatory before stimulant initiation.
Collateral evidence supports the diagnostic process.
Screen and treat comorbid mood, anxiety and substance disorders.
explanation.pearls: Women and girls are systematically under-diagnosed because inattentive presentations attract less referral than hyperactive ones; a normal childhood school record does not exclude ADHD in a woman presenting with adult functional decline.

subtopic_detail: First-line treatment of borderline personality disorder
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 22-year-old woman with a formal diagnosis of borderline personality disorder confirmed by a public mental health service. She describes recurrent self-harm by cutting, intense unstable relationships, fear of abandonment and chronic emptiness. She is currently on sertraline 100 mg with no significant change in symptoms after 4 months. She has no active suicidality today, no psychotic features and no substance use disorder. She is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Examination: Faint linear scars on volar forearms; no acute injuries; engaged with cooperative manner; no thought disorder
data_table.Investigations: TFTs and FBC normal; PHQ-9 score 12; GAD-7 score 10

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next management step?

options.text: Increase sertraline to 150 mg daily and review in 4 weeks for further response
options.rationale: Antidepressant escalation is unlikely to address the core symptoms of BPD; structured psychotherapy is the recommended first-line intervention. (Source: NHMRC Borderline Personality Disorder Guidelines)

options.text: Refer for structured dialectical behaviour therapy with a trained therapist or program
options.rationale: Australian NHMRC guidance places structured psychotherapy first-line for borderline personality disorder; dialectical behaviour therapy is the most studied program with effect on self-harm and emotion regulation. (Source: NHMRC Borderline Personality Disorder Guidelines)

options.text: Add quetiapine 200 mg at night for affective instability and sleep disturbance
options.rationale: Antipsychotics are not first-line for BPD; their use is restricted to short-term crisis management or specific symptom domains under specialist guidance. (Source: NHMRC Borderline Personality Disorder Guidelines)

options.text: Commence lithium 600 mg at night targeting a serum level of 0.6-0.8 mmol/L
options.rationale: Lithium is reserved for bipolar mood stabilisation; it has no role in BPD and adds toxicity and monitoring burden. (Source: NHMRC Borderline Personality Disorder Guidelines)

options.text: Refer for electroconvulsive therapy given persistent symptoms despite an SSRI trial
options.rationale: ECT has no place in BPD treatment; it is reserved for severe affective and psychotic illness unresponsive to other measures. (Source: NHMRC Borderline Personality Disorder Guidelines)

explanation.summary: NHMRC guidance positions structured psychotherapy as the core treatment for borderline personality disorder, with dialectical behaviour therapy, mentalisation-based therapy and schema therapy all evidence-supported. Pharmacotherapy is adjunctive and short-term, used for clearly defined comorbid disorders rather than core BPD symptoms. Crisis care plans, validation, and continuity of care reduce hospital use and self-harm. Carer involvement supports recovery when consented.
key_points: Structured psychotherapy is first-line for BPD.
DBT, MBT and schema therapy all have evidence.
Pharmacotherapy is adjunctive and time-limited.
Crisis plans and continuity reduce hospital use.
explanation.pearls: Brief admissions for BPD often worsen long-term outcomes by reinforcing self-harm cycles and disrupting therapy; a 'partial hospitalisation' day program or planned crisis respite is usually better than ad hoc inpatient stays.

stem: You are the GP reviewing a 28-year-old woman with schizophrenia stabilised on risperidone 4 mg daily for 18 months. Over the last 3 months she has developed amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea and reduced libido. Beta-hCG is negative. TFTs are normal. Pituitary MRI shows no mass. Serum prolactin is 1850 mIU/L. Her positive psychotic symptoms have remained well controlled and she has good insight. She is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Examination: Galactorrhoea on bilateral expression; no visual field defect; normal thyroid; no acanthosis nigricans
data_table.Investigations: Prolactin 1850 mIU/L (high), beta-hCG negative, TSH normal, MRI pituitary normal, fasting glucose 4.8 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue risperidone unchanged and add cabergoline 0.25 mg twice weekly for prolactin
options.rationale: Adding cabergoline risks worsening psychosis through dopamine agonism and is not preferred when antipsychotic substitution is available. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic)

options.text: Reduce risperidone to 1 mg daily to lower prolactin while accepting reduced antipsychotic cover
options.rationale: Reducing risperidone below the therapeutic threshold risks relapse of psychosis; dose reduction is only partially effective at lowering prolactin. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic)

options.text: Stop the antipsychotic entirely given the side effect and review again in 6 weeks
options.rationale: Antipsychotic cessation in well-controlled schizophrenia carries high relapse and rehospitalisation risk; substitution is preferred. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic)

options.text: Switch risperidone to aripiprazole with cross-titration and monitor for relapse and prolactin
options.rationale: Aripiprazole is prolactin-sparing through partial D2 agonism and is the preferred switch agent for prolactin-related side effects in stable patients with cross-titration. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic)

options.text: Refer to gynaecology for combined oral contraceptive to mask symptoms with risperidone
options.rationale: Masking symptoms with an oestrogen-containing pill does not address chronically elevated prolactin or its long-term consequences on bone density. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Risperidone and amisulpride raise prolactin substantially through D2 antagonism in the tuberoinfundibular pathway. Symptomatic hyperprolactinaemia (amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea, reduced libido, gynaecomastia, low bone density) warrants action. Aripiprazole, a partial D2 agonist, is the preferred switch in stable patients because it lowers prolactin and preserves antipsychotic cover. Cross-titration over 2 to 4 weeks reduces relapse risk. Cabergoline alone risks worsening psychosis.
key_points: Risperidone and amisulpride raise prolactin most.
Aripiprazole is prolactin-sparing through partial D2 agonism.
Cross-titrate to minimise relapse risk during switch.
Avoid cabergoline alone in psychotic illness.
explanation.pearls: Chronic untreated hyperprolactinaemia from antipsychotics can cause osteoporosis in young women; check bone density if levels stay above 1000 mIU/L for more than 6 months, particularly in women under 30 with no other osteoporosis risk.

subtopic_detail: Medical admission threshold for severe anorexia nervosa
stem: You are the inpatient psychiatric registrar reviewing a 16-year-old girl referred from her GP. She has restricting-type anorexia nervosa with 30 percent weight loss over 6 months and now refuses any oral intake. She presents with severe bradycardia, postural hypotension and significant electrolyte derangement. She is fully oriented but expresses distorted body image and intense fear of weight gain. She is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 38 supine, BP 80/50 with 30 mmHg postural drop, T 35.6 °C, SpO2 99% room air, BMI 13.5
data_table.Examination: Marked muscle wasting; lanugo hair; cool peripheries; dry mucous membranes; capillary refill 4 seconds
data_table.Investigations: K 2.8 mmol/L, phosphate 0.6 mmol/L, magnesium 0.6 mmol/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, glucose 3.2 mmol/L; ECG QTc 480 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Discharge home with outpatient family-based therapy and weekly weight monitoring
options.rationale: Family-based therapy is the gold standard outpatient model but cannot manage severe bradycardia, postural hypotension and electrolyte derangement; medical admission is required first. (Source: ANZAED Eating Disorders Guidelines)

options.text: Commence olanzapine 5 mg at night and arrange outpatient psychiatry follow-up next week
options.rationale: Olanzapine has only modest evidence in anorexia and does not address medical instability; medical admission and refeeding take precedence. (Source: ANZAED Eating Disorders Guidelines)

options.text: Admit for cardiac monitoring, electrolyte correction and supervised refeeding under refeeding precautions
options.rationale: Bradycardia under 40, postural hypotension, BMI under 14 and hypokalaemia or hypophosphataemia each independently meet admission criteria; supervised refeeding with phosphate and thiamine cover prevents refeeding syndrome. (Source: ANZAED Eating Disorders Guidelines)

options.text: Refer to a dietitian only for outpatient meal planning and review at the GP in 2 weeks
options.rationale: Dietetic input is essential but inadequate alone when medical instability is established; supervised refeeding requires a hospital environment. (Source: ANZAED Eating Disorders Guidelines)

options.text: Discharge with weekly weight checks and contingency plan if she loses more weight at home
options.rationale: Outpatient management is unsafe when admission criteria are met; medical complications including arrhythmia and death are well described in this group. (Source: ANZAED Eating Disorders Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Australian admission criteria for severe anorexia nervosa include any of HR under 40, BP under 80/50, postural drop above 20 mmHg, K under 3.0, phosphate under 0.5, BMI under 14, rapid weight loss or significant ECG changes. Refeeding syndrome risk peaks in the first week of nutritional restoration as intracellular electrolyte shift drives hypophosphataemia, hypomagnesaemia and hypokalaemia. Thiamine 100 mg daily and gradual calorie escalation reduce this risk. Family-based therapy remains the outpatient gold standard once medically stable.
key_points: HR under 40 or BP under 80/50 meets admission criteria.
K under 3.0 or phosphate under 0.5 mandates admission.
Refeeding syndrome peaks in the first week of restoration.
Family-based therapy follows medical stabilisation.
explanation.pearls: Always check phosphate, magnesium and potassium daily for the first week of refeeding; an asymptomatic phosphate of 0.4 on day 3 is the classic harbinger of cardiac arrest in refeeding syndrome and must trigger immediate replacement and pause in calorie advancement.

stem: You are the emergency department psychiatric registrar reviewing a 28-year-old man with a known schizoaffective disorder on quetiapine. His family brings him for 4 days of progressive muteness, immobility and bizarre posturing. He refuses oral intake. He is afebrile, has no muscle rigidity, no autonomic instability and a witnessed episode of waxy flexibility on examination. His creatine kinase is normal. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9 °C, HR 88, BP 122/78, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Mute and immobile; maintained postures imposed by examiner (waxy flexibility); no rigidity, no clonus, no tremor; no fever; clinically euvolaemic
data_table.Investigations: FBC normal, U&E normal, CK 110 U/L (normal), thyroid normal, urine drug screen negative; CT brain unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Intravenous lorazepam 2 mg challenge with reassessment of catatonic features within 10 minutes
options.rationale: A lorazepam challenge is both diagnostic and therapeutic for catatonia; 60 to 80 percent of patients with catatonia respond within minutes, supporting the diagnosis and guiding ongoing benzodiazepine therapy. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Guidance)

options.text: Commence ECT immediately as first-line therapy without any trial of benzodiazepine
options.rationale: ECT is highly effective in catatonia but is reserved for patients who fail or cannot tolerate benzodiazepine; the lorazepam challenge precedes ECT in routine pathways. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Guidance)

options.text: Increase quetiapine dose substantially to address residual psychotic illness in this patient
options.rationale: High-potency antipsychotics can worsen catatonia and risk neuroleptic malignant syndrome; benzodiazepine therapy is preferred. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Guidance)

options.text: Administer intravenous dantrolene 1 mg/kg now for suspected neuroleptic malignant syndrome
options.rationale: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome requires fever, muscle rigidity and raised creatine kinase; this clinical picture is catatonia, not neuroleptic malignant syndrome. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Guidance)

options.text: Give intravenous haloperidol 5 mg now for rapid tranquillisation of acute behavioural disturbance
options.rationale: Haloperidol can precipitate or worsen catatonia and risks neuroleptic malignant syndrome; it is not the right agent here. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Guidance)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a syndrome of motor immobility, mutism, posturing, waxy flexibility, negativism and stereotypy occurring in mood, psychotic, neurological and medical disorders. Diagnosis is supported by a positive lorazepam challenge: 1 to 2 mg intravenously with reassessment at 5 to 10 minutes typically produces clear improvement. Benzodiazepine therapy is then continued, often in escalating doses. ECT is highly effective for refractory or malignant catatonia and is the standard escalation step when benzodiazepines fail.
key_points: Lorazepam challenge is diagnostic and therapeutic.
Avoid high-potency antipsychotics during catatonia.
Escalate to ECT if lorazepam fails or malignant features develop.
Address underlying medical and psychiatric causes.
