explanation.pearls: Malignant catatonia presents with hyperthermia, autonomic instability and raised CK, and overlaps clinically with neuroleptic malignant syndrome; either way, withhold antipsychotics, support physiology and arrange urgent ECT because mortality without rapid treatment exceeds 50 percent.

subtopic_detail: Delusional disorder community management without involuntary admission
stem: You are the community psychiatric registrar reviewing a 52-year-old woman with an 18-month history of a fixed belief that her next-door neighbour is poisoning the water supply to her house. She has no auditory or visual hallucinations, no thought disorder, no negative symptoms and no mood disorder. Her husband reports she works, drives and socialises normally except for this belief. She uses no substances and her mini-mental status examination is normal. She is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Examination: Cooperative, well-groomed; no thought disorder; circumstantial speech around the persecutory belief; no perceptual disturbance; insight is poor for the belief but preserved elsewhere
data_table.Investigations: TFTs, B12, syphilis serology, HIV negative; urine drug screen negative; MRI brain unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next management step?

options.text: Admit involuntarily under the Mental Health Act despite there being no risk of harm to others
options.rationale: Involuntary admission requires risk to self or others or grave disability; isolated non-bizarre delusion with preserved function does not meet the legal threshold. (Source: RANZCP Psychotic Disorders Guidelines)

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg daily for likely psychotic depression with predominant delusions
options.rationale: There is no depressive syndrome here; sertraline alone will not treat persistent delusions and may delay appropriate antipsychotic therapy. (Source: RANZCP Psychotic Disorders Guidelines)

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy for psychosis alone without any pharmacotherapy
options.rationale: CBT for psychosis is a useful adjunct but is not first-line monotherapy for delusional disorder; antipsychotic therapy is the recommended core intervention. (Source: RANZCP Psychotic Disorders Guidelines)

options.text: Refer for electroconvulsive therapy given treatment resistance and chronicity of belief
options.rationale: ECT is not indicated as first-line for delusional disorder; antipsychotic trial should be undertaken before any ECT consideration. (Source: RANZCP Psychotic Disorders Guidelines)

options.text: Initiate aripiprazole 10 mg daily and arrange outpatient community psychiatric follow-up
options.rationale: An antipsychotic with strong tolerability is reasonable first-line; aripiprazole produces fewer metabolic and prolactin side effects than older agents and supports engagement in long-term community care. (Source: RANZCP Psychotic Disorders Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Delusional disorder is defined by one or more non-bizarre fixed false beliefs for at least 1 month without prominent hallucinations, thought disorder or negative symptoms, and with otherwise preserved functioning. Treatment combines antipsychotic medication with engagement-focused psychotherapy. Response rates to antipsychotics are lower than in schizophrenia but partial improvement supports ongoing care. Involuntary treatment is reserved for cases that meet the relevant Mental Health Act threshold.
key_points: Non-bizarre delusion for at least 1 month defines the disorder.
Antipsychotic is first-line; aripiprazole is well tolerated.
Response is partial; engagement strategies matter.
Involuntary care requires risk or grave disability.
explanation.pearls: The persecutory subtype most often presents to general practice through a third party such as a partner or police; refusal of treatment does not equate to grave disability, and forced admission of well-functioning patients risks harming the long-term therapeutic relationship.

stem: You are the community mental health registrar reviewing a 24-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia who started clozapine 8 weeks ago. He has tolerated the titration with mild constipation and sedation. He returns today for routine review. He reports no fever, sore throat or mouth ulcers. He has had blood tests done weekly since commencement under the central monitoring system.

data_table.Examination: Alert, no oropharyngeal lesions, no cervical lymphadenopathy, chest clear, abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Latest FBC: Hb 144 g/L, WCC 6.2 x10^9/L, neutrophils 3.4 x10^9/L, platelets 240 x10^9/L. Previous weekly results all within green-traffic-light range.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ongoing haematological monitoring schedule?

options.text: Continue weekly full blood examinations for the duration of his clozapine treatment because the agranulocytosis risk does not change over the course of the first year
options.rationale: Risk of clozapine-induced neutropenia falls after the first 18 weeks; weekly testing for the entire treatment duration is unnecessary and not part of the Australian monitoring schedule. (Source: ClopineCentral and ClozaCare Monitoring Schedules)

options.text: Continue weekly full blood examinations until 18 weeks of treatment, then space to fortnightly until 12 months and monthly thereafter while clozapine is continued
options.rationale: Australian clozapine monitoring requires weekly FBE for the first 18 weeks of treatment, fortnightly to 12 months and then monthly while clozapine continues; this matches the time-course of agranulocytosis risk. (Source: ClopineCentral and ClozaCare Monitoring Schedules)

options.text: Reduce to monthly full blood examinations now that he has completed 8 weeks because his neutrophil counts have been stable through the first two months of treatment
options.rationale: Monthly monitoring is not introduced until after 12 months of treatment in Australia; the agranulocytosis risk peaks between weeks 6 and 18, so monthly testing at 8 weeks is unsafe. (Source: ClopineCentral and ClozaCare Monitoring Schedules)

options.text: Stop routine full blood examinations and rely on patient-reported symptoms of fever, sore throat or mucosal ulcers to trigger any further investigations during clozapine treatment
options.rationale: Routine FBE monitoring is mandatory under the Australian clozapine monitoring scheme; symptom-only monitoring misses early neutropenia and is not permitted. (Source: ClopineCentral and ClozaCare Monitoring Schedules)

options.text: Add weekly C-reactive protein and procalcitonin to the existing full blood examination to capture early signs of cytokine-mediated myocarditis during titration through this period of treatment
options.rationale: Cardiac surveillance with troponin and C-reactive protein is recommended in the first month for myocarditis screening, not weekly thereafter, and is separate from the haematological monitoring schedule. (Source: ClopineCentral and ClozaCare Monitoring Schedules)

explanation.summary: Clozapine is the most effective antipsychotic for treatment-resistant schizophrenia but carries a 0.4 to 0.9% risk of agranulocytosis. The Australian central monitoring system (ClopineCentral, ClozaCare) mandates weekly full blood examinations for the first 18 weeks, fortnightly to 12 months, and monthly thereafter. Dispensing is contingent on a result-positive flag within the monitoring system. Myocarditis screening with troponin and C-reactive protein is performed during the first 4 weeks because of a separate cardiac risk.
key_points: Agranulocytosis risk peaks between weeks 6 and 18 of clozapine treatment
Australian monitoring: weekly to week 18, fortnightly to 12 months, monthly thereafter
Red traffic light is neutrophils under 1.5 x10^9/L and requires clozapine cessation
Cardiac monitoring with troponin and CRP screens for myocarditis in the first month
Constipation can progress to ileus, which is a leading cause of clozapine-related death
explanation.pearls: Clozapine-induced constipation is dose-related and managed with osmotic laxatives such as macrogol from initiation; stimulant laxatives are added if symptoms persist.

subtopic_detail: First-line psychological therapy for post-traumatic stress disorder
stem: You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 33-year-old woman with intrusive memories, nightmares, hypervigilance and avoidance for the past six months. The symptoms began after a serious motor vehicle accident in which a passenger died. She avoids driving and feels emotionally numb. She has no current suicidal ideation, no psychosis and no alcohol or substance misuse. She has not been on any psychotropic medication.

data_table.Examination: Mental state: anxious affect, congruent mood, intact thought form, no perceptual disturbance, future-oriented
data_table.Investigations: PCL-5 score 48 of 80. PHQ-9 score 12 of 27.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.text: Refer for trauma-focused cognitive behaviour therapy with a clinical psychologist over 8 to 12 weekly sessions and review her response in primary care after the course
options.rationale: Trauma-focused cognitive behaviour therapy and eye movement desensitisation reprocessing are first-line in Australian PTSD guidelines for adults; psychological therapy is preferred over pharmacotherapy as the initial intervention. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Start oral diazepam 5 mg three times daily for symptomatic control of hyperarousal and review at four weeks for response and tolerance with possible dose adjustments
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines do not improve PTSD outcomes, may worsen the trauma response and risk dependence; they are not recommended as monotherapy or first-line. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Commence quetiapine 50 mg at night for sleep and intrusive symptoms with planned uptitration to 200 mg over 4 weeks if tolerated by the patient at clinical review
options.rationale: Atypical antipsychotics are used as augmentation in treatment-resistant PTSD, not as a first-line monotherapy; first-line is psychological therapy. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Provide supportive psychoeducation only and review in 12 weeks because spontaneous remission occurs in most adults within the first six months of post-trauma symptoms
options.rationale: Symptoms persisting beyond one month with significant distress meet PTSD criteria and warrant active first-line therapy; watchful waiting alone is not appropriate at six months. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Start mirtazapine 30 mg at night and refer for generic supportive counselling sessions in the community over a course of weekly meetings spanning the next several months
options.rationale: Generic supportive counselling is not trauma-focused and shows inferior outcomes compared with trauma-focused cognitive behaviour therapy; pharmacotherapy alone is also not first-line. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Post-traumatic stress disorder is diagnosed by persistent intrusion, avoidance, negative cognitions and hyperarousal symptoms following trauma. Australian guidelines from Phoenix Australia recommend trauma-focused cognitive behaviour therapy or eye movement desensitisation reprocessing as first-line treatment for adults. Pharmacotherapy with a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor or venlafaxine is considered when psychological therapy is unavailable, declined, or insufficient. Benzodiazepines and stand-alone supportive counselling are explicitly not recommended.
key_points: Trauma-focused CBT and EMDR are first-line psychological therapies for adult PTSD
Sertraline, paroxetine and venlafaxine are first-line pharmacotherapies if medication is required
Benzodiazepines are not recommended because they impair fear extinction
Atypical antipsychotics are used as augmentation in treatment-resistant PTSD only
Comorbid depression and substance use are treated concurrently to avoid undertreatment
explanation.pearls: PTSD with complex presentations involving prolonged interpersonal trauma may meet criteria for complex PTSD in ICD-11 and benefits from phased therapy with stabilisation before trauma-focused processing.

subtopic_detail: Long-term lithium monitoring schedule for renal and thyroid function
stem: You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 45-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder who has been on lithium carbonate 750 mg nocte for 4 years. She is euthymic and continues to work full time. She takes no other regular medications and has no recent illnesses. Her last formal lithium level monitoring was nine months ago. She asks how often she needs ongoing tests.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic mood and affect, no tremor at rest, no peripheral oedema, abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Latest serum lithium 0.7 mmol/L (12-hour trough), TSH 2.4 mIU/L, creatinine 68 micromol/L, eGFR 92 mL/min/1.73 m^2, corrected calcium 2.34 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ongoing monitoring schedule?

options.text: Repeat serum lithium, urea and electrolytes and thyroid function tests now and then again every three months for the foreseeable course of treatment with this medication
options.rationale: Three-monthly monitoring is the initial schedule but not required indefinitely; once levels are stable, monitoring extends to six-monthly intervals. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Stop routine monitoring because she has been stable for four years and lithium levels have remained therapeutic at the most recent 12-hour trough level measurement
options.rationale: Routine surveillance must continue lifelong because of cumulative renal, thyroid and parathyroid toxicity; stopping monitoring is not safe. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Order serum lithium, urea, electrolytes, calcium and thyroid function every six months and an annual eGFR, with prompt repeat if dose, illness or new medications change
options.rationale: Six-monthly serum lithium, electrolytes, calcium and thyroid function with annual eGFR is the Australian long-term monitoring schedule for stable patients on lithium; additional testing is triggered by dose, illness or interacting medication changes. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Switch to lamotrigine 200 mg daily as long-term maintenance therapy because lithium causes inevitable progression to chronic kidney disease over more than 5 years of continuous use
options.rationale: Long-term lithium does not inevitably cause clinically significant chronic kidney disease in most patients; switching to lamotrigine in a euthymic patient with normal renal function is not indicated. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders Guidelines)

options.text: Continue annual serum lithium only because all other organ-system tests for this medication can be reasonably deferred when the patient is clinically euthymic and well
options.rationale: Annual lithium alone misses thyroid, parathyroid and renal complications; renal and thyroid screening at least 6-monthly remains the Australian standard. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Lithium remains the most effective long-term treatment for bipolar I disorder and is the only mood stabiliser with a clear anti-suicidal effect. Long-term toxicity affects the thyroid (hypothyroidism in around 20%), parathyroid (hypercalcaemia in around 10%) and kidney (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and slowly progressive chronic kidney disease). The Australian monitoring schedule pairs 6-monthly lithium with electrolytes, calcium and thyroid function, plus annual eGFR. Any dose, illness, diuretic or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory change triggers an interim level.
key_points: Therapeutic range is 0.6 to 1.0 mmol/L for maintenance and 0.8 to 1.2 mmol/L for acute mania
Monitoring: 6-monthly lithium, urea, electrolytes, calcium and thyroid; annual eGFR
Hypothyroidism occurs in around 20% and hypercalcaemia in around 10% on long-term lithium
Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus is the most common renal adverse effect
Drug interactions: non-steroidal anti-inflammatories, ACE inhibitors and thiazides raise levels
explanation.pearls: A 50% rise in lithium level with the introduction of a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory is common; advise patients to use paracetamol preferentially and to alert their prescriber before any new medication.

subtopic_detail: Opioid agonist therapy initial agent choice and safety
stem: You are the addiction medicine registrar reviewing a 28-year-old man with heroin use disorder for the past three years. He injects daily and wants to start opioid agonist therapy. He has hepatitis C antibody positive, but liver function and synthetic function are preserved. He has had no overdoses but has been using alone. He has no chronic respiratory disease or current benzodiazepine use. He has unstable housing and limited transport.

data_table.Examination: Mild withdrawal symptoms with dilated pupils, piloerection and yawning; no track marks of skin and soft tissue infection
data_table.Investigations: ALT 48 U/L, AST 52 U/L, bilirubin 14 micromol/L, INR 1.0, albumin 38 g/L. Urine toxicology positive for heroin; negative for benzodiazepines and methadone.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial opioid agonist therapy?

options.text: Start oral methadone 80 mg daily today and continue at this dose until next review with daily supervised dosing at his community pharmacy of usual choice
options.rationale: Methadone induction starts at 20 to 30 mg with cautious titration over weeks because of risk of accumulation and overdose; starting at 80 mg risks fatal respiratory depression. (Source: National Guidelines for MATOD)

options.text: Trial extended-release oral naltrexone 50 mg daily from tomorrow for relapse prevention because of its low risk of accumulation and once-daily oral dosing convenience
options.rationale: Naltrexone requires sustained opioid abstinence for 7 to 10 days before initiation to avoid precipitated withdrawal; it is not appropriate for a person currently using heroin daily. (Source: National Guidelines for MATOD)

options.text: Start oral diazepam 10 mg three times daily and oral clonidine for autonomic features and arrange community-based residential rehabilitation in the next available place
options.rationale: Detoxification without agonist therapy has high relapse and overdose rates; benzodiazepines plus opioids carry overdose risk. (Source: National Guidelines for MATOD)

options.text: Defer pharmacotherapy and refer to weekly cognitive behaviour therapy and peer support group meetings as the initial treatment of his opioid use disorder before any agonist therapy
options.rationale: Opioid agonist therapy is first-line for opioid use disorder and reduces mortality by around 50%; deferring it for psychological therapy alone is not best practice. (Source: National Guidelines for MATOD)

options.text: Induce sublingual buprenorphine-naloxone 4 mg when he is in objective withdrawal, uptitrate to 8 to 16 mg over the first day and arrange a depot formulation when stable
options.rationale: Sublingual buprenorphine-naloxone is the preferred initial agonist for most patients in Australia because of its safety ceiling and overdose protection; long-acting depot buprenorphine improves adherence in unstable housing. (Source: National Guidelines for MATOD)

explanation.summary: Opioid agonist therapy with buprenorphine or methadone reduces all-cause mortality by around 50% in people with opioid use disorder. Sublingual buprenorphine-naloxone is preferred initially because of its partial agonist ceiling effect, lower respiratory depression risk and intrinsic abuse deterrent through naloxone. Long-acting depot buprenorphine (weekly or monthly subcutaneous formulations) is particularly useful for unstable housing or poor adherence. Methadone is reserved for patients with high tolerance, failed buprenorphine response or specific clinical contexts.
key_points: Buprenorphine-naloxone is preferred initially because of its ceiling effect and lower overdose risk
Induction requires objective opioid withdrawal (COWS at least 12) to avoid precipitated withdrawal
Depot buprenorphine improves adherence in unstable housing and reduces takeaway diversion risk
Methadone induction starts at 20 to 30 mg with cautious uptitration over weeks
Naltrexone requires 7 to 10 days of opioid abstinence before initiation
explanation.pearls: Naloxone is offered to every patient at induction and to their household contacts; intranasal naloxone is now subsidised on the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme for take-home use in Australia.

subtopic_detail: Discriminating serotonin syndrome from neuroleptic malignant syndrome
stem: You are the medical registrar called to a 38-year-old woman on the psychiatric ward with sudden agitation, tremor and fever. She has bipolar I disorder and was started on tramadol 50 mg four-hourly for back pain yesterday in addition to her usual sertraline 100 mg and lithium 750 mg nocte. Symptoms began 6 hours ago and have worsened in the last hour. She has had no recent dose change of her antipsychotic.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.4 °C, HR 132, BP 168/96, RR 28, SpO2 97% room air
data_table.Examination: Agitated, diaphoretic, mydriasis, hyperreflexia and sustained clonus more marked in lower limbs, mild tremor, no lead-pipe rigidity
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 482 U/L, lactate 3.2 mmol/L, WCC 11.8 x10^9/L, Na 138, K 4.0, creatinine 78 micromol/L, lithium 0.9 mmol/L. ECG: sinus tachycardia.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Cease the offending serotonergic agents, give intravenous benzodiazepines for agitation, commence active cooling and admit for monitoring and supportive care
options.rationale: Hunter criteria with clonus, hyperreflexia, agitation and autonomic instability after addition of tramadol to sertraline confirm serotonin syndrome; cessation, benzodiazepines and supportive care are first-line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Start bromocriptine 2.5 mg orally three times daily and intravenous dantrolene 1 mg/kg as definitive treatment for neuroleptic malignant syndrome before any other escalation
options.rationale: Bromocriptine and dantrolene are reserved for neuroleptic malignant syndrome with lead-pipe rigidity and dopamine antagonist exposure; the clonus and hyperreflexia point to serotonin syndrome, not NMS. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Administer intravenous physostigmine 1 to 2 mg over 5 minutes targeting reversal of anticholinergic delirium and persisting tachycardia in this acutely confused febrile patient
options.rationale: Physostigmine reverses anticholinergic toxicity, which causes dry skin and absent bowel sounds rather than diaphoresis and clonus; it does not address serotonin syndrome. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Give intravenous haloperidol 5 mg for the acute behavioural disturbance and increase her usual sertraline to 150 mg today to address mood-related agitation in this acute presentation
options.rationale: Adding antipsychotics or increasing serotonergic agents in suspected serotonin syndrome will worsen the syndrome and risk neuroleptic malignant syndrome from haloperidol. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Hold lithium for 24 hours, continue sertraline and tramadol unchanged and recheck the lithium level in the morning before considering further changes to her medication regimen
options.rationale: Lithium is not the primary serotonergic agent here, and continuing tramadol and sertraline will perpetuate the syndrome; offending agents must be ceased immediately. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

explanation.summary: Serotonin syndrome arises within hours of a new serotonergic agent and is diagnosed by the Hunter criteria, which emphasise clonus, hyperreflexia, agitation, diaphoresis and autonomic instability. Tramadol is a common precipitant in patients already on selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors and should be flagged in medication review. Treatment is supportive: cease the agent, give benzodiazepines, cool and hydrate. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome by contrast develops over days, presents with lead-pipe rigidity and bradykinesia, and follows dopamine antagonist exposure.
key_points: Hunter criteria: spontaneous clonus, or inducible clonus with agitation or diaphoresis
Serotonin syndrome develops within hours; NMS develops over 1 to 3 days
Treatment is cessation, benzodiazepines, active cooling and supportive care
Cyproheptadine 12 mg orally is considered in refractory cases
Tramadol, fentanyl, pethidine, linezolid and St John's wort are common co-precipitants
explanation.pearls: MAO inhibitors plus serotonergic agents can cause life-threatening serotonin syndrome that persists for weeks; a 14-day washout is required before switching from a MAO inhibitor to a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor.

subtopic_detail: Acute mania with psychotic features adjunctive antipsychotic choice
stem: You are the psychiatry registrar on the consultation-liaison service reviewing a 36-year-old man with known bipolar I disorder. He has been on lithium 1000 mg nocte for two years with previous good response. He presents in florid mania for the past four days with grandiose delusions, reduced sleep and hyperactivity. He is medication adherent and his lithium level is in range. He has no diabetes or known cardiac disease. He has no acute medical issues.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 °C, HR 110, BP 132/82, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Pressured speech, flight of ideas, grandiose delusions, no perceptual disturbance reported, no extrapyramidal signs
data_table.Investigations: Serum lithium 0.9 mmol/L. TSH 2.2 mIU/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L, eGFR 95 mL/min/1.73 m^2, fasting glucose 4.8 mmol/L, fasting lipids unremarkable. ECG QTc 412 ms.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Increase his lithium dose to target a level of 1.2 mmol/L and continue this as monotherapy without addition of any antipsychotic agent during this episode
options.rationale: Lithium monotherapy is insufficient for severe mania with psychotic features and acute behavioural disturbance; combination with an antipsychotic is required. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders Guidelines)

options.text: Switch his lithium to sodium valproate 1 g twice daily and reassess his response over a fortnight after a routine therapeutic drug level has been obtained from his bloods
options.rationale: Switching mood stabilisers in someone with a previously good lithium response is inappropriate; combination treatment with an antipsychotic is preferred. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders Guidelines)

options.text: Add oral olanzapine 10 mg daily to his existing lithium and review the response over the following week with weekly weight, lipid and glucose monitoring
options.rationale: Adding a second-generation antipsychotic such as olanzapine to lithium is first-line for severe mania with psychotic features in Australia; combination therapy outperforms either agent alone. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders Guidelines)

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg daily in addition to current therapy to address irritability and mood lability that may be driving his presenting acute behavioural disturbance
options.rationale: Antidepressants are contraindicated in acute mania because they risk worsening the manic episode and inducing rapid cycling. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders Guidelines)

options.text: Add lamotrigine 25 mg daily, titrate over six weeks to 200 mg and continue ongoing monthly serum monitoring of his lithium level during the titration period
options.rationale: Lamotrigine has efficacy in bipolar maintenance and depressive episodes, not in acute mania; its slow titration over 6 weeks is unsuitable for acute control. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Acute mania with psychotic features is preferentially treated with combination therapy of a mood stabiliser plus a second-generation antipsychotic. Combination treatment achieves a higher response rate than either agent alone. Olanzapine, risperidone, quetiapine, aripiprazole and asenapine have evidence in acute mania; choice is guided by metabolic profile, sedation, prior response and patient preference. Antidepressants are avoided in acute mania because they can worsen the episode and induce rapid cycling.
key_points: Combination of a mood stabiliser and antipsychotic outperforms either alone in acute mania
Olanzapine, risperidone, quetiapine, aripiprazole and asenapine are first-line antipsychotic options
Antidepressants are contraindicated in acute mania because they worsen the episode
Lamotrigine is for bipolar maintenance and depressive episodes, not acute mania
Metabolic monitoring at baseline and 12 weekly is required with second-generation antipsychotics
explanation.pearls: Aripiprazole at 15 to 30 mg has the lowest metabolic burden among the second-generation antipsychotics used in mania; it is preferred when long-term cardiometabolic risk is a concern.

stem: You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 15-year-old non-Aboriginal girl with a four month history of persistent low mood, anhedonia, fatigue and reduced school attendance. She has had no manic features. She has been engaged in weekly trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy for eight weeks without improvement. She denies active suicidal ideation but has fleeting passive thoughts of being better off dead. Her parents are present and supportive of medication.

data_table.Examination: Mood low, affect restricted, no psychomotor agitation, thought form linear, no perceptual disturbance, denies plan or intent
data_table.Investigations: TSH normal, FBE normal, ferritin normal, urine pregnancy test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological choice?

options.text: Sertraline 25 mg orally daily titrated to 50 mg after 1 week with weekly clinical review for 4 weeks and shared safety planning
options.rationale: Sertraline is not the first-line antidepressant for adolescents in Australia because evidence for efficacy in this age group is strongest for fluoxetine, which is the recommended initial choice. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

options.text: Mirtazapine 15 mg orally at night titrated weekly with regular face-to-face review and explicit safety planning that includes a written crisis plan
options.rationale: Mirtazapine is not recommended first line in adolescents; the strongest randomised evidence in this age group supports fluoxetine, which is preferred. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

options.text: Continue psychological therapy alone for a further 8 weeks before reconsidering pharmacotherapy because medication carries a suicidality warning in adolescents
options.rationale: Failure of an adequate trial of psychological therapy in moderate adolescent depression is an indication to add pharmacotherapy; delay risks ongoing functional impairment. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

options.text: Venlafaxine 37.5 mg orally daily titrated weekly with face-to-face review at one week and explicit safety planning agreed with family and patient
options.rationale: Venlafaxine is not first line in adolescents because of higher rates of suicidality and discontinuation syndrome compared with fluoxetine. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

options.text: Fluoxetine 10 mg orally daily increased to 20 mg after one week, weekly clinical review for four weeks with explicit safety planning and continued psychological therapy
options.rationale: Fluoxetine is the first-line antidepressant for adolescent depression in Australia because it has the strongest evidence in this age group; weekly review covers the early increase in suicidality risk. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

explanation.summary: Australian RANZCP guidance recommends fluoxetine as the first-line antidepressant in adolescents because it has the strongest randomised controlled trial evidence in this age group, in particular the TADS trial. Combination therapy with cognitive behavioural therapy is more effective than either modality alone. Weekly face-to-face review is recommended for the first 4 weeks because of a small absolute increase in suicidality in the early weeks of treatment. A written safety plan and engagement of family or carers are integral to safe prescribing in this age group.
key_points: Fluoxetine is first-line antidepressant in adolescents
Combine pharmacotherapy with CBT for best outcomes
Weekly face-to-face review for first 4 weeks to monitor suicidality
Engage family and document a written safety plan
Other SSRIs and venlafaxine are second line because of evidence gaps and side effects
explanation.pearls: Fluoxetine 20 mg daily is the target dose in adolescents with response typically assessed at 4 to 6 weeks before considering increase or switch.

stem: You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 28-year-old non-Aboriginal woman with bipolar I disorder, currently euthymic six weeks after a manic episode requiring brief admission. She has been stable on quetiapine 600 mg daily but has gained 7 kg. She and her consultant agree to switch to lithium for relapse prevention. She is in a relationship and has had a Mirena IUD inserted last year. She has no past renal, thyroid or cardiac disease.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no abnormal movements, thyroid not palpably enlarged
data_table.Investigations: U&E pending, TSH pending, calcium pending, ECG pending, beta-hCG today negative

lead_in: Which baseline workup is required before commencing lithium?

options.text: Full blood examination, liver function tests and serum prolactin level before commencing lithium therapy at an initial dose of 250 mg twice daily
options.rationale: FBE, LFTs and prolactin are not the core baseline panel for lithium; the relevant tests are urea and electrolytes, thyroid function, calcium, ECG, weight and a pregnancy test. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

options.text: Urea, electrolytes and creatinine; thyroid function; serum calcium; ECG; weight and a pregnancy test before commencing lithium at an initial low dose
options.rationale: Lithium baseline panel covers renal function, thyroid function, calcium, ECG and pregnancy status because of long-term renal, thyroid, parathyroid, cardiac and teratogenic risks. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

options.text: Urea, electrolytes and creatinine alone without other tests because lithium's main adverse effect is nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and reduced glomerular filtration rate
options.rationale: Renal function alone misses thyroid and parathyroid screening required because of hypothyroidism and hyperparathyroidism risks, and pregnancy must be excluded because of Ebstein anomaly risk. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

options.text: Echocardiogram and exercise stress test to assess cardiac function before commencing lithium because of conduction abnormalities and risk of cardiomyopathy progression
options.rationale: Echocardiography and stress testing are not part of routine lithium initiation; a baseline 12-lead ECG suffices in patients without cardiac history. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

options.text: MRI brain and electroencephalogram to assess baseline neurological status before commencing lithium because of neurotoxicity risk and tremor reporting in many users
options.rationale: Neuroimaging and EEG are not part of routine lithium initiation; baseline neurological screening is clinical only and no imaging is required. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

explanation.summary: Lithium remains a first-line mood stabiliser for bipolar I relapse prevention. Baseline workup before initiation includes renal function (U&E and creatinine), thyroid function, calcium, ECG, weight and a pregnancy test in women of reproductive potential because lithium is teratogenic (Ebstein anomaly). Ongoing monitoring includes serum lithium level 5 to 7 days after each dose change, then every 3 months, and 6-monthly U&E plus thyroid plus calcium with annual eGFR thereafter. The narrow therapeutic window (0.6 to 1.0 mmol/L for maintenance) requires patient education about dehydration, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and diuretics.
key_points: Baseline: U&E, TFT, calcium, ECG, weight, pregnancy test
Ongoing: 3-monthly level, 6-monthly U&E plus TFT plus calcium
Therapeutic range 0.6 to 1.0 mmol/L maintenance, 0.4 to 0.8 mmol/L in older adults
Avoid in early pregnancy because of Ebstein anomaly
Counsel on dehydration, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and thiazides as toxicity precipitants
explanation.pearls: Lithium levels should be taken 12 hours post-dose (trough), with target 0.6 to 1.0 mmol/L for maintenance and 0.4 to 0.8 mmol/L in adults over 65 years.

stem: You are the addiction medicine registrar reviewing a 48-year-old non-Aboriginal man on day one of planned community alcohol detoxification. He has been drinking 200 g alcohol daily for 10 years. He has had two previous unprovoked alcohol withdrawal seizures. He has no liver decompensation and is keen to remain at home with carer support. His last drink was 12 hours ago and he is mildly tremulous but oriented.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 °C, HR 96, BP 142/86, RR 18, SpO2 98% room air
data_table.Examination: Mild tremor, anxious, no diaphoresis, oriented to time and place, no asterixis, no jaundice
data_table.Investigations: LFTs mildly deranged GGT 240 U/L, ALT 62, AST 70, INR 1.0, FBE normal, BSL 5.4 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate prescription?

options.text: Oral thiamine 300 mg daily and outpatient detox without sedative cover because his withdrawal severity is currently mild and he has carer supervision at home
options.rationale: A history of two previous withdrawal seizures makes seizure recurrence likely without benzodiazepine cover; thiamine alone is insufficient for prophylaxis. (Source: RACGP Alcohol Withdrawal Guidelines)

options.text: Oral diazepam loading 20 mg every 2 hours symptom-triggered using CIWA-Ar scoring with thiamine cover and admission to hospital because of his seizure history
options.rationale: Previous withdrawal seizures and high daily intake mandate inpatient detox with diazepam symptom-triggered dosing plus parenteral thiamine cover for Wernicke prevention. (Source: RACGP Alcohol Withdrawal Guidelines)

options.text: Oral lorazepam 1 mg every 6 hours for 5 days at home with general practitioner review every second day and thiamine 100 mg orally daily as outpatient support
options.rationale: Lorazepam at this dose is unlikely to control withdrawal in heavy drinkers with previous seizures, and outpatient management is unsafe in this risk profile. (Source: RACGP Alcohol Withdrawal Guidelines)

options.text: Oral carbamazepine 200 mg three times daily as primary withdrawal therapy and outpatient detoxification with daily clinic review and oral thiamine supplementation
options.rationale: Carbamazepine is occasionally used in mild withdrawal but is not first line in Australia and is inadequate alone for heavy drinkers with a seizure history. (Source: RACGP Alcohol Withdrawal Guidelines)

options.text: Oral chlordiazepoxide 25 mg every 6 hours fixed-schedule for 5 days at home with no thiamine because of his preserved nutritional status and normal full blood count
options.rationale: Outpatient fixed-schedule benzodiazepine in a patient with previous withdrawal seizures and heavy intake is unsafe, and thiamine cover is required regardless of nutritional appearance. (Source: RACGP Alcohol Withdrawal Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Alcohol withdrawal severity is predicted by daily intake, duration, previous withdrawal complications and concurrent illness. Patients with previous withdrawal seizures, delirium tremens, intake above 150 g daily, significant comorbidity or unstable home environment warrant inpatient detoxification with symptom-triggered diazepam (loaded 20 mg every 2 hours by CIWA-Ar score) and parenteral thiamine cover. Thiamine 300 mg intramuscular or intravenous daily for at least 3 days precedes any glucose-containing fluid to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy. Long-acting benzodiazepines are preferred for smoother withdrawal except in significant hepatic impairment where lorazepam or oxazepam are used.
key_points: Previous withdrawal seizures mandate inpatient detoxification with benzodiazepine cover
Diazepam 20 mg loading every 2 hours symptom-triggered is the Australian standard
Parenteral thiamine before any glucose-containing fluid to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy
Lorazepam or oxazepam in significant hepatic impairment because they avoid hepatic oxidation
CIWA-Ar score guides ongoing dosing
explanation.pearls: Parenteral thiamine 300 mg intramuscular daily for at least 3 days is given before any intravenous glucose to prevent precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy in chronic alcohol use.

stem: You are the consultation-liaison psychiatry registrar called to the emergency department to assess a 42-year-old non-Aboriginal man brought in with confusion and rigidity. He was started on haloperidol 10 mg three days ago for acute psychosis. He had received no other psychotropic medication. On arrival he is sweating, mute, and stiff with cogwheeling in all four limbs. Family deny illicit drug use and there has been no recent infection.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.4 °C, HR 132, BP 168/96, RR 28, SpO2 95% room air, GCS 12
data_table.Examination: Generalised lead-pipe rigidity, tremor, diaphoresis, no clonus, no neck stiffness, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 6200 U/L, WCC 13.5 x10^9/L, urea 9.2, creatinine 142 micromol/L, K 4.4, Na 142, urine myoglobin positive, CT brain normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue haloperidol at reduced dose with paracetamol and active cooling because pyrexia is from the acute psychosis rather than from the medication
options.rationale: Continuing the offending dopamine antagonist worsens neuroleptic malignant syndrome and risks death; immediate cessation is required. (Source: RANZCP Psychopharmacology Resources)

options.text: Add lorazepam 2 mg orally and observe for response with no other change in psychotropic medication because rigidity is characteristic of catatonia not NMS
options.rationale: Hyperthermia, autonomic instability and CK over 1000 with recent dopamine antagonist exposure point to NMS rather than isolated catatonia; haloperidol must be ceased and supportive care escalated. (Source: RANZCP Psychopharmacology Resources)

options.text: Cease haloperidol immediately, transfer to intensive care for active cooling, intravenous hydration, dantrolene or bromocriptine and electrolyte monitoring with myoglobinuric renal protection
options.rationale: NMS requires immediate cessation of the offending agent, aggressive supportive care including cooling and fluid resuscitation, and consideration of dantrolene or bromocriptine; renal protection addresses myoglobinuric injury. (Source: RANZCP Psychopharmacology Resources)

options.text: Switch haloperidol to olanzapine 10 mg, continue current observation in the medical ward and reassess in 24 hours after a single trial of cyproheptadine 12 mg orally
options.rationale: Switching to another antipsychotic continues dopamine blockade and worsens NMS; cyproheptadine treats serotonin syndrome, which has clonus and hyperreflexia rather than lead-pipe rigidity. (Source: RANZCP Psychopharmacology Resources)

options.text: Administer intramuscular procyclidine 10 mg as the first-line antidote and continue haloperidol in expectation that cogwheel rigidity will resolve within an hour
options.rationale: Procyclidine treats acute dystonia and parkinsonian extrapyramidal side effects, not NMS; continuing haloperidol perpetuates the syndrome. (Source: RANZCP Psychopharmacology Resources)

explanation.summary: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is a life-threatening idiosyncratic reaction to dopamine antagonists. Diagnosis rests on recent exposure plus the tetrad of hyperthermia, generalised rigidity, autonomic instability and altered mental state, with creatine kinase typically above 1000 U/L. Management is immediate cessation of the offending agent, supportive care (cooling, intravenous fluids, electrolyte correction, myoglobinuric renal protection), intensive care admission and pharmacological options of dantrolene, bromocriptine or amantadine. Distinguish from serotonin syndrome (clonus, hyperreflexia, recent serotonergic exposure) and malignant catatonia.
key_points: Immediate cessation of the offending dopamine antagonist is the first priority
Supportive care: cooling, intravenous fluids, electrolyte correction
Renal protection for rhabdomyolysis with myoglobinuria
Dantrolene or bromocriptine for severe cases in intensive care
Differentiate from serotonin syndrome (clonus, hyperreflexia) and catatonia
explanation.pearls: Rechallenge with a different antipsychotic is possible after at least 2 weeks of full recovery, ideally with a low-potency atypical agent and slow titration.

subtopic_detail: Borderline personality disorder with recurrent self-harm
stem: You are the emergency department registrar reviewing a 26-year-old non-Aboriginal woman with known borderline personality disorder who presents after superficial wrist lacerations following an argument with her partner. She is engaged in weekly dialectical behaviour therapy. She has had four similar presentations this year. She is now calm, engaged, declines admission and has a written safety plan in her phone. Her partner is present and supportive.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 °C, HR 78, BP 118/72, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Superficial linear lacerations to left forearm, no neurovascular compromise, no tendon injury; mood reactive, no current suicidal intent reported
data_table.Investigations: Bedside urine drug screen negative, BSL 5.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate disposition?

options.text: Admit involuntarily to the psychiatric unit under the relevant Mental Health Act because the repeated self-harm episodes constitute risk of serious harm
options.rationale: Hospital admission for chronic recurrent self-harm in borderline personality disorder is generally not therapeutic and can be iatrogenic; outpatient psychological therapy is the evidence-based core treatment. (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guidelines)

options.text: Prescribe diazepam 5 mg three times daily for two weeks and arrange general practitioner review without communication with her existing DBT therapist about the presentation
options.rationale: Routine benzodiazepines have no role in chronic borderline personality disorder and risk dependence and disinhibition; communication with the existing treating team is essential. (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guidelines)

options.text: Wound care, review and update of the existing safety plan, communication with her DBT therapist, and discharge with planned follow-up within 24 to 48 hours
options.rationale: Best-practice care for borderline personality disorder presenting after non-lethal self-harm involves wound management, brief safety planning, communication with the treating team and timely outpatient follow-up rather than admission. (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guidelines)

options.text: Initiate quetiapine 100 mg at night to reduce emotional dysregulation and arrange a private psychiatrist review within 6 weeks without contacting her current treating team
options.rationale: Pharmacotherapy has no first-line role for the core features of borderline personality disorder, and bypassing the existing treating team fragments care. (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guidelines)

options.text: Refer for an inpatient electroconvulsive therapy course because of the chronic and recurrent nature of the self-harm and limited response to weekly psychotherapy
options.rationale: ECT has no role in the treatment of borderline personality disorder; it is reserved for severe treatment-resistant depression or catatonia. (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Australian NHMRC guidelines establish structured psychological therapies, in particular dialectical behaviour therapy and mentalisation-based therapy, as the core treatment for borderline personality disorder. Hospital admission is generally avoided for chronic recurrent self-harm because it can reinforce maladaptive patterns and rarely changes long-term trajectory. Acute presentations focus on physical wound care, brief safety planning, communication with the existing treating team and timely outpatient follow-up. Pharmacotherapy has at most an adjunct role for comorbid conditions and short-term crisis use.
key_points: Structured psychological therapy is the core treatment for borderline personality disorder
Routine hospital admission for recurrent self-harm is not therapeutic
Acute care focus is wound management, brief safety planning, team communication, follow-up
Medications have at most adjunct roles for comorbid conditions
Benzodiazepines should generally be avoided because of dependence and disinhibition risk
explanation.pearls: Brief admission may be considered when there is a clear acute risk above baseline or comorbid major depression, but should be planned, time-limited and discharge focused.

stem: You are the early psychosis service registrar reviewing a 23-year-old non-Aboriginal man 3 months after starting olanzapine 15 mg nightly for a first episode of schizophrenia. Symptoms have improved and he is adherent. He has gained 5 kg since starting treatment. He smokes 10 cigarettes daily, eats takeaway most nights and walks only briefly. His parents and partner are supportive and he is back at his apprenticeship. He has no known cardiovascular disease and no family history of premature heart disease.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 132/82 mmHg, HR 84, RR 14, T 36.7 °C, BMI 27 kg/m2 (up from 25 baseline)
data_table.Examination: Mildly increased waist circumference 96 cm, no acanthosis nigricans, no peripheral oedema, no extrapyramidal signs
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 5.8 mmol/L, HbA1c 5.6%, total cholesterol 5.4 mmol/L, LDL 3.4 mmol/L, HDL 1.0 mmol/L, triglycerides 2.4 mmol/L, prolactin 380 mIU/L (normal up to 500), ECG QTc 432 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange dietitian and exercise physiologist input, schedule repeat fasting lipids and glucose at 6 months, and review olanzapine choice with the prescriber if metabolic indices worsen
options.rationale: RANZCP and Therapeutic Guidelines recommend 3-month then 6-monthly metabolic monitoring for second-generation antipsychotics with intervention via lifestyle and medication review when weight, glucose or lipid changes appear. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.text: Commence metformin 500 mg twice daily immediately to prevent further weight gain, continue olanzapine 15 mg unchanged, and review the FBC and renal function in 3 months
options.rationale: Metformin is considered after lifestyle measures fail or when significant insulin resistance is present; pre-emptive use in mild weight gain without dysglycaemia is not first-line. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.text: Switch immediately to risperidone 4 mg daily without dietitian input, withhold metabolic re-screening for 6 months, and review in psychiatric outpatient clinic in 12 weeks
options.rationale: Switching antipsychotic in stable first-episode response carries relapse risk and is reserved for significant intolerance; risperidone has different but not negligible metabolic and prolactin effects. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.text: Refer to cardiology for stress echocardiography given the elevated triglycerides and rising BMI, defer further psychiatry follow-up until that result is available
options.rationale: Stress echocardiography is not indicated in an asymptomatic 23-year-old; cardiovascular risk reduction in early psychosis hinges on lifestyle and medication selection, not advanced imaging. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.text: Cease olanzapine, prescribe diazepam 5 mg twice daily for symptom control, and refer back to the general practitioner for ongoing care of the metabolic side effects without psychiatry review
options.rationale: Stopping the antipsychotic in a first-episode patient with response risks relapse; benzodiazepines do not treat psychosis. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

explanation.summary: Second-generation antipsychotics, especially olanzapine and clozapine, cause weight gain, dyslipidaemia and dysglycaemia. RANZCP recommends weight, waist, BP, fasting glucose and lipids at baseline, 6 weeks, 3 months and then 6-monthly. Lifestyle intervention is first-line; metformin can be added when insulin resistance is established or weight gain progresses despite lifestyle. Switching antipsychotics is considered when metabolic harm exceeds psychiatric benefit.
key_points: Olanzapine has high metabolic risk; clozapine highest
Monitor weight, BP, fasting glucose and lipids at baseline, 6 weeks, 3 months, then 6-monthly
Lifestyle intervention is first-line for weight gain and dyslipidaemia
Metformin can be added when insulin resistance is established or weight gain progresses
Switching antipsychotic is considered when metabolic harm outweighs psychiatric benefit
explanation.pearls: Aripiprazole and ziprasidone have the lowest weight gain profile among second-generation antipsychotics and are favoured in first-episode psychosis when metabolic syndrome risk is high or already present.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

subtopic_detail: Cannabis-induced psychotic disorder vs first-episode schizophrenia
stem: You are the consultation-liaison psychiatry registrar called by ED about a 21-year-old non-Aboriginal man brought in by his housemates with 5 days of persecutory delusions and auditory hallucinations. He has used high-potency cannabis daily for 18 months and increased intake markedly over the past month. He has no past psychiatric history and no family history of psychosis. He is calm in the cubicle. Urine drug screen is positive for cannabinoids and negative for amphetamines.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/72 mmHg, HR 88, RR 16, T 36.6 °C, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Alert, oriented to person and time, mildly perplexed, no extrapyramidal signs, no fever, normal cardiovascular and neurological examination
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, CRP all normal, urine drug screen positive cannabinoids only, ECG QTc 410 ms, CT brain normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Order overnight observation in ED with diazepam 5 mg twice daily for sedation only, withhold antipsychotic and AOD counselling, and discharge in the morning to GP follow-up
options.rationale: Benzodiazepine monotherapy does not treat psychotic symptoms; same-day discharge from ED without an antipsychotic plan or specialist follow-up misses the early-intervention window. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.text: Discharge home with instructions to cease cannabis, withhold antipsychotic treatment, and review in early psychosis clinic in 2 weeks once a baseline assessment is complete
options.rationale: Active psychotic symptoms are unsafe to manage at home and warrant antipsychotic treatment; abstinence alone often does not resolve symptoms quickly. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.text: Detain under the Mental Health Act for compulsory inpatient treatment and commence intramuscular haloperidol 5 mg every 6 hours for symptom control on admission
options.rationale: Compulsory detention is reserved for refusal of treatment with risk; he is calm and agreeable. Haloperidol intramuscular every 6 hours is overaggressive and risks extrapyramidal side effects. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg daily for the perplexity and persecutory thoughts, recommend cannabis cessation, and arrange GP review in 1 week for medication titration
options.rationale: SSRIs do not treat psychosis and can worsen symptoms; antipsychotic is required. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.text: Admit voluntarily, commence olanzapine 10 mg nightly, arrange brief alcohol and other drug counselling, and plan psychiatric review in 4 weeks with abstinence advice
options.rationale: First-presentation psychosis in the context of heavy cannabis use needs antipsychotic treatment, abstinence support, and structured follow-up because around half of cannabis-induced psychoses transition to a primary psychotic disorder. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

explanation.summary: Cannabis-induced psychotic disorder and first-episode schizophrenia overlap significantly and are not reliably distinguishable at first presentation. Around half of cannabis-induced psychoses transition to a primary psychotic disorder within 3 years, so management mirrors first-episode psychosis with antipsychotic treatment, AOD intervention and structured follow-up. High-potency cannabis use confers the greatest risk. Voluntary admission is preferred when engagement allows.
key_points: Cannabis-induced and primary psychotic disorders overlap clinically at first presentation
Around 50% of cannabis-induced psychoses transition to primary psychotic disorder within 3 years
Treat with antipsychotic plus abstinence support and structured follow-up
High-potency cannabis use confers the greatest risk
Voluntary admission is preferred when the patient is engaging and safe
explanation.pearls: Daily use of high-potency cannabis (over 10% THC content) is associated with a nearly 5-fold increased risk of psychotic disorder compared with non-users; risk is highest under 18 years of age.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

stem: You are the consultation-liaison psychiatry registrar called to the medical ward to see a 28-year-old non-Aboriginal woman with bipolar I disorder admitted 4 days ago for refusing food and fluids. She has been mute, immobile and maintaining odd postures. She has not eaten or drunk anything. She has not had recent neuroleptic dose change. Medical causes have been excluded by neurology consult. She is on lithium 750 mg nightly.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.0 °C, HR 96, RR 18, BP 116/72 mmHg, SpO2 98% room air
data_table.Examination: Mute, eyes open without engagement, waxy flexibility with arms remaining where placed, mild echopraxia of examiner gestures, Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale score 14, no rigidity or pyrexia
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs normal, lithium level 0.72 mmol/L, CK 320 U/L, CRP 4 mg/L, CT brain normal, EEG without epileptiform activity

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence intramuscular haloperidol 5 mg twice daily for the immobility and mutism, observe for further extrapyramidal features, and review the response after 48 hours
options.rationale: Antipsychotics can precipitate malignant catatonia and worsen the syndrome; they are avoided in suspected catatonia until benzodiazepines are first trialled. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Clinical Memorandum)

options.text: Administer a lorazepam challenge with 1 mg intramuscularly and reassess at 30 minutes, planning ongoing scheduled lorazepam if responsive and ECT referral if not
options.rationale: The lorazepam challenge is the standard diagnostic and therapeutic test for catatonia; a marked reduction in catatonic features within 30 minutes confirms the diagnosis and supports continued benzodiazepine treatment, with ECT for non-response. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Clinical Memorandum)

options.text: Increase the lithium dose to 1000 mg nightly, recheck the level in 5 days, and continue ward observation pending mood stabiliser optimisation over the next week
options.rationale: Lithium augmentation is not the treatment for catatonia and the level is already therapeutic; a benzodiazepine challenge addresses the immediate problem. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Clinical Memorandum)

options.text: Commence intravenous valproate loading at 20 mg/kg in addition to lithium, withhold benzodiazepines, and reassess catatonic features after 4 hours of observation
options.rationale: Valproate is not first-line for catatonia and combined valproate-lithium does not address the syndrome; benzodiazepines plus ECT are the evidence-based path. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Clinical Memorandum)

options.text: Refer for nasogastric tube insertion for feeds and rehydration, withhold psychotropic intervention until oral intake resumes, and review with psychiatry team in 24 hours
options.rationale: NG feeding may be needed but does not treat catatonia; deferring psychotropic intervention prolongs the syndrome and risks complications such as pulmonary embolism and contractures. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Clinical Memorandum)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a neuropsychiatric syndrome of stupor, mutism, posturing, waxy flexibility and echophenomena, frequently associated with mood disorders, psychotic illness and medical conditions. The lorazepam challenge with 1 to 2 mg IM or IV provides rapid diagnostic confirmation and therapeutic effect; responders continue scheduled lorazepam. Non-responders or those with malignant features (autonomic instability, hyperthermia) need urgent ECT. Antipsychotics are avoided until catatonia resolves.
key_points: Catatonia features include stupor, mutism, posturing, waxy flexibility and echophenomena
Lorazepam challenge is the diagnostic and therapeutic standard
Scheduled lorazepam continues for responders; ECT for non-response or malignant features
Avoid antipsychotics until catatonia resolves due to malignant catatonia risk
Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale aids diagnosis and severity tracking
explanation.pearls: Malignant catatonia (autonomic instability, hyperthermia, severe rigidity) and neuroleptic malignant syndrome are increasingly viewed as variants of the same neurochemical spectrum; ECT is effective for both and should not be delayed in critically ill patients.

subtopic_detail: Valproate teratogenicity and pregnancy prevention in a woman of reproductive age
stem: You are the psychiatry registrar in the mood disorders clinic reviewing a 27-year-old non-Aboriginal woman with bipolar I disorder who has been stable for 18 months on sodium valproate 1000 mg nightly. She is in a new relationship and has stopped using contraception because she wants to start trying for a baby in the next 6 months. She has had no episodes for 18 months and is otherwise well. She works as a primary school teacher and has supportive parents nearby. There is no other medical or psychiatric history.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/76 mmHg, HR 76, RR 14, T 36.6 °C, BMI 24 kg/m2
data_table.Examination: Euthymic mental state, normal neurological examination, no signs of polycystic ovary syndrome, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: FBC normal, valproate level 480 micromol/L (therapeutic 350 to 700), LFTs normal, urine pregnancy test negative, TSH 1.6 mIU/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Switch to carbamazepine 400 mg daily as an alternative mood stabiliser with the rationale that it has a more favourable fetal safety profile in pregnancy planning settings
options.rationale: Carbamazepine has higher major malformation rates (around 5%) than lamotrigine (around 2%) and is not the preferred switch for pregnancy planning in bipolar disorder. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP Bipolar Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Continue valproate at the current dose, add folic acid 5 mg daily, and reassure that the medication is safer for the baby than a relapse during pregnancy in this stable patient
options.rationale: Folate does not mitigate valproate teratogenicity or neurodevelopmental risk; continuation in pregnancy planning is contraindicated outside extraordinary circumstances. (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Advice)
source_refs: Therapeutic Goods Administration Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Advice

options.text: Counsel that valproate is contraindicated in pregnancy planning, arrange specialist review to transition to a safer mood stabiliser such as lamotrigine, and continue effective contraception during the switch
options.rationale: Valproate carries 10% major congenital malformation risk and a 30 to 40% risk of neurodevelopmental impairment; women of reproductive potential planning pregnancy require transition to safer agents under specialist supervision with continued contraception. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP Bipolar Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline
Therapeutic Goods Administration Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Advice

options.text: Cease valproate immediately without replacement therapy, commence cognitive behavioural therapy fortnightly, and review for relapse with monthly mood diaries and clinic visits
options.rationale: Abrupt valproate cessation in bipolar I without bridging risks severe relapse; transition under specialist guidance to a maintenance-effective alternative is required. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP Bipolar Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Continue valproate during the periconceptional period only, switch to lamotrigine after the first trimester, and arrange detailed morphology scan at 20 weeks
options.rationale: Neural tube defect risk is highest in the first trimester so continuing valproate during that window is exactly the wrong sequence; safer agents must be in place before conception. (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Advice)
source_refs: Therapeutic Goods Administration Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Advice

explanation.summary: Valproate causes major congenital malformations in around 10% of exposed pregnancies and neurodevelopmental impairment in 30 to 40%, particularly autism spectrum and reduced IQ. The TGA pregnancy prevention program requires annual specialist review, documented contraception and a signed acknowledgement for women of reproductive potential. Pregnancy planning requires transition to safer agents such as lamotrigine under specialist supervision before conception. Folate does not mitigate teratogenicity.
key_points: Valproate causes around 10% major malformations and 30 to 40% neurodevelopmental impairment
TGA pregnancy prevention program mandates annual review and documented contraception
Transition to safer agents such as lamotrigine occurs before conception, not during pregnancy
Folate does not mitigate valproate teratogenicity
Lamotrigine has the lowest teratogenic risk of the mood stabilisers (around 2% major malformation)
explanation.pearls: Lamotrigine clearance increases by up to 250% during pregnancy due to glucuronidation induction; doses typically need to rise from second trimester and return to baseline within 2 weeks postpartum to avoid toxicity.

sources.label: RANZCP Bipolar Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline
Therapeutic Goods Administration Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Advice

subtopic_detail: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose with QRS widening
stem: You are the emergency registrar called to resus for a 32-year-old non-Aboriginal woman brought in 90 minutes after a deliberate overdose of approximately 50 amitriptyline 50 mg tablets. She is drowsy with a GCS of 11. Her partner found her with the empty bottle. She has a 5-year history of depression and previous self-harm by cutting. There is no other prescribed medication and no recreational drug use disclosed.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.5 °C, HR 132 sinus tachycardia, RR 16, SpO2 96% room air, BP 92/56 mmHg, GCS 11 (eyes 2, verbal 4, motor 5)
data_table.Examination: Dry mouth, mydriasis with sluggish pupils, dry warm skin, urinary retention, hyperreflexia, no clonus
data_table.Investigations: ECG QRS 132 ms with terminal R wave in aVR over 3 mm, QTc 480 ms, ABG pH 7.30 pCO2 30 mmHg HCO3 17 mmol/L, paracetamol level under 10 mg/L, alcohol negative, salicylate not detected, potassium 3.4 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus targeting QRS narrowing and arterial pH 7.45 to 7.55, intubate to protect the airway, and arrange ICU admission
options.rationale: QRS over 100 ms with terminal R in aVR over 3 mm signals significant TCA cardiotoxicity; sodium bicarbonate narrows QRS by sodium loading and pH-driven protein binding shift, intubation protects the airway with deteriorating GCS, and ICU is mandatory. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)
source_refs: Australasian College for Emergency Medicine Toxicology Reference

options.text: Administer activated charcoal 50 g orally, place on telemetry in the resus bay, and reassess the ECG and conscious state in 2 hours before deciding on further intervention
options.rationale: Charcoal at 90 minutes after overdose has limited benefit and is contraindicated with a falling GCS without airway protection; QRS widening already mandates bicarbonate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Administer intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg over 30 seconds for the reduced level of consciousness and reassess airway protective reflexes after each dose titration
options.rationale: Flumazenil is contraindicated in mixed overdose with TCA because it can precipitate seizures by lowering the seizure threshold against the proconvulsant TCA effect. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Administer intravenous physostigmine 1 mg slow push to reverse the anticholinergic syndrome and arrange continuous cardiac monitoring with intensive care liaison after dose
options.rationale: Physostigmine is contraindicated in TCA overdose due to the risk of asystole; reversal of anticholinergic features does not address the sodium channel blockade. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Administer intravenous amiodarone 300 mg over 20 minutes for the sinus tachycardia and broadening QRS, continue oxygen and intravenous fluids, and admit to a monitored ward bed
options.rationale: Class IA, IC and III antiarrhythmics worsen sodium channel blockade and are contraindicated in TCA toxicity; treatment is sodium bicarbonate and supportive care. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

explanation.summary: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose causes sodium channel blockade (wide QRS, terminal R in aVR), QT prolongation, hypotension, anticholinergic delirium, seizures and arrhythmias. Sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg is the antidote, narrowing QRS by sodium loading and alkalosis-driven protein binding. Airway protection precedes any procedure on a falling GCS. Class IA, IC and III antiarrhythmics, physostigmine and flumazenil are contraindicated.
key_points: QRS over 100 ms or terminal R in aVR over 3 mm signals significant TCA cardiotoxicity
Sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg is the antidote targeting QRS narrowing and pH 7.45 to 7.55
Intubate before lavage or charcoal if GCS is falling
Avoid class IA, IC and III antiarrhythmics, physostigmine and flumazenil
ICU admission until ECG is normal off bicarbonate for at least 6 hours
explanation.pearls: Intravenous lipid emulsion 1.5 mL/kg of 20% solution is a rescue therapy for refractory cardiovascular collapse from lipophilic drug toxicity including amitriptyline, and may be considered when bicarbonate and standard resuscitation are insufficient.

sources.label: Australasian College for Emergency Medicine Toxicology Reference

stem: You are the on-call psychiatry registrar in ED with a 26-year-old non-Aboriginal man brought in by police for violent and threatening behaviour in the community. He has a 3-year history of schizophrenia. He is shouting, intermittently striking the walls and refuses oral medication. De-escalation by experienced ED nursing staff has not reduced his agitation. He has no known medical conditions, no allergies and is otherwise physically well. Six security staff are present.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9 °C, HR 124, RR 22, SpO2 99% room air, BP 142/88 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Highly agitated, no signs of intoxication, no head injury, no needle marks, no pyrexia, no clonus, no rigidity
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 5.4 mmol/L, urine drug screen pending, ECG QTc 410 ms on previous admission

lead_in: What is the single best initial pharmacological intervention?

options.text: Intramuscular haloperidol 5 mg with promethazine 25 mg as a combined dose, no cardiac monitoring required, and admit to the psychiatric assessment unit immediately afterwards
options.rationale: Promethazine combinations are no longer preferred in Australian guidance due to lower efficacy than droperidol; cardiac monitoring is required for all parenteral antipsychotic use in this setting. (Source: NSW Health Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance)
source_refs: NSW Health Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance

options.text: Intramuscular midazolam 10 mg as a single dose without antipsychotic, observe airway and oximetry in the resus bay, and repeat at 10 minute intervals as needed
options.rationale: Benzodiazepine monotherapy at 10 mg carries higher airway and oversedation risks than droperidol at this dose in adult acute behavioural disturbance; combination or antipsychotic monotherapy is preferred. (Source: NSW Health Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance)
source_refs: NSW Health Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance

options.text: Oral olanzapine 20 mg wafer with lorazepam 2 mg by mouth and observe in the cubicle, repeating doses at 30 minute intervals if cooperation continues to improve
options.rationale: He has refused oral medication; oral routes are not appropriate in active behavioural disturbance requiring tranquillisation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Intramuscular droperidol 10 mg as a single dose with continuous pulse oximetry and cardiac monitoring, repeat dose available at 15 minutes if needed
options.rationale: Australian rapid tranquillisation guidance recommends intramuscular droperidol 10 mg as first-line for adult acute behavioural disturbance with cardiac monitoring; large RCT data (DORM trial) support efficacy and safety. (Source: NSW Health Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance)
source_refs: NSW Health Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance

options.text: Intravenous ketamine 100 mg as a sedative dose with anaesthetic standby, intubation kit prepared, and direct admission to ICU once sedated
options.rationale: Ketamine is a salvage option for failure of standard rapid tranquillisation, not first-line; its use mandates anaesthetic backup and is not the initial step. (Source: NSW Health Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance)
source_refs: NSW Health Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance

explanation.summary: Acute severe behavioural disturbance in Australia uses parenteral rapid tranquillisation when de-escalation fails. Intramuscular droperidol 10 mg is first-line in adults with cardiac monitoring and oximetry; the Druid 1 and Druid 2 trial program supports efficacy and acceptable QTc safety. Olanzapine intramuscular 10 mg is an alternative. Ketamine is reserved for refractory cases. Mechanical restraint and post-tranquillisation observation are mandatory components.
key_points: IM droperidol 10 mg is the Australian first-line for adult acute behavioural disturbance
Cardiac monitoring and oximetry are mandatory during and after rapid tranquillisation
Olanzapine IM 10 mg is an alternative first-line in adults
Ketamine is reserved for refractory cases with anaesthetic backup
De-escalation precedes pharmacological intervention; restraint is the last resort
explanation.pearls: Combined intramuscular olanzapine and benzodiazepines within 60 minutes of each other are associated with hypotension and respiratory depression; if recent IM lorazepam or midazolam has been given, droperidol is preferred over olanzapine.

sources.label: NSW Health Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance

subtopic_detail: Adult ADHD with comorbid stimulant use disorder
stem: You are the addiction psychiatry registrar in a tertiary clinic seeing a 29-year-old non-Aboriginal man referred for assessment of adult ADHD with comorbid methamphetamine use disorder. He has used methamphetamine intermittently for 6 years and was abstinent for the past 4 weeks following a residential withdrawal admission. He describes lifelong inattention, distractibility and impulsivity, with school records confirming attentional difficulties from age 8. His mother has untreated ADHD. He is engaged with an outpatient drug and alcohol service. He drives a delivery truck for work.

data_table.Examination: Normal cardiovascular and neurological examination, no signs of intoxication or withdrawal, no peripheral stigmata of long-term stimulant use
data_table.Investigations: Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS) score 18 of 24 inattentive features, structured diagnostic interview meets DSM-5 ADHD criteria with childhood symptom evidence, urine drug screen negative, ECG QTc 405 ms with normal sinus rhythm, FBC, UEC, LFTs normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological plan?

options.text: Commence guanfacine extended release 4 mg daily as a non-stimulant alternative, with the understanding that this is the preferred non-stimulant choice over atomoxetine in adults
options.rationale: Guanfacine ER is approved in Australia for children and adolescents but is not first-line for adult ADHD; atomoxetine is the standard adult non-stimulant. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Commence immediate-release dexamfetamine 5 mg twice daily and titrate weekly to symptom response, with monthly urine drug screens and direct supply through a single prescriber
