options.rationale: Immediate-release stimulants carry the highest diversion and misuse risk and are not first-line in active or recent stimulant use disorder. Long-acting formulations are preferred if a stimulant trial is later required. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Commence lisdexamfetamine 30 mg morning dose immediately with daily pharmacy dispensing and weekly urine screens, plus continued outpatient drug and alcohol engagement throughout therapy
options.rationale: Although long-acting stimulants have lower diversion risk than immediate-release, Australian guidance recommends a period of demonstrated stability and non-stimulant trial first in comorbid stimulant use disorder. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Defer ADHD pharmacotherapy until 12 months of abstinence, continue cognitive behavioural therapy and addiction support, and review at the end of that period for treatment planning
options.rationale: Indefinite deferral worsens ADHD symptom burden and risks return to methamphetamine self-medication; non-stimulant trial can proceed safely with addiction medicine engagement. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Commence atomoxetine titrated to 80 mg daily, continue addiction medicine engagement, and reassess in 8 weeks before considering stimulant trial if symptoms persist
options.rationale: Australian ADHD guidelines recommend non-stimulant first-line treatment in adults with comorbid stimulant use disorder due to diversion and relapse risk; atomoxetine is the standard non-stimulant choice. Reassessment after substance-use stabilisation guides any later stimulant decision. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

explanation.summary: ADHD and stimulant use disorder co-occur frequently and each worsens the other if untreated. Australian guidance prioritises non-stimulant pharmacotherapy (atomoxetine, less commonly bupropion) in adults with active or recent stimulant use disorder, with structured addiction medicine engagement throughout. Stimulant trial may be revisited after demonstrated stability, using long-acting formulations and tight prescriber controls. Driving capacity, cardiovascular screening and contraceptive counselling are part of standard ADHD initiation.
key_points: Atomoxetine is first-line for adult ADHD with comorbid stimulant use disorder
Indefinite deferral of pharmacotherapy worsens outcomes
Long-acting stimulants are preferred over immediate-release if later required
Baseline cardiovascular and driving screening is essential
Concurrent addiction medicine engagement is mandatory
explanation.pearls: Atomoxetine titration typically takes 4 to 6 weeks for full clinical effect, unlike stimulants which act within hours; this slow onset is a useful counselling point because patients often expect rapid stimulant-like response and disengage if not prepared.

sources.label: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

subtopic_detail: Anorexia nervosa medical admission criteria and refeeding syndrome
stem: You are the medical registrar reviewing a 19-year-old non-Aboriginal woman with a 3-year history of anorexia nervosa restricting subtype. Her parents have brought her in because of progressive fatigue, dizziness on standing and one syncopal episode while showering this morning. She has been eating around 400 kcal per day for the past month. She is medically stable but markedly underweight. She has been seeing an outpatient psychologist weekly but has not been admitted before.

data_table.Vital signs: T 35.6 °C, HR 38 supine resting, RR 14, SpO2 98% room air, BP 86/52 lying 70/40 standing, weight 38 kg height 168 cm BMI 13.5 kg/m2
data_table.Examination: Cachectic, lanugo on arms and back, cool peripheries, no oedema, alert and orientated but withdrawn, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: Na 134 K 2.9 Cl 96 HCO3 28 mmol/L, phosphate 0.65 mmol/L, magnesium 0.62 mmol/L, glucose 3.4 mmol/L, ALT 78 ALP 88 albumin 32 g/L, ECG QTc 478 ms, FBC unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management plan?

options.text: Discharge home with daily dietitian and psychologist input, immediate commencement of a high calorie oral nutritional supplement plan of 3000 kcal/day and review by adolescent psychiatry in the eating disorders day program within 48 hours
options.rationale: BMI 13.5 with bradycardia, hypotension, hypokalaemia, hypophosphataemia and QTc prolongation all meet inpatient admission criteria for anorexia nervosa. (Source: ANZAED Treatment Guidelines)

options.text: Admit to a general medical ward for cardiac monitoring, commence high-calorie nasogastric feeding at 30 kcal/kg/day, correct potassium and phosphate aggressively and start a benzodiazepine at night to manage refeeding anxiety
options.rationale: Starting feeds at 30 kcal/kg/day in a high-risk patient risks refeeding syndrome; initial feeds are 5-10 kcal/kg/day with cautious escalation. (Source: ANZAED Treatment Guidelines)

options.text: Admit to a monitored medical bed, commence oral thiamine 200 mg daily and a multivitamin, replace potassium phosphate and magnesium before feeding, start cautious refeeding at 5 to 10 kcal/kg/day and increase under daily electrolyte monitoring
options.rationale: Inpatient management of severe anorexia with multiple medical criteria includes thiamine, electrolyte correction before feeding and cautious refeeding starting at 5-10 kcal/kg/day with daily phosphate, potassium, magnesium and glucose monitoring. (Source: ANZAED Treatment Guidelines)
source_refs: MARSIPAN UK adapted Australian medical care of severe anorexia

options.text: Admit to the high-dependency unit, commence rapid parenteral nutrition at 40 kcal/kg/day to restore weight gain, correct electrolytes intravenously and request urgent compulsory inpatient treatment under the relevant state Mental Health Act
options.rationale: Parenteral nutrition is not first-line; oral or nasogastric refeeding is preferred. Use of the Mental Health Act is reserved for refusal of life-saving treatment without insight. (Source: ANZAED Treatment Guidelines)

options.text: Refer urgently to a private eating disorders inpatient program with daily outpatient electrolyte monitoring at her general practice surgery while a private psychiatric admission is being arranged over the next 7 days
options.rationale: Acute medical instability requires immediate medical admission rather than outpatient bridging while awaiting a private bed. (Source: ANZAED Treatment Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Medical admission criteria for anorexia nervosa include BMI under 14, bradycardia under 40, postural drop, hypothermia, electrolyte derangement, QTc over 450 and recent syncope. Inpatient care prioritises cautious refeeding to avoid refeeding syndrome, starting at 5-10 kcal/kg/day with daily electrolyte monitoring. Phosphate, potassium and magnesium are replaced before and during feeding, with prophylactic thiamine. Use of the Mental Health Act is reserved for refusal of life-saving treatment.
key_points: Admit if BMI under 14, HR under 40, postural drop, QTc over 450 or electrolyte derangement
Refeed at 5-10 kcal/kg/day, escalate slowly with daily electrolytes
Replace phosphate, potassium, magnesium before and during feeds
Thiamine 200 mg daily prophylaxis
Mental Health Act for refusal of life-saving treatment only
explanation.pearls: Phosphate is the single most reliable early biochemical marker of refeeding syndrome; a drop below 0.6 mmol/L in the first week of refeeding warrants dose reduction, supplementation and senior review.

sources.label: MARSIPAN UK adapted Australian medical care of severe anorexia

subtopic_detail: Complex PTSD therapy and pharmacotherapy choice
stem: You are the general practitioner reviewing a 34-year-old non-Aboriginal woman 4 months after a violent assault. She has nightmares, hypervigilance, intrusive flashbacks during the day, avoidance of public transport and difficulty sleeping. She has tried sertraline at 50 mg daily for the last 6 weeks with partial response on mood symptoms but persistent flashbacks. She is engaged with a clinical psychologist for supportive counselling and is willing to consider trauma-focused therapy. She has no current suicidal ideation and is working part-time.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 °C, HR 84, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air, BP 122/76 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Anxious affect with intermittent tearfulness, no psychomotor retardation, intact insight and judgement, no current suicidality
data_table.Investigations: PCL-5 score 48 (moderate-severe), PHQ-9 score 18 (moderate-severe), thyroid function and FBC within reference ranges, no substance use on history or urine drug screen

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Switch sertraline to mirtazapine 30 mg nocte targeting sleep and appetite improvement, and continue supportive counselling with the clinical psychologist as the sole talking therapy intervention going forward
options.rationale: Mirtazapine is not first-line in PTSD and supportive counselling alone is inferior to trauma-focused therapy for core PTSD symptoms. (Source: Phoenix Australia Australian PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Add olanzapine 5 mg nocte for adjunctive sleep and re-experiencing symptom control, and review SSRI dose titration in 4 weeks before considering any psychological therapy referral or non-pharmacological intervention
options.rationale: Atypical antipsychotic augmentation is third-line in PTSD and carries metabolic risk; first-line escalation is trauma-focused psychological therapy. (Source: Phoenix Australia Australian PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Increase sertraline to 100 mg daily, add prazosin 1 mg nocte for nightmares titrated to 5 mg over 4 weeks and review in 4 weeks for further dose adjustment without any change to her current psychological treatment
options.rationale: Prazosin is an option for refractory nightmares but does not substitute for first-line trauma-focused psychological therapy in PTSD. (Source: Phoenix Australia Australian PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Refer for trauma-focused CBT or EMDR with an experienced clinician, continue sertraline at 50 mg with a planned review of dose at the next appointment and arrange GP review in 4 weeks to monitor symptoms
options.rationale: Australian PTSD guidelines place trauma-focused CBT and EMDR as first-line therapy; supportive counselling is insufficient and pharmacotherapy is second-line or adjunctive. (Source: Phoenix Australia Australian PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Recommend a 6-week course of mindfulness-based stress reduction in a community group program as the primary therapy and discontinue sertraline because of the partial response and intolerance of medication side effects
options.rationale: MBSR is not first-line for PTSD and SSRI discontinuation in partial responders is not warranted; trauma-focused therapy is the next step. (Source: Phoenix Australia Australian PTSD Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Australian guidelines for PTSD recommend trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy or eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing as first-line treatment. SSRIs (sertraline or paroxetine) are second-line or used as adjuncts when trauma-focused therapy is unavailable or ineffective. Prazosin can target nightmares in refractory cases. Atypical antipsychotic augmentation is reserved for partial response after first- and second-line measures. Mindfulness and supportive counselling alone are not sufficient.
key_points: Trauma-focused CBT and EMDR are first-line in PTSD
Sertraline and paroxetine are second-line SSRIs
Prazosin can target nightmares in refractory cases
Atypical antipsychotic augmentation is third-line
Supportive counselling alone is inadequate for core PTSD symptoms
explanation.pearls: Eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing (EMDR) is non-inferior to trauma-focused CBT and may be preferred when patients find prolonged narrative exposure too distressing; benzodiazepines are not recommended in PTSD because they worsen recovery.

stem: You are the medical registrar admitting a 56-year-old non-Aboriginal man with a 30-year history of heavy alcohol use. He has been on the ward for 36 hours after self-presenting for detoxification and stopped drinking 48 hours ago. He is now confused, tremulous, sweating profusely and has had a witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure 30 minutes ago. He is intermittently agitated and seeing animals on the curtains. He has had two previous episodes of complicated alcohol withdrawal.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.2 °C, HR 132, RR 26, SpO2 96% room air, BP 168/108 mmHg, capillary glucose 4.8 mmol/L
data_table.Examination: Disoriented to time and place, marked tremor, profuse diaphoresis, visual hallucinations, GCS 14, no focal neurology, soft non-tender abdomen
data_table.Investigations: Na 132 K 3.2 Mg 0.62 phosphate 0.7 mmol/L, glucose 4.8 mmol/L, urea 7.2 creatinine 92 micromol/L, ALT 96 GGT 540 U/L, INR 1.4, FBC platelets 102 x10^9/L, head CT no acute pathology

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Commence oral diazepam 20 mg every 2 hours by symptom-triggered CIWA-Ar protocol on the general ward and arrange routine medical review by the consultant on the morning ward round in approximately 12 hours from now
options.rationale: Established delirium tremens with seizure and autonomic instability requires intravenous benzodiazepine titration in a high-dependency setting, not oral symptom-triggered dosing on a general ward. (Source: RACGP Alcohol Use Disorders)

options.text: Administer haloperidol 5 mg intramuscular for agitation, continue oral thiamine 100 mg daily and observe for further seizures on the ward with intramuscular diazepam available for clinician-initiated breakthrough as needed
options.rationale: First-generation antipsychotics lower seizure threshold and are inappropriate as primary therapy in delirium tremens; benzodiazepines remain the cornerstone. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Start phenytoin loading dose 18 mg/kg over 30 minutes for ongoing seizure prevention and continue an oral benzodiazepine taper with no need to escalate the level of care beyond the current general medical ward bed
options.rationale: Phenytoin is not effective for alcohol withdrawal seizures and does not treat the underlying autonomic instability; benzodiazepine titration is first-line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Transfer to the intensive care unit for sedation with continuous propofol infusion and elective intubation to control airway and autonomic features given the established delirium tremens with seizure and pyrexia
options.rationale: Intubation and propofol are reserved for refractory delirium tremens after high-dose benzodiazepine titration has failed; titration is the first step. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Transfer to a high-dependency or intensive care bed, give intravenous diazepam 10 mg titrated to RASS minus 1, administer parenteral thiamine 300 mg three times daily for 3-5 days before any glucose-containing fluids and replace magnesium and potassium
options.rationale: Established delirium tremens with seizure mandates HDU care, IV benzodiazepine titration, parenteral thiamine before glucose to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy and electrolyte correction. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Delirium tremens is a medical emergency with mortality up to 15% if untreated. Management requires high-dependency or intensive care monitoring, intravenous benzodiazepine titration (diazepam or midazolam), parenteral thiamine 300 mg three times daily before any glucose to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy, and electrolyte correction. Antipsychotics are avoided as primary therapy because they lower the seizure threshold. Intubation and propofol are reserved for refractory cases.
key_points: DT requires HDU or ICU monitoring
IV benzodiazepine titration is first-line
Parenteral thiamine 300 mg TDS before glucose
Correct magnesium, potassium, phosphate
Avoid first-generation antipsychotics as primary therapy
explanation.pearls: Score severity of withdrawal with CIWA-Ar but use the score to titrate benzodiazepine dose rather than to triage location; any seizure, autonomic instability or hallucinations escalate the patient to high-dependency or intensive care regardless of the numeric score.

stem: You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 28-year-old non-Aboriginal man who presents requesting an assessment for adult ADHD. He describes lifelong difficulties with sustained attention, frequent forgetfulness, restlessness, impulsivity at work, and three traffic infringements in the past 12 months for inattention while driving. He has not been previously assessed. Collateral from his mother confirms problems since primary school. He drinks alcohol on weekends only and uses no other substances. He has no current depression or anxiety on screening.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 °C, HR 76, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, BP 124/78 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Engaging in conversation, mildly restless, no thought disorder, no psychotic features, GCS 15, normal cardiac and neurological examination
data_table.Investigations: DIVA-5 structured interview supports ADHD combined presentation, ASRS-v1.1 screener positive in both inattentive and hyperactive-impulsive domains, no medical contraindications on baseline ECG and bloods, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step before initiating stimulant medication?

options.text: Refer to a psychiatrist or paediatrician with an authority to prescribe stimulant medication for confirmation of diagnosis and treatment initiation, and counsel on Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive obligations including notifying the driver licensing authority
options.rationale: Stimulant initiation requires a stimulant authority (psychiatrist or paediatrician) in Australia and Austroads requires patient notification of the driver licensing authority for treated ADHD with safety-relevant features. (Source: Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive 2022)

options.text: Commence methylphenidate immediate release 10 mg twice daily under your own prescription, with cardiac and blood pressure monitoring at 2 and 4 weeks, and continue community follow-up before any psychiatry referral is considered
options.rationale: General practitioners cannot independently initiate stimulant therapy for adult ADHD in Australia; this requires a stimulant authority. (Source: PBS Stimulants for ADHD authority)

options.text: Trial atomoxetine 40 mg daily for 6 weeks first and refer for stimulant prescriber only if atomoxetine has failed to control core ADHD symptoms because stimulants carry abuse potential and cardiovascular risk concerns
options.rationale: Stimulants are first-line for adult ADHD in Australia; atomoxetine is second-line when stimulants are contraindicated or not tolerated. (Source: RACGP: Adult ADHD)

options.text: Recommend cognitive behavioural therapy alone for 12 weeks with no pharmacotherapy until psychological therapy completion and review CBT outcomes before considering whether stimulant medication will be necessary at that future review
options.rationale: CBT is adjunctive in moderate-severe adult ADHD; pharmacotherapy is the primary intervention with greatest effect size. (Source: RACGP: Adult ADHD)

options.text: Advise the patient that ADHD diagnosis in adulthood requires symptoms appearing before age 7 years and cannot be diagnosed with first presentation at 28 years even with childhood history confirmed by collateral parental information
options.rationale: DSM-5 lowered the age-of-onset criterion to before age 12 and the diagnosis can be confirmed in adulthood with appropriate collateral. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

explanation.summary: Adult ADHD diagnosis requires a structured assessment, evidence of symptoms before age 12, functional impairment across two or more settings, and exclusion of mimics. Stimulant medication is first-line treatment and requires a stimulant authority held by a psychiatrist or paediatrician. Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive obligates notification of the driver licensing authority when ADHD has safety-relevant features or pharmacotherapy is being commenced. CBT and skills coaching are adjunctive.
key_points: DSM-5 onset before age 12 with cross-setting impairment
Stimulants are first-line; authority required to prescribe
Atomoxetine is second-line when stimulants contraindicated
Austroads driver licensing notification for safety-relevant ADHD
CBT and coaching are adjunctive
explanation.pearls: Baseline ECG is recommended before stimulant initiation in patients with family history of sudden cardiac death, structural heart disease, syncope, palpitations or pre-existing hypertension; stimulant cardiovascular safety in healthy adults is otherwise good.

subtopic_detail: Schizoaffective vs bipolar with psychosis discrimination
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 26-year-old non-Aboriginal man brought in by his family after 8 weeks of bizarre behaviour. He describes persistent persecutory delusions and auditory hallucinations of voices commenting on his actions. Over the last 3 weeks he has also developed elevated mood, decreased need for sleep, pressured speech and grandiose plans to start a new tech company.

His delusions persisted during a 5-week period when his mood and energy were normal earlier in this episode. He has had two previous similar episodes. There is no substance use confirmed on urine drug screen.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 °C, HR 92, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air, BP 124/76 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Pressured speech, distractible, grandiose, persistent auditory hallucinations of commentary type, persecutory delusions; no formal thought disorder, oriented to person place and time, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative, FBC UEC LFT TSH within reference ranges, head CT no acute findings, fasting glucose 4.8 mmol/L, lipids fasting cholesterol 4.6 mmol/L LDL 2.4 HDL 1.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Schizoaffective disorder (bipolar type) given two or more weeks of psychotic symptoms occurring in the absence of a major mood episode together with current concurrent manic and psychotic symptoms over the course of this illness
options.rationale: DSM-5 schizoaffective disorder requires two or more weeks of psychotic symptoms in the absence of a major mood episode, with mood episodes present for the majority of total illness duration. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Bipolar I disorder with psychotic features given the current manic episode with mood-congruent grandiose delusions and the absence of any persistent psychotic symptoms outside discrete mood episodes during the course of his illness
options.rationale: Psychotic symptoms persisted for 5 weeks during normal mood, which is incompatible with bipolar I psychotic features (where psychosis occurs only during mood episodes). (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Schizophrenia given the 8 week duration of psychotic symptoms with persistent auditory hallucinations and delusions of persecution and the absence of negative symptoms that have lasted at least 6 months at this present time
options.rationale: Schizophrenia requires significant mood symptoms to be brief relative to active and residual phases; sustained mania for 3 weeks excludes schizophrenia. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Substance-induced psychotic disorder given the relatively rapid onset of psychotic symptoms with concurrent mood elevation and the typical pattern observed in stimulant and cannabis use in young men of his age and demographic
options.rationale: Urine drug screen is negative and the persistence of psychotic symptoms during normal mood does not fit substance-induced psychosis. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Brief psychotic disorder given the rapid onset of psychotic symptoms with full return to premorbid functioning expected within one month and no requirement for ongoing antipsychotic maintenance therapy beyond resolution of symptoms
options.rationale: Brief psychotic disorder is by definition less than 1 month duration; this presentation has lasted 8 weeks. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

explanation.summary: Schizoaffective disorder is distinguished from bipolar I with psychotic features by the presence of 2 or more weeks of psychotic symptoms in the absence of a major mood episode. Mood episodes must be present for the majority of the total illness duration. Schizophrenia is distinguished by mood symptoms being brief relative to active and residual phases. Treatment of schizoaffective bipolar type uses a combination of antipsychotic and mood stabiliser. The diagnosis influences both pharmacotherapy and prognosis.
key_points: Schizoaffective: 2+ weeks of psychosis without mood episode plus mood episodes for majority of illness
Bipolar with psychotic features: psychosis only during mood episodes
Schizophrenia: mood symptoms brief relative to active and residual
Brief psychotic disorder: less than 1 month duration
Schizoaffective bipolar type: antipsychotic plus mood stabiliser
explanation.pearls: Lithium and lamotrigine are both reasonable mood-stabilising adjuncts in schizoaffective bipolar type; lithium has greater anti-manic and anti-suicide effect while lamotrigine targets depressive episodes with lower upfront monitoring burden.

stem: You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 79-year-old non-Aboriginal woman with a 6-week history of anhedonia, early morning waking, 4 kg weight loss and pervasive low mood since the death of her husband. Her past medical history includes well-controlled type 2 diabetes, atrial fibrillation on apixaban and stage 3 chronic kidney disease (eGFR 42 mL/min/1.73 m2). She lives alone, has good social supports through her church and has no current suicidal ideation. Her GDS-15 score is 11/15. There is no cognitive impairment on MoCA.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.6 °C, HR 72 irregularly irregular, RR 14, SpO2 98% room air, BP 132/78 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Tearful, psychomotor slowing, intact insight, no thought disorder, no psychotic features, GCS 15, MoCA 28/30
data_table.Investigations: Na 136 K 4.4 urea 6.8 creatinine 122 micromol/L eGFR 42, ALT 24 albumin 38 g/L, HbA1c 7.0%, TSH 2.4 mU/L, ECG sinus rhythm with QTc 460 ms, FBC within reference ranges

lead_in: Which antidepressant is the most appropriate first-line option?

options.text: Amitriptyline 25 mg nocte titrated to 75 mg over 4 weeks because tricyclic antidepressants have a long evidence base in older adults with biological depression features including early morning waking and significant weight loss
options.rationale: Tricyclics are avoided in older adults because of anticholinergic, cardiac and falls risk; they appear on the Beers list and STOPP/START criteria as potentially inappropriate. (Source: AGS Beers Criteria)

options.text: Sertraline 25 mg daily, titrating to 50 mg after 1 week with monitoring of serum sodium at 2 and 4 weeks, sleep and appetite, and review for response at 4 to 6 weeks before considering further dose adjustment
options.rationale: Sertraline is a first-line SSRI in older adults: no significant interaction with apixaban for bleeding (lower compared with paroxetine and fluoxetine), low anticholinergic burden, dose adjustment not required for moderate CKD. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Mirtazapine 30 mg nocte targeting appetite stimulation, weight gain and sleep restoration in geriatric depression with prominent vegetative features and minimal pharmacokinetic interaction with currently prescribed apixaban therapy at this stage
options.rationale: Mirtazapine is a reasonable second-line in older adults but is not preferred over sertraline as first-line; first-line remains SSRI per Australian guidance. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Citalopram 20 mg daily titrated to 40 mg over 2 weeks for fastest response with regular ECG monitoring to track QTc changes during dose increases over the next 6 weeks of antidepressant initiation and titration
options.rationale: Citalopram is restricted to 20 mg in adults over 65 due to dose-dependent QTc prolongation; her baseline QTc is already 460 ms. (Source: TGA citalopram QT prolongation safety advisory)
source_refs: TGA citalopram QT prolongation safety advisory

options.text: Venlafaxine extended release 75 mg daily titrated to 150 mg over 4 weeks combining SNRI efficacy with daily blood pressure monitoring and electrolyte review at 1 and 4 weeks for any hyponatraemia or treatment-emergent hypertension
options.rationale: SNRIs are reserved for second-line in older adults due to blood pressure effects and a higher discontinuation profile; SSRI is preferred first-line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: First-line antidepressant in geriatric depression is an SSRI, with sertraline typically preferred due to its favourable interaction profile with apixaban relative to other SSRIs, low anticholinergic burden and stability in moderate renal impairment. Citalopram is dose-restricted in older adults due to QTc prolongation. Tricyclics are avoided. Mirtazapine, venlafaxine and duloxetine are second-line. Monitoring of sodium at 2 and 4 weeks detects SSRI-induced hyponatraemia.
key_points: Sertraline is preferred first-line SSRI in older adults
Citalopram limited to 20 mg in over-65s due to QTc
Avoid tricyclics in older adults (Beers list)
Mirtazapine and SNRIs are second-line
Monitor sodium at 2 and 4 weeks for SSRI hyponatraemia
explanation.pearls: SSRIs increase upper gastrointestinal bleeding risk by approximately 2-fold; in older adults on concurrent anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy consider co-prescription of a proton pump inhibitor and document the risk-benefit discussion.

sources.label: TGA citalopram QT prolongation safety advisory

subtopic_detail: Clozapine red-result neutrophil threshold and immediate action
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar on a community clozapine clinic. A 34-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has been on clozapine 400 mg daily for 18 months with full symptom remission. His weekly FBC for the first 18 weeks was normal; after the first 6 months he was on 4-weekly monitoring and his most recent FBC 5 weeks ago was a green result.

Today's FBC, taken because of 2 days of sore throat and rigors, shows WBC 2.1 x10^9/L (was 6.8 x10^9/L last month), absolute neutrophil count 1.1 x10^9/L (was 4.2 x10^9/L last month), platelets 240 x10^9/L, Hb 142 g/L. He is afebrile (37.8 °C) but well in himself with no localising signs of infection.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.8 °C, BP 120/76 mmHg, HR 88, SpO2 98% room air, RR 18
data_table.Examination: Mild pharyngeal erythema, no exudate or tonsillar swelling, no cervical adenopathy, chest clear, no other findings
data_table.Investigations: WBC 2.1, ANC 1.1, plt 240, Hb 142, CRP 18; viral PCR pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Continue clozapine at current dose, repeat FBC in 24 hours and reassure that an isolated mild drop is common with viral illness in the first 18 months of treatment and resolves spontaneously without dose change
options.rationale: ANC of 1.1 x10^9/L is an amber result requiring twice-weekly monitoring and immediate review; clinical assumption of viral cause does not exempt from protocol. (Source: RANZCP: Clozapine treatment recommendations)

options.text: Halve clozapine to 200 mg daily as a precautionary dose reduction, repeat FBC in 7 days and review at the next routine clinic appointment after the protocol-required interval has elapsed for medication adjustment review
options.rationale: Reducing dose without proper protocol does not address agranulocytosis risk; the Australian clozapine monitoring system uses specific action thresholds, not arbitrary dose halving. (Source: RANZCP: Clozapine treatment recommendations)

options.text: Cease clozapine, admit to a medical ward for haematology consultation, take blood cultures, commence broad-spectrum IV antibiotics empirically and consider granulocyte colony-stimulating factor if ANC falls below 0.5 x10^9/L
options.rationale: This is the appropriate action for a red result (ANC under 1.0 x10^9/L) or for clinical sepsis; the current result is amber and not yet red. (Source: RANZCP: Clozapine treatment recommendations)

options.text: Switch to olanzapine 20 mg daily today and arrange weekly FBC for 8 weeks to ensure recovery of haematological parameters before considering rechallenge with clozapine or alternative antipsychotic options
options.rationale: Switching antipsychotic on a single amber FBC bypasses the recommended monitoring escalation; abrupt cessation of clozapine also risks rebound psychosis. (Source: RANZCP: Clozapine treatment recommendations)

options.text: Continue clozapine at current dose, escalate to twice-weekly FBC monitoring until two consecutive green results, review for infection (chest X-ray, blood cultures if febrile or focal signs), and notify the clozapine coordinator and prescribing psychiatrist
options.rationale: ANC 1.0 to 1.5 x10^9/L (or WBC 2.0 to 3.0) is an amber result: continue clozapine, monitor twice weekly, review for infection and notify the clozapine coordinator. Stop only if ANC under 1.0 or there are clinical features of sepsis. (Source: RANZCP: Clozapine treatment recommendations)

explanation.summary: Clozapine carries a 1 to 2% lifetime risk of agranulocytosis and 3% of neutropenia. The Australian monitoring system uses traffic-light thresholds (specific thresholds may vary by manufacturer but a common scheme is): green WBC at least 3.5 and ANC at least 2.0, amber WBC 3.0 to 3.5 or ANC 1.5 to 2.0 (continue with weekly FBC) or WBC 2.0 to 3.0 or ANC 1.0 to 1.5 (continue with twice-weekly FBC, look for infection), red WBC under 2.0 or ANC under 1.0 (stop clozapine immediately, admit, haematology referral, sepsis workup, consider G-CSF). After 18 weeks monitoring drops to monthly, but any abnormal result reverts to weekly or more frequent.
key_points: Clozapine agranulocytosis risk 1-2% lifetime; highest in first 6 months
Green: WBC at least 3.5 AND ANC at least 2.0
Amber WBC 2.0-3.0 or ANC 1.0-1.5: continue, twice-weekly FBC
Red WBC under 2.0 or ANC under 1.0: STOP, admit, haematology, sepsis workup
After 18 weeks: monthly FBC, but abnormal reverts to weekly+
explanation.pearls: The lifetime clozapine rechallenge after stopping for haematological reasons is generally only permitted via the manufacturer's special-access scheme and after haematology and psychiatric MDT review; do not casually restart clozapine after a red result.

subtopic_detail: Lithium long-term monitoring schedule for renal, thyroid and calcium function
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a community mental health clinic seeing a 45-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder maintained on lithium carbonate 1000 mg nocte for 8 years. She has been euthymic on this dose throughout. Her last set of routine bloods 6 months ago showed lithium level 0.7 mmol/L (target 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L for maintenance), eGFR 78 mL/min/1.73m^2, TSH 3.4 mIU/L, corrected calcium 2.42 mmol/L.

She drinks 1.5 to 2 litres of water daily, no NSAID use, no recent dehydration, no new medications. She has no current symptoms of toxicity.

data_table.Examination: No tremor, normal reflexes, no goitre, no signs of dehydration
data_table.Investigations: Last set 6 months ago as above

lead_in: What is the recommended routine monitoring schedule for her stable maintenance lithium therapy?

options.text: Lithium level every 6 months together with UEC, TFTs and corrected calcium every 6 months; review for new medications (NSAIDs, ACE-inhibitors, diuretics) and dehydration at every appointment
options.rationale: RANZCP and AMH guidance is 6-monthly lithium level plus 6-monthly UEC, TFTs and corrected calcium in stable maintenance lithium beyond the first year. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Mood disorders (bipolar))

options.text: Lithium level monthly, UEC monthly, TFTs annually, corrected calcium annually; review for drug interactions at every visit because of the narrow therapeutic index of lithium therapy in older adults
options.rationale: Monthly lithium and UEC is unnecessarily frequent for a stable patient and not recommended; this schedule applies to initiation or dose change. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Mood disorders (bipolar))

options.text: Lithium level annually, UEC annually, TFTs annually, corrected calcium 2-yearly; counsel on hydration and to report tremor, nausea or polyuria immediately as warning signs of impending lithium toxicity
options.rationale: Annual monitoring intervals are too long; 6-monthly is the recommended minimum for stable maintenance. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Mood disorders (bipolar))

options.text: Lithium level every 3 months, UEC every 3 months, TFTs every 6 months, corrected calcium annually; review medication interactions, dehydration risk and lithium toxicity signs at every visit
options.rationale: Three-monthly lithium and UEC is more frequent than required for stable patients and not consistent with Australian guidance. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Mood disorders (bipolar))

options.text: Lithium level 4-weekly until 6 months from any dose change then 6-monthly thereafter, TFTs and UEC only if clinically symptomatic, corrected calcium not routinely required for long-term lithium
options.rationale: Routine TFTs, UEC and corrected calcium are required, not only if symptomatic, because hypothyroidism and hyperparathyroidism can be insidious. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Mood disorders (bipolar))

explanation.summary: Long-term lithium therapy requires monitoring for therapeutic level (narrow therapeutic index 0.4 to 1.0 mmol/L), nephrotoxicity (chronic interstitial nephritis, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus), hypothyroidism (around 10 to 20% over years), and hyperparathyroidism with hypercalcaemia. The recommended monitoring for stable maintenance therapy is 6-monthly lithium level, UEC, TFTs and corrected calcium. Initiation or dose change triggers more frequent monitoring (5 to 7 days after dose change). Drug interactions to flag are NSAIDs, ACE-inhibitors, ARBs, thiazides (all raise lithium), and dehydration (volume contraction raises lithium). Levels are measured 12 hours post-dose (trough).
key_points: Stable maintenance lithium: 6-monthly level, UEC, TFTs, corrected calcium
Therapeutic range: 0.6-0.8 maintenance, 0.8-1.0 acute
Level taken 12 hours post-dose (trough)
Watch interactions: NSAIDs, ACEI/ARBs, thiazides all raise lithium
Long-term risks: CKD, hypothyroidism, hyperparathyroidism, nephrogenic DI
explanation.pearls: If a patient on chronic lithium presents with polyuria and polydipsia, do not assume diabetes mellitus; a urine osmolality below serum osmolality despite hyperosmolar plasma confirms nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and may persist after lithium cessation.

subtopic_detail: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose ECG criteria for sodium bicarbonate
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar managing a 28-year-old woman brought in by ambulance 90 minutes after a witnessed ingestion of around 2 grams of dosulepin tablets with vodka. She is drowsy but rousable to voice, agitated when stimulated. Her partner reports she took the tablets after an argument and a long history of depression. Initial GCS 13, BP 92/58 mmHg, HR 128, T 36.6 °C, SpO2 95% room air.

The ECG just performed shows sinus tachycardia at 128 bpm, QRS duration 142 ms with a prominent R wave in aVR of 5 mm and a deep S wave in lead I.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 92/58 mmHg, HR 128, RR 22, SpO2 95%, T 36.6 °C, GCS 13
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, agitated on stimulation, dry mucous membranes, dilated pupils 6 mm reactive, no focal neurology, no seizure activity
data_table.Investigations: ECG: sinus tachycardia 128, QRS 142 ms, R in aVR 5 mm; VBG pH 7.32, pCO2 41, HCO3 21; Na 138, K 3.6; paracetamol level pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Administer activated charcoal 50 g via nasogastric tube and obtain repeat ECG and serum drug levels in 4 hours before any additional pharmacological intervention beyond standard supportive measures
options.rationale: QRS over 100 ms with hypotension and an R wave in aVR over 3 mm meets criteria for immediate sodium bicarbonate; activated charcoal alone is inadequate given the cardiac toxicity. (Source: Murray Toxicology Handbook 3rd ed)

options.text: Administer sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol (100 mL of 8.4%) IV bolus, repeat to keep QRS under 100 ms and serum pH 7.45 to 7.55, intubate for airway protection given GCS 13 and start IV crystalloid 1 L bolus
options.rationale: QRS over 100 ms, R in aVR over 3 mm, hypotension and CNS depression in TCA overdose are indications for sodium bicarbonate boluses titrated to QRS narrowing and pH 7.45-7.55, plus intubation for airway and crystalloid resuscitation. (Source: Murray Toxicology Handbook 3rd ed)

options.text: Commence IV metoprolol 5 mg slow bolus to control the tachycardia and reduce myocardial oxygen demand, repeat ECG in 30 minutes and titrate further beta-blockade based on heart rate response
options.rationale: Beta-blockade in TCA overdose worsens hypotension; tachycardia is compensatory for vasodilation and direct cardiac toxicity. (Source: Murray Toxicology Handbook 3rd ed)

options.text: Administer flumazenil 0.2 mg IV titrated to GCS over 15 and avoid sodium bicarbonate unless clearly seizing because rapid alkalinisation may precipitate cardiac arrhythmia in TCA toxicity
options.rationale: Flumazenil is contraindicated in mixed or unknown overdoses (precipitates seizures); rapid alkalinisation is the indicated treatment, not a hazard. (Source: Murray Toxicology Handbook 3rd ed)

options.text: Administer IV magnesium sulfate 2 g over 10 minutes to suppress polymorphic ventricular ectopy and reserve sodium bicarbonate for QRS over 160 ms or established ventricular tachycardia
options.rationale: Sodium bicarbonate is indicated at QRS over 100 ms, not over 160 ms; magnesium alone does not address sodium channel blockade. (Source: Murray Toxicology Handbook 3rd ed)

explanation.summary: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose presents with anticholinergic features, CNS depression, cardiovascular toxicity (sodium channel blockade) and seizures. ECG markers of significant toxicity include QRS over 100 ms (sensitivity ~80%), R wave in aVR over 3 mm, terminal R/S ratio in aVR over 0.7, and rightward axis. Sodium bicarbonate boluses (1 to 2 mmol/kg, often 100 mmol in adults) are indicated for QRS over 100 ms, hypotension, ventricular arrhythmia or seizures. Target pH 7.45 to 7.55. Intubation and hyperventilation aid alkalinisation. IV lipid emulsion and ECMO are last-line. Activated charcoal only if airway secured and within 1 to 2 hours of ingestion.
key_points: TCA toxicity ECG: QRS over 100 ms, R in aVR over 3 mm
Sodium bicarbonate: 1-2 mmol/kg bolus, target pH 7.45-7.55
Intubate for GCS under 9 or for hyperventilation to aid alkalinisation
Avoid: flumazenil, beta-blockers, class Ia/Ic antiarrhythmics, physostigmine
Refractory: lipid emulsion, ECMO support
explanation.pearls: Apparent benzodiazepine-responsive seizures in TCA overdose still trigger urgent sodium bicarbonate because the underlying mechanism is sodium channel blockade; once a TCA seizes the patient is at imminent risk of cardiac arrest from the same channel block.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists Toxicology Network

subtopic_detail: Lorazepam challenge for diagnosis and treatment of catatonia
stem:
You are the consultation-liaison psychiatry registrar called to the medical ward to see a 22-year-old woman with a recent first episode of psychotic depression on the psychiatric unit who was transferred to medicine 36 hours ago for poor oral intake. She has eaten almost nothing and drunk very little for 5 days. The medical team are concerned she may have an organic encephalopathy.

On examination she shows marked psychomotor retardation, will not respond to verbal commands, has waxy flexibility with maintenance of posed positions for over a minute, intermittent grimacing, mutism with occasional brief echolalia and posturing of the right arm. T 37.1 °C, BP 118/74 mmHg, HR 92. Bloods show no infection or metabolic cause; CT head is unremarkable. CK is 290 U/L.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.1 °C, BP 118/74 mmHg, HR 92, RR 16, SpO2 98%, GCS reported as 14
data_table.Examination: Waxy flexibility, mutism, posturing, grimacing, echolalia, Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale 18
data_table.Investigations: Bloods unremarkable, CK 290, CT head unremarkable, EEG pending, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence olanzapine 10 mg orally daily and review for response after 72 hours given that catatonia in psychotic depression usually resolves with effective antipsychotic monotherapy at adequate doses
options.rationale: Antipsychotics can worsen catatonia and may precipitate neuroleptic malignant syndrome; benzodiazepines (lorazepam challenge) are first-line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Initiate enteral feeding via nasogastric tube to address nutritional compromise from 5 days of minimal intake, monitor electrolytes daily for refeeding syndrome and delay specific catatonia treatment until oral intake is restored
options.rationale: Nutritional support is appropriate but should not delay catatonia-specific treatment; the catatonia itself is reversible with lorazepam in most cases and treating it will restore oral intake. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Refer for empirical immunotherapy with high-dose methylprednisolone 1 g IV daily for 5 days and consider plasma exchange given the possibility of NMDA receptor encephalitis presenting with catatonia and mutism
options.rationale: Autoimmune encephalitis is a consideration but lorazepam challenge is the recommended next step and gives both diagnostic and therapeutic information rapidly. NMDAR antibodies, EEG and LP are part of workup. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Administer lorazepam 1 to 2 mg IV (lorazepam challenge), observe over 10 to 15 minutes for partial or complete remission of catatonia (around 50% rate), then commence scheduled lorazepam 2 mg three times daily and refer for ECT if no response within 48 to 72 hours
options.rationale: Lorazepam challenge is the standard initial step for suspected catatonia; partial improvement supports the diagnosis and informs ongoing scheduled lorazepam. ECT is indicated if no response in 48-72 hours or for malignant catatonia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Continue current management without specific pharmacotherapy and arrange daily Bush-Francis Rating Scale assessment, planning ECT only if catatonia persists beyond 14 days and not responding to supportive care
options.rationale: Withholding pharmacotherapy delays both diagnosis and treatment; lorazepam challenge is recommended on the day of presentation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a treatable syndrome with motor, behavioural and autonomic features. Recognition relies on the Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale or DSM criteria (at least 3 of mutism, immobility, posturing, waxy flexibility, negativism, echolalia, echopraxia, mannerisms, stereotypy, grimacing, agitation, mutism). The lorazepam challenge (1-2 mg IV or sublingual) achieves partial or complete response in about 50% within 10 minutes; this both confirms the diagnosis and is the start of treatment. Scheduled lorazepam 2 mg three times daily is continued. ECT is highly effective and is recommended if there is no response in 48-72 hours, for malignant catatonia (autonomic instability, hyperthermia), or for life-threatening features. Avoid antipsychotics until catatonia resolves due to NMS risk.
key_points: Diagnosis: 3+ of mutism, immobility, posturing, waxy flexibility, echolalia (DSM)
Lorazepam 1-2 mg IV challenge: 50% partial response within 10 minutes
Scheduled lorazepam 2 mg TDS as ongoing first-line
ECT if no response in 48-72 hours or for malignant catatonia
Avoid antipsychotics until catatonia resolves (NMS risk)
explanation.pearls: Malignant catatonia (hyperthermia, autonomic instability, rhabdomyolysis) clinically overlaps with NMS and serotonin syndrome; in either picture, withhold antipsychotics, give benzodiazepines, and consider urgent ECT if there is no rapid improvement.

sources.label: Sienaert et al. A clinical review of catatonia

subtopic_detail: Adult ADHD diagnosis confirmation pathway and driving notification under Austroads
stem:
You are the GP registrar reviewing a 28-year-old woman who self-presented requesting assessment for adult ADHD after seeing content online. She describes lifelong inattention, distractibility and impulsivity that she now believes contributed to her difficulties at school and her current poor work performance at her professional services firm. She reports six or more inattentive symptoms (loses focus mid-task, forgets appointments, struggles to start tasks) and four hyperactive-impulsive symptoms with onset in primary school.

Her teachers' reports document poor concentration from age 8. She has no current substance use, no current depression or anxiety meeting criteria, and no medical comorbidities. She holds an unrestricted Australian car licence and drives daily to work.

data_table.Examination: Normal physical exam, no cardiovascular abnormality
data_table.Investigations: Hospital ECG normal; thyroid function normal; iron studies normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence a trial of methylphenidate immediate-release 10 mg twice daily and review response at 4 weeks to assess symptom improvement before referring to a psychiatrist for formal diagnosis and ongoing prescribing
options.rationale: GPs cannot initiate stimulants in adult ADHD in most Australian states; an authority psychiatrist (or in some states paediatrician) must confirm the diagnosis and initiate stimulant therapy under Schedule 8 authority. (Source: Australian evidence-based clinical practice guideline for ADHD (AADPA))
source_refs: Australian evidence-based clinical practice guideline for ADHD (AADPA)

options.text: Reassure her that adult-onset ADHD is uncommon and that her symptoms are more likely to reflect anxiety or burnout; provide CBT referral and reassess in 6 months without specific ADHD pathway investigation
options.rationale: She describes longstanding childhood-onset symptoms documented by teachers, not adult-onset, and meets symptom thresholds; CBT alone without considering ADHD misses the diagnosis. (Source: Australian evidence-based clinical practice guideline for ADHD (AADPA))
source_refs: Australian evidence-based clinical practice guideline for ADHD (AADPA)

options.text: Commence atomoxetine 40 mg daily titrated to 80 mg as a non-stimulant ADHD pharmacotherapy that does not require psychiatrist authority and can be initiated in GP practice for clear adult ADHD presentations
options.rationale: Atomoxetine still requires diagnostic confirmation before initiation; AADPA recommends formal diagnosis through a specialist with structured assessment, not GP commencement on screening features. (Source: Australian evidence-based clinical practice guideline for ADHD (AADPA))
source_refs: Australian evidence-based clinical practice guideline for ADHD (AADPA)

options.text: Order EEG, MRI brain and overnight polysomnography in primary care to exclude differential diagnoses including absence seizures, structural intracranial lesion and obstructive sleep apnoea before any referral for ADHD assessment
options.rationale: Routine EEG, MRI and polysomnography are not indicated unless specific clinical features suggest these diagnoses; this delays appropriate ADHD pathway. (Source: Australian evidence-based clinical practice guideline for ADHD (AADPA))
source_refs: Australian evidence-based clinical practice guideline for ADHD (AADPA)

options.text: Refer her to a psychiatrist for diagnostic confirmation by structured interview, screen with a validated adult ADHD tool (DIVA-5 or ASRS-v1.1), assess comorbidity, and counsel on the Austroads requirement to disclose untreated symptomatic ADHD if it impairs safe driving
options.rationale: AADPA recommends specialist diagnostic confirmation with validated tools (DIVA-5, ASRS), comorbidity assessment, and driver-licensing implications under Austroads should be discussed where symptoms could affect driving. (Source: Australian evidence-based clinical practice guideline for ADHD (AADPA))
source_refs: Australian evidence-based clinical practice guideline for ADHD (AADPA)

explanation.summary: Adult ADHD requires symptoms onset before age 12 (DSM-5), persistence into adulthood, functional impairment in two or more settings, and not better explained by another condition. The AADPA guideline (2022) is the current Australian standard. Diagnosis is by specialist (psychiatrist) using structured interview such as DIVA-5 plus screening tools (ASRS-v1.1). Stimulant initiation requires Schedule 8 authority; ongoing prescribing can be shared-care with GPs in some states. Atomoxetine, guanfacine and bupropion are non-stimulant options. Austroads requires disclosure when symptoms (with or without treatment) might affect safe driving; most well-controlled adults can hold an unconditional licence.
key_points: DSM-5 ADHD: childhood onset (under 12), persistent, impairing, 2+ settings
Specialist diagnosis with DIVA-5 or ASRS-v1.1
Stimulants are Schedule 8: authority psychiatrist (or paeds) initiates
Non-stimulants: atomoxetine, guanfacine, bupropion
Austroads: disclose if symptoms affect driving; conditional licence possible
explanation.pearls: Adult ADHD presentations in women are commonly missed because hyperactivity manifests as internal restlessness and inattention dominates; longstanding sense of underperformance, chronic disorganisation and burnout out of proportion to load is a soft red flag to screen formally rather than label as anxiety.

sources.label: Australian evidence-based clinical practice guideline for ADHD (AADPA)

subtopic_detail: Varenicline versus NRT versus bupropion choice in post-myocardial infarction smoker
stem:
You are the GP registrar reviewing a 56-year-old man 8 weeks after an inferior NSTEMI treated with primary PCI to the right coronary artery. He smokes 25 cigarettes daily and has been on aspirin, ticagrelor, atorvastatin, ramipril and metoprolol since discharge. He started smoking at 16 and has had 3 prior cessation attempts using cold turkey alone, each relapsing within 3 weeks.

His mood is stable and he has no history of seizures, depression or self-harm. He has no renal impairment. He scores 8 on the Fagerstrom test for nicotine dependence (high). He wants to quit and asks what works best for him given his recent heart attack.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/76 mmHg, HR 64, BMI 28, SpO2 98%, expired CO 28 ppm
data_table.Examination: Healthy male, no cardiac signs of decompensation, no neurological abnormality
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs normal; recent echocardiogram LVEF 50%; HbA1c 5.8%

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy for smoking cessation?

options.text: Prescribe nicotine inhalator alone titrated to cravings, suggest he sets a quit date 2 weeks from now and provide brief advice plus a self-help quit booklet for behavioural support over the next 12 weeks
options.rationale: Single-form NRT is less effective than combination NRT or varenicline; given high dependence (Fagerstrom 8) a more effective regimen should be offered. (Source: RACGP: Supporting smoking cessation guide)

options.text: Defer pharmacotherapy until 6 months post-MI because both varenicline and bupropion have been associated with neuropsychiatric and cardiovascular adverse events in the immediate post-infarct period and only NRT is appropriate now
options.rationale: Varenicline is safe and effective in stable post-MI patients beyond 2 weeks; deferral until 6 months loses a key teachable moment. (Source: RACGP: Supporting smoking cessation guide)

options.text: Commence varenicline 0.5 mg daily for 3 days, then 0.5 mg twice daily for 4 days, then 1 mg twice daily from day 8 for 12 weeks with quit date at day 8 to 14 and Quitline behavioural support throughout therapy
options.rationale: Varenicline has the highest evidence for sustained 6-month abstinence; the EAGLES trial confirmed cardiac and neuropsychiatric safety. Standard 12-week course with quit date at day 8-14 plus Quitline. (Source: RACGP: Supporting smoking cessation guide)

options.text: Prescribe bupropion 150 mg daily for 3 days then 150 mg twice daily for 12 weeks with quit date at day 8 to 14 and Quitline support, choosing bupropion because it has the best efficacy and safety profile in post-MI patients
options.rationale: Bupropion is effective but slightly less so than varenicline; it is contraindicated in seizure disorder, eating disorders and severe hepatic impairment. Varenicline has stronger evidence post-MI. (Source: RACGP: Supporting smoking cessation guide)

options.text: Prescribe combination NRT (21 mg/24h patch plus 4 mg gum as needed) with no behavioural support given his prior failed attempts and ask him to return only if cessation fails at 4 weeks for escalation of therapy
options.rationale: Combination NRT is a reasonable second choice but is less effective than varenicline and behavioural support (Quitline) significantly increases abstinence; not offering it is suboptimal. (Source: RACGP: Supporting smoking cessation guide)

explanation.summary: Combined behavioural support (Quitline) plus pharmacotherapy is the most effective approach. Varenicline (TGA-approved, 12-week course, quit date at day 8-14) has the highest 6-month abstinence rates per EAGLES and Cochrane network meta-analyses. Combination NRT (patch plus oral) is similar in efficacy. Bupropion is effective but contraindicated in seizure disorder, eating disorders and severe hepatic impairment. EAGLES confirmed varenicline and bupropion neuropsychiatric and cardiovascular safety in patients with and without mental health conditions. Post-MI is a high-leverage teachable moment; cessation halves 5-year mortality. Pregnant women are typically offered NRT (oral forms preferred), and adolescents NRT only.
key_points: First-line: varenicline OR combination NRT (patch + oral)
Bupropion: contraindicated in seizures, EDs, severe hepatic disease
EAGLES (2016): varenicline cardiovascular and neuropsychiatric safety confirmed
Behavioural support: Quitline 13 78 48 adds substantially to pharmacotherapy
Pregnancy: NRT (oral preferred); adolescents NRT only
explanation.pearls: Schedule the quit date 8 to 14 days after starting varenicline so the patient is steroid-stated on the medication; ramping the dose first reduces nausea, which is the main reason for early discontinuation.

sources.label: EAGLES trial: Anthenelli et al. Lancet 2016

subtopic_detail: Acute severe behavioural disturbance pharmacological choice in young adult male
stem: You are the emergency department registrar called to the resuscitation bay where a 25-year-old man with first-presentation psychosis is acutely agitated, threatening staff and other patients, attempting to leave despite an Inpatient Treatment Order. De-escalation by an experienced nurse and security has failed over 15 minutes. He is not currently taking any psychotropic medication and has no documented allergies. Collateral suggests no significant alcohol or substance use in the past 24 hours but possible methamphetamine use 3 days ago. He weighs around 80 kg and is haemodynamically stable. The duty psychiatrist has authorised chemical restraint.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 142/88 mmHg, HR 118, T 37.0 °C, RR 22, SpO2 99% room air, ECG sinus tachycardia QTc 430 ms
data_table.Examination: Pacing, fists clenched, verbally threatening, no signs of intoxication, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 5.2 mmol/L, urine drug screen pending, FBC and UEC pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate single first-dose chemical restraint?

options.text: Administer droperidol 10 mg intramuscularly, monitor continuous cardiac monitoring and SpO2, repeat 10 mg IM at 15 minutes if not settled, and review for further treatment after 30 minutes from the second dose
options.rationale: NSW Health rapid tranquillisation guidance for acute severe behavioural disturbance in adults endorses droperidol 10 mg IM as a first-line option, with repeat at 15 minutes and standard monitoring. (Source: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance in emergency departments)
source_refs: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance in emergency departments

options.text: Administer haloperidol 5 mg with promethazine 25 mg IM together as a combined sedation regimen, monitor for extrapyramidal effects and lower the threshold for ECG monitoring given the QT interval
options.rationale: Haloperidol-promethazine combination is no longer first-line in Australian ED rapid tranquillisation; droperidol IM (or olanzapine IM, midazolam IM in some protocols) is preferred. (Source: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance in emergency departments)
source_refs: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance in emergency departments

options.text: Administer midazolam 10 mg IM as a single agent without monitoring beyond intermittent vitals given that benzodiazepine monotherapy avoids the cardiac and extrapyramidal risks of antipsychotic chemical restraint
options.rationale: Midazolam IM monotherapy is an option in protocols but mandates continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring (respiratory depression risk); intermittent vitals are inadequate. (Source: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance in emergency departments)
source_refs: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance in emergency departments

options.text: Administer ketamine 4 mg/kg intramuscularly under anaesthetic supervision as the first-line agent for severe behavioural disturbance in a stimulant-related agitation given recent methamphetamine use
options.rationale: Ketamine is a tertiary option (failed other agents) and is given by experienced clinicians with airway capability; not first-line in standard ED protocols. (Source: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance in emergency departments)
source_refs: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance in emergency departments

options.text: Offer oral olanzapine wafer 20 mg with a glass of water and observe for cooperation before escalating to any parenteral medication, regardless of the failed de-escalation by experienced staff already attempted
options.rationale: Oral medication assumes cooperation that has clearly already failed; parenteral chemical restraint is required for documented refractory severe behavioural disturbance. (Source: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance in emergency departments)
source_refs: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance in emergency departments

explanation.summary: Australian ED protocols (NSW Health, Victorian DHHS) for acute severe behavioural disturbance prioritise de-escalation first. If failed, first-line parenteral options include droperidol 10 mg IM (repeat at 15 min, max 20 mg), olanzapine IM 10 mg or midazolam IM 5 to 10 mg, with continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring. Avoid combinations of benzodiazepines and antipsychotics where possible due to additive respiratory depression. Ketamine 4 to 5 mg/kg IM is a third-line option with airway-capable clinician present. Document indication, dose, monitoring and review interval. Apply restraint principles consistent with the local Mental Health Act.
key_points: De-escalation first (15 min); chemical restraint if failed
First-line IM: droperidol 10 mg (repeat at 15 min) OR olanzapine 10 mg OR midazolam 5-10 mg
Continuous SpO2 and cardiac monitoring required post-dose
Avoid routine combination of benzodiazepine + antipsychotic
Ketamine 4-5 mg/kg IM is tertiary option with airway support
explanation.pearls: Document the failure of de-escalation, the specific indication, the consent or legal authority (e.g. Mental Health Act ITO), the dose, route and time, and the planned review at 15 minutes; the audit trail matters as much as the choice of agent in subsequent medico-legal review.

sources.label: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance in emergency departments

subtopic_detail: First-line structured psychotherapy choice for established borderline personality disorder
stem:
You are the community mental health team registrar following up a 24-year-old woman with a 4-year history of borderline personality disorder confirmed on structured assessment 12 months ago. She has had three psychiatric admissions for self-harm and suicidal ideation in the past 2 years. She has been on sertraline 200 mg daily and quetiapine 100 mg at night for over a year with limited benefit.

Self-harm by cutting occurs around weekly. She is engaged in care, attends appointments and is keen to try therapy. She is not currently psychotic, severely depressed or in active crisis. She lives independently and has a part-time job.

data_table.Examination: Healed self-harm scars to forearms, no fresh wounds; mental state stable
data_table.Investigations: Routine bloods normal, no current intoxication

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Increase sertraline to 250 mg daily and add lithium 250 mg twice daily for emotion dysregulation and consider a long-acting injectable antipsychotic if self-harm persists at the next 3-month review
options.rationale: Pharmacotherapy is not first-line for BPD; structured psychotherapy is the recommended treatment. Polypharmacy without specific indication should be avoided. (Source: NHMRC clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder)
source_refs: NHMRC clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder

options.text: Refer for an evidence-based structured psychotherapy program (dialectical behaviour therapy or mentalisation-based therapy or schema-focused therapy) with a target of 12 months of treatment and review pharmacotherapy aiming to rationalise prescribing
options.rationale: NHMRC and RANZCP recommend evidence-based structured psychotherapies (DBT, MBT, SFT, transference-focused psychotherapy) as first-line for BPD with active rationalisation of pharmacotherapy. (Source: NHMRC clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder)
source_refs: NHMRC clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder

options.text: Plan a hospital admission for behavioural containment of self-harm with a 4 to 6 week structured ward program, ECT consideration and graded leave because community management has failed over the last 12 months
options.rationale: Long-stay psychiatric admission for BPD is generally counterproductive and not recommended; brief crisis admission only for acute risk. ECT is not indicated. (Source: NHMRC clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder)
source_refs: NHMRC clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder

options.text: Discharge to GP-led management with a written safety plan and crisis line numbers, on the basis that BPD generally responds best to non-specialist supportive care with minimal medical intervention
options.rationale: Recurrent self-harm and previous admissions indicate need for specialist structured psychotherapy, not discharge. (Source: NHMRC clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder)
source_refs: NHMRC clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder

options.text: Trial open-label naltrexone 50 mg daily and topiramate 100 mg twice daily for impulsivity and self-harm and reassess at 12 weeks before considering psychotherapy referral if symptoms persist on combination pharmacotherapy
options.rationale: Naltrexone and topiramate are not recommended as first-line for BPD; psychotherapy is first-line. (Source: NHMRC clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder)
source_refs: NHMRC clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder

explanation.summary: BPD is best managed by evidence-based structured psychotherapy programs delivered over at least 12 months: dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT, Linehan), mentalisation-based therapy (MBT, Bateman & Fonagy), schema-focused therapy (SFT, Young) or transference-focused psychotherapy (TFP, Kernberg). NHMRC guidelines recommend these as first-line over pharmacotherapy. Medications are used for specific comorbid disorders (depression, anxiety) or symptom targets (impulsivity), not for BPD as a whole; polypharmacy should be rationalised. Long-stay admissions are generally avoided; brief crisis admission only for acute risk that cannot be safely managed in community. Crisis plans and safety plans are core community components.
key_points: First-line: structured psychotherapy (DBT, MBT, SFT, TFP) 12+ months
Pharmacotherapy: comorbidity-targeted only; rationalise polypharmacy
Long-stay admission avoided; brief crisis admission for acute risk only
Safety plans and crisis lines as part of community care
Family/carer support is recommended
explanation.pearls: Stress prescribing in BPD (adding more drugs after crises) tends to accumulate sedating polypharmacy that worsens function and falls risk without changing self-harm rates; structured deprescribing in stable phases is as important as introducing therapy.

sources.label: NHMRC clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder

subtopic_detail: Anorexia nervosa long-term hypogonadism and bone mineral density management
stem:
You are the GP registrar reviewing a 22-year-old woman with anorexia nervosa restrictive subtype diagnosed at age 15. She has had two prior medical admissions for bradycardia and electrolyte derangement; her last admission was 14 months ago. She is now stable at BMI 17.2 and engaged with a community eating disorder specialist team for 18 months. Menses have been absent for 5 years; she has never tried to conceive.

Recent bloods show normal electrolytes, oestradiol low, LH and FSH low. DEXA scan from 3 months ago shows lumbar spine T-score -2.4 and femoral neck T-score -1.9.

data_table.Examination: No bradycardia symptoms, no lanugo, mild peripheral cyanosis, no fractures
data_table.Investigations: Oestradiol low, LH 1.2, FSH 1.8 (both low), TSH 1.8, prolactin 360 mIU/L, vitamin D 42 nmol/L, corrected calcium 2.30, PTH 4.2 pmol/L, urine pregnancy negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her bone health?

options.text: Commence a combined oral contraceptive pill 30 microgram ethinylestradiol/levonorgestrel as the primary treatment for low bone mineral density to provide systemic oestrogen replacement and improve T-scores over 12 months of therapy
options.rationale: COCP has not been shown to improve BMD in AN-related hypogonadism and may give false reassurance of normalised menstruation; transdermal physiological oestrogen replacement has better evidence in adolescents. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Eating disorders)

options.text: Commence alendronate 70 mg weekly as a first-line bisphosphonate for low T-score in a young woman with hypothalamic amenorrhoea regardless of nutritional restoration progress or her stated plans for future pregnancy in coming years
options.rationale: Bisphosphonates are not first-line in young women with AN due to long bone half-life and uncertainty around fetal exposure if she later conceives; weight restoration with adjunct physiological oestrogen replacement is preferred. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Eating disorders)

options.text: Refer to endocrinology for consideration of teriparatide 20 micrograms subcutaneously daily for 2 years as a bone-anabolic agent given her premenopausal age and persistent low BMD despite treatment of her primary eating disorder
options.rationale: Teriparatide is reserved for severe established osteoporosis with fragility fracture and is not first-line in young women with AN-related low BMD. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Eating disorders)

options.text: Continue to support weight restoration as the primary intervention, optimise vitamin D and calcium, consider physiological oestrogen replacement via transdermal oestradiol with cyclical progesterone if BMD does not improve or fractures occur, and repeat DEXA in 12 months
options.rationale: Weight restoration is the most effective intervention for BMD in AN; nutritional sufficiency, vitamin D and calcium optimisation, and physiological transdermal oestrogen replacement when BMD is persistently low or fractures occur are recommended adjuncts. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Eating disorders)

options.text: Commence denosumab 60 mg subcutaneously every 6 months as an antiresorptive agent because it has rapid onset compared with bisphosphonates and is not deposited in bone matrix to give long-term fetal risk
options.rationale: Denosumab is not first-line in premenopausal AN and has issues with rebound vertebral fracture risk if discontinued; not the recommended choice. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Eating disorders)

explanation.summary: AN causes hypothalamic amenorrhoea with low oestradiol, low gonadotropins and low IGF-1, plus relative hypercortisolaemia, all of which impair bone turnover. The most effective intervention for BMD is weight restoration; this should always be the primary target. Adjunct measures include optimisation of vitamin D and calcium, treatment of comorbid hypothyroidism or hyperprolactinaemia. Physiological transdermal oestradiol with cyclical progesterone has evidence for improving BMD in adolescents/young adults with persistent amenorrhoea despite weight restoration. COCP does not improve BMD. Bisphosphonates and denosumab are not first-line in premenopausal women with AN due to long-term safety in pregnancy and rebound concerns respectively. DEXA is repeated 1-2 yearly.
key_points: Primary intervention: weight restoration (highest impact on BMD)
Adjuncts: vitamin D, calcium, treat comorbid endocrinopathy
Persistent low BMD: transdermal oestradiol + cyclical progesterone (not COCP)
Avoid bisphosphonates and denosumab as first-line in premenopausal AN
DEXA every 12-24 months while underweight
explanation.pearls: Adolescents with AN can lose peak bone mass at the very age that determines lifetime fracture risk; aggressive weight restoration in the early years is the only intervention with long-term BMD benefit and the brief window before age 25 is when the gains are made.

sources.label: ANZAED clinical practice guideline for eating disorders

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing conversion (functional neurological) disorder from factitious disorder and malingering
stem:
You are the neurology registrar reviewing a 32-year-old woman in clinic with a 6-month history of intermittent left-sided weakness, episodes of unresponsiveness with eye closure and convulsive activity. MRI brain, EEG (including ictal recordings of 4 typical events), and CSF are all normal. She is not seeking financial compensation and there is no medico-legal context. On examination, the left-sided weakness shows Hoover's sign and give-way pattern; her grip strength is variable when distracted.

Her symptoms began after the death of her father from a stroke. She is distressed by the symptoms and wishes to return to work as a nurse. She does not knowingly produce symptoms and is not seeking medical attention as the primary motivator.

data_table.Examination: Hoover's sign positive on the left, give-way weakness, variable grip when distracted, normal cranial nerves, sensory exam non-anatomical distribution
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain, EEG (4 ictal recordings), CSF all normal

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Malingering, because the symptoms are inconsistent with any organic neurological process and the variability of weakness on examination indicates intentional production of symptoms for personal gain
options.rationale: Malingering requires intentional symptom production for external incentive (financial, legal, drug-seeking); there is no such incentive here. (Source: RANZCP: Somatic symptom and related disorders practice guidance)
source_refs: RANZCP: Somatic symptom and related disorders practice guidance

options.text: Factitious disorder imposed on self because the production of seizure-like events without any organic correlate on EEG suggests deliberate symptom feigning to assume the sick role rather than for any external incentive
options.rationale: Factitious disorder requires conscious symptom production with the internal motivation of assuming the sick role; this patient is distressed and wants to return to work, which is incongruous. (Source: RANZCP: Somatic symptom and related disorders practice guidance)
source_refs: RANZCP: Somatic symptom and related disorders practice guidance

options.text: Functional neurological disorder (conversion disorder) because the symptoms are not consciously produced, are inconsistent with neurological examination, have positive rule-in signs (Hoover's, variable weakness) and are associated with psychological precipitants
options.rationale: FND is diagnosed by positive rule-in signs (Hoover's, distractibility, video-EEG of typical event with normal EEG) without conscious symptom production; the patient is genuinely distressed. (Source: RANZCP: Somatic symptom and related disorders practice guidance)
source_refs: RANZCP: Somatic symptom and related disorders practice guidance

options.text: Generalised anxiety disorder with somatic symptoms because chronic worry can manifest as motor and sensory symptoms in the absence of an underlying organic neurological cause and CBT for anxiety would be first-line
options.rationale: Anxiety with somatic symptoms does not produce non-anatomical motor weakness with positive Hoover sign or non-epileptic seizures; FND is a separate, more specific diagnosis. (Source: RANZCP: Somatic symptom and related disorders practice guidance)
source_refs: RANZCP: Somatic symptom and related disorders practice guidance
