options.text: Multiple sclerosis with normal initial MRI, because MS can present with motor symptoms and atypical seizure-like episodes for years before brain lesions become radiologically apparent on standard imaging sequences
options.rationale: MS does not produce non-anatomical weakness with Hoover's sign or non-epileptic seizures with normal video-EEG; the rule-in signs identify FND positively. (Source: RANZCP: Somatic symptom and related disorders practice guidance)
source_refs: RANZCP: Somatic symptom and related disorders practice guidance

explanation.summary: Functional neurological disorder (DSM-5 conversion disorder) is a positive diagnosis made on demonstrating internal inconsistency or incongruence with recognised neurological disease using rule-in signs (Hoover's sign, hip abductor sign, tremor entrainment, video-EEG of typical seizure with normal ictal EEG). It is not a diagnosis of exclusion; relabelling "medically unexplained" symptoms as FND requires positive clinical signs. Distinguishing features from factitious disorder (conscious symptom production to assume sick role) and malingering (conscious production for external incentive) rest on intentionality and motivation. Treatment is multidisciplinary: physiotherapy, psychology (CBT or psychodynamic), patient education about the diagnosis and self-management strategies. Prognosis improves with early diagnosis and engaged treatment.
key_points: FND: positive rule-in signs (Hoover's, distractibility, normal ictal EEG)
Factitious: conscious symptom production for internal sick-role gain
Malingering: conscious production for external incentive (money, drugs, legal)
FND treatment: physiotherapy + psychology + patient education
Early diagnosis and engagement improve prognosis
explanation.pearls: Hoover's sign (involuntary extension of the affected leg when the contralateral leg is flexed against resistance) has very high specificity for functional weakness; demonstrate it to the patient and show that the muscle works, which is the start of treatment, not just diagnosis.

sources.label: RANZCP: Somatic symptom and related disorders practice guidance
Stone J. Functional neurological disorders. Practical Neurology 2016

subtopic_detail: Sodium valproate pregnancy prevention program and switch in woman of reproductive age
stem:
You are the GP registrar reviewing a 27-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder maintained on sodium valproate 1500 mg daily for 4 years. She is euthymic, currently studying full-time, in a stable relationship and not actively planning pregnancy but does not use any reliable contraception. She does not want to use combined hormonal contraception due to a family history of VTE.

She has tried lithium previously but stopped due to fine tremor and weight gain, and tried quetiapine briefly with sedation. She asks for your advice about staying on valproate.

data_table.Examination: Unremarkable, no tremor, no acne, no hirsutism
data_table.Investigations: Valproate level 540 micromol/L (therapeutic), FBC, LFTs, UEC normal, urine pregnancy negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue sodium valproate at current dose, advise her of teratogenic risks and document discussion in the medical record, and recommend she contacts you within 24 hours of any positive pregnancy test result for review
options.rationale: Continuing valproate without reliable contraception in a woman of reproductive age does not meet the TGA pregnancy prevention program requirements; alternative mood stabilisers or contraception planning is required. (Source: TGA: Sodium valproate (Epilim) pregnancy prevention program)
source_refs: TGA: Sodium valproate (Epilim) pregnancy prevention program

options.text: Switch to carbamazepine 200 mg twice daily over 4 weeks as a safer mood stabiliser option in pregnancy planning with lower teratogenic risk than sodium valproate and continue with regular review of mood symptoms during the transition period from valproate to carbamazepine over the next month
options.rationale: Carbamazepine is also teratogenic (neural tube defects, craniofacial); it is not a safer alternative for pregnancy planning. (Source: TGA: Sodium valproate (Epilim) pregnancy prevention program)
source_refs: TGA: Sodium valproate (Epilim) pregnancy prevention program

options.text: Discontinue valproate today and start lamotrigine 25 mg daily with rapid titration to 200 mg daily over 2 weeks to avoid bipolar relapse during transition and minimise the window of unprotected reproductive exposure to teratogenic valproate during the changeover period
options.rationale: Lamotrigine must be titrated slowly over at least 6 weeks to avoid Stevens-Johnson syndrome; rapid titration is unsafe and abrupt valproate cessation risks relapse. (Source: TGA: Sodium valproate (Epilim) pregnancy prevention program)
source_refs: TGA: Sodium valproate (Epilim) pregnancy prevention program

options.text: Continue valproate at her current dose but enrol her in the formal pregnancy prevention program with monthly pregnancy testing and document a risk discussion review annually; if she fails to comply with the program transition to a non-teratogenic alternative
options.rationale: Pregnancy prevention program requires highly effective contraception; this patient does not use any reliable contraception, so enrolment alone is insufficient. (Source: TGA: Sodium valproate (Epilim) pregnancy prevention program)
source_refs: TGA: Sodium valproate (Epilim) pregnancy prevention program

options.text: Counsel on teratogenic risks of valproate (around 10% major malformation, 30 to 40% neurodevelopmental delay), arrange psychiatric review to plan transition to lamotrigine or olanzapine, and recommend a long-acting reversible contraceptive such as an IUD in the interim
options.rationale: TGA pregnancy prevention program requires risk discussion, transition to non-teratogenic alternative (lamotrigine, olanzapine etc) and effective contraception. LARC (copper IUD or LNG-IUS) is appropriate given her wish to avoid CHC. (Source: TGA: Sodium valproate (Epilim) pregnancy prevention program)
source_refs: TGA: Sodium valproate (Epilim) pregnancy prevention program

explanation.summary: Sodium valproate is associated with major congenital malformation in around 10% of in-utero exposed pregnancies and neurodevelopmental delay in 30 to 40%. The TGA pregnancy prevention program (since 2023) requires that valproate is not used in women of reproductive age unless other treatments are ineffective or not tolerated, the woman is using highly effective contraception, and risks are discussed annually using a risk acknowledgement form. For bipolar disorder in women of reproductive age, lamotrigine (depression-predominant), olanzapine or quetiapine are typical alternatives. Lithium is also teratogenic (Ebstein anomaly, ~0.1% absolute risk) but has lower overall teratogenicity than valproate. Lamotrigine titration is slow (25 mg, 50 mg, 100 mg, 200 mg over weeks).
key_points: Valproate teratogenic risk: 10% major malformation, 30-40% neurodevelopmental delay
TGA PPP: only use if other Rx ineffective AND effective contraception AND annual risk form
Alternatives in reproductive-age women: lamotrigine, olanzapine, quetiapine, lithium
Lamotrigine titration: slow over 6+ weeks to avoid SJS
LARC options if avoiding CHC: copper IUD, LNG-IUS, depot implant
explanation.pearls: The risk acknowledgement form must be signed annually and at each new prescription, not just at initiation; failure to document at each renewal is the most common compliance failure flagged in TGA audits of valproate prescribing.

sources.label: TGA: Sodium valproate (Epilim) pregnancy prevention program

subtopic_detail: Schizoaffective disorder versus bipolar I with psychotic features diagnostic discrimination
stem: You are the inpatient psychiatry registrar reviewing a 32-year-old man with a 6-year illness history with recurrent psychotic episodes. Records confirm: 2017 first episode lasting 7 weeks of grandiose delusions and auditory hallucinations of God speaking to him, accompanied by elevated mood, decreased sleep, pressured speech and overspending; 2019 a 6-week depressive episode with low mood, anhedonia and suicidal ideation, during which auditory hallucinations persisted; 2022 a 4-week period of persistent persecutory delusions and auditory hallucinations with no concurrent mood symptoms (no mania, no depression). Between episodes he has had mild residual negative symptoms but no severe mood disturbance.

data_table.Examination: Mental state on admission: psychotic with ideas of reference, currently low mood and reduced sleep over 10 days
data_table.Investigations: Bloods routine; no substance use on urine screen; no organic cause identified

lead_in: Which diagnosis is most consistent with his longitudinal illness pattern?

options.text: Schizoaffective disorder bipolar type, because his illness includes mood episodes (mania, depression) with concurrent psychosis and a 4-week period of psychosis in the absence of mood symptoms during the lifetime of the illness
options.rationale: Schizoaffective disorder requires (i) concurrent mood episode with psychosis at some time, (ii) at least 2 weeks of psychosis in the absence of major mood episode during lifetime illness, (iii) mood episodes are present majority of total illness time; his pattern fits. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia and related disorders

options.text: Bipolar I disorder with mood-congruent psychotic features, because the psychosis is part of his mood episodes (mania and depression) and the periods of inter-episode psychosis are unrelated negative symptoms rather than schizoaffective psychosis
options.rationale: Bipolar I with psychotic features requires psychosis only during mood episodes; the documented 4 weeks of pure psychosis without mood symptoms excludes pure bipolar with psychotic features. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia and related disorders

options.text: Schizophrenia with comorbid mood episodes, because his persistent residual negative symptoms between episodes are more consistent with schizophrenia and the mood episodes are reactive demoralisation rather than primary affective illness
options.rationale: Schizophrenia requires mood symptoms to be present only briefly during total illness; this patient has substantial mood episodes (mania and depression) constituting a major part of his course. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia and related disorders

options.text: Major depressive disorder with mood-incongruent psychotic features, because his current presentation includes low mood and the persistent delusions and hallucinations represent treatment-resistant psychotic depression following inadequate antidepressant therapy
options.rationale: MDD with psychotic features does not account for the prior manic episode in 2017; the diagnosis must encompass the entire illness course. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia and related disorders

options.text: Substance-induced psychotic and mood disorder because chronic substance use produces both psychotic and mood phenomena and the patient's current presentation likely represents withdrawal-related affective and psychotic symptoms
options.rationale: No substance use is documented on urine screen and history is not consistent; the diagnosis must be primary. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia and related disorders

explanation.summary: Schizoaffective disorder DSM-5 criteria require: (A) uninterrupted illness with major mood episode (depressive or manic) concurrent with active phase psychotic symptoms, (B) delusions or hallucinations for 2 or more weeks in the absence of major mood episode during the lifetime of the illness, (C) mood episodes present for majority of total active and residual illness, and (D) not attributable to substance or medical condition. Schizoaffective bipolar type includes manic episodes; depressive type only depressive. Treatment combines antipsychotic plus mood stabiliser or antidepressant as appropriate. Distinguishing from bipolar with psychotic features hinges on criterion B (mood-independent psychosis), and from schizophrenia hinges on criterion C (substantial mood component).
key_points: Schizoaffective DSM-5: mood + psychosis concurrent, plus 2+ weeks pure psychosis lifetime
Mood episodes must be majority of total illness time (active + residual)
Type: bipolar type (mania) vs depressive type
Bipolar I with psychosis: psychosis only during mood episodes
Schizophrenia: mood symptoms brief over total course
explanation.pearls: Documenting the exact temporal relationship between mood and psychotic symptoms over years is essential; without longitudinal records, distinguishing schizoaffective from bipolar with psychotic features is often impossible in cross-section.

sources.label: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia and related disorders

subtopic_detail: First-episode schizophrenia antipsychotic selection and monitoring
stem: You are the psychiatry registrar in an early-psychosis service reviewing a 21-year-old engineering student who was admitted involuntarily 2 weeks ago after a first-episode psychosis with 6 months of persecutory delusions and auditory hallucinations. He has fully cooperated with treatment, has no medical comorbidities and his BMI is 24. He has gained 1 kg in two weeks and his symptoms are partially improved on oral olanzapine 10 mg nocte. He smokes 10 cigarettes per day and has no family history of diabetes or cardiac disease.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72, HR 84, BMI 24, weight 76 kg (up from 75)
data_table.Examination: Affect blunted but engaged, no EPS, no abnormal involuntary movements, normal cardiovascular and neurological examination
data_table.Investigations: Baseline ECG QTc 412 ms, FBC, UEC, LFTs normal, fasting lipids: total cholesterol 4.6, LDL 2.8, fasting glucose 5.0 mmol/L, HbA1c 5.4%, prolactin 410 mIU/L (slightly elevated)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue oral olanzapine at the current dose, provide brief smoking cessation advice with nicotine replacement therapy and arrange baseline-plus-3-monthly metabolic monitoring with weight, waist circumference, fasting lipids and glucose for at least the first year of treatment
options.rationale: RANZCP and Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic recommend continuing the initial effective antipsychotic with structured metabolic monitoring (weight monthly for 3 months then 3-monthly, lipids and glucose at baseline, 3 months and 12 months) for all first-episode patients on second-generation agents. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia

options.text: Switch immediately to first-generation haloperidol 5 mg daily because second-generation antipsychotics in young adult males consistently produce greater metabolic and prolactin morbidity than first-generation agents at equivalent symptomatic doses
options.rationale: FGAs cause more EPS and tardive dyskinesia and similar long-term metabolic concerns; switching after a partial response in 2 weeks is premature. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia

options.text: Add a mood stabiliser such as sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily as augmentation for partial response at 2 weeks because combination therapy from the outset shortens time to remission in first-episode schizophrenia and reduces relapse risk
options.rationale: Valproate is not first-line augmentation for first-episode schizophrenia and adds teratogenicity, weight gain and hepatotoxicity risks without clear benefit at 2 weeks. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia

options.text: Discontinue antipsychotic medication entirely and commence weekly cognitive behavioural therapy alone because psychological therapy is now first-line in first-episode psychosis if symptoms partially improve during the initial 2-week admission period
options.rationale: CBT for psychosis is an adjunct to antipsychotic medication, not a substitute; discontinuation risks rapid relapse in first-episode schizophrenia. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia

options.text: Start a long-acting injectable depot antipsychotic such as paliperidone palmitate 150 mg deep IM at first dose, omit further oral antipsychotic and discharge home without further specialist follow up because depot reduces relapse risk most effectively
options.rationale: LAI is appropriate in selected first-episode patients with adherence concerns, but is given alongside specialist multidisciplinary follow up, not discharge without it. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia

explanation.summary: First-episode schizophrenia is treated with a second-generation antipsychotic at the lowest effective dose, allowed at least 4 to 6 weeks to assess full response. Olanzapine, risperidone, aripiprazole and amisulpride are common first-line choices; clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant illness after two failed trials. Baseline workup includes ECG (QTc), FBC, UEC, LFTs, fasting lipids, glucose, prolactin and weight/waist. RANZCP monitoring is weekly weight for 6 weeks, lipids and glucose at baseline, 3 months and 12 months, prolactin if symptomatic. Smoking cessation, exercise, dietitian and metabolic syndrome prevention are integral. CBT for psychosis, family therapy and supported employment are added.
key_points: SGA at lowest effective dose; allow 4-6 weeks for full effect
Baseline: ECG (QTc), FBC, UEC, LFTs, lipids, glucose, prolactin, weight
Monitor weight weekly to 6 weeks then 3-monthly
Lipids and glucose at baseline, 3 months, 12 months
Clozapine after two failed trials
explanation.pearls: Olanzapine has the largest weight gain and metabolic effect of common SGAs; aripiprazole is most weight-neutral but more activating. Prolactin elevation is greatest with risperidone and amisulpride.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia

subtopic_detail: Serotonin syndrome from SSRI plus tramadol
stem: You are the consult-liaison psychiatry registrar called by the emergency department about a 48-year-old man on sertraline 200 mg daily for major depressive disorder who attended his general practitioner two days ago for low back pain and was prescribed tramadol 50 mg three times daily. Today he presents with tremor, agitation, sweating, dilated pupils and inducible ankle clonus that is more marked on the right. His vital signs show hyperthermia at 38.6 degrees C, tachycardia and hypertension. He has had no recent alcohol or illicit drug use.

data_table.Examination: Tremor, hyperreflexia greater in lower limbs, inducible ankle clonus, dilated pupils, diaphoretic, agitated and restless, mild abdominal hyperactive bowel sounds
data_table.Investigations: FBC normal, CK 320 U/L, UEC normal, ECG sinus tachycardia QTc 420 ms, toxicology screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Commence intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g infusion and oral propranolol 40 mg three times daily as first-line therapy for serotonin syndrome and continue both serotonergic agents at reduced doses with ongoing twice-daily monitoring of vital signs
options.rationale: Magnesium and beta-blockers are not first-line; cessation of serotonergic agents and benzodiazepines are the foundation of treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology - Serotonin syndrome)

options.text: Continue both medications because tramadol plus an SSRI does not produce clinically significant serotonin syndrome at standard doses and treat the autonomic features with intravenous beta blocker and oral paracetamol for the hyperthermia
options.rationale: Tramadol is a known serotonergic agent and combination with high-dose SSRI causes serotonin syndrome; treating symptoms without ceasing the precipitants risks progression. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology - Serotonin syndrome)

options.text: Treat as neuroleptic malignant syndrome with intravenous dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg and oral bromocriptine 2.5 mg every 8 hours and arrange transfer to intensive care because the autonomic instability is identical to NMS in clinical presentation
options.rationale: NMS is associated with antipsychotic dopamine antagonism, with lead-pipe rigidity not the lower-limb-predominant clonus, hyperreflexia and dilated pupils of serotonin syndrome. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology - Serotonin syndrome)

options.text: Cease sertraline and tramadol immediately, provide intravenous benzodiazepine sedation with diazepam or midazolam, active cooling and supportive intravenous fluids, and consider oral cyproheptadine 12 mg as a serotonin antagonist if symptoms persist
options.rationale: Serotonin syndrome management is cessation of all serotonergic agents, benzodiazepine sedation for agitation, active cooling, IV hydration; cyproheptadine 12 mg orally as a 5-HT2A antagonist is added for moderate to severe cases per Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology - Serotonin syndrome)

options.text: Administer single dose intravenous physostigmine 1 mg over 5 minutes as the specific cholinergic antidote for serotonin syndrome and continue intravenous hydration only with no further pharmacological cessation or substitution of any kind
options.rationale: Physostigmine is the antidote for anticholinergic toxicity, not serotonin syndrome; the dilated pupils, sweating and hyperactive bowels here are pro-serotonergic. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology - Serotonin syndrome)

explanation.summary: Serotonin syndrome is a clinical diagnosis using the Hunter Criteria: serotonergic agent plus one of spontaneous clonus, inducible clonus with agitation or diaphoresis, ocular clonus, tremor and hyperreflexia, or hypertonia with temperature above 38 and either ocular or inducible clonus. Lower-limb-predominant clonus and hyperreflexia distinguish it from neuroleptic malignant syndrome (lead-pipe rigidity). Management is cessation of all serotonergic agents, benzodiazepine sedation, active cooling, IV hydration, and cyproheptadine 12 mg PO load then 2 mg every 2 hours for moderate to severe cases (max 32 mg/day). ICU and paralysis with intubation are required for hyperthermia over 41.1 degrees C.
key_points: Hunter Criteria: serotonergic agent + characteristic neuromuscular signs
Clue: clonus and hyperreflexia greater in lower limbs
Cease all serotonergic agents (SSRIs, SNRIs, tramadol, linezolid, MAOIs)
Benzodiazepines first-line for agitation and autonomic features
Cyproheptadine 12 mg PO load, 2 mg q2h for moderate to severe
explanation.pearls: Common SSRI plus tramadol is a high-yield combination at GP-prescribing interfaces; education at the SSRI prescription stage helps the patient flag risk if subsequently offered tramadol.

subtopic_detail: Inpatient alcohol withdrawal management with CIWA-Ar guidance
stem: You are the medical registrar admitting a 52-year-old man with daily heavy alcohol use (estimated 14 standard drinks per day for 12 years) who has come in for elective inpatient detoxification. His last drink was 14 hours ago. He has no history of seizures or delirium tremens. He is fully oriented but tremulous and anxious. His CIWA-Ar score is 18 currently. He has no other medical comorbidities, no known liver disease and no pregnancy is possible.

data_table.Examination: Coarse tremor of outstretched hands, mildly anxious, mild diaphoresis, oriented to time place and person, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: FBC normal, LFTs ALT 78 AST 96 GGT 240, INR 1.0, UEC normal, BSL 5.4, ethanol level 0.04% on admission, CIWA-Ar 18

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Commence symptom-triggered oral diazepam 10 to 20 mg every 1 to 2 hours guided by CIWA-Ar score, plus intramuscular thiamine 300 mg daily for 3 days before oral thiamine 100 mg three times daily, and monitor for delirium tremens or seizure
options.rationale: RACP and Therapeutic Guidelines Addiction recommend symptom-triggered diazepam (or chlordiazepoxide) loading guided by CIWA-Ar at or above 8 to 10, with parenteral thiamine 300 mg IM/IV daily for at least 3 days before oral, and monitoring for AWS complications. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction - Alcohol withdrawal)

options.text: Commence oral chlorpromazine 100 mg every 6 hours as first-line therapy because chlorpromazine treats both the autonomic features and any subsequent delirium tremens with a lower risk of respiratory depression than benzodiazepines
options.rationale: Antipsychotics lower seizure threshold and do not prevent the GABA-mediated complications of withdrawal; benzodiazepines are first-line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction - Alcohol withdrawal)

options.text: Commence intravenous 10% dextrose at maintenance rate prior to thiamine and continue without benzodiazepine cover because adequate carbohydrate restoration alone will prevent Wernicke encephalopathy and reduce the severity of subsequent withdrawal symptoms
options.rationale: Glucose before thiamine in a chronic alcohol user precipitates Wernicke encephalopathy; thiamine before any glucose is the order. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction - Alcohol withdrawal)

options.text: Commence oral baclofen 10 mg three times daily and oral acamprosate 666 mg three times daily for relapse prevention before the patient develops further withdrawal features and as initial monotherapy without benzodiazepine cover during the acute period
options.rationale: Baclofen and acamprosate are relapse-prevention agents started after acute withdrawal is complete, not during it; benzodiazepines are needed for acute management. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction - Alcohol withdrawal)

options.text: Commence a small daily ration of oral alcohol via 30 mL whisky four times daily and gradual taper over 14 days as the safest method of avoiding the GABAergic rebound seen with abrupt cessation of long-term heavy alcohol use
options.rationale: Alcohol tapering is not endorsed in Australian inpatient detox protocols; benzodiazepine cover is the standard substitute. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction - Alcohol withdrawal)

explanation.summary: Acute alcohol withdrawal management uses symptom-triggered benzodiazepine dosing guided by the CIWA-Ar score (or equivalent AWS scale). Diazepam 10 to 20 mg orally every 1 to 2 hours is given until CIWA-Ar falls below 8 to 10. Parenteral thiamine 300 mg IM or IV daily for at least 3 days then 100 mg orally three times daily prevents Wernicke encephalopathy. Glucose-containing fluids must be preceded by thiamine. Magnesium and folate are replaced if low. Antipsychotics lower seizure threshold and are avoided unless severe agitation persists despite adequate benzodiazepine. Severe AWS, history of delirium tremens or seizures or significant medical comorbidity warrant ICU consideration.
key_points: CIWA-Ar score 8-10 triggers benzodiazepine dosing
Diazepam 10-20 mg PO q1-2h symptom-triggered
Thiamine 300 mg parenteral daily for at least 3 days before glucose
Avoid antipsychotics (lower seizure threshold)
ICU if severe, prior DT or seizures, comorbidity
explanation.pearls: Phenobarbital is reserved for benzodiazepine-refractory withdrawal under specialist supervision; propofol intubation is used in delirium tremens not controlled by maximal benzodiazepines.

sources.label: Australian guidelines for the treatment of alcohol problems (NHMRC)

subtopic_detail: Antidepressant choice in pregnancy after MDD relapse
stem: You are the perinatal psychiatry registrar reviewing a 31-year-old G2P1 at 10 weeks gestation with recurrent moderate to severe major depressive disorder. Her current episode began 6 weeks ago. She stopped citalopram 20 mg daily 4 weeks ago when she discovered she was pregnant, after which her mood, sleep and appetite have deteriorated and she now reports passive suicidal ideation without plan or intent. She has a history of postpartum depression after her first child. She is breastfeeding-naive currently. She has no other mental or physical health diagnoses.

data_table.Examination: Anxious mood, congruent affect, slowed speech and thought, no perceptual disturbance, no active suicidal ideation or intent, oriented
data_table.Investigations: FBC, TFTs, UEC normal; routine antenatal bloods unremarkable, beta-hCG appropriate for gestation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence paroxetine 20 mg daily as first-line because paroxetine has the largest sample of pregnancy outcome data of any SSRI and has been used successfully across all trimesters in international guidelines without major safety concerns
options.rationale: Paroxetine has been associated with a small absolute increase in cardiac malformations (RR around 1.5) and is not first-line in Australian perinatal guidelines. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guidelines)
source_refs: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guidelines

options.text: Defer all pharmacotherapy until after delivery because antidepressant exposure in the first trimester causes major congenital malformations and the safest approach is psychological therapy alone for the duration of the pregnancy
options.rationale: SSRIs (except paroxetine, with some cardiac concerns) do not significantly increase major malformation risk; deferring treatment of relapsed moderate-severe MDD with SI is unsafe. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guidelines)
source_refs: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guidelines

options.text: Restart citalopram at the previous 20 mg daily dose because she had a documented good response to citalopram before pregnancy and any switch of agent at the start of pregnancy risks unnecessary delay in symptom remission with second-line agents
options.rationale: Citalopram is acceptable but sertraline has more pregnancy and breastfeeding data and is generally preferred for new initiation in pregnancy; previous response is a reasonable argument to restart citalopram, but RANZCP and Australian Prescriber lean to sertraline as first-line in perinatal initiation. The more correct answer is sertraline as the safer first-line choice when starting fresh in pregnancy after a gap. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guidelines)
source_refs: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guidelines

options.text: Restart antidepressant therapy with sertraline 50 mg daily, refer to a perinatal mental health service and arrange combined obstetric and psychiatric follow up, with brief psychological therapy as a concurrent adjunct over the next 6 weeks
options.rationale: Sertraline is the preferred SSRI in pregnancy and breastfeeding due to extensive data and the lowest milk-to-plasma ratio of SSRIs; treating moderate-severe MDD with relapse and passive SI in pregnancy is mandated rather than expectant. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guidelines)
source_refs: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guidelines

options.text: Commence venlafaxine 75 mg modified-release daily as first-line because SNRIs are more effective than SSRIs for moderate to severe MDD and the cardiovascular and persistent pulmonary hypertension risks in the neonate are reassuringly negligible
options.rationale: Venlafaxine is used in pregnancy when SSRIs fail but is not first-line; SSRI (sertraline) is preferred as first-line. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guidelines)
source_refs: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guidelines

explanation.summary: Untreated moderate to severe depression in pregnancy is itself associated with preterm birth, low birthweight and poor mother-infant attachment; treatment is therefore indicated when the depression is more than mild. Sertraline is the preferred SSRI in pregnancy and breastfeeding due to its low placental transfer, low milk-to-plasma ratio and extensive safety data. Citalopram and escitalopram are acceptable alternatives, especially with documented prior response. Paroxetine is avoided in the first trimester due to a small increase in cardiac malformations. SNRIs (venlafaxine, duloxetine) are used when SSRIs fail. Lithium and antipsychotics may be required for bipolar relapse or psychotic depression. Perinatal mental health teams provide stepped care including CBT, IPT and shared decision making.
key_points: Untreated moderate-severe MDD in pregnancy is harmful: treat
Sertraline is the preferred first-line SSRI in pregnancy and breastfeeding
Avoid paroxetine first trimester (small cardiac malformation increase)
SNRIs as second line if SSRI fails
Perinatal mental health team + psychological therapy alongside drug
explanation.pearls: Neonatal poor adaptation syndrome (jitteriness, feeding difficulty, transient respiratory distress) occurs in 10 to 30 percent of SSRI-exposed neonates and is self-limiting over 1 to 2 weeks - not a reason to stop the SSRI in the third trimester.

sources.label: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guidelines

stem:
You are the on-call psychiatry registrar called by the obstetric team to review a 29-year-old G1P1 day 8 postpartum who was discharged 5 days ago after an uncomplicated normal vaginal delivery. Her partner reports she has had two days of progressively reduced sleep, perplexity, fluctuating mood, and tonight she has been talking about the baby having a special spiritual purpose she must protect.

She is bewildered and has trouble following conversation. She has no past psychiatric history but her mother had bipolar I disorder. The baby is currently with the grandmother.

data_table.Examination: Perplexed, restless, intermittent thought blocking, mood labile, fleeting persecutory and grandiose delusions about the infant, no objective auditory hallucinations elicited, cognitively impaired on bedside testing, no neurological signs
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, TFTs, B12/folate, calcium, magnesium, BSL all normal; urine drug screen negative; CT head unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate plan?

options.text: Diagnose postpartum thyroiditis presenting with neuropsychiatric features and commence oral propranolol 40 mg three times daily while awaiting repeat thyroid function tests at 6 weeks postpartum before consideration of psychiatric pharmacotherapy
options.rationale: Normal TFTs exclude postpartum thyroiditis as the cause; even if thyroiditis coexisted, antipsychotic management of psychosis is still required. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guidelines)
source_refs: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guidelines

options.text: Diagnose severe postnatal depression with psychotic features and prescribe sertraline 50 mg daily with brief community psychological therapy by the perinatal mental health team while continuing her exclusive home care with her infant
options.rationale: Symptoms of perplexity, fluctuating mood and delusions days after delivery are characteristic of postpartum psychosis, not psychotic depression; home management is unsafe due to infanticide and suicide risk. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guidelines)
source_refs: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guidelines

options.text: Reassure the family that this presentation is consistent with severe baby blues that affect up to 80 percent of women in the first two weeks postpartum and arrange general practitioner review in 7 days if symptoms persist
options.rationale: Baby blues is mild mood lability without psychotic features or perplexity and resolves by day 10; this is psychosis and demands urgent specialist care. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guidelines)
source_refs: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guidelines

options.text: Arrange urgent involuntary admission to a mother-baby unit (or psychiatric ward if MBU unavailable), commence a second-generation antipsychotic such as olanzapine and consider lithium for prophylaxis under specialist psychiatric supervision
options.rationale: Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency due to risk of suicide and infanticide; urgent MBU admission, antipsychotic initiation and lithium prophylaxis (especially in those with bipolar diathesis) is the RANZCP standard. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guidelines)
source_refs: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guidelines

options.text: Recommend her partner takes parental leave and provides 24-hour supervision at home while she initiates community lithium under shared general practitioner and community psychiatric team care for the coming 6 to 8 weeks of recovery
options.rationale: Home supervision is inadequate for postpartum psychosis given the rapid and unpredictable risk trajectory; inpatient MBU admission is needed. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guidelines)
source_refs: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guidelines

explanation.summary: Postpartum psychosis affects 1 to 2 per 1000 deliveries and presents in the first 2 weeks postpartum with rapid onset of insomnia, perplexity, fluctuating mood, delusions (often centred on the baby) and confusion. Family or personal history of bipolar disorder increases risk 10 to 25 fold. It is a psychiatric emergency due to elevated risk of suicide and infanticide. Management is urgent admission to a mother-baby unit (or general psychiatric unit if MBU not available), second-generation antipsychotic (olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone) with consideration of lithium for prophylaxis. ECT is highly effective for refractory or catatonic presentations. Pregnancy planning with mood stabiliser prophylaxis from delivery onwards reduces recurrence in subsequent pregnancies.
key_points: Psychiatric emergency due to suicide and infanticide risk
Urgent MBU admission (or general unit if unavailable)
Antipsychotic + consider lithium for prophylaxis
ECT for refractory or catatonic illness
Recurrence risk in next pregnancy 30 to 50 percent without prophylaxis
explanation.pearls: Lithium initiated within the first 48 hours postpartum in women with bipolar history reduces postpartum psychosis recurrence from around 50 percent to under 15 percent and is given despite breastfeeding considerations with neonatal monitoring.

sources.label: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guidelines
COPE Australia: Perinatal mental health guideline

subtopic_detail: Dementia with Lewy bodies antipsychotic sensitivity
stem: You are the consult-liaison registrar reviewing a 76-year-old man with progressive cognitive decline over 18 months, fluctuating attention, recurrent vivid visual hallucinations of cats in his bedroom, and recent-onset rest tremor with bradykinesia. His GP started haloperidol 1.5 mg twice daily five days ago for the hallucinations. Today he is hyperthermic, has marked rigidity in all limbs, is mute and barely responsive. His baseline cognition four months ago showed a MoCA of 19 out of 30 with prominent visuospatial deficits. He has no other psychotropic medications.

data_table.Examination: Severe cogwheel rigidity in all 4 limbs, mute, barely responsive, marked diaphoresis, no clonus, brisk reflexes
data_table.Investigations: CK 4800 U/L, WCC 12.4, UEC creatinine 122 (baseline 88), CT head old age-related changes only, urinalysis negative, blood cultures pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase haloperidol to 5 mg three times daily for refractory psychosis, add a benzodiazepine for the rigidity and transfer to a closed dementia ward for ongoing antipsychotic titration and behavioural containment over the next 7 days
options.rationale: Increasing the antipsychotic worsens the antipsychotic-sensitivity reaction; rigidity is part of NMS-like physiology not just behavioural agitation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Dementia with Lewy bodies)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Dementia with Lewy bodies

options.text: Cease haloperidol immediately, treat as neuroleptic malignant syndrome with intravenous fluids and active cooling, transfer to a high-dependency setting, and once stabilised commence rivastigmine for the underlying dementia with Lewy bodies
options.rationale: Severe antipsychotic sensitivity reaction with NMS-like features in a man with parkinsonism, fluctuating cognition and visual hallucinations is classical for DLB; haloperidol must be ceased and cholinesterase inhibitor (rivastigmine) is the disease-targeted treatment per RANZCP. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Dementia with Lewy bodies)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Dementia with Lewy bodies

options.text: Switch to risperidone 1 mg twice daily because risperidone is a safer antipsychotic in older patients with parkinsonian features than haloperidol and is recommended first-line for behavioural and psychological symptoms in dementia
options.rationale: All dopamine-receptor-blocking antipsychotics can cause severe sensitivity reactions in DLB; risperidone is not safer here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Dementia with Lewy bodies)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Dementia with Lewy bodies

options.text: Add oral carbidopa-levodopa 25/100 three times daily as treatment for newly recognised idiopathic Parkinson disease and continue haloperidol for the psychotic symptoms until levodopa shows benefit in the limbs over the next fortnight
options.rationale: L-dopa would worsen psychosis, and continuing haloperidol perpetuates the antipsychotic-sensitivity NMS-like reaction; cessation of haloperidol is the priority. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Dementia with Lewy bodies)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Dementia with Lewy bodies

options.text: Continue haloperidol at the current dose but add intravenous dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg six-hourly and oral bromocriptine 5 mg three times daily as specific antidotal therapy for ongoing NMS rather than ceasing the precipitating agent
options.rationale: Cessation of the precipitating antipsychotic is the foundation of NMS treatment; dantrolene and bromocriptine are second-line in severe cases but never used while continuing the antipsychotic. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Dementia with Lewy bodies)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Dementia with Lewy bodies

explanation.summary: Dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) is characterised by fluctuating cognition, recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations, REM sleep behaviour disorder and spontaneous parkinsonism. Antipsychotic medications (especially first-generation and high-D2-occupancy SGAs like risperidone) can precipitate severe extrapyramidal reactions and NMS-like presentations in 30 to 50 percent of patients with DLB. First-line treatment of cognitive and hallucinatory symptoms is a cholinesterase inhibitor (rivastigmine or donepezil), with quetiapine as the safest antipsychotic if pharmacotherapy of psychosis is essential. Levodopa for motor symptoms is used cautiously because it can exacerbate hallucinations. Multidisciplinary care addresses falls risk, autonomic dysfunction and carer support.
key_points: DLB: fluctuating cognition + visual hallucinations + parkinsonism + REM sleep behaviour disorder
Severe antipsychotic sensitivity in 30-50% (NMS-like reactions)
First-line for cognitive/psychotic features: cholinesterase inhibitor (rivastigmine)
If antipsychotic essential: low-dose quetiapine
L-dopa cautiously for motor symptoms
explanation.pearls: DaT-SPECT (dopamine transporter scan) showing reduced striatal uptake supports DLB and PD over Alzheimer disease; it is the imaging biomarker used to distinguish DLB from AD with parkinsonian features.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Dementia with Lewy bodies
Dementia Australia: Dementia with Lewy bodies

stem:
You are the adult psychiatry registrar in an outpatient clinic seeing a 26-year-old man referred for assessment of long-standing inattention, distractibility and disorganisation that have persisted from childhood and now substantially impair his postgraduate study and ability to hold steady employment. A structured diagnostic interview using DIVA confirms adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder with childhood-onset symptoms documented on school reports.

Comorbid depression and anxiety have been excluded on screening. He drinks under 4 standard drinks weekly, uses no other substances, has no personal or family history of cardiac disease, and his cardiovascular and neurological examinations are entirely normal with no resting tachycardia, no murmur, and no documented hypertension.

data_table.Examination: Normal cardiovascular and neurological examination, no tremor, no thyromegaly, no Cushingoid features, alert and cooperative
data_table.Investigations: ECG: sinus rhythm rate 76, normal axis, QTc 412 ms; routine bloods and TFTs within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Bupropion 150 mg daily as off-label augmentation given its dopaminergic and noradrenergic profile, with monthly blood-pressure monitoring and an expectation of a clinically meaningful response within 4 to 6 treatment weeks
options.rationale: Bupropion is not first-line for adult ADHD in Australian guidance; stimulants and atomoxetine have stronger evidence and clear regulatory positioning. (Source: Australian Evidence-based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Atomoxetine 40 mg daily with uptitration to 80 mg daily over 2 weeks as a noradrenergic non-stimulant first-line option given the duration of his symptoms and the long-acting nature of this pharmacological treatment choice
options.rationale: Atomoxetine is second-line; reserved for patients who do not tolerate or respond to stimulants, who have a substance use disorder, or where stimulant diversion is a major concern. (Source: Australian Evidence-based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Methylphenidate immediate-release starting at 10 mg twice daily with structured uptitration to a therapeutic dose, with monitoring of weight, blood pressure, heart rate and sleep, and a discussion about driving and stimulant-class diversion risks
options.rationale: Stimulants (methylphenidate or lisdexamfetamine) are first-line for adult ADHD in Australian guidance; immediate-release methylphenidate with cardiovascular and weight monitoring is a standard initial choice. (Source: Australian Evidence-based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Defer all pharmacotherapy and commence 12 sessions of cognitive behavioural therapy specifically adapted for adult ADHD, then reassess for pharmacotherapy if his symptoms persist following completion of the therapy course
options.rationale: Psychological therapy is recommended in combination with pharmacotherapy rather than as a delay strategy when the diagnosis is clear and functional impairment is substantial. (Source: Australian Evidence-based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Clonidine 50 microgram twice daily titrated to effect with weekly blood pressure monitoring at home and ongoing review for postural symptoms or fatigue or any clinically meaningful changes in his sleep architecture
options.rationale: Clonidine is not a first-line agent for adult ADHD; alpha-2 agonists are used in paediatric ADHD, often as adjuncts, and rarely as monotherapy in adults. (Source: Australian Evidence-based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

explanation.summary: First-line pharmacotherapy for adult ADHD in Australia is a stimulant (methylphenidate or lisdexamfetamine), titrated to effect with monitoring of blood pressure, heart rate, weight and sleep. Atomoxetine is second-line and reserved for stimulant intolerance, contraindications, or significant misuse risk. Psychological therapy is combined with pharmacotherapy, not used to delay it when impairment is significant. Authority and prescriber registration requirements apply by jurisdiction. Pre-treatment ECG is indicated when cardiovascular risk factors or family history are present.
key_points: First-line: stimulant (methylphenidate or lisdexamfetamine) titrated to effect
Second-line: atomoxetine (noradrenergic non-stimulant), preferred if substance use disorder or diversion risk
Monitor: BP, HR, weight, sleep, appetite, mood, diversion risk; ECG if cardiac history
Combine pharmacotherapy with psychoeducation and ADHD-adapted CBT for best outcomes
explanation.pearls: Adult ADHD stimulants are Schedule 8 with state-specific authority requirements; in NSW and several other states only psychiatrists or paediatricians can initiate, with GP shared care possible once stable - know your state's pathway before promising to start.

sources.label: Australian Evidence-based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

subtopic_detail: Borderline personality disorder self-harm crisis management
stem:
You are the consultation-liaison psychiatry registrar reviewing a 24-year-old woman with established borderline personality disorder, currently engaged in a structured DBT program, who has self-presented to ED after a self-inflicted superficial right forearm laceration in the context of a relationship conflict 4 hours ago. She is calm now, expresses regret and embarrassment, denies current suicidal intent or plan, has no access to means at home, and asks to be discharged so she can attend her individual DBT session in the morning.

Wound assessment shows superficial linear cuts requiring closure with steristrips only. She has a supportive housemate at home, attends regular skills group, and her DBT therapist is contactable for handover within working hours.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72, HR 78, SpO2 99% in air, T 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Superficial right forearm lacerations closed with steristrips, no tendon or neurovascular involvement, no other injuries on torso or limbs, no signs of intoxication
data_table.Investigations: Bedside alcohol breath test negative; urine drug screen not indicated; routine bloods not required

lead_in: What is the most appropriate disposition?

options.text: Admit her voluntarily for 72 hours to the psychiatric short stay unit for crisis stabilisation and arrange a clozapine titration to begin during the inpatient stay to address her recurrent self-harm pattern observed today
options.rationale: Clozapine has no role in BPD self-harm management; even short admissions can reinforce unhelpful patterns when chronic suicidality is the presentation rather than an acute crisis. (Source: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD)
source_refs: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD

options.text: Discharge her home without further follow-up and advise her to ring 000 if she has any further self-harm or suicidal thoughts; the wound has been dressed and her observations are within normal limits today
options.rationale: Discharge without a structured safety plan and handover to her existing treating team fails to leverage the strongest predictor of safety in BPD: continuity of therapeutic relationships. (Source: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD)
source_refs: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD

options.text: Arrange involuntary admission to a closed psychiatric unit under the Mental Health Act for ongoing risk management and recommend a trial of quetiapine 50 mg twice daily as a chemical containment intervention for the next 4 weeks
options.rationale: Inpatient admission for chronic suicidality in BPD without an acute imminent risk often worsens long-term outcomes; routine pharmacotherapy is not first-line and BPD-specific psychotherapy carries the evidence. (Source: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD)
source_refs: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD

options.text: Discharge home with a written DBT-aligned safety plan, contact her DBT therapist by phone with her consent now to hand over and arrange a clinic review the next morning, and provide acute care service contact numbers for overnight use
options.rationale: She has chronic suicidality with no acute imminent risk, an existing therapeutic relationship and engaged DBT plan; structured handover and discharge with a clear safety plan is the evidence-based response. (Source: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD)
source_refs: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD

options.text: Refer for an electroconvulsive therapy work-up given the recurrent self-harm and a probable underlying treatment-resistant depressive component, and admit her until the first ECT treatment can be scheduled during the week
options.rationale: ECT is not indicated for BPD self-harm without a clear concurrent severe depressive episode meeting criteria; this would be over-treatment and not aligned with BPD-specific guidance. (Source: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD)
source_refs: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD

explanation.summary: BPD self-harm in the absence of acute imminent risk is best managed by a structured discharge that maintains continuity with the patient's existing therapy. Brief admission is reserved for an acute change in risk profile, severe comorbid depression or psychosis, or when no community supports exist. BPD-specific psychotherapies (DBT, MBT, schema-focused therapy) carry the strongest evidence; pharmacotherapy is targeted at specific comorbid syndromes rather than the personality disorder itself. Safety planning, handover to the treating team and clear next contact are the disposition essentials.
key_points: Chronic suicidality without acute change usually does not warrant admission in BPD
Continuity with existing therapist and structured safety plan are highest-value interventions
Pharmacotherapy targets specific comorbidities only; no medication is first-line for BPD itself
DBT, MBT, schema-focused therapy and TFP are the evidence-based BPD-specific psychotherapies
explanation.pearls: When in doubt about admit vs discharge in BPD, ask: has the risk changed acutely from baseline? If chronic suicidality is at the patient's baseline and a coherent therapy plan exists, discharge with a safety plan and same-day handover is almost always safer than admission.

sources.label: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guideline for BPD
RANZCP: Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of BPD

subtopic_detail: Dementia with Lewy bodies recognition and antipsychotic avoidance
stem:
You are the geriatric psychiatry registrar reviewing a 76-year-old man brought in by his wife with 12 months of progressive cognitive decline characterised by marked fluctuations in attention and arousal, recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations of small animals and children, and a recently diagnosed REM sleep behaviour disorder confirmed on polysomnography. Over the last 4 months he has developed mild Parkinsonian signs with bradykinesia and rigidity.

He has had two falls in the past month. On the ward he has become agitated overnight and his treating team is asking your advice. He has no preceding psychiatric history; his Addenbrooke's Cognitive Examination score has fallen from 86 to 72 over 12 months, with relative preservation of memory but impaired visuospatial function.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 142/82 lying with 22 mmHg systolic drop on standing, HR 78, T 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Bradykinesia, mild cogwheel rigidity bilaterally, no tremor, soft visual hallucinations described non-distressingly, no focal neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain: mild generalised atrophy, no significant vascular load, no hippocampal predominance; DAT scan: bilateral reduced striatal uptake; routine bloods normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of his cognitive symptoms and overnight agitation?

options.text: Commence rivastigmine starting at 1.5 mg twice daily with stepwise dose titration, avoid first-generation and most second-generation antipsychotics due to severe neuroleptic sensitivity, and address modifiable triggers for his nocturnal agitation
options.rationale: Rivastigmine has the best evidence for cognitive and neuropsychiatric symptoms in DLB; neuroleptic sensitivity is severe in DLB and includes risk of NMS-like reactions, so antipsychotics are largely avoided and modifiable triggers addressed first. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Dementia)

options.text: Commence memantine 5 mg daily titrated to 20 mg daily over 4 weeks and add a benzodiazepine such as diazepam 2 mg at night to address both his cognitive symptoms and the overnight behavioural agitation episodes
options.rationale: Memantine has weaker evidence in DLB than cholinesterase inhibitors and benzodiazepines worsen falls, cognition and confusion in older people, particularly in DLB. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Dementia)

options.text: Defer all pharmacotherapy and arrange a 4-week trial of one-on-one behavioural therapy and a structured cognitive stimulation program before considering any specific pharmacological interventions in this clinical presentation today
options.rationale: Non-pharmacological interventions are important but the rapid functional decline and characteristic symptom cluster warrant prompt rivastigmine initiation rather than deferral. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Dementia)

options.text: Commence levodopa-carbidopa for the Parkinsonian signs and add risperidone 0.5 mg at night for the visual hallucinations and the overnight agitation, with periodic review of both treatments at the local clinic
options.rationale: Levodopa can worsen psychosis in DLB and risperidone carries neuroleptic sensitivity risk; cholinesterase inhibitor first and antipsychotics avoided are the standard package. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Dementia)

options.text: Commence haloperidol 0.5 mg orally twice daily for the visual hallucinations and agitation, and add donepezil 5 mg daily for the cognitive component once the agitation has been brought under reasonable control over time
options.rationale: Haloperidol can precipitate severe neuroleptic sensitivity reactions including NMS-like syndromes in DLB and is specifically discouraged; rivastigmine has the strongest evidence base. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Dementia)

explanation.summary: Dementia with Lewy bodies presents with the core features of fluctuating cognition, recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations, REM sleep behaviour disorder and spontaneous parkinsonism. Cholinesterase inhibitors (rivastigmine first, donepezil second) have the strongest evidence for both cognitive and neuropsychiatric symptoms. Neuroleptic sensitivity in DLB is severe and includes NMS-like reactions; antipsychotics are largely avoided and, if absolutely required, quetiapine at very low dose is preferred. Levodopa worsens psychosis; benzodiazepines worsen cognition and falls. Address modifiable triggers (pain, infection, environment) before any pharmacology.
key_points: DLB core features: fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, REM sleep behaviour disorder, parkinsonism
First-line cognitive Rx: rivastigmine; donepezil second
Antipsychotics largely avoided due to severe neuroleptic sensitivity; quetiapine very low dose if essential
Benzodiazepines and levodopa worsen DLB outcomes; address modifiable triggers first
explanation.pearls: If a person with new-onset dementia has well-formed visual hallucinations, REM behaviour disorder and falls, suspect DLB and never reach for haloperidol or risperidone first - the neuroleptic sensitivity reaction can be fatal.

subtopic_detail: Severe anorexia nervosa refeeding syndrome prevention
stem:
You are the consultation-liaison psychiatry registrar reviewing a 19-year-old woman admitted to the general medical ward 2 hours ago with severe restrictive anorexia nervosa. Her current BMI is 13.1 with a 12 kg weight loss over 4 months and a daily intake estimated at 350 kcal for the past 3 weeks. Pulse is 42 sitting, blood pressure 88/52 lying with 22 mmHg systolic postural drop, and her temperature is 35.4 degrees C.

Her phosphate is 0.62 mmol/L, magnesium 0.66 mmol/L, potassium 3.1 mmol/L, sodium 134 mmol/L; ECG shows a prolonged QTc of 488 ms; her glucose is 3.3 mmol/L. She is medically and cognitively cooperative, accepts the plan in principle, and wishes to engage with the eating-disorders service team during admission.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 88/52 lying (postural drop 22 mmHg systolic), HR 42, T 35.4 degrees C, SpO2 99% in air
data_table.Examination: BMI 13.1, severe muscle wasting, dry skin, lanugo, no peripheral oedema, alert and cooperative, normal cranial nerve exam
data_table.Investigations: Phosphate 0.62 (RR 0.8-1.5), Mg 0.66 (RR 0.7-1.0), K 3.1 (RR 3.5-5.0), Na 134, glucose 3.3, albumin 32, INR 1.2, ECG: sinus bradycardia, QTc 488 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial nutritional and electrolyte plan?

options.text: Defer the nutritional plan until she has been transferred to a tertiary eating-disorders unit for inpatient psychiatric admission under the Mental Health Act, maintaining her on a clear-fluids-only diet without electrolyte replacement
options.rationale: Delay risks rapid deterioration; medical stabilisation and prophylactic electrolyte replacement must begin immediately at the current facility, and involuntary admission is decided on capacity grounds rather than as a transfer device. (Source: ANZAED Practice Standards for the Treatment of Eating Disorders)
source_refs: ANZAED Practice Standards for the Treatment of Eating Disorders

options.text: Commence oral feeding at 35 kcal/kg/day from the first meal with structured supervised meal support and replace phosphate and magnesium and potassium only after the first 48 hours of feeding to allow biochemical re-equilibration
options.rationale: Starting above 30 kcal/kg/day in a severely underweight patient with established hypophosphataemia exceeds the safe initial caloric load; prophylactic electrolyte replacement should precede feeding. (Source: ANZAED Practice Standards for the Treatment of Eating Disorders)
source_refs: ANZAED Practice Standards for the Treatment of Eating Disorders

options.text: Commence full nutritional rehabilitation with nasogastric feeding at 50 kcal/kg/day from admission to reverse her catabolic state as quickly as possible and replace electrolytes only if her biochemistry confirms deficits beyond initial values
options.rationale: Aggressive initial feeding precipitates refeeding syndrome with potentially fatal hypophosphataemia, cardiac arrhythmias and Wernicke encephalopathy; current Australian guidance favours cautious initial caloric load with prophylactic replacement. (Source: ANZAED Practice Standards for the Treatment of Eating Disorders)
source_refs: ANZAED Practice Standards for the Treatment of Eating Disorders

options.text: Start at approximately 20 kcal/kg/day with the multidisciplinary team, supplement oral phosphate and magnesium and potassium before significant feeding, give intravenous thiamine 300 mg daily for 5 days, monitor electrolytes 12-hourly initially
options.rationale: MARSIPAN and Australian eating-disorders guidance recommend low-rate initial feeding (around 20 kcal/kg/day) with empirical electrolyte and thiamine replacement, frequent biochemistry, and continuous cardiac monitoring in patients with established hypophosphataemia and a prolonged QTc. (Source: ANZAED Practice Standards for the Treatment of Eating Disorders)
source_refs: ANZAED Practice Standards for the Treatment of Eating Disorders

options.text: Commence intravenous 10% dextrose at maintenance rate for the next 24 hours to correct her low blood glucose and only commence oral feeding once her electrolytes have been fully normalised on biochemistry without further loading
options.rationale: Intravenous dextrose without prior thiamine and electrolyte replacement can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy and rebound hypophosphataemia; thiamine must precede or accompany any glucose load. (Source: ANZAED Practice Standards for the Treatment of Eating Disorders)
source_refs: ANZAED Practice Standards for the Treatment of Eating Disorders

explanation.summary: Severe anorexia nervosa with BMI under 13, marked bradycardia, postural hypotension and electrolyte derangement is medically high risk for refeeding syndrome. Initial nutritional rehabilitation starts at approximately 20 kcal/kg/day (5 to 10 kcal/kg/day in extreme cases), with empirical replacement of phosphate, magnesium, potassium and thiamine before significant feeding, frequent biochemistry, continuous cardiac monitoring, and a multidisciplinary plan. Wernicke prophylaxis precedes any carbohydrate load. Feeding is uptitrated as biochemistry tolerates over 5 to 7 days.
key_points: Refeeding syndrome risk factors: BMI under 16, weight loss above 15% in 3 to 6 months, low baseline phosphate/Mg/K
Start at approximately 20 kcal/kg/day; even lower (5-10 kcal/kg/day) in extreme malnutrition
Prophylactic thiamine 300 mg IV daily for 5 to 7 days before or with carbohydrate load
Replace phosphate, magnesium, potassium pre-emptively; monitor biochemistry 12-hourly initially
explanation.pearls: Thiamine before glucose is non-negotiable in severely malnourished patients - giving carbohydrate first risks precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy that can leave permanent amnestic deficits even after good nutritional recovery.

sources.label: ANZAED Practice Standards for the Treatment of Eating Disorders
RANZCP: Eating Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

subtopic_detail: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose with QRS prolongation
stem:
You are the ED registrar reviewing a 28-year-old woman brought in by paramedics 90 minutes after a witnessed ingestion of approximately 50 tablets of amitriptyline 25 mg from her own prescription. On arrival she is drowsy but rousable, has dilated pupils, dry warm skin and decreased bowel sounds. Her observations show tachycardia, mild hypotension and a wide-complex tachycardia on the cardiac monitor with the 12-lead ECG showing sinus tachycardia at 132/min with a QRS of 128 ms, an R wave in aVR of 6 mm, and a rightward terminal axis.

She has been intubated for airway protection. Activated charcoal was not given pre-hospital due to her drowsiness. There is no co-ingestion history of paracetamol or alcohol on initial assessment.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 92/56, HR 132, T 37.6 degrees C, SpO2 100% on FiO2 0.4 (intubated and ventilated)
data_table.Examination: Drowsy then intubated, dilated pupils, dry skin, decreased bowel sounds, no clonus, no rigidity, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: ECG: sinus tachycardia QRS 128 ms, R wave aVR 6 mm, terminal R wave rightward axis; ABG pH 7.32, pCO2 4.6 kPa, HCO3 18, Na 140, K 3.8, BSL 7.8, paracetamol level pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg as a bolus and repeat to narrow the QRS to under 100 ms while monitoring blood pH between 7.45 and 7.55 and titrating ongoing infusion to clinical and ECG response
options.rationale: QRS prolongation above 100 ms in TCA overdose predicts seizures and ventricular arrhythmias; sodium bicarbonate is the first-line antidote, with the dual mechanism of alkalinisation and increased extracellular sodium to overcome sodium channel blockade. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology - Tricyclic antidepressants)

options.text: Administer intravenous physostigmine 1 to 2 mg slowly to reverse the central anticholinergic syndrome and improve her drowsiness, with continuous cardiac monitoring and resuscitation equipment available throughout administration of the medication
options.rationale: Physostigmine is contraindicated in TCA overdose because it can precipitate asystole through bradyarrhythmia in the setting of TCA-induced conduction abnormalities. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology - Tricyclic antidepressants)

options.text: Commence intravenous lipid emulsion 20% as a 1.5 mL/kg bolus followed by an ongoing infusion at 0.25 mL/kg/min as the first-line specific antidote intervention for amitriptyline-associated cardiotoxicity in this overdose presentation
options.rationale: Intravenous lipid emulsion is a rescue therapy for refractory cardiovascular collapse, not first-line; sodium bicarbonate should be tried first and titrated to QRS narrowing and pH 7.45 to 7.55. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology - Tricyclic antidepressants)

options.text: Administer intravenous amiodarone 300 mg over 20 minutes for the wide-complex tachycardia and prepare for synchronised DC cardioversion if there is no improvement in the cardiac rhythm or her haemodynamic status
options.rationale: Class III antiarrhythmics worsen TCA cardiotoxicity by prolonging QT and depressing conduction; sodium bicarbonate is the indicated antidote and most antiarrhythmics are contraindicated in TCA overdose. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology - Tricyclic antidepressants)

options.text: Administer intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg titrated to reverse her drowsiness and improve her airway protection so she can be extubated promptly and avoid the morbidity associated with prolonged mechanical ventilation in the ED
options.rationale: Flumazenil is contraindicated in mixed overdoses and in TCA toxicity because it can precipitate seizures; airway management is the priority and chemical reversal is not appropriate here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology - Tricyclic antidepressants)

explanation.summary: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose causes a sodium-channel-blocker cardiotoxicity (QRS widening, terminal R wave in aVR, ventricular arrhythmias) plus anticholinergic and alpha-blocking effects. QRS above 100 ms predicts seizures and ventricular arrhythmias and is the trigger for sodium bicarbonate boluses targeted to narrow the QRS to under 100 ms and a serum pH 7.45 to 7.55. Lipid emulsion is reserved for refractory cardiovascular collapse. Flumazenil, physostigmine, and class I/III antiarrhythmics are contraindicated. Supportive care includes airway protection, fluid resuscitation and seizure management with benzodiazepines.
key_points: QRS over 100 ms or R wave aVR over 3 mm: high risk of seizures and ventricular arrhythmias
First-line antidote: sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg boluses, target QRS under 100 ms and pH 7.45 to 7.55
Avoid flumazenil, physostigmine, class I/III antiarrhythmics; benzodiazepines for seizures
Lipid emulsion as rescue therapy for cardiovascular collapse refractory to standard measures
explanation.pearls: Look at aVR on the 12-lead: a terminal R wave above 3 mm with rightward terminal axis is the TCA-toxicity signature and predicts arrhythmias - it is the cleanest single trigger for early sodium bicarbonate.

sources.label: Australian Poisons Information Centre: TCA overdose

stem:
You are the perinatal psychiatry registrar reviewing a 29-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder, stable for 4 years on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily as monotherapy with two prior depressive episodes and one manic episode in her early 20s. She has been in a stable relationship for 3 years and is now planning a first pregnancy within the next 6 to 12 months.

She uses no other medications, has no contraindications to lithium, has had no thyroid or renal disease, and her family history is unremarkable. She has read patient information that suggests valproate carries risks in pregnancy and asks for your advice on what to do. She is a non-smoker, drinks no alcohol, and her partner is supportive of her decisions.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic affect, normal speech, no thought disorder, no perceptual disturbance, no parkinsonism, mood elevated to baseline range
data_table.Investigations: Routine bloods including TFTs, eGFR, valproate level 460 micromol/L (RR 300-700) all within target range

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue valproate at the current dose throughout pregnancy and add high-dose folic acid 5 mg daily preconceptionally, and arrange detailed second-trimester anatomy ultrasound to detect any neural-tube or other structural anomalies that may arise
options.rationale: Folic acid does not fully mitigate valproate teratogenicity; valproate use in pregnancy carries unacceptable risk in women planning conception when alternative effective agents exist. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal Mental Health Position Statement)
source_refs: RANZCP: Perinatal Mental Health Position Statement

options.text: Continue valproate at a reduced dose of 500 mg daily and add lamotrigine titrated to 200 mg daily, hoping that the combination will protect against relapse while halving the dose-dependent teratogenic risk profile during pregnancy planning today
options.rationale: Risk reduction with valproate is not proportionate to dose reduction at clinically effective doses, and any continued valproate in pregnancy carries unacceptable teratogenicity when alternatives exist. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal Mental Health Position Statement)
source_refs: RANZCP: Perinatal Mental Health Position Statement

options.text: Plan a switch from valproate to lithium pre-conception with overlap and gradual cross-titration, baseline thyroid and renal function with ongoing therapeutic drug monitoring, and high-dose folic acid 5 mg daily preconceptionally
options.rationale: Valproate carries a 10% major malformation rate (especially neural tube defects) and a 30 to 40% neurodevelopmental impact; pre-conception switch to lithium (preferred maintenance in childbearing women with bipolar I) with cross-titration and high-dose folate is recommended Australian practice. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal Mental Health Position Statement)
source_refs: RANZCP: Perinatal Mental Health Position Statement

options.text: Switch from valproate to topiramate 100 mg twice daily as a non-teratogenic mood stabiliser alternative and arrange detailed pre-conception genetic counselling before any further changes to her medication regimen at this stage in her care
options.rationale: Topiramate is itself teratogenic (oral clefts, low birth weight), is not licensed as a mood stabiliser in Australia, and is not first-line in bipolar maintenance. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal Mental Health Position Statement)
source_refs: RANZCP: Perinatal Mental Health Position Statement

options.text: Cease valproate abruptly and rely on lifestyle measures and structured psychological therapy for relapse prevention until she has completed her pregnancy and lactation period before resuming maintenance pharmacotherapy at any later point
options.rationale: Discontinuation of mood stabiliser in bipolar I carries high relapse risk, particularly in pregnancy and the postpartum period; treatment is changed to a safer agent rather than stopped. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal Mental Health Position Statement)
source_refs: RANZCP: Perinatal Mental Health Position Statement

explanation.summary: Sodium valproate is the most teratogenic of the mood stabilisers, with 10% major malformation rate (notably neural tube defects), and 30 to 40% adverse neurodevelopmental outcomes (lower IQ, autism spectrum disorders). Australian regulators have implemented pregnancy prevention programs requiring documented contraception in women of childbearing potential. For pre-conception planning in bipolar I, lithium is the preferred maintenance agent (with anomaly scan and serial monitoring), with lamotrigine the alternative for predominantly depressive presentations. Cross-titration to lithium with overlap, baseline renal and thyroid function, high-dose preconception folate, and counselling about Ebstein anomaly (lithium first-trimester risk is modest at around 1 in 1000) are key.
key_points: Valproate: 10% major malformation rate, 30 to 40% neurodevelopmental impact; pregnancy prevention program required
Lithium: preferred maintenance in bipolar I planning pregnancy; Ebstein anomaly risk around 1 in 1000
Lamotrigine: alternative for predominantly depressive bipolar; safer than valproate but less effective for mania prevention
High-dose folate 5 mg daily preconceptionally for women on any anti-seizure medication
explanation.pearls: Folic acid does not rescue valproate teratogenicity - the combination is misleadingly reassuring and the patient still carries a 10% major malformation risk; switching to lithium pre-conception is the right ask, not adding folate.

sources.label: RANZCP: Perinatal Mental Health Position Statement
TGA: Valproate use and pregnancy prevention

stem:
You are the acute psychiatry registrar reviewing a 22-year-old man brought in by police after he was found running through traffic shouting at unseen voices and accusing strangers of conspiring against him. Collateral from his housemate confirms 12 months of daily high-potency cannabis use with a sharp escalation in the past 3 weeks coinciding with a relationship breakdown. He has no prior psychiatric history, no family history of psychotic illness, no other substance use beyond occasional alcohol, no head injury, and a normal medical and neurological examination.

Urine drug screen is positive for THC only. Acute behavioural disturbance has now settled with calm verbal de-escalation in the ED; he is paranoid but able to engage with the interview process today.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/84, HR 96, T 36.9 degrees C, SpO2 98% in air
data_table.Examination: Alert, paranoid, mild psychomotor agitation, conjunctival injection, no nystagmus or rigidity, no neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen: THC positive, all other drugs of abuse negative; routine bloods unremarkable; CT brain normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Discharge home with his housemate, prescribe diazepam 5 mg three times daily for 7 days for sedation and arrange follow-up with the local alcohol and other drug service within the next 2 weeks for cannabis cessation support
