options.rationale: Active psychotic symptoms with paranoia and recent dangerous behaviour preclude direct discharge to a housemate without specialist follow-up; benzodiazepine monotherapy does not treat psychotic symptoms. (Source: RANZCP: Substance use and psychosis position statement)
source_refs: RANZCP: Substance use and psychosis position statement

options.text: Admit him under the Mental Health Act involuntarily for 4 weeks of inpatient stabilisation with risperidone 4 mg daily and a low-dose sodium valproate mood stabiliser added from admission as a substance-induced episode mood stabiliser
options.rationale: Involuntary admission is reserved for patients lacking capacity or with risk profiles unsafe for voluntary care; he is engaging with assessment, and mood stabiliser addition is not indicated in substance-induced psychosis. (Source: RANZCP: Substance use and psychosis position statement)
source_refs: RANZCP: Substance use and psychosis position statement

options.text: Discharge with a 4-week supply of olanzapine 10 mg daily and rely on his general practitioner to arrange specialist mental health follow-up, with reattendance only if there are any further psychotic symptoms after the discharge today
options.rationale: Direct discharge without specialist follow-up risks decompensation and undertreatment; assertive early intervention in psychosis with specialist follow-up improves long-term outcomes. (Source: RANZCP: Substance use and psychosis position statement)
source_refs: RANZCP: Substance use and psychosis position statement

options.text: Commence clozapine 12.5 mg daily titrated as inpatient and continue for at least 6 months given the severity of the psychotic episode and the high risk of relapse with ongoing cannabis use after his discharge from hospital
options.rationale: Clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia after failure of two adequate trials of other antipsychotics; first-episode cannabis-induced psychosis should not be treated with clozapine. (Source: RANZCP: Substance use and psychosis position statement)
source_refs: RANZCP: Substance use and psychosis position statement

options.text: Admit him voluntarily for short-term observation, commence olanzapine 10 mg orally daily, arrange brief intervention and motivational interviewing for cannabis cessation, and plan early community mental health team follow-up after discharge
options.rationale: Acute cannabis-induced psychosis with significant symptoms warrants short admission, an antipsychotic to treat acute symptoms (olanzapine is a reasonable choice), cessation counselling, and structured follow-up given the elevated risk of progression to a primary psychotic illness. (Source: RANZCP: Substance use and psychosis position statement)
source_refs: RANZCP: Substance use and psychosis position statement

explanation.summary: Cannabis-induced psychotic disorder presents with paranoia, perceptual disturbances and disorganised behaviour in the context of cannabis use, classically with high-potency THC products and adolescent or young-adult onset. Acute management combines short admission for safety and observation, antipsychotic treatment (commonly olanzapine or risperidone), substance use intervention with motivational interviewing, and assertive early intervention follow-up. A substantial proportion (around 20 to 40%) of cannabis-induced psychoses progress to a schizophrenia-spectrum disorder over the following decade, particularly with ongoing cannabis use, so longitudinal follow-up is essential.
key_points: Cannabis-induced psychosis: paranoia and perceptual disturbances with cannabis use, especially high-potency THC
Acute management: short voluntary admission, antipsychotic (olanzapine or risperidone), cessation intervention
Risk of progression to primary psychotic illness: 20 to 40% over the next decade
Assertive early intervention follow-up improves long-term function and reduces relapse
explanation.pearls: Even when psychosis is clearly substance-induced, the appropriate disposition is short admission with antipsychotic and early intervention follow-up - not direct discharge - because the cumulative risk of progression to schizophrenia warrants longitudinal engagement.

sources.label: RANZCP: Substance use and psychosis position statement

subtopic_detail: Gamma-hydroxybutyrate withdrawal recognition and inpatient management
stem:
You are the addiction medicine registrar called to ED for a 32-year-old man with a 4-year history of daily gamma-hydroxybutyrate use, dosing every 2 to 3 hours including overnight, who ran out of supply 18 hours ago. He has been profoundly anxious, tremulous and diaphoretic; in the last 4 hours he has become confused with visual hallucinations of insects on the wall and a brief generalised seizure self-terminating after 60 seconds.

Standard alcohol-withdrawal-style diazepam loading at 60 mg over the past 2 hours has produced only modest improvement in his agitation and autonomic features. He has no past psychiatric history, no other substance use beyond moderate alcohol, and no metabolic, neurological or infective focus identified on a comprehensive bedside workup.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 168/104, HR 132, T 38.3 degrees C, SpO2 96% in air, RR 24
data_table.Examination: Confused, GCS 14 with intermittent worsening, diaphoretic, coarse tremor, hyperreflexia without sustained clonus, visual hallucinations
data_table.Investigations: Routine bloods, CK, lactate, BSL, electrolytes within acceptable limits; CT brain normal; LP not yet performed; urine drug screen GHB-positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer haloperidol 5 mg intramuscularly with promethazine for behavioural control and arrange a CT brain and lumbar puncture before any further sedation is given, in case there is an undetected intracranial cause for delirium
options.rationale: Antipsychotics lower seizure threshold and worsen delirium in GHB withdrawal; the syndrome is recognised clinically and sedation with high-dose benzodiazepines plus baclofen is the appropriate next step. (Source: Australian Clinical Guidelines: GHB withdrawal management)
source_refs: Australian Clinical Guidelines: GHB withdrawal management

options.text: Escalate to high-dose benzodiazepine loading guided by sedation and seizure response, add a GABAergic adjunct such as baclofen, and discuss urgent ICU transfer for ongoing sedation, airway monitoring and ventilation if required
options.rationale: Severe GHB withdrawal is benzodiazepine-resistant and progresses rapidly to seizures, delirium and autonomic instability; high-dose benzodiazepines with GABAergic adjuncts (baclofen) and ICU admission for airway management are the recognised escalation pathway. (Source: Australian Clinical Guidelines: GHB withdrawal management)
source_refs: Australian Clinical Guidelines: GHB withdrawal management

options.text: Commence clonidine 75 microgram four times daily and dexmedetomidine infusion in a monitored bed, with hourly observations and a low threshold for repeating his routine bloods overnight if his agitation has not improved on this regimen
options.rationale: Alpha-2 agonists alone do not control GHB withdrawal-related seizures and delirium; the central problem is GABA-B underactivity and benzodiazepine-resistant agitation, requiring high-dose benzodiazepines and GABAergic adjuncts. (Source: Australian Clinical Guidelines: GHB withdrawal management)
source_refs: Australian Clinical Guidelines: GHB withdrawal management

options.text: Commence intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g over 30 minutes and intravenous thiamine 300 mg daily for 5 days as the primary pharmacological intervention for his withdrawal syndrome and assess his progress 12 hours after this loading regimen
options.rationale: Magnesium and thiamine are supportive only; severe GHB withdrawal requires high-dose benzodiazepines, GABAergic adjuncts and ICU-level monitoring rather than magnesium and thiamine as the primary intervention. (Source: Australian Clinical Guidelines: GHB withdrawal management)
source_refs: Australian Clinical Guidelines: GHB withdrawal management

options.text: Discharge him to a community withdrawal facility with twice-daily nursing review and oral diazepam taper over the next 7 days, with explicit instructions about return precautions for seizures or worsening behaviour after the discharge
options.rationale: Severe GHB withdrawal with seizures and delirium has a mortality risk and is not safe for community withdrawal; it requires inpatient and often intensive care management with airway support available. (Source: Australian Clinical Guidelines: GHB withdrawal management)
source_refs: Australian Clinical Guidelines: GHB withdrawal management

explanation.summary: GHB withdrawal in heavy daily users can begin within 4 to 6 hours of last dose, escalates rapidly over 24 to 72 hours, and produces an alcohol-withdrawal-like syndrome that is characteristically benzodiazepine-resistant with delirium, autonomic instability and seizures. Management is inpatient with high-dose benzodiazepine loading guided by sedation and seizure response, GABAergic adjuncts (baclofen or, in some centres, pharmaceutical sodium oxybate where available), and ICU-level monitoring for airway and ventilation. Antipsychotics worsen the delirium and lower seizure threshold. Mortality without appropriate inpatient management is significant.
key_points: GHB withdrawal in heavy daily users: onset 4 to 6 hours, peak 24 to 72 hours, prolonged course
Classically benzodiazepine-resistant; high-dose loading with baclofen adjunct often required
ICU monitoring for airway, autonomic instability and prolonged sedation requirements
Avoid antipsychotics: lower seizure threshold, worsen delirium; magnesium and thiamine are supportive only
explanation.pearls: If 60 mg of diazepam over 2 hours has barely touched the agitation in a daily GHB user, do not just keep stepping benzodiazepines - add baclofen and call ICU early, because the syndrome can progress to refractory delirium and respiratory arrest within hours.

sources.label: Australian Clinical Guidelines: GHB withdrawal management

subtopic_detail: Varenicline initiation for smoking cessation in a patient with treated depression
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 52-year-old man who has decided to make another quit attempt after smoking 20 cigarettes per day for 30 years. His depression has been stable on sertraline 100 mg daily for the past three years with no recent suicidal ideation, self-harm, or psychiatric admission, and his GP-led mental health plan is current. He has no history of seizures, no significant renal impairment (eGFR 88), and no cardiovascular events.

He has previously tried nicotine replacement therapy patches alone for two weeks but resumed smoking due to severe cravings. He asks for the most effective evidence-based pharmacotherapy.

data_table.Examination: Mood euthymic on sertraline, no current suicidal ideation, normal cardiovascular and respiratory exam, no recent cardiac events documented
data_table.Investigations: Recent eGFR 88, normal LFTs, normal ECG, exhaled CO 28 ppm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Varenicline 0.5 mg daily for three days then 0.5 mg twice daily for four days then 1 mg twice daily for a 12-week course, with quit date in week two and monitoring for neuropsychiatric symptoms and abnormal dreams at routine review
options.rationale: Varenicline has the strongest evidence for sustained abstinence in moderate to heavy smokers who have failed monotherapy NRT, with no excess neuropsychiatric risk in stable treated depression per the EAGLES trial. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines)

options.text: Bupropion sustained release 150 mg daily for three days then 150 mg twice daily for nine weeks with quit date in week two, and counsel on the increased seizure risk if he has any past head injury or eating disorder history
options.rationale: Bupropion is effective but is generally less efficacious than varenicline and is relatively contraindicated with current serotonergic antidepressants due to seizure threshold and serotonergic interactions. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines)

options.text: Nicotine patch 21 mg per 24 hours combined with short-acting nicotine lozenges as needed for cravings for 8 to 12 weeks, with weekly review and gradual tapering of the patch dose over the final four weeks of treatment
options.rationale: Combination NRT is a reasonable option and is more effective than patch alone, but varenicline still has the strongest evidence of efficacy for heavy smokers with prior NRT failure. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines)

options.text: Nortriptyline 25 mg nocte titrated to 75 mg nocte commencing two weeks before quit date for a 12-week course, with baseline ECG to assess QTc and monitoring for orthostatic hypotension and anticholinergic adverse effects
options.rationale: Nortriptyline is a second-line option only when first-line therapies are contraindicated or have failed; it should not be combined with sertraline due to additive serotonergic and adverse effect risks. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines)

options.text: Brief motivational counselling alone without pharmacotherapy with structured weekly review for the first month and referral to the Quitline 13 78 48 telephone counselling service to consolidate the patient's stated motivation to quit
options.rationale: Brief advice without pharmacotherapy has low quit rates in heavy smokers and would represent under-treatment given his history of NRT failure and clear motivation. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Varenicline is the most effective single pharmacotherapy for smoking cessation, with sustained quit rates roughly twice those of placebo and superior to single-agent NRT. The EAGLES trial demonstrated no excess neuropsychiatric adverse events in stable treated depression. Initiation is by titration to 1 mg twice daily with a quit date in week two, and treatment continues for 12 weeks with extension if abstinence achieved. Combination NRT is a reasonable alternative when varenicline is contraindicated.
key_points: Varenicline most effective; EAGLES showed safety in stable treated depression
Bupropion contraindicated with seizure risk and SSRI co-prescription is cautious
Combination NRT (patch + short-acting) > patch alone, but varenicline > combination NRT
explanation.pearls: Monitor for abnormal dreams, nausea, and any new suicidal ideation; warn that nicotine plasma levels may shift causing transient mood changes.

subtopic_detail: Long-term lithium monitoring with renal decline and parathyroid disturbance
stem: You are the community psychiatrist reviewing a 35-year-old woman on lithium 750 mg nocte for 8 years for bipolar I disorder, who is currently euthymic with no relapse during this time. Her routine annual monitoring shows progressive renal decline (eGFR fallen from 95 three years ago to 65 today), a lithium level within range at 0.7 mmol/L, subclinical hypothyroidism with TSH 7.2 and normal free T4, mildly elevated corrected calcium 2.68 mmol/L with raised PTH 9.8 pmol/L, BMI 28 and BP 130/82. She is asymptomatic, takes no other medications, and is planning a family within 12 months.

data_table.Investigations: Lithium 0.7 mmol/L, eGFR 65 (95 three years ago), TSH 7.2 (RR 0.4-4.0) free T4 normal, corrected calcium 2.68 (RR 2.20-2.60), PTH 9.8 (RR 1.6-6.9), urine ACR 4 mg/mmol, fasting glucose 5.2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue lithium at current dose and recheck eGFR, lithium level, TSH and calcium in 12 months as part of standard annual monitoring, with no immediate change to therapy given her euthymia and lithium level within range
options.rationale: Progressive renal decline plus emerging hyperparathyroidism and subclinical hypothyroidism warrants a change in approach rather than another 12 months of unchanged therapy. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders

options.text: Discuss with the patient cross-titration from lithium to an alternative mood stabiliser (e.g., quetiapine), continue lithium until the new agent is at therapeutic dose and stable for at least 6 weeks, and refer to nephrology and endocrinology for parallel management
options.rationale: Lithium-related progressive renal decline, hyperparathyroidism and subclinical hypothyroidism in a woman planning pregnancy warrant gradual cross-titration with specialist input rather than abrupt discontinuation. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders

options.text: Reduce lithium dose to 500 mg nocte to limit further renal injury and recheck eGFR and lithium level in 4 weeks while continuing the same drug as lower dose is generally renoprotective with preserved mood stabilising effect
options.rationale: Dose reduction alone does not reliably reverse lithium nephropathy and risks subtherapeutic levels and relapse; it does not address parathyroid pathology. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders

options.text: Add amiloride 5 mg daily as prophylaxis against lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and continue lithium at current dose, with no other change to therapy or referral and routine reassessment in 6 months
options.rationale: Amiloride may be considered for established nephrogenic DI but does not address the broader pattern of multi-organ lithium toxicity here, especially with pregnancy planned. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders

options.text: Stop lithium abruptly today and commence sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily as alternative mood stabiliser with serum level check at 1 week, while accepting some risk of mood relapse from abrupt change in maintenance therapy
options.rationale: Abrupt lithium discontinuation markedly increases relapse risk, and valproate is contraindicated in women planning pregnancy due to major teratogenicity. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders

explanation.summary: Long-term lithium use can cause progressive interstitial nephropathy, primary hyperparathyroidism and hypothyroidism, all of which are present here. In a woman planning pregnancy with multi-organ lithium effects and stable mood, cross-titration to an alternative mood stabiliser with multidisciplinary input (psychiatry, nephrology, endocrinology, obstetrics) is appropriate rather than continuing unchanged or abrupt cessation. Lithium should never be stopped abruptly outside of life-threatening toxicity due to high relapse risk.
key_points: Lithium long-term effects: nephropathy, hyperparathyroidism, hypothyroidism, NDI
Never stop lithium abruptly; cross-titrate over weeks
Valproate contraindicated in women of childbearing age unless pregnancy-prevention program in place
explanation.pearls: Annual monitoring: eGFR, electrolytes, calcium, PTH, TSH; lithium level 12 hours post-dose every 3-6 months; weight, BP, ECG as clinically indicated.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders

subtopic_detail: IM rapid tranquillisation for severe acute behavioural disturbance
stem: You are the emergency department registrar called to a 25-year-old man brought in by police on a Mental Health Act order following methamphetamine use earlier today. He is paranoid, threatening security staff, pacing, shouting and has thrown a chair. Verbal de-escalation by the senior nurse over 20 minutes has been unsuccessful and he is refusing oral medication. He has no past medical history, takes no regular medications, and there is no known QT prolongation or cardiac disease, but he will not allow ECG, vital sign measurement or IV cannulation. The team has decided to administer parenteral medication for safety.

data_table.Vital signs: Refusing measurement; visibly agitated, tachypnoeic, sweating
data_table.Examination: Aggressive, paranoid, pacing, shouting threats, throwing furniture, no obvious injury, no recent ETOH ingestion known
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen pending; no ECG available; collateral from family confirms first presentation, no known cardiac history or QT prolonging medications

lead_in: What is the most appropriate parenteral pharmacological choice?

options.text: Intramuscular droperidol 10 mg as a single dose with continuous physical observation for sedation, repeat 10 mg dose at 15 minutes if behaviour has not de-escalated, and arrange cardiac monitoring as soon as it can be safely applied
options.rationale: Droperidol 10 mg IM is Australian first-line for acute severe behavioural disturbance with a faster onset, fewer EPS than haloperidol, and a strong evidence base from emergency department trials. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic: Acute behavioural disturbance)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic: Acute behavioural disturbance

options.text: Intramuscular haloperidol 5 mg plus IM lorazepam 2 mg given concurrently into separate sites with cardiac monitoring planned as soon as possible, and clinical observation for extrapyramidal adverse effects over the following 4 hours
options.rationale: Haloperidol plus lorazepam is older practice and is associated with higher EPS, dystonia, and more cumulative sedation than droperidol monotherapy in Australian protocols. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic: Acute behavioural disturbance)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic: Acute behavioural disturbance

options.text: Intramuscular diazepam 10 mg as a single agent with intensive observation for respiratory depression and resedation, with consideration of additional doses every 30 minutes until sedation is achieved and assessment can proceed
options.rationale: IM diazepam is erratically absorbed and not recommended for acute behavioural disturbance; lorazepam IM is the preferred benzodiazepine if one is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic: Acute behavioural disturbance)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic: Acute behavioural disturbance

options.text: Intravenous midazolam 5 mg titrated against sedation in 2 mg aliquots with continuous pulse oximetry and respiratory monitoring, and IV access established under restraint by the security team before drug administration
options.rationale: IV access in a violently agitated patient before sedation is high risk for staff and patient; IM is preferred until safe sedation is achieved. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic: Acute behavioural disturbance)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic: Acute behavioural disturbance

options.text: Intramuscular zuclopenthixol acetate 100 mg as a longer-acting agent to control behaviour over several days while a longer-term plan is made, with observation for prolonged extrapyramidal adverse effects and slowed elimination
options.rationale: Zuclopenthixol acetate is not first-line for acute behavioural disturbance and is reserved for established psychosis when shorter-acting agents have failed and longer effect is genuinely desired. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic: Acute behavioural disturbance)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic: Acute behavioural disturbance

explanation.summary: Australian first-line parenteral therapy for acute severe behavioural disturbance is IM droperidol 10 mg (or IM olanzapine 10 mg as alternative); both have superior evidence to haloperidol-based regimens. The dose can be repeated at 15-minute intervals if needed. Continuous observation for sedation, respiratory rate and oxygen saturation is essential. IM is preferred over IV when restraint is required because IV cannulation in an agitated patient is unsafe.
key_points: First-line IM: droperidol 10 mg or olanzapine 10 mg
Avoid combining IM olanzapine with parenteral benzodiazepine (excess sedation/respiratory depression)
Continuous observation: airway, breathing, circulation, sedation score
explanation.pearls: Droperidol has a black box warning for QT prolongation but Australian ED trials (e.g., DORM study) have shown it is safe at 10 mg IM with appropriate monitoring.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic: Acute behavioural disturbance
Calver et al DORM Study Annals Emerg Med

subtopic_detail: Functional neurological disorder diagnosis with positive Hoover sign
stem:
You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar asked to review a 28-year-old woman with sudden onset left-sided 'paralysis' three days ago following an argument with her partner. Detailed neurological examination demonstrates a positive Hoover sign (involuntary left hip extension when contralateral hip flexion is tested against resistance), inconsistent power across formal versus distracted testing, normal reflexes and tone with no atrophy, and dragging non-physiological gait.

MRI brain and whole spine are normal, EMG and nerve conduction studies are normal. She is genuinely distressed by her symptoms, is not seeking compensation, has no pending legal matters, has not deliberately produced symptoms for medical attention, and has no prior psychiatric history.

data_table.Examination: Inconsistent power on distraction, positive Hoover sign on left, normal reflexes and tone, no muscle wasting, dragging non-physiological gait, intact sensation in non-anatomical pattern
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain and spine normal, EMG and NCS normal, CSF examination normal, autoimmune encephalitis panel pending and unlikely given chronology

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Malingering with deliberate production of motor symptoms for an external secondary gain such as financial compensation, time off work, or avoidance of an ongoing legal or relational obligation by the patient
options.rationale: Malingering requires an external incentive (compensation, legal, drug-seeking) which is absent here; the patient is genuinely distressed and not seeking external benefit. (Source: DSM-5-TR Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder)

options.text: Factitious disorder imposed on self with deliberate falsification of motor symptoms in order to assume the sick role and receive medical attention, in the absence of any obvious external incentive other than the sick role itself
options.rationale: Factitious disorder requires deliberate production of symptoms, which is excluded here by history; functional symptoms in FND are involuntary and genuinely experienced. (Source: DSM-5-TR Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder)

options.text: Functional neurological symptom disorder (also known as conversion disorder) diagnosed on positive clinical signs including a positive Hoover sign and inconsistency on distraction, with normal structural neurological investigations and an identifiable stressor
options.rationale: FND is now diagnosed by positive clinical signs (e.g., Hoover sign, tremor entrainment, give-way weakness) rather than by exclusion alone, and structural investigations are typically normal. (Source: DSM-5-TR Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder)

options.text: Somatic symptom disorder with one or more distressing physical symptoms accompanied by excessive disproportionate thoughts feelings and behaviours focused on those symptoms persisting more than six months in the typical clinical course
options.rationale: Somatic symptom disorder involves excessive worry about symptoms; here the disorder is a discrete motor deficit with positive neurological FND signs, not excessive symptom focus per se. (Source: DSM-5-TR Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder)

options.text: Acute stress reaction with psychomotor manifestations occurring within the first month after an interpersonal stressor and resolving spontaneously within four weeks without specific intervention beyond psychoeducation about the natural course
options.rationale: Acute stress disorder requires a traumatic event and a different symptom profile of intrusive, avoidant, mood and arousal symptoms; not a discrete motor deficit. (Source: DSM-5-TR Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder)

explanation.summary: Functional neurological symptom disorder (conversion disorder) is diagnosed by positive clinical signs of inconsistency and incongruence with neurological disease, such as Hoover sign for functional leg weakness or tremor entrainment for functional tremor. It is not a diagnosis of exclusion. Symptoms are genuinely experienced and not deliberately produced. Management is via clear non-stigmatising explanation, physiotherapy, and psychological therapy.
key_points: FND: diagnosed by positive signs (Hoover, entrainment), not exclusion
Malingering requires external incentive; factitious requires deliberate production
Treatment: explanation, physiotherapy, CBT, treat comorbid mood/anxiety
explanation.pearls: Communicating the diagnosis as a 'software not hardware' problem of the nervous system improves engagement and outcome; avoid 'all in your head' framing.

sources.label: Stone et al BMJ Functional Symptoms

subtopic_detail: Postpartum depression with active suicidal ideation requiring inpatient mother-baby admission
stem:
You are the GP reviewing a 28-year-old woman 8 weeks postpartum after her first baby, a healthy term boy now exclusively breastfed. She presents with low mood, anhedonia, marked guilt about being 'a bad mother', insomnia beyond infant sleep disruption, and weight loss. EPDS score today is 22 with item 10 endorsed. On further interview she describes recurrent suicidal thoughts with a tentative plan involving medications at home.

She denies any intent or thoughts to harm the baby. Her husband works long hours and there is no extended family nearby. She has no prior psychiatric history and is taking no medications.

data_table.Examination: Flat affect, tearful, slowed speech, denies psychotic symptoms, denies thoughts to harm baby, infant settled and well-cared-for at this visit
data_table.Investigations: EPDS 22 with positive item 10, TSH 1.8 (normal), Hb 122, ferritin 38, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Commence oral fluoxetine 20 mg daily, arrange community perinatal mental health team review tomorrow and ensure husband is aware to provide support, with discharge home today and follow-up safety planning by phone in 48 hours
options.rationale: Active suicidal ideation with plan in the context of severe postpartum depression and limited social support warrants admission, not community follow-up; fluoxetine also has a long half-life and is not first-line during breastfeeding. (Source: COPE Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines)

options.text: Arrange same-day admission to a mother-baby unit for combined inpatient assessment and treatment, commence sertraline as the SSRI most compatible with breastfeeding, and involve the perinatal psychiatry team for ongoing management
options.rationale: Severe postpartum depression with active suicidal ideation and plan requires inpatient care; mother-baby units in Australia allow continued breastfeeding and bonding while ensuring safety. (Source: COPE Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines)

options.text: Refer for outpatient cognitive behavioural therapy through the Better Access program with focus on cognitive restructuring and behavioural activation, with weekly EPDS reassessment by GP for the next 6 weeks before considering medication or admission
options.rationale: Psychological therapy alone is inadequate for severe postpartum depression with active suicidal ideation; safety must be addressed first via admission and pharmacotherapy. (Source: COPE Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines)

options.text: Admit to general adult psychiatry inpatient unit with separation of mother and baby for the duration of admission, commence sertraline 50 mg daily, and arrange community follow-up with paediatric review for the infant after discharge
options.rationale: Separation of mother and baby is harmful to bonding and breastfeeding; mother-baby units are preferred where available in Australia. (Source: COPE Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines)

options.text: Commence diazepam 5 mg twice daily for anxiety and insomnia, with brief sleep advice, and reassess in 1 week with view to commencing antidepressant therapy once sleep has been restored and mood appears more stable on benzodiazepine cover
options.rationale: Diazepam is not first-line for postpartum depression and crosses into breastmilk significantly; it does not treat the underlying condition and delays definitive care. (Source: COPE Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Postpartum depression with active suicidal ideation and a plan, particularly with limited social support, is a psychiatric emergency requiring admission to a mother-baby unit where available. Sertraline is the SSRI of choice during breastfeeding due to minimal infant exposure. Fluoxetine is avoided because of its long half-life and active metabolite. Psychological therapy and community follow-up have a role only when safety is established.
key_points: EPDS >=13 plus active suicidal ideation = high risk; consider admission
Mother-baby units preserve bonding and breastfeeding
Sertraline preferred SSRI in breastfeeding; avoid fluoxetine (long half-life)
explanation.pearls: Item 10 of EPDS (thoughts of self-harm) endorsement always warrants direct safety assessment and explicit suicide risk evaluation, regardless of total score.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Perinatal Mental Health

subtopic_detail: Continuing lithium in pregnancy for bipolar I with manic relapse history
stem:
You are the perinatal psychiatry registrar providing pre-conception counselling to a 32-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder, well controlled on lithium 750 mg nocte for the past 5 years with no mood episodes during this time. Her recent lithium level is 0.8 mmol/L, eGFR 90, TSH 2.4, corrected calcium normal. Three years ago she self-discontinued lithium for 6 weeks because of weight concerns and developed a severe manic episode requiring involuntary admission with psychosis.

She has had two earlier hospitalised manic episodes pre-lithium. She and her partner plan to commence trying to conceive within 2 months and she asks for advice on her medication during pregnancy.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no current suicidal ideation, no psychotic symptoms, insightful, motivated for pregnancy planning
data_table.Investigations: Lithium 0.8 mmol/L, eGFR 90, TSH 2.4, corrected calcium 2.40, FBC and UEC normal, urine bHCG negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pre-conception plan for her mood stabiliser?

options.text: Switch immediately to lamotrigine 25 mg daily with planned titration to 200 mg over 6 weeks as a safer mood stabiliser during conception and pregnancy, since lamotrigine has the most reassuring safety profile in pregnancy
options.rationale: Lamotrigine is more effective for depressive than manic episodes; her manic-predominant phenotype with severe manic relapses makes lamotrigine inadequate prophylaxis. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Perinatal Mental Health)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Perinatal Mental Health

options.text: Switch to sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily for the duration of pregnancy and the postpartum period, accepting some teratogenic risk in exchange for superior mood stabilisation across both manic and depressive episodes
options.rationale: Valproate has the highest teratogenic risk of any mood stabiliser (around 10 percent major congenital malformations plus neurodevelopmental risk) and is contraindicated in women planning pregnancy. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Perinatal Mental Health)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Perinatal Mental Health

options.text: Continue lithium at the lowest effective dose throughout pregnancy with fetal echocardiography at 18-20 weeks, monthly lithium levels with rising frequency near term, hydration counselling, and planned dose adjustment around delivery to avoid toxicity
options.rationale: Continuing lithium is appropriate given high relapse risk off lithium; absolute Ebstein anomaly risk is small (around 1 in 1000) and is screened with fetal echocardiography, with maternal benefit outweighing fetal risk in manic-predominant disease. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Perinatal Mental Health)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Perinatal Mental Health

options.text: Stop lithium abruptly at confirmation of pregnancy and restart only at the beginning of the second trimester after organogenesis is complete, with close monitoring for early mood relapse and re-titration of lithium dose at that time
options.rationale: First-trimester relapse risk is substantially higher than Ebstein risk; abrupt discontinuation also markedly increases relapse risk and has been associated with reduced response when lithium is restarted. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Perinatal Mental Health)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Perinatal Mental Health

options.text: Switch to quetiapine 300 mg nocte as a non-teratogenic atypical antipsychotic with mood-stabilising effect, with cross-titration off lithium over 4 weeks prior to conception and ongoing monitoring for metabolic adverse effects in pregnancy
options.rationale: Quetiapine is a reasonable alternative when lithium cannot be continued, but switching introduces relapse risk unnecessarily in a patient already well-controlled with severe manic recurrence history. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Perinatal Mental Health)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Perinatal Mental Health

explanation.summary: Lithium in early pregnancy is associated with a small absolute increase in Ebstein anomaly (background risk roughly 1 in 20,000; with first-trimester lithium roughly 1 in 1000-2000). This is detectable by fetal echocardiography at 18-20 weeks. In a patient with severe manic-predominant bipolar I and recent relapse off lithium, the maternal relapse risk on withdrawal far outweighs the small fetal cardiac risk. Continue lithium at the lowest effective dose, monitor levels monthly (then more frequently approaching term), maintain hydration, and reduce dose around delivery to avoid toxicity from volume contraction.
key_points: Continue lithium when manic-predominant illness and high relapse risk
Ebstein risk ~1:1000 with first-trimester lithium - screen at 18-20 weeks
Valproate contraindicated in women of childbearing age (10% major malformations)
explanation.pearls: Lithium clearance increases in second and third trimesters then plummets after delivery; check levels weekly in final weeks and reduce or hold dose at labour onset to avoid maternal toxicity post-partum.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Perinatal Mental Health
COPE Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines: Bipolar disorder in pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Lorazepam challenge for catatonia in a patient on aripiprazole
stem: You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar asked to review a 24-year-old woman with chronic schizophrenia on aripiprazole 30 mg daily, brought in by her family with one week of progressive mutism, immobility, posturing, waxy flexibility on examination, echolalia, and refusal of food and fluids. Examination shows BFCRS score 14 with prominent immobility, mutism, posturing, staring and grimacing. She is afebrile and haemodynamically stable. CK is 1200 with normal renal function and otherwise normal investigations including TSH, calcium, and a non-contrast CT brain.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7, HR 88, BP 118/72, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air, BFCRS 14
data_table.Examination: Mute, immobile, posturing with waxy flexibility, echolalia, staring, grimacing, no fever, no autonomic instability, no muscular rigidity beyond posturing
data_table.Investigations: CK 1200 (RR <200), eGFR 95, TSH 1.8, corrected calcium 2.38, FBC and UEC normal, urine drug screen negative, CT brain unremarkable, BFCRS 14

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological intervention?

options.text: Increase the aripiprazole dose to 30 mg daily intramuscularly with concurrent prophylactic benzatropine 2 mg IM to reduce extrapyramidal side effects and target the underlying psychotic illness that is presumably driving the catatonic state
options.rationale: Antipsychotics can worsen catatonia and risk progression to malignant catatonia or NMS; they should be reduced or paused while catatonia is treated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic: Catatonia)

options.text: Administer lorazepam 1-2 mg IV (or IM) as a challenge test, observe for clinical response over 30 minutes (improvement in mutism, immobility, posturing), commence regular lorazepam 6-8 mg/day if response is positive, and escalate or proceed to ECT if no response
options.rationale: Lorazepam challenge is the first-line test and treatment for catatonia; a partial response within 30 minutes guides ongoing scheduled lorazepam dosing, with ECT for refractory or malignant catatonia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic: Catatonia)

options.text: Administer haloperidol 5 mg IM as initial treatment for the underlying psychotic symptoms with planned regular dosing every 6 hours, monitoring for extrapyramidal side effects and dystonia in the first 24 hours of therapy
options.rationale: Haloperidol can precipitate malignant catatonia or NMS in a catatonic patient; antipsychotics should not be used to treat catatonia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic: Catatonia)

options.text: Commence clozapine 12.5 mg with planned titration over 2 weeks given the failure of aripiprazole to control her psychotic illness, with weekly FBC monitoring per the clozapine protocol and adjunctive lorazepam if needed
options.rationale: Clozapine is used in treatment-resistant schizophrenia after multiple trials but is not the first-line agent for catatonia; lorazepam challenge precedes any antipsychotic change. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic: Catatonia)

options.text: Proceed directly to electroconvulsive therapy after Mental Health Tribunal authorisation as the most rapidly effective therapy for catatonia, without trial of lorazepam first, given the severity of her clinical state and the urgency of treatment
options.rationale: ECT is the next step after lorazepam challenge failure (or for malignant catatonia or rapid deterioration); lorazepam trial precedes ECT in non-malignant catatonia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic: Catatonia)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is recognised by motor (immobility, posturing, waxy flexibility), behavioural (mutism, negativism, echolalia, echopraxia) and autonomic features. The Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale (BFCRS) supports recognition. First-line treatment is a lorazepam challenge (1-2 mg IV or IM), with positive response within 30 minutes guiding scheduled lorazepam at 6-8 mg/day (sometimes higher). Antipsychotics can worsen catatonia and risk progression to malignant catatonia or NMS. ECT is the definitive treatment in lorazepam non-responders and in malignant catatonia.
key_points: First-line: lorazepam 1-2 mg IV/IM challenge then 6-8 mg/day scheduled
Avoid antipsychotics in catatonia (risk of malignant catatonia/NMS)
ECT for refractory or malignant catatonia
explanation.pearls: Malignant catatonia (catatonia plus fever and autonomic instability) overlaps clinically with NMS and serotonin syndrome; immediate cessation of antipsychotics, supportive care, lorazepam and urgent ECT are required.

subtopic_detail: Antipsychotic metabolic monitoring at 12 weeks on olanzapine
stem:
You are the community mental health team registrar reviewing a 28-year-old man who has been on olanzapine 10 mg nocte for 12 weeks for a first episode of schizophrenia. He is settled mentally, has good adherence and minimal residual psychotic symptoms. Since starting treatment he has gained 6 kg in weight and reports daytime sedation, increased appetite and reduced exercise.

His baseline 12 weeks ago showed normal weight, normal fasting glucose, normal lipid panel and a normal ECG. He has no chest pain, no orthostatic symptoms, no galactorrhoea and no gynaecomastia. He has no past medical history and is not on any other regular medications.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 128/82, HR 78, BMI 27 (baseline 23), waist circumference 96 cm (up 8 cm)
data_table.Examination: Settled affect, no extrapyramidal side effects, no orthostatic hypotension, normal cardiovascular and abdominal examination, no obvious tardive dyskinesia
data_table.Investigations: Baseline 12 weeks ago: fasting glucose 4.9 normal, lipids normal, ECG QTc 410 ms, prolactin not done

lead_in: What is the most appropriate panel of monitoring investigations to request at this 12-week review?

options.text: HbA1c alone as the most sensitive marker for olanzapine-related glucose dysregulation, given that fasting glucose may miss postprandial hyperglycaemia in early metabolic disturbance and is more practical in the community mental health setting
options.rationale: HbA1c alone is insufficient; the recommended panel is fasting glucose (or HbA1c), fasting lipid profile, weight, BMI and waist circumference at 12 weeks. (Source: RANZCP: Antipsychotic Monitoring Guidelines)

options.text: Thyroid function tests including TSH free T4 free T3 and thyroid antibodies given the weight gain, sedation and possible iatrogenic hypothyroidism related to olanzapine treatment, and assessment of any underlying thyroid contribution to ongoing symptoms
options.rationale: Thyroid testing is not indicated as routine antipsychotic monitoring without specific clinical features of thyroid disease; metabolic panel is the priority. (Source: RANZCP: Antipsychotic Monitoring Guidelines)

options.text: Fasting glucose or HbA1c, fasting lipid profile, body weight, BMI and waist circumference, with consideration of metformin and clozapine review if metabolic parameters have deteriorated significantly compared to the baseline values taken before olanzapine commencement
options.rationale: RANZCP and Maudsley antipsychotic metabolic monitoring at 12 weeks comprises fasting glucose or HbA1c, fasting lipid panel, weight, BMI and waist circumference. (Source: RANZCP: Antipsychotic Monitoring Guidelines)

options.text: Serum prolactin level alone as the primary monitoring test given that olanzapine carries a class warning for hyperprolactinaemia and patients may not volunteer sexual dysfunction or galactorrhoea symptoms without specific prompting at review consultations
options.rationale: Olanzapine is not a high-prolactin antipsychotic; routine prolactin is for prolactin-elevating agents such as risperidone or amisulpride or when clinically symptomatic. (Source: RANZCP: Antipsychotic Monitoring Guidelines)

options.text: Repeat 12-lead ECG for assessment of QTc prolongation as the highest priority safety check on antipsychotic therapy at this stage, given that 12 weeks corresponds to the typical timeframe for delayed cardiac repolarisation changes to manifest fully
options.rationale: Olanzapine is low QTc risk; routine repeat ECG is not standard antipsychotic monitoring at 12 weeks unless QTc-prolonging factors are present. (Source: RANZCP: Antipsychotic Monitoring Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Antipsychotic metabolic monitoring at the 12-week mark of treatment in Australia follows the RANZCP and Maudsley guidance: fasting glucose or HbA1c, fasting lipid profile, body weight, body mass index, and waist circumference. Olanzapine and clozapine are the highest-risk second-generation agents for weight gain, dyslipidaemia and glucose dysregulation. If metabolic parameters deteriorate beyond a 5% increase in weight or new metabolic syndrome criteria, options include lifestyle support, metformin add-on, and switching to lower-risk antipsychotics such as aripiprazole. Prolactin and ECG are reserved for specific agent profiles or clinical features.
key_points: 12-week panel: fasting glucose or HbA1c, fasting lipids, weight, BMI, waist circumference
Olanzapine and clozapine are highest metabolic risk; aripiprazole lowest
Metformin add-on indicated for weight gain greater than 5% on antipsychotic
explanation.pearls: RANZCP suggests metabolic monitoring at baseline, 6 weeks, 12 weeks, 6 months and annually thereafter; consider switching agent if BMI rises by 1 kg/m^2 or other metabolic criteria emerge.

subtopic_detail: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose sodium bicarbonate for QRS prolongation
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar managing a 19-year-old woman brought in 2 hours after ingesting 50 tablets of her grandmother's amitriptyline 25 mg as a deliberate self-poisoning. She is drowsy but rouses to voice. Her airway is patent and she is breathing spontaneously. A 12-lead ECG taken now shows sinus tachycardia at 122 with a QRS duration of 130 ms, a terminal R wave of 4 mm in aVR, and no other ischaemic features.

There is no significant past medical history, no allergies, and no other co-ingestants identified or admitted. Activated charcoal was not given as ingestion was more than an hour ago. Senior emergency consultant and clinical toxicologist have been called.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8, HR 122, BP 92/58, RR 16, SpO2 97% room air, GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6), bedside glucose 5.6 mmol/L
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, dilated pupils 6 mm bilaterally reacting sluggishly, dry mucous membranes, hypoactive bowel sounds, no clonus, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: 12-lead ECG: sinus tachycardia 122, QRS 130 ms, terminal R wave 4 mm in aVR; VBG pH 7.32 pCO2 38 HCO3 18; potassium 3.4, sodium 138, creatinine 78

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Administer intravenous physostigmine 2 mg slowly with continuous cardiac monitoring to reverse the central and peripheral anticholinergic features, with atropine immediately available at the bedside to manage any clinically significant bradycardia
options.rationale: Physostigmine is contraindicated in TCA overdose because it can precipitate asystole or seizures; sodium bicarbonate is the antidote. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology: TCA Overdose)

options.text: Activated charcoal 50 g via nasogastric tube to bind the remaining tricyclic antidepressant in the gastrointestinal tract, with intubation prior to administration if the patient's Glasgow Coma Scale falls further during preparation for the procedure
options.rationale: Activated charcoal beyond 1-2 hours post-ingestion has limited benefit and risks aspiration; cardiac stabilisation with sodium bicarbonate is the priority. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology: TCA Overdose)

options.text: Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate 8.4% 1 to 2 mmol/kg as a bolus aiming to narrow the QRS and alkalinise serum pH to 7.45 to 7.55, intubate and ventilate to support pH if needed, continuous cardiac monitoring and intensive care admission
options.rationale: Sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol/kg is the antidote for TCA-induced QRS prolongation and hypotension; aim for pH 7.45-7.55 with narrowing of QRS as the endpoint. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology: TCA Overdose)

options.text: Commence intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg titrated to GCS improvement, with continuous cardiac monitoring during administration and observation in resuscitation for 4 hours, alongside intravenous fluids to support blood pressure and reverse the anticholinergic syndrome
options.rationale: Flumazenil is contraindicated in mixed overdose where TCA is involved due to seizure risk and has no role in TCA toxicity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology: TCA Overdose)

options.text: Commence haemodialysis urgently with vascular access via right internal jugular vein quad-lumen catheter to clear the tricyclic antidepressant from the systemic circulation, with continuous cardiac monitoring and intensive care admission for the procedure
options.rationale: TCAs have a large volume of distribution and high protein binding so are not effectively cleared by haemodialysis; sodium bicarbonate is the antidote. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology: TCA Overdose)

explanation.summary: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose causes cardiotoxicity through sodium channel blockade leading to QRS prolongation, terminal R wave in aVR, hypotension and arrhythmias. Sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol/kg bolus is the antidote, working through both sodium loading and serum alkalinisation (target pH 7.45-7.55). The endpoint is QRS narrowing to under 100 ms. Intubation may be needed to maintain controlled ventilation and pH. Activated charcoal is reserved for ingestions within 1-2 hours of presentation; flumazenil and physostigmine are contraindicated; haemodialysis does not work due to high volume of distribution.
key_points: Sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol/kg for QRS over 100 ms or hypotension; target pH 7.45-7.55
Endpoint is QRS narrowing under 100 ms
Flumazenil and physostigmine contraindicated; haemodialysis ineffective
explanation.pearls: Persistent hypotension despite sodium bicarbonate is treated with intravenous lipid emulsion 20% as a 1.5 mL/kg bolus and consideration of intra-aortic balloon pump or VA-ECMO in severe refractory cases.

subtopic_detail: Borderline personality disorder DBT first-line outpatient referral
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 24-year-old woman with five emergency department presentations over the past 8 months for recurrent superficial cutting and overdose threats following relationship conflicts. She describes a pervasive sense of emptiness, marked identity disturbance, intense unstable interpersonal relationships, and impulsive episodes of binge eating, spending and sexual activity. Her affect varies sharply over hours.

She has been on three different antidepressants and a low-dose antipsychotic over the last 2 years with no sustained benefit. She has no current intent or plan to end her life today, and has agreed to engage with outpatient mental health services for a sustainable longer-term plan.

data_table.Examination: Multiple superficial linear scars on the forearms in different stages of healing, no fresh wounds, mildly tearful affect, clear sensorium, no thought disorder, no psychotic symptoms, no current suicidal ideation
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, TFTs all within normal limits; urine drug screen negative; ECG normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Increase her current sertraline to 200 mg daily with addition of quetiapine 100 mg nocte for affective instability and impulsivity, with weekly general practice review for the first month and mental health care plan referral for supportive counselling
options.rationale: Pharmacotherapy is not first-line for core borderline personality disorder symptoms; structured psychotherapy such as DBT is first-line per RANZCP guidance. (Source: RANZCP: Personality Disorders)

options.text: Admit voluntarily to an acute psychiatric inpatient unit for 4 to 6 weeks to provide containment and intensive day-long therapy with daily group work and individual sessions, with discharge planning back to the community mental health team
options.rationale: Prolonged psychiatric admission for borderline personality disorder is associated with worse outcomes and regression; outpatient structured psychotherapy is preferred. (Source: RANZCP: Personality Disorders)

options.text: Initiate weekly cognitive behavioural therapy alone delivered through a 10-session mental health care plan with the general practitioner, given the high prevalence of cognitive distortions and maladaptive coping strategies underpinning the personality presentation
options.rationale: Standard CBT is less evidence-based for borderline personality disorder than dialectical behaviour therapy or other structured personality-disorder-specific therapies. (Source: RANZCP: Personality Disorders)

options.text: Refer to a community-based dialectical behaviour therapy program as first-line treatment with planned 12-month duration involving weekly individual therapy, weekly skills group and between-session coaching, with general practice mental health care plan as the funding pathway
options.rationale: Dialectical behaviour therapy is first-line evidence-based treatment for borderline personality disorder per RANZCP and NHMRC, reducing self-harm and ED presentations over 12 months. (Source: RANZCP: Personality Disorders)

options.text: Discharge to general practice care only with planned mental health care plan and supportive counselling, given that personality disorders typically do not respond to specialist mental health input and management is primarily through chronic disease care frameworks
options.rationale: Borderline personality disorder is treatable with structured psychotherapy; declining specialist referral underestimates evidence base for therapeutic response. (Source: RANZCP: Personality Disorders)

explanation.summary: Borderline personality disorder is treatable, with structured psychotherapy as first-line care according to RANZCP and NHMRC guidance. Dialectical behaviour therapy (Linehan), with weekly individual therapy, weekly skills group, between-session coaching and therapist consultation team, has the strongest evidence base, reducing self-harm, emergency presentations and hospitalisation over 12-month courses. Other evidence-based therapies include mentalisation-based therapy, schema therapy, and transference-focused psychotherapy. Pharmacotherapy is not first-line and is reserved for short-term management of comorbid depression, anxiety or psychotic features.
key_points: DBT is first-line for borderline personality disorder
Pharmacotherapy is adjunctive, not core treatment
Prolonged inpatient admission worsens outcomes; outpatient structured psychotherapy preferred
explanation.pearls: Brief crisis admissions of 1 to 3 days for acute risk are acceptable but should be structured with a clear discharge plan back to outpatient psychotherapy to avoid iatrogenic regression.

sources.label: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder

subtopic_detail: Cannabis-induced psychosis observation off substance before antipsychotic
stem:
You are the early psychosis team registrar reviewing a 19-year-old man brought to the assessment unit by his family for a 2-week history of persecutory delusions, auditory hallucinations and disorganised behaviour. He has been smoking high-potency cannabis daily for the past 2 years and increased to multiple uses per day in the month prior to symptom onset. There is no family history of schizophrenia or other psychotic illness.

He has had no previous psychotic episodes, no suicidal or homicidal intent today, has no acute aggression, and has agreed voluntarily to inpatient assessment with his family supportive. Urine drug screen is positive for THC only. He has had a negative test for methamphetamine and other stimulants.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.0, HR 98, BP 124/78, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air, BMI 22
data_table.Examination: Mildly anxious, persecutory delusions, occasional auditory hallucinations, no thought disorder evident on examination, no extrapyramidal signs, no neurology deficit, no signs of intoxication or withdrawal currently
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen THC positive, all other substances negative; FBC, UEC, LFTs and TFTs normal; ECG normal; non-contrast CT head normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management plan?

options.text: Admit to an inpatient psychiatric unit voluntarily, cease all cannabis use with structured withdrawal support, observe for up to 4 weeks off cannabis, commence low-dose olanzapine 5 mg nocte if symptoms persist, and refer to early psychosis intervention service
options.rationale: Cannabis-induced psychotic disorder is managed with abstinence and observation; antipsychotic is started for persistent symptoms with planned weaning; early psychosis service follow-up captures transition to primary psychotic illness. (Source: RANZCP: Substance-induced Psychosis)

options.text: Commence clozapine 12.5 mg nocte titrating up over 2 weeks under the early psychosis service for treatment-resistant first-episode psychosis given the chronicity of cannabis use, with weekly FBC monitoring and cardiac monitoring per protocol
options.rationale: Clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia after failure of two adequate antipsychotic trials; it is not first-line for any psychosis presentation. (Source: RANZCP: Substance-induced Psychosis)

options.text: Commit to involuntary detention under the Mental Health Act and arrange urgent electroconvulsive therapy for severe disorganised psychotic features, given the failure of community management to date and the chronic high-potency cannabis use pattern documented
options.rationale: He is engaging voluntarily without acute risk, so involuntary detention is inappropriate; ECT is not first-line for substance-induced psychosis. (Source: RANZCP: Substance-induced Psychosis)

options.text: Commence outpatient management with a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor for likely underlying mood and anxiety symptoms, with cognitive behavioural therapy referral and harm-minimisation cannabis counselling through the local drug and alcohol service
options.rationale: SSRI is not indicated for psychosis; the presentation requires psychiatric assessment, abstinence support and possible antipsychotic, not outpatient SSRI alone. (Source: RANZCP: Substance-induced Psychosis)

options.text: Refer urgently for schizoaffective disorder workup including mood charting and family interview, commence lithium 750 mg nocte after baseline renal and thyroid testing, and arrange outpatient psychiatric follow-up within the next 2 weeks for definitive diagnostic clarification
options.rationale: Schizoaffective diagnosis requires sustained mood episodes alongside psychotic symptoms; presenting picture is acute substance-induced psychosis. (Source: RANZCP: Substance-induced Psychosis)

explanation.summary: Cannabis-induced psychotic disorder requires abstinence and observation for at least 4 weeks before assigning a primary psychotic illness diagnosis. Inpatient admission supports cessation, monitoring and family education. Antipsychotic medication (low-dose olanzapine, risperidone or aripiprazole) is added if symptoms persist beyond 1 to 2 weeks or are severe. Early psychosis intervention services in Australia (such as headspace and EPPIC) provide structured follow-up; approximately 25 to 50% of cannabis-induced psychotic episodes transition to a primary psychotic illness, with younger age, longer duration of use and family history increasing risk.
key_points: Cease cannabis and observe 4 weeks before committing to primary psychotic illness diagnosis
Low-dose antipsychotic if symptoms persist or are severe
Approximately 25-50% transition to primary psychotic illness; early psychosis service follow-up
explanation.pearls: Synthetic cannabinoids (such as Spice and K2) cause severe agitation, seizures, hyperthermia, and rhabdomyolysis, with longer-duration psychotic symptoms than natural cannabis and resistance to standard urine drug screens.

subtopic_detail: Adult ADHD methylphenidate initiation with driving counselling
stem:
You are the consultant psychiatrist completing the new diagnosis of adult attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (combined presentation) in a 26-year-old IT engineer who has had longstanding inattention, impulsivity and emotional dysregulation. He drives 1 hour each way for his daily commute. There is no history of cardiac disease, no family history of sudden cardiac death, no current substance misuse, and no current depression or anxiety requiring treatment.

His baseline ECG is normal with QTc 410 ms and his blood pressure is 130/80. He is keen to start medication and understands stimulants are first-line. He has read consumer information and consented to monitoring.

data_table.Examination: Mildly restless, no thought disorder, no psychotic features, no neurology deficit, no signs of intoxication
data_table.Investigations: ECG normal QTc 410 ms, FBC, UEC, LFTs, TFTs all within normal limits; urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy plan and accompanying counselling?

options.text: Counsel that stimulants are contraindicated for daily drivers due to the impact on cognition and reaction time, and commence atomoxetine 40 mg daily as a non-stimulant first-line therapy with planned 6-week review of symptom response and tolerability
options.rationale: Stimulants generally improve, not impair, driving performance in adult ADHD; they remain first-line. Atomoxetine is second-line per RANZCP and Australian Practice Standards. (Source: RANZCP: ADHD in Adults)

options.text: Commence methylphenidate immediate-release 10 mg twice daily titrating weekly to symptom response and tolerability, counsel that driving while titrating is acceptable once side effects have stabilised, and arrange 4-week review with repeat BP, HR and side-effect assessment
options.rationale: Stimulants such as methylphenidate are first-line for adult ADHD per RANZCP; titration with side-effect monitoring is standard; driving advice is to take dose before driving once tolerated. (Source: RANZCP: ADHD in Adults)

options.text: Refer to a private neuropsychologist for cognitive testing and computerised continuous performance task to confirm diagnostic uncertainty before commencing any pharmacotherapy, with planned review after the formal cognitive assessment results are available
options.rationale: Diagnosis of adult ADHD is clinical per DSM-5 criteria; neuropsychological testing is an adjunct, not required to start treatment once diagnosis is established. (Source: RANZCP: ADHD in Adults)

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg daily for likely comorbid anxiety or depression as the most parsimonious treatment for adult ADHD-like presentations, given the substantial overlap of symptoms and the favourable side-effect profile of SSRIs as a first step
options.rationale: SSRIs are not effective for core ADHD symptoms; pharmacotherapy targets ADHD with stimulants or atomoxetine, with SSRI reserved for comorbid depression or anxiety. (Source: RANZCP: ADHD in Adults)

options.text: Commence clonidine 50 micrograms three times daily for adult ADHD, with planned 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring during titration and dose escalation, and a planned outpatient review at 4 weeks for symptom and side-effect assessment
options.rationale: Clonidine is third-line for ADHD, mainly used in children with tic disorders or sleep onset; not first-line in adult ADHD per Australian practice. (Source: RANZCP: ADHD in Adults)

explanation.summary: Adult ADHD diagnosis is clinical and based on DSM-5 criteria. Stimulant medications (methylphenidate or lisdexamfetamine) are first-line per RANZCP and the Australian ADHD Professionals Association guidelines, with non-stimulant atomoxetine or guanfacine as second-line, and clonidine third-line. Pre-treatment workup includes baseline BP, HR, ECG, and screening for cardiac and psychiatric risk factors. Driving is generally improved by stimulant treatment but patients should be counselled to take their dose before driving once tolerability is established. Comorbid depression, anxiety and substance use disorders are screened for and treated alongside.
key_points: Methylphenidate or lisdexamfetamine first-line per RANZCP
Atomoxetine and guanfacine second-line; clonidine third-line
Pre-treatment: baseline BP, HR, ECG; screen for cardiac and psychiatric comorbidity
explanation.pearls: Schedule 8 stimulant prescribing requires state-based authority (e.g. NSW Pharmaceutical Services Branch) for adults newly diagnosed with ADHD; clinicians must verify their state's authority requirements before prescribing.

sources.label: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

stem: A 15-year-old girl is reviewed by her general practitioner with her mother. Over the past 4 months she has had persistent low mood, anhedonia, fatigue, mid-afternoon naps, dropping school grades, and irritability. She denies suicidal ideation. She has tried 8 weeks of psychological therapy with no improvement. There is no substance use. Her mother is keen to consider medication.

data_table.Examination: Affect dysphoric, mood subjectively low, reactive, no psychomotor retardation, insight preserved, no psychotic features, MSE otherwise normal
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, TFTs, B12, vitamin D, urine drug screen all normal

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate pharmacological first step?

options.text: Sertraline 50 mg orally daily, titrated upward as clinically tolerated
options.rationale: Sertraline is a reasonable second-line SSRI in adolescent depression but does not have the same level of trial evidence as fluoxetine, which is the only SSRI approved for under-18s in Australia. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Mood Disorders)

options.text: Mirtazapine 15 mg orally at night to address sleep difficulty and appetite
options.rationale: Mirtazapine is not first-line in adolescent depression; its sedating and weight-gain effects are not preferred, and SSRIs have stronger paediatric evidence. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Mood Disorders)

options.text: Fluoxetine 10 mg orally daily with weekly review during the first 4 weeks
options.rationale: Fluoxetine is the first-line SSRI in adolescent moderate-severe depression with the strongest efficacy evidence and is the only SSRI specifically approved in this age group in Australia. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Mood Disorders)

options.text: Venlafaxine 75 mg orally daily as a sustained-release titration schedule
options.rationale: SNRIs are not first-line in adolescent depression and carry a higher discontinuation syndrome and blood-pressure burden; SSRIs are preferred initially. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Mood Disorders)

options.text: Amitriptyline 25 mg orally at night for low mood and insomnia management
options.rationale: Tricyclic antidepressants have not shown efficacy in adolescent depression and carry significant overdose risk, so are not recommended in this age group. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Mood Disorders)

explanation.summary: Australian guidance for moderate-severe adolescent depression that has not responded to 6 to 8 weeks of psychological therapy recommends fluoxetine as the first-line SSRI, with weekly initial reviews because of a small absolute increase in suicidal ideation in the first month of treatment. Sertraline and escitalopram are reasonable second-line SSRIs if fluoxetine is not tolerated. Combining medication with continued CBT or interpersonal therapy improves response. TCAs and MAOIs are not used in adolescents.
key_points: Fluoxetine is the only SSRI specifically approved in Australian adolescents
Combine pharmacotherapy with continued psychological therapy
Weekly review in the first month to monitor suicidal ideation and side effects
explanation.pearls: Black-box warnings for suicidal ideation with SSRIs in under-25s reflect a small absolute risk increase confined mostly to the first 1 to 4 weeks; weekly review during that window mitigates the risk.

stem: A 36-year-old paramedic presents 4 months after a critical-incident motor vehicle collision in which a colleague died. He describes intrusive memories, nightmares, hypervigilance, avoidance of the highway, and emotional numbing. Symptoms are present most days. He has had no previous mental illness, no substance use, and is currently on leave from work. There is no suicidal ideation. He prefers a non-pharmacological starting point.

data_table.Examination: Affect anxious, mood subjectively low, sleep poor with nightmares 4 nights/week, no psychotic features, insight preserved
data_table.Investigations: PCL-5 score 52

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate first-line therapy?

options.text: Supportive counselling without trauma-focused techniques over 12 weeks
options.rationale: Generic supportive counselling without trauma-focused techniques is inferior to trauma-focused CBT or EMDR for PTSD symptom reduction. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines 2020)

options.text: Critical incident stress debriefing delivered as a single-session intervention
options.rationale: Single-session psychological debriefing is not effective for PTSD prevention or treatment and may worsen outcomes; it is no longer recommended. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines 2020)

options.text: Sertraline 50 mg orally daily as first-line pharmacological monotherapy
options.rationale: Sertraline has evidence in PTSD but Australian guidance positions it as second-line after trauma-focused psychological therapy in patients who can engage with therapy, and the patient prefers a non-pharmacological start. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines 2020)

options.text: Trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy weekly for 8 to 12 sessions
options.rationale: Trauma-focused CBT is a Phoenix Australia and RANZCP first-line recommendation for adult PTSD, with consistent strong evidence across military and civilian populations. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines 2020)

options.text: Prazosin 1 mg orally at night targeting trauma nightmares as sole therapy
options.rationale: Prazosin is an adjunct for trauma-related nightmares but is not a stand-alone PTSD treatment; primary therapy is trauma-focused psychological intervention. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines 2020)

explanation.summary: PTSD requires symptoms for at least 1 month after a Criterion A traumatic exposure, with intrusion, avoidance, negative cognitions/mood and hyperarousal clusters. Australian Phoenix guidelines and RANZCP recommend trauma-focused CBT or EMDR as first-line treatment for adult PTSD. SSRIs (sertraline, paroxetine) and venlafaxine are second-line, used when psychological therapy is unavailable, declined, or insufficient. Prazosin is an adjunct for nightmares. Critical incident debriefing is no longer recommended.
key_points: Trauma-focused CBT and EMDR are first-line for adult PTSD
SSRIs (especially sertraline) are second-line pharmacotherapy
Single-session debriefing is not recommended and may worsen outcomes
explanation.pearls: Phoenix Australia recommends 8 to 12 weekly sessions of trauma-focused CBT for adult PTSD; a typical course incorporates psychoeducation, in-vivo and imaginal exposure, and cognitive restructuring.

stem: A 52-year-old man with bipolar I disorder has been on lithium 750 mg at night for 6 years. Two days ago he started ramipril 5 mg for newly diagnosed hypertension. Today he attends with 24 hours of coarse hand tremor, nausea, vomiting and ataxia. He has been struggling to keep down fluids. His last lithium level 3 weeks ago was 0.7 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 37.0 degrees Celsius, HR 88, BP 130/82 mmHg, RR 16
data_table.Examination: Coarse tremor of both hands, mild ataxia on standing, normal mental status, mild dehydration, no nystagmus, deep tendon reflexes brisk
data_table.Investigations: Lithium level pending, Na 138, K 4.2, urea 8.4 mmol/L, creatinine 132 micromol/L (baseline 92)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer oral activated charcoal 50 g to bind any further absorbed lithium
options.rationale: Activated charcoal does not bind lithium meaningfully and is not used in lithium toxicity. (Source: AMH: Lithium)

options.text: Continue lithium and administer ondansetron 4 mg intravenously for nausea
options.rationale: Continuing lithium in a symptomatic patient with rising creatinine and a likely toxic level worsens neurological injury; the precipitant must be withdrawn. (Source: AMH: Lithium)

options.text: Arrange urgent haemodialysis now without waiting for the lithium level result
options.rationale: Haemodialysis is indicated for severe lithium toxicity (level above 4 mmol/L, level 2.5 to 4 with severe symptoms or renal failure, or impaired clearance) but is not first-line for mild-moderate toxicity that may respond to fluid resuscitation. (Source: AMH: Lithium)

options.text: Switch the antihypertensive to a thiazide diuretic and continue the lithium
options.rationale: Thiazides also raise lithium levels by reducing distal tubular sodium delivery; switching to a thiazide worsens lithium retention rather than helping it. (Source: AMH: Lithium)

options.text: Hold lithium and give intravenous normal saline at 1 L per hour and recheck
options.rationale: Acute on chronic lithium toxicity from ACE-inhibitor-induced renal lithium retention and dehydration is treated with stopping the precipitant, lithium hold and IV crystalloid to enhance renal excretion. (Source: AMH: Lithium)

explanation.summary: Acute on chronic lithium toxicity classically follows the addition of an ACE inhibitor, ARB, thiazide or NSAID to a chronic lithium user. Renal lithium retention plus dehydration tips levels into the toxic range. Early features are coarse tremor, GI upset, ataxia and confusion; severe toxicity includes seizures, coma and arrhythmia. Initial management is to stop the precipitant, hold lithium, give intravenous crystalloid, and check lithium and renal function. Haemodialysis is reserved for severe toxicity (level above 4 mmol/L, severe symptoms, renal failure).
key_points: ACEi, ARB, thiazide and NSAID raise lithium levels
Early features: tremor, GI symptoms, ataxia
Haemodialysis if level above 4 mmol/L or severe symptoms with renal impairment
explanation.pearls: Therapeutic lithium range is 0.4 to 1.0 mmol/L for maintenance and up to 1.2 mmol/L for acute mania; symptoms generally appear above 1.5 mmol/L and dialysis is considered above 4 mmol/L or above 2.5 mmol/L with renal failure.

stem: A 19-year-old woman with severe anorexia nervosa (BMI 13.5) is admitted to a medical ward for refeeding. Day 2 of structured refeeding at 30 kcal/kg/day, she develops new-onset peripheral oedema, calf cramps and palpitations. She is conscious and oriented. Her electrolytes were normal on admission.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 36.4 degrees Celsius, HR 110, BP 100/64 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 98% in room air
data_table.Examination: Bilateral pitting ankle oedema, calf tenderness on stretch, normal heart sounds, no peripheral neuropathy, abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Phosphate 0.42 mmol/L (1.05 on admission), magnesium 0.58 mmol/L, potassium 3.1, glucose 4.4, ECG shows QTc 480 ms with no arrhythmia

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Replace phosphate, magnesium and potassium intravenously and reduce calories
options.rationale: This is biochemical refeeding syndrome with hypophosphataemia, hypomagnesaemia and hypokalaemia; standard practice is IV replacement of the three electrolytes plus thiamine, with reduced (not stopped) caloric load. (Source: ANZAED Guidelines)

options.text: Stop nutrition entirely until serum phosphate is above 1.0 mmol/L overnight
