options.rationale: Stopping nutrition risks further metabolic collapse and reverses the gains of feeding; the correct response is to reduce caloric load and aggressively replace electrolytes, not zero feeding. (Source: ANZAED Guidelines)

options.text: Administer intravenous furosemide 40 mg for the new bilateral peripheral oedema
options.rationale: Refeeding oedema is from sodium and water retention plus reduced oncotic pressure; loop diuretics worsen electrolyte derangements and are contraindicated in this context. (Source: ANZAED Guidelines)

options.text: Increase the caloric load to compensate for any ongoing weight loss observed
options.rationale: Increasing calories during active refeeding syndrome will accelerate metabolic complications; the correct move is to reduce caloric load while replacing electrolytes. (Source: ANZAED Guidelines)

options.text: Commence a beta blocker for the tachycardia with serial QTc monitoring
options.rationale: Beta blockers in severe anorexia carry hypotension and bradycardia risks and do not address the underlying electrolyte problem driving the tachycardia and QT prolongation. (Source: ANZAED Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Refeeding syndrome is the rapid intracellular shift of phosphate, potassium and magnesium that follows reintroduction of carbohydrate in severely malnourished patients, classically those with BMI under 14 or rapid weight loss. Manifestations include hypophosphataemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypokalaemia, thiamine deficiency (Wernicke), peripheral oedema, cardiac arrhythmia and acute heart failure. Management is electrolyte replacement (intravenous if severe), thiamine 100 to 200 mg daily, reduction in caloric load (not cessation), and twice-daily biochemistry monitoring during the high-risk window of the first week.
key_points: Hypophosphataemia is the hallmark electrolyte derangement
Replace phosphate, magnesium, potassium and give thiamine; reduce calories, do not stop
Twice-daily electrolytes for the first 5 to 7 days of refeeding in high-risk patients
explanation.pearls: ANZAED guidance recommends starting refeeding at 20 to 30 kcal/kg/day with twice-daily electrolytes and pre-emptive thiamine 100 mg, increasing calories cautiously by 10 kcal/kg/day if biochemistry stays stable.

stem: A 38-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia on clozapine 450 mg at night for 5 years was admitted to a general ward after a road traffic collision. He has been nil by mouth for 65 hours pending surgery and has not received any clozapine. Surgery is now postponed for 24 hours and oral intake can resume. He has had no agitation or psychotic relapse, his ECG is normal and he has a normal white cell count.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 36.7 degrees Celsius, HR 84, BP 124/76 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Calm, oriented, no psychotic symptoms
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 6.4, neutrophils 4.1, ECG normal sinus rhythm, troponin normal, no QTc prolongation

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate clozapine prescription tonight?

options.text: Restart clozapine at his usual maintenance dose of 450 mg tonight only
options.rationale: After more than 48 hours off clozapine, tolerance is lost and restarting at the previous full dose risks severe orthostatic hypotension, sedation and respiratory depression. (Source: Clopine Connect / Australian Clozapine Treatment Guidelines)

options.text: Restart clozapine at 12.5 mg tonight with day-by-day retitration as new
options.rationale: After 48 hours or more of missed clozapine, retitration is mandatory from a low test dose (12.5 to 25 mg) with day-by-day escalation, as if starting clozapine from scratch. (Source: Clopine Connect Prescribing Information)

options.text: Give clozapine 225 mg tonight as a half-dose then 450 mg from tomorrow
options.rationale: Halving the dose for one night is insufficient to manage lost tolerance; the patient remains at risk of hypotension and over-sedation with any dose larger than the test dose. (Source: Clopine Connect Prescribing Information)

options.text: Switch to intramuscular olanzapine pamoate 300 mg as a temporary bridge
options.rationale: Long-acting olanzapine is not used as a bridge in clozapine-eligible patients and carries its own post-injection syndrome risk requiring 3 hours of supervised observation. (Source: AMH: Olanzapine)

options.text: Restart clozapine at 200 mg tonight without using a test-dose initial step
options.rationale: Skipping the test dose at restart bypasses the safety check for hypotension and over-sedation in someone who has lost tolerance; Australian product information mandates test-dose retitration after 48 hours. (Source: Clopine Connect Prescribing Information)

explanation.summary: Clozapine tolerance to hypotension, sedation and respiratory depression is lost after 48 hours without dosing. Australian product information and Clopine Connect mandate retitration as if commencing from scratch: a 12.5 to 25 mg test dose followed by daily incremental increases (50 mg, 100 mg etc.) targeting the previous maintenance dose. Concurrent enzyme inducers (smoking, carbamazepine) and inhibitors (ciprofloxacin, fluvoxamine) affect plasma levels significantly. Re-baseline FBC and ECG before re-initiation when restarting after prolonged interruption.
key_points: More than 48 hours off clozapine = retitrate from 12.5 mg test dose
Tolerance loss applies to hypotension, sedation and respiratory effects
Re-baseline FBC and ECG before extended re-initiation
explanation.pearls: Smoking cessation during hospitalisation can double clozapine plasma levels because tobacco induces CYP1A2; a clozapine plasma level 2 weeks after admission is mandatory when a smoker is admitted to a non-smoking ward.

subtopic_detail: Capacity and the NSW Mental Health Act 2007
stem: A 28-year-old woman is admitted to a NSW medical ward after a paracetamol overdose. She has severe major depressive disorder and says she wants to die. She refuses intravenous fluids and N-acetylcysteine, understands what is proposed, but says nothing will work. There are no psychotic features. She is calm and engaging.

data_table.Examination: Affect flat, suicidal ideation with intent, no psychotic features, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Paracetamol above the nomogram line, ALT 240 U/L, INR 1.3, lactate 1.6 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Accept her refusal as competent and move to symptom-focused palliation
options.rationale: Severe depression with active suicidal intent distorts the appreciating and weighing limbs of capacity even when the patient can recite the facts, so this refusal is not a competent one. (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007)

options.text: Seek a Supreme Court order before starting any treatment at all
options.rationale: The Supreme Court is for enduring or contested incapacity questions. Where mental illness is driving an acute refusal the Mental Health Act 2007 and the duty of care are the working mechanisms. (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007)

options.text: Complete a schedule under the NSW Mental Health Act and treat actively
options.rationale: A medical practitioner who has examined her may complete a mental health certificate, Schedule 1, so she can be detained in a declared mental health facility: she is a mentally ill person under section 14, or at least mentally disordered under section 15, and no less restrictive care is appropriate and available. The Act carries the psychiatric care while the antidote is given without delay under the duty of care. (Source: NSW Mental Health Rights Manual: initial detention and transport)
source_refs: NSW Mental Health Rights Manual: initial detention and transport

options.text: Apply to the NCAT Guardianship Division before starting the antidote infusion
options.rationale: Guardianship consent is for enduring incapacity and takes days to arrange. It is neither quick enough for paracetamol toxicity nor the right instrument for refusal driven by acute mental illness. (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007)

options.text: Allow 48 hours of reflection with capacity reviewed at every shift
options.rationale: Delaying N-acetylcysteine beyond 8 hours from ingestion sharply raises the risk of hepatic failure, and capacity impaired by acute suicidal depression rarely returns within hours. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

explanation.summary: Capacity requires the person to understand, retain, weigh and communicate a decision. In severe depression with suicidal intent the weighing limb is typically the one that fails, so refusal of life-saving treatment is not competent. In NSW the pathway is a mental health certificate, Schedule 1, completed by a medical practitioner or accredited person who has examined the person, authorising detention in a declared mental health facility. An authorised medical officer must then examine her as soon as practicable and within 12 hours. The Act authorises her care and treatment for mental illness; the antidote itself is given under the duty of care and must not wait on legal process.
key_points: Severe depression most often impairs the weighing limb of capacity.
NSW detention starts with a mental health certificate, not an assessment order.
Detention requires that no less restrictive care is appropriate and available.
Paracetamol toxicity is time-critical: do not delay N-acetylcysteine for paperwork.
explanation.pearls: Scheduling and treating are separate decisions. The schedule secures her psychiatric care; the N-acetylcysteine goes up on the duty of care while the paperwork is still being written.

sources.label: NSW Mental Health Rights Manual: initial detention and transport

stem: A 38-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has been stable on lithium carbonate 750 mg nocte for 4 years (steady-state level 0.7 mmol/L). She presents to her GP for routine review. She has noticed increasing thirst and polyuria over the last 6 months and is now drinking 4 L of fluid daily. She is otherwise well, sleeping normally with no mood symptoms. Her partner reports no behavioural change. She is concerned about her kidneys.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 36.7 degrees Celsius, HR 76, RR 14, BP 124/76 mmHg, SpO2 99% in room air
data_table.Examination: Well, hydrated, no peripheral oedema, no tremor, thyroid not enlarged
data_table.Investigations: Lithium 0.68 mmol/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L (baseline 62), eGFR 84 mL/min, TSH 2.6 mIU/L, calcium 2.42 mmol/L, urine osmolality 220 mosmol/kg after overnight fluid restriction

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to psychiatry for review of lithium dose and consider switching to an alternative mood stabiliser
options.rationale: Polyuria with reduced urine osmolality after fluid restriction in a lithium-treated patient indicates lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus; psychiatric review is needed to balance ongoing mood stabilisation against renal toxicity and consider dose reduction or switching. (Source: RANZCP Lithium Position Statement)

options.text: Ignore the symptoms because the lithium level is within range and continue routine 6-monthly testing
options.rationale: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus occurs in long-term lithium use regardless of therapeutic level and signals nephron damage; ignoring symptoms risks irreversible decline. (Source: RANZCP Lithium Position Statement)

options.text: Recommend further fluid restriction to under 1.5 L daily as treatment of polyuria from lithium therapy
options.rationale: Fluid restriction is dangerous in nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and risks hypernatraemic dehydration; treatment is to reduce or stop lithium under specialist supervision. (Source: RANZCP Lithium Position Statement)

options.text: Commence desmopressin 100 microgram nocte without specialist review for symptomatic relief at home
options.rationale: Desmopressin is largely ineffective in nephrogenic DI because the defect is renal tubular resistance, and specialist input is required before commencing. (Source: RANZCP Lithium Position Statement)

options.text: Increase lithium dose to 1000 mg nocte to maintain mood stability if level remains under 1.2 mmol/L
options.rationale: Increasing the lithium dose worsens renal effects; the current level is therapeutic and increasing it without reason is contraindicated, especially with emerging nephrogenic DI. (Source: RANZCP Lithium Position Statement)

explanation.summary: Polyuria and polydipsia in a long-term lithium-treated patient with reduced urine osmolality after fluid restriction indicate lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Joint psychiatric and renal review is needed to consider dose reduction, switching to an alternative mood stabiliser, or adding amiloride. Fluid restriction is dangerous and desmopressin is largely ineffective because the defect is tubular resistance.
key_points: Lithium causes nephrogenic DI by reducing aquaporin-2 expression in collecting ducts
Long-term lithium also causes chronic interstitial nephritis and reduced eGFR
Joint psychiatric and renal review is required before dose change or switching
explanation.pearls: Amiloride 5 to 10 mg orally daily reduces lithium uptake in the principal cell and improves nephrogenic DI; thiazides can be used cautiously but raise lithium levels.

stem: A 28-year-old man presents to a psychiatrist with longstanding inattention, disorganisation and restlessness that have impaired his university and work performance since adolescence. Symptoms are present at home and at work. A structured clinical interview and ASRS confirm features of ADHD with onset in childhood. Substance use, mood and anxiety disorders are excluded. He has no personal or family history of cardiac disease, hypertension or seizure. He prefers a once-daily medication. ECG is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 36.7 degrees Celsius, HR 72, RR 14, BP 122/76 mmHg, SpO2 99% in room air
data_table.Examination: Mental state - mildly fidgety, mood euthymic, no psychotic features, insight preserved
data_table.Investigations: 12-lead ECG normal sinus rhythm, FBC, UEC and TSH all within normal limits

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Bupropion 150 mg sustained release each morning as off-label first-line therapy for adult ADHD
options.rationale: Bupropion has limited evidence in adult ADHD and is not endorsed as first-line in Australian guidelines. (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guidelines)

options.text: Atomoxetine 40 mg orally each morning titrated up to 80 mg over 4 weeks for symptom control
options.rationale: Atomoxetine is an alternative non-stimulant agent and is reserved for stimulant intolerance, substance use risk, or comorbid anxiety; it is not first-line. (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guidelines)

options.text: Immediate-release methylphenidate 10 mg three times daily as initial therapy for adult ADHD
options.rationale: Immediate-release stimulants are second-line in adults because of multiple daily doses and diversion risk; long-acting forms are preferred. (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guidelines)

options.text: Clonidine 75 microgram orally twice daily as a non-stimulant alternative to amphetamine-based therapy
options.rationale: Clonidine is used as augmentation in paediatric ADHD; it is not a first-line monotherapy in adults. (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guidelines)

options.text: Lisdexamfetamine 30 mg orally each morning, titrated up over 4 weeks to symptom response
options.rationale: Long-acting stimulants such as lisdexamfetamine are first-line for adult ADHD in Australia, offering once-daily dosing and lower abuse potential than immediate-release amphetamine. (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Adult ADHD is treated first-line with a long-acting stimulant such as lisdexamfetamine or methylphenidate modified release in Australia. Pre-treatment cardiovascular assessment includes history, BP and ECG; ongoing monitoring tracks BP, pulse and weight. Non-stimulants (atomoxetine, guanfacine) are reserved for stimulant contraindication or intolerance.
key_points: Long-acting stimulants (lisdexamfetamine, methylphenidate MR) are first-line in adult ADHD
Pre-treatment cardiovascular history, BP and ECG are required before stimulant initiation
Non-stimulants are reserved for stimulant contraindication or substance use risk
explanation.pearls: Diversion risk should be discussed at every visit; in Australia, stimulant prescribing for adults is restricted and requires authority from the relevant state regulatory body.

sources.label: Australian Evidence-based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

stem: A 24-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has been stable on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily for 2 years. She presents to her psychiatrist saying she is considering pregnancy in the next year. She is on no other psychotropic medications. Her last manic episode was 18 months ago; she has had no depressive episodes for 2 years. She is sexually active with one male partner using condoms. She has no other medical conditions.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 36.6 degrees Celsius, HR 72, RR 14, BP 116/74 mmHg, SpO2 99% in room air
data_table.Examination: Mental state - euthymic, no psychotic or suicidal features, full insight
data_table.Investigations: Valproate level 480 micromol/L, LFTs normal, FBC normal, beta-hCG negative

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Plan a cross-titration to lithium or lamotrigine with effective contraception until the new agent is established
options.rationale: Valproate has the highest teratogenic potential of mood stabilisers (about 10 percent major malformations, dose-related neurodevelopmental impact); women planning pregnancy are switched to a safer agent under cover of effective contraception. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar Guidelines)

options.text: Continue valproate at the current dose and recommend high-dose folate 5 mg daily for 3 months pre-conception
options.rationale: High-dose folate does not offset the malformation and neurodevelopmental risk of valproate; switching to a safer agent before conception is required. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar Guidelines)

options.text: Reduce valproate to 600 mg daily and continue this dose throughout pregnancy as a minimal teratogenic dose
options.rationale: There is no safe dose of valproate in pregnancy; even reduced doses carry a substantial risk of structural and neurodevelopmental harm. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar Guidelines)

options.text: Stop valproate immediately without cross-titration and review in 4 weeks for clinical mood relapse
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation risks relapse of bipolar disorder; cross-titration under cover of contraception is the safer pathway. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar Guidelines)

options.text: Insert a copper IUD and continue valproate indefinitely as long as effective contraception is maintained
options.rationale: While the pregnancy prevention program requires effective contraception, the woman is planning pregnancy and a switch is required, not indefinite continuation. (Source: TGA Valproate)

explanation.summary: Sodium valproate carries the highest teratogenic and neurodevelopmental risk among mood stabilisers. The risk is approximately 10 percent for major malformations and 30 to 40 percent for impaired cognitive development. Women of reproductive potential must be on a pregnancy prevention program. Women planning pregnancy are cross-titrated to a safer agent (lithium or lamotrigine) under cover of effective contraception before stopping contraception.
key_points: Valproate is contraindicated in pregnancy unless no effective alternative exists
Lithium and lamotrigine are the preferred mood stabilisers in pregnancy planning
Cross-titration occurs under cover of effective contraception, not abrupt cessation
explanation.pearls: Lamotrigine requires slow titration (25 mg/day increments) over 6 weeks to minimise the risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome; pre-conception planning should allow this lead time.

stem: A 26-year-old man with first-episode schizophrenia was commenced on olanzapine 10 mg nocte 11 weeks ago. He is being reviewed at the community mental health clinic. His positive symptoms have improved markedly. He has gained 5 kg since starting olanzapine. He reports increased appetite and lethargy but no new physical symptoms. He has no personal or family history of cardiometabolic disease. He smokes 10 cigarettes daily and is not physically active.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 36.7 degrees Celsius, HR 84, RR 16, BP 128/82 mmHg, SpO2 99% in room air
data_table.Examination: BMI 28 kg/m^2 (up from 26.5), no acanthosis, no tremor or rigidity, mental state stable
data_table.Investigations: Baseline pre-treatment - fasting BSL 4.8 mmol/L, total cholesterol 4.2 mmol/L, ECG QTc 410 ms

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate set of monitoring tests at this 12-week review?

options.text: Liver function tests, thyroid function and serum creatinine only as the 12-week metabolic screen
options.rationale: LFTs, TFTs and creatinine are baseline and yearly tests rather than the 12-week metabolic screen, which focuses on glucose, lipids, weight and BP. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia Guidelines)

options.text: Serum prolactin and bone densitometry as the 12-week metabolic screen for second-generation antipsychotics
options.rationale: Olanzapine has relatively low prolactin-raising effect; the 12-week screen is metabolic and DEXA is not part of routine 12-week monitoring. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia Guidelines)

options.text: Annual ECG with QTc, clozapine level and full blood examination as the 12-week monitoring panel
options.rationale: Clozapine levels are irrelevant on olanzapine; FBC is mandatory for clozapine but not for olanzapine, and annual ECG is not the 12-week tool. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia Guidelines)

options.text: Fasting glucose, lipid profile, weight, waist circumference and blood pressure as the 12-week metabolic screen
options.rationale: Australian RANZCP guidance recommends a fasting metabolic screen (glucose, lipids, weight, waist circumference, BP) at 12 weeks after starting an antipsychotic, then 6-monthly. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia Guidelines)

options.text: Symptom rating scale (PANSS) and a Simpson-Angus scale with no metabolic blood tests required at 12 weeks
options.rationale: Symptom and EPS rating are important but do not substitute for metabolic blood and anthropometric monitoring which is the highest yield at 12 weeks. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Second-generation antipsychotics, especially olanzapine and clozapine, cause weight gain, dyslipidaemia and impaired glucose metabolism. Australian RANZCP guidance schedules a metabolic screen at baseline, 12 weeks and 6-monthly comprising fasting glucose, lipid profile, weight, waist circumference and BP. Early identification at 12 weeks allows lifestyle intervention or antipsychotic switch before sustained metabolic disease develops.
key_points: 12-week metabolic screen on antipsychotic - fasting glucose, lipids, weight, waist, BP
Olanzapine and clozapine have the highest cardiometabolic burden
Weight gain over 5 percent in 12 weeks should prompt lifestyle and medication review
explanation.pearls: Metformin can be added to mitigate antipsychotic-induced weight gain (around 3 kg average effect) when lifestyle measures are insufficient and switching is undesired.

stem: A 24-year-old woman known to the community mental health team for borderline personality disorder presents to ED after superficial cutting of her forearm following an argument with her partner. She has had multiple similar presentations and is engaged in weekly dialectical behaviour therapy with her usual psychologist. She denies suicidal intent and asks to go home. She has no medical injury requiring suturing. She is calm at interview and has a safety plan she co-developed with her DBT therapist.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 36.7 degrees Celsius, HR 82, RR 16, BP 118/72 mmHg, SpO2 99% in room air
data_table.Examination: Superficial linear lacerations on left forearm, no deep injury, no signs of intoxication, mental state - distressed but engaged, mood reactive, no psychotic features

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate ED management?

options.text: Commence a low-dose quetiapine 25 mg as required regimen for her presentation today and on discharge
options.rationale: Pharmacotherapy has limited evidence in BPD and as-needed sedative-antipsychotic use risks dependence; first-line management is psychological. (Source: NHMRC BPD Guideline)

options.text: Admit to the inpatient psychiatry ward overnight for crisis stabilisation and review by the on-call team in the morning
options.rationale: Routine admission for self-harm in BPD often reinforces help-seeking via crisis and disrupts therapeutic work; admission is reserved for acute psychiatric emergency or comorbid acute condition. (Source: NHMRC BPD Guideline)

options.text: Validate her distress, review her safety plan with her, dress the wounds and discharge to her usual DBT clinician with rapid follow-up
options.rationale: Evidence-based BPD care prioritises continuity with the primary therapist, validation, brief crisis interventions and use of the patient's existing safety plan; routine hospital admission for self-harm in BPD does not improve outcomes. (Source: NHMRC BPD Guideline)

options.text: Make her an involuntary patient under the Mental Health Act because of her history of repeated self-harm
options.rationale: BPD without acute serious risk does not warrant involuntary admission; her presentation is non-life-threatening and she has insight, capacity and a safety plan. (Source: NHMRC BPD Guideline)

options.text: Discharge without follow-up because she is engaged in ongoing private psychology and has no acute medical injury
options.rationale: Discharge is appropriate but should be coordinated with the usual treating team and include rapid follow-up rather than disengaging from acute care. (Source: NHMRC BPD Guideline)

explanation.summary: Australian NHMRC guidance for borderline personality disorder prioritises a structured, evidence-based psychological therapy (DBT, MBT, schema therapy) with continuity of care. Acute presentations with non-life-threatening self-harm are managed by validating distress, supporting the patient's existing safety plan, and rapid follow-up with the primary clinician. Admission and involuntary measures are reserved for acute psychiatric emergency.
key_points: Continuity with the primary therapist is the highest-leverage acute intervention
Routine inpatient admission for self-harm in BPD does not improve outcomes
Pharmacotherapy is adjunctive and lacks BPD-specific efficacy in the long-term
explanation.pearls: Brief admission of 24 to 72 hours may be useful in acute suicidal crisis to prevent imminent harm; planned and time-limited stays reduce reinforcement of crisis presentations.

stem: A 32-year-old man with a 4-year history of schizoaffective disorder is admitted to a general medical ward from a psychiatric inpatient unit because he has stopped eating, drinking and moving over 48 hours. He has been on risperidone 6 mg daily for 2 years. Physical examination shows mutism, waxy flexibility and persistent staring. He resists passive arm movement but yields once the arm is positioned. CK is 480 U/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, glucose 5.0 mmol/L, urinalysis normal and there is no fever or autonomic instability.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 36.9 degrees Celsius, HR 86, RR 18, BP 118/74 mmHg, SpO2 99% in room air
data_table.Examination: Mute, immobile, eyes open and tracking, waxy flexibility on arm posturing, no fever, no diaphoresis, no rigidity, no tremor
data_table.Investigations: CK 480 U/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L, glucose 5.0 mmol/L, CRP 4 mg/L

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange MRI brain and CSF examination before any treatment to exclude autoimmune encephalitis as the cause
options.rationale: Autoimmune encephalitis warrants investigation in atypical or refractory cases, but does not delay urgent treatment of the catatonic state; lorazepam is safe and aids diagnosis. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Position)

options.text: Cease risperidone and commence dantrolene 1 mg/kg intravenously for suspected neuroleptic malignant syndrome
options.rationale: NMS requires fever, autonomic instability and significant rigidity with a markedly elevated CK; their absence here makes catatonia more likely than NMS. (Source: RANZCP NMS Position)

options.text: Commence electroconvulsive therapy this morning without further pharmacological challenge first
options.rationale: ECT is highly effective in catatonia but is reserved for lorazepam non-response, life-threatening features (malignant catatonia) or recurrent catatonia; trial of lorazepam comes first. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Position)

options.text: Increase risperidone to 8 mg daily for inadequate antipsychotic effect causing residual negative symptoms
options.rationale: Increasing antipsychotic dose may worsen catatonia (and could precipitate NMS); catatonia in psychosis is treated by stopping or reducing antipsychotic and adding benzodiazepine. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Position)

options.text: Administer lorazepam 2 mg intravenously and reassess catatonic features at 10 minutes for a positive response
options.rationale: A lorazepam challenge (1 to 2 mg IV) is the diagnostic and first-line treatment step for catatonia; partial or full response within minutes confirms the diagnosis and guides further benzodiazepine dosing. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Position)

explanation.summary: Catatonia presents with mutism, immobility, waxy flexibility and posturing and may complicate psychotic or mood disorders. The lorazepam challenge (1 to 2 mg IV with reassessment at 5 to 10 minutes) is both diagnostic and therapeutic. Lack of fever, autonomic instability and severe rigidity argues against NMS. ECT is reserved for benzodiazepine non-responders, malignant or recurrent catatonia.
key_points: Lorazepam 1 to 2 mg IV is first-line diagnostic and therapeutic test for catatonia
NMS requires fever, autonomic instability and significant rigidity with marked CK rise
ECT is reserved for non-response, malignant or recurrent catatonia
explanation.pearls: Excited catatonia (hyperkinetic variant) presents with frenzied motor activity rather than stupor; lorazepam still works but the differential broadens to include serotonin syndrome and acute psychosis.

stem: A 48-year-old man presents to the emergency department 36 hours after his last drink. He had been consuming approximately 200 g of alcohol daily for 25 years. He has tremor, sweating, anxiety, nausea, and feels his heart racing. He has had no hallucinations, seizures or recent head injury. His LFTs are mildly deranged but there are no clinical features of decompensated cirrhosis.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 165/95, HR 110 sinus, RR 18, SpO2 99% in room air, temp 37.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Coarse tremor of outstretched hands, diaphoretic, anxious; no asterixis, no jaundice, abdomen soft with no ascites; orientated to time, person and place
data_table.Investigations: CIWA-Ar score 18 of 67; ALT 80, AST 110, GGT 240, bilirubin 16, albumin 36, INR 1.1; glucose 5.4, Mg 0.7

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?

options.text: IV haloperidol 5 mg for agitation control as the primary withdrawal treatment
options.rationale: Haloperidol does not treat the underlying GABA-glutamate imbalance and lowers seizure threshold; benzodiazepines are first-line in alcohol withdrawal. (Source: eTG Psychotropic: Alcohol withdrawal)

options.text: Atenolol 50 mg daily as monotherapy targeting autonomic withdrawal symptoms only
options.rationale: Beta-blockers mask tachycardia without preventing seizures or delirium tremens and are not adequate as monotherapy. (Source: eTG Psychotropic: Alcohol withdrawal)

options.text: Chlordiazepoxide 100 mg single dose then PRN regimen without further scheduled dosing
options.rationale: Single-dose chlordiazepoxide without titration or symptom-triggered repeat dosing under-treats moderate withdrawal; structured symptom-triggered or front-loaded regimens are recommended. (Source: RACP: Management of alcohol withdrawal)

options.text: IV chlormethiazole infusion titrated to sedation as the inpatient withdrawal regimen
options.rationale: IV chlormethiazole is no longer recommended for alcohol withdrawal in Australia due to respiratory depression risk and abuse potential. (Source: eTG Psychotropic: Alcohol withdrawal)

options.text: Oral diazepam 20 mg loading dose with repeat dosing per CIWA-Ar and IV thiamine 300 mg daily
options.rationale: Symptom-triggered diazepam loading (20 mg orally every 1-2 hours guided by CIWA-Ar) with parenteral thiamine 300 mg daily for at least 3 days is the Australian first-line regimen for moderate alcohol withdrawal. (Source: eTG Psychotropic: Alcohol withdrawal)

explanation.summary: Moderate alcohol withdrawal (CIWA-Ar 10-20) is managed with symptom-triggered or front-loaded diazepam, parenteral thiamine 300 mg daily before any carbohydrate, hydration, magnesium and folate replacement, and monitoring for delirium tremens and seizures. In hepatic failure, shorter-acting benzodiazepines such as oxazepam are preferred.
key_points: Diazepam is first-line in alcohol withdrawal without significant hepatic impairment
Parenteral thiamine 300 mg daily prevents Wernicke encephalopathy
Oxazepam or lorazepam are preferred in significant liver disease
explanation.pearls: Always give thiamine before glucose in malnourished alcohol-dependent patients to avoid precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy; oral thiamine has poor absorption when intake is poor.

subtopic_detail: Serotonin syndrome from SSRI plus tramadol
stem: A 35-year-old woman with major depressive disorder has been on sertraline 100 mg daily for 6 months. Her GP prescribed tramadol 50 mg four-times daily for back pain 36 hours ago. She now presents to the emergency department with fever, agitation, tremor, sweating and intermittent involuntary lower limb jerking. She has not started any other new medication and denies illicit substance use.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 39.5 degrees Celsius, HR 130 sinus, BP 160/95, RR 24, SpO2 98% in room air
data_table.Examination: Agitated, mydriasis, hyperreflexia, sustained ankle clonus, tremor of outstretched hands, diaphoretic; no muscular rigidity
data_table.Investigations: CK 800, creatinine 95, sodium 138, potassium 4.0, glucose 6.2; ECG sinus tachycardia

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Stop both serotonergic agents, IV fluids and benzodiazepines, active cooling, and consider cyproheptadine if persistent
options.rationale: Serotonin syndrome from SSRI plus tramadol is managed by ceasing all serotonergic agents, supportive care with IV fluids, benzodiazepines for agitation and hyperthermia, active cooling and oral cyproheptadine 12 mg loading if symptoms persist. (Source: eTG Psychotropic: Serotonin syndrome)

options.text: IV dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg as first-line treatment for hyperthermia and muscle rigidity in this setting
options.rationale: Dantrolene is used in malignant hyperthermia and severe neuroleptic malignant syndrome; serotonin syndrome lacks rigidity and is managed differently. (Source: eTG Psychotropic: Serotonin syndrome)

options.text: IV bromocriptine 2.5 mg three times daily to reverse dopaminergic blockade and stabilise the syndrome
options.rationale: Bromocriptine is used in NMS where there is dopamine antagonism; it is not indicated in serotonin syndrome where the issue is excess serotonin. (Source: eTG Psychotropic: Serotonin syndrome)

options.text: Continue sertraline and add propranolol 40 mg three times daily for ongoing autonomic instability
options.rationale: Continuing the serotonergic drug perpetuates the syndrome; cessation of all serotonergic agents is essential to recovery. (Source: AMH: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors)

options.text: Empiric IV ceftriaxone and vancomycin for presumed sepsis with confirmatory blood cultures pending
options.rationale: Sepsis is a differential and cultures should be sent but the clinical syndrome (clonus, hyperreflexia, mydriasis, hyperthermia, serotonergic drug exposure) fits serotonin toxicity, which is treated by drug cessation and supportive care. (Source: eTG Psychotropic: Serotonin syndrome)

explanation.summary: Serotonin syndrome is recognised by the triad of neuromuscular excitability (clonus, hyperreflexia, tremor), autonomic instability (tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, mydriasis) and altered mental status, in the setting of serotonergic drug exposure. Tramadol combined with SSRIs is a common trigger. Management is drug cessation, IV fluids, benzodiazepines, active cooling and cyproheptadine if severe.
key_points: Hunter criteria identify serotonin syndrome (clonus, hyperreflexia, tremor)
Tramadol plus SSRI is a high-risk combination
Differentiate from NMS by rigidity and rate of onset
explanation.pearls: NMS develops over days to weeks with rigidity and bradyreflexia; serotonin syndrome develops over hours with clonus and hyperreflexia; getting this distinction right changes management to dantrolene/bromocriptine in NMS or cyproheptadine in serotonin syndrome.

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents to her GP with 8 months of excessive worry about work, family, finances and her own health. She describes restlessness, fatigue, irritability, muscle tension and insomnia most nights. She has had 2 episodes of panic in the last month. Her mood is anxious but she denies persistent low mood, anhedonia or thoughts of self-harm. She uses no substances. GAD-7 score is 16.

data_table.Examination: Vital signs within normal limits; mental state: anxious affect, normal speech, no psychotic features, no suicidal ideation; cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: TSH 1.8, full blood count and electrolytes normal; urine drug screen negative; ECG normal

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Benzodiazepine diazepam 5 mg three times daily for 6 weeks as first-line monotherapy
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are not first-line in GAD due to tolerance, dependence and impaired psychomotor function; SSRIs or SNRIs and CBT are preferred. (Source: eTG Psychotropic: Generalised anxiety disorder)

options.text: Sertraline 50 mg daily titrating to 100-200 mg with referral for cognitive behavioural therapy
options.rationale: An SSRI such as sertraline combined with cognitive behavioural therapy is first-line treatment for GAD per Australian guidelines; expected onset of benefit is 4 to 6 weeks. (Source: eTG Psychotropic: Generalised anxiety disorder)

options.text: Olanzapine 5 mg daily as augmentation for severe anxiety symptoms ongoing despite GP review
options.rationale: Antipsychotics are not first-line in GAD and carry significant metabolic and motor side effects. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline: Anxiety disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline: Anxiety disorders

options.text: Beta-blocker propranolol 40 mg three times daily as first-line monotherapy for somatic symptoms
options.rationale: Propranolol may help performance anxiety but is not first-line for GAD where SSRIs and CBT address core cognitive and worry symptoms. (Source: eTG Psychotropic: Generalised anxiety disorder)

options.text: Refer for inpatient psychiatric admission given the severity score on GAD-7 questionnaire
options.rationale: GAD-7 of 16 is severe but does not by itself indicate admission; outpatient pharmacotherapy and psychotherapy is appropriate given employment and absence of suicidality. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline: Anxiety disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline: Anxiety disorders

explanation.summary: First-line treatment of moderate to severe generalised anxiety disorder is an SSRI or SNRI combined with cognitive behavioural therapy. Benzodiazepines are limited to short-term use due to dependence risk. Antipsychotics and beta-blockers are not first-line. Treatment effect for SSRIs is typically seen at 4 to 6 weeks with dose titration as needed.
key_points: SSRI plus CBT is first-line for moderate-severe GAD
Benzodiazepines are short-term adjuncts only due to dependence risk
Treatment response is typically assessed at 4-6 weeks
explanation.pearls: Counsel patients about possible initial worsening of anxiety in the first 1-2 weeks of SSRI initiation; lower starting doses (sertraline 25 mg) may reduce activation symptoms.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline: Anxiety disorders

stem: A 24-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia is on day 18 of clozapine titration, currently at 175 mg daily. He has been responding well to treatment but today presents to the emergency department with fever, malaise, persistent tachycardia and mild dyspnoea on exertion. He denies cough, sputum or urinary symptoms. He has no source of infection on examination.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 38.7 degrees Celsius, HR 120 sinus, BP 110/68, RR 22, SpO2 96% in room air
data_table.Examination: No focus of infection on ENT or chest examination; chest clear; heart sounds soft with no murmur; abdomen soft; no rash
data_table.Investigations: Troponin I 250 ng/L (less than 14), ECG: sinus tachycardia with non-specific T wave flattening, CXR: clear, WCC 9.5 with no left shift, CRP 60, BNP 200, blood cultures sent

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Continue clozapine and treat symptomatically with paracetamol given non-specific viral picture
options.rationale: Persistent tachycardia, fever and elevated troponin in the first 4 weeks of clozapine titration is suggestive of clozapine-induced myocarditis and requires immediate cessation. (Source: RANZCP Clozapine treatment guidelines)

options.text: Reduce clozapine dose by 50 percent and recheck the troponin level in 48 hours review
options.rationale: Dose reduction is inadequate when myocarditis is suspected; immediate cessation and urgent cardiac assessment are required given the mortality risk. (Source: RANZCP Clozapine treatment guidelines)

options.text: Cease clozapine immediately, admit for cardiac assessment with echocardiogram, and never rechallenge
options.rationale: Clozapine-induced myocarditis presents in the first 4 weeks of titration with tachycardia, fever and elevated troponin; immediate cessation, cardiology referral with echocardiogram, and avoidance of any future clozapine rechallenge is required. (Source: RANZCP Clozapine treatment guidelines)

options.text: Add propranolol 40 mg three times daily for tachycardia and continue clozapine titration as planned
options.rationale: Symptomatic beta-blockade does not address the underlying myocarditis and continued exposure increases mortality risk. (Source: RANZCP Clozapine treatment guidelines)

options.text: Switch directly to olanzapine 20 mg daily and discharge with outpatient cardiology follow-up review
options.rationale: Outpatient management is unsafe in suspected myocarditis; admission for cardiac assessment is required before any switch is made. (Source: eTG Psychotropic: Clozapine)

explanation.summary: Clozapine-induced myocarditis typically presents in the first 4 weeks of titration with persistent tachycardia, fever, elevated troponin and constitutional symptoms. Mandatory monitoring includes baseline and weekly CRP, troponin and FBC for the first 4 weeks. Suspected myocarditis requires immediate clozapine cessation, urgent cardiac assessment with echocardiogram, and lifelong avoidance of rechallenge.
key_points: Suspect clozapine myocarditis in weeks 1-4 with fever, tachycardia and high troponin
Immediate cessation and cardiac assessment is mandatory
Rechallenge with clozapine is contraindicated after myocarditis
explanation.pearls: Monitoring during titration includes baseline echocardiogram, weekly CRP and troponin for 4 weeks, and weekly FBC for 18 weeks then monthly for the duration of treatment.

stem: A 26-year-old woman on risperidone 4 mg daily for 6 months for schizophrenia has had a good symptomatic response. She presents to the early psychosis clinic with 4 months of amenorrhoea, milk discharge from both breasts and reduced libido. She wishes to retain antipsychotic efficacy. She is sexually active and uses condoms; pregnancy test is negative.

data_table.Examination: Breast examination: bilateral expressible non-bloody galactorrhoea, no palpable mass; visual fields full to confrontation; mental state stable with no psychotic relapse features
data_table.Investigations: Prolactin 1800 mIU/L (less than 500), TSH 1.6, beta-hCG negative, FSH and LH suppressed; MRI pituitary normal; LFTs and renal function normal

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Add cabergoline 0.25 mg twice weekly to reduce prolactin while continuing risperidone unchanged
options.rationale: Dopamine agonists may precipitate psychotic relapse in schizophrenia and are not the preferred approach when an alternative antipsychotic option exists. (Source: eTG Psychotropic: Antipsychotic adverse effects)

options.text: Stop risperidone and commence oral oestradiol-progestogen combined contraceptive only
options.rationale: Stopping the antipsychotic without substitution risks psychotic relapse; hormonal therapy alone does not address the underlying dopamine D2 blockade. (Source: AMH: Risperidone)

options.text: Reduce risperidone to 2 mg and add bromocriptine 2.5 mg daily as combination management
options.rationale: Combination dopamine agonist plus antipsychotic risks psychotic relapse and is less preferred than switching to a prolactin-sparing agent. (Source: eTG Psychotropic: Antipsychotic adverse effects)

options.text: Switch from risperidone to aripiprazole and titrate to symptom control over 4-6 weeks
options.rationale: Risperidone is a strong dopamine D2 antagonist causing prolactin elevation; aripiprazole is a partial dopamine D2 agonist and is prolactin-sparing, making it the preferred switch when antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinaemia is symptomatic. (Source: eTG Psychotropic: Antipsychotic adverse effects)

options.text: Continue risperidone and reassure as hyperprolactinaemia is asymptomatic and benign here
options.rationale: The patient is symptomatic with amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea and reduced libido; long-term hyperprolactinaemia also raises concerns about hypogonadism and reduced bone density. (Source: AMH: Risperidone)

explanation.summary: Symptomatic antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinaemia is best managed by switching to a prolactin-sparing antipsychotic such as aripiprazole, which is a partial D2 agonist. Cabergoline carries a risk of precipitating psychotic relapse. Long-term untreated hyperprolactinaemia leads to hypogonadism and reduced bone mineral density.
key_points: Aripiprazole is prolactin-sparing due to partial D2 agonism
Risperidone, paliperidone and amisulpride are high-prolactin agents
Untreated hyperprolactinaemia causes hypogonadism and bone loss
explanation.pearls: Olanzapine, quetiapine and clozapine are also relatively prolactin-sparing options if aripiprazole is unsuitable; baseline prolactin should be checked before commencing any antipsychotic with high prolactin liability.

subtopic_detail: Severe anorexia nervosa medical admission criteria
stem: A 19-year-old female university student presents to her GP with 8 months of progressive restrictive eating and 30 percent weight loss from baseline. She has weakness, dizziness on standing and feels cold. She denies binging or purging. Mental state shows intense fear of weight gain and distorted body image. She does not feel suicidal.

data_table.Vital signs: BMI 12.8 kg/m2; HR 38 sinus, BP 85/55 supine and 70/40 standing, temp 35.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Cachectic, lanugo hair, cold peripheries, slow capillary refill 3 seconds, proximal weakness on squat test; abdomen soft and non-tender
data_table.Investigations: K 2.8, PO4 0.6, Mg 0.6, Na 134, glucose 3.2, urea 4.2, creatinine 50, LFTs ALT 90 AST 110, albumin 28; ECG sinus bradycardia QTc 470 ms

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate disposition and initial management?

options.text: Refer to specialist outpatient eating disorder team with weekly weights and dietitian reviews scheduled
options.rationale: Outpatient management is unsafe when patients meet MARSIPAN medical instability criteria; inpatient medical admission is required. (Source: RANZCP MARSIPAN guidance: Management of really sick patients with anorexia nervosa)
source_refs: RANZCP MARSIPAN guidance: Management of really sick patients with anorexia nervosa

options.text: Discharge with family-based therapy referral and weekly GP review for weight monitoring at home
options.rationale: FBT is an appropriate longer-term therapy but does not address acute medical instability which requires immediate medical admission. (Source: ANZAED: Eating disorder medical management)

options.text: Admit to a general adult ward with a standard three-meal regimen at full calories from day one
options.rationale: Full caloric refeeding from day 1 in severe anorexia nervosa risks refeeding syndrome including hypophosphataemia, cardiac arrhythmia and Wernicke encephalopathy. (Source: RANZCP MARSIPAN guidance: Management of really sick patients with anorexia nervosa)
source_refs: RANZCP MARSIPAN guidance: Management of really sick patients with anorexia nervosa

options.text: Cognitive behavioural therapy for eating disorders intensive outpatient program with weekly therapy
options.rationale: CBT-ED is an evidence-based outpatient therapy in less severe disease; it is not appropriate when MARSIPAN criteria for medical instability are met. (Source: ANZAED: Eating disorder medical management)

options.text: Admit to medical ward with cardiac monitoring, electrolyte correction and slow refeeding with daily monitoring
options.rationale: MARSIPAN medical instability criteria (BMI under 13, HR under 40, postural BP drop above 20, hypothermia, K under 3.0, hypoglycaemia, prolonged QTc) require medical admission with cardiac monitoring, slow refeeding from 5-10 kcal/kg/day, electrolyte correction and daily monitoring for refeeding syndrome. (Source: RANZCP MARSIPAN guidance: Management of really sick patients with anorexia nervosa)
source_refs: RANZCP MARSIPAN guidance: Management of really sick patients with anorexia nervosa

explanation.summary: Severe anorexia nervosa meeting MARSIPAN medical instability criteria requires medical admission with continuous cardiac monitoring, slow refeeding from 5-10 kcal/kg/day, electrolyte and thiamine supplementation, daily bloods and clinical review for refeeding syndrome. Outpatient and standard ward management without monitoring are unsafe.
key_points: MARSIPAN criteria identify need for medical admission in severe AN
Refeeding starts at 5-10 kcal/kg/day with daily phosphate monitoring
Cardiac monitoring is required for QTc prolongation or bradycardia
explanation.pearls: Family-based therapy, CBT-ED and specialist outpatient eating disorder programs are evidence-based long-term treatments but only after medical stabilisation; involve mental health services early to plan post-admission care.

sources.label: RANZCP MARSIPAN guidance: Management of really sick patients with anorexia nervosa

subtopic_detail: Long-term lithium monitoring frequency in stable bipolar I disorder
stem: A 38-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has been stable on lithium 1000 mg nightly for 5 years with no acute mood episodes. Her most recent 12-hour trough lithium level is 0.7 mmol/L. She is otherwise well and on no other regular medications. She has no symptoms of polyuria or polydipsia. Her primary care GP is reviewing her chronic disease management plan and asks about monitoring intervals. She has had no surgery or significant illness in the past year.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no fine tremor, no weight gain over 12 months
data_table.Investigations: Most recent (3 months ago): lithium 0.7 mmol/L, TSH 2.4 mIU/L, eGFR 92, calcium corrected 2.34 mmol/L; ECG normal

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate monitoring plan?

options.text: Six-monthly lithium level, TSH, eGFR and calcium, with a 12-hourly trough lithium level taken 5 to 7 days after any dose change or new interacting medication
options.rationale: AU practice on stable lithium recommends 6-monthly serum lithium, renal, thyroid and calcium monitoring with trough levels 12 hours post dose, and additional levels around dose or interacting-medication changes. (Source: RANZCP clinical practice guidelines on mood disorders; AMH lithium monograph)

options.text: Annual TSH and lithium level only, with no renal or calcium monitoring required and no additional monitoring around dose or interacting-medication changes
options.rationale: Lithium causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, chronic kidney injury and hyperparathyroidism; renal and calcium monitoring is mandatory. (Source: RANZCP mood disorders guideline)

options.text: Five-yearly lithium level only with no other monitoring intervals, on the basis that her current ranges have been stable for 5 consecutive years at therapeutic targets without symptoms
options.rationale: Lithium toxicity, renal injury and thyroid disease can develop silently; long intervals miss reversible harms. (Source: RANZCP mood disorders guideline)

options.text: Replace lithium with sodium valproate empirically without further monitoring of any chemistry, levels or organ function and discontinue all bipolar-specific reviews going forward
options.rationale: Stable disease on lithium is a reason to continue lithium with monitoring, not to switch agents. (Source: RANZCP mood disorders guideline)

options.text: Monthly lithium level and ECG indefinitely as the default monitoring schedule for any patient on lithium, regardless of stability or duration of therapy
options.rationale: Monthly testing is reserved for initiation, dose change or instability; routine stable monitoring is at 6 to 12 monthly intervals. (Source: RANZCP mood disorders guideline)

explanation.summary: Long-term lithium monitoring in a stable patient is at 6-monthly intervals and covers a 12-hour trough lithium level (target 0.4 to 1.0 mmol/L for maintenance), eGFR, TSH and calcium. Additional levels are drawn around dose changes, new interacting medications (NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, thiazides), and intercurrent illness. Toxicity risk rises with dehydration, infection and renal injury. Annual cardiometabolic review and review of contraception remain relevant.
key_points: Stable lithium: 6-monthly lithium, eGFR, TSH and calcium
Trough lithium 12 hours post dose; therapeutic 0.4 to 1.0 mmol/L for maintenance
Monitor more frequently around dose changes, new interacting drugs and intercurrent illness
explanation.pearls: Maintenance lithium trough 0.4 to 1.0 mmol/L drawn 12 hours post dose with 6-monthly eGFR, TSH and calcium balances relapse prevention with the risks of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, chronic kidney injury and hyperparathyroidism.

subtopic_detail: First-line pharmacotherapy for tobacco use disorder in an adult smoker
stem: A 47-year-old man smokes 20 cigarettes a day, has done so for 25 years, and wants to quit. He has tried nicotine patches without behavioural support twice in the past with relapse within weeks. He has no history of seizures, no eating disorder, no recent myocardial infarction in the last month and no severe renal impairment. He has a remote episode of mild depression 8 years ago, fully resolved without treatment. He is on no regular medications.

data_table.Examination: No respiratory distress, breath sounds normal; mild dental staining
data_table.Investigations: FEV1/FVC 0.74; eGFR 88; HbA1c 5.5%; PHQ-9 score 3 (minimal symptoms)

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Encourage transition to electronic cigarettes (vapes) without any other pharmacological cessation aid as the recommended first-line strategy in this patient with prior NRT failures
options.rationale: RACGP positions vaping as a second-line cessation aid, considered only when first-line approved pharmacotherapies fail; not first-line. (Source: RACGP supporting smoking cessation)

options.text: Varenicline 0.5 mg daily for 3 days, then 0.5 mg twice daily for 4 days, then 1 mg twice daily for 12 weeks, with a quit date set for day 8, alongside behavioural support
options.rationale: Varenicline plus behavioural support is the AU first-line pharmacotherapy for tobacco use disorder, with the licensed titration to 1 mg twice daily for 12 weeks. (Source: RACGP supporting smoking cessation; AMH varenicline)

options.text: Brief nicotine replacement therapy for 3 days only at low dose to minimise systemic exposure, with no concurrent behavioural support, no extended duration, and no longer-acting agent considered
options.rationale: Standard NRT is 8 to 12 weeks at full dose combining a patch with short-acting formulation; 3 days is sub-therapeutic. (Source: RACGP supporting smoking cessation)

options.text: Bupropion sustained-release 150 mg daily as monotherapy in a patient with an active eating disorder requiring close psychiatric follow-up and concurrent low-dose benzodiazepine support
options.rationale: Bupropion is contraindicated in active eating disorders and is not first-line here; behavioural support is also needed. (Source: RACGP supporting smoking cessation)

options.text: Oral naltrexone 50 mg daily indefinitely as monotherapy specifically targeting nicotine craving, with no other cessation aid or behavioural support added at this initial visit
options.rationale: Naltrexone is not an approved nicotine cessation pharmacotherapy in Australia. (Source: RACGP supporting smoking cessation)

explanation.summary: First-line AU pharmacotherapy for tobacco use disorder is varenicline (12 weeks at 1 mg twice daily after titration), combination NRT (patch plus short-acting formulation for 8 to 12 weeks), or bupropion sustained-release. Behavioural support roughly doubles quit rates compared with pharmacotherapy alone. Quitline and brief intervention models support adherence. Vaping is a second-line aid considered when first-line pharmacotherapies fail. Bupropion is contraindicated in active eating disorders and seizure disorders.
key_points: Varenicline 12 weeks with behavioural support is AU first-line
Combination NRT (patch plus short-acting) doubles quit rates over patch alone
Bupropion is contraindicated in active eating disorders or seizure history
explanation.pearls: Varenicline 1 mg twice daily for 12 weeks (titrated over the first week) achieves around 25 percent abstinence at 6 months, roughly double the rate of NRT patch monotherapy.

subtopic_detail: Adult ADHD assessment and stimulant initiation pathway
stem: A 27-year-old graphic designer reports lifelong inattention, frequent task-switching and procrastination that now impair his work. He recalls academic difficulties from primary school. He drinks alcohol moderately and uses no other substances. He has no cardiac history, no significant mood symptoms today and no anxiety disorder requiring treatment. He has no first-degree relative with sudden cardiac death. His GP is the first doctor to assess these concerns formally.

data_table.Examination: Mental state: euthymic, no thought disorder, concentration intermittently poor on serial 7s; PHQ-9 score 4, GAD-7 score 5
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus rhythm, normal QTc; AUDIT score 5; collateral history from mother confirms childhood inattention at school

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Commence a trial of oral methylphenidate immediate-release 10 mg twice daily empirically at this initial visit without further diagnostic workup, collateral history or specialist referral
options.rationale: Australian regulations require psychiatrist or paediatrician initiation of stimulants for ADHD; GPs cannot initiate. (Source: RACGP ADHD position; Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)

options.text: Commence an SSRI as first-line pharmacotherapy for adult ADHD symptoms with no further specialist assessment, no further investigation and no plan to consider stimulants for this presentation
options.rationale: SSRIs are not first-line for ADHD; they may treat comorbid depression or anxiety but do not address core ADHD symptoms. (Source: AADPA ADHD clinical guideline)

options.text: Complete a structured DSM-5 ADHD interview, gather corroborating childhood history, screen for comorbid mood, anxiety and substance use, then refer to a psychiatrist for stimulant initiation under AU prescribing restrictions
options.rationale: Adult ADHD diagnosis requires DSM-5 symptoms in childhood and adulthood with corroborating history; comorbidity screening guides management. Stimulant initiation must be by a psychiatrist (or paediatrician) under state authority and PBS rules. (Source: AADPA ADHD clinical guideline)

options.text: Refer for CBT alone without any consideration of stimulant or non-stimulant pharmacotherapy, regardless of severity, functional impairment or response to non-pharmacological interventions over time
options.rationale: CBT is adjunctive in moderate to severe ADHD; pharmacotherapy remains the most effective core treatment. (Source: AADPA ADHD clinical guideline)

options.text: Trial of lithium for impulse control as the first pharmacological intervention with no specialist referral, no structured ADHD diagnostic interview, and no consideration of stimulant or non-stimulant agents
options.rationale: Lithium has no role in primary ADHD pharmacotherapy. (Source: AADPA ADHD clinical guideline)

explanation.summary: Adult ADHD diagnosis requires DSM-5 symptoms beginning before age 12, persisting into adulthood with functional impairment across more than one setting, after exclusion of competing diagnoses. Corroborative childhood history (parent, school reports) strengthens diagnostic confidence. Comorbidity with mood, anxiety, substance use and learning disorders is the rule rather than the exception. Treatment is multimodal: psychoeducation, environmental modification, and pharmacotherapy (stimulants first-line in non-substance-use comorbidity, atomoxetine for substance use risk). Stimulant initiation is restricted to psychiatrists and paediatricians under Australian state authorities.
key_points: Adult ADHD diagnosis requires DSM-5 symptoms from childhood persisting into adulthood
Corroborative childhood history strengthens the diagnosis
Stimulants are initiated by a psychiatrist or paediatrician under AU state authorities
explanation.pearls: The AADPA 2022 guideline anchors adult ADHD diagnosis in structured DSM-5 interviewing with corroborative childhood history; GP-initiated stimulants are not legal in any Australian state.

subtopic_detail: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose with QRS prolongation and hypotension
stem: A 24-year-old woman is brought to ED 2 hours after ingestion of an estimated 4 grams of amitriptyline. She is now drowsy, hypotensive and tachycardic. She had a single seizure in the ambulance. The ECG demonstrates sinus tachycardia with a QRS duration of 140 ms and a right axis. She has no significant past medical history, no allergies and is not pregnant. There is no concurrent alcohol or other drug ingestion documented.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 86/52, HR 124, RR 22, SpO2 96% on room air, Temp 36.8 degrees Celsius, GCS 11
data_table.Examination: Dilated pupils 6 mm, dry mucous membranes, urinary retention; ECG QRS 140 ms, right axis
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.30, lactate 3.6 mmol/L, K 3.6 mmol/L, Na 138 mmol/L; salicylate and paracetamol levels negative; serum amitriptyline pending

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Intravenous lipid emulsion 20 percent at 1.5 mL/kg as a sole agent with no concurrent bicarbonate, no airway support and no antiarrhythmic therapy in this presentation
options.rationale: Lipid emulsion is a salvage option for refractory toxicity; it is not the first-line for QRS widening. (Source: NSW Health Poisons Information Centre TCA monograph; Murray Toxicology 4e)
source_refs: NSW Poisons Information Centre TCA guideline

options.text: Single dose activated charcoal 50 g orally 4 hours after the ingestion as the sole and primary intervention, with no other haemodynamic or cardiac stabilising therapy commenced at this time
options.rationale: Activated charcoal at 4 hours after an ingestion of a slow-absorbed drug is of marginal benefit and does not address the cardiotoxicity. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre TCA guideline)
source_refs: NSW Poisons Information Centre TCA guideline

options.text: Intravenous diazepam 10 mg as a single dose for the seizure with no further cardiovascular intervention beyond observation in a monitored bay over the next 4 hours
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines treat seizures but do not address the sodium channel blockade driving QRS widening and hypotension. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre TCA guideline)
source_refs: NSW Poisons Information Centre TCA guideline

options.text: Intravenous 8.4 percent sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg as a bolus to narrow the QRS and target arterial pH 7.45 to 7.55, with airway support and crystalloid resuscitation as adjuncts
options.rationale: TCA cardiotoxicity from fast sodium channel blockade is reversed with hypertonic sodium bicarbonate aiming for QRS narrowing and arterial pH 7.45 to 7.55; airway and circulation support continue alongside. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre TCA guideline)
source_refs: NSW Poisons Information Centre TCA guideline

options.text: Initiation of urgent haemodialysis as the sole and primary management strategy for TCA cardiotoxicity, with no concurrent bicarbonate therapy and no specific airway or cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: TCAs are highly protein-bound with a large volume of distribution; haemodialysis is not effective. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre TCA guideline)
source_refs: NSW Poisons Information Centre TCA guideline

explanation.summary: TCA overdose produces sodium channel blockade with QRS prolongation, ventricular arrhythmia, seizures, anticholinergic and alpha-blocker effects. Hypertonic sodium bicarbonate (1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus, repeated as needed) reverses sodium channel blockade by both pH alkalinisation and sodium loading, targeting QRS under 100 ms and arterial pH 7.45 to 7.55. Adjuncts: airway protection, crystalloid plus noradrenaline for hypotension, benzodiazepines for seizures, lipid emulsion in refractory shock. Haemodialysis is ineffective due to high protein binding and large volume of distribution.
key_points: QRS over 100 ms in TCA overdose indicates sodium channel blockade
Hypertonic sodium bicarbonate is the first-line antidote
Target arterial pH 7.45 to 7.55 and QRS narrowing
explanation.pearls: QRS over 100 ms in suspected TCA overdose predicts seizures and arrhythmia and is the trigger for sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg IV bolus; an R wave over 3 mm in aVR is corroborative.

sources.label: NSW Poisons Information Centre TCA guideline

subtopic_detail: Catatonia in major depression with positive lorazepam challenge
stem: A 58-year-old woman with a history of recurrent major depressive disorder is admitted after 6 days of becoming progressively mute, immobile and refusing food. She maintains odd postures and exhibits waxy flexibility. There is no fever. Investigations exclude infection, hypoglycaemia, electrolyte disturbance and intoxication. CT brain is unremarkable. She has been off her usual sertraline for 3 weeks before admission. There is no history of antipsychotic exposure.

data_table.Examination: Mutism, immobility, posturing, waxy flexibility; no rigidity, no tremor, no autonomic instability; Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale 14
data_table.Investigations: Na 139 mmol/L, K 4.0, glucose 5.4 mmol/L, CK 220 U/L, CRP 4 mg/L, ammonia 28 micromol/L, TSH 1.8 mIU/L; CT brain unremarkable

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate initial step?

options.text: Commence electroconvulsive therapy this afternoon without any pharmacological trial first, with no informed consent or capacity assessment process performed before treatment in this patient
options.rationale: ECT is highly effective for catatonia but follows a lorazepam challenge in most pathways and requires informed consent or substitute decision-maker authorisation. (Source: RANZCP catatonia clinical resource; Australian ECT guidelines)

options.text: Initiate sertraline 50 mg daily as the sole intervention with the expectation of full response within 72 hours and no other pharmacological or psychiatric measures arranged at this admission
options.rationale: SSRI initiation does not address acute catatonia and may delay effective treatment. (Source: RANZCP catatonia clinical resource)

options.text: Commence haloperidol 5 mg intramuscular every 6 hours as monotherapy for catatonia, with no benzodiazepine challenge and no other pharmacological measure considered at this point in admission
options.rationale: Antipsychotics, especially typical agents, can precipitate neuroleptic malignant syndrome in catatonic patients; they are reserved for psychotic catatonia under specialist guidance after a benzodiazepine trial. (Source: RANZCP catatonia clinical resource)

options.text: Commence a single dose of biperiden 5 mg intramuscularly as the sole pharmacological intervention for catatonia and reassess in 24 hours with no other immediate measures
options.rationale: Anticholinergics have no established role in catatonia. (Source: RANZCP catatonia clinical resource)

options.text: Intravenous lorazepam 1 to 2 mg challenge with reassessment of catatonia score at 5 to 10 minutes; if responsive, scheduled lorazepam and plan for ECT if symptoms persist or recur
options.rationale: A lorazepam challenge (1 to 2 mg IV with reassessment within 10 minutes) confirms benzodiazepine-responsive catatonia in 60 to 80 percent of cases; ECT follows for non-responders. (Source: RANZCP catatonia clinical resource)

explanation.summary: Catatonia presents with mutism, immobility, posturing, waxy flexibility, negativism and stupor; the Bush-Francis scale aids diagnosis. After exclusion of medical mimics (infection, NMS, encephalitis, hypoactive delirium, drug effects), the first-line treatment is a lorazepam challenge (1 to 2 mg IV with reassessment within 10 minutes), followed by scheduled lorazepam typically 6 to 24 mg per day. ECT is the most effective second-line treatment when lorazepam fails or for malignant catatonia. Antipsychotics are deferred unless psychotic features require treatment with concurrent benzodiazepines.
key_points: Bush-Francis catatonia rating helps quantify response to treatment
Lorazepam challenge 1 to 2 mg IV reverses catatonia in 60 to 80 percent within minutes
Antipsychotic monotherapy risks neuroleptic malignant syndrome in catatonic patients
explanation.pearls: A 1 to 2 mg IV lorazepam challenge with reassessment at 5 to 10 minutes confirms benzodiazepine-responsive catatonia in around 70 percent and titrates to scheduled lorazepam 6 to 24 mg per day.

subtopic_detail: Discriminating schizoaffective disorder from bipolar I with mood-congruent psychosis
stem: A 32-year-old man has had three discrete depressive episodes over 4 years, each with mood-congruent paranoid delusions and auditory hallucinations. Between episodes, his depressive symptoms have remitted but the paranoid delusions and auditory hallucinations have persisted continuously for at least 3 weeks at a time, in the absence of an acute mood episode. He has no history of manic or hypomanic episodes. He uses no substances. There is no first-degree family history of bipolar disorder.

data_table.Examination: Today: persecutory delusions present; mood euthymic; speech normal; no manic features
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative; TSH 1.6 mIU/L; CT brain normal; PANSS positive 28

lead_in: Which is the single most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Schizoaffective disorder, depressive type, given the persistence of psychotic symptoms for 2 weeks or longer in the absence of an acute major depressive episode in this patient
options.rationale: DSM-5 schizoaffective disorder requires major mood episodes during a substantial portion of the illness with at least 2 weeks of psychotic symptoms in the absence of an acute mood episode. (Source: DSM-5; RANZCP schizoaffective disorder clinical resource)

options.text: Bipolar I disorder with mood-congruent psychotic features, given his recurrent psychotic mood symptoms with full remission of psychotic symptoms between acute mood episodes in his presentation
options.rationale: He has had no manic or hypomanic episodes and psychosis persists between mood episodes; bipolar I does not fit. (Source: DSM-5)

options.text: Brief psychotic disorder, given the episodic nature of his psychotic symptoms over 4 years of intermittent illness, with mood symptoms considered incidental in this patient
options.rationale: Brief psychotic disorder is by definition under 1 month and does not recur over years. (Source: DSM-5)

options.text: Major depressive disorder with psychotic features, given the depressive episodes and concurrent psychotic features, with psychosis considered episode-bound in this patient's longitudinal course of illness
options.rationale: MDD with psychotic features requires psychosis to occur only during depressive episodes; persistent psychosis between episodes excludes this. (Source: DSM-5)

options.text: Schizophreniform disorder, given the under-6-month duration of any individual psychotic episode in this patient with intermittent mood symptoms and recurring discrete intervals of psychosis
options.rationale: Schizophreniform applies for psychotic episodes lasting 1 to 6 months in total; the longitudinal course here exceeds this. (Source: DSM-5)

explanation.summary: Schizoaffective disorder requires DSM-5 criteria of an uninterrupted period of illness with a major mood episode (manic or depressive) concurrent with schizophrenia A criteria, plus at least 2 weeks of delusions or hallucinations in the absence of a major mood episode. Mood episodes are present for the majority of the active and residual phases. Differentiation from bipolar I with psychotic features rests on persistence of psychosis outside of mood episodes; from MDD with psychotic features on the same point; from schizophrenia on the prominence and duration of mood symptoms.
key_points: Schizoaffective disorder requires psychosis for 2 weeks or more in the absence of an acute mood episode
Mood episodes must be present for the majority of the illness's active and residual phases
Mood-congruent psychosis confined to mood episodes points to MDD or bipolar I with psychotic features
explanation.pearls: Schizoaffective disorder is identified longitudinally: at least 2 weeks of psychosis without an active mood episode, with mood symptoms across the majority of the total illness duration distinguishing it from primary psychotic disorders.

subtopic_detail: Acute behavioural disturbance in the ED requiring rapid tranquillisation
stem: A 36-year-old man brought in by police is highly agitated, shouting and pacing in the ED short-stay unit. He has paranoid delusions and a history of treatment-resistant schizophrenia, with intermittent methamphetamine use. He is intermittently approaching staff aggressively but has not yet assaulted anyone. He is refusing oral medication and verbal de-escalation has failed. There is no documented allergy, no current QT prolongation on ECG, and no concurrent CNS depressant ingestion suspected.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 142/86, HR 108, SpO2 98% on room air, Temp 37.0 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, dilated pupils 5 mm, ECG sinus tachycardia QTc 412 ms, blood alcohol 0
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen pending; previous ECG 3 weeks ago QTc 408 ms; weight 80 kg

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Single oral diazepam 2 mg only without any antipsychotic, with no further escalation pathway and no re-evaluation interval planned for this patient with acute behavioural disturbance
options.rationale: A low oral benzodiazepine dose alone is sub-therapeutic for severe acute behavioural disturbance and lacks a planned escalation pathway. (Source: NSW Health acute behavioural disturbance clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: NSW Health acute behavioural disturbance CPG

options.text: De-escalation first, then offer oral olanzapine 10 mg or oral lorazepam 1 to 2 mg; if refused or unsafe, intramuscular olanzapine 10 mg or droperidol 10 mg with cardiac and respiratory monitoring
options.rationale: AU stepped pathway prioritises de-escalation and oral options before parenteral therapy; IM olanzapine or droperidol is the preferred parenteral option with monitoring of airway and ECG. (Source: NSW Health acute behavioural disturbance clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: NSW Health acute behavioural disturbance CPG

options.text: Single intramuscular haloperidol 20 mg as a one-off dose without ECG, without monitoring and without re-evaluation, regardless of comorbid stimulant intoxication or QTc status
options.rationale: High-dose haloperidol risks dystonia, QT prolongation and torsades, especially with stimulant intoxication; not recommended as a first-line single dose. (Source: NSW Health acute behavioural disturbance CPG)
source_refs: NSW Health acute behavioural disturbance CPG

options.text: Rapid IV midazolam infusion at 5 mg/hour without monitoring, escalation plan or airway support, in a general ward bed with no immediate access to flumazenil or other airway adjuncts
options.rationale: IV midazolam infusion outside a high-acuity bed risks respiratory arrest; IM benzodiazepines or olanzapine are safer first-line parenteral choices. (Source: NSW Health acute behavioural disturbance CPG)
source_refs: NSW Health acute behavioural disturbance CPG

options.text: Physical restraint indefinitely without medication, with no clear monitoring plan, no medical review interval and no de-escalation attempt offered to the patient before restraint is applied
options.rationale: Mechanical restraint without pharmacotherapy and ongoing medical review is unsafe and ethically untenable; it is a last-resort short-term measure with chemical and behavioural alternatives. (Source: NSW Health acute behavioural disturbance CPG)
source_refs: NSW Health acute behavioural disturbance CPG

explanation.summary: Acute behavioural disturbance is managed by a stepped pathway: assess for medical or substance causes, attempt verbal de-escalation and environmental measures, offer oral medication (olanzapine, lorazepam or risperidone), then escalate to intramuscular olanzapine or droperidol if refused or unsafe. Monitoring includes airway, conscious level, SpO2, BP, HR, ECG (for QT), temperature and post-restraint review. Mechanical restraint is a last resort and time-limited. Specific AU pathways (NSW Health, Victorian DHHS, Queensland Health) operationalise this approach with consistent agents and review timing.
