key_points: De-escalation and oral medication precede parenteral options where safe
IM olanzapine or droperidol is the preferred parenteral option with monitoring
Mechanical restraint is a last resort, time-limited and requires ongoing medical review
explanation.pearls: Intramuscular olanzapine 10 mg or droperidol 10 mg with airway, SpO2 and ECG monitoring is the AU-preferred parenteral rapid tranquillisation when oral medication is refused or unsafe.

sources.label: NSW Health acute behavioural disturbance CPG
RANZCP guideline on management of acute behavioural disturbance

subtopic_detail: Schizoaffective disorder vs bipolar I with psychotic features
stem: A 24-year-old woman is admitted with a third episode of acute psychosis with prominent persecutory delusions, third-person auditory hallucinations, and disorganised behaviour. Collateral from her sister indicates these psychotic symptoms have been present for the past 6 weeks. During the first 3 weeks of this episode she was sleeping 3 hours nightly, spending compulsively, and grandiose. Over the past 3 weeks her mood has stabilised but the psychotic symptoms persist unchanged.

data_table.Examination: Mental state: thought disorder, persecutory delusions held with full conviction, third-person auditory hallucinations; mood euthymic for the past 3 weeks; no current suicidal ideation
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative; CT brain normal; TSH, B12, FBC, calcium, electrolytes normal; structured interview confirms two prior episodes of mania each lasting at least 7 days

lead_in: What is the single most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Schizoaffective disorder bipolar type because the psychosis has persisted at least 2 weeks in the absence of prominent mood symptoms during a longitudinal course with mood episodes
options.rationale: Schizoaffective disorder requires psychosis without prominent mood symptoms for at least 2 weeks alongside mood episodes meeting full criteria over the illness course. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia Clinical Practice Guideline)

options.text: Bipolar I disorder with mood-congruent psychotic features because mania was clearly present in the first 3 weeks of this index episode of illness
options.rationale: Bipolar I with psychotic features requires psychosis to occur only within mood episodes; persistence of psychosis after mood remits points to schizoaffective. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia Clinical Practice Guideline)

options.text: Schizophreniform disorder because the psychotic symptoms have been present for over 1 month but less than 6 months in total since the prodromal onset
options.rationale: Schizophreniform disorder does not include episodes meeting full mania or major depression criteria during the course of psychosis. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia Clinical Practice Guideline)

options.text: Substance-induced psychotic disorder because methamphetamine remains detectable for up to 3 months in clinical practice despite a current negative screen
options.rationale: Methamphetamine is undetectable in urine after 72 to 96 hours; substance-induced psychosis would also be expected to remit fully within weeks of cessation. (Source: RANZCP: Psychostimulant Position Statement)

options.text: Major depressive disorder with psychotic features and mood incongruent persecutory delusions despite the absence of depressive symptoms over recent weeks
options.rationale: Major depression with psychotic features requires the psychosis to occur during a current depressive episode, which this presentation lacks. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

explanation.summary: Schizoaffective disorder requires psychosis to persist for at least 2 weeks in the absence of prominent mood symptoms within a course that also includes mood episodes meeting major depressive or manic criteria for a substantial part of the illness. Bipolar disorder with psychotic features confines psychotic symptoms within the duration of mood episodes. Treatment for schizoaffective bipolar type usually combines a mood stabiliser with an antipsychotic; clozapine is considered for treatment resistance. The diagnosis often requires longitudinal data because of significant overlap with bipolar disorder with psychotic features.
key_points: Schizoaffective requires 2 weeks of psychosis without prominent mood symptoms
Mood episodes must be present for a substantial part of the illness
Treatment combines mood stabiliser plus antipsychotic; consider clozapine for resistance
explanation.pearls: Longitudinal collateral history outperforms cross-sectional assessment for distinguishing schizoaffective from bipolar with psychotic features.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

stem: A 47-year-old smokes 25 cigarettes daily for 28 years and presents for cessation support after a hospital admission for a non-ST elevation myocardial infarction 4 weeks ago. He has previously tried nicotine patches and tried cold turkey twice without success. He is on aspirin, atorvastatin, metoprolol, perindopril. His mood is euthymic with no previous depression or suicidal thoughts. He has no renal impairment.

data_table.Examination: BMI 28, BP 132/82, no signs of withdrawal, no respiratory disease on examination
data_table.Investigations: eGFR 78 mL/min/1.73 m2, normal liver function, recent echocardiogram with preserved ejection fraction

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate plan for varenicline?

options.text: Start varenicline 1 mg twice daily today and stop smoking immediately on the same day as the first dose to maximise medication coverage at the receptor
options.rationale: Varenicline requires a 1 week titration from 0.5 mg daily to 1 mg twice daily and the quit date is set within that first or second week, not immediately at first dose. (Source: AMH: Varenicline)

options.text: Substitute varenicline 1 mg twice daily for his metoprolol because beta-blockers interfere with the action of varenicline at nicotinic receptors
options.rationale: Beta-blockers do not interact pharmacologically with varenicline; both are continued and metoprolol is essential after recent myocardial infarction. (Source: AMH: Varenicline)

options.text: Avoid varenicline entirely after recent acute coronary syndrome and recommend nicotine inhalator plus oral nortriptyline combination instead
options.rationale: Recent meta-analyses show no excess cardiovascular events with varenicline; it remains a first-line option after acute coronary syndrome. (Source: RACGP: Smoking Cessation)

options.text: Begin varenicline 2 mg daily with a planned cessation date 6 weeks after starting to allow gradual tapering of cigarettes during titration
options.rationale: The standard quit date is set 1 to 2 weeks after starting, not 6 weeks; the dose of 2 mg daily is also non-standard. (Source: AMH: Varenicline)

options.text: Start varenicline 0.5 mg daily for 3 days then 0.5 mg twice daily for 4 days then 1 mg twice daily, with a quit date 8 to 14 days from first dose, for 12 weeks
options.rationale: Standard titration is 0.5 mg daily for 3 days, 0.5 mg twice daily for 4 days, then 1 mg twice daily; the quit date is set 8 to 14 days after starting for 12 weeks. (Source: AMH: Varenicline)

explanation.summary: Varenicline is a partial nicotinic agonist that is started 1 to 2 weeks before the planned quit date with a standard titration to allow tolerance. Standard duration is 12 weeks; an additional 12 weeks may be considered to consolidate abstinence. Australian post-acute coronary syndrome guidance still considers varenicline first-line because cardiovascular safety is established. Common adverse effects include nausea, vivid dreams, and insomnia; severe psychiatric adverse effects are rare and historic boxed warnings have been substantially revised.
key_points: Set the quit date 1 to 2 weeks after starting varenicline
Titrate over 7 days then continue 1 mg twice daily for 12 weeks
Cardiovascular safety after acute coronary syndrome is established
explanation.pearls: Nausea peaks in the first 2 weeks of varenicline; taking the dose with food and a full glass of water reduces it markedly.

subtopic_detail: Cannabis-induced psychosis vs first episode schizophrenia
stem: A 19-year-old male is admitted with 5 days of persecutory delusions about being followed by police and second-person command auditory hallucinations. He uses high-potency cannabis daily and his last use was 12 hours ago. He has had previous brief paranoid episodes after heavy cannabis sessions that resolved within 48 hours of cessation. His older brother was diagnosed with schizophrenia at age 22.

data_table.Examination: Mental state: marked paranoia, third-person auditory hallucinations, blunted affect, formal thought disorder; appears internally preoccupied
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen positive for cannabis only; CT brain normal; TSH and electrolytes normal; collateral confirms no premorbid functional decline before recent cannabis escalation 9 months ago

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate diagnostic and management approach now?

options.text: Diagnose first episode schizophrenia and commence long-acting paliperidone palmitate intramuscular depot before discharge home with community mental health follow-up
options.rationale: Premature labelling and depot initiation before observing the post-substance withdrawal trajectory is not best practice; substance-induced psychosis often resolves with abstinence. (Source: RANZCP: First Episode Psychosis Guideline)

options.text: Diagnose cannabis intoxication and discharge home today with cessation counselling alone and review at the local community mental health team within 1 month
options.rationale: Acute psychosis with command hallucinations requires admission for safety and observation regardless of substance use cause. (Source: RANZCP: First Episode Psychosis Guideline)

options.text: Admit to a specialist youth early psychosis service for low-dose oral antipsychotic, cannabis cessation support, and longitudinal review for emerging psychosis
options.rationale: Australian early intervention practice supports admission, low-dose oral antipsychotic, structured cannabis cessation, and longitudinal review because up to 40% of cannabis-induced psychoses convert to schizophrenia. (Source: Orygen: First Episode Psychosis)

options.text: Diagnose substance-induced psychotic disorder definitively and avoid antipsychotic medication entirely while encouraging abstinence over the next 4 weeks
options.rationale: Antipsychotic medication relieves distressing symptoms and reduces risk during active psychosis even when substance use is implicated. (Source: RANZCP: First Episode Psychosis Guideline)

options.text: Commence high-dose intramuscular zuclopenthixol acuphase 100 mg with physical restraint maintained for the duration of all acute behavioural symptoms
options.rationale: Acuphase is reserved for severe acute behavioural disturbance unresponsive to oral therapy; oral first-line antipsychotic is preferred when the patient can engage. (Source: NSW Health: Acute Behavioural Disturbance)

explanation.summary: Cannabis-induced psychosis and first episode schizophrenia can be indistinguishable cross-sectionally. Australian early intervention practice favours admission to a specialist youth early psychosis service, low-dose oral antipsychotic to manage acute symptoms, structured cannabis cessation support, and longitudinal review. Approximately 40% of cannabis-induced psychoses convert to schizophrenia within 5 years, particularly with high-potency cannabis exposure, family history, and prodromal functional decline. Early intervention reduces transition rates and improves outcomes.
key_points: Admit acute psychosis with command hallucinations regardless of substance use
Use low-dose oral antipsychotic plus structured cannabis cessation
Up to 40% of cannabis-induced psychosis converts to schizophrenia within 5 years
explanation.pearls: Family history of schizophrenia and prodromal functional decline strongly raise transition risk after cannabis-induced psychosis; track these explicitly.

subtopic_detail: Augmentation strategy in treatment-resistant unipolar depression
stem: A 52-year-old has had inadequate response to two adequate trials of antidepressant: sertraline 200 mg daily for 10 weeks then venlafaxine extended release 225 mg daily for 12 weeks. She has a current Hamilton Depression Rating Scale of 22. She remains in partial remission with persistent low mood, anhedonia, and middle insomnia. She has no psychotic features, no bipolarity in personal or family history, and no suicidal ideation. Her thyroid function, vitamin B12, and full blood count are normal.

data_table.Examination: BMI 27, BP 124/78, no parkinsonism, no acute distress
data_table.Investigations: TSH 1.9 mIU/L, B12 320 pmol/L, fasting glucose 4.8 mmol/L, lithium not previously tried, cardiac echo normal, ECG QTc 410 ms

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Cross-titrate to oral fluoxetine 60 mg daily over 2 weeks before reassessing for a further antidepressant switch
options.rationale: A third sequential antidepressant monotherapy switch has lower remission rates than augmentation after two adequate antidepressant trials. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Augment with aripiprazole 2.5 mg daily, titrating to 10 mg as tolerated, with metabolic and akathisia monitoring at 4 and 8 weeks
options.rationale: Atypical antipsychotic augmentation, typically aripiprazole or quetiapine, has the strongest evidence base for treatment-resistant unipolar depression in current Australian guidance. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Combine venlafaxine with a tricyclic antidepressant such as amitriptyline 75 mg nightly to maximise noradrenergic effect over the next 6 weeks
options.rationale: Combining serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor with tricyclic antidepressant has significant serotonergic and cardiovascular risk and is not a routine augmentation. (Source: AMH: Antidepressants)

options.text: Augment with the dopamine agonist pramipexole 0.125 mg three times daily as a first-line augmentation strategy
options.rationale: Pramipexole augmentation has limited evidence and is not first-line in current Australian guidance. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Recommend immediate electroconvulsive therapy as initial next step without further pharmacological augmentation trials
options.rationale: Electroconvulsive therapy is appropriate for severe, psychotic, or treatment-resistant depression but is generally considered after augmentation trials in non-psychotic moderate cases. (Source: RANZCP: Electroconvulsive Therapy Guideline)

explanation.summary: Treatment-resistant unipolar depression after two adequate antidepressant trials benefits more from augmentation than a third sequential monotherapy switch. Atypical antipsychotic augmentation with aripiprazole or quetiapine has the strongest evidence base and is preferred in current Australian guidance. Lithium augmentation remains an option, particularly with comorbid suicidal ideation. Electroconvulsive therapy is considered for severe, psychotic, or treatment-resistant depression unresponsive to augmentation. Monitor metabolic side effects, akathisia, and movement disorders during augmentation.
key_points: After two adequate antidepressant trials, augment rather than switch
Aripiprazole and quetiapine have the strongest augmentation evidence
Monitor for metabolic syndrome and akathisia during antipsychotic augmentation
explanation.pearls: Quetiapine extended release has additional sedative benefit in middle insomnia; aripiprazole is more activating and may worsen insomnia in some patients.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

stem: A 32-year-old has been stable on clozapine 350 mg nightly for 8 months for treatment-resistant schizophrenia. His routine weekly bloods today show an absolute neutrophil count of 1.4 x10^9/L, down from 2.1 x10^9/L a week ago. White cell count is 3.0. He is afebrile, asymptomatic, and has had no recent infections. He uses no other myelosuppressive medications. He continues to attend his weekly clozapine clinic.

data_table.Examination: No oral ulceration, no lymphadenopathy, no infective focus, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Today: WCC 3.0, neutrophils 1.4 x10^9/L, lymphocytes 1.3, platelets 220, Hb 142; previous week: WCC 4.1, neutrophils 2.1 x10^9/L; clozapine level 540 microgram/L

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next action?

options.text: Continue clozapine unchanged and resume routine 4-weekly bloods after a single repeat full blood count tomorrow morning
options.rationale: An absolute neutrophil count below 1.5 x10^9/L requires increased haematological surveillance regardless of asymptomatic status. (Source: ClozapinePMC Australia Protocol)

options.text: Stop clozapine permanently and switch to oral aripiprazole 10 mg daily, starting cross-titration today before discharge home
options.rationale: Permanent cessation is reserved for the red zone with absolute neutrophil count below 1.0 x10^9/L or other evidence of agranulocytosis. (Source: ClozapinePMC Australia Protocol)

options.text: Hospitalise and commence intravenous filgrastim 300 microgram daily until neutrophil recovery without changing the clozapine dose
options.rationale: Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor is reserved for the red zone with severe neutropenia, not amber zone monitoring; clozapine should be ceased in the red zone. (Source: ClozapinePMC Australia Protocol)

options.text: Continue clozapine at the current dose, repeat full blood count twice weekly, and notify the clozapine program as the patient is now in the amber zone
options.rationale: Absolute neutrophil count between 1.0 and 1.5 x10^9/L is the amber zone; continue clozapine, increase monitoring to twice weekly, and notify the clozapine program. (Source: ClozapinePMC Australia Protocol)

options.text: Halve the clozapine dose to 175 mg nightly and continue routine 4-weekly bloods, with general practitioner review only if febrile illness emerges
options.rationale: Dose reduction does not reverse clozapine-induced neutropenia; increased monitoring frequency is required and routine 4-weekly bloods are inadequate. (Source: ClozapinePMC Australia Protocol)

explanation.summary: Clozapine haematological monitoring uses a traffic light system. Absolute neutrophil count over 2.0 x10^9/L is green and continues routine monitoring. Counts between 1.5 and 2.0 x10^9/L are yellow with twice-weekly bloods and physician review. Counts between 1.0 and 1.5 x10^9/L are amber with twice-weekly bloods, continued clozapine, and clozapine program notification. Counts below 1.0 x10^9/L are red and clozapine is ceased; granulocyte colony-stimulating factor and intravenous antibiotics are considered if febrile.
key_points: Green over 2.0, yellow 1.5 to 2.0, amber 1.0 to 1.5, red below 1.0 x10^9/L for absolute neutrophil count
Cease clozapine in red zone and consider granulocyte colony-stimulating factor
Notify the clozapine program for amber or red zone events
explanation.pearls: Benign ethnic neutropenia in some Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander, African, and Middle Eastern patients warrants program-approved lower thresholds rather than clozapine cessation.

stem:
You are a GP registrar reviewing a 47-year-old woman who has been on lithium carbonate 1000 mg daily for bipolar I disorder for 4 years. Her mood has been stable on this dose with no relapses. She presents for an annual review and reports fatigue, mild constipation, modest weight gain, and dry skin over the past 6 months. She has no tremor, no polyuria, and no neurological symptoms.

Her psychiatrist last reviewed her 6 months ago and was happy with her mood state. Her most recent lithium level 3 months ago was 0.7 mmol/L. The annual monitoring bloods have just been performed.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/76 mmHg, HR 64 bpm, BMI 28 kg/m2
data_table.Examination: No goitre, no tremor, no peripheral oedema, slow ankle jerk relaxation
data_table.Investigations: TSH 18.2 mIU/L, free T4 9 pmol/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L, eGFR 78 mL/min/1.73m2, calcium corrected 2.42 mmol/L, lithium level 0.7 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Cease lithium immediately and substitute sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily as mood stabiliser
options.rationale: Abrupt lithium cessation is associated with high rates of bipolar relapse, especially in a stable patient. Lithium-induced hypothyroidism is reversible with thyroxine while continuing lithium. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines - Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines - Mood Disorders

options.text: Commence levothyroxine 50 micrograms orally daily and continue lithium at current dose
options.rationale: Lithium-induced hypothyroidism affects up to 20% of patients on long-term lithium and is managed with levothyroxine replacement rather than lithium cessation, given the lithium is providing effective mood stabilisation. Starting dose of 50 micrograms is appropriate in a woman without cardiovascular disease. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines - Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines - Mood Disorders

options.text: Reduce lithium to 500 mg daily to allow thyroid recovery and continue close monitoring of mood
options.rationale: Subtherapeutic lithium risks bipolar relapse without reversing the autoimmune component of lithium-induced hypothyroidism, which is more reliably treated with thyroxine. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines - Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines - Mood Disorders

options.text: Recheck thyroid function in 6 weeks before considering replacement therapy in this asymptomatic phase
options.rationale: She has clear clinical hypothyroidism with fatigue, constipation, and dry skin alongside a TSH of 18 and low T4. Delaying replacement worsens symptoms unnecessarily. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines - Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines - Mood Disorders

options.text: Refer to endocrinology for thyroid autoantibodies and ultrasound before starting any treatment
options.rationale: Thyroid autoantibodies and imaging do not change the management of overt hypothyroidism. Thyroxine should commence promptly with monitoring through general practice. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines - Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines - Mood Disorders

explanation.summary: Lithium causes thyroid dysfunction in around 15 to 20% of patients on long-term therapy, predominantly hypothyroidism, and a smaller minority develop hyperparathyroidism. Australian best practice is to monitor TSH, calcium, creatinine, and lithium level every 6 to 12 months. When lithium-induced hypothyroidism develops in a patient with sustained mood stability, levothyroxine replacement is preferred over lithium cessation. Renal monitoring is for nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and chronic interstitial nephritis; baseline and annual eGFR are standard.
key_points: Lithium-induced hypothyroidism affects approximately 15 to 20% of long-term patients
Manage with thyroxine; do not stop lithium if mood stability has been hard-won
Annual monitoring: TSH, calcium, creatinine, lithium level, weight
Lithium also causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and chronic interstitial nephritis
explanation.pearls: In a patient stable on lithium who develops hypothyroidism, add levothyroxine rather than stopping lithium - bipolar relapse risk after lithium cessation is approximately 50% within 12 months, far exceeding the morbidity of treated hypothyroidism.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines - Mood Disorders

stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar called to review a 24-year-old man with a first episode of psychosis admitted 5 days ago. He was started on olanzapine 10 mg daily 3 days ago. Today he is mute, staring, and immobile. The nurse reports he has not eaten or drunk since this morning and has held his arm in an awkward position for over an hour without complaint.

There is no fever and no rigidity. He has no past medical history and takes no other medications. His vital signs are stable. The medical registrar saw him this morning and excluded delirium with a normal collateral history of acute onset and stable medical workup.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88 bpm, BP 122/78 mmHg, Temp 37.0 degrees C, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Mute, immobile, posturing, waxy flexibility, no tremor, no rigidity, no clonus
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 180 U/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, glucose 5.2 mmol/L, urinalysis clear, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer haloperidol 5 mg intramuscularly for behavioural disturbance and continue olanzapine
options.rationale: Haloperidol can precipitate or worsen catatonia and may cause neuroleptic malignant syndrome in this state. It is not appropriate as a catatonia treatment or diagnostic test. (Source: RANZCP Guideline - Catatonia)

options.text: Increase olanzapine to 20 mg daily for presumed exacerbation of underlying psychotic illness
options.rationale: Antipsychotics can worsen catatonia and precipitate neuroleptic malignant syndrome, particularly in malignant catatonia. The first step is benzodiazepine challenge, with cautious antipsychotic dose review thereafter. (Source: RANZCP Guideline - Catatonia)

options.text: Cease olanzapine and commence intravenous dantrolene 2 mg/kg as muscle relaxant for rigidity
options.rationale: Dantrolene treats malignant hyperthermia and may be used adjunctively in severe NMS, but is not indicated in catatonia without hyperthermia or marked rigidity. The pathognomonic finding here is waxy flexibility, not rigidity. (Source: RANZCP Guideline - Catatonia)

options.text: Administer lorazepam 2 mg intramuscularly and reassess catatonic features at 30 to 60 minutes
options.rationale: The lorazepam challenge is both diagnostic and therapeutic for catatonia. A response within 30 to 60 minutes (loosening of posturing, return of speech, ability to move) confirms catatonia and supports ongoing benzodiazepine treatment. This is the recommended first-line approach in Australian psychiatry. (Source: RANZCP Guideline - Catatonia)

options.text: Defer pharmacological intervention and arrange brain MRI to exclude structural neurological cause
options.rationale: MRI is appropriate in atypical presentations but does not replace immediate symptomatic and diagnostic lorazepam challenge in clear-cut catatonia. The patient is at risk of dehydration, aspiration, and venous thromboembolism if left immobile. (Source: RANZCP Guideline - Catatonia)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a syndrome of motor, behavioural, and affective disturbance characterised by features such as mutism, immobility, posturing, waxy flexibility, negativism, echolalia, and stereotypy. It complicates affective, psychotic, and medical illness and can be precipitated or worsened by antipsychotics. The lorazepam challenge (1 to 2 mg parenteral with response assessed at 30 to 60 minutes) is both diagnostic and first-line treatment. Refractory cases or malignant catatonia respond to electroconvulsive therapy. Antipsychotics are reduced or temporarily withdrawn until catatonia resolves.
key_points: Catatonia features include mutism, immobility, posturing, waxy flexibility, negativism
Lorazepam 1 to 2 mg challenge is first-line diagnostic and therapeutic
ECT is second-line, particularly for malignant catatonia or non-response
Antipsychotics can precipitate or worsen catatonia; consider holding during workup
explanation.pearls: Malignant catatonia (with autonomic instability, hyperthermia, rigidity) clinically overlaps with neuroleptic malignant syndrome but responds rapidly to electroconvulsive therapy with 80 to 100% remission rates.

stem: You are the emergency registrar reviewing a 28-year-old woman brought in 90 minutes after deliberate ingestion of approximately 50 amitriptyline 50 mg tablets. She is drowsy with GCS 11 but maintaining her airway. Her observations are concerning. She was charcoal-treated by paramedics 30 minutes after the ingestion. The poisons information centre advice has been sought and a plan formulated. An arterial blood gas and ECG have just been performed. The toxicology registrar is on the phone for consultation about further management. She has no past medical history.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 132 bpm, BP 92/56 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 96% room air, Temp 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Dilated pupils, dry mucous membranes, no clonus, no focal deficit
data_table.Investigations: pH 7.30, pCO2 32 mmHg, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, lactate 3.4 mmol/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 3.8 mmol/L, ECG: sinus tachycardia 132 bpm with QRS 130 ms and R wave in aVR 4 mm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Administer intravenous lipid emulsion 20% as bolus then infusion for lipid sink rescue
options.rationale: Intralipid is a second-line rescue therapy for refractory cardiovascular collapse not responding to bicarbonate. It is not first-line in haemodynamically borderline TCA overdose where bicarbonate is the priority. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology - Tricyclic Antidepressants)

options.text: Administer intravenous lidocaine 1 mg/kg bolus followed by an infusion for ventricular ectopy
options.rationale: Class IA and IC antiarrhythmics are contraindicated in TCA overdose because they share sodium channel blockade. Lidocaine has limited evidence and is not first-line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology - Tricyclic Antidepressants)

options.text: Administer sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg intravenously and target a serum pH of 7.50 to 7.55
options.rationale: QRS prolongation over 100 ms and R wave in aVR over 3 mm are markers of severe sodium channel blockade in tricyclic overdose and predict arrhythmia and seizure. Hypertonic sodium bicarbonate is first-line, alkalinising serum to enhance dissociation from cardiac sodium channels and providing a sodium load. Target pH is 7.50 to 7.55. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology - Tricyclic Antidepressants)

options.text: Administer activated charcoal 50 g via nasogastric tube as second dose to improve drug binding
options.rationale: Single-dose charcoal within 1 to 2 hours has limited benefit and a further dose 90 minutes post-ingestion in a drowsy patient risks aspiration. The priority is sodium bicarbonate for the cardiotoxicity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology - Tricyclic Antidepressants)

options.text: Commence intravenous physostigmine 1 mg over 5 minutes to reverse anticholinergic toxicity
options.rationale: Physostigmine is contraindicated in TCA overdose because it can precipitate asystole and seizures. Anticholinergic features are managed supportively. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology - Tricyclic Antidepressants)

explanation.summary: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose causes sodium channel blockade, anticholinergic syndrome, alpha-adrenergic blockade, and central nervous system depression. ECG markers of severity include QRS over 100 ms (seizure and arrhythmia risk) and R wave in aVR over 3 mm. Sodium bicarbonate is the cornerstone treatment, working through both serum alkalinisation and sodium loading. Hypotension is treated with crystalloid and noradrenaline; benzodiazepines for seizures; intralipid for refractory cardiovascular collapse. Charcoal is reserved for early presentations with protected airway.
key_points: QRS over 100 ms or R wave in aVR over 3 mm predict arrhythmia and seizure
Sodium bicarbonate is first-line - alkalinise to pH 7.50 to 7.55
Class IA and IC antiarrhythmics and physostigmine are contraindicated
Intralipid 20% is rescue therapy for refractory cardiovascular collapse
explanation.pearls: An R wave over 3 mm in lead aVR within 6 hours of tricyclic overdose has a positive predictive value of approximately 81% for seizures or arrhythmias, making it a stronger predictor than QRS duration alone.

sources.label: Murray L, Daly F - Toxicology Handbook

stem:
You are a psychiatry registrar reviewing a 32-year-old IT consultant referred by his GP for assessment of possible adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. He reports lifelong difficulty completing tasks, frequent careless mistakes, and being easily distracted. He has held his current job 8 years but says he relies on tight deadlines and a self-built reminder system. He achieved high school graduation with average results despite his difficulties.

He drinks 2 standard drinks per week and uses no other substances. His mood is euthymic. He has no anxiety or sleep disturbance. His mother reports he was always restless in primary school but managed academically.

data_table.Examination: Mental state normal, no thought disorder, no psychomotor abnormality
data_table.Investigations: Standardised adult ADHD rating scale: 18 of 18 inattentive items endorsed at threshold severity, 6 of 9 hyperactive-impulsive items, symptoms present since age 7, impairment present in occupational and home domains

lead_in: Which feature is essential to support an adult ADHD diagnosis under the Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline?

options.text: Documented IQ below 90 to establish baseline cognitive impairment before stimulant therapy
options.rationale: ADHD is diagnosed regardless of IQ. Many adults with ADHD have above-average IQ and have compensated for impairment until adult demands exceed their capacity. (Source: AADPA Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: AADPA Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: At least 6 of 9 symptoms in BOTH inattentive and hyperactive-impulsive domains for adult diagnosis
options.rationale: DSM-5 lowers the adult threshold to 5 of 9 in either domain (not both). The combined-presentation requirement of 6 of 9 in both applies only to children under 17. (Source: AADPA Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: AADPA Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Persistent functional impairment in two or more settings attributable to symptoms present before 12 years old
options.rationale: The Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD aligns with DSM-5 in requiring symptoms before age 12, present in two or more settings, with clear functional impairment. Without childhood onset and cross-setting impairment, an adult presentation of inattention is more likely explained by other conditions. (Source: AADPA Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: AADPA Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Normal brain MRI and electroencephalogram excluding structural and epileptiform causes
options.rationale: Routine MRI and EEG are not part of the standard ADHD workup. They are reserved for atypical features such as focal neurology or possible seizures. (Source: AADPA Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: AADPA Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Failed trial of nonpharmacological strategies including cognitive behavioural therapy and coaching
options.rationale: Behavioural and educational strategies can be used in parallel with or before pharmacotherapy but are not a diagnostic prerequisite. The diagnosis is based on history, examination, and ratings, not therapy response. (Source: AADPA Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: AADPA Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

explanation.summary: Adult ADHD diagnosis under the Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline requires DSM-5 criteria: at least 5 of 9 inattentive or hyperactive-impulsive symptoms (lower threshold than child criteria of 6), symptoms before age 12, present in 2 or more settings, with clear functional impairment, not better explained by another disorder. Collateral history (school reports, parent interview) anchors the childhood onset criterion. Stimulant treatment in adults requires ECG only if cardiovascular risk factors or symptoms, BP/HR monitoring before and during treatment, and substance use assessment.
key_points: Adult DSM-5 threshold: 5 of 9 symptoms in either domain (vs 6 of 9 in children)
Symptoms must be present before age 12 with cross-setting impairment
Routine MRI and EEG not required
Stimulants require BP/HR monitoring; ECG only if cardiovascular risk
explanation.pearls: Roughly 60 to 70% of adults with ADHD have at least one comorbid psychiatric condition (depression, anxiety, substance use, or personality disorder), and untreated comorbidities significantly worsen functional outcomes.

sources.label: AADPA Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

subtopic_detail: ECT consent in severe depression under NSW law
stem: You are the consultation-liaison registrar. A 68-year-old woman detained in a NSW mental health facility has psychotic depression with nihilistic delusions, has lost 11 kg in 3 months and refuses food and fluids. Three antidepressant trials have failed over 6 months. She is drowsy from dehydration and declines ECT, saying it will erase her memories. Her family supports treatment.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 96/58 mmHg, HR 102 bpm, SpO2 97% room air
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 132 mmol/L, urea 12 mmol/L, creatinine 102 micromol/L

lead_in: Under the NSW Mental Health Act 2007, what is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start ECT today under emergency provisions without any Tribunal involvement
options.rationale: The Act sets no emergency route to a course of ECT for a detained patient. Her deterioration is serious but an urgent Tribunal inquiry can be listed within days. (Source: NSW Mental Health Review Tribunal: electro convulsive therapy)
source_refs: NSW Mental Health Review Tribunal: electro convulsive therapy

options.text: Respect her refusal and continue antidepressant escalation with intravenous fluids
options.rationale: Three trials have failed and she is at imminent risk from food and fluid refusal. Repeating a failed strategy is not least restrictive care when ECT could remit the psychotic depression. (Source: RANZCP Position Statement on ECT)

options.text: Obtain her next of kin's written consent and proceed with ECT now
options.rationale: Next of kin, designated carers and the principal care provider must be notified of an ECT application, but none of them can consent to ECT for an adult in NSW. (Source: NSW Health: designated carers and principal care providers)
source_refs: NSW Health: designated carers and principal care providers

options.text: Apply to the Mental Health Review Tribunal for an ECT administration inquiry
options.rationale: For any involuntary or detained patient the authorised medical officer applies to the Tribunal, which determines whether she can give informed consent and, if she cannot, whether ECT is a reasonable and proper treatment necessary or desirable for her safety or welfare. Nihilistic delusions driving her refusal, failed pharmacotherapy and physical deterioration are exactly the evidence that application needs. (Source: NSW Mental Health Review Tribunal: electro convulsive therapy)
source_refs: NSW Mental Health Review Tribunal: electro convulsive therapy

options.text: Transfer for nasogastric feeding and defer ECT until her capacity returns
options.rationale: Feeding corrects the dehydration but not the psychotic depression driving the food refusal, and the ECT application can be prepared at the same time as the physical resuscitation. (Source: RANZCP Position Statement on ECT)

explanation.summary: ECT in Australia is governed by state legislation and the instruments differ. In NSW the authorised medical officer applies to the Mental Health Review Tribunal for an ECT administration inquiry whenever ECT is proposed for an involuntary patient, a detained person who has not yet had a mental health inquiry, or a person under 16. Capacity is decision-specific and psychotic depression with nihilistic delusions usually destroys the ability to weigh information about ECT. Remission rates in severe psychotic depression are roughly 80 to 90%, faster than any drug regimen, and most cognitive effects settle within weeks.
key_points: NSW ECT for a detained patient goes to the Mental Health Review Tribunal.
A determination lasts 6 months and ordinarily allows up to 12 treatments.
Designated carers and the principal care provider must be notified of the application.
ECT remission in severe psychotic depression is around 80 to 90%.
explanation.pearls: Psychotic depression with food refusal responds to ECT in about 2 to 4 weeks, against 6 to 8 weeks for antidepressant and antipsychotic combinations, which is why the physical deterioration belongs in the Tribunal application rather than in the progress notes alone.

sources.label: NSW Mental Health Review Tribunal: electro convulsive therapy
NSW Health: designated carers and principal care providers

stem: You are the community mental health team registrar reviewing a 28-year-old man four months after commencing olanzapine 15 mg nightly for a first episode of schizophrenia. He reports improved sleep and reduced positive symptoms. He has gained 8 kg, with new central adiposity and increased thirst. He smokes 20 cigarettes daily and has a family history of premature ischaemic heart disease.

data_table.Examination: Central adiposity, no acanthosis nigricans, no peripheral neuropathy
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 6.4 mmol/L, HbA1c 6.0%, triglycerides 2.6, HDL 0.9, LDL 3.4, ALT 64, prolactin 320 mIU/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Switch to an antipsychotic with a lower metabolic risk profile such as aripiprazole and continue lifestyle intervention with monitoring
options.rationale: Olanzapine has the highest metabolic risk and the patient meets at least three metabolic syndrome criteria; switching to a lower-risk agent (aripiprazole or ziprasidone) is RANZCP first-line. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia Guidelines)

options.text: Continue olanzapine and add metformin titrated to 1500 mg daily for weight management without any change to the antipsychotic regimen at this stage
options.rationale: Metformin may be considered as adjunct but switching the offending antipsychotic is the more impactful first step. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia Guidelines)

options.text: Reduce olanzapine to 5 mg nightly to minimise side effects and reassess weight and metabolic parameters at the next six-monthly clinic review
options.rationale: Subtherapeutic doses risk relapse and do not reliably reverse metabolic effects. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia Guidelines)

options.text: Add clozapine at low dose as an augmentation strategy with weekly haematological monitoring and continue olanzapine at the current daily dose
options.rationale: Clozapine has highest metabolic risk of all antipsychotics and is for treatment-resistant schizophrenia, not as augmentation. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia Guidelines)

options.text: Refer for bariatric surgery assessment and continue current antipsychotic regimen unchanged given the response to therapy for the primary psychiatric illness
options.rationale: Bariatric assessment is premature without first switching to a lower-risk antipsychotic and trialling lifestyle and metformin. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Antipsychotic-associated metabolic syndrome is a major contributor to premature mortality in schizophrenia (around 15 to 20 year reduction in life expectancy). Olanzapine and clozapine have the highest metabolic risk; aripiprazole, ziprasidone, and lurasidone have the lowest. RANZCP recommends baseline metabolic screening then every 3 months in first year, then 6-monthly. When metabolic syndrome develops, first-line is switching to a lower-risk agent before adding metformin.
key_points: Olanzapine and clozapine highest metabolic risk; aripiprazole and ziprasidone lowest
Switch antipsychotic first; add metformin if switch contraindicated or insufficient
Metabolic screening baseline, 3-monthly in year 1, then 6-monthly
explanation.pearls: Clozapine-induced metabolic effects can occur within the first 6 weeks; baseline weight, lipids, and glucose should be repeated at 6 weeks, 3 months, and 6 months.

stem: You are the GP registrar reviewing a 48-year-old woman who smokes 25 cigarettes daily and wants to quit. Her past medical history includes major depressive disorder in remission on sertraline, well-controlled hypertension on perindopril, and stable angina with an ETT performed last year that was reassuring. She has tried nicotine patches alone twice without success.

data_table.Examination: Unremarkable, no signs of depression on current review
data_table.Investigations: Recent FBC, UEC, LFTs all within normal range; ECG normal
data_table.Medications: Sertraline 100 mg, perindopril 5 mg, GTN PRN, aspirin 100 mg

lead_in: Which smoking cessation pharmacotherapy has the strongest evidence and is most appropriate here?

options.text: Recommend electronic cigarettes as primary smoking cessation aid given previous nicotine replacement therapy has failed in this patient with stable cardiac disease
options.rationale: Electronic cigarettes have limited evidence and are not first-line; RACGP recommends approved pharmacotherapy first. (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation)

options.text: Repeat nicotine patches alone at higher 21 mg dose and provide written information about quitting and a follow-up appointment in four weeks for review
options.rationale: Single-form NRT has failed twice; combination NRT or varenicline or bupropion should be offered. (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation)

options.text: Commence bupropion 150 mg daily titrated to twice daily after one week with weekly review to monitor for mood deterioration and seizure threshold change
options.rationale: Bupropion is a valid option but interacts with sertraline through serotonergic effects; varenicline is preferred when both are available. (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation)

options.text: Commence varenicline with structured dose titration over twelve weeks alongside behavioural support and counsel about possible neuropsychiatric monitoring
options.rationale: Varenicline is the most effective single agent and is no longer thought to increase neuropsychiatric risk per the EAGLES trial; appropriate with stable depression and behavioural support. (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation)

options.text: Refer to a residential drug and alcohol service for inpatient withdrawal management with intensive nursing and counselling provided over a four-week admission
options.rationale: Inpatient withdrawal for nicotine is not appropriate; community pharmacotherapy with behavioural support is first-line. (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation)

explanation.summary: Varenicline is the most effective monotherapy for smoking cessation (OR around 2.9 vs placebo for 6-month abstinence). The EAGLES trial showed no significant neuropsychiatric harm in patients with stable psychiatric illness compared to NRT or placebo. Combination NRT (patch plus short-acting) is the next most effective. Bupropion is an alternative but carries seizure threshold lowering and serotonergic interaction risk with SSRIs. RACGP recommends pharmacotherapy + behavioural support for all motivated smokers.
key_points: Varenicline most effective monotherapy; standard 12-week course with structured titration
EAGLES trial showed neuropsychiatric safety in stable psychiatric illness
Combination NRT (patch + short-acting) is next most effective after varenicline
explanation.pearls: Varenicline dosing: 0.5 mg daily for 3 days, then 0.5 mg twice daily for 4 days, then 1 mg twice daily; start 1 to 2 weeks before quit date and continue for 12 weeks.

stem: You are the ED registrar managing a 24-year-old woman who presents 90 minutes after ingesting approximately 3 grams of her grandmother's amitriptyline in a deliberate self-harm context. She is drowsy with GCS 12. The intern shows you the ECG, which has triggered immediate concern for cardiotoxicity. She has had no seizures.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 96/52, HR 128, RR 22, SpO2 98% on 4 L/min, T 36.4
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, GCS E3 V4 M5, dry mucous membranes, dilated pupils, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: ECG: QRS 132 ms with terminal R wave in aVR over 3 mm, sinus tachycardia; venous pH 7.32, sodium 138, potassium 3.6, glucose 8.4

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Administer activated charcoal 50 g via nasogastric tube after airway protection without other immediate pharmacological intervention for the cardiac findings
options.rationale: Charcoal may be considered within 1 hour with airway protection but does not address established cardiotoxicity; alkalinisation is the time-critical action. (Source: TPCH Poisons Information)

options.text: Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate boluses titrated to QRS narrowing and arterial pH 7.50 to 7.55 with continuous cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: QRS over 100 ms or terminal R in aVR over 3 mm indicates cardiotoxicity needing alkalinisation with sodium bicarbonate to overcome sodium channel blockade. (Source: TPCH Poisons Information)

options.text: Administer intravenous flumazenil to reverse central nervous system depression and assess for improvement in conscious state before further management
options.rationale: Flumazenil is contraindicated in mixed or unclear overdose due to seizure risk; it does not address TCA toxicity. (Source: TPCH Poisons Information)

options.text: Administer intravenous amiodarone 300 mg for the wide complex tachycardia and titrate further therapy to electrocardiograph response over the next hour
options.rationale: Class IA, IC, and III antiarrhythmics including amiodarone can worsen TCA cardiotoxicity and are contraindicated. (Source: TPCH Poisons Information)

options.text: Administer intravenous physostigmine to reverse anticholinergic toxicity given the dilated pupils and tachycardia and follow with observation in the resuscitation bay
options.rationale: Physostigmine is contraindicated in TCA overdose due to risk of asystole and seizures. (Source: TPCH Poisons Information)

explanation.summary: TCA toxicity is dominated by sodium channel blockade (wide QRS, terminal R in aVR), anticholinergic effects, alpha blockade (hypotension), and CNS depression with seizures. Sodium bicarbonate boluses targeting pH 7.50 to 7.55 overcome sodium channel blockade and are the cornerstone of treatment. Avoid amiodarone, flumazenil, and physostigmine. Lipid emulsion may be considered as rescue in refractory cardiotoxicity.
key_points: QRS over 100 ms or terminal R in aVR over 3 mm triggers sodium bicarbonate
Target pH 7.50 to 7.55 with boluses 1 to 2 mmol/kg
Avoid class IA, IC, III antiarrhythmics, flumazenil, and physostigmine
explanation.pearls: Intralipid 20% may be used as rescue therapy in refractory TCA cardiotoxicity (1.5 mL/kg bolus then 0.25 mL/kg/min infusion); contact Poisons Information for advice.

stem: You are the community mental health registrar reviewing a 56-year-old woman on lithium 1000 mg nightly for bipolar I disorder for 22 years. She has been stable on this dose. Her routine bloods show a steady deterioration in renal function over the past three years. She is otherwise well, has no polyuria or polydipsia, and lives independently. She does not want to risk relapse.

data_table.Examination: Fine tremor, no nystagmus, no ataxia
data_table.Investigations: Lithium level 0.7 mmol/L 12 hours post-dose, eGFR 42 mL/min/1.73 m^2 (52 one year ago, 64 three years ago), TSH 4.8, calcium 2.65, urine ACR 6
data_table.Medications: Lithium 1000 mg nightly, perindopril 5 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg

lead_in: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence high-dose amiloride for presumed nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and continue lithium at the current daily dose with routine monitoring
options.rationale: Amiloride is used for lithium-induced NDI but there is no polyuria here, and amiloride does not reverse chronic interstitial nephropathy. (Source: KHA-CARI Lithium Nephropathy Statement)

options.text: Stop lithium abruptly and commence sodium valproate at therapeutic dose with monitoring of mood and laboratory parameters over the next four weeks
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation of lithium markedly increases relapse risk; valproate is contraindicated in women of reproductive potential without strict criteria. (Source: KHA-CARI Lithium Nephropathy Statement)

options.text: Continue current lithium dose and recheck renal function in three months without additional specialist input given the patient's wellness and longstanding stability
options.rationale: Progressive eGFR decline warrants escalation rather than watchful waiting; reaching CKD stage 4 risks irreversible disease. (Source: KHA-CARI Lithium Nephropathy Statement)

options.text: Increase fluid intake to four litres daily and recheck renal function in six months without making any changes to the current lithium dose or specialist input
options.rationale: Increased fluid alone does not reverse chronic interstitial nephropathy and risks further sodium dilution and lithium variability. (Source: KHA-CARI Lithium Nephropathy Statement)

options.text: Refer to nephrology and psychiatry jointly to plan a slow lithium taper or switch in the context of progressive lithium-associated kidney disease
options.rationale: Progressive eGFR decline with long-term lithium use suggests chronic interstitial nephritis; joint nephrology and psychiatry input plans a controlled taper or switch to balance relapse and renal risks. (Source: KHA-CARI Lithium Nephropathy Statement)

explanation.summary: Long-term lithium causes chronic interstitial nephritis with progressive eGFR decline in around 20% of users after 20 years. Risk factors include duration over 10 years, episodes of toxicity, and lithium levels at the higher end. Joint specialist input is recommended once eGFR falls below 60 with progressive decline. Switching agents (valproate, lamotrigine, atypical antipsychotic) is balanced against relapse risk, which is highest after lithium discontinuation.
key_points: Long-term lithium causes chronic interstitial nephritis in around 20% of patients after 20 years
Joint nephrology and psychiatry input when eGFR falling below 60 with progressive decline
Slow taper preferred; abrupt cessation increases relapse risk substantially
explanation.pearls: Lithium also causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, hyperparathyroidism with hypercalcaemia, and hypothyroidism; check calcium, PTH, TSH, urinary concentrating ability annually.

stem: You are the psychiatry consultant assessing a 32-year-old solicitor self-referred for poor focus and procrastination that has worsened with increasing job demands. School reports from her primary school show comments about daydreaming, organisation difficulties, and underachievement relative to expected ability. She has tried mindfulness and study planners without sustained improvement. She has no cardiac history or family sudden death history.

data_table.Examination: Mental state shows good rapport, normal mood, no anxiety disorder identified on screening tools, no substance use
data_table.Investigations: WURS (childhood retrospective) and DIVA-5 (adult interview) both meet ADHD criteria, ECG normal, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan after sharing the diagnosis?

options.text: Trial methylphenidate immediate release with structured titration, ECG and BP monitoring, and adjunctive psychological support and workplace accommodations
options.rationale: Stimulants (methylphenidate or lisdexamfetamine) are first-line for adult ADHD with structured titration and cardiovascular monitoring per RANZCP. (Source: RANZCP ADHD Guidelines)

options.text: Commence atomoxetine as first-line therapy to avoid the abuse potential associated with stimulant medication in a professional patient with longstanding symptoms
options.rationale: Atomoxetine is second-line for adult ADHD; stimulants have greater effect size and are first-line. (Source: RANZCP ADHD Guidelines)

options.text: Recommend ongoing cognitive behavioural therapy alone without pharmacotherapy given the patient is functional and the symptoms are likely related to occupational stress
options.rationale: Diagnosis meets criteria and prior non-pharmacological strategies have been tried; pharmacotherapy is indicated. (Source: RANZCP ADHD Guidelines)

options.text: Trial sertraline 50 mg daily for presumed inattention secondary to subthreshold anxiety symptoms identified on the clinical interview at the initial consultation
options.rationale: Anxiety screening was negative and SSRIs do not treat core ADHD symptoms. (Source: RANZCP ADHD Guidelines)

options.text: Refer for sleep study to exclude obstructive sleep apnoea before considering pharmacotherapy or further psychological intervention for the presenting symptoms
options.rationale: BMI 22 and no snoring or fatigue features make OSA unlikely; deferring treatment is not appropriate. (Source: RANZCP ADHD Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Adult ADHD requires confirmation of childhood onset (before age 12) and symptoms across two settings. DIVA-5 plus collateral or school records are standard. Pharmacotherapy is first-line for moderate to severe symptoms; methylphenidate and lisdexamfetamine have largest effect sizes. ECG and BP monitoring at baseline and during titration. Atomoxetine and guanfacine are second-line. Psychological strategies augment but do not replace pharmacotherapy in moderate to severe cases.
key_points: Childhood onset before 12 years required for adult diagnosis
Methylphenidate or lisdexamfetamine first-line; atomoxetine second-line
ECG and BP monitoring at baseline and during dose escalation
explanation.pearls: Stimulants are PBS streamlined authority for adult ADHD when criteria met and require an accredited prescriber in some states; check state-specific S8 prescribing requirements.

sources.label: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

stem: You are the consult-liaison psychiatry registrar called to a general medical ward for a 64-year-old man admitted three days ago with severe depression who has now become mute and immobile. He has not eaten for 24 hours and his fluid intake is minimal. He keeps the position his arm is moved into for prolonged periods. He has no fever and is otherwise haemodynamically stable.

data_table.Examination: Mute, immobile, eyes open, waxy flexibility with sustained arm positioning, mild rigidity, no clonus, GCS technically 11 (E4 V1 M6) but neurologically intact when assessed indirectly
data_table.Investigations: CK 320 (slightly raised), FBC, UEC, LFTs, calcium, glucose, urine drug screen all unremarkable, CT brain normal
data_table.Medications: Sertraline 200 mg started three weeks ago for severe MDD

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence intravenous fluids and nutritional support while awaiting routine review by the inpatient psychiatry team at the start of the following week
options.rationale: Waiting risks malignant catatonia and complications; lorazepam challenge should not be delayed. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Guidance)

options.text: Commence intravenous haloperidol 5 mg followed by repeat dosing every twenty minutes until the patient demonstrates clear response to behavioural redirection on the ward
options.rationale: Antipsychotics worsen catatonia and risk precipitating neuroleptic malignant syndrome; they are contraindicated as first-line. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Guidance)

options.text: Administer intravenous lorazepam 2 mg as a diagnostic and therapeutic challenge with formal reassessment for catatonia response within ten minutes
options.rationale: Lorazepam challenge (1 to 2 mg IV) is the standard diagnostic and therapeutic intervention; response within 10 minutes confirms catatonia and guides ongoing therapy. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Guidance)

options.text: Refer urgently for ECT as primary treatment without trialling pharmacotherapy first given the severe presentation and degree of functional incapacity observed on the ward
options.rationale: ECT is highly effective and may be needed; however, lorazepam challenge is the first-line initial step and may be sufficient on its own. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Guidance)

options.text: Increase sertraline to 300 mg daily and add olanzapine 10 mg nightly to augment the antidepressant response while continuing observation on the medical ward
options.rationale: SSRI increase does not treat catatonia rapidly; olanzapine risks worsening catatonia and precipitating NMS. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Guidance)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is identified by Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale features including mutism, immobility, waxy flexibility, posturing, staring, and negativism. Lorazepam 1 to 2 mg IV is both diagnostic (response within 10 minutes) and therapeutic, with up to 80% response rates. ECT is the next step if lorazepam fails or if malignant catatonia features (fever, autonomic instability, rigidity, raised CK) develop. Antipsychotics worsen catatonia and may precipitate NMS.
key_points: Lorazepam 1 to 2 mg IV is first-line diagnostic and therapeutic
Antipsychotics worsen catatonia and risk NMS
ECT is highly effective for refractory or malignant catatonia
explanation.pearls: Malignant catatonia (fever, autonomic instability, raised CK) shares features with NMS; treatment is the same with lorazepam, supportive care, and early ECT if no rapid response.

stem: You are the community psychiatry registrar reviewing a 28-year-old man with schizophrenia who was started on olanzapine 10 mg nocte three months ago. He has had no further hallucinations and is sleeping well. He reports a 7 kg weight gain and increased thirst. His mother has type 2 diabetes. Baseline metabolic screen at olanzapine commencement showed fasting glucose 4.9 mmol/L, HbA1c 5.4%, total cholesterol 4.6 mmol/L, and waist circumference 88 cm. He has no chest pain and no polyuria overnight.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 128/82, HR 78, weight 87 kg (baseline 80 kg), waist 96 cm
data_table.Examination: Acanthosis nigricans absent, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Pending today

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in metabolic monitoring?

options.text: Repeat fasting lipids, fasting glucose, HbA1c and waist circumference today and review
options.rationale: RANZCP and Australian Diabetes Society monitoring for second-generation antipsychotics recommends fasting glucose, HbA1c, lipids and waist at 3 months, then at least annually; weight gain at 3 months is the trigger to recheck full panel and consider intervention. (Source: RANZCP CPG Schizophrenia)

options.text: Defer metabolic bloods until the 12 month review since baseline was normal and recheck waist now
options.rationale: Deferring to 12 months ignores the recommended 3 month repeat for fasting glucose, HbA1c and lipids on olanzapine, which carries the highest metabolic risk of the SGAs. (Source: RANZCP CPG Schizophrenia)

options.text: Order random glucose, total cholesterol and weight only and review by phone in one week
options.rationale: Random glucose and isolated total cholesterol do not meet RANZCP monitoring standards, which specify fasting glucose plus HbA1c and a full fasting lipid panel. (Source: RANZCP CPG Schizophrenia)

options.text: Switch immediately to aripiprazole today and arrange repeat fasting bloods in one month
options.rationale: Switching without first quantifying metabolic change risks destabilising remission; rescreen first, then consider a lower metabolic risk SGA if the panel is deranged. (Source: RANZCP CPG Schizophrenia)

options.text: Start metformin 500 mg twice daily empirically and recheck waist circumference at 6 months
options.rationale: Metformin for antipsychotic-induced weight gain is reasonable in selected patients but is not first action before measuring fasting glucose and HbA1c to confirm dysglycaemia or prediabetes. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Olanzapine carries one of the highest metabolic risk profiles of all antipsychotics, with weight gain, dyslipidaemia and incident type 2 diabetes overrepresented compared with aripiprazole or lurasidone. Australian monitoring frameworks recommend a baseline metabolic panel, repeat at 3 months, then at least annually thereafter while on treatment, with more frequent monitoring if any parameter is abnormal or trending. A 7 kg gain by 3 months is a red flag for emerging metabolic syndrome and should drive a full repeat panel before adjusting therapy. Decisions about switching, adding metformin, or pursuing lifestyle interventions follow the panel, not precede it. Family history of diabetes raises pretest probability of progression.
key_points: Olanzapine and clozapine are the SGAs with highest metabolic burden
Monitor fasting glucose, HbA1c, fasting lipids, weight and waist at baseline, 3 months, then annually
>5 kg gain or >5% body weight gain at 3 months should trigger early intervention
Metformin and aripiprazole augmentation have evidence for SGA-induced weight gain
Family history of diabetes lowers the threshold for switching to a lower metabolic risk SGA
explanation.pearls: Olanzapine produces a mean weight gain of about 3 to 4 kg by 10 weeks in first-episode treatment; a 7 kg gain at 3 months sits well above average and predicts persistent metabolic harm if untreated.

stem: You are the consultation-liaison psychiatry registrar reviewing a 58-year-old woman on lithium carbonate 750 mg nocte for bipolar I disorder for 18 years. She had her last episode 6 years ago and remains euthymic. Routine bloods today show eGFR 47 mL/min/1.73 m2 (53 six months ago, 62 two years ago) with a lithium level of 0.78 mmol/L taken 12 hours post-dose. She takes ramipril for hypertension. She is fearful of relapse if lithium is stopped.

data_table.Examination: Fine tremor of outstretched hands, no oedema
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 118, eGFR 47 (53 at 6 months, 62 at 24 months); lithium 0.78 mmol/L; TSH 3.1; corrected calcium 2.42
data_table.Medications: Lithium carbonate 750 mg nocte, ramipril 5 mg mane

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue lithium at current dose and recheck eGFR and lithium level in 12 months as planned
options.rationale: A sustained downward trend in eGFR over 24 months with eGFR now <60 mandates earlier review than annual, not routine continuation. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar CPG)

options.text: Refer to nephrology for shared review and discuss reducing lithium or switching mood stabiliser
options.rationale: Progressive eGFR decline (CKD stage 3a with downward trend) on long-term lithium warrants joint nephrology and psychiatry review; options include dose reduction with closer level monitoring or switch to valproate or lamotrigine after discussing relapse risk. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar CPG)

options.text: Stop lithium today and start sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily titrated against levels weekly
options.rationale: Abrupt lithium cessation increases relapse risk substantially; any switch should be planned with overlapping cover and patient consent after multidisciplinary review. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar CPG)

options.text: Reduce lithium to 500 mg nocte without further investigation and recheck level in two weeks
options.rationale: Unilateral dose reduction without nephrology input or imaging risks subtherapeutic levels and does not address possible structural lithium nephropathy. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar CPG)

options.text: Stop ramipril and recheck eGFR in two weeks since ACE inhibitors lower eGFR through haemodynamic effect
options.rationale: ACE inhibitor-mediated eGFR drop is usually small and stable; a progressive decline over 24 months is not explained by ramipril alone. (Source: KHA-CARI)

explanation.summary: Long-term lithium produces a clinically meaningful chronic interstitial nephropathy in a minority of patients after 10 to 20 years, with the dominant risk factors being duration of exposure, episodes of toxicity, and concurrent nephrotoxins. RANZCP guidelines recommend renal function monitoring 6 monthly, with thyroid and calcium annually, and earlier review when eGFR trend declines or absolute eGFR drops below 60. Sustained decline below 60 with continued lithium use warrants shared nephrology review and a frank discussion of switching mood stabilisers, accepting elevated relapse risk especially in patients with multiple prior manic episodes. Lamotrigine and valproate are reasonable alternatives but neither equals lithium for suicide-reduction in bipolar disorder. Decisions hinge on the relapse vs renal risk trade-off and patient preference.
key_points: Lithium nephropathy is a chronic interstitial nephritis from cumulative exposure
RANZCP: eGFR, TSH and calcium 6 to 12 monthly on maintenance lithium
Sustained eGFR fall below 60 triggers nephrology referral and switch consideration
Abrupt lithium cessation has high (>50%) relapse risk over 12 months
Lithium retains a unique anti-suicide signal over valproate and lamotrigine
explanation.pearls: Cumulative lithium exposure over 15 years roughly doubles the risk of CKD stage 3, with the strongest predictor being prior episodes of lithium toxicity (level >1.5 mmol/L) rather than maintenance level.

subtopic_detail: Valproate in women of reproductive potential
stem: You are the early psychosis registrar reviewing a 23-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder commenced on sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily by the inpatient team three weeks ago following a manic episode. She is now euthymic. She is in a new sexual relationship and uses condoms only intermittently. She is not pregnant on testing today. She has no prior trial of lithium or other mood stabilisers and her mother had similar episodes managed with lithium.

data_table.Examination: Nil acute
data_table.Investigations: Beta-hCG negative; valproate level 380 micromol/L; LFTs normal
data_table.Medications: Sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily; combined OCP discontinued 2 years ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in mood stabiliser management?

options.text: Continue valproate at current dose with monthly pregnancy testing and folate 5 mg daily
options.rationale: Folate and monthly testing do not mitigate the 10% major congenital malformation rate or 30 to 40% neurodevelopmental harm if she conceives on valproate. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar CPG)

options.text: Continue valproate but add the combined oral contraceptive pill and review in three months
options.rationale: Even with reliable contraception the TGA and RANZCP advise against valproate in women of reproductive potential when alternatives exist, because unintended pregnancy still occurs and exposure is teratogenic from the first weeks. (Source: TGA Valproate Warning 2024)

options.text: Switch valproate to lithium with overlapping cover and arrange contraception counselling now
options.rationale: Valproate is contraindicated in women of reproductive potential unless no effective alternative exists and a pregnancy prevention program is in place; lithium is a guideline-supported first-line maintenance option in bipolar I and aligns with her family history of response. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar CPG; TGA Valproate Warning 2024)

options.text: Reduce valproate to 250 mg twice daily as a lower teratogenic risk maintenance dose for now
options.rationale: Valproate teratogenicity is dose-related but no maintenance dose is considered safe in pregnancy; reduction does not solve the contraindication and risks relapse. (Source: TGA Valproate Warning 2024)

options.text: Continue valproate and refer to obstetrics for preconception counselling at her annual review
options.rationale: Preconception counselling does not address the immediate teratogenic exposure window if she conceives between reviews; switch first. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar CPG)

explanation.summary: Valproate exposure during pregnancy is associated with about a 10% rate of major congenital malformations and a 30 to 40% rate of neurodevelopmental impairment, including autism spectrum disorder and reduced IQ. The TGA strengthened warnings in 2024 to align with European regulators, recommending valproate is only used in women of reproductive potential where no effective alternative exists and only within a documented pregnancy prevention program. For maintenance treatment of bipolar I disorder, lithium remains the first-line option in most women, with lamotrigine an alternative if depressive polarity predominates. Family history of lithium response is a relevant prognostic factor. Switching should occur with overlapping cover and lithium loading with weekly levels until therapeutic range is reached.
key_points: Valproate: 10% major malformation rate, 30-40% neurodevelopmental harm
TGA 2024: contraindicated in women of reproductive potential without pregnancy prevention program
Lithium is the preferred maintenance switch in bipolar I, especially with family response
Lamotrigine is preferred if depressive polarity dominates
Switch with overlapping cover; do not stop valproate abruptly during ongoing manic stabilisation
explanation.pearls: Sodium valproate plasma levels above 700 micromol/L during the first trimester carry the highest neural tube defect risk, but no level is considered safe in early pregnancy.

stem: You are the emergency registrar in a metropolitan ED at 2 am. A 34-year-old man arrives 90 minutes after ingesting an estimated 60 of his amitriptyline 25 mg tablets with two cans of beer. He is drowsy but rousable. He has a history of major depressive disorder. He has no prior cardiac history. ECG shows sinus tachycardia at 124 bpm with QRS 124 ms and a terminal R wave of 4 mm in aVR.

data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, sluggish pupils, hyporeflexic, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: VBG: pH 7.32, pCO2 38, HCO3 19, K 3.4, Na 138; paracetamol level pending; ethanol 22 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: IV flumazenil 0.2 mg titrated to reversal of sedation and improve airway protection
options.rationale: Flumazenil in mixed overdose with TCAs precipitates seizures by unmasking proconvulsant effects; it is contraindicated in this setting. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Activated charcoal 50 g via nasogastric tube with airway protection after sedation
options.rationale: Charcoal beyond one hour post-ingestion in a patient with reduced GCS increases aspiration risk and offers limited benefit; addressing cardiotoxicity is the immediate priority. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: IV intralipid 20% bolus 1.5 mL/kg with infusion 0.25 mL/kg/min over 30 minutes
options.rationale: Intralipid is reserved for cardiovascular collapse refractory to bicarbonate and standard resuscitation; it is not first-line for QRS prolongation alone. (Source: Australian Poisons Centre TCA Guideline)

options.text: IV sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus with continuous cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: QRS >100 ms (and especially >120 ms) plus terminal R wave in aVR confirms significant TCA cardiotoxicity, where bicarbonate boluses targeting pH 7.50 to 7.55 reduce sodium channel blockade and prevent ventricular arrhythmia. (Source: Australian Poisons Centre TCA Guideline)

options.text: IV magnesium sulfate 2 g over 10 minutes with potassium replacement to 4.5 mmol/L target
options.rationale: Magnesium is useful for torsades or refractory ventricular arrhythmia but does not address the underlying sodium channel block driving QRS prolongation. (Source: Australian Poisons Centre TCA Guideline)

explanation.summary: TCA overdose toxicity is dominated by sodium channel blockade, anticholinergic features and alpha-1 antagonism, producing the classic constellation of QRS prolongation, tachycardia, hypotension, sedation and seizures. ECG predictors of serious toxicity include QRS >100 ms, terminal R wave >3 mm in aVR, and R/S ratio >0.7 in aVR. Sodium bicarbonate works by both increasing extracellular sodium gradient and alkalinising plasma to displace TCA from sodium channels; the target serum pH is around 7.50 to 7.55. Hypertonic saline is an alternative if bicarbonate is unavailable. Intralipid is reserved for refractory cardiovascular collapse and is not first-line. Seizures are managed with benzodiazepines, not phenytoin, which shares sodium-channel-blocking properties.
key_points: QRS >100 ms or terminal R wave aVR >3 mm = significant TCA cardiotoxicity
Sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol/kg boluses target pH 7.50-7.55
Avoid flumazenil in mixed TCA overdose (seizure risk)
Avoid phenytoin for seizures - use benzodiazepines
Intralipid is rescue therapy for refractory collapse only
explanation.pearls: A terminal R wave in aVR >3 mm at presentation predicts seizure and arrhythmia in TCA overdose with about 80% sensitivity, outperforming QRS duration alone.

stem:
You are the inpatient psychiatry registrar reviewing a 32-year-old woman three weeks into admission. Her mood and energy have normalised on lithium and olanzapine after a manic episode characterised by reduced sleep, grandiose religious delusions and pressured speech. Her mood symptoms have settled but she continues to describe persecutory delusions about her neighbours bugging her flat and reports auditory hallucinations commenting on her movements.

There is a clear premorbid 9 month period over the past two years where she described persistent persecutory beliefs in the absence of any mood episode. She has been sleeping a full 8 hours nightly for the past 10 days.

data_table.Examination: Mental state: euthymic affect, no pressure of speech, persecutory delusions intact, auditory hallucinations present, insight partial
data_table.Investigations: Lithium 0.84; TSH 1.8; FBC normal
data_table.Medications: Lithium 750 mg nocte, olanzapine 15 mg nocte

lead_in: Which diagnosis best fits this presentation?

options.text: Bipolar I disorder with mood congruent psychotic features in remission
options.rationale: Persistent psychotic symptoms outside mood episodes, especially the documented 9 month pre-manic persecutory delusions, are incompatible with bipolar I with mood-congruent features which confines psychosis to mood episodes. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Brief psychotic disorder superimposed on bipolar I disorder
