options.rationale: Brief psychotic disorder duration is <1 month with full return to premorbid function; this patient has had psychotic symptoms for months across separate periods. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Schizophrenia with comorbid substance-induced mood episode
options.rationale: Schizophrenia is not the best fit because the patient has had a sustained manic episode meeting DSM-5-TR criteria, which is not adequately captured by schizophrenia plus a substance-induced episode. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Delusional disorder with superimposed lithium-responsive mood episode
options.rationale: Delusional disorder requires absence of marked impairment in functioning outside the delusion and absence of prominent hallucinations; auditory commentary makes this diagnosis untenable. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Schizoaffective disorder bipolar type with persistent psychotic features
options.rationale: Schizoaffective disorder requires psychotic symptoms for >=2 weeks in the absence of a mood episode (the pre-manic 9 month period) and mood episodes that occupy the majority of the total illness duration, with current persistent psychotic symptoms in remitted mood. (Source: DSM-5-TR; RANZCP CPG Schizophrenia)

explanation.summary: Schizoaffective disorder is the diagnosis when DSM-5-TR criterion A for schizophrenia is met alongside mood episodes, AND psychotic symptoms persist for >=2 weeks in the absence of a major mood episode at some point in the illness, AND mood episodes occupy the majority of the total illness duration. The bipolar subtype requires a manic episode, while the depressive subtype requires only depressive episodes. Distinguishing schizoaffective from bipolar with mood-congruent psychotic features hinges on whether psychotic symptoms persist outside mood episodes; this is the single most discriminating feature. Treatment usually combines a mood stabiliser with a second-generation antipsychotic and carries an intermediate prognosis between bipolar I and schizophrenia. Cross-sectional review during one admission is rarely sufficient; the longitudinal history is decisive.
key_points: Schizoaffective dx requires >=2 weeks of psychosis without a mood episode
Mood episodes must occupy the MAJORITY of total illness duration
Bipolar I with mood-congruent psychosis confines psychosis to mood episodes
Delusional disorder excludes prominent hallucinations
Brief psychotic disorder = <1 month with full return to baseline
explanation.pearls: Schizoaffective disorder bipolar type has prognosis closer to bipolar I than to schizophrenia, while the depressive type tracks closer to schizophrenia outcomes over 10 year follow-up.

stem: You are the GP registrar seeing a 48-year-old woman who smokes 20 cigarettes per day and wants to quit. She has tried nicotine patches before with only a 3 week period of abstinence. She has a history of major depressive disorder, currently in remission on sertraline 100 mg daily for 18 months. She has no history of seizures or eating disorder. She is not pregnant and does not breastfeed. She has no cardiovascular disease and no recent ACS. She wants the most effective option.

data_table.Examination: Nil
data_table.Investigations: Recent fasting lipids and HbA1c normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy to recommend?

options.text: Varenicline 0.5 mg daily titrated to 1 mg twice daily with set quit date 1 week in
options.rationale: Varenicline has the highest single-agent quit rate in head-to-head trials and is safe in stable depression on an SSRI; the EAGLES trial demonstrated no excess neuropsychiatric events compared with placebo. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guideline)

options.text: Bupropion SR 150 mg daily titrated to twice daily with quit date set 1 week into therapy
options.rationale: Bupropion is an option but is contraindicated or relatively contraindicated with concurrent serotonergic medication due to seizure threshold and serotonergic load considerations, and is less effective than varenicline as monotherapy. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guideline)

options.text: Single 21 mg nicotine patch daily with brief behavioural counselling for relapse prevention
options.rationale: Single-form NRT has lower efficacy than varenicline or combination NRT; she has already failed patches alone, so single patch is suboptimal as the next step. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guideline)

options.text: Combination NRT with 21 mg patch and 4 mg gum as needed for cravings throughout the day
options.rationale: Combination NRT is more effective than single-form NRT and is a reasonable alternative, but evidence places varenicline ahead of combination NRT for quit rates in head-to-head trials. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guideline)

options.text: Nortriptyline 25 mg nocte titrated up against tolerability with quit date set 2 weeks in
options.rationale: Nortriptyline is a second-line cessation aid not registered on PBS for this indication and risks serotonergic interaction with sertraline. (Source: AMH)

explanation.summary: Australian guidelines and the 2024 Cochrane network meta-analysis place varenicline at the top of first-line smoking cessation pharmacotherapy, ahead of combination NRT and bupropion. Varenicline is a partial agonist at the alpha-4 beta-2 nicotinic receptor and approximately doubles continuous abstinence rates at 6 months compared with placebo. The 2016 EAGLES trial dispelled earlier concerns about neuropsychiatric events in stable depression and schizophrenia, allowing confident use in mental illness in remission. Bupropion lowers seizure threshold and has relative contraindications with concurrent SSRIs. NRT remains a valid first-line option, especially in combination, and is the default in pregnancy where varenicline is not recommended. Behavioural support roughly doubles the efficacy of any pharmacotherapy.
key_points: Varenicline > combination NRT > bupropion > single-form NRT (Cochrane 2024)
EAGLES trial: varenicline safe in stable depression and schizophrenia
Set quit date 1-2 weeks into varenicline; titrate over first week
Combination NRT (patch + short-acting) > patch alone
Add behavioural counselling (Quitline 13 7848) for additive effect
explanation.pearls: Varenicline reaches steady state at 4 days and is renally excreted; dose reduce to 1 mg daily when eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m2.

stem: You are the psychiatry registrar in an adult ADHD clinic seeing a 29-year-old software engineer who self-referred. She describes lifelong difficulty starting tasks, frequent loss of personal items, frequent procrastination on important emails, and inability to follow long meetings. School reports from age 9 documented daydreaming and disorganisation. She has never met criteria for major depressive disorder, generalised anxiety, autism, intellectual disability or substance use disorder. She is in stable employment but routinely works late to catch up. Symptoms are present at home and at work.

data_table.Examination: Mental state: attentive in clinic, organised speech
data_table.Investigations: TSH 1.8; FBC normal; urine drug screen negative

lead_in: Which DSM-5-TR criterion is the most important to confirm before making the diagnosis?

options.text: Symptoms present in two or more settings causing functional impairment in current adult life
options.rationale: Multi-setting impairment is required and present here (home and work), but it is not the differentiating step; the developmental onset criterion is the most commonly missed and most often disputed at diagnosis. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Several inattentive symptoms present before age 12 documented by collateral or records
options.rationale: DSM-5-TR requires several inattentive or hyperactive-impulsive symptoms present before age 12; this is the criterion most often inadequately documented in adult presentations and is the strongest differentiator from acquired attentional impairment. (Source: DSM-5-TR; RANZCP ADHD Position)

options.text: Five or more inattentive symptoms in the last six months for adults aged 17 years or older
options.rationale: Five-of-nine is correct for adult diagnosis but is straightforward from current symptom report; the developmental criterion is the harder step to verify. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Symptoms not better explained by another mental disorder or substance use disorder
options.rationale: Exclusion criteria are necessary and the history already addresses depression, anxiety, autism and substance use; the development-onset criterion is more often missed. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Symptoms interfere with academic or occupational function as evidenced by collateral report
options.rationale: Functional interference is required and apparent, but does not by itself separate adult-onset attentional complaints from true ADHD; only childhood onset does. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

explanation.summary: Adult ADHD diagnosis under DSM-5-TR requires five or more symptoms from inattentive and/or hyperactive-impulsive lists for >=6 months, symptoms present before age 12 (often the hardest criterion to evidence), symptoms present in two or more settings, clear functional impairment, and exclusion of other better explanations. Australian adult ADHD assessment combines structured clinical interview with collateral from a parent or sibling where possible, plus school records when accessible. The 2024 Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD endorses stimulants (lisdexamfetamine, methylphenidate) as first-line pharmacotherapy in adults without contraindication. Comorbidity rates are high; screen routinely for anxiety, depression and substance use. Driving and cardiovascular risk are key safety considerations before stimulant initiation.
key_points: DSM-5-TR adult: 5+ symptoms, onset before age 12, two+ settings, impairment, not better explained
Childhood-onset evidence is the hardest and most-missed criterion
Use collateral and school records to verify
Australian Guidelines 2024: stimulants first-line for adult ADHD
Screen for comorbid anxiety, depression and substance use at diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Adult ADHD symptom threshold is 5/9 inattentive or 5/9 hyperactive-impulsive symptoms, lowered from the paediatric 6/9 to reflect developmental attenuation of overt hyperactivity.

stem: You are the psychiatry registrar in a community mental health team seeing a 26-year-old woman with borderline personality disorder confirmed by structured assessment 12 months ago. She has had six self-harm episodes in the past year (superficial cutting) without suicidal intent, recurrent unstable relationships, chronic feelings of emptiness, and recurrent fears of abandonment. She has previously trialled sertraline without benefit and is on no current medication. She is now stable from substance use and has reliable transport to weekly appointments. She wants help to reduce self-harm and emotional storms.

data_table.Examination: Mental state: anxious, organised, no current SI
data_table.Investigations: FBC, TSH, EUC normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line intervention to recommend?

options.text: Commence sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily for emotional dysregulation and labile affect
options.rationale: Mood stabilisers have weak and inconsistent evidence in BPD; the principal indication is psychotherapy and valproate has teratogenic risk in this patient. (Source: NHMRC BPD Guideline; TGA Valproate Warning 2024)

options.text: Commence olanzapine 5 mg nocte for affective instability and review in eight weeks
options.rationale: Pharmacotherapy is not first-line for BPD and SGAs have limited evidence; targeted short courses may be used adjunctively for crises but not as primary treatment. (Source: NHMRC BPD Guideline)

options.text: Twelve months of structured dialectical behaviour therapy with skills group and weekly individual
options.rationale: NHMRC and RANZCP guidance: structured psychotherapy (DBT, MBT, schema-focused, transference-focused) is first-line for BPD with self-harm; DBT has the strongest evidence for reducing self-injury and ED presentations. (Source: NHMRC BPD Guideline; RANZCP CPG Personality Disorders)

options.text: Refer for inpatient admission to structured ward-based program for six weeks of containment
options.rationale: Brief inpatient admission for BPD is generally discouraged outside acute crisis; longer hospitalisation reinforces dependence and rarely reduces self-harm. (Source: NHMRC BPD Guideline)

options.text: Restart sertraline 100 mg daily and continue with monthly GP review as primary treatment
options.rationale: Sertraline failed previously and SSRIs are not first-line for BPD; psychotherapy is the intervention with proven efficacy. (Source: NHMRC BPD Guideline)

explanation.summary: BPD is best managed with structured, time-limited evidence-based psychotherapy delivered by trained clinicians. DBT (12 months, weekly individual plus skills group plus telephone coaching) has the strongest evidence for reducing self-injurious behaviour and ED presentations. Mentalisation-based therapy, schema-focused therapy, and transference-focused therapy are also evidence-based first-line options. Pharmacotherapy plays a limited adjunctive role for specific symptom targets, with no medication approved by TGA for core BPD treatment. Brief crisis admissions are appropriate for safety, but longer admissions are usually counterproductive. The 2024 NHMRC BPD guideline emphasises continuity of care, written crisis plans, and primary care involvement.
key_points: DBT, MBT, schema-focused, TFP = first-line for BPD
DBT has the strongest evidence for self-harm reduction
Pharmacotherapy is adjunctive only - no TGA-approved core medication
Avoid long admissions; use brief crisis admissions only
Written crisis plan should accompany psychotherapy
explanation.pearls: Structured DBT reduces self-injurious behaviour frequency by about 50% over 12 months compared with treatment as usual in randomised trials.

subtopic_detail: ED first-line response in young adult
stem: You are the ED registrar at a regional hospital. A 24-year-old man arrives by ambulance with police following an alleged amphetamine use earlier that evening. He is shouting at staff, pacing, and threatening to leave. He has no known medical conditions. He has not been violent toward staff yet but is making fists. He has no IV access. There is a private interview room available. The mental health and security teams are 3 and 6 minutes away respectively.

data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, dilated pupils, no focal neurology, no obvious injuries
data_table.Investigations: Pending; blood glucose 6.2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate next step?

options.text: Allow him to self-discharge under supervision since he has not yet been violent to staff
options.rationale: Allowing exit when he is intoxicated and at risk of harm to self or others would breach duty of care; assessment under Mental Health Act may be required if he refuses to stay. (Source: NSW Health ABD Guideline)

options.text: Intramuscular olanzapine 10 mg with midazolam 5 mg now and document the rationale
options.rationale: Parenteral sedation is for severe agitation where de-escalation has failed or is not safe; combining olanzapine with midazolam increases hypotension and respiratory depression risk. (Source: NSW Health ABD Guideline)

options.text: Place a Mental Health Act schedule and immediately apply mechanical restraints to the trolley
options.rationale: Restraints are a last resort and should follow failed less-restrictive options; restraints in stimulant-intoxicated patients raise rhabdomyolysis and sudden death risk. (Source: NSW Health ABD Guideline)

options.text: Verbal de-escalation in the private room with a single calm clinician and clear space
options.rationale: Australian acute behavioural disturbance guidelines place verbal de-escalation as the first-line response when there is no immediate physical threat and resources allow; lower stimulation and a clear exit reduce the need for restraint. (Source: NSW Health ABD Guideline; ACEM Guidelines)

options.text: Wait for the mental health team to attend in 3 minutes before any intervention is started
options.rationale: Initial de-escalation by the treating ED clinician should commence immediately and not wait; the mental health team should join when available. (Source: NSW Health ABD Guideline)

explanation.summary: Australian acute behavioural disturbance frameworks (NSW Health, ACEM, RANZCP) emphasise a stepped approach: environmental modification (reduce stimulation, clear space, exits for both patient and staff), verbal de-escalation, oral medication if accepted, then parenteral medication if needed, with mechanical restraint as a last resort. Stimulant intoxication confers higher risk of rhabdomyolysis, hyperthermia and sudden death, especially with restraint. When parenteral sedation is required, options include droperidol 10 mg IM, olanzapine 10 mg IM, or midazolam 5 to 10 mg IM, used as monotherapy in preference to combinations to reduce respiratory depression. Continuous monitoring and rapid medical reassessment are mandatory post-sedation.
key_points: Stepped approach: environment, verbal de-escalation, oral, parenteral, restraint last
Stimulant intoxication + restraint = high rhabdomyolysis and sudden death risk
Droperidol 10 mg IM or olanzapine 10 mg IM monotherapy preferred
Avoid combination olanzapine + benzodiazepine (cardiorespiratory depression)
Continuous monitoring required post-sedation
explanation.pearls: Droperidol 10 mg IM achieves adequate sedation within 15 to 30 minutes in 80% of acute behavioural disturbance cases in Australian EDs, with a lower respiratory depression rate than midazolam at equivalent sedation depth.

stem: You are the consultation-liaison psychiatry registrar called to the medical ward for a 42-year-old woman with schizophrenia who has become mute, immobile and resistant to passive limb movement over the past 36 hours. She has not eaten or drunk in 24 hours and is intermittently maintaining bizarre postures with her arm raised. She has not received antipsychotics for one week as she stopped olanzapine on a recent admission. She has no fever and her observations are otherwise stable. There is no rigidity outside the limb posturing and her CK is 220 U/L.

data_table.Examination: Mute, posturing left arm, waxy flexibility on examination, no rigidity, no clonus
data_table.Investigations: CK 220, FBC normal, EUC normal, CRP 4, TSH 2.1, urine drug screen negative
data_table.Medications: Olanzapine 15 mg ceased 1 week ago; nil current

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate diagnostic and therapeutic next step?

options.text: Resume olanzapine 15 mg nocte and add diazepam 5 mg orally three times daily for posturing
options.rationale: Reintroducing antipsychotic during active catatonia carries risk of conversion to NMS; benzodiazepine alone should be tried first with response assessment. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Position)

options.text: IV haloperidol 5 mg as urgent rapid tranquillisation for prolonged psychotic posturing
options.rationale: Antipsychotics worsen catatonia and increase the risk of converting to neuroleptic malignant syndrome; first-line is benzodiazepine, not antipsychotic. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Position)

options.text: MRI brain with contrast urgently to exclude structural causes before any pharmacotherapy
options.rationale: While neuroimaging is part of catatonia workup, it is not the immediate next step when the lorazepam challenge can simultaneously diagnose and treat; imaging can follow once acute features are addressed. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Position)

options.text: Empiric IV dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg with bromocriptine to treat presumed neuroleptic malignant syndrome
options.rationale: NMS requires fever, autonomic instability, marked rigidity and elevated CK; her temperature, CK, and observations do not support NMS as primary diagnosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Lorazepam 2 mg IV with observation for response within 10 to 30 minutes as a diagnostic challenge
options.rationale: The lorazepam challenge is both diagnostic and therapeutic in catatonia, with response in 60-80% of cases; partial response supports diagnosis and guides ongoing benzodiazepine titration with ECT as the next step if no response. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Position; BFCRS evidence)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is recognised by combinations of immobility, mutism, posturing, waxy flexibility, negativism, echolalia and echopraxia, formally assessed using the Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale. It complicates major depression, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, and a wide range of medical conditions including autoimmune encephalitis, metabolic derangement and substance toxicity. The lorazepam challenge of 1 to 2 mg IV, repeated as needed, both confirms the diagnosis (partial or full response in 60 to 80%) and provides initial treatment. Antipsychotics worsen catatonia and may precipitate NMS, so they are avoided until catatonic features resolve. ECT is the second-line treatment if benzodiazepines fail and is the first-line for malignant catatonia with autonomic instability or hyperthermia. Workup includes EEG, MRI, autoimmune panel and metabolic screen.
key_points: BFCRS quantifies catatonia; >=3 features = diagnosis
Lorazepam 1-2 mg IV is both diagnostic challenge and treatment
Avoid antipsychotics in active catatonia - NMS risk
ECT is second-line; first-line in malignant catatonia
Investigate organic causes: autoimmune encephalitis, metabolic, drug-induced
explanation.pearls: Malignant catatonia (catatonia with fever, autonomic instability, rigidity and elevated CK) carries a mortality of about 20% if not treated promptly with ECT, and is essentially indistinguishable on presentation from NMS.

subtopic_detail: Functional neurological vs malingering vs factitious
stem: You are the neurology registrar reviewing a 38-year-old woman with sudden onset right leg weakness for 4 weeks. Examination shows give-way weakness with positive Hoover sign and intact reflexes. MRI brain and spine are normal. She is genuinely distressed by the symptoms and wants help. She does not seek work cover and has no pending litigation. She is not a healthcare worker. She has a remote history of anxiety. She tells you the leg moves freely when she is distracted reaching for her drink bottle.

data_table.Examination: Right leg 4/5 give-way weakness, positive Hoover, normal reflexes, normal tone, normal sensation in non-anatomical distribution
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain and spine: nil acute; nerve conduction studies normal

lead_in: Which diagnosis best fits this presentation?

options.text: Functional neurological disorder with positive Hoover sign supporting the diagnosis
options.rationale: Functional neurological disorder is now a rule-in diagnosis based on positive clinical signs (Hoover, distractibility, give-way weakness) rather than exclusion; the patient has genuine symptoms and seeks help, distinguishing from factitious and malingering. (Source: RACP Position FND; DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Factitious disorder imposed on self with intentional production of weakness for sick role
options.rationale: Factitious disorder requires conscious symptom production motivated by the sick role; the patient is genuinely distressed and lacks evidence of deception. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Malingering with intentional symptom production motivated by an external incentive
options.rationale: Malingering requires identifiable external incentive (financial, legal, work avoidance); none is present in this case. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Somatic symptom disorder predominantly characterised by pain in absence of weakness
options.rationale: Somatic symptom disorder centres on excessive thoughts, feelings or behaviours about somatic symptoms; the dominant feature here is the motor deficit with positive functional signs. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Multiple sclerosis with normal initial imaging that requires repeat MRI in three months
options.rationale: MS is unlikely with normal MRI, intact reflexes, give-way weakness and positive Hoover; functional signs are specific rule-in features. (Source: McDonald Criteria 2024)

explanation.summary: Functional neurological disorder (FND) is the contemporary term for what was previously called conversion disorder. DSM-5-TR reframed it as a rule-in diagnosis based on positive clinical features incompatible with neurological disease, not a diagnosis of exclusion. Positive features include Hoover sign, hip abductor sign, tremor entrainment, give-way weakness, distractibility, and seizure features inconsistent with electroclinical correlation. The patient has genuine symptoms and distress, and motivation is not consciously to assume the sick role (factitious) or to obtain external gain (malingering). Treatment combines clear positive communication of the diagnosis, physiotherapy with FND-trained therapists, and addressing predisposing and perpetuating psychological factors. Misdiagnosis rate of FND on long-term follow-up is approximately 4%.
key_points: FND = rule-in diagnosis from positive signs (Hoover, distractibility, give-way)
Factitious = conscious symptom production for sick role
Malingering = conscious symptom production for external incentive
Long-term misdiagnosis rate of FND ~4% (no higher than other neuro disorders)
Treatment: clear positive communication + FND-trained physiotherapy
explanation.pearls: Hoover sign has sensitivity around 63% and specificity around 100% for functional leg weakness, making it the single highest-yield bedside test.

stem: You are the paediatric medicine registrar admitting a 16-year-old girl with anorexia nervosa for medical stabilisation. Her BMI is 14.2 with weight loss of 25% over six months. She has been eating <500 kcal per day for four weeks. She is bradycardic and hypotensive. The dietitian plans to start nasogastric feeds at 1200 kcal per day, increasing by 200 kcal every 48 hours.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 88/52 supine, HR 42 supine, T 35.8, RR 14
data_table.Examination: Cachectic, lanugo, cold peripheries, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Na 138, K 3.4, phosphate 0.95, magnesium 0.74, glucose 3.6, LFTs mildly deranged

lead_in: Which electrolyte requires the most frequent monitoring during the first 5 days of refeeding?

options.text: Sodium, with twice daily measurement to avoid central pontine myelinolysis from rapid correction
options.rationale: Sodium derangements occur but are not the primary driver of refeeding cardiac events; phosphate is. (Source: ANZAED Refeeding Guideline)

options.text: Phosphate, with daily measurement and proactive supplementation as required
options.rationale: Hypophosphataemia is the hallmark of refeeding syndrome and drives cardiac arrhythmia and respiratory failure; daily monitoring with proactive supplementation is the cornerstone of safe refeeding. (Source: ANZAED Refeeding Guideline)

options.text: Potassium, with three times daily measurement to maintain a level above 4.0 mmol/L
options.rationale: Hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia also occur in refeeding but phosphate is the marker most predictive of refeeding syndrome severity. (Source: ANZAED Refeeding Guideline)

options.text: Magnesium, with twice daily measurement to maintain a level above 0.85 mmol/L target
options.rationale: Magnesium is monitored but is not the most predictive marker; phosphate is the single most important electrolyte during early refeeding. (Source: ANZAED Refeeding Guideline)

options.text: Bicarbonate, with daily venous gas to monitor for refeeding-induced lactic acidosis early
options.rationale: Bicarbonate trend is informative but is not the primary monitored parameter; refeeding lactic acidosis is rare compared with refeeding hypophosphataemia. (Source: ANZAED Refeeding Guideline)

explanation.summary: Refeeding syndrome is driven by an insulin surge when carbohydrate is reintroduced after starvation, shifting phosphate, magnesium and potassium intracellularly. Hypophosphataemia is the hallmark electrolyte disturbance and the strongest predictor of cardiac and respiratory complications. Australian Eating Disorder guidelines (ANZAED) recommend daily phosphate, magnesium, potassium and glucose for the first 5 to 7 days, with proactive phosphate supplementation if levels fall below 0.85 mmol/L or rapidly trend down. Thiamine should be given before any carbohydrate to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy. Cardiac monitoring is recommended for the first 72 hours in severely malnourished patients. ECG should be repeated daily until refeeding is established.
key_points: Refeeding syndrome: insulin-driven intracellular shift of PO4, K, Mg
Hypophosphataemia is the hallmark and strongest mortality predictor
ANZAED: daily PO4, K, Mg, glucose for first 5-7 days
Give thiamine 100 mg IV before any carbohydrate (Wernicke prevention)
Cardiac monitoring for first 72 hours if severely malnourished
explanation.pearls: Serum phosphate below 0.5 mmol/L during refeeding carries a 30% risk of cardiac arrhythmia and warrants IV replacement (e.g. potassium phosphate 20 mmol over 6 hours) rather than oral.

stem: You are the community mental health registrar seeing a 52-year-old man, brought in by his daughter. For 18 months he has been convinced his neighbour is poisoning his garden vegetables and has been writing letters to the council. He has continued working as a successful accountant throughout. He denies hallucinations and his speech is organised. His self-care and occupational function are intact. There is no mood episode. There is no substance use. He has no first-rank symptoms of schizophrenia.

data_table.Examination: Mental state: organised speech, persecutory delusion of garden poisoning, no hallucinations, no thought disorder
data_table.Investigations: FBC, EUC, TSH, B12, syphilis serology, CT brain normal

lead_in: Which diagnosis best fits this presentation?

options.text: Brief psychotic disorder with single persecutory delusion lasting beyond one month
options.rationale: Brief psychotic disorder is by definition <1 month duration; 18 months excludes this diagnosis. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Schizophrenia paranoid type with preserved cognitive function on testing
options.rationale: Schizophrenia requires criterion A symptoms (delusions, hallucinations, disorganised speech, grossly disorganised behaviour or negative symptoms) for >=1 month with functional decline >=6 months; preserved high-level work function and isolated delusion does not fit. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Delusional disorder persecutory type with preserved psychosocial function
options.rationale: Encapsulated non-bizarre delusion >1 month, preserved function outside the delusion, no prominent hallucinations and absence of mood episode satisfies DSM-5-TR delusional disorder criteria. (Source: DSM-5-TR; RANZCP CPG Schizophrenia)

options.text: Late-onset schizophrenia with negative symptoms predominating over positive symptoms
options.rationale: Late-onset schizophrenia features prominent positive symptoms and functional decline; this patient has neither functional decline nor multiple criterion A symptoms. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Substance-induced psychotic disorder with persistent residual persecutory beliefs
options.rationale: There is no history of substance use; substance-induced psychotic disorder requires temporal association with intoxication or withdrawal. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

explanation.summary: Delusional disorder is characterised by one or more delusions for at least 1 month, in the absence of other criterion A symptoms of schizophrenia, preserved psychosocial function outside the delusion, and no prominent hallucinations. Subtypes include persecutory (most common), erotomanic, grandiose, jealous, somatic, and mixed. Mean age of onset is later than schizophrenia (40s to 50s). Treatment combines antipsychotic medication (response rates 30 to 50%) with engagement-focused psychotherapy. Distinguishing features from schizophrenia are absence of negative symptoms, preserved function and encapsulated delusion. Excluding organic causes (frontal lobe lesion, B12 deficiency, neurosyphilis) is mandatory.
key_points: Delusional disorder = >=1 delusion, >=1 month, preserved function, no other criterion A
Onset typically 40s-50s vs schizophrenia onset late teens to early 20s
Persecutory subtype is most common
Response to antipsychotic 30-50%; engagement is the limiting factor
Always exclude organic cause (frontal lesion, B12, neurosyphilis)
explanation.pearls: Delusional disorder shared with a close contact (folie à deux) is now coded under 'Other Specified Schizophrenia Spectrum and Other Psychotic Disorder' in DSM-5-TR rather than as a separate entity.

stem: You are the GP registrar seeing a 36-year-old man with PTSD following a workplace assault 6 months ago. He has intrusive memories, avoidance of the workplace, hypervigilance and nightmares. He has not yet had any trial of psychotherapy or pharmacotherapy. He has no comorbid alcohol use, no dissociative symptoms and no suicidal ideation. He prefers an evidence-based approach without medication initially.

data_table.Examination: Mental state: anxious, organised, no SI, no dissociation
data_table.Investigations: FBC, TSH, EUC normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line psychotherapy to recommend?

options.text: Dialectical behaviour therapy with skills training group for emotion dysregulation in PTSD
options.rationale: DBT is first-line for borderline personality disorder; in uncomplicated PTSD without comorbid BPD, trauma-focused therapy is preferred first. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Supportive counselling weekly with relaxation training for hypervigilance and arousal symptoms
options.rationale: Generic supportive counselling is not first-line for PTSD; trauma-focused therapy demonstrates superior outcomes for PTSD symptom reduction. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Critical incident stress debriefing in a single session focused on the recent workplace event
options.rationale: Single-session debriefing is not recommended and may worsen outcomes; trauma-focused therapy delivered over multiple sessions is preferred. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy with prolonged exposure components over 8 to 12 weeks
options.rationale: Australian PTSD guidelines (Phoenix Australia / NHMRC) endorse trauma-focused CBT and EMDR as first-line for adult PTSD, with TF-CBT having the largest evidence base; EMDR is an equally valid alternative. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Mindfulness-based stress reduction with somatic experiencing as primary trauma-focused therapy
options.rationale: Mindfulness and somatic experiencing have weaker evidence and are second-line; TF-CBT and EMDR are first-line. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Australian PTSD treatment guidelines (Phoenix Australia, endorsed by RANZCP and NHMRC) place trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy (which includes prolonged exposure and cognitive processing therapy variants) and eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing (EMDR) as first-line psychotherapies for adult PTSD. SSRIs (sertraline, paroxetine) and SNRIs (venlafaxine) are first-line pharmacotherapy and can be combined with trauma-focused therapy when symptoms are severe or in patient preference. Single-session debriefing is not recommended. Adjunctive prazosin can reduce trauma-related nightmares. Comorbidity (depression, substance use) often co-exists and may need parallel treatment. NDIS and workers compensation pathways may apply in workplace-related PTSD.
key_points: TF-CBT (prolonged exposure, cognitive processing) = first-line
EMDR = equally effective first-line alternative
SSRIs (sertraline, paroxetine) and SNRIs (venlafaxine) first-line pharmacotherapy
Avoid single-session critical incident debriefing
Prazosin can be added for persistent nightmares
explanation.pearls: Prazosin 1 to 6 mg at night reduces PTSD-related nightmares with NNT around 4; titrate from 1 mg, monitor for orthostatic hypotension.

stem: You are the psychiatry registrar starting a 42-year-old man on lisdexamfetamine for adult ADHD confirmed at multi-source assessment. He has a 10 year history of essential hypertension on amlodipine, with last clinic BP 138/84. He has no history of ischaemic heart disease, arrhythmia or stroke. His ECG is unremarkable. His brother had sudden cardiac death at age 38 with no autopsy diagnosis. He has stable employment as a long-distance truck driver requiring an unrestricted commercial driver's licence.

data_table.Examination: Cardiovascular examination unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: ECG: sinus rhythm 78, QTc 416 ms, no LVH, no ischaemic change

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step before starting lisdexamfetamine?

options.text: Start lisdexamfetamine 30 mg daily and monitor BP and HR at 2 weeks, 4 weeks, then 3 monthly
options.rationale: Family history of unexplained sudden cardiac death under 40 requires cardiology review before stimulant initiation, regardless of normal baseline ECG. (Source: Australian ADHD Guideline 2024)

options.text: Request transthoracic echocardiogram and 24 hour Holter monitor then start stimulant if normal
options.rationale: Ordering investigations without cardiology input for inherited arrhythmia evaluation is suboptimal; cardiology review directs appropriate testing including genetic considerations. (Source: Australian ADHD Guideline 2024)

options.text: Switch amlodipine to perindopril and recheck BP and HR in two weeks before starting stimulant
options.rationale: Antihypertensive switch is not the limiting factor; cardiology review for family history is the gating step before stimulant initiation. (Source: Australian ADHD Guideline 2024)

options.text: Start atomoxetine 40 mg daily instead and avoid all stimulants in commercial truck drivers
options.rationale: Atomoxetine is a reasonable alternative but commercial driving status alone is not a contraindication to stimulants; cardiology review for family history is the appropriate immediate step. (Source: Australian ADHD Guideline 2024)

options.text: Refer to cardiology for review of unexplained sudden cardiac death in first-degree relative
options.rationale: First-degree relative with unexplained sudden cardiac death under 40 is a flag for inherited cardiac conditions (long QT, HCM, ARVC) and warrants cardiology workup before stimulant initiation per Australian ADHD Guideline 2024. (Source: Australian ADHD Guideline 2024)

explanation.summary: Australian ADHD Guideline 2024 (AADPA) recommends cardiovascular history, examination and baseline BP/HR before stimulant initiation in adults. Routine ECG is not mandatory in the absence of red flags, but red flags trigger cardiology review and further investigation. Red flags include syncope on exertion, palpitations on exertion, known structural heart disease, family history of sudden cardiac death under age 40, family history of cardiomyopathy or channelopathy, and inadequately controlled hypertension. Stimulants typically raise BP by 2 to 5 mmHg and HR by 3 to 7 bpm. Monitoring after initiation includes BP and HR at 2 weeks, 4 weeks, 3 months, then 6 monthly. Driving authority disclosure follows state rules (DVA in NT, RMS NSW, VicRoads, TMR Qld).
key_points: Cardiac history + examination + BP/HR baseline before stimulant
Routine ECG not required in absence of red flags
First-degree SCD under 40 = cardiology review before starting
Stimulants typically raise BP 2-5 mmHg and HR 3-7 bpm
Disclose to driving authority per state rules (e.g. AustRoads)
explanation.pearls: Lisdexamfetamine vs immediate-release dexamfetamine: lisdexamfetamine is a prodrug requiring red-cell esterase cleavage, giving a smoother 10 to 12 hour profile and lower abuse potential, which favours it in adult ADHD.

stem:
You are the consultation-liaison psychiatry registrar called to ICU for a 28-year-old man with schizophrenia. He was admitted three days ago with acute psychosis and started on olanzapine 10 mg daily. Twelve hours ago he became mute and immobile with rigid posturing and waxy flexibility, then over the past six hours has developed fever and autonomic instability. He had a similar episode of mutism and posturing two years ago that responded to lorazepam.

Total dose of antipsychotic in this admission has been 30 mg olanzapine in divided doses. CK has risen from 180 to 3200 over 12 hours.

data_table.Vital signs: BP fluctuating 92/56 to 168/102, HR 124, T 39.6, RR 28, SpO2 96% RA
data_table.Examination: Mute, posturing, lead-pipe rigidity, waxy flexibility, no clonus, no hyperreflexia
data_table.Investigations: CK 3200 (rising), WCC 14.8, CRP 26, EUC: Cr 132, K 4.8, lactate 3.2; venous gas: pH 7.30, HCO3 18; urine myoglobin positive
data_table.Medications: Olanzapine 10 mg daily x 3 days (total 30 mg this admission)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Stop olanzapine and arrange urgent electroconvulsive therapy with IV fluids and supportive care
options.rationale: Malignant catatonia and NMS overlap clinically and pathophysiologically; in a patient with prior lorazepam-responsive catatonia who now has rigidity, fever, autonomic instability and elevated CK, ECT is the indicated first-line treatment after stopping antipsychotic, with mortality reduction over pharmacotherapy alone. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Position; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Continue olanzapine at reduced dose and start IV dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg with bromocriptine
options.rationale: Continuing antipsychotic in suspected NMS or malignant catatonia is contraindicated; dantrolene + bromocriptine have weak evidence and do not replace ECT for malignant catatonia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Stop olanzapine and trial IV lorazepam 4 mg now with planned escalation to 16 mg over 24 hours
options.rationale: High-dose benzodiazepine alone in malignant catatonia with autonomic instability is unlikely to reverse the syndrome promptly enough; ECT is the definitive treatment with the lowest mortality. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Position)

options.text: Stop olanzapine and switch to quetiapine 100 mg daily once afebrile and CK falling consistently
options.rationale: Reintroducing any antipsychotic before complete resolution of malignant catatonia or NMS risks recurrence and death; antipsychotic rechallenge must wait >=2 weeks after full resolution. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Continue current management and observe in ICU for 24 hours before deciding on ECT referral
options.rationale: Delaying definitive treatment of malignant catatonia or NMS increases mortality substantially; ECT should be expedited within 24 to 48 hours of recognition. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Position)

explanation.summary: Malignant catatonia and neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) are now widely considered overlapping conditions on a single spectrum, with shared features of rigidity, hyperthermia, autonomic instability, altered consciousness and elevated CK. The temporal association with antipsychotic, presence of lead-pipe rigidity, and rapid rise in CK favour NMS as the proximate trigger, while prior lorazepam-responsive catatonia favours an underlying catatonic substrate. Management is identical: cease the offending antipsychotic, aggressive supportive care (cooling, IV fluids, monitoring for rhabdomyolysis-induced AKI), and definitive treatment with ECT, particularly when there is autonomic instability or failure to respond to high-dose benzodiazepine. Bromocriptine and dantrolene have limited evidence and are second-line adjuncts. Antipsychotic rechallenge must be delayed by at least 2 weeks after full resolution and is usually with a lower-potency D2 antagonist or a partial agonist.
key_points: Malignant catatonia and NMS overlap clinically and pathophysiologically
Stop offending antipsychotic; aggressive supportive care; monitor for AKI
ECT is the definitive treatment; bromocriptine/dantrolene weakly supported
Antipsychotic rechallenge >=2 weeks after resolution
Prior catatonia response to lorazepam predicts catatonic substrate
explanation.pearls: ECT for malignant catatonia or NMS typically requires daily or bilateral treatments rather than the standard 3-times-weekly schedule, with first response often seen after 3 to 6 treatments.

stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 28-year-old woman self-referred for assessment after her 6-year-old child was diagnosed with ADHD. She reports lifelong difficulty sustaining attention at school and work, forgetfulness with deadlines, losing belongings, procrastination, frequent task-switching, restlessness, and impulsive decisions. She failed to complete two TAFE courses despite high IQ. Symptoms are present at work, at home, and in her relationship.

She was always called daydreamy at primary school but had no school disciplinary issues. School reports from age 8 confirm distractibility, untidy work, and frequent careless mistakes.

data_table.Examination: Normal mental state: euthymic, no psychomotor abnormality beyond restlessness, no psychotic features, no anxiety beyond performance-related
data_table.Investigations: K10 score 14 (mild distress, non-clinical); ASRS-V1.1 part A 5 of 6 positive; collateral from mother confirms childhood symptoms; school reports from age 8 documenting inattentive features; no significant developmental, perinatal, or head injury history

lead_in: What is the most appropriate basis for diagnosing adult ADHD in this patient?

options.text: Adult onset symptoms within the last 12 months are sufficient to diagnose ADHD if 5 of 9 criteria are met
options.rationale: DSM-5 requires several symptoms present BEFORE age 12 (not necessarily impairing) plus current persistence; truly adult-onset presentation without childhood symptoms is not ADHD by current criteria. (Source: DSM-5; Australian ADHD Guideline)

options.text: At least 5 of 9 inattentive or hyperactive symptoms in adults, with several symptoms before age 12 across settings
options.rationale: DSM-5 adult ADHD: >=5 of 9 inattentive AND/OR hyperactive-impulsive symptoms (vs 6 in children), several symptoms present before age 12, symptoms in 2 or more settings, impairing function, not better explained by another disorder. (Source: DSM-5; Australian ADHD Guideline)

options.text: Positive Conners Adult ADHD Rating Scale alone is sufficient to confirm ADHD diagnosis in primary care
options.rationale: Rating scales (Conners, ASRS) screen but do not replace structured clinical interview, collateral history, and DSM-5 criteria assessment for diagnosis. (Source: Australian ADHD Guideline)

options.text: Neuropsychological testing showing impaired sustained attention is required for adult ADHD diagnostic confirmation
options.rationale: Neuropsychological tests are supportive but not required; many patients with ADHD have normal continuous performance test results due to compensation strategies. (Source: Australian ADHD Guideline)

options.text: All 9 inattentive or all 9 hyperactive symptoms must be present in adulthood to meet diagnostic threshold
options.rationale: Threshold is 5 of 9 in adults (DSM-5 lowered from 6 of 9 for children to reflect symptom attenuation with maturation). (Source: DSM-5)

explanation.summary: DSM-5 adult ADHD criteria require >=5 of 9 inattentive AND/OR >=5 of 9 hyperactive-impulsive symptoms (vs 6 of 9 in children under 17 to reflect symptom attenuation), with several symptoms present before age 12 (not necessarily impairing), symptoms in >=2 settings (work, home, social, study), clear impairment of social/academic/occupational function, and not better explained by another mental disorder. Three presentations: inattentive, hyperactive-impulsive, combined. Adult women often present with predominantly inattentive symptoms missed in childhood (daydreaminess vs disruptive hyperactivity in boys); diagnosis often follows child diagnosis. The Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD (AADPA 2022) recommends structured clinical interview using DSM-5 plus validated rating scales (ASRS, Conners), collateral history (parent, partner, school reports), screening for comorbid mood/anxiety, sleep, substance use, autism, and learning disorders. Pharmacotherapy is methylphenidate or lisdexamfetamine first-line; atomoxetine non-stimulant alternative; behavioural therapy and coaching adjunctive.
key_points: DSM-5 adult: >=5 of 9 inattentive AND/OR >=5 hyperactive-impulsive
Several symptoms before age 12 required (not necessarily impairing)
Symptoms in >=2 settings, clear impairment, not better explained
Women often missed: inattentive presentation, daydreamy phenotype
Australian AADPA guideline + DSM-5 + collateral history + rating scales
explanation.pearls: Adult ADHD prevalence in Australia is approximately 2 to 5%, persisting from childhood in about 50% of paediatric cases; lifetime stimulant exposure does not increase substance use disorder risk and may reduce it in treated populations.

stem: You are the ED registrar reviewing a 32-year-old man brought by ambulance 90 minutes after intentional overdose of his partner's amitriptyline (estimated 50 tablets of 25 mg, so 1250 mg) found beside an empty wine bottle. He is drowsy (GCS 12), tachycardic, and hypotensive. ECG shows sinus tachycardia at 132 bpm with QRS duration of 130 ms and terminal R wave in lead aVR of 4 mm. VBG shows pH 7.28, lactate 3.1, HCO3 18. He has not had a seizure yet. He is intubated for airway protection.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 88/56, HR 132, RR 22 (intubated and ventilated), SpO2 99%, T 37.0, GCS 12 before intubation
data_table.Examination: Dilated pupils 6 mm sluggishly reactive, dry mucous membranes, urinary retention, no focal neurology before sedation, abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: ECG: sinus tachycardia 132, QRS 130 ms, terminal R wave aVR 4 mm, QTc 480; VBG: pH 7.28, HCO3 18, lactate 3.1, K 3.6, glucose 7.2; troponin pending; paracetamol level negative
data_table.Medications: (Partner) amitriptyline 25 mg nocte; patient on no regular medications

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological intervention?

options.text: IV flumazenil 200 mcg titrated up to 1 mg total as reversal for sedation effects with continued ECG monitoring
options.rationale: Flumazenil is benzodiazepine antidote, irrelevant to TCA; also precipitates seizures in TCA overdose and is contraindicated. (Source: Poisons Information Centre)

options.text: IV magnesium sulfate 2 g loading then 2 g/hour infusion for prolonged QTc and risk of torsades de pointes
options.rationale: Magnesium is given for documented torsades but is not the priority intervention for sodium channel blockade with widened QRS; bicarbonate addresses the primary toxicity. (Source: Poisons Information Centre)

options.text: IV intralipid 20% 1.5 mL/kg bolus then infusion at 0.25 mL/kg/min for lipid soluble TCA overdose
options.rationale: Intralipid is reserved for cardiac arrest or refractory haemodynamic collapse with TCA; not first-line before bicarbonate trial. (Source: Poisons Information Centre)

options.text: IV physostigmine 1 mg titrated as antidote for anticholinergic toxidrome to reverse neurological effects rapidly
options.rationale: Physostigmine is CONTRAINDICATED in TCA overdose due to risk of asystole, seizures, and worsening conduction; never used in this setting. (Source: Poisons Information Centre)

options.text: IV sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol (8.4%) bolus then infusion targeting QRS narrowing and arterial pH 7.45 to 7.55
options.rationale: QRS >100 ms, terminal R in aVR >3 mm, hypotension and acidosis are all indications for sodium bicarbonate in TCA overdose; mechanism is sodium loading (sodium channel blockade reversal) and alkalinisation (decreases protein binding, free drug); target pH 7.45-7.55. (Source: ANZICS Tox Guidelines; Poisons Information Centre)

explanation.summary: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose causes cardiotoxicity through sodium channel blockade (QRS widening, terminal R wave in aVR, ventricular arrhythmia), potassium channel blockade (QTc prolongation), alpha-1 blockade (hypotension), and anticholinergic toxidrome (dilated pupils, dry skin, urinary retention, tachycardia, ileus, agitation, hyperthermia). Mortality risk markers: QRS >100 ms (seizure risk), QRS >160 ms (ventricular arrhythmia risk), terminal R wave aVR >3 mm. Management: airway protection (intubate for GCS <12 or seizures); IV sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus then infusion to target pH 7.45 to 7.55 - sodium loads the channel and alkalinisation decreases protein binding and free active drug; benzodiazepines for seizures and agitation; vasopressors (noradrenaline) for refractory hypotension; intralipid for cardiac arrest. Activated charcoal within 1 to 2 hours if airway protected. Physostigmine and flumazenil are CONTRAINDICATED. ICU admission for at least 24 hours; QRS normalisation precedes safe discharge.
key_points: TCA cardiotoxicity: QRS widening, terminal R aVR, QTc long, hypotension
Bicarbonate indications: QRS >100, terminal R aVR >3 mm, hypotension, acidosis
Target pH 7.45-7.55 with bicarbonate bolus + infusion
Physostigmine and flumazenil CONTRAINDICATED
Intralipid reserved for cardiac arrest or refractory shock
explanation.pearls: Terminal R wave in lead aVR >3 mm has approximately 80% sensitivity and 75% specificity for predicting seizure or arrhythmia in TCA overdose, and triggers immediate sodium bicarbonate even when QRS is borderline at 100 to 120 ms.

subtopic_detail: Valproate use in women of childbearing potential
stem: You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 27-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder who has been stable on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily for 4 years following 2 previous severe manic episodes requiring inpatient admission. She has a new long-term partner and tells you they are planning to start a family within the next 12 months. She has had no further mood episodes on valproate. Her contraception is condoms only. Her mother also had bipolar disorder. She asks about continuing her medication during a planned pregnancy and breastfeeding.

data_table.Examination: Mental state: euthymic, no psychomotor abnormality, no psychotic features
data_table.Investigations: Valproate level 540 micromol/L (therapeutic); FBC, LFTs, EUC normal; pregnancy test today negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Continue valproate at lowest effective dose with high-dose folate 5 mg daily commenced 3 months pre-conception
options.rationale: Valproate teratogenicity (NTD risk 1-2%, IQ loss about 7 to 10 points, ADHD/ASD risk) cannot be mitigated by folate; valproate is contraindicated in pregnancy planning unless no alternative. (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention; AMH)

options.text: Switch to carbamazepine 400 mg twice daily for safer pregnancy and breastfeeding profile than valproate
options.rationale: Carbamazepine also has substantial teratogenicity (NTD risk about 1%, similar developmental risks); lithium or lamotrigine are preferred alternatives in pregnancy. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar Guideline)

options.text: Switch to lithium with serum-level monitoring monthly antenatally and consider TFTs 3-monthly during pregnancy
options.rationale: Lithium is preferred mood stabiliser in pregnancy for bipolar maintenance (lower teratogenicity than valproate; Ebstein anomaly relative risk historically overstated, actual risk about 0.6% with first-trimester exposure); monthly levels (rising volume of distribution), TFTs 3-monthly, fetal echo at 16 to 20 weeks. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar Guideline; TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention)

options.text: Cease all mood stabilisers and rely on close clinical monitoring with rapid restart of valproate if relapse occurs
options.rationale: Discontinuation of mood stabiliser in stable bipolar I carries 50-70% relapse risk; pregnancy and postpartum are high-risk periods for relapse, so maintenance is required. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar Guideline)

options.text: Continue valproate, ensure long-acting reversible contraception, and counsel against pregnancy with both partners
options.rationale: This patient has expressed clear intent to conceive; appropriate response is medication switch to a safer alternative rather than denying her reproductive autonomy. (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention)

explanation.summary: Valproate is highly teratogenic with major malformation rate of 10% (vs 2 to 3% background), neural tube defects 1 to 2%, mean IQ loss 7 to 10 points, and substantially increased risk of autism spectrum disorder and ADHD in exposed offspring. The TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program (and equivalent EMA program) mandates: avoid in women of childbearing potential unless no effective alternative AND patient is on highly effective contraception (LARC preferred) AND annual specialist review using risk acknowledgement form AND patient information document signed. For bipolar I maintenance in women planning pregnancy, switch options include lithium (preferred, monitoring intensified during pregnancy), lamotrigine (excellent pregnancy profile, less effective for mania prevention), or atypical antipsychotic (quetiapine, olanzapine). Lithium pregnancy management: monthly levels (rising volume of distribution; lithium clearance increases in pregnancy then falls postpartum), TFTs every trimester, fetal echo at 16 to 20 weeks (Ebstein anomaly risk about 0.6%), continue throughout pregnancy at lowest effective dose, hold during labour or reduce dose 24 to 48 hours pre-delivery, restart with reduced dose immediately postpartum.
key_points: Valproate teratogenicity: 10% major malformations, NTD 1-2%, IQ -7 to -10
TGA Pregnancy Prevention Program mandatory for valproate in WOCBP
Alternatives: lithium (preferred), lamotrigine, atypical antipsychotic
Lithium pregnancy: monthly levels, TFTs/trimester, fetal echo 16-20 weeks
Postpartum is highest risk for bipolar relapse; maintain mood stabiliser
explanation.pearls: Valproate first-trimester exposure carries a neural tube defect risk of approximately 1 to 2%, which is 10 times the background population rate, and is not preventable by even high-dose 5 mg folate.

stem: A 48-year-old man with a 30-pack-year smoking history presents requesting help to quit. He has attempted to quit twice before using nicotine patches, relapsing within 2 weeks both times. He has a history of stable ischaemic heart disease managed with aspirin, bisoprolol, and atorvastatin. His last MI was 4 years ago. He has no psychiatric history and no current depressive symptoms. He is motivated to quit.

data_table.History: 30 pack-years, Fagerstrom Test for Nicotine Dependence score 7/10 (high dependence), two prior quit attempts with NRT patches both relapsing within 2 weeks, stable IHD (MI 4 years ago), no psychiatric history

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy for this quit attempt?

options.text: Varenicline 0.5 mg daily for 3 days then titrated to 1 mg twice daily
options.rationale: Varenicline is the most effective single-agent smoking cessation pharmacotherapy, with superior quit rates compared to NRT monotherapy and bupropion. The EAGLES trial and subsequent meta-analyses confirmed no excess cardiovascular risk in patients with stable CVD. Given this patient's high nicotine dependence and NRT failure, varenicline is the appropriate escalation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Bupropion sustained-release 150 mg daily for 3 days then twice daily
options.rationale: Bupropion is a reasonable alternative but is less effective than varenicline, particularly in highly dependent smokers. It also lowers the seizure threshold and has more drug interactions. Given the availability of varenicline and this patient's NRT failure, varenicline is preferred. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Combination NRT with 21 mg patch plus 4 mg nicotine lozenges as needed
options.rationale: Combination NRT (patch plus short-acting form) is more effective than patch alone and is a reasonable option. However, this patient has already failed NRT twice, and combination NRT still has lower quit rates than varenicline in head-to-head trials. Escalation to varenicline is more appropriate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Nortriptyline 25 mg nightly titrated to 75 mg as a cessation adjunct
options.rationale: Nortriptyline has some evidence for smoking cessation but is a third-line agent with significant side effects including cardiac conduction changes, which are particularly concerning in a patient with ischaemic heart disease. It is not preferred over varenicline or bupropion. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Nicotine patch 21 mg daily with concurrent behavioural counselling only
options.rationale: While behavioural support improves quit rates, repeating NRT monotherapy after two failures without escalating pharmacotherapy is unlikely to succeed. High nicotine dependence (Fagerstrom 7/10) and repeated NRT failure warrant pharmacological escalation to a more effective agent. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Varenicline is the most effective single-agent smoking cessation pharmacotherapy, acting as a partial agonist at the alpha-4-beta-2 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor. It reduces both craving and the rewarding effects of smoking. The EAGLES trial (2016) established that varenicline does not increase neuropsychiatric adverse events compared to NRT or placebo, and subsequent cardiovascular safety data support its use in stable CVD. Australian PBS listing requires at least one prior quit attempt. Standard course is 12 weeks with an optional 12-week extension for relapse prevention.
key_points: Varenicline has the highest single-agent quit rates (approximately 25% at 12 months vs 15% for NRT)
EAGLES trial confirmed cardiovascular and neuropsychiatric safety profile
Standard titration: 0.5 mg daily for 3 days, 0.5 mg twice daily for 4 days, then 1 mg twice daily
PBS listing requires documented prior quit attempt and Quitline referral
explanation.pearls: Setting a quit date 1-2 weeks after starting varenicline allows steady-state plasma levels to be reached before the target quit date; if the patient reduces smoking spontaneously during this lead-in period, quitting earlier is encouraged rather than waiting for the planned date.

subtopic_detail: Autism spectrum disorder in adult woman - masking and diagnostic pathway
stem: A 32-year-old woman is referred by her GP after self-identifying with autism content online. She has a history of treatment-resistant anxiety and depression since adolescence, with multiple SSRI trials. She describes lifelong difficulty reading social cues, intense focused interests (currently entomology), sensory overwhelm in crowded spaces, and exhaustion after social events. She performed well academically, maintained employment, and has one close friend. Previous clinicians attributed her difficulties to social anxiety disorder.

data_table.History: Lifelong social difficulties masked by learned compensatory strategies, intense focused interests since childhood, sensory sensitivities (noise, textures), social exhaustion, GAD and MDD diagnosed age 16, multiple SSRI trials with partial response, no intellectual disability, employed as a research librarian

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in assessment?

options.text: Trial of higher-dose SSRI for treatment-resistant social anxiety disorder
options.rationale: This patient has had multiple SSRI trials with partial response, and her social difficulties have been lifelong rather than onset-related as in social anxiety disorder. Escalating SSRIs without considering the underlying neurodevelopmental explanation perpetuates diagnostic overshadowing. Autism assessment should precede further pharmacological trials. (Source: RANZCP: ASD in Adults)

options.text: Referral for comprehensive autism diagnostic assessment by a specialist team
options.rationale: The presentation is consistent with autism spectrum disorder with masking (camouflaging) - a pattern frequently seen in women who develop compensatory social strategies that delay diagnosis. Comprehensive assessment should include developmental history (ideally with informant), standardised tools adapted for the female phenotype, and assessment of co-occurring conditions. Diagnosis enables targeted support and explains the partial SSRI response. (Source: RANZCP: ASD in Adults)

options.text: Cognitive behavioural therapy for social skills with exposure hierarchy
options.rationale: Standard CBT for social anxiety uses exposure to reduce avoidance, but in autism the social difficulties are neurodevelopmental, not anxiety-driven avoidance. Forcing neurotypical social exposure without recognising the autistic need for recovery time can worsen burnout. Assessment should precede therapy planning. (Source: RANZCP: ASD in Adults)

options.text: Personality disorder assessment given lifelong interpersonal difficulties
options.rationale: While lifelong interpersonal difficulties can suggest personality disorder, the specific pattern of social communication differences, restricted interests, and sensory sensitivities is more consistent with ASD. Misdiagnosis of ASD as personality disorder is a recognised pattern, particularly in women. Assessment for ASD should precede personality disorder formulation. (Source: RANZCP: ASD in Adults)

options.text: Neuropsychological testing for intellectual giftedness as explanation
options.rationale: While intellectual giftedness can coexist with social differences, it does not explain sensory sensitivities, social exhaustion after masking, or the specific pattern of restricted intense interests. Giftedness and autism are not mutually exclusive and can co-occur, but the clinical features warrant autism-specific assessment. (Source: RANZCP: ASD in Adults)

explanation.summary: Autism spectrum disorder in women is frequently diagnosed late due to the female autism phenotype, which features more effective social masking (camouflaging), internalising rather than externalising behaviours, and focused interests that may appear more socially conventional. Women with undiagnosed ASD are commonly misdiagnosed with anxiety disorders, depression, BPD, or eating disorders. The RANZCP recognises that standard diagnostic tools may be less sensitive in women, and assessment should include female-specific presentations, developmental history, and recognition of camouflaging as a compensatory strategy.
key_points: Women with ASD frequently develop effective masking strategies that delay diagnosis by an average of 5-10 years compared to men
Diagnostic overshadowing occurs when ASD traits are attributed to anxiety, depression, or personality disorder
Camouflaging is associated with autistic burnout, depression, and suicidality independent of the underlying autism
Assessment tools such as the CAT-Q (Camouflaging Autistic Traits Questionnaire) can identify masking behaviour
explanation.pearls: Autistic burnout - characterised by chronic exhaustion, loss of previously acquired skills, and reduced tolerance for sensory input - is increasingly recognised as a distinct phenomenon from depression; it typically follows periods of sustained masking or increased social demands and may not respond to antidepressant therapy.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Autism Spectrum Disorder

subtopic_detail: Catatonia recognition - lorazepam challenge and ECT consideration
stem:
A 24-year-old man with a 2-year history of schizophrenia managed on olanzapine is brought to the emergency department by his family. Over the past 48 hours he has become increasingly mute and immobile. On examination he is awake with open eyes but does not respond to verbal commands or painful stimuli. He maintains an uncomfortable arm position when passively raised for over 2 minutes.

He intermittently exhibits purposeless repetitive hand movements. His temperature is 37.2 degrees C and vital signs are otherwise stable. He has not changed or missed any medications recently.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88, BP 130/82 mmHg, Temp 37.2 degrees C, RR 16
data_table.Examination: Mute, immobile, waxy flexibility (catalepsy), stereotypy present, negativism to passive movement, no rigidity, no tremor, Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale score 22 (significant catatonia)
data_table.Investigations: WCC 9.2 x10^9/L, CK 320 U/L (mildly elevated, ref <200), CRP 8 mg/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Increase olanzapine dose to address worsening psychotic symptoms
options.rationale: Catatonia is not psychotic agitation and should not be treated by increasing antipsychotics. In fact, antipsychotics can worsen catatonia and increase the risk of progression to malignant catatonia or NMS. The antipsychotic should be continued at current dose but not increased. (Source: RANZCP: Catatonia Management)

options.text: Cease olanzapine and commence IV dantrolene for suspected NMS
options.rationale: While catatonia and NMS share features, NMS typically presents with severe rigidity, high fever (>38 degrees C), markedly elevated CK (usually >1000 U/L), and autonomic instability. This patient has mild temperature elevation, mild CK rise, waxy flexibility rather than rigidity, and no medication changes - features more consistent with catatonia than NMS. (Source: RANZCP: Catatonia Management)

options.text: Administer lorazepam 2 mg IV as a diagnostic and therapeutic challenge
options.rationale: The lorazepam challenge is both diagnostic and therapeutic for catatonia. A positive response (improvement in catatonic signs within 10-30 minutes of IV or IM lorazepam) confirms the diagnosis and guides treatment. Benzodiazepines are first-line for catatonia, with 60-80% responding to lorazepam. The Bush-Francis score of 22 confirms significant catatonia warranting immediate treatment. (Source: RANZCP: Catatonia Management)

options.text: Urgent CT brain and lumbar puncture to exclude organic encephalitis
options.rationale: While organic causes of catatonia (such as anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis) should be considered, the clinical presentation with known schizophrenia history and classic catatonic signs warrants a lorazepam challenge first. The lorazepam challenge does not delay workup and provides immediate diagnostic information. If there is no response or atypical features emerge, organic workup should follow. (Source: RANZCP: Catatonia Management)

options.text: Electroconvulsive therapy referral as first-line definitive treatment
options.rationale: ECT is highly effective for catatonia (response rates >80%) but is a second-line treatment, reserved for patients who do not respond to an adequate trial of benzodiazepines or who present with malignant catatonia (high fever, severe autonomic instability, markedly elevated CK). The lorazepam challenge should be attempted first. (Source: RANZCP: Catatonia Management)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a neuropsychiatric syndrome characterised by motor, behavioural, and autonomic abnormalities. Key features include stupor, mutism, catalepsy (waxy flexibility), stereotypy, negativism, and posturing. The Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale quantifies severity. The lorazepam challenge (1-2 mg IV) is both diagnostic and therapeutic: improvement within 10-30 minutes confirms the diagnosis. Benzodiazepines are first-line treatment with 60-80% response rates. ECT is reserved for benzodiazepine-refractory cases or malignant catatonia. Antipsychotics should not be increased as they can worsen the syndrome.
key_points: Catalepsy, mutism, stereotypy, and negativism are cardinal features of catatonia
Lorazepam challenge (1-2 mg IV) is both diagnostic and first-line therapeutic
ECT is second-line for benzodiazepine-refractory catatonia with >80% response rate
Antipsychotics should not be increased during catatonia as they may worsen the condition
explanation.pearls: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis should be considered in all first presentations of catatonia, particularly in young women; CSF anti-NMDA receptor antibodies, MRI, and EEG should be performed if there is no response to lorazepam within 48 hours or if seizures, dysautonomia, or orofacial dyskinesia develop.

stem: A 24-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has been stable on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily for 3 years with no manic or depressive episodes. She presents for routine review. She is currently single and not planning pregnancy. She uses condoms inconsistently as her only contraception. She was not counselled about the pregnancy prevention program when valproate was first prescribed.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no psychotic features, BMI 26, well-groomed, good rapport
data_table.Investigations: Valproate level 72 mg/L (target 50-100), LFTs normal, FBC normal, pregnancy test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate action regarding her valproate prescription?

options.text: Enrol in the pregnancy prevention program and ensure effective contraception before continuing
options.rationale: Australian TGA and ACSQHC requirements mandate that all women of childbearing potential on valproate must be enrolled in the valproate pregnancy prevention program, have an annual acknowledgement of risk form signed, and use highly effective contraception (LARC or combined methods). Condoms alone are insufficient. Valproate can be continued if the patient provides informed consent and uses effective contraception. Abrupt cessation risks destabilising her bipolar disorder. (Source: ACSQHC Valproate Safety; AMH)

options.text: Immediately cease valproate and switch to lithium as a safer alternative for her age
options.rationale: While lithium is preferred for bipolar disorder in women of childbearing age, abruptly ceasing valproate in a stable patient without establishing an alternative mood stabiliser risks precipitating mania or depression. If a switch is planned, it should be done gradually with overlapping treatment. The immediate priority is to address the missing pregnancy prevention program requirements. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines; AMH)

options.text: Continue valproate unchanged as pregnancy is not currently planned by the patient
options.rationale: The pregnancy prevention program applies to ALL women of childbearing potential on valproate, regardless of current pregnancy plans. Unplanned pregnancies account for a significant proportion of pregnancies, and valproate exposure in early pregnancy causes neural tube defects in approximately 5-10% and neurodevelopmental effects in up to 40% of exposed children. Inconsistent condom use provides inadequate protection. (Source: ACSQHC Valproate Safety; AMH)

options.text: Add high-dose folic acid 5 mg daily to mitigate the teratogenic risk while continuing valproate
options.rationale: While folic acid supplementation is recommended for all women of childbearing potential, evidence does not support that it adequately mitigates valproate-specific teratogenicity. Valproate's teratogenic mechanism involves histone deacetylase inhibition and is not solely folate-mediated. Folic acid is an adjunct, not a substitute for effective contraception and the pregnancy prevention program. (Source: AMH; ACSQHC Valproate Safety)

options.text: Reduce valproate to the minimum effective dose of 500 mg daily to lower teratogenic risk
options.rationale: Dose reduction may lower the risk somewhat (teratogenicity is dose-dependent above 700-1000 mg/day) but does not eliminate it, and reducing from an effective dose risks destabilisation. The priority is enrollment in the pregnancy prevention program with effective contraception. Dose optimisation is a secondary consideration in the context of established efficacy at the current dose. (Source: AMH; RANZCP)

explanation.summary: Valproate carries the highest teratogenic risk of any commonly used mood stabiliser, causing neural tube defects in 5-10% and neurodevelopmental effects in up to 40% of exposed pregnancies. The Australian pregnancy prevention program mandates informed consent, effective contraception, and annual review for all women of childbearing potential. These requirements apply regardless of current pregnancy planning status due to the high rate of unplanned pregnancies.
key_points: Valproate pregnancy prevention program is mandatory for all women of childbearing potential
Highly effective contraception (LARC or combined methods) is required, not condoms alone
Annual risk acknowledgement form must be signed
Abrupt cessation of stable mood stabiliser risks relapse and should be avoided
explanation.pearls: Valproate exposure in the first trimester causes neural tube defects at a rate of approximately 5-10% (vs 0.1% background risk), with the critical window being weeks 3-4 post-conception, often before pregnancy is recognised - underlining why effective contraception must be established proactively.

stem: A 32-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by ambulance after her housemate found her drowsy next to an empty blister pack of amitriptyline. The housemate estimates she may have taken up to 3 g approximately 90 minutes ago. She is drowsy but rousable. She has a history of depression and chronic back pain. An IV cannula has been placed and blood tests sent.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128 (sinus tachycardia), BP 92/58, RR 16, SpO2 97% on room air, T 37.2, GCS 12 (E3 V4 M5)
data_table.Examination: Dilated pupils 7 mm bilaterally, dry flushed skin, urinary retention on bladder scan (450 mL), no clonus, mild generalised hyperreflexia
data_table.Investigations: ECG: sinus tachycardia 128, QRS duration 118 ms, right axis deviation, positive R wave in aVR 4 mm, QTc 488 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate pharmacological intervention?

options.text: IV physostigmine 1 mg to reverse the anticholinergic toxidrome causing the tachycardia
options.rationale: Physostigmine is contraindicated in TCA overdose despite the anticholinergic features. It can precipitate seizures, bradycardia, and asystole by potentiating the cholinergic effects in the setting of sodium channel blockade. The anticholinergic features are managed supportively. (Source: Toxicology Guidelines; AMH)

options.text: IV sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol/kg bolus targeting a serum pH of 7.50-7.55
options.rationale: Sodium bicarbonate is the specific antidote for TCA-induced sodium channel blockade. The QRS duration of 118 ms (>100 ms) and positive R wave in aVR >3 mm indicate significant sodium channel blockade with risk of ventricular arrhythmias. Sodium bicarbonate works by alkalinisation (reducing drug-receptor binding) and providing a sodium load to overcome the channel blockade. Target serum pH 7.50-7.55 with repeated boluses. (Source: Toxicology Guidelines; Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology; Austin Health Toxicology)

options.text: Activated charcoal 50 g via nasogastric tube for gastrointestinal decontamination
