options.rationale: Activated charcoal may be considered within 1-2 hours of TCA ingestion if the airway is protected. However, this patient has reduced GCS (12) with risk of further deterioration. The immediate priority is treating the sodium channel blockade with sodium bicarbonate, not gastrointestinal decontamination. Charcoal may be given concurrently if safe airway conditions permit. (Source: Toxicology Guidelines)

options.text: IV amiodarone 300 mg over 20 minutes to prevent ventricular tachyarrhythmia
options.rationale: Amiodarone and all Class IA and IC antiarrhythmics are contraindicated in TCA overdose. They worsen sodium channel blockade and prolong the QRS and QT intervals further, increasing arrhythmia risk. Sodium bicarbonate is the correct treatment for QRS widening in TCA toxicity. (Source: Toxicology Guidelines; AMH)

options.text: IV lipid emulsion 20% at 1.5 mL/kg bolus as rescue therapy for lipophilic toxicity
options.rationale: IV lipid emulsion may be considered in severe TCA toxicity refractory to sodium bicarbonate, particularly in cardiac arrest. However, it is not first-line therapy. Sodium bicarbonate is the established first-line treatment for TCA cardiotoxicity with QRS prolongation. Lipid emulsion is a rescue therapy for refractory cases. (Source: Toxicology Guidelines; Austin Health Toxicology)

explanation.summary: TCA overdose causes a distinctive toxidrome combining anticholinergic effects, cardiovascular toxicity (sodium channel blockade, alpha-blockade), and CNS depression. The ECG is the critical prognostic tool - QRS >100 ms and R wave in aVR >3 mm indicate significant cardiotoxicity with risk of seizures and ventricular arrhythmias. IV sodium bicarbonate is the specific treatment for sodium channel blockade, working through alkalinisation and sodium loading.
key_points: QRS >100 ms and R wave in aVR >3 mm indicate significant TCA cardiotoxicity
IV sodium bicarbonate is the specific antidote for TCA sodium channel blockade
Target serum pH 7.50-7.55 with repeated boluses
Class IA/IC antiarrhythmics and physostigmine are contraindicated
explanation.pearls: The R wave amplitude in aVR >3 mm has a sensitivity of 81% and specificity of 73% for predicting seizures in TCA overdose, and is a more reliable early marker of severe toxicity than the QRS duration alone.

subtopic_detail: Schizoaffective disorder vs bipolar I with psychosis
stem: A 29-year-old man is reviewed in the outpatient psychiatry clinic. Over the past 4 years, he has had three manic episodes with prominent grandiose and persecutory delusions and auditory hallucinations. Between these episodes, he has extended periods of 3-4 months where his mood is completely euthymic, yet he continues to experience persistent auditory hallucinations (commentary voices) and referential delusions. He is adherent with his medications. His mother has schizophrenia and his maternal uncle has bipolar I disorder.

data_table.Examination: Well-groomed, euthymic affect, engaged in conversation, describes ongoing auditory hallucinations present daily despite euthymic mood, referential ideation regarding television broadcasts, no thought disorder, insight partial
data_table.Investigations: Nil new - recent TFTs, FBC, metabolic panel all normal

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Bipolar I disorder with psychotic features limited to mood episodes only
options.rationale: In bipolar I with psychotic features, psychotic symptoms occur exclusively during mood episodes (mania or depression) and resolve completely during euthymia. This patient has persistent hallucinations and delusions during extended euthymic periods, which is the key discriminating feature that points away from bipolar I with psychotic features. (Source: RANZCP; DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Schizophrenia with secondary mood episodes attributable to substance misuse
options.rationale: There is no mention of substance use, and the manic episodes are described as distinct episodic events consistent with a primary mood component. Schizophrenia does not include full manic episodes as part of its presentation. The co-occurrence of full affective episodes and persistent psychosis between them points to schizoaffective disorder. (Source: RANZCP; DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Delusional disorder with grandiose subtype and coincidental mood instability
options.rationale: Delusional disorder involves non-bizarre delusions without prominent hallucinations, and functioning is generally preserved apart from the delusional system. This patient has prominent auditory hallucinations (commentary voices) and full manic episodes, which exceed the criteria for delusional disorder. (Source: DSM-5-TR; RANZCP)

options.text: Schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type, with inter-episode psychotic symptoms
options.rationale: Schizoaffective disorder requires: (1) a major mood episode concurrent with Criterion A schizophrenia symptoms, (2) delusions or hallucinations for at least 2 weeks in the absence of a mood episode during the illness lifetime, and (3) mood symptoms present for the majority of the total illness duration. This patient meets all criteria: manic episodes with psychotic features, persistent psychosis during 3-4 month euthymic periods, and recurrent mood episodes comprising a substantial portion of his illness. (Source: RANZCP; DSM-5-TR; BMJ Best Practice: Schizoaffective Disorder)

options.text: Schizophrenia with comorbid cyclothymic disorder causing mood fluctuations
options.rationale: The manic episodes described are full manic episodes (with grandiosity and psychosis), not the hypomanic-depressive fluctuations of cyclothymia. Additionally, schizophrenia with a separate cyclothymia diagnosis does not account for the temporal relationship between psychotic and mood symptoms. The integrated diagnosis of schizoaffective disorder better captures this presentation. (Source: RANZCP; DSM-5-TR)

explanation.summary: Schizoaffective disorder occupies the diagnostic boundary between schizophrenia and mood disorders with psychotic features. The key discriminator from bipolar I with psychotic features is the presence of psychotic symptoms during extended euthymic periods (at least 2 weeks without mood symptoms). From schizophrenia, it is distinguished by the presence of prominent mood episodes comprising a substantial portion of the total illness. It is subtyped as bipolar or depressive type.
key_points: Psychosis persisting during euthymia distinguishes schizoaffective from bipolar with psychotic features
At least 2 weeks of psychosis without mood symptoms is required for schizoaffective diagnosis
Mood episodes must be present for the majority of the total illness duration
Family history often spans both schizophrenia and mood disorders spectrum
explanation.pearls: The DSM-5-TR criterion requiring delusions or hallucinations for >=2 weeks in the absence of a mood episode is the single most important discriminator; a careful longitudinal history documenting psychotic symptoms during euthymic intervals is more diagnostically valuable than any cross-sectional assessment.

stem: A 21-year-old male university student is brought to the emergency department by police after being found agitated and disoriented in a public park. His friends report he smoked a large quantity of high-potency cannabis at a party 6 hours ago. He has no prior psychiatric history and no family history of psychotic illness. He believes people at the party poisoned him and that police are conspiring against him. He is visually distressed and pacing around the cubicle.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 108, BP 142/88, RR 18, SpO2 99% on room air, T 37.0
data_table.Examination: Agitated, paranoid, disorganised speech, persecutory delusions, no hallucinations elicited, conjunctival injection, dry mouth, pupils mildly dilated, oriented to person only, urine drug screen positive for THC
data_table.Investigations: FBC normal, UEC normal, LFTs normal, BSL 6.2 mmol/L, urine drug screen THC positive, alcohol level undetectable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management approach?

options.text: Commence oral olanzapine 10 mg for psychosis and arrange psychiatric admission
options.rationale: While antipsychotic medication may be needed if agitation is severe and unresponsive to de-escalation, committing to a full antipsychotic treatment course and psychiatric admission is premature. Cannabis-induced psychosis typically resolves within hours to days of cessation. The priority is supportive management in a low-stimulus environment with benzodiazepines for agitation. (Source: RANZCP; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Administer IM haloperidol 10 mg and IM midazolam 10 mg for rapid tranquillisation
options.rationale: This patient is agitated but pacing and verbally communicable. Aggressive parenteral rapid tranquillisation at these high doses is disproportionate. Oral medications and de-escalation should be attempted first. IM haloperidol 10 mg is a high dose with risk of acute dystonia and oversedation. Graduated response is the recommended approach per Australian guidelines. (Source: NSW Health Acute Behavioural Disturbance Guidelines; RANZCP)

options.text: Discharge with safety-netting as cannabis psychosis is self-limiting and requires no treatment
options.rationale: While cannabis-induced psychosis is often self-limiting, this patient is currently acutely psychotic, paranoid, and disoriented. Discharge without adequate observation is unsafe. He requires monitoring in a low-stimulus environment until psychotic symptoms resolve and he is oriented and safe for discharge with appropriate follow-up. (Source: RANZCP; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Administer IV flumazenil to reverse the cannabis intoxication effects on GABA receptors
options.rationale: Flumazenil is a benzodiazepine antagonist with no activity at cannabinoid receptors. Cannabis acts primarily on CB1 receptors, not GABA receptors. There is no specific pharmacological antagonist for cannabis intoxication. Flumazenil administration is inappropriate and could precipitate seizures if unreported benzodiazepine co-ingestion is present. (Source: AMH; Toxicology Guidelines)

options.text: Place in a low-stimulus environment with verbal de-escalation and oral diazepam as needed
options.rationale: The initial management of cannabis-induced psychosis centres on supportive care in a low-stimulus environment with verbal de-escalation. Oral benzodiazepines (diazepam 5-10 mg) are first-line for agitation, providing anxiolysis and sedation without the extrapyramidal risks of antipsychotics. Observation until symptoms resolve (typically 6-24 hours for uncomplicated cannabis psychosis) with reassessment for ongoing psychotic symptoms is the standard approach. (Source: RANZCP; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Cannabis-induced psychosis typically presents with paranoia, disorganisation, and anxiety within hours of use, particularly with high-potency products. Management is primarily supportive with a calm environment, de-escalation, and benzodiazepines for agitation. Symptoms usually resolve within hours to days. However, cannabis-induced psychosis is a significant risk factor for subsequent primary psychotic disorder, with approximately 20-30% of patients developing schizophrenia within 3 years. Follow-up is essential.
key_points: Supportive care in a low-stimulus environment is the initial priority
Benzodiazepines are first-line for cannabis-induced agitation
Symptoms typically resolve within 6-24 hours of cessation
20-30% of cannabis-induced psychosis cases progress to primary psychotic disorder
explanation.pearls: High-potency cannabis (THC >10% with low CBD content) carries approximately 5 times the psychosis risk of low-potency cannabis, and daily use of high-potency products accounts for a significant population-attributable fraction of first-episode psychosis presentations.

stem: A 36-year-old woman with a history of bipolar I disorder is brought to the emergency department by her partner. She has been increasingly withdrawn over the past 3 days and for the past 18 hours has been mute, refusing food and fluids, and staring blankly. Her bipolar disorder is managed with lithium 900 mg daily. She has no history of substance use. She was under the care of her community mental health team for a depressive episode over the past 4 weeks.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96, BP 148/92, T 37.4, RR 16, SpO2 98% on room air
data_table.Examination: Mute, immobile in bed, eyes open and staring, waxy flexibility present on limb positioning (arms remain in passively placed positions for >30 seconds), negativism when attempts made to open her mouth, no response to verbal commands, maintains posture despite apparent discomfort
data_table.Investigations: Lithium level 0.8 mmol/L (therapeutic), FBC normal, UEC normal, CRP 8 mg/L, TFTs normal, urinalysis no infection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial diagnostic and therapeutic intervention?

options.text: Administer IV lorazepam 1-2 mg and observe for improvement in catatonic signs within 30 minutes
options.rationale: The lorazepam challenge is both diagnostic and therapeutic for catatonia. This patient displays classic catatonic features: mutism, immobility, waxy flexibility, negativism, and posturing. A positive response to IV lorazepam (improvement in at least one catatonic sign within 10-30 minutes) supports the diagnosis and guides ongoing treatment with scheduled benzodiazepines. The Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale should be scored before and after the challenge. (Source: RANZCP; BMJ Best Practice: Catatonia)

options.text: Commence oral olanzapine 10 mg for presumed psychotic depression with catatonic features
options.rationale: Antipsychotics should be used with caution in catatonia as they may worsen symptoms and precipitate neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS), which shares features with malignant catatonia. Antipsychotics are not first-line treatment for catatonia. The initial intervention should be a benzodiazepine challenge. (Source: RANZCP; BMJ Best Practice: Catatonia)

options.text: Arrange urgent brain MRI to exclude organic causes before any pharmacological treatment
options.rationale: While organic causes of catatonia should be investigated, the clinical presentation in the context of known bipolar disorder with a recent depressive episode is consistent with psychiatric catatonia. Brain imaging is appropriate but should not delay the lorazepam challenge, which is both safe and diagnostically informative. Investigation and treatment proceed in parallel. (Source: RANZCP; BMJ Best Practice: Catatonia)

options.text: Increase lithium dose to achieve a higher therapeutic level for the depressive episode
options.rationale: The lithium level is therapeutic at 0.8 mmol/L. Increasing the dose would risk toxicity without addressing the catatonia. Catatonia is a distinct syndrome requiring specific treatment (benzodiazepines or ECT) and does not respond to mood stabiliser dose escalation alone. The depressive episode context is important but the catatonia takes treatment priority. (Source: AMH; RANZCP)

options.text: Commence IV antibiotics empirically for possible autoimmune encephalitis presenting as catatonia
options.rationale: While autoimmune encephalitis (particularly anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis) can present with catatonic features, the clinical context of known bipolar disorder with a recent depressive episode makes psychiatric catatonia more likely. Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis would typically also include seizures, dysautonomia, and movement disorders. A lorazepam challenge is the appropriate first step. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Catatonia)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a psychomotor syndrome that can occur in the context of mood disorders, psychotic disorders, medical conditions, or autoimmune encephalitis. The key features include mutism, immobility, waxy flexibility, negativism, posturing, and stereotypy. The lorazepam challenge (1-2 mg IV with repeat scoring) is the gold standard diagnostic and initial therapeutic intervention. Benzodiazepines are first-line treatment, with ECT reserved for refractory cases. Antipsychotics should be avoided as they can worsen catatonia and precipitate NMS.
key_points: Lorazepam challenge is both diagnostic and therapeutic for catatonia
Benzodiazepines are first-line treatment; antipsychotics may worsen catatonia
Bipolar disorder is the most common psychiatric cause of catatonia
Malignant catatonia requires urgent ECT referral
explanation.pearls: The lorazepam challenge has a sensitivity of approximately 60-80% for catatonia; a negative challenge does not exclude the diagnosis, and patients who fail to respond to benzodiazepines should be referred for ECT, which has response rates exceeding 80% in catatonia.

subtopic_detail: Functional neurological disorder diagnosis and management
stem: A 28-year-old woman presents to the neurology clinic with a 3-week history of left-sided leg weakness causing difficulty walking. Symptoms began after a minor workplace injury. She has no history of neurological disease. MRI brain and spine are normal. Nerve conduction studies are normal. On examination, her left leg gives way inconsistently, and she has a positive Hoover sign. She appears genuinely distressed by her symptoms and is unable to work.

data_table.Examination: Inconsistent left leg weakness (gives way on direct testing but normal involuntary patterns during distraction), positive Hoover sign (hip extension weakness reverses with contralateral hip flexion), normal reflexes, downgoing plantars bilaterally, intact sensation, La belle indifference not present
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain and complete spine normal, nerve conduction studies normal, FBC/UEC/TFTs/B12 normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach to communicating the diagnosis?

options.text: Explain the symptoms are stress-related and refer for psychological therapy alone
options.rationale: Framing FND as purely stress-related is reductive and may be perceived as dismissive. While psychological factors can contribute, FND is understood as a disorder of nervous system function, not simply a stress response. Management requires a multidisciplinary approach including physiotherapy, not psychology alone. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: FND; NICE)

options.text: Explain the positive diagnostic signs, name the condition, and plan multidisciplinary treatment
options.rationale: Best practice for FND diagnosis involves naming the condition (functional neurological disorder), explaining the positive clinical signs that support the diagnosis (e.g. Hoover sign demonstrates the nervous system has the capacity for normal function but is not sending signals correctly in the usual way), validating the patient's experience as real and not fabricated, and planning multidisciplinary care including specialist physiotherapy. This approach reduces diagnostic uncertainty and improves engagement. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: FND; NICE; Lancet Neurology FND consensus)

options.text: Reassure that all tests are normal and the weakness should resolve spontaneously over time
options.rationale: Dismissive reassurance based on normal investigations is unhelpful and may reinforce the patient's distress. FND is a positive diagnosis made on clinical signs, not a diagnosis of exclusion. Without active multidisciplinary treatment, symptoms may persist or worsen. Spontaneous resolution occurs in only a minority of cases with established symptoms. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: FND; Lancet Neurology FND consensus)

options.text: Request repeat MRI with contrast and electromyography before committing to a functional diagnosis
options.rationale: The diagnosis is supported by positive clinical signs (Hoover sign, inconsistency) with normal investigations. Repeating investigations delays treatment and may reinforce illness behaviour. FND is a rule-in diagnosis based on positive examination findings, not a rule-out diagnosis requiring exhaustive investigation. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: FND; NICE)

options.text: Confront the patient with the examination inconsistencies to demonstrate symptom fabrication
options.rationale: FND symptoms are not fabricated or under voluntary control. Confronting the patient with inconsistencies as evidence of fabrication is both clinically incorrect and therapeutically harmful. It damages the therapeutic alliance and may worsen symptoms. The inconsistency on examination is a positive diagnostic sign, not evidence of malingering. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: FND; Lancet Neurology FND consensus)

explanation.summary: Functional neurological disorder is diagnosed based on positive clinical signs demonstrating internal inconsistency of neurological function, such as the Hoover sign. It is not a diagnosis of exclusion. Communication of the diagnosis should name the condition, demonstrate the positive signs to the patient, validate their experience, and establish a treatment plan including specialist physiotherapy. Outcomes are improved by early diagnosis, clear communication, and multidisciplinary treatment.
key_points: FND is a positive diagnosis based on clinical signs, not a diagnosis of exclusion
Hoover sign and other inconsistency signs are rule-in diagnostic features
Symptoms are real and involuntary, not fabricated
Multidisciplinary treatment including specialist physiotherapy is the evidence-based approach
explanation.pearls: The Hoover sign has a sensitivity of approximately 63% and specificity of 100% for functional leg weakness; it demonstrates that involuntary hip extension (during contralateral flexion) is normal, confirming intact motor pathways that are not activated during voluntary testing.

stem: A 52-year-old woman with stable schizophrenia managed on clozapine 400 mg daily presents requesting support to quit smoking. She smokes 30 cigarettes per day. She previously tried varenicline but discontinued it after 2 weeks due to severe nausea and vomiting despite dose adjustment. She has no history of cardiovascular disease or seizures. Her clozapine level is 0.52 mg/L. She is motivated to attempt quitting again.

data_table.Examination: Stable mental state, no psychotic symptoms, BMI 32, PHQ-9 score 6
data_table.Investigations: Clozapine level 0.52 mg/L (target 0.35-0.60), FBC: WCC 5.8 x10^9/L, neutrophils 3.2 x10^9/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate smoking cessation pharmacotherapy for this patient?

options.text: Retry varenicline at a lower maintenance dose of 0.5 mg twice daily long-term
options.rationale: The patient discontinued varenicline due to severe nausea and vomiting despite dose adjustment. While reduced-dose varenicline is an option, severe GI intolerance that led to discontinuation suggests an alternative approach is more appropriate. Forcing re-trial of a poorly tolerated medication reduces adherence. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction; RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines)

options.text: Commence bupropion 150 mg twice daily as an alternative first-line cessation agent
options.rationale: Bupropion lowers the seizure threshold and may interact with clozapine, which also lowers seizure threshold. The combination increases the risk of seizures. Additionally, bupropion inhibits CYP2D6, which may affect clozapine metabolism. Combination NRT is a safer alternative in this context. (Source: AMH; Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction)

options.text: Advise nicotine e-cigarette use as a harm reduction strategy without other pharmacotherapy
options.rationale: While e-cigarettes are used by some as a harm reduction tool, they are not a recommended first-line smoking cessation strategy in Australian clinical guidelines. Evidence-based pharmacotherapy should be offered first. The long-term safety profile of e-cigarettes remains uncertain, and TGA-approved cessation aids have stronger evidence. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines; Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction)

options.text: Commence nicotine patch 21 mg daily plus nicotine mouth spray for breakthrough cravings
options.rationale: Combination NRT (long-acting patch plus short-acting oral form) is an evidence-based approach with efficacy approaching that of varenicline. It avoids the seizure risk of bupropion in a clozapine-treated patient and the GI intolerance of varenicline. Importantly, smoking cessation reduces the induction of CYP1A2, which will increase clozapine levels - the clozapine dose must be reduced by approximately 30-50% and levels monitored closely after quitting. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction; RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines; AMH)

options.text: Defer smoking cessation until clozapine is switched to a less metabolically affected antipsychotic
options.rationale: Smoking cessation should not be deferred due to clozapine treatment. The interaction between smoking cessation and clozapine metabolism is well-characterised and manageable with proactive dose reduction and level monitoring. The health benefits of smoking cessation far outweigh the inconvenience of clozapine dose adjustment. (Source: AMH; Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction)

explanation.summary: Smoking cessation in patients on clozapine requires careful pharmacokinetic management. Cigarette smoke induces CYP1A2, which metabolises clozapine. Cessation reduces this induction, causing clozapine levels to rise by 50-70% if the dose is not adjusted. Combination NRT is preferred when varenicline is not tolerated and bupropion carries seizure risk. Clozapine dose should be reduced by approximately 30-50% at the quit date with close monitoring of levels and clinical state.
key_points: Combination NRT achieves efficacy approaching varenicline
Bupropion and clozapine both lower seizure threshold, making their combination risky
Smoking cessation increases clozapine levels by 50-70% via reduced CYP1A2 induction
Clozapine dose must be reduced proactively when a patient quits smoking
explanation.pearls: The CYP1A2 induction by cigarette smoke (polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, not nicotine) means that NRT does not affect clozapine metabolism, but stopping smoking does - clozapine levels must be checked within 72 hours of the quit date and the dose typically reduced by 30-50% to avoid toxicity.

stem: A 30-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has been stable on sodium valproate 1500 mg daily for 5 years. She presents at 6 weeks gestation having just discovered an unplanned pregnancy. Her pregnancy test was positive 3 days ago. She is enrolled in the pregnancy prevention program but her LARC (Implanon) was removed 2 months ago when she changed GPs and a replacement was not organised. She is distressed and wants to continue the pregnancy. She has had three severe manic episodes requiring hospitalisation before stabilisation on valproate.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic, anxious about pregnancy, no psychotic features, well-engaged
data_table.Investigations: Valproate level 92 mg/L, beta-hCG consistent with 6-week gestation, FBC and LFTs normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Continue valproate at the current dose as the risk period for neural tube defects has passed
options.rationale: Neural tube closure occurs at approximately 28 days post-conception (6 weeks gestational age). While the critical period for neural tube defects may have passed, valproate exposure throughout pregnancy is associated with additional risks including cardiac malformations, cleft palate, hypospadias, and - most significantly - neurodevelopmental impairment affecting IQ and risk of autism spectrum disorder. Continued exposure must be weighed against relapse risk. (Source: ACSQHC Valproate Safety; AMH; RANZCP)

options.text: Immediately cease valproate without replacement and commence folic acid 5 mg daily
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation of valproate in a patient with a history of three severe manic episodes risks precipitating mania or psychosis during the critical first trimester. A manic relapse during pregnancy poses its own risks to mother and fetus. Any medication change must be gradual with concurrent introduction of a safer alternative. Folic acid should be commenced but is insufficient alone. (Source: RANZCP; COPE Guidelines; AMH)

options.text: Plan cross-taper from valproate to lithium with close psychiatric and obstetric monitoring
options.rationale: A collaborative decision involving the patient, psychiatrist, and obstetrician is needed. Cross-tapering from valproate to lithium is the recommended approach when valproate must be ceased in pregnancy. Lithium has a lower overall teratogenic risk (cardiac malformation rate approximately 1-2% vs valproate's 5-10% major malformation rate and 30-40% neurodevelopmental effects). The cross-taper should be gradual to minimise relapse risk. Folic acid 5 mg daily should be commenced. High-resolution ultrasound at 18-20 weeks is recommended. (Source: RANZCP; COPE Guidelines; AMH)

options.text: Reduce valproate to 500 mg daily as a dose-dependent risk reduction strategy throughout pregnancy
options.rationale: While valproate teratogenicity shows some dose-dependence (higher risk above 700-1000 mg daily), even low-dose valproate carries substantially higher risk than alternatives such as lithium. Dose reduction without switching still exposes the fetus to the ongoing neurodevelopmental risks of valproate. If the pregnancy is to continue, switching to a safer agent is the recommended approach. (Source: ACSQHC Valproate Safety; AMH; RANZCP)

options.text: Continue valproate and add lamotrigine as augmentation to allow later valproate cessation
options.rationale: Adding lamotrigine while continuing valproate delays the removal of the teratogenic agent. Valproate also inhibits the metabolism of lamotrigine, requiring the lamotrigine dose to be halved and complicating titration. The priority is to cease valproate exposure as quickly as is safely achievable, with direct transition to an alternative mood stabiliser. (Source: AMH; RANZCP)

explanation.summary: Valproate in pregnancy carries a 5-10% major malformation rate and a 30-40% risk of neurodevelopmental effects including reduced IQ and autism spectrum disorder. When pregnancy is discovered, the priority is a collaborative plan to transition to a safer mood stabiliser while minimising relapse risk. Lithium is the preferred alternative for bipolar I disorder. The cross-taper must be gradual, and close psychiatric monitoring is essential throughout. Specialist perinatal mental health involvement is recommended.
key_points: Valproate causes 5-10% major malformations and 30-40% neurodevelopmental effects
Cross-taper to lithium is the recommended strategy in bipolar I pregnancy
Abrupt cessation risks manic relapse which poses its own fetal and maternal risks
Specialist perinatal psychiatry and high-risk obstetric care should be involved
explanation.pearls: The NICE-MHRA valproate data show that valproate at doses above 1000 mg/day is associated with a major congenital malformation rate of approximately 10-11%, compared with 2-3% at doses below 700 mg/day, though neurodevelopmental risk persists at all doses.

subtopic_detail: TCA overdose with wide QRS specific management
stem: A 28-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after an intentional overdose of his mother's dosulepin. His housemate found him 90 minutes after ingestion. He was initially drowsy but has since had a 30-second generalised tonic-clonic seizure in the ambulance that self-terminated. He has received IV sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol on arrival. His post-bicarbonate ECG still shows a QRS duration of 148 ms with a prominent R wave in aVR. His pH is now 7.52. He then develops a broad complex tachycardia at a rate of 156 bpm with a BP of 72/44.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 156 (broad complex tachycardia), BP 72/44, RR 22, SpO2 96% on 10 L/min, GCS 8
data_table.Examination: Dilated pupils, dry skin, obtunded, broad complex tachycardia on monitor, no response to voice
data_table.Investigations: ABG: pH 7.52, pCO2 28 mmHg, HCO3 24 mmol/L, lactate 4.8 mmol/L, K+ 3.2 mmol/L, ECG: wide QRS 148 ms, R aVR 6 mm, broad complex tachycardia 156 bpm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next intervention for the arrhythmia?

options.text: Administer IV amiodarone 300 mg over 20 minutes for the broad complex tachycardia
options.rationale: Amiodarone is a Class III antiarrhythmic that also has sodium channel blocking properties (Class IA effect). In TCA overdose, any agent that further blocks sodium channels will worsen QRS prolongation and may precipitate intractable VF. Amiodarone is specifically contraindicated in sodium channel blocker toxicity. (Source: Toxicology Guidelines; Austin Health Toxicology)

options.text: Perform synchronised DC cardioversion at 150 J for the haemodynamically unstable VT
options.rationale: While cardioversion is indicated for haemodynamically unstable VT from other causes, TCA-induced wide complex tachycardia is often resistant to electrical cardioversion because the arrhythmia mechanism is sodium channel blockade rather than a re-entrant circuit. Further sodium bicarbonate to overcome the channel blockade is the specific treatment. Cardioversion may be attempted if bicarbonate fails, but sodium loading is the priority. (Source: Toxicology Guidelines; ANZCOR)

options.text: Administer IV procainamide 15 mg/kg to convert the broad complex tachycardia
options.rationale: Procainamide is a Class IA sodium channel blocker that is absolutely contraindicated in TCA overdose. It will compound the existing sodium channel blockade, widen the QRS further, and likely precipitate cardiac arrest. Class IA, IC, and III antiarrhythmics are all contraindicated. (Source: Toxicology Guidelines; AMH)

options.text: Administer IV magnesium sulfate 2 g for the broad complex tachycardia and hypokalaemia
options.rationale: While magnesium may be appropriate for torsades de pointes, the primary arrhythmia mechanism in TCA toxicity is sodium channel blockade producing a wide complex tachycardia, not a magnesium-responsive rhythm. The hypokalaemia should be corrected concurrently, but the arrhythmia-specific treatment is further sodium loading. (Source: Toxicology Guidelines; Austin Health Toxicology)

options.text: Administer a further 100 mmol IV sodium bicarbonate bolus and consider 20% lipid emulsion
options.rationale: Further sodium bicarbonate is indicated despite the alkalotic pH because the mechanism of benefit is dual: alkalinisation (reducing drug-receptor binding) AND sodium loading (overcoming the sodium channel blockade with excess extracellular sodium). Hypertonic saline can be used if pH exceeds 7.55. IV lipid emulsion (20%, 1.5 mL/kg bolus then infusion) is the appropriate rescue therapy for severe TCA toxicity refractory to bicarbonate, acting as a lipid sink for the highly lipophilic drug. (Source: Toxicology Guidelines; Austin Health Toxicology; ANZCOR)

explanation.summary: Severe TCA overdose with refractory wide complex tachycardia after initial sodium bicarbonate requires escalation of sodium loading. The sodium channel blockade mechanism means that standard antiarrhythmics (Class IA, IC, III) worsen toxicity. Further sodium bicarbonate remains the first-line approach; when pH exceeds 7.55, hypertonic saline provides sodium loading without further alkalinisation. IV lipid emulsion is the second-line rescue therapy. Cardioversion has poor efficacy for sodium channel blocker-induced arrhythmias.
key_points: Sodium bicarbonate works via both alkalinisation and sodium loading mechanisms
All Class IA, IC, and III antiarrhythmics are contraindicated in TCA overdose
IV lipid emulsion is rescue therapy for refractory TCA cardiotoxicity
If pH >7.55, switch to hypertonic saline for sodium loading without further alkalinisation
explanation.pearls: Dosulepin (dosulepin) is the most toxic TCA in overdose per unit dose ingested, with the lowest therapeutic index; ingestion of 35 mg/kg (approximately 2.5 g in a 70 kg adult) carries a significant risk of fatal arrhythmia, making it the most dangerous commonly prescribed antidepressant in overdose.

stem: A 34-year-old woman with established schizoaffective disorder, depressive type, presents for medication review. She has been on paliperidone long-acting injection 150 mg monthly for psychotic symptoms with good effect - her hallucinations and paranoia are well controlled. However, she is experiencing a persistent depressive episode with low mood, anhedonia, insomnia, poor concentration, and feelings of hopelessness lasting 10 weeks. She denies suicidal ideation. She has no history of mania or hypomania. Her previous trial of sertraline was ineffective at 200 mg daily for 8 weeks.

data_table.Examination: Flat affect, psychomotor retardation, no psychotic features currently, PHQ-9 score 18 (moderately severe depression), no thought disorder, GAF 48
data_table.Investigations: Prolactin mildly elevated at 680 mIU/L, TFTs normal, metabolic panel normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological adjustment for her depressive symptoms?

options.text: Add venlafaxine 75 mg daily, titrating to 150-225 mg over 4 weeks for the depression
options.rationale: For schizoaffective disorder depressive type with an inadequate response to SSRI, switching to or adding an SNRI (venlafaxine) is an appropriate next step. The antipsychotic should be maintained for psychotic symptom control. SNRIs have broader mechanism of action (serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibition) that may be effective where SSRIs have failed. The paliperidone LAI should continue unchanged as psychosis is well controlled. (Source: RANZCP; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines)

options.text: Switch paliperidone to clozapine 25 mg daily titrating for combined antipsychotic and antidepressant effect
options.rationale: Switching from a well-tolerated and effective antipsychotic to clozapine is inappropriate when psychotic symptoms are well controlled. Clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia/schizoaffective disorder refractory to two adequate antipsychotic trials. The current issue is inadequate depression treatment, not antipsychotic failure. (Source: RANZCP; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Increase paliperidone LAI to 200 mg monthly to address the depressive component through dopamine modulation
options.rationale: Increasing the antipsychotic dose is unlikely to improve the depressive episode and may worsen side effects including extrapyramidal symptoms, sedation, and further prolactin elevation. Paliperidone has minimal antidepressant properties. The depression requires specific antidepressant treatment as an adjunct. (Source: RANZCP; AMH)

options.text: Add lithium 500 mg daily as augmentation targeting both mood stabilisation and antidepressant effect
options.rationale: Lithium augmentation of an antidepressant is an established strategy in treatment-resistant depression. However, this patient has not yet trialled an adequate alternative antidepressant class after SSRI failure. An SNRI trial is a more appropriate next step before considering augmentation strategies. Additionally, lithium augmentation is typically added to an existing antidepressant, not to an antipsychotic alone. (Source: RANZCP; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Cease paliperidone and commence quetiapine 300 mg nocte for combined antipsychotic and antidepressant benefit
options.rationale: Switching from an effective LAI antipsychotic to an oral agent risks both psychotic relapse (due to adherence challenges) and inadequate antipsychotic efficacy. While quetiapine has some antidepressant properties, it would not provide the same level of psychotic symptom control as paliperidone in this patient. Maintaining the effective antipsychotic and adding a dedicated antidepressant is the safer strategy. (Source: RANZCP; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Schizoaffective disorder depressive type requires treatment of both psychotic and mood components, often with separate agents. When psychotic symptoms are controlled on an antipsychotic, the depressive component should be managed with standard antidepressant principles. After SSRI failure, switching antidepressant class (e.g. to an SNRI) is the recommended next step before considering augmentation strategies. The effective antipsychotic should be maintained to prevent psychotic relapse.
key_points: Maintain the effective antipsychotic while addressing the depression separately
After SSRI failure, switch to an SNRI (venlafaxine) as next-step antidepressant
Increasing antipsychotic dose does not adequately treat depressive episodes
Lithium augmentation is a later-stage strategy after adequate antidepressant trials
explanation.pearls: Paliperidone (9-hydroxyrisperidone) has high D2 and 5-HT2A affinity but minimal noradrenaline or histamine receptor binding, which means it provides antipsychotic efficacy but has negligible intrinsic antidepressant activity, necessitating a separate antidepressant for the depressive component of schizoaffective disorder.

stem: A 19-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by friends after smoking a substance purchased online described as herbal incense. Within 20 minutes of use, he became severely agitated, vomited, and developed a generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting 2 minutes that self-terminated. His friends deny other substance use. He has no psychiatric history. On arrival, he is tachycardic, hypertensive, and alternating between extreme agitation and obtundation. His urine drug screen is negative for THC.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 142, BP 176/104, T 38.8, RR 24, SpO2 95% on room air, GCS fluctuating 8-12
data_table.Examination: Agitated then obtunded cycling over minutes, diaphoretic, dilated pupils 6 mm, generalised hyperreflexia, dry mucous membranes, CK 2840 U/L, no clonus
data_table.Investigations: UDS negative for THC, amphetamines, opioids, benzodiazepines, ECG: sinus tachycardia QTc 468 ms, VBG: pH 7.32 lactate 5.2 mmol/L, creatinine 128 micromol/L, CK 2840 U/L

lead_in: Which substance class most likely explains this clinical presentation?

options.text: Natural high-potency cannabis with an atypically severe reaction to THC
options.rationale: Natural cannabis, even high-potency strains, rarely causes seizures, significant hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, or the rapidly fluctuating consciousness seen here. The negative THC on urine drug screen also argues against natural cannabis. Additionally, natural cannabis intoxication does not typically cause the severe sympathomimetic features present. (Source: RANZCP; Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Synthetic cannabinoid receptor agonist with full agonist activity at CB1 receptors
options.rationale: Synthetic cannabinoid receptor agonists (SCRAs) are full agonists at CB1 receptors (versus THC which is a partial agonist), producing markedly more severe effects. They commonly cause seizures, severe agitation, rhabdomyolysis, hyperthermia, tachycardia, and obtundation - all present in this case. Crucially, they are NOT detected on standard urine THC immunoassays because their chemical structure differs from THC metabolites. The product description as herbal incense is a classic marketing term for SCRAs. (Source: Toxicology Guidelines; RANZCP; BMJ Best Practice)

options.text: MDMA with serotonin syndrome causing the seizure and hyperthermia presentation
options.rationale: MDMA-associated serotonin syndrome typically presents with clonus (absent here), hyperreflexia, hyperthermia, and agitation. However, the urine drug screen would be expected to detect MDMA via the amphetamines assay (though sensitivity varies). The route of exposure (smoking herbal product) is inconsistent with MDMA, which is typically ingested or insufflated. (Source: Toxicology Guidelines)

options.text: Anticholinergic toxidrome from a plant-based alkaloid in the herbal product
options.rationale: Anticholinergic toxidrome includes mydriasis and dry mucous membranes (present) but classically features absent bowel sounds, urinary retention, and warm dry skin with minimal diaphoresis. This patient is diaphoretic, which is inconsistent with a pure anticholinergic toxidrome. The seizure and rhabdomyolysis pattern is more consistent with synthetic cannabinoid toxicity. (Source: Toxicology Guidelines)

options.text: Cathinone derivative (bath salts) contaminating the herbal product as an adulterant
options.rationale: Synthetic cathinones can produce a similar sympathomimetic toxidrome with agitation, tachycardia, and hyperthermia. However, the product was smoked as a herbal incense product, which is the characteristic delivery system for synthetic cannabinoids rather than cathinones. Cathinones are typically insufflated or ingested. The overall pattern is more consistent with SCRA toxicity. (Source: Toxicology Guidelines; RANZCP)

explanation.summary: Synthetic cannabinoid receptor agonists (SCRAs) are full agonists at CB1 receptors, producing far more severe and dangerous effects than natural cannabis. Key distinguishing features include seizures, severe agitation alternating with obtundation, rhabdomyolysis, hyperthermia, and negative standard urine THC assays. They are commonly sold as herbal incense or potpourri. Management is supportive with benzodiazepines for agitation and seizures, cooling for hyperthermia, and IV fluids for rhabdomyolysis prevention.
key_points: SCRAs are full CB1 agonists versus THC's partial agonism, causing more severe effects
Standard urine drug screens do NOT detect synthetic cannabinoids
Seizures, rhabdomyolysis, and severe sympathomimetic features distinguish SCRAs from natural cannabis
Management is supportive with benzodiazepines, cooling, and IV fluid resuscitation
explanation.pearls: Synthetic cannabinoid receptor agonists such as JWH-018 and AB-FUBINACA have binding affinities 4-100 times greater than THC at CB1 receptors and act as full rather than partial agonists, explaining the dramatically more severe clinical toxicity including seizures and organ damage not seen with natural cannabis.

subtopic_detail: Malignant catatonia vs neuroleptic malignant syndrome
stem: A 42-year-old man with chronic schizophrenia was commenced on haloperidol 10 mg daily 5 days ago after a psychotic relapse. He is now rigid, mute, and febrile. His CK is markedly elevated. The treating team is debating whether this is neuroleptic malignant syndrome or malignant catatonia. His premorbid psychiatric notes document two prior episodes of catatonia associated with psychotic relapses, both responsive to lorazepam. A lorazepam challenge (2 mg IV) has been administered with no improvement after 30 minutes.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128, BP 168/102 (labile, ranging 90/60-170/110), T 39.6, RR 24, SpO2 94% on room air
data_table.Examination: Generalised lead-pipe rigidity (not waxy flexibility), mute, diaphoretic, GCS 9, pupils mid-size and reactive, no tremor at rest, autonomic instability with fluctuating BP and HR
data_table.Investigations: CK 14,200 U/L, WCC 16.4 x10^9/L, creatinine 186 micromol/L, LDH 890 U/L, AST 128 U/L, lactate 3.8 mmol/L, myoglobinuria on dipstick

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management approach?

options.text: Continue haloperidol and add bromocriptine 2.5 mg TDS plus dantrolene 1 mg/kg IV
options.rationale: Continuing haloperidol in the setting of either NMS or malignant catatonia is inappropriate. The antipsychotic must be ceased immediately. While bromocriptine and dantrolene are specific NMS treatments, the history of prior catatonic episodes and the timeline suggest this may be malignant catatonia precipitated by or overlapping with NMS. The priority is ceasing the causative agent. (Source: RANZCP; BMJ Best Practice: NMS)

options.text: Administer further lorazepam 4 mg IV and repeat the challenge in 2 hours if no response
options.rationale: The initial lorazepam challenge at 2 mg was negative at 30 minutes. In malignant catatonia with NMS overlap, lorazepam alone may be insufficient. While higher doses of benzodiazepines can be tried, this patient has severe autonomic instability, markedly elevated CK with renal impairment, and is deteriorating. Urgent escalation to ECT should not be delayed by repeated benzodiazepine challenges. (Source: RANZCP; BMJ Best Practice: Catatonia)

options.text: Switch to oral clozapine 12.5 mg twice daily as a low D2-affinity alternative antipsychotic
options.rationale: Initiating any antipsychotic during an acute NMS or malignant catatonia episode is contraindicated. Even low D2-affinity agents carry risk of worsening the neuroleptic-mediated component of the presentation. Antipsychotic rechallenge can only be considered weeks after full resolution, typically with a structurally dissimilar agent at low dose. (Source: RANZCP; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Cease haloperidol, provide aggressive supportive care, and arrange urgent ECT consultation
options.rationale: This presentation likely represents a NMS-malignant catatonia overlap. The history of prior catatonic episodes suggests underlying catatonia vulnerability, with haloperidol precipitating a malignant progression. Management requires: (1) immediate cessation of haloperidol, (2) aggressive supportive care (IV fluids for rhabdomyolysis, cooling, ICU monitoring), (3) benzodiazepines may continue, and (4) urgent ECT referral for lorazepam-refractory malignant catatonia, which has response rates exceeding 80%. ECT can be lifesaving in this context. (Source: RANZCP; BMJ Best Practice: Catatonia; BMJ Best Practice: NMS)

options.text: Transfer to ICU for IV dantrolene and bromocriptine as definitive NMS pharmacotherapy alone
options.rationale: While ICU transfer and NMS-specific pharmacotherapy (dantrolene for rigidity, bromocriptine for dopaminergic support) are appropriate components of care, treating this purely as NMS misses the underlying catatonia vulnerability. The history of prior catatonic episodes and lorazepam-unresponsive malignant catatonia indicates that ECT should be part of the treatment plan. Pharmacotherapy for NMS and ECT for catatonia can be pursued concurrently. (Source: RANZCP; BMJ Best Practice: NMS; BMJ Best Practice: Catatonia)

explanation.summary: Malignant catatonia and NMS share features (rigidity, fever, autonomic instability, elevated CK) and may represent overlapping syndromes. The key discriminator is the clinical context: NMS occurs after antipsychotic initiation while malignant catatonia arises from escalation of untreated catatonia. They may coexist, as antipsychotics can both cause NMS and worsen underlying catatonia. Management requires antipsychotic cessation, aggressive supportive care, and urgent ECT for the catatonic component when benzodiazepines fail.
key_points: NMS and malignant catatonia share clinical features and may overlap
Prior catatonic episodes suggest underlying vulnerability to catatonia
ECT is the definitive treatment for lorazepam-refractory malignant catatonia
All antipsychotics must be ceased immediately in both conditions
explanation.pearls: Lead-pipe rigidity (constant resistance throughout passive movement) is more typical of NMS, while waxy flexibility (initial resistance then maintained posturing) is more typical of catatonia; when lead-pipe rigidity develops in a patient with known catatonia vulnerability after antipsychotic exposure, NMS-catatonia overlap should be strongly suspected.

stem: You are a paediatric registrar reviewing a 3-year-old girl who has been admitted 8 times in 12 months for recurrent episodes of unexplained vomiting, lethargy, and dehydration. Each admission resolves rapidly with IV fluids and observation. The mother is a former enrolled nurse and is very engaged with the medical team, often suggesting diagnoses and requesting investigations. A nursing colleague has observed the mother injecting an unknown substance into the child's IV line during a previous admission. The child's father is estranged and has no contact. Baseline investigations including metabolic panels, coeliac screen, and neuroimaging have been consistently normal.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 112, BP 88/52, T 36.8, weight tracking below the 3rd centile (previously 25th)
data_table.Examination: Mild dehydration, otherwise normal examination, developmental milestones appropriate, no bruising or skin lesions, interactive when mother leaves the room
data_table.Investigations: Repeated admissions: FBC normal, UEC normal, LFTs normal, coeliac screen negative, MRI brain normal, urinalysis normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Confront the mother with the nursing staff observation and request a psychiatric evaluation
options.rationale: Direct confrontation with the suspected perpetrator risks escalation, absconding with the child, destruction of evidence, or harm to the child. The priority is safeguarding the child through appropriate institutional and statutory processes. Confrontation should occur only after child protection services are involved and a safety plan is established. (Source: RANZCP; RACP Child Protection Guidelines)

options.text: Arrange a case conference and covert video surveillance to gather definitive evidence first
options.rationale: Covert video surveillance raises significant ethical and legal issues and requires institutional ethics approval, legal advice, and cannot be implemented unilaterally. While it has been used in some jurisdictions, the immediate priority is the child's safety through mandatory reporting and institutional child protection processes. Waiting for definitive evidence should not delay protective action. (Source: RACP Child Protection Guidelines)

options.text: Ensure the child's safety and make an immediate mandatory report to child protection services
options.rationale: When there is a reasonable suspicion of factitious disorder imposed on another (formerly Munchausen by proxy), the immediate priority is the child's safety. As a medical practitioner, you are a mandatory reporter in all Australian states and territories. The nursing observation of injection into the IV line, combined with 8 unexplained admissions, failure to thrive, and rapid resolution with separation, constitutes reasonable grounds for concern. A mandatory report to the relevant state child protection authority should be made immediately. Hospital-level child protection processes should also be activated. (Source: RACP Child Protection Guidelines; RANZCP; State/Territory Mandatory Reporting Legislation)

options.text: Discharge the child and arrange increased community health nurse visits for ongoing monitoring
options.rationale: Discharging a child where there is a reasonable suspicion of factitious disorder imposed on another without protective intervention places the child at ongoing risk. Community monitoring is insufficient when there is an observation of potential direct harm. The child should remain in a safe environment until child protection services assess the situation. (Source: RACP Child Protection Guidelines)

options.text: Order a comprehensive toxicology screen and await results before taking any further action
options.rationale: While a toxicology screen may provide supporting evidence, waiting for results before acting on a reasonable suspicion of harm is inappropriate. Mandatory reporting obligations are triggered by reasonable suspicion, not confirmed diagnosis. The child's safety cannot wait for laboratory results. Investigations and protective action should proceed simultaneously. (Source: RACP Child Protection Guidelines; State Mandatory Reporting Legislation)

explanation.summary: Factitious disorder imposed on another (FDIA) is a form of child abuse where a caregiver fabricates or induces illness in a child. Key warning signs include multiple unexplained admissions, symptoms occurring only in the caregiver's presence, a caregiver with medical knowledge, and failure to thrive. The child's safety is the absolute priority. Australian mandatory reporting laws require medical practitioners to report reasonable suspicions of child abuse to the relevant state or territory authority. The diagnosis is confirmed through the process of child protection investigation, not through medical confrontation.
key_points: Child safety is the absolute first priority in suspected FDIA
Mandatory reporting is triggered by reasonable suspicion, not confirmed diagnosis
Never confront the suspected perpetrator before child protection involvement
FDIA carries a mortality rate of approximately 6-9% in case series
explanation.pearls: A key diagnostic feature of FDIA is that the child's symptoms resolve when separated from the perpetrating caregiver, and recur upon reunification; this pattern of admission resolution should prompt clinicians to review the temporal relationship between symptom episodes and caregiver presence.

stem: A 45-year-old man with schizophrenia is reviewed in his community mental health clinic. He smokes 40 cigarettes per day and has COPD with an FEV1 of 52% predicted. His schizophrenia has been stable on olanzapine 20 mg daily for 2 years with no psychotic symptoms. He is motivated to quit smoking but his GP has declined to prescribe varenicline due to concerns about worsening his psychosis. He has tried NRT patches without success. His treating psychiatrist is now asked to consider prescribing varenicline.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 82, BP 142/88, SpO2 94% on room air
data_table.Examination: Stable mental state, no psychotic symptoms, BMI 34, tar staining fingers, barrel chest, PHQ-9 score 5
data_table.Investigations: Spirometry: FEV1 52% predicted, FEV1/FVC 0.62, olanzapine level therapeutic, FBC normal, LFTs normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate response regarding varenicline prescribing?

options.text: Agree with the GP that varenicline is contraindicated in schizophrenia due to psychosis risk
options.rationale: This is based on outdated safety concerns. The EAGLES trial (2016, 8144 participants including those with stable psychiatric illness) demonstrated no significant increase in neuropsychiatric adverse events with varenicline compared with NRT, bupropion, or placebo in participants with psychiatric diagnoses. The FDA removed the black box warning based on these results. (Source: EAGLES trial; RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines; Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction)

options.text: Prescribe bupropion as it has a better safety profile than varenicline in schizophrenia
options.rationale: Bupropion has lower efficacy than varenicline for smoking cessation and carries a seizure risk that is of concern in patients on antipsychotics, which also lower the seizure threshold. The EAGLES trial showed no safety advantage of bupropion over varenicline in psychiatric populations. Bupropion is not preferred over varenicline in this context. (Source: EAGLES trial; AMH)

options.text: Recommend a nicotine e-cigarette as the safest cessation option for psychiatric patients
options.rationale: E-cigarettes are not a TGA-approved smoking cessation aid and are not recommended as first-line therapy by Australian guidelines. While harm reduction is a valid consideration, evidence-based pharmacotherapy with proven efficacy should be offered first, particularly in a patient with severe COPD where smoking cessation is critical. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines; Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction)

options.text: Advise that smoking cessation is too risky given potential antipsychotic level changes
options.rationale: While smoking cessation affects CYP1A2 metabolism (relevant to clozapine and to a lesser extent olanzapine), this is a manageable pharmacokinetic interaction requiring monitoring, not a reason to deny smoking cessation. Olanzapine is partially metabolised by CYP1A2; levels may rise modestly after quitting but the effect is smaller than with clozapine. The health benefits of cessation far outweigh this manageable risk. (Source: AMH; Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction)

options.text: Prescribe varenicline with standard titration and monitor mental state closely during treatment
options.rationale: Varenicline should be prescribed with standard titration in this patient with stable schizophrenia. The EAGLES trial provides strong evidence for its safety in psychiatric populations. Given severe COPD (FEV1 52%), smoking cessation is a clinical imperative. Olanzapine levels should be monitored as CYP1A2 induction from smoking will decrease after cessation, potentially increasing olanzapine levels. Close mental state monitoring during the quit attempt is good practice but not a barrier to prescribing. (Source: EAGLES trial; RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines; Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction; AMH)

explanation.summary: The EAGLES trial was a landmark safety study that compared varenicline, bupropion, NRT, and placebo in 8144 smokers with and without psychiatric illness. It found no significant increase in neuropsychiatric adverse events with varenicline in either group, leading to removal of the FDA black box warning. Patients with stable psychiatric illness should be offered the most effective cessation therapy available. Monitoring for mental state changes during a quit attempt is good practice regardless of the pharmacotherapy used.
key_points: EAGLES trial confirmed varenicline safety in stable psychiatric illness
Varenicline is the most effective single-agent cessation therapy
CYP1A2 changes after smoking cessation may increase olanzapine levels requiring monitoring
COPD with FEV1 52% makes smoking cessation a clinical imperative
explanation.pearls: Smoking induces CYP1A2 via polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (not nicotine); olanzapine is approximately 30-40% metabolised by CYP1A2, so cessation may increase levels by 20-30%, compared with clozapine's 50-70% increase, requiring therapeutic drug monitoring but not contraindicating cessation.

subtopic_detail: Delusional disorder recognition and initial management
stem: A 54-year-old woman is referred by her GP for psychiatric assessment. She has a fixed belief that her neighbour has been installing surveillance cameras in her home, which she has held for 8 months. She has called the police multiple times but no evidence has been found. She otherwise functions well at work, maintains friendships, and her behaviour is not obviously bizarre apart from issues relating to the belief about her neighbour. She has never experienced auditory hallucinations, thought disorder, or negative symptoms.

data_table.Examination: Well-groomed, cooperative, euthymic affect, fixed non-bizarre delusion of persecution, no hallucinations, no formal thought disorder, no negative symptoms, MMSE 30/30

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Schizophrenia with predominantly positive symptoms and preserved functioning
options.rationale: Schizophrenia requires at least two of: delusions, hallucinations, disorganised speech, disorganised or catatonic behaviour, and negative symptoms, for a significant portion of one month. This patient has only a single isolated delusion without hallucinations, thought disorder, or negative symptoms, and her functioning is preserved. This pattern favours delusional disorder. (Source: RANZCP CPG Schizophrenia; DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Delusional disorder, persecutory type, with preserved psychosocial functioning
options.rationale: Delusional disorder is characterised by one or more non-bizarre delusions lasting at least 1 month, without prominent hallucinations, formal thought disorder, or negative symptoms. Functioning is relatively preserved apart from the impact of the delusion itself. The persecutory subtype involves conviction that one is being conspired against, spied on, or harassed. This patient meets all criteria: fixed persecutory delusion for 8 months, no other psychotic symptoms, preserved functioning. (Source: DSM-5-TR; RANZCP CPG Schizophrenia)

options.text: Brief psychotic disorder with a persecutory delusion as the sole symptom feature
options.rationale: Brief psychotic disorder by definition lasts at least 1 day but less than 1 month, with full return to premorbid functioning. This patient's symptoms have persisted for 8 months, well beyond the 1-month threshold. The chronicity points to delusional disorder. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Paranoid personality disorder with transient stress-related paranoid ideation
options.rationale: Paranoid personality disorder involves pervasive distrust and suspiciousness but the beliefs are typically overvalued ideas rather than fixed delusions. This patient has a fixed false belief that surveillance equipment has been installed, which is a frank delusion rather than personality-level suspiciousness. Additionally, the delusion is focused and specific rather than pervasive. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Late-onset schizophrenia given her age and isolated persecutory content
options.rationale: While late-onset schizophrenia (after age 40) can present with prominent persecutory delusions, it still requires the presence of at least two criterion A symptoms and is typically accompanied by auditory hallucinations. An isolated delusion without hallucinations or other psychotic features in a well-functioning individual is better classified as delusional disorder regardless of age of onset. (Source: RANZCP CPG Schizophrenia; DSM-5-TR)

explanation.summary: Delusional disorder is characterised by the presence of one or more non-bizarre delusions persisting for at least 1 month, in the absence of other prominent psychotic symptoms. Functioning is generally preserved except where directly related to the delusion. Subtypes include persecutory, jealous, erotomanic, grandiose, somatic, and mixed. Treatment involves antipsychotic medication (often low-dose) combined with CBT for psychosis, though engagement can be challenging as patients often lack insight. Prognosis is better than schizophrenia with many patients maintaining employment and social relationships.
key_points: Delusional disorder requires delusions lasting at least 1 month without other prominent psychotic symptoms
Functioning is relatively preserved apart from the direct impact of the delusion
Non-bizarre delusions involve situations that could theoretically occur in real life
Persecutory subtype is the most common form of delusional disorder
Treatment combines low-dose antipsychotic with CBT for psychosis
explanation.pearls: Delusional disorder has a lifetime prevalence of approximately 0.2% and typically presents in middle to late adulthood - the persecutory subtype accounts for approximately 50% of cases and can be distinguished from paranoid personality disorder by the presence of fixed false beliefs rather than pervasive suspiciousness.

subtopic_detail: Brief psychotic disorder recognition and recovery expectations
stem: A 26-year-old woman with no prior psychiatric history is brought to the emergency department by her family. Three days ago she experienced an acute onset of persecutory delusions, auditory hallucinations, and disorganised speech following the sudden death of her mother. She has not slept in 3 days. Prior to this event she was functioning normally with no prodromal symptoms.

data_table.Examination: Agitated, disorganised speech with loose associations, persecutory delusions (believes hospital staff are poisoning her), auditory hallucinations (third-person commentary), no substance use on UDS, normal physical examination and bloods
data_table.Investigations: UDS negative, TFTs normal, FBC and UEC normal, CT brain normal

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis and the expected clinical course?

options.text: First-episode schizophrenia - expect chronic relapsing course requiring long-term antipsychotic therapy
options.rationale: While this presentation includes multiple criterion A symptoms of schizophrenia, the duration of only 3 days is too short for a schizophrenia diagnosis, which requires symptoms for at least 1 month (with at least 6 months of disturbance). The acute onset following a clear psychosocial stressor and absence of prodromal symptoms favour brief psychotic disorder. (Source: DSM-5-TR; RANZCP CPG Schizophrenia)

options.text: Acute stress disorder with psychotic features - treat with trauma-focused therapy alone
options.rationale: Acute stress disorder presents with dissociative, intrusive, avoidance, and arousal symptoms following trauma, but frank psychotic symptoms (delusions, hallucinations, formal thought disorder) are not part of the ASD diagnostic criteria. The presence of hallucinations and disorganised speech indicates a primary psychotic disorder. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Brief psychotic disorder with marked stressor - expect full remission within 1 month of onset
options.rationale: Brief psychotic disorder is characterised by sudden onset of at least one psychotic symptom (delusions, hallucinations, disorganised speech, or grossly disorganised behaviour) lasting between 1 day and 1 month, with eventual full return to premorbid functioning. The specifier 'with marked stressor' applies when onset closely follows a significant psychosocial stressor. Short-term antipsychotic treatment is typically required during the acute episode, but the prognosis is good with expected full recovery. (Source: DSM-5-TR; RANZCP CPG Schizophrenia)

options.text: Schizophreniform disorder - expect resolution within 6 months with uncertain long-term prognosis
options.rationale: Schizophreniform disorder requires symptom duration of at least 1 month but less than 6 months. At only 3 days, the duration is too short for schizophreniform disorder. If symptoms persist beyond 1 month, the diagnosis would be revised. The acute onset with clear stressor and no prodrome makes brief psychotic disorder more likely. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Dissociative identity disorder presenting with hallucination-like experiences and identity disruption
options.rationale: Dissociative identity disorder involves disruption of identity with two or more distinct personality states and recurrent gaps in recall. While it can include hallucination-like experiences, the formal thought disorder, persecutory delusions, and acute presentation with clear stressor are more consistent with a primary psychotic disorder. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

explanation.summary: Brief psychotic disorder is a time-limited psychotic episode lasting 1 day to 1 month with full return to premorbid functioning. It can occur with or without a marked stressor. The acute onset, often in response to severe psychosocial stress, and the absence of prodromal symptoms distinguish it from schizophrenia spectrum disorders. Treatment involves short-term low-dose antipsychotic medication for symptom control, with benzodiazepines for agitation and insomnia. Most patients recover fully, though approximately 20% may eventually meet criteria for a longer-duration psychotic disorder on follow-up.
key_points: Duration is 1 day to 1 month with full return to premorbid function
Can be specified as with or without a marked stressor
Short-term antipsychotic treatment is typically sufficient
Approximately 80% of patients recover fully without recurrence
If symptoms persist beyond 1 month the diagnosis is revised to schizophreniform disorder
explanation.pearls: Approximately 20% of patients initially diagnosed with brief psychotic disorder are eventually rediagnosed with schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder on longitudinal follow-up - good prognostic features include acute onset, identifiable psychosocial stressor, preserved premorbid functioning, and absence of flat affect.

subtopic_detail: Schizophreniform disorder management and prognostic features
stem: A 22-year-old male university student is brought by his parents for psychiatric review. Over the past 3 months he has developed persecutory delusions that his lecturers are conspiring against him, auditory hallucinations of derogatory voices, and social withdrawal. His academic performance has declined markedly. He had no psychiatric symptoms before this episode and had been performing well academically. There is no substance use history. Physical examination and investigations are normal.

data_table.Examination: Flat affect, guarded, persecutory delusions (believes lecturers are sabotaging his grades), auditory hallucinations (second-person derogatory), social withdrawal for 3 months, no insight into illness
data_table.Investigations: UDS negative, TFTs normal, FBC and UEC normal, MRI brain normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate diagnosis and management approach at this stage?

options.text: First-episode schizophrenia - commence antipsychotic with plan for indefinite treatment
options.rationale: Schizophrenia requires at least 6 months of disturbance, including at least 1 month of active-phase symptoms. At 3 months, this patient meets duration criteria for schizophreniform disorder but not yet schizophrenia. Presumptively diagnosing schizophrenia and committing to indefinite treatment is premature. (Source: DSM-5-TR; RANZCP CPG Schizophrenia)

options.text: Brief psychotic disorder - expect spontaneous resolution and avoid antipsychotic medication
options.rationale: Brief psychotic disorder requires symptoms lasting less than 1 month. This patient has had symptoms for 3 months, exceeding the 1-month limit. Additionally, the presence of negative symptoms (flat affect, social withdrawal) and the duration make this diagnosis inappropriate. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Delusional disorder with comorbid depression causing the functional decline and psychotic features
options.rationale: Delusional disorder requires absence of other prominent psychotic symptoms beyond the delusion itself. This patient has auditory hallucinations, flat affect, and social withdrawal in addition to delusions, which goes beyond the isolated delusion pattern of delusional disorder. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Schizophreniform disorder - commence antipsychotic and reassess diagnosis at 6 months
options.rationale: Schizophreniform disorder is diagnosed when the full criteria for schizophrenia are met (at least two criterion A symptoms for at least 1 month) but the total duration of illness is less than 6 months. Treatment involves antipsychotic medication similar to first-episode schizophrenia. The diagnosis should be reviewed at 6 months: if symptoms persist, the diagnosis is changed to schizophrenia; if remission occurs, schizophreniform disorder is confirmed. Approximately 60% of patients with schizophreniform disorder eventually meet criteria for schizophrenia. (Source: DSM-5-TR; RANZCP CPG Schizophrenia)

options.text: Substance-induced psychotic disorder despite negative drug screen, requiring repeat testing
options.rationale: The urine drug screen is negative and there is no substance use history. A 3-month course of symptoms with progressive negative symptoms and functional decline is not consistent with substance-induced psychosis, which typically resolves within weeks of cessation. Repeat testing without clinical indication is not warranted. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

explanation.summary: Schizophreniform disorder occupies a diagnostic space between brief psychotic disorder and schizophrenia, with a duration of at least 1 month but less than 6 months. It requires at least two criterion A schizophrenia symptoms. Treatment mirrors first-episode schizophrenia with low-dose second-generation antipsychotic medication and psychosocial support. The diagnosis is provisional and should be reviewed at 6 months. Good prognostic features include acute onset, confusion at the height of the psychotic episode, good premorbid functioning, and absence of blunted affect.
key_points: Schizophreniform disorder lasts at least 1 month but less than 6 months
Requires the same criterion A symptoms as schizophrenia
Approximately 60% of cases eventually progress to a schizophrenia diagnosis
Good prognostic features include acute onset and preserved premorbid functioning
Treatment is similar to first-episode schizophrenia with planned diagnostic review at 6 months
explanation.pearls: The provisional specifier in schizophreniform disorder allows clinicians to initiate appropriate treatment without prematurely committing to a schizophrenia diagnosis - the 6-month reassessment point is the key decision node where approximately 40% achieve full remission and 60% transition to schizophrenia.

subtopic_detail: Schizoaffective depressive type vs MDD with psychotic features discrimination
stem: A 36-year-old woman has a 7-year psychiatric history with multiple hospitalisations. During her first admission she presented with persecutory delusions and auditory hallucinations for 3 months without any mood symptoms, which resolved with risperidone. Since then she has had three major depressive episodes, each lasting 2 to 4 months, during which her psychotic symptoms returned alongside severe depressed mood, anhedonia, and suicidal ideation. Between mood episodes she continues to experience intermittent auditory hallucinations and paranoid ideation despite euthymic mood.

data_table.Current presentation: Depressed mood for 6 weeks with psychotic symptoms, PHQ-9 22, continues to hear derogatory voices outside of mood episodes
data_table.Medications: Risperidone 4 mg daily, sertraline 150 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most accurate diagnosis based on the longitudinal course?

options.text: Major depressive disorder with psychotic features and inter-episode residual symptoms
options.rationale: In MDD with psychotic features, psychotic symptoms occur exclusively during depressive episodes and resolve with mood recovery. This patient has psychotic symptoms (hallucinations and paranoia) that persist during euthymic periods between mood episodes, which is inconsistent with MDD with psychotic features and points to schizoaffective disorder. (Source: DSM-5-TR; RANZCP CPG Schizophrenia)

options.text: Schizophrenia with comorbid recurrent major depressive disorder as a separate diagnosis
options.rationale: While this patient has persistent psychotic symptoms, the mood episodes are prominent, prolonged (2 to 4 months each), and constitute a major proportion of the total illness duration. Schizoaffective disorder is the appropriate diagnosis when major mood episodes are present for a majority of the total illness duration in the setting of persistent psychotic symptoms. Schizophrenia with comorbid MDD would be considered only if mood symptoms were brief relative to psychosis. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Bipolar I disorder with psychotic features occurring during depressive episodes only
options.rationale: Bipolar I disorder requires at least one manic episode. This patient has had depressive episodes only, with no history of mania or hypomania. Additionally, bipolar disorder with psychotic features would not explain the persistent psychotic symptoms during euthymic periods. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Recurrent brief psychotic disorder occurring alongside major depressive episodes
options.rationale: Brief psychotic disorder episodes last less than 1 month and result in full return to premorbid functioning. This patient has persistent psychotic symptoms between mood episodes, which is not consistent with brief psychotic disorder. The longitudinal course requires a single integrated diagnosis. (Source: DSM-5-TR)
