While many patients with BPD have trauma histories, the core treatment targets in BPD (emotional dysregulation, self-harm, interpersonal dysfunction) require BPD-specific therapies. Trauma processing may be integrated later within a DBT or schema therapy framework. (Source: NHMRC BPD Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Dialectical behaviour therapy is the gold-standard psychotherapy for BPD, with the strongest evidence for reducing self-harm, suicidal behaviour, ED presentations, and improving emotional regulation. Standard DBT comprises four components: individual therapy (weekly), skills group (weekly), phone coaching (between sessions), and therapist consultation team. Other evidence-based therapies include mentalisation-based therapy (MBT), schema therapy, and transference-focused psychotherapy. Pharmacotherapy has a limited role in BPD and is not first-line.
key_points: DBT is first-line psychotherapy for BPD with self-harm
Standard DBT has four components: individual, skills group, phone coaching, therapist team
Treatment duration is typically 12 months
Pharmacotherapy has limited evidence in BPD and is not first-line
explanation.pearls: DBT's four skills modules (mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation, interpersonal effectiveness) target distinct BPD features - distress tolerance specifically addresses the 'action urge' that drives self-harm by teaching crisis survival strategies as alternatives to self-injury.

subtopic_detail: ECT cognitive side effects and electrode placement
stem: A 62-year-old man with severe treatment-resistant depression is being considered for electroconvulsive therapy. He has failed adequate trials of sertraline, venlafaxine, and lithium augmentation. He is currently experiencing psychomotor retardation, anhedonia, and passive suicidal ideation. He is a retired accountant who is concerned about cognitive side effects, particularly memory impairment, as he is writing his memoirs. He has no contraindications to anaesthesia.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate counselling regarding electrode placement and cognitive effects?

options.text: Bilateral ECT is the only effective placement with no memory loss
options.rationale: While bilateral (bitemporal) ECT may have slightly higher efficacy, it is associated with greater cognitive side effects, particularly retrograde amnesia and anterograde memory impairment, compared to right unilateral (RUL) ECT. Stating that it causes no memory impairment is inaccurate. (Source: RANZCP ECT Position Statement; NICE ECT Guideline)

options.text: RUL brief-pulse ECT has equivalent efficacy with less cognitive impact
options.rationale: Standard brief-pulse RUL ECT has lower efficacy than bilateral ECT. However, RUL with ultra-brief pulse width at adequate suprathreshold dosing approaches bilateral efficacy while significantly reducing cognitive side effects. The pulse width distinction is important. (Source: RANZCP ECT Position Statement)

options.text: All cognitive effects are permanent and he should weigh this carefully
options.rationale: Most cognitive effects of ECT are transient. Anterograde memory impairment typically resolves within weeks to months of completing treatment. Some retrograde amnesia (particularly for events around the treatment period) may persist, but widespread permanent cognitive impairment is not typical. (Source: RANZCP ECT Position Statement; NICE ECT Guideline)

options.text: TMS would be equally effective and should be tried first before ECT
options.rationale: TMS has evidence for treatment-resistant depression but has lower efficacy than ECT, particularly for severe or psychotic depression. In a patient with severe TRD with psychomotor retardation and suicidal ideation who has failed multiple adequate trials, ECT is the more appropriate intervention. TMS may be considered for less severe presentations. (Source: RANZCP; NICE Depression Guideline)

options.text: Ultra-brief pulse RUL ECT offers good efficacy with less cognitive impact
options.rationale: Right unilateral ECT with ultra-brief pulse width (0.3 ms vs standard 0.5-1.0 ms), delivered at 5-6 times seizure threshold, approaches bilateral efficacy while producing significantly less cognitive impairment. Anterograde memory effects typically resolve within weeks. Some retrograde amnesia for the treatment period may persist, but autobiographical memory is generally preserved. This is the most accurate and balanced counselling. (Source: RANZCP ECT Position Statement; NICE ECT Guideline)

explanation.summary: ECT remains the most effective treatment for severe, treatment-resistant depression, with response rates of 50-70%. The choice between right unilateral (RUL) and bilateral (BT) electrode placement involves a trade-off between efficacy and cognitive effects. Ultra-brief pulse RUL ECT (0.3 ms pulse width) at adequate suprathreshold dosing offers a favourable balance. Most cognitive effects are transient. Informed consent should include discussion of expected memory effects, their typical duration, and the option to switch placement if response is inadequate.
key_points: Ultra-brief pulse RUL ECT reduces cognitive effects while maintaining efficacy
Most anterograde memory impairment resolves within weeks to months
Bilateral ECT may be more effective but has greater cognitive impact
Some retrograde amnesia for the treatment period may persist
explanation.pearls: Ultra-brief pulse width (0.3 ms) compared to standard brief pulse (0.5-1.0 ms) reduces the charge delivered per seizure by approximately 50% - this narrower pulse selectively activates neural membranes with less indiscriminate depolarisation, which is the proposed mechanism for reduced cognitive side effects.

stem: An 18-year-old woman with anorexia nervosa is admitted to a medical ward. Her BMI is 13.8 kg/m2. She has been restricting intake to less than 500 kcal/day for the past 3 months. On examination, she is bradycardic, hypotensive, and hypothermic. Her sit-to-stand test shows a heart rate rise from 52 to 96 bpm. Blood tests reveal phosphate 0.62 mmol/L, potassium 3.0 mmol/L, and magnesium 0.58 mmol/L.

data_table.Investigations: BMI 13.8, Phosphate 0.62 mmol/L, K 3.0 mmol/L, Mg 0.58 mmol/L, Na 137, glucose 3.4 mmol/L, sit-stand HR rise 52 to 96

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial nutritional management strategy?

options.text: Commence nasogastric feeding at 2000 kcal/day to restore weight
options.rationale: Commencing at 2000 kcal/day in a severely malnourished patient (BMI 13.8, prolonged starvation) carries extreme risk of refeeding syndrome. Refeeding syndrome causes rapid intracellular shifts of phosphate, potassium, and magnesium, potentially fatal cardiac arrhythmias, and fluid overload. Initial refeeding must start at a very low rate. (Source: MARSIPAN Guidelines; NICE Eating Disorders Guideline)

options.text: Correct electrolytes only and defer feeding until she is stable
options.rationale: While electrolyte correction is essential, deferring refeeding entirely is dangerous. Patients with severe anorexia are catabolic with depleted glycogen stores and may develop life-threatening hypoglycaemia if feeding is further delayed. Electrolyte replacement and cautious refeeding should commence simultaneously. (Source: MARSIPAN Guidelines)

options.text: Total parenteral nutrition to bypass the gastrointestinal tract
options.rationale: TPN carries its own risks (line sepsis, metabolic complications) and does not eliminate refeeding syndrome risk. The enteral route is preferred whenever possible. TPN is reserved for patients with genuine inability to use the GI tract. Cautious oral or nasogastric refeeding is appropriate. (Source: MARSIPAN Guidelines)

options.text: Start 10-15 kcal/kg/day with electrolyte supplementation and monitoring
options.rationale: For patients at extreme refeeding risk (BMI below 14, negligible intake, electrolyte derangement), MARSIPAN recommends starting nutrition at 10-15 kcal/kg/day (approximately 500-750 kcal for this patient). Pre-emptive phosphate, potassium, and magnesium supplementation is essential. Thiamine 200-300 mg daily should be given before and during refeeding. Continuous cardiac monitoring is required due to the risk of arrhythmias. Caloric intake is increased gradually over 5-7 days. (Source: MARSIPAN Guidelines; NICE Eating Disorders Guideline; RANZCP)

options.text: Start refeeding at 20 kcal/kg/day with daily electrolyte monitoring
options.rationale: 20 kcal/kg/day (approximately 1000 kcal) is the starting rate for moderate refeeding risk. This patient is at extreme risk (BMI 13.8, prolonged starvation, existing electrolyte derangement, cardiovascular instability). A lower starting rate of 10-15 kcal/kg/day is recommended with more frequent electrolyte monitoring (twice daily initially). (Source: MARSIPAN Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Refeeding syndrome is a potentially fatal metabolic complication of nutritional rehabilitation in severely malnourished patients. It results from rapid intracellular shifts of phosphate, potassium, and magnesium driven by insulin release during carbohydrate reintroduction. The MARSIPAN guidelines stratify refeeding risk and recommend starting at 10-15 kcal/kg/day for extreme-risk patients (BMI <14, negligible intake, baseline electrolyte derangement). Pre-emptive supplementation, thiamine, and cardiac monitoring are essential. Caloric intake is increased gradually.
key_points: Extreme refeeding risk: start 10-15 kcal/kg/day
Pre-emptive phosphate, potassium, and magnesium supplementation
Thiamine 200-300 mg daily before and during refeeding
Continuous cardiac monitoring for arrhythmia risk
explanation.pearls: The hallmark of refeeding syndrome is a precipitous drop in serum phosphate within 24-72 hours of nutritional reintroduction - phosphate below 0.32 mmol/L is a medical emergency requiring IV replacement, as it causes ATP depletion affecting cardiac and respiratory muscle function.

stem: A 48-year-old man is referred by his GP for management of delusional disorder, persecutory type, diagnosed 2 years ago. He has the fixed belief that his neighbours are surveilling him through hidden cameras and contaminating his water supply. He has no hallucinations, thought disorder, or negative symptoms. His functioning is preserved in all domains except his relationship with neighbours, which has deteriorated. He has been trialled on risperidone 4 mg daily for 8 weeks with no improvement in his delusions, though he has been adherent.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Increase risperidone to 8 mg daily as higher dose may be needed
options.rationale: Increasing risperidone beyond 6 mg daily generally does not improve efficacy but significantly increases side effects, particularly EPS and hyperprolactinaemia. If a standard dose of an antipsychotic has not been effective, switching to a different antipsychotic is more appropriate than dose escalation. (Source: RANZCP CPG for Schizophrenia; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Add an SSRI to the antipsychotic as combination therapy trial
options.rationale: Adding an SSRI is not evidence-based for delusional disorder. SSRIs are used when comorbid depression or anxiety is present but do not treat delusions. The priority is optimising antipsychotic management. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Switch antipsychotic and combine with CBT for psychosis treatment
options.rationale: Delusional disorder is notoriously treatment-resistant, with only 30-50% partial response to antipsychotics. Switching to a different antipsychotic (e.g. olanzapine or amisulpride) is reasonable after failure of an adequate first trial. CBT for psychosis (CBTp) has evidence for reducing distress associated with delusions and improving functioning, even when delusions persist. The combination approach addresses both pharmacological and psychological dimensions. (Source: RANZCP CPG for Schizophrenia; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; NICE Psychosis Guideline)

options.text: Commence clozapine for treatment-resistant psychotic presentation
options.rationale: Clozapine is indicated for treatment-resistant schizophrenia after failure of two adequate antipsychotic trials. This patient has only failed one trial and does not have schizophrenia. The evidence for clozapine in delusional disorder is limited. A second antipsychotic trial should be attempted before considering clozapine. (Source: RANZCP CPG for Schizophrenia; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Cease antipsychotic as delusional disorder is medication-resistant
options.rationale: While delusional disorder has lower response rates than schizophrenia, approximately 30-50% of patients achieve partial response. Ceasing treatment after one failed trial is premature. A trial of a different antipsychotic is warranted. Additionally, antipsychotics may reduce the distress and preoccupation associated with delusions even when the delusional content persists. (Source: RANZCP CPG for Schizophrenia)

explanation.summary: Delusional disorder has a lower antipsychotic response rate (30-50% partial response) compared to schizophrenia (70-80%). Management requires a multimodal approach combining antipsychotic therapy with psychological interventions. CBTp can reduce delusional distress and improve functioning even when delusions persist. The therapeutic relationship is particularly important as patients with delusional disorder often have limited insight. Second-generation antipsychotics are preferred due to the better side-effect profile for this population that often requires long-term treatment.
key_points: Delusional disorder response rate to antipsychotics is only 30-50%
Switch antipsychotic before considering clozapine (need 2 failed trials)
CBTp reduces distress and improves functioning alongside medication
Therapeutic relationship and rapport are crucial for engagement
explanation.pearls: CBT for psychosis (CBTp) in delusional disorder targets the distress and behavioural impact of delusions rather than the belief itself - reducing the emotional salience and occupying nature of the delusion can significantly improve functioning even when the delusional content remains unchanged.

stem: A 32-year-old man is newly diagnosed with ADHD, combined presentation, after comprehensive neuropsychological assessment. He works as a delivery driver and holds a commercial vehicle licence. He is commenced on methylphenidate modified-release 18 mg daily. At his 4-week review, he reports improved concentration and reduced impulsivity. He asks about the implications for his driving licence and whether he needs to notify the road transport authority.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice regarding his driving licence?

options.text: Notification to the road transport authority required for commercial licence
options.rationale: Under Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive guidelines, ADHD that may impair driving (particularly with a commercial licence) should be assessed regarding fitness to drive. Stimulant medication use must be declared for commercial licence holders. The patient should notify the relevant state authority and provide a medical report confirming that the condition is well-controlled on treatment. Private licence holders with well-controlled ADHD on stable medication may not need to notify, but commercial licence holders have stricter requirements. (Source: Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive; State Road Transport Authority guidelines)

options.text: No notification required as ADHD does not affect driving ability
options.rationale: ADHD significantly affects driving performance, with studies showing increased crash risk. Inattention, impulsivity, and risk-taking behaviours all impair driving safety. The Austroads guidelines specifically address ADHD as a condition that may affect fitness to drive, particularly for commercial licence holders. (Source: Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive)

options.text: He must cease driving immediately and permanently lose his licence
options.rationale: ADHD does not require permanent driving cessation. When effectively treated with medication and the patient demonstrates adequate symptom control, driving (including commercially) can continue. The Austroads guidelines provide a framework for conditional licences with periodic medical review. (Source: Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive)

options.text: Stimulant medication is incompatible with any driving licence at all
options.rationale: Prescribed stimulant medication at therapeutic doses is not a barrier to driving. In fact, treated ADHD has better driving outcomes than untreated ADHD. The concern is about the condition itself affecting driving fitness, not the therapeutic medication. However, recreational stimulant use or abuse would be a concern. (Source: Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive)

options.text: Only notify if he has had a motor vehicle accident in the past year
options.rationale: The obligation to notify is based on having a medical condition that may affect driving fitness, not contingent on having had an accident. Proactive notification and fitness assessment are required for commercial licence holders with conditions that may impair driving. Waiting for an accident to occur is not an acceptable approach. (Source: Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive)

explanation.summary: ADHD is associated with a 1.5-2 fold increase in motor vehicle accident risk due to inattention, impulsivity, and risk-taking. Treatment with stimulant medication significantly reduces this risk. Under Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive guidelines, conditions that may impair driving require assessment. Commercial licence holders have stricter obligations and must declare medical conditions and medications. A conditional licence with periodic review is the typical outcome for well-treated ADHD. The treating doctor has a duty to advise the patient about notification obligations.
key_points: ADHD increases motor vehicle accident risk 1.5-2 fold
Stimulant medication reduces driving risk - treated ADHD drives better than untreated
Commercial licence holders must notify the road transport authority
Conditional licence with periodic medical review is typical for well-treated ADHD
explanation.pearls: Methylphenidate reduces the crash risk in ADHD drivers by approximately 40% on medicated versus unmedicated days (Lancet Psychiatry 2017 Swedish register study) - this is one of the strongest arguments for pharmacological treatment in adults with ADHD who drive.

subtopic_detail: ADHD adult diagnosis and stimulant initiation
stem:
A 28-year-old graphic designer is referred to a community psychiatrist with 12 years of inattention, procrastination and disorganisation. She has just been retrenched after losing her third role for missed deadlines. She meets DSM-5 criteria for adult ADHD with childhood symptoms documented in school reports. She has no cardiovascular history, BP 124/76, ECG sinus rhythm with QTc 410 ms. She is not pregnant and uses condoms reliably.

She drives daily for work and to a child-care centre. She has a remote history of cocaine use in her early 20s, with no substance use for 5 years. Her younger brother takes methylphenidate.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 76, BP 124/76, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7 degrees C, BMI 23
data_table.Examination: Engaged, eye contact good, no extrapyramidal features, no thyroid enlargement
data_table.Investigations: FBC, U&E, LFTs, TFTs normal; urine drug screen negative; ECG sinus rhythm QTc 410 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological choice?

options.text: Commence bupropion 150 mg daily as a stimulant-sparing strategy
options.rationale: Bupropion has limited evidence in adult ADHD; it is not a first-line agent in Australian guidelines and not PBS-listed for ADHD. (Source: RANZCP ADHD Practice Guidelines)

options.text: Commence atomoxetine 40 mg daily and titrate to 80 mg over 2 weeks
options.rationale: Atomoxetine is non-stimulant alternative with slower onset and lower response rate; reserved for stimulant contraindication or comorbid anxiety with stimulant intolerance. (Source: RANZCP ADHD Practice Guidelines)

options.text: Commence immediate-release dexamfetamine 5 mg three times daily
options.rationale: Immediate-release formulations carry higher diversion and misuse potential than long-acting pro-drugs, especially in patients with past stimulant misuse; long-acting formulations are preferred. (Source: RANZCP ADHD Practice Guidelines; AMH Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence cognitive behavioural therapy only and review in 8 weeks
options.rationale: Although CBT for adult ADHD adds skills training and is recommended as adjunct, evidence supports stimulant pharmacotherapy as core treatment for moderate to severe adult ADHD. (Source: RANZCP ADHD Practice Guidelines)

options.text: Commence lisdexamfetamine 30 mg mornings, advise driving disclosure obligations
options.rationale: Lisdexamfetamine is first-line in Australian adult ADHD; her past stimulant misuse is in sustained remission and a long-acting pro-drug carries lower diversion and misuse potential than immediate-release formulations. Driving disclosure under Austroads guidelines is mandatory. (Source: RANZCP ADHD Practice Guidelines; AMH Psychotropic; Austroads 2022)

explanation.summary: Adult ADHD treatment in Australia uses long-acting stimulants (lisdexamfetamine, methylphenidate-MR) as first-line, with non-stimulants (atomoxetine, guanfacine-XR) for stimulant contraindications or non-response. Baseline assessment includes cardiovascular history, BP, ECG (especially QTc), substance use history and driving. Schedule 8 prescribing requires state authority and individual prescriber accreditation in most jurisdictions. Driving disclosure under Austroads is mandatory because stimulants can affect concentration and reaction time during titration. Monitor BP, weight and sleep at 4-weekly visits initially. Past sustained-remission substance use is not an absolute contraindication; choose long-acting pro-drug formulations to reduce diversion.
key_points: First-line: lisdexamfetamine or methylphenidate-MR (long-acting)
Non-stimulants: atomoxetine, guanfacine-XR
Schedule 8 - state authority required
Cardiovascular and QTc screen before starting
Austroads driving disclosure mandatory
explanation.pearls: Lisdexamfetamine 30 mg mornings is the standard adult starting dose - titrate to clinical response monitoring BP, weight and sleep; lower diversion risk than immediate-release dexamfetamine.

stem: A 32-year-old female teacher presents to a community psychiatry clinic at her partner's suggestion after 8 weeks of escalating exhaustion, social withdrawal and meltdowns at home after work. She has been treated by a GP for generalised anxiety disorder and recurrent depression since age 19 with multiple SSRI trials of partial benefit. She describes feeling 'always overwhelmed by sensory input' (lights, noise, clothing tags), having intense interests in classical opera and tortoises, and rehearses social scripts before meetings. She has had two long-term partners and one close friend since childhood. Her younger brother has a confirmed autism diagnosis.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78, BP 118/72, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Engaged eye contact (described as effortful), no thought disorder, mood mildly low, no psychotic features, no acute risk
data_table.Investigations: FBC, U&E, LFTs, TFTs normal; PHQ-9 score 14, GAD-7 score 16

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for borderline personality disorder evaluation given mood lability
options.rationale: Sensory overwhelm, special interests and social rehearsal point to autism not BPD; misdiagnosis as BPD is well-described in autistic women and delays appropriate support. (Source: AU National Autism Guideline)

options.text: Increase SSRI to high-dose sertraline 200 mg and continue management
options.rationale: Pharmacological escalation without considering underlying autism risks ongoing burnout and missed diagnosis; female autistic adults are frequently treated for anxiety/depression rather than the autism. (Source: AU National Autism Guideline)

options.text: Refer for structured ADOS-2 and ADI-R adult assessment with autism specialist
options.rationale: Female presentations of autism are commonly missed because of social masking; structured tools (ADOS-2, ADI-R) and clinicians experienced in adult and female autism are the recommended pathway when DSM-5 criteria appear met. (Source: Australian National Guideline for Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Adults)

options.text: Recommend 6 months of cognitive behavioural therapy before further assessment
options.rationale: Generic CBT without recognition of autism context risks reinforcing masking and worsening burnout; adapted approaches are preferred after assessment. (Source: AU National Autism Guideline)

options.text: Discuss antipsychotic augmentation with low-dose aripiprazole therapy
options.rationale: Antipsychotics are not indicated for adult autism diagnosis or core features; they are reserved for severe comorbid irritability or psychotic features. (Source: AU National Autism Guideline)

explanation.summary: Adult autism diagnosis, particularly in women and gender-diverse adults, requires structured assessment by clinicians experienced in adult presentations. The Australian National Guideline (Autism CRC) endorses ADOS-2 and ADI-R alongside developmental history and observation. Female masking - active suppression of autistic traits to fit social norms - leads to delayed diagnosis (median age 30s), misdiagnosis as anxiety, depression or borderline personality disorder, and chronic exhaustion or 'autistic burnout'. Diagnosis enables identity recognition, reasonable adjustments, NDIS eligibility for those significantly impaired, and adapted therapies. Co-occurring ADHD, anxiety, depression and chronic pain are common.
key_points: Adult diagnosis via ADOS-2 + ADI-R + developmental history
Female masking causes delayed and missed diagnosis
Common misdiagnoses: anxiety, depression, BPD
Diagnosis enables NDIS eligibility (when functional impairment present)
Adapted therapies preferred over generic CBT
explanation.pearls: Sensory overwhelm + special interests + social rehearsal in a woman with 'treatment-resistant' anxiety and depression is autism until structured assessment proves otherwise.

subtopic_detail: GHB intoxication: airway and avoiding flumazenil
stem:
A 24-year-old man is brought to a metropolitan ED by ambulance at 0330 from a nightclub. He was found unresponsive in the bathroom. His friends report he had been drinking heavily and had taken something they called 'G'. On arrival he is deeply sedated, with shallow breathing, snoring respirations and no response to voice. He has a strong gag reflex when suctioned.

There is no evidence of opioid use on examination (pupils 3 mm). Naloxone 0.4 mg IV produced no response 5 minutes ago. IV access is patent.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 62, BP 108/64, RR 8, SpO2 91% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C, GCS 6 (E1 V1 M4)
data_table.Examination: Snoring respirations, gag reflex present, pupils 3 mm equal reactive, no needle marks, no head injury signs
data_table.Investigations: VBG: pH 7.31, pCO2 56 mmHg, lactate 1.6 mmol/L, glucose 5.8 mmol/L, ethanol 0.18 g/dL

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Proceed directly to rapid sequence intubation and ventilation now
options.rationale: Intubation is reserved for failure of supportive airway management, persistent hypoxia or absent gag; he has a gag and is responsive to suction, so supportive management is appropriate first. (Source: Poisons Information Centre - GHB)

options.text: Administer IV flumazenil 0.2 mg as a benzodiazepine reversal agent
options.rationale: Flumazenil does not reverse GHB and risks precipitating seizures in coingestion of benzodiazepines or in chronic users; supportive care is preferred. (Source: Poisons Information Centre - GHB)

options.text: Administer repeat IV naloxone 2 mg and admit for opioid withdrawal
options.rationale: Pupils are mid-size and there has been no opioid response; further naloxone is unlikely to help and signs do not suggest opioids. (Source: Poisons Information Centre - GHB)

options.text: Recovery position and supportive airway care with continuous capnography
options.rationale: GHB intoxication causes deep but typically brief sedation that resolves over 2 to 6 hours; supportive airway management with capnography and avoiding intubation when feasible is the standard approach. (Source: Poisons Information Centre - GHB; eTG Toxicology)

options.text: Activated charcoal 50 g via nasogastric tube to bind ingested toxin
options.rationale: Activated charcoal in a deeply sedated patient without a protected airway risks aspiration; GHB is rapidly absorbed and charcoal has limited utility beyond 1 hour. (Source: Poisons Information Centre - GHB)

explanation.summary: GHB (gamma-hydroxybutyrate) and its precursors GBL and 1,4-butanediol cause GABA-B receptor mediated sedation, with characteristic brief deep coma (often 2 to 6 hours) followed by rapid recovery and combativeness. The therapeutic-to-toxic dose ratio is narrow. Coingestion with alcohol, ketamine or benzodiazepines markedly increases respiratory depression. There is no antidote. Management is airway support with simple manoeuvres, side positioning, suction and capnography. Intubation is reserved for failed supportive care. Withdrawal from chronic GHB use is severe (similar to alcohol withdrawal) and may require benzodiazepine treatment.
key_points: GHB: brief deep coma 2 to 6 hours then rapid recovery
No antidote - supportive care only
Avoid flumazenil and naloxone unless coingestion likely
Coingestion (alcohol, ketamine, benzos) markedly worsens depression
Chronic users may develop severe withdrawal needing inpatient treatment
explanation.pearls: GHB intoxication typically produces patients who wake up suddenly and walk out - keep them in a monitored bed until they are fully alert, and do not give flumazenil even if benzodiazepine coingestion is suspected because of seizure risk.

stem: A 56-year-old man is reviewed in cardiac rehabilitation 4 weeks after an uncomplicated anterior NSTEMI managed with primary PCI. He has smoked 25 cigarettes a day for 35 years. He has tried unassisted cessation twice in his 40s but relapsed within 2 months. He has no history of depression, suicidal ideation, or psychiatric disease. He is taking aspirin, ticagrelor, atorvastatin, perindopril and bisoprolol. He says he is highly motivated to quit and asks for the most effective pharmacotherapy.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 64, BP 122/78, RR 14, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C, BMI 28
data_table.Examination: Recovering well, no chest pain, ECG sinus rhythm
data_table.Investigations: PHQ-9 score 3, no suicidal ideation, FBC, U&E, LFTs normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Brief intervention with motivational interviewing and review in 3 months
options.rationale: Behavioural support alone has lower quit rates than pharmacotherapy + behavioural support; in a high-risk post-MI patient combined treatment is the standard. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation)

options.text: Nicotine replacement patch 21 mg daily with oral lozenges as required
options.rationale: Combination NRT is effective but lower efficacy than varenicline; in a highly-motivated patient post-MI varenicline gives the best chance of long-term abstinence. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation)

options.text: Bupropion 150 mg daily for 6 days then twice daily for 12 weeks
options.rationale: Bupropion is an option but lower efficacy than varenicline; it has greater seizure risk and is reserved for varenicline contraindication or NRT failure. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation)

options.text: Varenicline with 7-day titration, then 1 mg twice daily for 12 weeks
options.rationale: Varenicline has the highest efficacy among smoking cessation agents and EAGLES data show it is safe in established cardiovascular disease without an increased cardiac event signal. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation; eTG)

options.text: Electronic cigarettes (nicotine vaping) as primary cessation therapy
options.rationale: Australian regulation requires prescription nicotine vaping and it is not first-line; therapeutic-strength NRT or varenicline is preferred. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation; TGA Vaping Reforms 2024)

explanation.summary: Australian smoking cessation guidance recommends combining behavioural support (Quitline, brief intervention) with pharmacotherapy. Varenicline has the highest efficacy (quit rates roughly double of placebo and higher than bupropion or single-agent NRT). The EAGLES trial demonstrated safety in patients with established cardiovascular disease and in those with stable mental illness. Combination NRT (patch plus short-acting oral form) is an effective alternative when varenicline is contraindicated or not tolerated. Bupropion is third-line. Nicotine vaping products require prescription in Australia under TGA reforms and are not first-line.
key_points: Varenicline is first-line, highest efficacy
Safe in cardiovascular disease (EAGLES)
Combination NRT alternative (patch + lozenge/gum)
Bupropion third-line; seizure threshold caution
Vaping is prescription-only in Australia; not first-line
explanation.pearls: After EAGLES, the 'do not use varenicline in heart disease or depression' caveat is gone - it is now first-line in both groups, with the usual titration over the first week.

stem: A 31-year-old man is brought to a metropolitan ED at 2200 by police after threatening a stranger in the street. He is shouting incoherently, threatening staff, has assaulted two security officers and is at high risk of self-harm. De-escalation by experienced senior staff has failed. There is no available collateral. He has not responded to offered oral medication. The team has him in a safe assessment room with adequate staffing. He has no known cardiac history and no documented allergies; his weight is estimated at 80 kg. The senior nurse is preparing IM medication.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 124, BP 152/94, RR 22, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 37.0 degrees C, GCS 15
data_table.Examination: Highly aroused, pacing, no overt psychotic features identifiable, no medic-alert, no injection sites noted
data_table.Investigations: Not yet obtained

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological choice?

options.text: IM droperidol 10 mg as a single dose with continuous monitoring
options.rationale: IM droperidol 10 mg is first-line for acute behavioural disturbance in Australian EDs per RAFT and Calver studies; sedation is rapid and reliable with continuous cardiac monitoring. (Source: RAFT/Calver Acute Behavioural Disturbance; eTG Psychotropic)

options.text: IM olanzapine 10 mg with concurrent IM lorazepam 2 mg simultaneously
options.rationale: Combining IM olanzapine with IM benzodiazepine carries excess risk of respiratory depression and cardiovascular collapse (PBS and product information warning); avoid co-administration within 1 hour. (Source: AMH Psychotropic; eTG Psychotropic)

options.text: IM ketamine 4 mg/kg as sole sedative without an antipsychotic
options.rationale: Ketamine alone is reserved for failure of first-line agents; routine first-line use risks emergence delirium and is not Australian first-line. (Source: RAFT/Calver Acute Behavioural Disturbance)

options.text: Oral haloperidol 5 mg in liquid form offered again with verbal encouragement
options.rationale: Repeating an oral offer after a previous refusal is unlikely to be effective and delays definitive sedation; the IM route is needed in acute behavioural disturbance where oral therapy has failed. (Source: eTG Psychotropic)

options.text: IM midazolam 10 mg as sole agent without an antipsychotic
options.rationale: Midazolam alone gives shorter and less reliable sedation than droperidol with comparable respiratory risk; droperidol is preferred as monotherapy. (Source: RAFT/Calver Acute Behavioural Disturbance)

explanation.summary: Acute behavioural disturbance management in Australian EDs follows a stepwise approach: de-escalation, oral medication offered, IM monotherapy, then IM combination or IV escalation in a high-dependency setting. The Calver/RAFT trials established IM droperidol 10 mg as first-line because it provides rapid reliable sedation, has a low rate of cardiovascular complications when used with appropriate monitoring, and the historical QTc concern is overstated. IM olanzapine plus IM benzodiazepine should not be co-administered within 1 hour because of respiratory and cardiovascular risk. Always treat in a safe space with adequate staffing, monitor vital signs and SpO2 every 10 minutes for 1 hour, and investigate underlying organic causes (delirium, intoxication, withdrawal).
key_points: First-line IM droperidol 10 mg (Calver/RAFT)
IM olanzapine + IM benzo NOT co-administered within 1 hour
Continuous monitoring post-medication
Always exclude organic cause: delirium, intoxication, withdrawal
Restraint duration kept minimum, documented and reviewed
explanation.pearls: In Australian EDs IM droperidol 10 mg is more effective than IM midazolam alone and avoids the IM olanzapine + benzodiazepine interaction - just remember 15 minute observations and continuous SpO2.

subtopic_detail: Aboriginal social and emotional wellbeing engagement
stem:
A 19-year-old Aboriginal man from a remote NSW community is brought to a regional ED by his auntie after a third presentation in 4 weeks with self-harm by superficial cutting. His parents died in a motor vehicle crash 18 months ago. He has not engaged with the community psychologist after a single appointment, declined antidepressant prescription, and was discharged each time within 4 hours.

He says he does not want to talk to 'another whitefella in a clinic'. He is calm at presentation and denies suicidal intent currently. He has no formal psychiatric diagnosis. He worked in mine maintenance until 6 months ago.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 76, BP 118/72, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Engaged with auntie but minimal eye contact with clinician, superficial linear cuts on forearm, no active bleeding, no acute medical issue
data_table.Investigations: K10 score declined, alcohol audit pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial approach?

options.text: Involuntary admission under the Mental Health Act for involuntary treatment
options.rationale: Involuntary admission is not justified for a calm patient without acute risk of harm and would breach least-restrictive-care principles and worsen engagement. (Source: NSW Mental Health Act; AISP)

options.text: Provide a written safety plan and discharge with GP follow-up only
options.rationale: A discharge with written plan replicates the pattern that has not engaged him; without cultural and family connection the safety plan is unlikely to be enacted. (Source: National SEWB Framework)

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg daily and review again in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Pharmacological intervention without engagement and without a clear diagnosis is unlikely to be accepted and ignores the social and cultural drivers of distress. (Source: National SEWB Framework)

options.text: Refer to the local ACCHO and offer engagement with an Aboriginal Health Worker
options.rationale: Engagement with an Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Organisation (ACCHO) and an Aboriginal Health Worker/cultural broker addresses the social and emotional wellbeing framework and supports self-determination; this aligns with national strategy. (Source: National SEWB Framework 2017-2023; Lowitja Institute Yarning)

options.text: Refer for inpatient psychotherapy with a metropolitan trauma team
options.rationale: Relocation to a metropolitan setting away from family and country is likely to worsen distress and is not the recommended approach; community-based engagement is preferred. (Source: National SEWB Framework)

explanation.summary: The Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander social and emotional wellbeing (SEWB) framework recognises seven interconnected domains: body, mind and emotions, family and kinship, community, culture, country, and spirituality and ancestors. Effective mental health care for Aboriginal people centres on partnership with Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Organisations (ACCHOs), engagement with Aboriginal Health Workers and cultural brokers, family involvement (where appropriate), and respect for cultural identity, country and grief. The Yarning method is a culturally grounded conversational approach that supports trust and self-determination. Suicidality and self-harm in young Aboriginal people often relate to historical and intergenerational trauma, dispossession, racism, and incomplete grief; addressing these drivers improves engagement and outcomes more than pharmacotherapy alone.
key_points: SEWB framework: 7 interconnected domains
Engage ACCHO and Aboriginal Health Worker / cultural broker
Family and kinship inclusion (with consent)
Yarning as culturally grounded approach
Address dispossession, grief and racism as drivers
explanation.pearls: When an Aboriginal patient disengages from mainstream services, the first step is to bring an Aboriginal Health Worker into the conversation and to refer to the local ACCHO - relocation to metropolitan services almost always worsens engagement.

stem: A 24-year-old man was diagnosed with ADHD combined type three months ago and started on dexamfetamine 10 mg twice daily. He reports significant improvement in concentration at work and asks about his driver licence obligations. He holds a private (Class C) licence in New South Wales. He has had no accidents or traffic infringements. His prescriber confirms stable dosing with no adverse effects.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice regarding his driving licence?

options.text: He must notify the RMS and obtain a conditional licence with annual medical review with ongoing clinical monitoring
options.rationale: Austroads Fitness to Drive guidelines require drivers on Schedule 8 stimulants for ADHD to notify the licensing authority. A conditional licence is typically granted if the condition is stable and managed, with annual review confirming adherence and absence of side effects impacting driving. (Source: Austroads Fitness to Drive 2022)

options.text: No notification is required provided his prescriber documents fitness to drive in the medical record
options.rationale: Documentation in the medical record alone does not satisfy the statutory obligation for the driver to notify the licensing authority. Austroads guidelines place the notification duty on the driver, not the treating doctor. (Source: Austroads Fitness to Drive 2022)

options.text: He must cease driving for six months after commencing the stimulant before reapplying for a conditional licence
options.rationale: There is no mandatory six-month non-driving period for stimulant initiation. The requirement is notification plus medical certification of fitness, not a fixed stand-down period. A stand-down applies to conditions like seizures, not uncomplicated ADHD treatment. (Source: Austroads Fitness to Drive 2022)

options.text: He must downgrade to a non-stimulant medication such as atomoxetine before he can retain his unrestricted licence
options.rationale: There is no requirement to switch to a non-stimulant to retain a licence. Stimulant medications are acceptable provided the driver meets Austroads conditional licence criteria. Atomoxetine would still require notification as it is prescribed for a medical condition affecting driving. (Source: Austroads Fitness to Drive 2022)

options.text: No action is needed because ADHD treated with a stable stimulant dose does not meet the threshold for a reportable medical condition
options.rationale: ADHD is explicitly listed as a condition that may affect driving fitness in Austroads guidelines. The use of a Schedule 8 medication further triggers the reporting obligation regardless of stability. (Source: Austroads Fitness to Drive 2022)

explanation.summary: Australian drivers with ADHD must self-report the condition to their licensing authority under Austroads Fitness to Drive. A conditional licence is granted if the prescriber certifies stable treatment, absence of impairing side effects, and adequate attention for driving. Annual review is standard. The doctor's role is to provide the medical report, not to decide licensure.
key_points: ADHD is a reportable medical condition under Austroads regardless of treatment type
Schedule 8 stimulant use independently triggers disclosure obligations
Conditional licence requires annual prescriber review confirming fitness
No mandatory stand-down period for stimulant commencement
explanation.pearls: Dexamfetamine and methylphenidate at stable doses generally improve driving performance in ADHD, but Austroads mandates conditional licensing with annual review - the obligation is on the driver to report within the timeframe specified by their state authority.

stem: A 32-year-old woman with newly diagnosed ADHD predominantly inattentive type also has comorbid generalised anxiety disorder managed with escitalopram 20 mg daily. She is a registered nurse and expresses concern about Schedule 8 prescribing implications for her AHPRA registration. She prefers to avoid stimulant medication. Her resting heart rate is 84 bpm and blood pressure is 118/72 mmHg.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line non-stimulant pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Guanfacine extended-release 1 mg daily at bedtime at this stage
options.rationale: Guanfacine is TGA-approved for ADHD in children and adolescents aged 6-17 years but is not first-line in adults. Its evidence base in adult ADHD is limited compared to atomoxetine. Sedation and hypotension make it less ideal as a first choice in adults. (Source: AMH; TGA Product Information)

options.text: Clonidine 100 mcg twice daily with dose adjustment to sedation
options.rationale: Clonidine has some evidence in paediatric ADHD but is not approved or recommended as monotherapy for adult ADHD. Its primary role in adults is adjunctive for stimulant-related insomnia or tic disorders, not as first-line standalone treatment. (Source: AMH; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Bupropion sustained-release 150 mg daily for dual ADHD and anxiety benefit
options.rationale: Bupropion is not TGA-approved for ADHD in Australia and evidence for its efficacy is weaker than atomoxetine. It is primarily indicated for smoking cessation and depression. It may worsen anxiety symptoms rather than improve them. (Source: AMH; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Atomoxetine 40 mg daily, titrated over four weeks to target dose
options.rationale: Atomoxetine is the first-line non-stimulant for adult ADHD in Australia. It is TGA-approved, has evidence for concurrent anxiety symptom improvement, and avoids Schedule 8 regulatory concerns. Starting dose is typically 40 mg daily for adults over 70 kg, titrated to a target of 80-100 mg over 4 or more weeks. (Source: AMH; RANZCP ADHD Guidelines)

options.text: Venlafaxine extended-release 75 mg daily for combined ADHD and anxiety coverage
options.rationale: Venlafaxine has noradrenergic activity but is not approved or recommended for ADHD treatment. It would address anxiety but not core ADHD symptoms with adequate efficacy. Off-label use for ADHD is not supported by guideline evidence. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Atomoxetine is the preferred first-line non-stimulant for adult ADHD in Australia. It is a selective noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor with TGA approval for adults. It has additional anxiolytic properties that benefit patients with comorbid anxiety and avoids Schedule 8 regulatory issues. Titration is gradual over 4 weeks to minimise gastrointestinal side effects.
key_points: Atomoxetine is the only TGA-approved non-stimulant for adult ADHD
Concurrent anxiety often improves with atomoxetine unlike stimulants which may worsen it
Target dose is 80-100 mg daily for adults over 70 kg
Guanfacine extended-release is TGA-approved only for ages 6-17
explanation.pearls: Atomoxetine takes 4-6 weeks to reach full efficacy - counsel patients that unlike stimulants there is no immediate effect, and titrate from 40 mg to 80-100 mg over at least 4 weeks to reduce nausea.

stem: A 41-year-old man with ADHD has been on methylphenidate extended-release 54 mg daily for eight months with good symptom control. He presents for routine review. He is otherwise healthy with no cardiac history and no family history of sudden death. He denies chest pain, palpitations, or exercise intolerance.

data_table.Observations: HR 92, BP 142/88 mmHg (previous visit: HR 76, BP 126/78 mmHg)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Repeat blood pressure on two further occasions over the next two weeks before making changes
options.rationale: While a single elevated reading may warrant confirmation, the combination of a significant rise from baseline (126/78 to 142/88 mmHg) plus an elevated resting heart rate (92 bpm) on stimulant therapy warrants immediate action rather than passive monitoring. (Source: RANZCP; AMH)

options.text: Arrange a 12-lead ECG and echocardiogram before any medication changes at this stage
options.rationale: Cardiac investigations are warranted when there are symptoms or a family history of sudden cardiac death. In an asymptomatic patient with stimulant-related hypertension and tachycardia, the correct response is dose adjustment rather than cardiac workup. (Source: RANZCP ADHD Guidelines)

options.text: Switch to atomoxetine 40 mg daily given the cardiovascular concerns at this stage
options.rationale: Switching agent is premature before attempting dose reduction. Atomoxetine also carries cardiovascular effects including raised blood pressure and tachycardia and would not necessarily resolve the issue. Dose reduction of the current effective medication should be trialled first. (Source: AMH)

options.text: Add amlodipine 5 mg daily to manage the hypertension while maintaining the current stimulant dose
options.rationale: Adding an antihypertensive to maintain a stimulant dose is not first-line. Guidelines recommend dose reduction or cessation of the causative agent before introducing additional medications to treat the side effect. (Source: AMH; Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Reduce methylphenidate to 36 mg daily and review blood pressure in two weeks
options.rationale: A sustained increase in blood pressure above 140/90 mmHg or a rise of more than 15 mmHg systolic from baseline warrants dose reduction as first step. This patient has risen 16 mmHg systolic and 10 mmHg diastolic with concurrent tachycardia, meeting threshold for intervention. Dose reduction with close follow-up is the standard approach. (Source: AMH; RANZCP ADHD Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Stimulant medications for ADHD can raise blood pressure and heart rate as a dose-dependent effect. Monitoring at every visit is essential. When blood pressure exceeds 140/90 mmHg or rises significantly from baseline, dose reduction is the first intervention. Switching agents or adding antihypertensives are second-line if dose reduction is ineffective or the patient has pre-existing hypertension.
key_points: Check BP and HR at every stimulant review visit
A rise of more than 15/10 mmHg from baseline warrants intervention
Dose reduction is first-line for stimulant-induced hypertension
Atomoxetine also raises BP so is not necessarily safer
Cardiac workup reserved for symptomatic patients or those with family history of sudden death
explanation.pearls: Methylphenidate raises systolic BP by a mean of 3-5 mmHg but individual responses vary widely - a rise exceeding 15 mmHg systolic from pre-treatment baseline triggers dose reduction before any add-on antihypertensive is considered.

stem: A 29-year-old woman with ADHD combined type controlled on dexamfetamine 15 mg twice daily presents at 6 weeks gestation in an unplanned but desired pregnancy. She works as a paramedic and reports that without medication she cannot safely perform clinical tasks. She has no other psychiatric comorbidities. Her obstetrician has referred her for psychiatric review regarding medication continuation.

data_table.Medications: Dexamfetamine 15 mg BD, folate 5 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Cease dexamfetamine immediately given first-trimester teratogenicity and implement workplace adjustments
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation is not mandated. While stimulants are category B3 in Australia, current evidence does not show major teratogenicity. The decision requires shared risk-benefit discussion balancing occupational safety against uncertain fetal risk, rather than automatic cessation. (Source: AMH; COPE Guidelines)

options.text: Discuss shared decision-making with lowest effective dose, occupational risk assessment, and trimester-by-trimester review
options.rationale: COPE perinatal mental health guidelines recommend an individualised risk-benefit approach. For this patient whose occupation involves safety-critical tasks, cessation poses its own risk. The approach is to use the lowest effective dose, provide informed consent about limited data, involve the multidisciplinary team, and review at each trimester. (Source: COPE Guidelines; AMH)

options.text: Continue dexamfetamine at current dose without modification as the evidence shows no teratogenic risk
options.rationale: While major teratogenicity has not been demonstrated, the data is limited and does not support blanket reassurance. Best practice is to use the lowest effective dose with ongoing risk-benefit review each trimester, not to continue without modification. (Source: COPE Guidelines; AMH)

options.text: Switch to atomoxetine which has a safer pregnancy profile than amphetamines and review clinical response accordingly
options.rationale: Atomoxetine is category B3 and has less pregnancy safety data than dexamfetamine. It also takes 4-6 weeks to reach efficacy, during which time the patient's occupational function would be impaired. Switching introduces a new agent with uncertain benefit and no clear safety advantage. (Source: AMH; TGA Prescribing Medicines in Pregnancy)

options.text: Cease dexamfetamine and commence cognitive behavioural therapy for ADHD as sole management at this stage
options.rationale: CBT for ADHD has some evidence as an adjunct but limited efficacy as monotherapy for moderate-severe ADHD, particularly in a role requiring sustained vigilance. Non-pharmacological strategies alone are insufficient for her functional demands. (Source: RANZCP; COPE Guidelines)

explanation.summary: ADHD stimulant use in pregnancy requires individualised risk-benefit analysis. Current evidence does not confirm major teratogenicity but data is limited. Where the functional consequences of cessation are severe, continuation at the lowest effective dose with informed consent and multidisciplinary review is appropriate. COPE guidelines emphasise shared decision-making in perinatal psychotropic prescribing.
key_points: Dexamfetamine is TGA category B3 - limited data but no confirmed teratogenicity
Cessation poses occupational safety risk in safety-critical roles
Lowest effective dose with trimester-by-trimester review is recommended
Atomoxetine has no proven safety advantage over stimulants in pregnancy
COPE guidelines emphasise shared decision-making and informed consent
explanation.pearls: Dexamfetamine in pregnancy is associated with possible small increases in preterm birth and low birth weight, but registry data shows no signal for major congenital malformations - the clinical decision rests on functional impairment severity versus uncertain fetal risk.

stem: A 26-year-old man is referred by his GP for assessment of possible ADHD. He reports lifelong difficulties with concentration, organisation, and impulsivity. However, his partner describes distinct episodes lasting 5-7 days every few months where he sleeps 3 hours per night, starts multiple business ventures simultaneously, spends excessively, and speaks rapidly. Between episodes his concentration difficulties persist. He has no substance use. His mother has bipolar I disorder.

data_table.History: Childhood school reports describe persistent inattention since age 7. Three hospitalisations in the past two years for agitation and grandiosity with spontaneous resolution after one week each.

lead_in: What is the most likely primary diagnosis?

options.text: Adult ADHD combined type with episodic hyperfocus misidentified as mania
options.rationale: ADHD hyperfocus is not episodic in 5-7 day blocks and does not present with reduced sleep need, grandiosity, or excessive spending. The discrete episodes with clear onset and offset are characteristic of mania rather than ADHD fluctuation. (Source: DSM-5-TR; RANZCP CPG Mood Disorders)

options.text: Bipolar I disorder with comorbid ADHD given childhood-onset inattention predating mood episodes
options.rationale: While this has features of both conditions, the inattention between episodes may reflect inter-episode cognitive dysfunction of bipolar disorder rather than true comorbid ADHD. Given hospitalisations for mania, bipolar I is the priority diagnosis requiring mood stabilisation before ADHD can be reliably confirmed. (Source: RANZCP CPG Mood Disorders; DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Adult ADHD with episodic anxiety misinterpreted as mood cycling at this stage
options.rationale: The episodes include grandiosity, reduced sleep need, excessive spending, and pressured speech lasting 5-7 days with hospitalisations. These are not anxiety features. This is mania, not ADHD-related emotional dysregulation. (Source: DSM-5-TR; RANZCP CPG Mood Disorders)

options.text: Cyclothymic disorder with ADHD as the primary attentional diagnosis at this stage
options.rationale: Cyclothymia involves hypomanic and depressive symptoms that do not meet full criteria for mania. This patient has had episodes meeting full manic criteria with hospitalisation, ruling out cyclothymia. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Bipolar I disorder with inter-episode cognitive dysfunction mimicking ADHD symptoms
options.rationale: The discrete manic episodes with hospitalisations meet DSM-5 criteria for bipolar I. Persistent concentration difficulties between episodes are well-documented in bipolar disorder as inter-episode neurocognitive impairment affecting 40-60% of euthymic patients. Mood stabilisation takes diagnostic and therapeutic priority. (Source: RANZCP CPG Mood Disorders; DSM-5-TR)

explanation.summary: Discriminating bipolar disorder from ADHD is a common clinical challenge as both present with impulsivity, distractibility, and hyperactivity. Key discriminators include episodicity (bipolar has discrete episodes, ADHD is persistent), reduced sleep need (bipolar) versus difficulty sleeping (ADHD), and grandiosity (specific to mania). Inter-episode cognitive impairment in bipolar mimics ADHD and requires longitudinal assessment after mood stabilisation.
key_points: Discrete episodes with clear onset and offset suggest bipolar rather than ADHD
Reduced sleep NEED (feeling refreshed on 3 hours) is a manic feature not seen in ADHD
Inter-episode cognitive dysfunction occurs in 40-60% of bipolar patients
Stimulants for ADHD can precipitate mania in undiagnosed bipolar
Family history of bipolar I raises pre-test probability significantly
explanation.pearls: Inter-episode neurocognitive impairment affects 40-60% of euthymic bipolar I patients, predominantly in attention and executive function - mood stabilisation must precede ADHD assessment to distinguish true comorbidity from bipolar cognitive residua.

stem: A 35-year-old woman has been commenced on methylphenidate immediate-release 5 mg twice daily for newly diagnosed ADHD. At two-week review she reports mild improvement in focus during the morning dose but symptoms return by midday. She tolerates the medication well with no appetite suppression, insomnia, or cardiovascular concerns. She works full-time requiring sustained concentration across an 8-hour day.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Convert to methylphenidate extended-release 18 mg each morning with review in two weeks
options.rationale: Converting to an extended-release formulation addresses both partial efficacy and inadequate duration. The 18 mg ER dose provides approximately equivalent exposure to her current regimen with a slight increase reflecting partial response, covers 8-12 hours, and maintains conservative titration. This is the standard next step when IR dosing reveals good tolerability but insufficient duration. (Source: AMH; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Add a third dose of methylphenidate IR 5 mg at 4pm to extend afternoon coverage
options.rationale: Adding a third IR dose extends coverage but introduces complexity, risks insomnia, and provides uneven blood levels. For a patient requiring all-day coverage, conversion to an extended-release formulation simplifies the regimen and provides smoother pharmacokinetics. (Source: AMH)

options.text: Switch to methylphenidate extended-release 20 mg each morning at this stage
options.rationale: Her current total daily dose is 10 mg (5 mg BD), so jumping straight to 20 mg ER doubles exposure without confirming tolerability at that level. A conservative conversion to approximately equivalent total daily dose with modest titration is appropriate. (Source: AMH)

options.text: Increase to methylphenidate IR 10 mg twice daily and review in two weeks
options.rationale: While dose increase addresses inadequate efficacy, the core issue is also duration of coverage. Immediate-release methylphenidate lasts 3-4 hours per dose, meaning two doses cannot cover an 8-hour day. Formulation change to extended-release provides superior coverage. (Source: AMH; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Switch to lisdexamfetamine 30 mg daily as it provides longer duration of action
options.rationale: Switching drug class is premature when the current medication shows partial efficacy with good tolerability. Guidelines recommend optimising the current agent before switching to an alternative stimulant. Lisdexamfetamine would be appropriate if methylphenidate ER fails at adequate doses. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; AMH)

explanation.summary: When immediate-release methylphenidate shows partial response with good tolerability, the next step is conversion to an extended-release formulation rather than simply increasing the IR dose. Extended-release provides smoother all-day coverage suitable for occupational demands. The conversion dose should approximate the current total daily IR dose with adjustment for partial response.
key_points: IR methylphenidate duration is 3-4 hours - insufficient for full-day coverage
ER formulation covers 8-12 hours with single morning dosing
Convert at approximately equivalent total daily dose before further titration
Optimise current agent before switching to alternative stimulant class
Titration steps should occur at 1-2 week intervals
explanation.pearls: Methylphenidate ER (Concerta) uses an osmotic-release system delivering 22% immediate and 78% extended - the 18 mg formulation is pharmacokinetically equivalent to approximately 5 mg IR three times daily, making it the natural conversion from a 5 mg BD IR regimen.

stem: A 22-year-old university student presents requesting assessment for ADHD. He reports difficulty concentrating during lectures and failing two subjects. He mentions his flatmate gave him dexamfetamine tablets before exams which he found helpful. He drinks 10-15 standard drinks each weekend. He denies other substance use. His childhood school reports do not mention attentional or behavioural concerns.

data_table.History: No childhood symptoms documented. AUDIT score 14. PHQ-9 score 8. No prior psychiatric contact. No family history of ADHD.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial approach?

options.text: Decline ADHD assessment as the absence of childhood symptoms excludes the diagnosis at this stage
options.rationale: While DSM-5 requires symptom onset before age 12, the absence of documented symptoms does not exclude ADHD. Assessment should proceed but with attention to competing explanations. (Source: DSM-5-TR; RANZCP)

options.text: Complete full ADHD assessment with collateral history, and address hazardous alcohol use and academic stress concurrently
options.rationale: The correct approach is comprehensive assessment including collateral sources, validated rating scales, and concurrent evaluation of differentials. Hazardous alcohol use (AUDIT 14) must be addressed as it independently impairs concentration and is a relative contraindication to stimulant prescribing. (Source: RANZCP ADHD Guidelines; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence a dexamfetamine 5 mg trial as his positive response supports the ADHD diagnosis at this stage
options.rationale: Therapeutic response to stimulants is not diagnostic of ADHD - stimulants enhance concentration in neurotypical individuals. Prescribing based on self-reported benefit from diverted medication, without formal assessment and in the presence of hazardous drinking, is inappropriate. (Source: RANZCP ADHD Guidelines; AMH)

options.text: Refer directly for neuropsychological testing as the definitive diagnostic tool for ADHD at this stage
options.rationale: Neuropsychological testing is not required for ADHD diagnosis and is not the definitive diagnostic tool. Clinical interview with collateral history and rating scales remains the gold standard. Testing may support clinical assessment but has limited sensitivity and specificity. (Source: RANZCP ADHD Guidelines)

options.text: Prescribe atomoxetine as it has lower misuse potential while the ADHD assessment proceeds at this stage
options.rationale: Prescribing any ADHD medication before completing a thorough diagnostic assessment is inappropriate. The diagnosis is not yet established, differentials have not been excluded, and hazardous alcohol use requires attention first. (Source: RANZCP ADHD Guidelines; AMH)

explanation.summary: ADHD assessment in young adults requires careful evaluation given high rates of stimulant diversion on university campuses. A positive response to diverted stimulants does not confirm ADHD. Comprehensive assessment must include developmental history with collateral informants, screening for competing explanations, and validated rating scales. Hazardous alcohol use is both a differential and a relative contraindication to stimulant prescribing.
key_points: Stimulant response is not diagnostic - neurotypical individuals also benefit cognitively
AUDIT score 14 indicates hazardous drinking requiring intervention
Collateral history from childhood is essential for DSM-5 onset criterion
Alcohol-related cognitive impairment mimics ADHD inattention
Assessment must precede any treatment decision
explanation.pearls: AUDIT score 8-15 indicates hazardous alcohol use which independently impairs attention and executive function - addressing alcohol before diagnosing ADHD prevents misattribution of alcohol-related cognitive dysfunction to a neurodevelopmental disorder.

stem: A 38-year-old man with ADHD combined type has trialled methylphenidate ER titrated to 72 mg daily over 12 weeks with only partial response. He then trialled dexamfetamine titrated to 40 mg daily over 8 weeks with modest improvement but developed significant appetite suppression and 6 kg weight loss. His psychiatrist now wishes to trial lisdexamfetamine.

data_table.Medications: Currently dexamfetamine 40 mg daily (to be ceased)
data_table.History: Two adequate stimulant trials failed. No substance use. No cardiac history.

lead_in: What PBS criterion must be met for lisdexamfetamine authority prescription?

options.text: Failure of at least one adequate trial of methylphenidate at maximum tolerated dose for a minimum of four weeks at this stage
options.rationale: PBS criteria for lisdexamfetamine in adults require failure of BOTH methylphenidate AND dexamfetamine, not just one agent. A single failed trial is insufficient for PBS authority. (Source: PBS Schedule; AMH)

options.text: A neuropsychological assessment confirming ADHD diagnosis within the preceding 12 months with regular monitoring of clinical parameters
options.rationale: Neuropsychological testing is not a PBS requirement for lisdexamfetamine authority. The criteria relate to failed adequate trials of first-line stimulants and ongoing functional impairment confirmed by a specialist. (Source: PBS Schedule)

options.text: Failure of methylphenidate plus documented cardiovascular contraindication to dexamfetamine as the sole alternative pathway
options.rationale: Cardiovascular contraindication is one possible intolerance pathway but is not the sole alternative. The standard pathway is inadequate response or intolerance to both agents. Lisdexamfetamine is a prodrug of dexamfetamine and would carry the same cardiovascular precautions. (Source: PBS Schedule)

options.text: Prior authority approval for atomoxetine with documented failure before stimulant class escalation and review clinical response accordingly
options.rationale: PBS criteria do not require atomoxetine trial before lisdexamfetamine. The pathway is through failure of methylphenidate and dexamfetamine specifically, not non-stimulants. (Source: PBS Schedule; AMH)

options.text: Documented inadequate response to both methylphenidate and dexamfetamine at adequate doses with specialist confirmation of ongoing functional impairment
options.rationale: PBS authority for lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse) in adults requires documented inadequate response or intolerance to both methylphenidate and dexamfetamine, prescribed by or in consultation with a psychiatrist or paediatrician, with confirmation of ongoing significant functional impairment. (Source: PBS Schedule; AMH)

explanation.summary: Lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse) is PBS-listed for adult ADHD only after documented failure of both methylphenidate and dexamfetamine. The authority requires specialist prescribing, evidence of adequate trials at therapeutic doses, and confirmation of ongoing functional impairment. Understanding PBS authority pathways is essential for Australian prescribers managing treatment-resistant ADHD.
key_points: PBS authority requires failure of BOTH methylphenidate AND dexamfetamine
Lisdexamfetamine is a prodrug hydrolysed to dexamfetamine in vivo
Specialist (psychiatrist or paediatrician) must prescribe or be consulted
Neuropsychological testing is not a PBS prerequisite
Atomoxetine failure is not required before lisdexamfetamine
explanation.pearls: Lisdexamfetamine PBS authority in adults requires documented failure of both methylphenidate and dexamfetamine at adequate doses for at least 4 weeks each - the authority is obtained by phone from Services Australia with the specialist confirming criteria are met.

stem: A 62-year-old woman with severe melancholic depression has not responded to two adequate antidepressant trials and lithium augmentation over 16 weeks. She is severely psychomotor retarded and has lost 12 kg. Her psychiatrist recommends ECT. She has capacity and understands the recommendation but refuses, stating she does not want general anaesthesia. She is an involuntary patient under the NSW Mental Health Act 2007.

data_table.History: Failed escitalopram 20 mg 8 weeks, venlafaxine 225 mg 8 weeks, lithium augmentation 8 weeks. BMI 17.2.

lead_in: What is the correct legal position regarding ECT administration?

options.text: ECT can proceed under the treating psychiatrist's authority alone as she is involuntary at this stage
options.rationale: Under the NSW MHA 2007, a treating psychiatrist cannot unilaterally authorise ECT for an involuntary patient who refuses. The Mental Health Review Tribunal must authorise treatment when a patient does not consent. (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007; RANZCP ECT Position Statement)

options.text: ECT cannot be given as she has capacity and has refused regardless of involuntary status at this stage
options.rationale: While her refusal carries significant weight, the NSW MHA allows the Mental Health Review Tribunal to authorise ECT for involuntary patients who refuse, provided specific criteria are met. A capacitous refusal does not create an absolute bar. (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007)

options.text: Her designated person responsible can provide substitute consent for ECT with multidisciplinary team involvement
options.rationale: Substitute consent applies only when the patient LACKS capacity. This patient has capacity and actively refused. Substitute consent cannot override a capacitous refusal under the MHA framework. (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007; NSW Guardianship Act 1987)

options.text: ECT can proceed under emergency provisions given her malnutrition poses immediate risk to life
options.rationale: Emergency ECT provisions (s97) apply only when life is at immediate risk and it is not practicable to obtain Tribunal authorisation in time. While she is deteriorating, the scenario describes chronic severe illness rather than an imminent emergency. Tribunal application is appropriate. (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007 s97)

options.text: Application must be made to the Mental Health Review Tribunal which can authorise ECT despite her refusal if criteria are met
options.rationale: Under NSW MHA s96, ECT for an involuntary patient who does not consent requires Mental Health Review Tribunal authorisation. The Tribunal must be satisfied treatment is necessary, alternatives have been considered, and benefit outweighs risk. The patient's refusal is considered but not an absolute bar. (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007 s96; RANZCP ECT Position Statement)

explanation.summary: In NSW, ECT for involuntary patients who refuse requires Mental Health Review Tribunal authorisation under s96. This applies even when treatment is clearly indicated. The Tribunal balances patient autonomy against illness severity and likelihood of benefit. Emergency provisions exist for imminent life-threatening situations only.
key_points: Involuntary status does not give automatic authority for ECT
Capacitous refusal triggers Tribunal pathway under NSW MHA s96
Person responsible consent only applies when patient lacks capacity
Emergency ECT (s97) reserved for imminent life threat where Tribunal impracticable
Tribunal must consider necessity, alternatives tried, and benefit versus risk
explanation.pearls: Under NSW MHA s96, the Mental Health Review Tribunal must hear ECT applications within 3 business days of a category A referral - involuntary patients who refuse can have treatment authorised within a working week if clinical need is demonstrated.

stem: A 55-year-old man with treatment-resistant major depression with psychotic features has consented to ECT. He works as a barrister and expresses strong concern about cognitive side effects, particularly retrograde amnesia affecting case recall. He has no contraindications to anaesthesia. His psychiatrist is planning treatment parameters.

data_table.History: Treatment-resistant MDD with persecutory delusions. No prior ECT. MMSE 28/30 at baseline.

lead_in: What electrode placement offers the best balance of efficacy and cognitive preservation?

options.text: Right unilateral at six times seizure threshold with standard brief pulse width of 1.0 ms
options.rationale: Right unilateral at 6x threshold with standard brief pulse provides good efficacy but ultra-brief pulse width (0.3 ms) offers equivalent remission rates with significantly less retrograde amnesia. For a patient prioritising cognitive preservation, ultra-brief pulse is preferred. (Source: RANZCP ECT Guidelines; Lancet Psychiatry)

options.text: Right unilateral at six times seizure threshold with ultra-brief pulse width of 0.3 ms
options.rationale: Right unilateral at 6x seizure threshold with ultra-brief pulse width (0.3 ms) provides efficacy comparable to bilateral ECT while producing significantly less retrograde amnesia. This combination represents current best practice for maximising efficacy while minimising cognitive effects. (Source: RANZCP ECT Guidelines; Lancet Psychiatry)

options.text: Bifrontal at 1.5 times seizure threshold as the lowest cognitive impact option
options.rationale: Bifrontal has been studied as a compromise but evidence does not consistently show superiority over right unilateral ultra-brief for cognitive preservation. Its efficacy advantage over RUL ultra-brief is not established. (Source: RANZCP ECT Guidelines; Cochrane Review ECT)

options.text: Bilateral bitemporal at 1.5 times seizure threshold with ultra-brief pulse width
options.rationale: Bilateral placement produces the most retrograde amnesia regardless of pulse width. While it may have marginally faster response speed, it does not offer the best cognitive-efficacy balance. Bilateral is reserved for urgent cases or when unilateral fails. (Source: RANZCP ECT Guidelines)

options.text: Left unilateral to preserve non-dominant hemisphere verbal memory function
options.rationale: Left unilateral ECT is not used because the left hemisphere is dominant for language in most people. Stimulating the dominant hemisphere causes MORE verbal memory impairment. Right unilateral is chosen to spare dominant hemisphere language circuits. (Source: RANZCP ECT Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Right unilateral ECT at high dose (6x seizure threshold) with ultra-brief pulse width (0.3 ms) provides the optimal balance of efficacy and cognitive preservation. Ultra-brief pulse stimulates neurons more selectively. High dosing relative to threshold compensates for reduced charge delivery. This achieves remission rates approaching bilateral ECT while preserving retrograde memory significantly better.
key_points: RUL at 6x threshold with ultra-brief pulse is current best practice for cognitive preservation
Ultra-brief pulse width is 0.3 ms versus standard brief pulse of 1.0 ms
High dose (6x threshold) compensates for reduced charge with ultra-brief pulse
Bilateral causes most retrograde amnesia - reserved for urgent or refractory cases
Right (non-dominant) unilateral spares left hemisphere verbal memory
explanation.pearls: Ultra-brief pulse (0.3 ms) RUL ECT at 6x seizure threshold produces 50-70% less retrograde amnesia than bilateral ECT with comparable remission rates of 55-65% for major depression - the advantage is most pronounced for autobiographical memory.

stem: A 48-year-old woman on lithium carbonate 900 mg daily (level 0.7 mmol/L) for bipolar depression is scheduled to commence ECT. Her anaesthetist raises concerns about continuing lithium. She has previously relapsed within weeks of lithium cessation. Her renal and thyroid function are normal.

data_table.Investigations: Lithium 0.7 mmol/L, eGFR 92, TSH 2.1 mIU/L, Na 139 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach to lithium management during ECT?

options.text: Continue lithium at current dose throughout the ECT course without modification
